Schooten then gives this practical rule, from Descartes, for finding amicable numbers, viz. assume the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> 2, or some power of the number 2, such that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> unity or 1 be subtracted from each of these three following quantities, viz. from three times the assumed number, also from 6 times the assumed number, and from 18 times the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> of the assumed number, the three remainders may be all prime numbers; then the last prime number being multiplied by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> the assumed number, the product <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be one of the amicable numbers sought, and the sum of its aliquot parts will be the other. That is, if $a$ be put = the number 2, and $n$ some integer number, such that $3an - 1$, and $6an - 1$, and $18a^2n - 1$, be all three prime numbers; then is $18a^2n - 1 \times 2an$ one of the amicable numbers; and the sum of its aliquot parts is the other.

AMICTUS

Pages 154-154

in Roman antiquity, was any upper garment worn over the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUNICA">tunica</a>. Amictus, among <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> writers, the uppermost garment anciently worn by the clergy; the other five being the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBA">alba</a>, singulum, stola, manipulus, and plauta. The amictus was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> garment, of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, covering the head, neck, and shoulders, and buckled, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> clasped before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>. It is still worn by the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> abroad.

AMICULUM

Pages 154-154

in Roman antiquity, a woman's upper garment, which differed from the pala. It was worn both by matrons and courtezans.

AMICUS CURIAE

Pages 154-154

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a>, to denote a by-stander who informs the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> in law that is doubtful <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> mistaken.

AMID-AMID

Pages 154-154

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a lofty ridge of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABYSSINIA">Abyssinia</a>. See ABYSSINIA.

AMIDA

Pages 154-155

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Mesopotamia, otherwise called Ammoea; situated on a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> mountain, on the borders of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASSYRIA">Assyria</a>, on the Tigris, where it receives the Nymphius. It was taken from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Constans, by Saporos <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>. The siege is said to have cost him 30,000 men; however, it reduc... ced it to such ruin, that the emperor afterwards wept over it. According to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMMIANUS_MARCELLINUS">Ammianus Marcellinus</a>, the city was razed; the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> officers were crucified; and the rest, with the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> and inhabitants, either put to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> carried into <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTIVITY">captivity</a>, except our historian himself, and two or three more, who, in the dead of the night, escaped through a postern unperceived by the enemy. The inhabitants of Nisibis, however, being obliged to leave their own city by Jovian's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> with the Persians, soon restored Amida to its former strength, but it was again taken by Cavades in 501, but was restored to the Romans in 503. On the declension of the Roman power, it fell again into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the Persians; but was taken from them by the Saracens in 899. It is now in the possession of the Turks. Here are above 20,000 <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, who are better treated by the Turks than in other places. A <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> trade is carried on in this city of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, and cotton cloth of the same <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. The Arabian name of Amida is <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIARBEKIR">Diarbekir</a>, and the Turkish one Kard-Amed. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 39°. O. N. Lat. 36°. 58'.

AMIENS

Pages 155-155

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> handsome <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of France, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the department of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOMME">Somme</a>. It is agreeably situated on the river Somme, and said to have received its Latin name Ambianum from being everywhere encompassed with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. It is a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> antiquity; being mentioned by Cæsar as a town that had made a vigorous resistance against the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, and where he convened a general <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> of the Gauls after having made himself <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of it. The emperors Antoninus and Marcus Aurelius enlarged it; and Constantine, Constans, Julian, and several others, resided here a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. The town is encompassed with a wall and other fortifications; and the ramparts are planted with trees, which form a delightful walk. The river Somme enters Amiens by three different channels, under as many bridges; and these channels, after washing the town in several places, where they are of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> in its different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>, unite at the other end by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> of St Michael. Here is a quay for the boats that come from <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABBEVILLE">Abbeville</a> with goods brought by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. At the gate of Noyon there is a suburb remarkable for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a> of St Achen. Next to this gate you come to that of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, where they have a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> mall between two rows of trees. The houses are well built; the streets spacious, embellished with handsome squares and good buildings; and the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of inhabitants in 1817 was 39,000. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>, dedicated to our Lady, is one of the largest and most magnificent churches in France; adorned with handsome paintings, fine pillars, chapels, and tombs; particularly the nave is greatly admired. The other places worth seeing are the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of the bailiwick, the town-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> des Fleurs, and the great market place. Amiens was taken by the Spaniards, in 1597, by the following stratagem: <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">Soldiers</a>, disguised like peasants, conducted a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CART">cart</a> laden with nuts, and let a bag of them <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> as the gate was opened. While the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> was busy in gathering up the nuts, the Spaniards entered and became masters of the town. It was retaken by Henry IV, who built a citadel here. The definitive <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of peace, entered into by the different European powers in 1802, was negociated here. The town is the seat of a bishop, suffragan of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHEIMS">Rheims</a>, as also of a presidial, bailiwick, vidam, a chamber of accounts, and a generality. The bishop's revenue is 30,000 livres. They have some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> and woollen manufactures, and they also make a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> and green <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOAP">soap</a>. It lies in E. Long. 2°. 18'. N. Lat. 49°. 53'.

AMILCAR

Pages 155-155

the name of several Carthaginian captains. The most celebrated of them is Amilcar Barcas, the father of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HANNIBAL">Hannibal</a>, who, during five years, infested the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>; when the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> sending out their whole naval strength defeated him near Trapani, 242 years before Christ; and this put an end to the first Punic <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. Amilcar began the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, and landed in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, where he subdued the most warlike nations; but as he was preparing for an expedition against Italy, he was killed in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, 218 years before the Christian era. He left three sons, whom he had educated, as he said, like three lions, to tear Rome in pieces; and made Hannibal, his eldest son, swear an eternal enmity against the Romans.

AMILICTI

Pages 155-155

in the Chaldaic <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>, denote a kind of intellectual powers, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> persons in the divine <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HIERARCHY">hierarchy</a>. The amilicti are represented as three in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>; and constitute one of the triads, in the third order of the hierarchy.

AMIRANTE

Pages 155-155

in the Spanish polity, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> officer of state, answering to our <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a>.

AMISUS

Pages 155-155

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the ancient <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Pontus. It was built by the Milesians, and peopled partly by them and partly by a colony from <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>. It was at first a free city, like the other Greek cities in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>; but afterwards subdued by Pharnaces <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Pontus, who made it his <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a>. It was taken by Lucullus in the Mithridatic <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, who restored it to its ancient <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">Close</a> by Amisus stood another city called Eupatoria, from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MITHRIDATES">Mithridates</a> Eupator its founder. This city was likewise taken by Lucullus, who levelled it with the ground; but it was afterwards rebuilt by Pompey, who united it with Amisus, giving them the name of Pompeiopolis. It was taken during the war between Caesar and Pompey, by Pharnaces king of Pontus, who put most of its inhabitants to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>; but Caesar, having conquered Pharnaces, made it again a free city.

AMITERNUM

Pages 155-155

a town of the Sabines, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> (Livy, Pliny); now extinct. The ruins are to be seen on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> ridge of a mountain, near St Vittorino, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> of the Aternus; not far from <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AQUILA">Aquila</a>, which rose out of the ruins of Amiternum. AMITTERE LEGEM TERRÆ, among lawyers, a phrase importing the loss of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of swearing in any <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>: The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> of a champion overcome <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> yielding in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, of jurors found guilty in a writ of attain, and of a person outlawed.

AMMIANUS MARCELLINUS

Pages 156-156

a Roman historian of the fourth century, was a native of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, born in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Antioch. Having served several years in the early <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, he was afterwards promoted to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> station of protector domesticus. In the year 350 he entered the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of Constantius, the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> of the east, and, under the command of Ursicinus, a general of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, he served during several expeditions. According to his own modest relation, it appears that he acquired considerable <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> fame, and that he deserved well of his sovereign. He attended the emperor Julian in his expedition into <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, but <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> is silent whether <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> not he rose to any higher military <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> than that which has already been mentioned. He was either in the city or the vicinity of Antioch when the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSPIRACY">conspiracy</a> of Theodorus was discovered, under the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VALENS">Valens</a>, and was an eye-witness of the severe torments to which many persons were exposed by the emperor on that account. But his lasting reputation was not to be acquired from military exertions. He left the army, and retired to Rome, where he employed his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> and talents in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> the history of that empire during the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of three centuries. Though a native of Greece, he wrote in the Latin <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>; but, according to the remark of Vossius, his Latin shows that he was a Greek, and also a soldier. His history begins with the reign of Nerva, and continues to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Valens; and the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> was originally divided into 31 books. Of these the first 13 have perished, and the 18 which remain commence with the 17th year of the reign of Constantius, and terminate at the year 375. But there are several facts mentioned in the history which prove that the author was alive in the year 390. Of this <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> are the accession of Theodosius to the eastern empire, the character of Gratian, and the consulate of Neotherius. Similar to the manner in which <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a>, the father of Grecian history, read his history, Marcellinus read his books in public with general approbation. Some have reckoned the style harsh and redundant, but this may easily be excused, from his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> and military life; and the valuable information communicated abundantly compensates for that defect. Candour and impartiality are leading features in his history. The character given him by Mr Gibbon appears to be accurate, when he says that he is "an accurate and faithful guide, who composed the history of his own times without indulging the prejudices and passions which usually affect the mind of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a>." A <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> has obtained, whether or not our historian was a Christian or a Pagan. But the respectful manner in which he speaks of Pagan deities, and of the advantage of heathen auguries to foretell future events, render it abundantly evident that he was a heathen. The favourable account which he gives of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, manners, and fortitude of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, are the result of his candour and impartiality as an historian. The work of Marcellinus has passed through several editions; but that printed at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a> in 1693, with explanatory notes, is esteemed the best. (Gen. Ammianus Biog.)

AMMIRATO

Pages 156-156

SCIPIO, an eminent Italian historian, born at Lecca in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a> in 1531. After travelling over <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, without settling to his satisfaction, he was engaged by the great <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUSCANY">Tuscany</a> to write The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a>; for which he was presented to a canonry in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> there. He wrote other works while in this station: and died in 1600.

AMMOCHRYOS

Pages 156-156

from ἀμμός sand, and χρυσός <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, a name given by authors to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> very <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> in Germany, and seeming to be composed of a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> sand. It is of a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> gold-like <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, and its particles are very glossy, being all fragments of a coloured talc. It is usually so soft as to be easily rubbed to a powder in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>; sometimes it requires <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRINDING">grinding</a> to powder in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MORTAR">mortar</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> otherwise. It is used only as sand to strew over <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>. The Germans call it katzengold. There is another kind of it less common, but much more beautiful, consisting of the same sort of glossy spangles; not however of a gold colour, but of a bright <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> like <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERMILION">vermilion</a>.

AMMON

Pages 156-157
or HAMMON, in heathen mythology, the name of the Egyptian Jupiter, worshipped under the figure of a ram. Bacchus having subdued Asia, and passing with his army through the deserts of Africa, was in great want of water: but Jupiter, his father, assuming the shape of a ram, led him to a fountain, where he refreshed himself and his army; in gratitude for which favour, Bacchus built there a temple to Jupiter, under the title of Ammon, from the Greek ἀμμός, which signifies sand, alluding to the sandy desert where it was built. In this this temple was an oracle of great note, which Alexander the Great consulted, and which lasted till the time of Theodosius. Hammon the god of the Egyptians, was the same with the Jupiter of the Greeks; for which reason these latter denominate the city which the Egyptians call No-Hammon, or the habitation of Ammon, Diospolis or the city of Jupiter. He is thought to be the same with Ham, who peopled Africa, and was the father of Mizraim, the founder of the Egyptians. Ammon, or Ben-Ammi, the son of Lot, was the father of the Ammonites, and dwelt to the east of the Dead sea, in the mountains of Gilead. See Ammonitis and Ammonites. Ammon, or Ammonius, Andreas, an excellent Latin poet, born at Lucca in Italy, was sent by Pope Leo X. to England, in the characters of prothonotary of the apostolic see, and collector-general of that kingdom. He was a man of singular genius and learning, and soon became acquainted with the principal literati of those times; particularly with Erasmus, Colet, Grocin, and others, for the sake of whose company he resided some time at Oxford. The advice which Erasmus gives him, in regard to pushing his fortune, has a good deal of humour in it, and was certainly intended as a satire on the artful methods generally practised by the selfish and ambitious part of mankind: "In the first place (says he), throw off all sense of shame; thrust yourself into every one's business, and allow out whomever you can, neither love nor hate any one; measure every thing by your own advantage; let this be the scope and drift of all your actions. Give nothing but what is to be returned with usury, and be complaisant to every body. Have always two strings to your bow. Feign that you are solicited by many from abroad, and get every thing ready for your departure. Show letters inviting you elsewhere, with great promises." Ammon was Latin secretary to Henry VIII., but at what time he was appointed does not appear. In 1512 he was made canon and prebendary of the collegiate chapel of St Stephen, in the palace of Westminster. He was likewise prebendary of Wells; and in 1514 was presented to the rectory of Dychial in that diocese. About the same time, by the king's special recommendation, he was also made prebendary of Salisbury. He died in the year 1517, and was buried in St Stephen's chapel in the palace of Westminster. He was esteemed an elegant Latin writer, and an admirable poet. The epistles of Erasmus to Ammon abound with encomiums on his genius and learning. His works are, 1. Epistolae ad Erasmus, lib. i. 2. Scotici conflictus historia, lib. i. 3. Bucolicae vel eclogae, lib. i. Basil, 1546, 8vo. 4. De rebus nihil, lib. i. 5. Panegyricus quidam, lib. i. 6. Varii generis epigrammata, lib. i. 7. Poemata diversa, lib. i.

AMMONIAC

Pages 157-158

some suspect there never was any such thing: But this suspicion is removed, by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> quantities of a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, nearly of the same <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, thrown out by Mount Etna. The <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> sal ammoniac is entirely factitious. See <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>, and Sal Ammoniac, Supplement. AMMONIAN <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMMONIUS">Ammonius</a>. AMMONITÆ, in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>. See Cornu Ammonis.

AMMONITES

Pages 158-158

a people descended from <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMMON">Ammon</a> the son of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">Lot</a>. The Ammonites destroyed those giants which they called Zanzummims (Deut. ii. 19—21.), and seized upon their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. God forbade Moses, and by him the children of Israel (Judg. xii. 19), to attack the Ammonites; because he did not intend to give their lands unto the Hebrews. Before the Israelites entered the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANAAN">Canaan</a>, the Amorites had by conquest got <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the countries belonging to the Ammonites and Moabites. This Moses retook from the Amorites, and divided between the tribes of Gad and Reuben. In the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Jephtha, the Ammonites declared <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> against the Israelites (Judg. xi.), under pretence that they detained a great part of the country which had formerly been theirs before the Amorites possessed it. Jephtha declared, that as this was an acquisition which the Israelites had made in a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> war, and what they had taken from the Amorites, who had <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> enjoyed it by <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of conquest, he was under no obligation to restore it. The Ammonites were not satisfied with this reason; wherefore Jephtha gave them <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> and defeated them. The Ammonites and Moabites generally united whenever there was any <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> set afloat of attacking the Israelites. After the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Othniel (Judg. iii.), the Ammonites and Amalekites joined with Eglon <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Moab to oppress the Hebrews; whom they subdued, and governed for the space of 18 years, till they were delivered by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EHUD">Ehud</a> the son of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GERA">Gera</a>, who slew Eglon king of Moab. Some time after this, the Ammonites made war against the Israelites, and greatly distressed them. But these were at last delivered by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of Jephtha; who having attacked the Ammonites, made a very great slaughter among them (Judges xi.). In the beginning of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAUL">Saul</a>’s reign (1 Sam. xi.), Nahash king of the Ammonites having sat <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> before <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JABESH">Jabesh</a>-gilead, reduced the inhabitants to the extremity of demanding a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITULATION">capitulation</a>. Nahash answered, that he would capitulate with them upon no other conditions than their submitting to have every one his right eye plucked out, that so they might be made a reproach to Israel: but Saul coming seasonably to the relief of Jabesh, delivered the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> and people from the barbarity of the king of the Ammonites. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a> had been the king of Ammon’s friend; and after the death of this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, he sent ambassadors to make his compliments of condolence to Hanun his son and successor; who, imagining that David’s ambassadors were come as spies to observe his strength, and the condition of his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, treated them in a very injurious manner (2 Sam. x. 4.). David revenged this indignity thrown upon his ambassadors, by subduing the Ammonites, the Moabites, and the Syrians their allies. Ammon and Moab <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> under the obedience of the kings David and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a>; and, after the separation of the ten tribes, were subject to the kings of Israel till the death of Ahab in the year of the world 3107. Two Ammonites years after the death of Ahab, Jehoram his son, and successor of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AHAZIAH">Ahaziah</a>, defeated the Moabites (2 Kings Ammon iii.); but it does not appear that this victory was so complete as to reduce them to his obedience. At the same time, the Ammonites, Moabites, and other people, made an irruption into the lands belonging to Judah; but were forced back and routed by Jehoshaphat (2 Ch. xx. 1, 2.). After the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and the half tribe of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANASSEH">Manasseh</a>, were carried into <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTIVITY">captivity</a> by Tiglath-pilneser in the year 3264, the Ammonites and Moabites took possession of the cities belonging to these tribes. Jeremiah (xlix. i.) reproaches them for it. The ambassadors of the Ammonites were some of those to whom this prophet (chap. xxviii. 2—4.) presented the cup of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>’s fury, and directed to make bonds and yokes for themselves; exhorting them to submit themselves to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEBUCHADNEZZAR">Nebuchadnezzar</a>, and threatening them, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they did not, with captivity and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EZEKIEL">Ezekiel</a> (xxv. 4—10.) denounces their entire destruction; and tells them that God would give them up to the people of the east, who should set their palaces in their country, so that there should be no more mention of the Ammonites among the nations. It is believed that these misfortunes happened to the Ammonites in the fifth year after the taking of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>, when Nebuchadnezzar made war against all the people that dwelt upon the confines of Judea, in the year of the world 3420. It is also thought probable, that <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CYRUS">Cyrus</a> gave the Ammonites and Moabites the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of returning into their own country, from whence they had been removed by Nebuchadnezzar; for we see them in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of their former settlement, exposed to those revolutions which were <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> to the people of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALESTINE">Palestine</a>; subject sometimes to the kings of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, and at other times to the kings of Syria. We are told by Polybius, that Antiochus the Great took Rabbeth, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILADELPHIA">Philadelphia</a>, their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, demolished the walls, and put a garrison in it in 386. During the persecutions of Antiochus Epiphanes, Josephus informs us, that the Ammonites showed their hatred to the Jews, and exercised great cruelties against such of them as lived about their country. <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol13.html#article-JUSTIN_MARTYR">Justin <a cla</a>ss="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARTYR">Martyr</a> says, That in his time there were still many Ammonites remaining; but <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORIGEN">Origen</a> assures us, that when he was living they were known only under the general name of Arabians. Thus was the prediction of Ezekiel (xxv. 10.) accomplished; who said that the Ammonites should be destroyed in such a manner as not to be remembered among the nations.

AMMONITIS

Pages 158-158

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a> Petraea, occupied by the children of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMMON">Ammon</a>, whence the appellation. Its limits partly to the west and partly to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> were the river Jabbok, whose course is nowhere determined; though Josephus says, that it runs between Rabbeth-Ammon <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILADELPHIA">Philadelphia</a>, and Gerase, and falls into the Jordan.

AMMONIUS

Pages 158-159

surnamed SACCAS, was born in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>, and flourished about the beginning of the third century. He was one of the most celebrated philosophers of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>; and, adopting with alterations the Eclectic <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, laid the foundation of that <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a> which was distinguished by the name of the New Platonics. See Eclectics and Platonism. This learned <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> was born of Christian parents, and educated in their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>; the outward profession of which, it is said, he never entirely deserted. As his genius was vast and comprehensive, so were his projects bold and singular: For he attempted a general coalition of all sects, whether philosophical <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a>, by framing a system of doctrines which he imagined calculated to unite them all, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> not excepted, in the most perfect <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a>. In pursuance of this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, he maintained, that the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> principles of all philosophical and religious <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> were to be found equally in all sects; that they differed from each other only in their method of expressing them, and in some opinions of little or no importance; and that, by a proper interpretation of their respective sentiments, they might easily be united into one body. Accordingly all the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENTILE">Gentile</a> religions, and even the Christian, were to be illustrated and explained by the principles of this universal philosophy; and the fables of the priests were to be removed from Paganism, and the comments and interpretations of the disciples of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> from Christianity. In conformity to this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>, he insisted, that all the religious systems of all nations should be restored to their original purity, and reduced to their primitive standard, viz. the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> philosophy of the east, preserved uncorrupted by <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a>: and he affirmed, that this project was agreeable to the intentions of Jesus Christ; whose sole view in descending upon <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> was to set bounds to the reigning <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>, to remove the errors that had blended themselves with the religions of all nations, but not to abolish the ancient <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a> from which they were derived. He therefore adopted the doctrines which were received in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> concerning the universe and the Deity, considered as constituting one great whole; concerning the eternity of the world, the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of souls, the empire of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of the world by demons. He also established a system of moral <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a>; which allowed the people in general to live according to the laws of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> and the dictates of nature; but required the wise to exalt their minds by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPLATION">contemplation</a>, and to mortify the body, so that they might be capable of enjoying the presence and assistance of the demons, and of ascending after <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> to the presence of the Supreme <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARENT">Parent</a>. In order to reconcile the popular religion, and particularly the Christian, with this new system, he made the whole <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the Heathen gods an allegory; maintaining that they were only celestial ministers, entitled to an inferior kind of worship. And he acknowledged that Jesus Christ was an excellent man, and the friend of God; but alleged that it was not his design entirely to abolish the worship of demons, and that his only intention was to purify the ancient religion. This system, so plausible in its first rise, but so comprehensive and complying in its progress, has been the source of innumerable errors and corruptions in the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. At its first establishment it is said to have had the approbation of Athenagoras Pantenus, and Clemens the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIAN">Alexandrian</a>, and all who had the care of the public school belonging to the Christians at Alexandria. It was afterwards adopted by Longinus the celebrated author of the treatise on the Sublime, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLOTINUS">Plotinus</a>, Herennius, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORIGEN">Origen</a>, Porphyry, Jamblichus the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of Porphyry, Sopater, Edisius, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUSTATHIUS">Eustathius</a>, Maximus of Ephesus, Priscus, Chrysanthius the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of Julian, Julian the Apostate, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIEROCLES">Hierocles</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCLUS">Proclus</a>, and many others both Pagans and Christians. The above opinions of Ammonius are collected from the writings and disputations of his disciples the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> Platonics: for he himself left nothing in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> behind him; nay, he imposed a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> upon his disciples not to divulge his doctrines among the multitude; which <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INJUNCTION">injunction</a>, however, they made no scruple to neglect and violate.

AMMUNITION

Pages 159-159

a general name for all warlike <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>; but more particularly powder, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a>, &c. Ammunition, arms, utensils of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUNPOWDER">gunpowder</a>, imported without license from his majesty, are, by the laws of England, forfeited, and triple the value. And again, such license obtained, except for furnishing his majesty's public stores, is to be void, and the offender to incur a premunire, and to be disabled to hold any office of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>. AMMUNITION <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">Bread</a>, Shoes, &c., such as are served out to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> of an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> garrison.

AMNESTY

Pages 159-159

in matters of policy, denotes a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a> granted by a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> to his rebellious subjects, usually with some exceptions; such was that granted by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II. at his restoration.—The word is formed from the Greek ἀμνηστία, the name of an edict of this kind published by Thrasybulus, on his expulsion of the tyrants out of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>.

AMNIOS

Pages 159-159

in Anatomy, a thin pellucid membrane which surrounds the fetus in the womb. See Fetus.

AMOEBAEUM

Pages 159-159

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, a kind of poem representing a dispute between two persons, who are made to answer each other alternately; such are the third and seventh of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>'s eclogues.

AMOMUM

Pages 159-159

Ginger. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. AMOMUM Vulgare. See Stium, Botany Index.

AMONTONS

Pages 159-160

William, an ingenious experimental <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, the son of a lawyer of Normandy, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in the year 1663. From his childhood he laboured under the infirmity of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> dulness, which led him to amuse himself, in the want of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, by studying <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICS">mechanics</a>. He learned <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGNING">designing</a> and surveying, and was employed in many public works. He presented to the Academy of Sciences, in the year 1687, an hygrometer upon a new <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a>, which was highly approved. In 1696, he published in French, a treatise, entitled, "Observations on a new <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">Hour</a>-Glass, and Barometers, Thermometers, and Hygrometers." This <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> was dedicated to the Academy of Sciences, of which he became a member in the year 1699. Upon his admission, he read a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> on friction, in which a new <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> upon that subject is proposed: the paper <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be found in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMOIRS">memoirs</a> of the academy. He discovered a method of conveying intelligence speedily to a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> distance by means of signals, from one person to another, placed at as great a distance as they could be seen by means of telescopes: he may therefore be esteemed the inventor of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TELEGRAPH">telegraph</a>. This ingenious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, who was distinguished for his ingenuity in inventing, and his accuracy in executing experiments, died in the year 1705. His pieces, which are numerous, AMORÆANS, a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> order of Gemaric doctors, or commentators on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TALMUD">Talmud</a>. The Amoræans succeeded the Mischnic doctors. They subsisted 250 years; and were succeeded by the Sebureans.

AMORGOS

Pages 160-160
or AMURGUS, in Ancient Geography, now Mergo, not far from Naxus to the east, one of the European Sporades; the country of Simonides the iambic poet. To this island criminals were banished. It was famous for a fine flax called Emorgis.

AMORITES

Pages 160-160

a people descended from Amoræus, according to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEPTUAGINT">Septuagint</a> and Vulgate; Emoræus, according to other expositors; Hæmoræus, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Emorites, according to our version of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a>, who was the fourth son of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANAAN">Canaan</a>, Gen. x. 16. The Amorites first of all peopled the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> lying to the west of the Dead <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. They had likewise establishments to the east of the same sea, between the brooks of Jabbok and Arnon, from whence they forced the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMMONITES">Ammonites</a> and Moabites, Numb. xiii. 30. xvi. 29. Josh. v. 1, and Judges xi. 19. 20. Moses made a conquest of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> from their kings Sihon and Og, in the year of the world 2553. The prophet <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMOS">Amos</a> (ii. 9.) speaking of the gigantic stature and valour of the Amorites, compares their height with that of cedars, and their strength with that of an oak. The name Amorite is often taken in Scripture for all Canaanites in general. The lands which the Amorites possessed on this side Jordan were given to the tribe of Judah, and those which they had enjoyed beyond this river were distributed between the tribes of Reuben and Gad.

AMORIUM

Pages 160-160

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHRYGIA">Phrygia</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">Major</a>, near the river Sangarius, on the borders of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GALATIA">Galatia</a>.—It was taken from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> by the Saracens in 668; but soon after retaken by the Romans. A <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> breaking out again between these two nations in 837, the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Theophilus destroyed Sozopetra; the birthplace of the caliph Al Mutasem, notwithstanding his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARNEST">earnest</a> entreaties to him to spare it. This so enraged the caliph, that he ordered every one to engrave upon his shield the word Amoriun, the birthplace of Theophilus, which he resolved at all events to destroy. Accordingly he laid siege to the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, but met with a vigorous resistance. At length, after a siege of 55 days, it was betrayed by one of the inhabitants who had abjured the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. The caliph, exasperated at the loss he had sustained during the siege, put most of the men to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, carried the women and children into <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTIVITY">captivity</a>, and levelled the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> with the ground. His forces being distressed for want of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> on their return home, the Christian prisoners rose upon some of them and murdered them; upon which the caliph put 6000 of the prisoners to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. According to the eastern historians, 30,000 of the inhabitants of Amorium were slain, and as many carried into captivity.

AMORTIZATION

Pages 160-160

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, the alienation of lands <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> tenements to a corporation or fraternity and their successors. See <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MORTMAIN">Mortmain</a>.

AMOS

Pages 160-161

the fourth of the smaller prophets, who in his youth had been a herdsman at Tekoa, a small town about four leagues southward of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>, was sent to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Bashan, that is, to the people of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAMARIA">Samaria</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Israel, to bring them back to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REPENTANCE">repentance</a> and an amendment of their lives; whence it is thought probable, that he was born within the territories of Israel, and only retired to Tekoa on his being driven from <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BETHEL">Bethel</a>, by Amaziah the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> calves at Bethel. The prophet being thus returned to Tekoa, in the kingdom of Judah, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to prophesy. He complains in many places of the violence offered him, by endeavouring to oblige him to silence. He boldly remonstrates against the crying sins that prevailed among the Israelites, as idolatry, oppression, wantonness, and obstinacy. He likewise reproves those of Judah, such as their carnal security, sensuality, and injustice. He terrifies them both with frequent threatenings, and pronounces that their sins <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> at last end in the ruin of Judah and Israel, which he illustrates by the visions of a plumb-line and a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASKET">basket</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>-fruit. It is observable in this prophecy, that as it begins with denunciation of judgment and destruction against the Syrians, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILISTINES">Philistines</a>, Tyrians, and other enemies of the Jews, so it concludes with comfortable promises of restoring the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABERNACLE">tabernacle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a>, and erecting the kingdom of Christ. Amos was chosen to the prophetic office in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-UZZIAH">Uzziah</a> king of Judah, and Jeroboam the son of Joash king of Israel, two years before the earthquake (Amos i. 1.), which happened in the 24th or 25th year of Uzziah, according to the rabbins and most of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> commentators; or the year of the world 3219, when this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> usurped the priest’s office, and attempted to offer incense to the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>: but it is observed, that this cannot be the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, because Jotham the son of Uzziah, who was born in 3221, was of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> to govern, and consequently was between 15 and 20 years of age, when his father undertook to offer incense, and was struck with a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEPROSY">leprosy</a>. The first of the prophecies of Amos, in order of time, are those of the 7th <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a>: the rest he pronounced in the town of Tekoa, whither he retired. He foretold the misfortunes which the kingdom of Israel should <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> into after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Rehoboam II., who was then living; he foretold the death of Zechariah, the invasion of the lands belonging to Israel by Pul and Tiglath-pileser kings of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASSYRIA">Assyria</a>: and he speaks of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTIVITY">captivity</a> of the ten tribes, and their return. The time and manner of this prophet’s death are not known. Some old authors relate that Amaziah, priest of Bethel, provoked by the discourses of the prophet, had his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> broke, in order to silence him. Others say, that Hosea or Uzziah, the son of Amaziah, struck him with a stake upon the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>, knocked him <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, and wounded him much; in which condition he was carried to Tekoa, where he died, and was buried with his fathers; but it is generally thought that he prophesied a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> time at Tekoa, after the adventure which he had with Amaziah; and the prophet himself taking no notice of the ill treatment. ment which he is said to have received, is an argument that he did not suffer in the manner they relate. St Jerome observes, that there is nothing <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> or sublime in the style of Amos. He applies the words of St Paul (2 Cor. vi. 6.) to him, "rude in speech though not in knowledge." And he farther observes, that he borrows his comparisons from the state and profession to which he belonged.

AMOY

Pages 161-161

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Fokien, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, where the English had a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACTORY">factory</a>; but they have abandoned it on account of the impositions of the inhabitants. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 118. O. N. Lat. 24. 30. It has a fine port, that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> contain many thousand vessels. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> has a garrison here of 7000 men.

AMPELITES

Pages 161-161

Cannel-coal, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANDLE">Candle</a>-coal, a hard, opaque, fossil, inflammable substance, of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. It does not effervesce with <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACIDS">acids</a>. The ampelites, though much inferior to jet in many respects, is yet a very beautiful fossil; and, for a body of so <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a> a structure, remarkably <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>. Examined by the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MICROSCOPE">microscope</a>, it appears composed of innumerable very thin and small plates, laid closely and firmly on one another; and full of very small specks of a blacker and more shining <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> than the rest, which is evidently a purer bitumen than the general <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASS">mass</a>. These specks are equally diffused over the different parts of the masses. There is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARRY">quarry</a> of it near Alençon in France. It is dug in many parts of England, but the finest is in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANCASHIRE">Lancashire</a> and Cheshire; it lies usually at considerable depths. It makes a very brisk fire, flaming violently for a short <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, and after that continuing <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> and glowing hot a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> while; and finally is reduced into a small proportion of gray ashes, the greater <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of its substance having flown off in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a>. It is capable of a very <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> and elegant polish; and in the countries where it is produced, is turned into a vast <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of toys, as snuff-boxes and the like, which bear all the nicety of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a>, and are made to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> for jet. Husbandmen smear their vines with it, as it kills the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VERMIN">vermin</a> which infests them. It is likewise used for the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DYEING">dyeing</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> black. In medicine, it is reputed good in colics, against <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORMS">worms</a>, and as being in general an emollient and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISSOLVENT">dissolvent</a>; but the present practice takes no notice of it.

AMPELUSIA

Pages 161-161

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a promontory of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MAURITANIA">Mauritania</a> Tingitana, called Cottes by the natives, which is of the same signification with a town of the same name not far from the river <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-LIXUS">Lixus</a>, near the straits of Gibraltar, now <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> Spartel. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 6. 30. N. Lat. 36. 0.

AMPERES

Pages 161-161

in antiquity, a kind of vessels wherein the rowers plied two oars at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, one with the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> and another with the left.

AMPHIARAUS

Pages 161-161

in Pagan <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">Mythology</a>, a celebrated prophet, who possessed <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARGOS">Argos</a>. He was believed to excel in divining by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DREAMS">dreams</a>, and is said to be the first who divined by fire. Amphiarous knowing, by the spirit of prophecy, that he should lose his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> against Thebes, hid himself in order to avoid engaging in that expedition; but his wife Eriphyle, being prevailed upon by a present, discovered the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in which he had concealed himself; so that he was obliged to accompany the other Amphiarus princes who marched against Thebes. This proved fatal to him; for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> being split asunder by a thunderbolt, both he and his chariot were swallowed up in the opening. Amphiarus, after his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, was ranked among the gods; <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a> were dedicated to him; and his oracle, as well as the sports instituted to his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, were very famous.

AMPHIARTHROSIS

Pages 161-161

in Anatomy, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> for such junctures of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> as have an evident <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, but different from the diarthrosis, &c. See DIARTHROSIS.

AMPHIBIA

Pages 161-164

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZOOLOGY">Zoology</a>, the name of Linnaeus's third class of animals; including all those which live partly in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> and partly on <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>. This class he subdivides into four orders, viz. the amphibia reptiles; the amphibia serpentes; the amphibia nantes; and the amphibia meantes. It has been a question whether the animals <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called amphibious, live most in the water <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> on land. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> we consider the words ἀμφί (utrinque, both ways) and βιος (vita, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>), from which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> amphibious is derived; we should understand, that animals, having this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a>, should be capable of living as well by land, or in the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>, as by water; or of dwelling in either constantly at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a>; but it will be difficult to find any animal that can fulfil this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-DEFINITION">definition</a>, as being equally qualified for either. An ingenious naturalist *, therefore, Dr. Parson, in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> read before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>, considers their economy respectively, divides them into two orders, viz. 1. Such as enjoy their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> functions by land, but occasionally go into the water; 2. Such as chiefly inhabit the water, but occasionally go ashore. What he advances on this subject is curious, and well illustrates the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of this class. 1. Of the first order, he particularly considers the phœnix; and endeavours to show, that none of them can live chiefly in the water, but that their chief enjoyment of the functions of life is on shore. These animals (he observes) are really <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUADRUPEDS">quadrupeds</a>; but, as their chief food is fish, they are under a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of going out to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> to hunt their prey, and to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> distances from shore; taking care that, however great the distance, rocks or small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> are at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, as resting places when they are tired, or when their bodies become too much macerated in the water; and they return to the places of their usual <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a>, copulate, and bring forth their young, for the following reasons, viz. It is well known, that the only essential <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> (as to the general structure of the heart) between amphibious and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> land animals, or such as never go into the water, is, that in the former the oval hole remains always open. Now, in such as are without this hole, if they were to be immersed in water for but a little <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, respiration would cease, and the animal must die; because a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of blood passes from the heart by the pulmonary artery through the lungs, and by the pulmonary veins returns to the heart, while the aorta is carrying the greater part of the mass to the head and extremities, &c. Now, the blood passes through the lungs in a continual uninterrupted stream, while respiration is gentle and moderate; but when it is violent, then the circulation is interrupted, for <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSPIRATION">inspiration</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPIRATION">expiration</a> are now carried to their <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>; and in this state the blood cannot <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through the lungs either during the total inspiration. Amphibian inspiration or total expiration of the air in breathing; for, in the former <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, the inflation compresses the returning veins; and in the latter, by the collapse of the lungs, these veins are interrupted also; so that it is only between these two violent actions that the blood can pass; and hence it is, that the lives of animals are shortened, and their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> impaired, when they are subjected to frequent violent inspiration; and thus it is, that when animals have thus breathed, they must continue to respire ever after, for life is at an end when that ceases. There are three necessary and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> uses of respiration in all land animals, and in those kinds that are counted amphibious. The first is that of promoting the circulation of the blood through the whole body and extremities. In real fishes, the force of the heart is alone capable of sending the blood to every part, as they are not furnished with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMBS">limbs</a> or extremities; but in the others mentioned, being all furnished with extremities, respiration is an assistant force to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTERIES">arteries</a> in sending blood to the extremities; which, being so remote from the heart, have need of such assistance, otherwise the circulation would be very languid in these parts: thus we see, that in persons subject to asthmatic complaints, the circulation grows languid, the legs grow <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a> and edematous, and other parts suffer by the defect in respiration.—A <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of breathing is, that in respiration, the variety of particles, of different qualities, which float always in the air, might be drawn into the lungs, to be insinuated into the mass of blood, being highly necessary to contemplate and cool the agitated mass, and to contribute refined palatum to the finer parts of it, which, meeting with the daily supply of chyle, serves to assimilate and more intimately mix the mass, and render its <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> the fitter for supporting the life of the animal. Therefore it is, that valetudinarians, by changing foul or unwholesome air for a free, good, open air, often recover from lingering diseases.—A third principal use of respiration is, to promote the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXHIBITION">exhibition</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> in animals: which all those that live on the land do according to their specific natures. From these considerations it appears that the phoca of every kind are under an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> necessity of making the land their principal residence. But there is another very convincing argument why they reside on shore the greatest part of their time; namely, that the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> of these creatures is analogous to that of other land animals; and therefore, by over <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> maceration, added to the fatigue of their chasing their prey, they would suffer such a relaxation as would destroy them. It is well known, that animals which have lain long under water are reduced to a very lax and even putrid state; and the phoca must bask in the air on shore: for while the solids are at rest, they acquire their former <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of tension, and the vigour of the animal is restored; and while he has an uninterrupted placid respiration, his blood is refreshed by the new supply of air, as explained above, and he is rendered fit for his next cruise: for <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> wastes the most exalted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a> of the body, more or less, according to its <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DURATION">duration</a> and violence: and the restorative rest must continue a longer or shorter time, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of the previous fatigue. Let us now examine by what power these animals are capable of remaining longer under water than land Amphibian animals. All these have the oval hole open between the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> and left auricles of the heart; and in many, the canalis arteriosus also; and while the phoca remains under water, which he may continue an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> or two more or less, his respiration is stopped; and the blood, not finding the passage through the pulmonary artery free, rushes through the hole from the right to the left auricle, and partly through the arterial canal, being a short passage to the aorta, and thence to every part of the body, maintaining the circulation; but, upon rising to come ashore, the blood finds its passage again through the lungs the moment he respires. Thus the fetus in utero, during its confinement, having the lungs compressed, and consequently the pulmonary arteries and veins impervious, has the circulation of the blood carried on through the oval hole and the arterial canal. Now, so far the phoca in the water, and the fetus in utero, are analogous; but they differ in other material circumstances. One is, that the fetus having never respired, remains sufficiently nourished by the maternal blood circulating through him, and continues to grow till the time of his birth, without any want of respiration during <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> months confinement: the phoca, having respired the moment of his birth, cannot live very long without it, for the reasons given before; and this hole and canal would be closed in them, as it is in land animals, if the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DAM">dam</a> did not, soon after the birth of the cub, carry him so very frequently into the water to teach him; by which practice these <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> are kept open during life, otherwise they would not be capable of attaining the food designed for them by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a>. Another difference is, that the phoca, as we have said before, would be relaxed by maceration in remaining too long in the water; whereas the fetus in utero suffers no injury from continuing its full <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of months in the fluid it swims in: the reason is, that water is a powerful solvent, and penetrates the pores of the skins of land animals, and in time can dissolve them; whereas the liquor amnii is an insipid soft fluid, impregnated with particles more or less mucilaginous, and utterly incapable of making the least <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CUTIS">cutis</a> of the fetus. Otters, beavers, and some kind of rats, go occasionally into the water for their prey, but cannot remain very long under water. "I have often gone to shoot otters (says our author), and watched all their motions; I have seen one of them go softly from a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> into the river, and dive <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>: and in about two minutes rise at 10 or 15 yards from the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> he went in, with a middling salmon in his mouth, which he brought on shore: I <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> him, and saved the fish whole." Now, as all tetanuses have these passages open, if a whelp of a true water spaniel was, immediately after its birth, served as the phoca does her cubs, and immersed in water, to stop respiration for a little time every <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, it is probable that the hole and canal would be kept open, and the dog be made capable of remaining as long under water as the phoca. Frogs, how capable soever of remaining in the water, yet cannot avoid living on land, for they respire; and if a frog be thrown into a river, he makes to the shore as fast as he can. The lizard kind, such as may be called water <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIZARDS">lizards</a> (see <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LACERTA">Lacerta</a>), are all obliged to come to land, in order to deposit their eggs, to rest, and to sleep. Even the crocodiles, who dwell much in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, sleep and lay their eggs on shore; and, while in the water are compelled to rise to the surface to breathe; yet, from the texture of their sealy covering, they are capable of remaining in the water longer by far than any <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of the phoca, whose skin is analogous to that of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> or cow. The hippopotamus, who wades into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a> or rivers, is a quadruped, and remains under the water a considerable time; yet his chief residence is upon land, and he must come on shore for respiration. The testudo, or sea-tortoise, though he goes out to sea, and is often found far from land; yet being a respiring animal, cannot remain long under water. He has indeed a power of rendering himself specifically heavier or <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> than the water, and therefore can let himself down to avoid an enemy or a storm; yet he is under a necessity of rising frequently to breathe, for reasons given before; and his most usual situation, while at sea, is upon the surface of the water, feeding upon the various substances that float in great abundance everywhere about him: these animals sleep securely upon the surface, but not under water; and can remain longer at sea than any other of this class, except the crocodile, because, as it is with the latter, his covering is not in danger of being too much macerated; yet they must go on shore to copulate and lay their eggs. 2. The consideration of these is sufficient to inform us of the nature of the first order of the class of amphibious animals; let us now see what is to be said of the second in our <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of them, which are such as chiefly inhabit the waters, but occasionally go on shore; These are but of two kinds: the eels, and water <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERPENTS">serpents</a> or snakes of every kind. It is their form that qualifies them for loco-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> on land, and they know their way back to the water at will: for by their structure they have a strong peristaltic motion, by which they can go forward at a pretty good rate; whereas all other kinds of fish, whether vertical or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a>, are incapable of a voluntary loco-motion on shore; and therefore, as soon as such fish are brought out of the water, after having flounced a while, they <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> motionless and soon die. Let us now examine into the reason why these vernacular fish, the eel and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SERPENT">serpent</a> kinds, can live a considerable time on land, and the vertical and horizontal kinds die almost immediately when taken out of the water: and, in this research, we shall come to know what <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANALOGY">analogy</a> there is between land animals and those of the waters. All land animals have lungs, and can live no longer than while these are inflated by the ambient air, and alternately compressed for its expulsion; that is, while respiration is duly carried on, by a regular inspiration and expiration of air.
