In like manner, the fish in general have, instead of lungs, gills or branchiae: and as in land animals the lungs have a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> portion of the mass of blood circulating through them, which must be stopped if the air has not a free ingress and egress into and from them; so, in fish, there is a great number of blood-vessels that pass through the branchiae, and a great portion of their blood circulates through them, which must in like manner be totally stopped, if the branchiae are not perpetually wet with water. So that, as the air is to the lungs in land animals a constant assistant to the circulation; so is the water to the branchiae of those of the rivers and seas: for when these are out of the water, the branchiae very soon grow crisp and dry, the blood-vessels are shrunk, and the blood is obstructed in its passage; so, when the former are immersed in water, or otherwise prevented from having respiration, the circulation ceases, and the animal dies. Again, as land animals would be destroyed by too much maceration in water; so fishes would, on the other hand, be ruined by too much desiccation: the latter being, from their general structure and constitution, made fit to bear, and live in, the water; the former, by their constitution and form, to breathe and dwell in the air. But it may be asked, Why eels and water snakes are capable of being longer in the air than the other kinds of fish! This is answered, by considering the providential care of the great Creator for these and every one of his creatures: for since they were capable of locomotion by their form, which they need not be if they were never to go on shore, it seemed necessary that they should be rendered capable of living a considerable time on shore, otherwise their locomotion would be in vain. How is this provided for? Why, in a most convenient manner; for this order of fishes have their branchiae well covered from the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> drying air; they are also furnished with a slimy mucus, which hinders their becoming crisp and dry for many hours; and their very skins always emit a mucous liquor which keeps them supple and moist for a long time: whereas the branchiae of other kinds of fish are much exposed to the air, and want the slimy <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> to keep them moist. Now, if any of these, when brought out of the water, were laid in a vessel without water, they might be preserved alive a considerable time, by only keeping the gills and surface of the skin constantly wet, even without any water to swim in. It has been advanced, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> may, by art, be rendered amphibious, and able to live under water as well as frogs. As the fetus lives in utero without air, and the circulation is there <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> by means of the foramen ovale; by preserving the passage open, and the other parts in statu quo, after the birth, the same <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> would still continue. Now, the foramen, it is alleged, would be preserved in its open state, were people accustomed, from their infancy, to hold their breath a considerable time once a day, that the blood might be forced to resume its pristine passage, and prevent its drying up as it usually does. This conjecture seems, in some <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, supported by the practice of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a>, who are taught from their childhood to hold their breath, and keep long under water, by which means the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> channel is kept open.—A Calabrian monk at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MADRID">Madrid</a> laid claim to this amphibious capacity, making an offer to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, to continue twice twenty-four hours under water, without ever coming up to take breath. Kircher gives an account of a Sicilian, named the fish Colas, who by a long habitude from his youth, had so accustomed himself to live in water, that his nature seemed to be quite altered; so that he lived rather after the manner of a fish than a man. AMPHIBOLE. See <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINERALOGY">Mineralogy</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

AMPHIBOLOGY

Pages 164-164

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">Rhetoric</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> used to denote a phrase susceptible of two different interpretations. Amphibology arises from the order of the phrase, rather than from the ambiguous meaning of a word. Of this kind was that answer which Pyrrhus received from the oracle: Ἀτό τε, Ἐακίδα, Ῥωμανος νικήσει ποσε; where the amphibology consists in this, that the words te and Romanos, may either of them precede, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> either of them follow, the words posse vincere, indifferently. See Oracle. The English <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> usually speaks in a more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> manner, and is not capable of any amphibologies of this kind: nor is it so liable to amphibologies in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> as the French and most other <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> tongues.

AMPHIBRACHYS

Pages 164-164

in Greek and Latin <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, the name of a foot consisting of three syllables, whereof that in the middle is <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and the other two short; such are the words [ἀβίρε, ἀμάρε].

AMPHICOME

Pages 164-164

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, a kind of figured <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, of a round shape, but rugged, and beset with eminences, celebrated on account of its <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVINATION">divination</a>. The word is originally Greek, ἀμφικόμην, q. d. utrinque comata, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a>, "hairy on all sides." This stone is also called Erotylus, Εὐλογεῖς, Amatoria, probably on account of its supposed power of creating <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a>. The amphicome is mentioned by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEMOCRITUS">Democritus</a> and Pliny. Mercatus takes it for the same with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAPIS">lapis</a> umbriacus, of which he gives a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>.

AMPHICTYONS

Pages 164-164

in Grecian antiquity, an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> composed of deputies from the different states of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>; and resembling, in some <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, the diet of the German empire. Some suppose the word Amphictyons to be formed of ἀπό, "about," and κύων <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> κύων, in regard the inhabitants of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> round about met here in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>: others, with more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a>, from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMPHICTYON">Amphictyon</a>, son of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEUCALION">Deucalion</a>, whom they suppose to have been the founder of this assembly; though others <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> have Acrisius, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of the Argives, to have been the first who gave a form and laws to it. Authors give different accounts of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of the Amphictyons, as well as of the states who were entitled to have their representatives in this council. According to Strabo, Harpocrateon, and Suidas, they were twelve from their first <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a>, sent by the following cities and states; the Ionians, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DORIANS">Dorians</a>, Periæans, Boeotians, Magnesians, Achæans, Phthians, Melians, Dolopians, Ænianians, Delphians, and Phocians. Æschines reckons no more than eleven: instead of the Achæans, Ænianians, Delphians, and Dolopians, he only gives the Thessalians, Oetians, and Locrians. Lastly, Pausanias's <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIST">list</a> contains only ten, viz. the Ionians, Dolopians, Thessalians, Ænianians, Magnesians, Melians, Phthians, Dorians, Phocians, and Locrians. In the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> of Macedon, the Phocians were excluded the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a>, for having plundered the Delphian temple, and the Lacedemonians were admitted in their <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>; but the Phocians, 60 years after, having behaved gallantly against Brennus and his Gauls, were restored to their seat in the Amphictyonic council. Under Augustus, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NICOPOLIS">Nicopolis</a> was admitted into the body; and to make room for it, the Magnesians, Melians, Phthians, and Ænianians, who till then had distinct voices, were ordered to be numbered with the Thessalians, and to have only one <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> representative. Strabo speaks as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> this council were extinct in the times of Augustus and Tiberius: but Pausanias, who lived many years after, under <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANTONINUS_PIUS">Antoninus Pius</a>, assures us it remained entire in his time, and that the number of Amphictyons was then 30. The members were of two kinds. Each city sent two deputies, under different denominations; one called Ἱερομνημον, whose business seems to have been more immediately to inspect what related to sacrifices and ceremonies of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>; the other, Πολιχρόνος, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with hearing and deciding of causes and differences between private persons. Both had an equal <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to deliberate and vote, in all that related to the common interests of Greece. The hieromnemon was elected by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">lot</a>, the pylagoras by plurality of voices. Though the Amphictyons were first instituted at Thermopylae, M. de Valois maintains, that their first place of residence was at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DELPHI">Delphi</a>; where, for some ages, the tranquillity of the times found them no other employment than that of being, if we may so call it, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>-wardens of the temple of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a>. In after times, the approach of armies frequently drove them to Thermopylae, where they took their station, to be nearer at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> to oppose the enemies progress, and order timely succour to the cities in danger. Their ordinary residence, however, was at Delphi. Here they decided all public differences and disputes between any of the cities of Greece; but before they entered on business, they jointly sacrificed an ox cut into small pieces, as a symbol of their union. Their determinations were received with the greatest veneration, and even held sacred and inviolable. The Amphictyons, at their admission, took a solemn oath never to divest any city of its right of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPUTATION">deputation</a>; never to avert its running waters: and if any attempts of this kind were made by others, to make mortal <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> against them: more particularly, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of any attempt to rob the temple of any of its ornaments, that they would employ <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, feet, tongue, their whole power to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> it.—This oath was backed with terrible imprecations against such as should violate it; e.g. May they meet all the vengeance of Apollo, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIANA">Diana</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a>, &c. their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> produce no fruit, their wives bring forth nothing but monsters, &c. The stated terms of their meeting were in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> and autumn: The spring meeting was called Εἰρήνη Πυλαία, that in autumn Μελέταια. On extraordinary occasions, however, they met at any time of the year, or even <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> sitting all the year round. Philip of Macedon usurped the right of presiding in the assembly of the Amphictyons, and of first consulting the oracle, which was called Προφήτης.

AMPHIDROMIA

Pages 164-164

a feast celebrated by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> on the first <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> after the birth of a child.

AMPHIDRYON

Pages 164-164

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> writers, denotes the veil <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> curtain which was drawn before the door of the bema in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> churches.

AMPHILOCHIA

Pages 164-165

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, the territory of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARGOS">Argos</a> in Acarnania: Amphilocheum, (<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUCYDIDES">Thucydides</a>); called Amphilochi (from the people), in the lower <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, (Stephanus). A town also of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GALICIA">Galicia</a>, built by Teucer, and denominated nated from Amphilocheus one of his companions, (Strabo): now Orense. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 8. 25. Lat. 42. 36.

AMPHILOCHIUS

Pages 165-165

bishop of Iconium, in the fourth century, was the friend of St Gregory Nazianzen and St <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASIL">Basil</a>. He assisted at the first general <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of Constantinople in 381; presided at the council of Sida; and was a strenuous opposer of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARIANS">Arians</a>. He died in 394; and his works were published in Greek and Latin at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, 1644, by Francis Combesis.

AMPHILOCHUS

Pages 165-165

son of Amphiarans and Eriphyle, was a celebrated diviner. He had an altar erected to him at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, and an oracle at Mallus in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CILICIA">Cilicia</a>, which <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> was founded by him and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOPSUS">Mopsus</a>. The answers of this oracle were given by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DREAMS">dreams</a>; the party inquiring used to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> a night in the temple, and that night's dream was the answer. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DION">Dion</a> Cassius mentions a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> done by order of Sextus Condianus, representing the answer he received of the oracle, in the reign of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Commodus.

AMPHIMACER

Pages 165-165

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, a foot consisting of three syllables; whereof the first and last are <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and that in the middle short; such is the word [cástiás].

AMPHION

Pages 165-165

son of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> and Antiope; who, according to the poets, made the rocks follow his music; and at his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HARP">harp</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a> of Thebes danced into walls and a regular <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>.

AMPHIPHIPI

Pages 165-165

in Grecian antiquity, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> who, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, used two horses without saddles, and were dexterous enough to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAP">leap</a> from one to the other. AMPHIPRORÆ, in the naval affairs of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, vessels with a prow at each end. They were used chiefly in rapid <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> and narrow channels, where it was not easy to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TACK">tack</a> about.

AMPHIPOLES

Pages 165-165

in antiquity, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> magistrates of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRACUSE">Syracuse</a>. They were established by Timoleon in the 109th Olympiad, after the expulsion of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a> Dionysius. They governed Syracuse for the space of 300 years: and Diodorus Siculus assures us, that they subsisted in his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>.

AMPHIPOLIS

Pages 165-165

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, on the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUPHRATES">Euphrates</a>, built by Seleucus, called by the Syrians Turmeda, (Stephanus): the same with Thapsacus, (Pliny); and supposed to have been only renewed and adorned by Seleucus, because <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> famous before his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, (Xenophon).

AMPHIPROSTYLES

Pages 165-165

in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, a temple which had four columns in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a>, and as many in the aspect behind. AMPHISBENA. See OPHIOLOGY <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. AMPHISBENA Aquatica. See Gordius, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HELMINTHOLOGY">Helminthology</a> Index.

AMPHISCII

Pages 165-165

among geographers, a name applied to the people who inhabit the torrid zone. The Amphiscii, as the word imports, have their shadows one <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the year towards the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, and the other towards the south, according to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the ecliptic. They are also called Ascii. See Ascii.

AMPHISSA

Pages 165-165

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the Locri Ozolae, 120 stadia (<a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 15 miles) to the west of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DELPHI">Delphi</a>, (Pausanias). So called, because surrounded on all sides by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, (Stephanus). Hence Amphissæi, the inhabitants; who plundered the temple at Delphi (<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEMOSTHENES">Demosthenes</a>).—Also a town of Magna Graecia at the mouth of the Sagra, on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of the Farther <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALABRIA">Calabria</a>, situated between Locri and Caulonia; now called Rocelia. Amphissius the epithet, (Ovid).

AMPHITHEATRE

Pages 165-168

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> of an elliptic form, of two <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> more stories of open arcades, with a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of interior galleries and arched <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a>, which served both as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> and support to several rows of seats which rose above each other, and were arranged round a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> space called the arena. The derivation of the word amphitheatre, indicates that it is a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where the spectators, circumspectly arranged, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> the performance equally well on all sides. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of amphitheatres is of considerable importance, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of its connexion with ancient manners. These structures owed their origin to the barbarity of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, and their ruin to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> of the moderns. They are the production of Roman <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> in the last ages of the republic. The ferocious disposition of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> was immoderately fond of every <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of amusement; but especially that which was of a bloody and horrible <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> rulers improved this general feature in the Roman character, to rouse and foster that martial spirit which rendered them masters of the world. After the Samnite <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> had extended the Roman sceptre over Etruria and the whole <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, the first gladiatorial conflicts were exhibited in Rome in the year of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> 490. Lucius Metellus brought into the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CIRCUS">circus</a> the elephants which were <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the spoil of the Carthaginians, in the year 502, and this proved the introduction of wild beasts into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SPECTACLES">spectacles</a> of Rome. This addition was equally agreeable to the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>; and those who courted the popular favour, vied with each other in entertaining the people in this barbarous manner. This soon gave birth to a profession of men denominated gladiators, who were trained to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a>, and for reward slaughtered one another in the forum, whilst every devouring animal which the wilds of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a> produced, added to the horrid <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a>. In the days of Pompey and Caesar these barbarous amusements were given with an astonishing profusion. In these games given by Pompey, the elephants attempted to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARRIER">barrier</a> between them and the people, and the situation of the circus prevented the people from seeing equally well: this induced Caesar to alter the original form, and construct edifices where the people might be entertained without danger or interruption. Amphitheatres were suited to this purpose; therefore they were adopted, and became the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> place for the exhibitions both of gladiators and wild beasts. It is supposed that the first amphitheatre was composed of those singular <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MACHINES">machines</a>, formed by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAIUS">Caius</a> Curio, for the games which Caesar presented among the funeral honours of his father. In a semicircular form Caius made two large <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-THEATRES">theatres</a>, and opposed their backs to each other: and, having amused the people in these the one half of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, then they wheeled round, forming one spacious <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a> where the gladiators contended during the remainder of the day. Pliny is the only one who makes mention of this amphitheatre; and from his account it is difficult to ascertain whether this was the first idea of an amphitheatre, or whether the previous sight of one had suggested this huge and wonderful structure. It is reported, that Julius Caesar, a few years after, formed a hunting theatre of wood; and, in consequence of the circular position of the seats, it obtained the name of an amphitheatre. This appears to have been of very superior kind and in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> estimation. In the reign of Augustus, Statilius Taurus erected one of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, but it seems to have been seldom used; and, from its being consumed by fire in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Nero, it is evident that it was not wholly of stone. These wooden buildings appear to have been temporary, and a few of them permanent from the establishment conferred upon them. The politic spirit of Augustus induced him to erect several of these, and Caligula began one, which he left unfinished. Nero formed a large and spacious one, which is said to have been a year in building. Herod of Judea erected amphitheatres both in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a> and in Caesarea. During the reign of Tiberius, one was built at Fidene, which Tacitus informs us fell while the games were performing, and slew or hurt about 50,000 persons. There was another at <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACENTIA">Placentia</a>, reported to have been the most spacious in Italy; but it was destroyed by fire in the contest between Vitellius and Otho. The unfortunate accidents, which happened to these wooden buildings, led the public to construct others of a more durable and stronger nature, where the crowd might be entertained without danger. This <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> was reserved to Vespasian and Titus. In his eighth consulate, the former began the amphitheatre, which the latter finished during his reign. It is said, that the expense of this building would have erected a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> city; and it is deservedly esteemed one of the most celebrated edifices of ancient times. Dio says, that 9200 wild beasts were destroyed at the dedication of this huge building, but Eutropius restricts their number to 5000. After the hunting of these ferocious animals was ended, instantly the arena was filled with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> animals were made to contend, and a sea-fight exhibited. This immense building obtained the appellation of the Coliseum. See Plate XX. fig. 1. This amphitheatre became the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODEL">model</a> of other amphitheatres throughout the empire. Compared with the original model, these were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> valleys, with seats formed in the surrounding heights similar to the amphitheatre at Corinth. On the declivity of two hills seats of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a> were sometimes placed, and the extremes formed by regular works of stone. Of this kind was that of Gortyna in Candia. One in the vicinity of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SANDWICH">Sandwich</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KENT">Kent</a> had its benches formed of turf; and similar must have been those amphitheatres, which were formed along with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMPS">camps</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> stations of the Roman <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>. When Christianity became the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> of the empire, it meliorated the dispositions of the Romans, and induced them to lay aside this barbarous <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>. Constantine the Great terminated the gladiatorial combats in the east during his reign; but they were not finally abolished at Rome until the beginning of the fifth century, in the reign of Honorius. The combats of wild beasts <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a>, however, some time longer; but during the progress of the fifth century these gradually declined, until they were finally abolished, and the amphitheatres were abandoned to the ravages of time and accident. During the middle ages they were sometimes employed for judicial conflicts, tilts, and tournaments; but these practices having been discontinued, the amphitheatres experienced universal neglect and ruin. It is very difficult to give an accurate <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of an amphitheatre. It is scarcely possible to give a clear idea of the manner in which such immense crowds of people were seated and arranged, and how they had a convenient entrance and a returning. It has already been mentioned, that these buildings were circuitous, and that the exterior circuit was composed of two or more stories of arcades; and it may now be added, that the number of these stories varied according to the nature of the building. A corresponding number of arched passages and staircases opened upon the ground <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a> towards these stories in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of radii towards the arena. These communications were again intersected by arched passages which encircled the whole structure, and afforded an uninterrupted entrance to every part of the amphitheatre. Sometimes an intermediate gallery surrounded the whole in the centre of the fabric, and served as a common place of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> to all the stairs which led to the higher galleries. This was the form of one at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NISMES">Nismes</a>. Sometimes each staircase had its distinct communication by itself. Such was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> with one at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERONA">Verona</a>. See Plate XX. fig. 2. The four radiating entries on the diameter were usually more capacious; and by the two <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of these the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>, and other persons of distinction, were conducted to their seats on a place which was called the podium. The other two led to the arena, and by these the gladiators and beasts made their entrance. The various ranks of the people passed by the staircases, which led to their respective seats. The doors which opened from the staircases were called vomitories, and varied in magnitude, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of the amphitheatre, and the number of exterior <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a>. The number of seats between the several vomitories was unequal, and seems to have been subject to no positive regulation. These benches were about one foot and eight inches in height, and about two feet four inches in breadth. A <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATFORM">platform</a> four feet eight inches <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> was formed of one of these benches, which served as a circular communication to the whole building. These obtained the name of precincts, and the boundaries on the side were called belts. The latter were surrounded by balustrades, to protect the persons from falling who occupied occupied the benches in the vicinity. The podium was more spacious than the precincts, and was a platform encircling the arena. From one precinct to the belt of another, a flight of stairs two feet six inches in breadth descended opposite to every vomitory. Small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a> were cut in the tops of the benches, by which the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> and urine were conducted from <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENCH">bench</a> to bench, until they reached the instruments prepared to convey them to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DRAINS">drains</a> below. These stairs radiated from the highest bench to the podium; so that, with the precincts, they separated the whole cavity into wedge-like divisions, which the people occupied according to their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>. The amphitheatre called the Coliseum, was of an elliptical form, whose longest diameter was about 615 English feet six inches, and the shortest 510. The length of the diameter of the arena was about 281 feet, and the breadth 176, reserving a space for the seats and galleries of about 157 feet in breadth. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> circumference covered a superficies of about five acres and a half, and could scarcely be included in a parallelogram of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> acres. Three stories of arcades, adorned with columns of the Doric, Ionic, and Corinthian orders, and enclosed with a pilasterade of the Corinthian order, composed the external elevation. The first story rose about four feet from the ground, and the pavement supported the basis of the columns. The columns which supported the upper stories were placed upon pedestals. A stylobata supported the pilasterade, in which were the windows of an intermediate gallery, and in every <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> interpilaster was a window to illuminate the highest gallery. A cantaliver cornice, perforated with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> holes, through which the erect pieces of wood passed that supported the awning to a range of corbels, about the centre of the pilasterade, crowned the building. These various columns, pilasters, and stories, appear to have been continued without interruption around the whole edifice. The height of the first story is about 33 feet six inches, the second about 39, and the third about 38; the pilasterade about 46; and the whole, including the blocking course and the steps, was about 164 feet in height. An ellipse of 80 open arches formed the exterior circuit of the ground <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>; the piers, with three-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> columns in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a>, of about two feet 10 inches diameter. The four which corresponded to the four semi-diameters formerly mentioned, were about 14 feet two inches, and 76 of the arches were about 13 feet eight inches. These arches led to a large <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> corridor, that encircled the whole; this corridor is a magnificent and distinguishing feature in the Coliseum theatre. Square openings in the precinct above, illuminated the interior corridor; and the corridor which was united with the wall of the podium appears to have been illuminated in a similar manner. A double corridor was seen on the floor of the second story directly above the corridor of the lower floor, and an interior corridor which sent forth stairs leading to a range of vomitories on the one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and on the other hand an intermediate corridor which formed a mezzanine floor above the double corridor of the interior circuit. Here the stairs began to ascend to the next story, and square holes in the upper floor enlightened this gallery. A double corridor formed the third story, and it appears that here the stairs commenced that led to the galleries above. There were also some windows in the interior wall, and vomitories which opened to the uppermost cunei of benches. In a similar manner were other three stories constructed and filled above, the whole composing a most magnificent and spacious structure. Justus Lipsius supposes that this amphitheatre was capable of containing 87,000 spectators on the benches; and Fontana adds 22,000 for the galleries and other passages. Upon a fair calculation it appears that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> all was crowded, it might contain about 80,000. This magnificent structure certainly excelled the monuments both of Grecian and Egyptian genius which have reached our times. When this amphitheatre was in its <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a>, and crowded with Romans, the sight must have been magnificent and striking. If the report is accurate, that this was completed in two years and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> months, it affords an astonishing instance of Roman vigour and persevering industry. Besides former depredations, Michael Angelo removed near the one half of the external wall to build the Palazzo Farnese. To prevent these depredations, Pope Benedict XIV consecrated these ruins, and erected several altars, which were much frequented on the Sundays and Fridays, before the revolution in France. To <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> these relics, a hermit was stationed in a small dwelling near the centre. The different kinds of amusement have already been mentioned during the progress of the history. Gladiators contended together, or entered the lists with wild beasts. These wild animals were hunted or encountered, or left to devour each other, according to the humour of the times or the taste of him who gave the entertainment. It appears also, that criminals were sometimes forced to fight with these ferocious creatures for the entertainment of the people of Rome; and, in the dawn of Christianity, many of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> suffered <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> in this brutal manner. It is also reported, that <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> were sometimes constructed with caves below, from whence these devouring animals rushed forth to attack their prey. Information concerning the laws that regulated the amphitheatre is rather scanty; but the following are among the number. In the centre of one side of the podium was the emperor's seat, called the suggestum, and highly adorned. The remainder of the podium was occupied by senators; and when this space was not sufficient, several of the adjacent wedges were appropriated to the other senators and to persons of distinction. The equestrians, and the civil and military tribunes, had their places next assigned them. From this order both the liberti and the legati were excluded. The married men sat by themselves. The young men were also arranged by themselves, and their tutors sat near them to observe their conduct. The attendants and servants occupied the highest gallery. The vestals were seated, and frequently the princesses and the ladies of distinguished rank sat along with them. The front of the gallery was assigned to the women, who were placed on chairs, and the lowest order of plebeians stood behind them. It appears also, that for the better accommodation of the people, the different tribes had particular wedges allotted to them. It is also proper to remark, that the arrangement in the different provinces was different from that of Rome. AMP The general direction of the amphitheatre was under the care of an officer, named *vilicus amphitheatri*; and different officers, who were called *locarii*, had the direction of the cuniculi. By carefully preventing any person from occupying a place to which he was not entitled, all confusion was prevented, and strict order maintained. The means used by Pope Benedict to preserve the Coliseum at Rome, have already been mentioned. Of one which was erected at Verona, only four arches of the external circuit remained at the commencement of the eighteenth century. These consist of three stories of about 90 English feet. The whole building was erected without cement, and joined and secured by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> cramps, overlaid with <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>. The whole superstructure is about four stories and nearly one-third. One has been erected at Nîmes, which has suffered much dilapidation; but the remains are yet worthy of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> of the traveller. In the year 1533, Francis I. gave orders to have the rubbish removed; but his misfortunes prevented this order from being carried into execution. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XVI. issued a similar order, but the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> is not yet finished. This amphitheatre is said by Governor Pownall, to be occupied with houses arranged in the form of streets, and resembles a small walled town. The galleries are converted in wretched dwellings, but the exterior gallery of the second story, and that of the attic, were in their original state. At Pola in Istria, there are the remains of an amphitheatre built on the declivity of a hill. The whole of the exterior circuit was standing, except a few yards of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARAPET">parapet</a>, when Massi visited these remains. It was erected of stone, with cramps of iron; and all the benches and other parts constructed of wood, have been destroyed. **Amphitheatre**, in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARDENING">Gardening</a>, certain dispositions of trees and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHRUBS">shrubs</a> on the sides of hilly places, which, if the hill or rising be naturally of a circular <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, always have the best effect. They are to be formed of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVERGREENS">evergreens</a>, such as hollies, phillireys, laurustines, bays, and such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, observing to plant the shortest growing trees in the front, and those which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be the tallest behind, such as pines, firs, cedars of Lebanon, &c. Amphitheatres are also sometimes formed of slopes on the sides of hills, covered only with turf; and, when well kept, they are a great ornament to large gardens. **<a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-AMPHITRITE">Amphitrite</a>**, (from *amphi*, circumferendo), in the heathen <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">mythology</a>, the wife of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEPTUNE">Neptune</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> of the sea, sometimes taken for the sea. **Amphitryon**, son of Alceus, and the father of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>, less known by his own exploits than from his wife Alcmena's adventure. See Alcmena. **<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMPHORA">Amphora</a>**, in antiquity, a liquid <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> among the Greeks and Romans. The Roman amphora contained 48 sextaries, equal to about seven gallons one pint English wine measure; and the Grecian or Attic amphora contained one-third more. Amphora was also a dry measure used by the Romans, and contained about three bushels. Amphora, among the Venetians, is the largest measure used for liquids, containing about 16 quarts. **Amphorarium vinum**, in antiquity, denotes that which is drawn or poured into *amphora* or pitchers; by way of distinction from *vinum doliare*, or cask wine.—The Romans had a method of keeping wine in *amphora* for many years to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIPEN">ripen</a>, by fastening the lids tight down with pitch or gypsum, and placing them either in a situation within reach of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a>, or under ground. **Amphotides**, in antiquity, a kind of armour or covering for the ears, worn by the ancient pupilles, to prevent their adversaries from laying hold of that part. **Amphrysus**, or **Amphryssus**, in Ancient <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a river of Phthiotis, a district of Thessaly, running by the foot of Mount Othrys, from south to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, into the Enipeus at Thebes of Thessaly; where <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a> fed the herds of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> Admetus (<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>, Lucan). Another Amphrysus in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHRYGIA">Phrygia</a>, rendering women barren, according to Pliny: Hence the epithet *Amphryssacus* (Statius). Also a town of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHOCIS">Phocis</a>, at the foot of Mount <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARNASSUS">Parnassus</a>, encompassed with a double wall by the Thebans in the war with <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> (Pausanias): *Amphryssia Vates*, in Virgil, denotes the Sibyl. **Amphthill**, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEDFORDSHIRE">Bedfordshire</a> in England, situated pleasantly between two hills, near the centre of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>, but in a barren <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">Population</a> 1277 in 1811. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 0° 29'. N. Lat. 52° 2'. **Ampliation**, in a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, denotes the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of enlarging or extending the compass of a thing. On a medal of the emperor <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANTONINUS_PIUS">Antoninus Pius</a>, we find the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> *Ampliator civium* given him, on account of his having extended the *jus civitatis*, or <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of citizenship, to many states and people before excluded from that privilege. In effect, it is generally supposed to have been this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> that made the famous <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, whereby all the subjects of the empire were made citizens of Rome. **Ampliation**, in Roman antiquity, was the deferring to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> in certain causes. This the judge did, by pronouncing the word *amplius*; or by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> the letters *N. L.* for *non liquet*; thereby signifying, that, as the cause was not clear, it would be necessary to bring farther <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a>. **Amplification**, in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">Rhetoric</a>, part of a discourse or speech, wherein a crime is aggravated, a praise or commendation heightened, or a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NARRATION">narration</a> enlarged, by an enumeration of circumstances: so as to excite the proper emotions in the souls of the auditors. Such is the passage in Virgil, where, instead of saying merely that Turnus died, he amplifies the circumstances of his death: > Ast illi solvuntur frigore membra, > Vitaque cum gemitu fugit indignata sub umbras. The masters of eloquence make an amplification to be the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> of discourse. See Oratory. **Amplitude**, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> of the horizon intercepted between the east or west point and the centre of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> or a planet, at its rising or setting; and so is either north and south, or orte and occasive. **Magnetic Amplitude**, the different rising or setting of the sun from the east or west <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of the compass. It is found by observing the sun, at his rising and setting, by an amplitude compass. **Ampsaga**, a river of ancient <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMIDIA">Numidia</a>. See Algiers. **Ampancti**

AMPSANCTI VALLIS

Pages 169-171
or AMPSANCTI LACUS, a cave or lake in the heart of the Hirpinii, or Principato Ultra, near the city Tricentum (Cicero, Virgil, Pliny); it is now called Mofletta, from Mephitis, the goddess of stench, who had a temple there. The ancient poets imagined that this gulf led to hell. The Mofletta is thus described by Mr Swinburne: "We were led into a narrow valley, extending a considerable way to the south-west, and pressed in on both sides by high ridges thickly covered with copses of oak. The bottom of the dell is bare and arid: in the lowest part, and close under one of the hills, is an oval pond of muddy ash-coloured water, not above fifty feet in diameter; it boils up in several places with great force in irregular fits, which are always preceded by a hissing sound. The water was several times spouted up as high as our heads in a diagonal direction; a whirlpool being formed round the tube, like a basin, to receive it as it fell. A large body of vapour is continually thrown out with a loud rumbling noise. The stones on the rising ground that hangs over the pool are quite yellow, being stained with the fumes of sulphur and sal ammoniac. A most nauseous smell rising with the steam obliged us to watch the wind, and keep clear of it, to avoid suffocation. The water is quite insipid both as to taste and smell; the clay at the edge is white, and carried into Puglia to rub upon scabby sheep, on which account the lake is farmed out at 100 ducats a-year. On a hill above this lake stood formerly a temple dedicated to the goddess Mephitis: but I perceived no remains of it."

AMPULLA

Pages 171-171

among <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> writers, denotes one of the sacred vessels used at the altars. Ampullae were also used for holding the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> used in chrismation, consecration, coronation, &c. Among the ornaments of churches we find frequent mention made of ampuls <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> vials. In the inventory of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LINCOLN">Lincoln</a> we meet with ampuls of crystal, variously enriched with silver feet and covers; one containing a tooth of St Christopher, another a tooth of St Cecily, another a bone of the head of St John Baptist. Knights of St AMPULLA, belong to an order instituted by Clovis I., <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of France; at the coronation they bear up the canopy under which the ampulla is carried in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESSION">procession</a>.

AMPURA

Pages 171-171

a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERU">Peru</a>, before its conquest by the Spaniards. Here the inhabitants worshipped two lofty <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> from a principle of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a>, because of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> from them by which their lands were fertilized. It is said to have been conquered by Viracocha the eighth inca.

AMPURIAS

Pages 171-171

the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the territory of Ampurdan, in Catalonia, seated at the mouth of the river Fluvia, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2° 56'. N. Lat. 42° 5'. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> about it is barren, full of briars and bulrushes, except in some places which produce <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>.

AMPUTATION

Pages 171-171

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> off a limb, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> any <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a>, from the body. See SURGERY <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

AMRAPHEL

Pages 171-171

the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Shinar, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BABYLONIA">Babylonia</a>, confederated with Chedorlaomer, king of the Elamites, and two other kings, to make <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> against the kings of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENTAPOLIS">Pentapolis</a>; that is to say, of Sodom, Gomorrah, and the three neighbouring cities. The kings who were in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> with Amraphel worsted those of Pentapolis, plundered their <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, and carried off abundance of captives, among whom was <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">Lot</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABRAHAM">Abraham</a>'s nephew: but Abraham pursued them, retook Lot, and recovered all the spoil. See ABRAHAM.

AMRAS

Pages 171-171

a strong castle of Germany, seated in Tirol; by some German writers called Arx Ambrosiana, which was a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> for the archdukes to retire to in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>. By others this fort is called Ombrossa; a name derived from the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of it, which was to be a shady summer-house. It is most delightfully situated at the foot of a mountain, but has no <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>. All the furniture of ordinary <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> has been carried away; yet it is still remarkable for its galleries, which contain a very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> collection of antiquities, and both <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> curiosities. It excels all others in its curious collection of armour and coats of mail, many of which belonged to very great men. There is also a great collection of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> medals, which weigh, as they affirm, about 16 pounds; there are also 3000 cameos and intaglios, but few of them very fine. A great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of these antiquities were sent to this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> V. On the walls and ceiling there are some very good paintings; and, among the rest, they have an admirable <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOAH">Noah</a>'s ark, done by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BASSANO">Bassano</a>, for which the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUSCANY">Tuscany</a> is said to have offered 100,000 crowns. They have a library, which is not in very good order; and a gallery full of busts and other pieces of antiquity, besides many other apartments adorned with pictures of great value. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 11° 40'. N. Lat. 47°.

AMRU-EBN-AL-AS

Pages 171-173

one of the most famous of the first <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of Saracen leaders, was descended of Asai, of the tribe of Koreish, by a notorious prostitute. In his youth he indulged in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, and wrote satirical verses against the person and doctrine of Mahomet. His zeal in opposing the new <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> prompted him to undertake an embassy to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Ethiopia, to stimulate him against the converts whom he had taken under his protection. It is uncertain by what arguments he was induced to change his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> sentiments; but he returned a convert to the Mahometan <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, and, along with Caled, joined the fugitive prophet at Medina. The <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> talents of Amru had begun to attract general <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>, when <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABUBEKER">Abubeker</a> resolved to make a new attack upon <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, in which he obtained the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> command. After several displays of his military valour and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> in some successful enterprises, he rose to the elevated station of chief in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-IRAK">Irak</a>, when Caled requested the attendance of all the Arabian generals before Damascus. During the caliphate of Omar, he also served in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALESTINE">Palestine</a>, under Abu Obeidah. While besieging Cesarea, he held a memorable conference with Constantine, the son of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Heraclius. Historians mention that their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> was chiefly occupied in producing genealogical arguments to prove the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFFINITY">affinity</a> of the Greeks and Arabians, and the consequent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> of the latter as their descendants. Amru concluded with the candid <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a> "That the Arabians were tired of living..." in their scorching deserts, and were resolved to re-enter into the possession of the delightful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> which was the inheritance of their forefathers." He withdrew from the conference, after denouncing perpetual enmity against the Greeks, unless they should either become converts to the Mahometan faith <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> tributaries to that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. In the year of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HEGIRA">Hegira</a> 17, A.D. 638, Amru took Cesarea, and reduced to subjection all the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> of Syria. After the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Obeidah, Amru assumed the chief command in Syria, in which he was confirmed by the caliph, notwithstanding the opposition of Othman. An expedition against <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> being formerly resolved upon, Amru wrote to the caliph, informing him that he would instantly <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a> into Egypt. During the progress of his march, attended only by 4000 Arabs, a messenger from Omar arrived with a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a>, containing directions to return, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he should receive this letter in the territories of Syria; but if he should receive it in those of Egypt, he might advance, and all needful assistance would be instantly sent him. Anticipating the contents, he hastened on to the frontiers of Egypt, and read the instructions of the caliph. Then requesting some of the inhabitants to be brought before him, and inquiring at them in what country they were; and being informed that they were in Egypt, Amru replied, "Let us, then, continue our march." Having taken Pharna, he advanced to Misrah, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMPHIS">Memphis</a>, and besieged it during the space of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> months. Although numerous reinforcements arrived, he would have found it very difficult to storm the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> previous to the inundation of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NILE">Nile</a>, if Mokawkas had not treacherously lessened the forces of the citadel, which was accordingly taken by storm; and the Greeks who remained there were either made prisoners or put to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>. On the same spot Amru erected a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> named Fostat, the ruins of which are now known by the name of Old <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAIRO">Cairo</a>. The Coptic <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, who composed the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> majority of the Egyptian natives, and who were enemies to the Catholic Greeks, after this victory submitted to Amru, and engaged to provide <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> and support for the Mussulman <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>. Amru pursued the Greeks to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>, and, after an obstinate and bloody siege of 14 months, the city was taken, A.D. 642. During the siege, the general, along with one of his officers and a slave, was taken prisoner, and brought before the governor, who was at that time ignorant of the value of his prisoner. The manner, however, in which the general at first conducted himself induced the governor to suppose that he was a person of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>, therefore he ordered him to be beheld. This order would have immediately been carried into effect, had not the slave, who understood the Greek tongue, in which the command was given, fortunately chastised the imprudent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of Amru by giving him a box on the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-EAR">ear</a>. This circumstance changed the mind of the governor, and obtained a repeal of his order. By an engagement to propose an accommodation, the captive officer obtained the release of all the three; and the acclamations of the army on the return of their general first informed the governor of his egregious mistake. Amru prevailed upon his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> to refrain from the pillage of Alexandria, and to content themselves with the preservation of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, jewels, and other valuable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>, to defray the expense of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. Amru was disposed to preserve the famous library, and to have given it in a present to John the grammarian, but, by the command of the caliph, he was obliged to commit it to the flames. If the relation is not exaggerated, such was the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of books in that famous library, that they afforded <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a> to 5000 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a> during the space of six months. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> being taken, all Egypt soon fell into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the conqueror. Amru observed a wise and equitable policy, although his pecuniary demands were great. Egypt became the storehouse to famishing <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a>, and camels carrying <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> covered the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> from Memphis to Medina. Amru also employed his army in opening the canal from the Nile to the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RED_SEA"><a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">Red</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. The adjacent parts of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a> next felt the conquering power of Amru, but, upon the elevation of Othman, he was succeeded in the government of Egypt by Abdallah-ebn-Said. The inhabitants were so displeased with this change, that they formed a confederacy, and delivered up the city to a Grecian fleet. Amru was dispatched in haste to retake Alexandria, which, after an obstinate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>, was taken with great slaughter. The general at length interposing his authority, the slaughter was stopped, and upon the spot where the massacre ceased the Mosque of Mercy was erected. To prevent future rebellion, he dismantled the town, and was again succeeded by Abdallah; and he himself retired to Medina. When <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALI">Ali</a> ascended the throne, he became an adversary, and united himself to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of Moawiyah, whom he acknowledged caliph, and swore <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLEGIANCE">allegiance</a> to him. Ali proposed to decide the quarrel by single <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a>, and the valour of Amru inclined him to urge his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> to accept of the proposal; but Moawiyah positively declined the challenge. Amru, however, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> firm to the interest of Moawiyah, and took possession of Egypt in his name, having defeated the governor of Ali. About this time, he fortunately escaped assassination by the hands of the frantic Charegites, who had marked him out as one of the three who, by their death, were to restore peace to the contending parties. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSASSIN">assassin</a> waited his arrival at the mosque, but being prevented by a fit of the colic, his friend who was sent to officiate for him was slain in his stead. In the year 663, of the Hegira 43, he died in his government of Egypt, highly esteemed, and much regretted by his countrymen. In a pathetic <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORATION">oration</a> to his children on his deathbed, he bitterly lamented his youthful offence in satirizing the prophet, although Mahomet had forgiven the offence, and had frequently affirmed "that there was no Mussulman more sincere and steadfast in the faith than Amru." It is reported, that one <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> the caliph desired to see the sword of Amru, which had cut in pieces so many Christians. Amru drew his sword, which was a short and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> scimitar; and when Omar manifested signs of unusual surprise, he exclaimed, "Alas! the sword itself, without the arm of its master, is neither sharper nor more weighty than the sword of Pharezdak the poet." The greatness of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, the firmness of the friend, the valour of the general, the policy of the statesman, and the sanctity of the Mahometan moralist, were united in the character of Amru. (Mod. Univ. Hist. Gen. Biog.) AMSANCTI. See Ampsancti.

AMSDORFIANS

Pages 173-173

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a> in the 16th century, who took their name from Amsdorf their leader. They maintained, that good works were not only unprofitable, but were obstacles to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALVATION">salvation</a>.

AMSTERDAM

Pages 173-176

the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a> and of the United <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, is seated on the river Amstel and an arm of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> called the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WYE">Wye</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> is but indifferent, on account of the marshes that surround it, and render the city almost inaccessible; but this inconvenience is abundantly recompensed by the utility of its <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, which the port serves greatly to promote; for it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> contain above 1000 <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> ships. In 1204, it was nothing but a small castle, called Amstel from the name of the river, which its lords made a retreat for fishermen, who at first lived in huts covered with thatch; but it soon became considerable, and had a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> and towers built upon it, insomuch that it rose to a small city; though, till the year 1490, it was surrounded with nothing but a weak pallisado. The walls were then built with brick, to defend it from the incursions of the inhabitants of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-UTRECHT">Utrecht</a>, with whom the Hollanders were often quarrelling; but some months afterwards it was almost reduced to ashes. In 1512, it was besieged by the people of Guelderland; who not being able to take it, set fire to the ships in the harbour. In 1525, an Anabaptist leader, with 600 of his followers, got into the city in the night-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, attacked the townhouse, and defeated those that made any resistance. At length they barricaded, with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a> and hop sacks, the avenues to the market <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, where these enthusiasts were posted; and so put a stop to their fury till <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> appeared, at which time the citizens fell upon them on all sides, and forced them to retire into the townhouse, where most of them were cut to pieces. About ten years after, there was another tumult raised by a parcel of fanatics, consisting of men and women, who ran about the streets stark naked, and had a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of making themselves masters of the townhouse. Their shrieks and cries, which were dreadful enough, soon alarmed the inhabitants, who seized the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of them, and gave them the chastisement they deserved. Amsterdam was one of the last cities that embraced the reformed <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. It was besieged by the Hollanders in 1578, and submitted after a siege of ten months. One article of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITULATION">capitulation</a> was, a free <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of the Roman Catholic religion; but this was not observed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>; for they soon drove the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICS">ecclesiastics</a>, monks, and nuns, out of the city, broke the images, and demolished the altars. From this time it became the general rendezvous of all nations and of every <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a>, which raised it to that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a> and opulence it <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> enjoyed. The inhabitants were often obliged to enlarge the bounds of their city, and in 1675 it was increased to its present <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>. It was surrounded with a brick wall, and a large ditch 80 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> full of running <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. The walls were fortified with 26 bastions, on each of which there is now a windmill. There are eight gates towards the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>, and one towards the water. Amsterdam being seated on a marshy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, is built on piles of wood; for which reason no coaches are allowed, except to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> men and physicians, who pay a tax for that privilege; and all kinds of goods are drawn on sledges. It stands so low, that they would be exposed to inundations, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they did not secure themselves by dykes and sluices. The finest streets are, the Keysar's Graft, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">Emperor</a>'s Canal; the Heer Graft, or Lords Canal; the Cingel; and the street of Haerlem. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> canal is remarkable for its houses, which are magnificent structures of an equal height. Here are three prodigious sluices, and a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a> which <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> the city in many parts, and render the streets clean and pleasant. The canals are deep, their sides are lined with hewn <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, they have generally rows of trees planted on each side, and many stone bridges over different parts of them. The finest is that called the Amarrack, which is formed by the waters of the Amstel, into which the tide comes up, and on the sides of which are two large quays. This canal has several bridges. The principal is that next the sea, called Pont Neuf, or the New Bridge: it is 600 feet long, and 70 broad, with <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> balustrades on each side; it has 56 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a>, of which 11 are very <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, and eight are shut up to enclose the yachts. From this bridge there is a most charming prospect of the city, port, and sea. The port is a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a> and a half in length, and above 1000 paces in breadth. It is always filled with a multitude of vessels, which look like a forest, or rather a floating city. The streets in general are well paved, and the houses built of brick or stone. Towards the sides of the haven, the city is enclosed with great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a> driven into the ground, which are joined by large beams placed horizontally. There are openings to let the ships in and out, which are shut every night at the ringing of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELL">bell</a>. Amsterdam, including its fortifications, occupies a large space of ground; and is inhabited by very various <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a>.
