There are people here of almost every <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> and religion in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, who are all tolerated in their respective persuasions; but none admitted to any share in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> except the Calvinists. There are 11 churches for the Dutch of the established or Calvinstical religion, with two French and one High Dutch. The English have also three churches in this city: one for the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRESBYTERIANS">Presbyterians</a>, whose ministers are paid by the magistrates; a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> for those of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of England, whose minister is paid by his Britannic majesty; and a third for the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWNISTS">Brownists</a>, who maintain their own ministers. None but the Calvinists are allowed to have bells, and their ministers are maintained by the magistrates. All these churches or congregations make up only a third part of the inhabitants of the city. The <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ROMAN_CATHOLICS">Roman Catholics</a>, who have 27 houses or chapels for their worship, form another third part. Here they have a long <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> of houses for their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEGUINES">beguines</a> (a kind of nuns) to live in; who are not shut up in cloisters as other nuns in Roman Catholic countries, but have <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to walk abroad, and may even marry when they are tired of this kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. These chapels of the Roman Catholics have no bells allowed. lowed them, being looked upon as conventicles, and may be shut up and opened according as the government pleases. The other third part of the city is made up of Jews, Lutherans, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMINIANS">Arminians</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANABAPTISTS">Anabaptists</a>, &c., none of whom, as was said of the Roman Catholics, are allowed to have bells in their churches. Those who marry, and are not of the established religion, are obliged to be joined first by the magistrates, and then they may perform the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> in their own assemblies. The Jews, who are very considerable in this place, have two synagogues; one of which, namely the Portuguese, is the largest in Europe. Within the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> yard, where their synagogue stands, they have several rooms or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, where their children are taught <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a>, and very carefully instructed in the Jewish religion. The most remarkable of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> buildings is the New Church, dedicated to St Catharine. It was begun in the year 1408, others say 1414; and was 100 years in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>. It had the misfortune of being burnt in the year 1645, but was in a short time after built in a more magnificent manner. The foundation of a steeple is laid before this church, which was designed to be very high. The piles on which it was to be erected are not above 100 feet square, and yet they are 6334 in number, and those very large. Nevertheless it was thought that these vast piles, or rather the ground, were not able to support the prodigious <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> they intended to lay upon it; for which reason the steeple remains unfinished. The pulpit is a masterpiece of the kind, where the four evangelists and many other curious pieces of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a> are represented. The glass windows are adorned with paintings, among which the emperor Maximilian is described, presenting an imperial <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> to the burgomasters of Amsterdam for the crest of the arms of this city. The organ is very large, and reckoned one of the best in the world. It has a set of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a> that counterfeit a chorus of voices, and has 52 whole stops besides half stops, with two rows of keys for the feet, and three rows of keys for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. Those who hear it play for the first time imagine they hear a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>. The grate dividing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCEL">chancel</a> from the body of the church is all of Corinthian <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>. The branches of candlesticks are the richest in the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">Seven</a> Provinces. There is a very fine marble monument erected to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADMIRAL">Admiral</a> Ruyter, who was killed at Messina. The public buildings of a civil <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> are very magnificent. The stadthouze was founded in 1648. It is built upon 14,000 wooden piles; and its <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a> is 282 feet long, its sides 255 feet, and its height to the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> 116. There is a marble pediment in the front, whereon a woman is carved in relievo, holding the arms of the city; she is seated in a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a>, supported by two lions, with an olive branch in her <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>; on each side are four Naiads who present her with a crown of palm and laurel, and two other marine goddesses present her with different sorts of fruit; besides, there is <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEPTUNE">Neptune</a> with his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIDENT">trident</a>, accompanied with Tritons, a sea-unicorn, and a sea-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>. On the top stand three <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRONZE">bronze</a>, representing <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">Justice</a>, Strength, and Plenty. On the top of the structure is a round tower, 50 feet above the roof, adorned with statues, and an harmonious chime of bells, the biggest of which weighs about 7000 pounds, and the next 6000. They are made to play different tunes every <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a>. It has not one handsome gate, but only seven doors to answer to the number of the United Provinces. On the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a> of the great <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALL">hall</a> are two globes, the celestial and terrestrial, which are 22 feet in diameter and 69 in circumference. They are made of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> marble, and are inlaid with jasper and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>. In general, all the chambers are enriched with paintings, carvings, and gildings. While this stadthouze was building, the old one was set on fire, and consumed with all the archives and registers. Under the stadthouze is a prodigious vault, wherein is kept the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of Amsterdam, where there is a vast <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of ingots both of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver, as also bags which are supposed to be full of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>. The doors are <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> against petards, and are never opened but in the presence of one of the burgomasters. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRISONS">prisons</a> for debtors and criminals are likewise under the stadthouze; as also the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> room for the citizens, wherein the keys of the city are locked every night. At the end of the great hall is the sche-pens or aldermen's chamber, where civil causes are tried. Besides these, there are the chambers of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, the burgomasters chamber, the chamber of accounts, &c. In the second story is a large <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGAZINE">magazine</a> of arms; and on the top of the building are six large cisterns of water, which may be conveyed to any room in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of fire; to prevent which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIMNEYS">chimneys</a> are lined with copper. The bourse, or <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a>, where the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> assemble, is all of free-stone, and built upon 2000 wooden piles. Its length is about 250 feet, and its breadth 140. The galleries are supported by 26 marble columns, upon each of which are the names of the people that are to meet there. They are all numbered; and there is a place fixed for every merchandise under some one of these numbers. On the right hand of the gate is a superb staircase which leads to the galleries; on one side of which there are several shops, and on the other a place to sell clothes. It is not unlike the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> exchange in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADMIRALTY">admiralty</a> office is a house which belonged formerly to the princes of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a>. The arsenal for their men of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> is in the harbour. This is a very handsome building, 200 feet long, and 22 broad. The ground floor is filled with bullets; the second floor contains the arms and cordage; the third their sails, pulleys, flags, &c. This arsenal contains a great many curiosities; among the rest an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> canoe brought from the straits of Davis, and a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSERVATORY">conservatory</a> of water on the top of the house that holds 1600 tuns of water, which may be distributed in case of fire into 16 different parts by leaden pipes. Hard by this edifice you see the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOCK">dock</a> or yard where they build their men of war. The dock is 508 feet long, and contiguous to it are houses for lodging the ship carpenters. The dock is plentifully supplied with every thing necessary for the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of ships. The East <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">Company</a> occupy a large building divided into several offices or apartments. In some of those they have great stores of packed goods, and likewise a room with all sorts of drugs, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEA">tea</a>, wax, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBERGRIS">ambergris</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSK">musk</a>. Here they have a magazine full of medicaments for surgeons chests, to furnish the Company's ships and garrisons in the Indies; as also large large magazines of nutmegs, cloves, mace, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CINNAMON">cinnamon</a>. In the court yard there is a guard chamber, where every night the housekeeper has a watch; and on the other side of the gate there is a chemist, who with his men prepares medicines for the Indies; and adjoining to this court-yard is their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARE">ware</a>-house and packhouse for <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEPPER">pepper</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROSS">gross</a> goods. In the new part of this city they have a magazine or <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, which may properly be called an arsenal. The ground on which this building stands is 2000 feet, and square every way, reckoning the moats or burgwall about it. The two rope-alleys are 1800 feet long, on the back-side of which is a store of 500 large anchors besides small ones. In this arsenal they build the ships belonging to the Indian chamber of Amsterdam; for which reason they have all sorts of workhouses here for the artificers that serve the Company. The academy called the Illustrious School, is likewise a very fine building. It was formerly a convent belonging to the Nuns of St Agnes. Here they teach Latin, the oriental languages, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, &c. The lawyers and physicians have likewise their schools. Besides these, there are several <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">hospitals</a> or houses for orphans, for <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> widows, for sick persons, and for mad people; all which are regulated with much <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a>. The Rasp-house, which was formerly a nunnery, is now a sort of workhouse for men that behave ill. They are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> set to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> or rasp Brasil wood; and if they will not perform their task, they are put into a cellar which the water runs into, where if they do not almost constantly ply the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUMP">pump</a>, they run the risk of being drowned. There is likewise a spin-house for debauched women, where they are obliged to spin wool, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>, and do other <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>. All the hospitals are extremely neat, and richly adorned with pictures. They are maintained partly by voluntary contributions, which are raised by putting money into the poor's boxes fixed up all over the city; and partly by taxing all public diversions, as well at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a> as elsewhere. Likewise every person that passes through any of the gates at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANDLE">candle</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> pays a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENNY">penny</a> for the same <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>. The charities are taken care of by certain officers called deacons. The governors are nominated by the magistrates out of the most considerable men in the city. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> sort have places of diversion called Spiel-houses, where there are music and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DANCING">dancing</a>. They are much of the same kind as the hops which were so frequent about London. If strangers go there, they must take care not to make their addresses to a woman that is engaged to any other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>. There are two suburbs to this city; one at the gate of the regulars; and the other goes as far as Overtoon, a village a little way from Amsterdam, where boats which come from <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a> are rolled over land upon wooden rollers. There is likewise in this city an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a> for those that are infected with the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAGUE">plague</a>; which was built in the year 1630, and has 360 windows. The city is governed by a senate and council, which consists of 36 persons, called a Vroedshop, who enjoy their places for life; and when any of them dies, the remainder choose another in his stead. This senate elects deputies to be sent to the states of Holland, and appoints the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> magistrates of the city called Burgomasters or Echevins, who are like our aldermen. The number is twelve; out of which some are chosen every year to execute the office, and are called Burgomasters-regent. Three of these are discharged every year, to make room for three others. One of the four is kept in to inform the new ones of the state of affairs, and also presides the three first months in the year, and the others three months each; so that when they are in this office, they may be compared to the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> mayor of the city of London. These alterations and appointments are made by their own body. They dispose of all inferior offices which become vacant during their regency. They have likewise the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of all public works, which regard the safety, tranquillity, and embellishment of this city. The keys of the famous bank of this city are in the hands of these magistrates. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> consists of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> burgomasters or echevins, who are judges in all criminal affairs, without <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a>; but in civil causes they may appeal to the council of the province. There are two treasurers, a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAILIFF">bailiff</a>, and a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENSIONARY">pensionary</a>. The bailiff continues in his office three years; and searches after criminals, takes care to prosecute them, and sees their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> executed. The pensionary is the minister of the magistracy, is well versed in the laws, makes public harangues, and is the defender of the interests of the city. The city of Amsterdam contributes to the public income above 50,000 livres per day, besides the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXCISE">excise</a> of beer, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>, and corn; which in all amounts to above 1,600,000l. a-year. This is more than is paid by all the rest of the provinces put together; and yet Amsterdam bears but the fifth <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> of the states of Holland, with this distinction, that, whereas other cities send two members, this sends four. The <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITIA">militia</a> of Amsterdam is very considerable. They have 60 companies, each of which has from 200 to 300 men. Jews and Anabaptists are excluded from this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, not being admitted to bear arms: But they are obliged to contribute to the maintenance of the city-guard, which consists of 1400 <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>; as also to the night-watch, who patrol about the streets and proclaim the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>. Besides these, there are trumpeters on every church steeple who <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> every half hour; and if there happens a fire, they <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RING">ring</a> the fire-bell, and show where it is. The inhabitants have excellent contrivances to extinguish it speedily. The trade of Amsterdam was formerly very great: for almost the whole trade of the East India Company centred in this city, which besides carried on a commerce with all the rest of the world. The richest spices were entirely in the hands of the East India Company, who furnished all Europe therewith. They had vast quantities of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> stores, with which they supplied several nations; which was owing to their engrossing most of the iron-works on the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a> and other great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> that run into Holland. Such was the state of Amsterdam before the late revolution. Since that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, however, its trade has greatly declined. The long war with England, the consequent <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLOCKADE">blockade</a> of the port, the loss of the colonies, and the harassing consequences of the French occupation, gave a blow to the prosperity of the city. Its population, which amounted to 230,000 in 1785, was reduced below 200,000 in 1812. The <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a> of Amsterdam is 4° 30' E; the latitude, 52° 25' N. Amsterdam, or Tongataboo, is also the name of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> island in the South sea, said to have been discovered by Tasman a Dutch navigator. It was also visited by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Cook. Its greatest extent from east to west is about 21 miles, and from <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> to south about 13. It is broad at the east end, and runs <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TAPER">taper</a> towards the west, where it turns, and runs to a point due north. It is about six leagues to the west of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MIDDLEBURG">Middleburg</a>. The shore is surrounded by a coral rock, and its most elevated parts are not above six or eight yards above the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> of the sea. S. Lat. 21. 11. W. Long. 175. It is wholly laid out in plantations, in which are cultivated some of the richest productions of nature. Here are <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>-fruit, cocoa-<a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUT">nut</a> trees, plantains, bananas, sladdocks, yams, and some other roots, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>-canes, and a fruit like a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NECTARINE">nectarine</a>, called by the natives fighega. There did not appear an inch of waste ground: the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a> occupied no more space than was absolutely necessary: the fences did not take up above four inches each; and even these were not wholly lost, for in many grew some useful trees or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>; it was everywhere the same, change of place altered not the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a>: nature, assisted by a little art, nowhere appeared with more splendour than on this island. Water is not so plentiful here as at the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>; but the chief pointed out a pool of fresh water unasked, to supply the ships with that necessary article. Casuarinas, pandangs, and wild sago palms, appear here with their various tints of green, and baringtonia as big as the loftiest oaks. The bread-fruit does not, however, thrive here with the same luxuriance as at the Society islands; the coral rock, which composes the basis of this spot, being much more thinly covered with mould. Both men and women are of the common size of Europeans, and their <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> is that of lightish copper; they are well-shaped, have regular features, are <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a>, brisk, and lively. They have fine eyes, and in general good <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>, even to an advanced <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. The women are the merriest creatures imaginable, and incessant talkers. In general they appear to be modest; although there was no want of those of a different stamp. Among the natives, who swam about the ship very vociferously, were a considerable number of women, who wanted in the water like amphibious creatures, and were easily persuaded to come on board perfectly naked; but none of them ventured to stay there after sunset, but returned to the shore to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> the night, like the greater part of the inhabitants, under the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a> of the wild wood which lined the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a>. There they lighted great fires, and were heard conversing almost the whole night. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> of both sexes in general is black, but especially that of the women; both sexes wear it short, except a single lock on the top of the head, and a small quantity on each side. The men cut or shave their beards quite <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a>; which operation they perform with two shells. The hair of many was observed to be burnt at the ends, and strewed with a white powder, which was found, on examining it, to be lime made of shells or coral, which had corroded or burnt the hair; some made use of a blue powder, and others, both men and women, of an orange-coloured powder made of turmeric. The dress of both sexes consists of a piece of cloth or matting wrapped round the waist, and hanging <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> below the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNEES">knees</a>. From the waist upwards they are generally naked; and it seems to be a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMULET">amulet</a> these parts every morning. The practice of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TATTOOING">tattooing</a>, or puncturing the skin, likewise prevails. The men are tattooed from the middle of the thigh to above the hips; the women have it only on their arms and fingers, and on these parts but very slightly. Their ornaments were amulets, necklaces, and bracelets, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a>, shells, and beads of mother-of-<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEARL">pearl</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TORTOISE_SHELL">tortoise-shell</a>, &c. which are worn by men as well as women. The women also wear on their fingers neat rings made of tortoise-shell, and pieces in their ears about the size of a small quill; but here ornaments are not commonly worn, though all have their ears pierced. They have also a curious apron, made of the cocoa-nut shell; and composed of a number of small pieces sewed together in such a manner as to form stars, half-moons, little squares, &c.; it is studded with beads and shells, and covered with <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> feathers, so as to have a pleasing effect. They make the same kind of cloth, and of the same materials, as at Otaheite, though they have not such a variety, nor do they make any so fine; but as they have a method of glazing it, it is more durable, and will resist <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> for some time, which the other cloth would not. Their colours are black, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>, purple, and red; all made from vegetables. They make various sorts of matting, some of a very fine texture, which is generally used for clothing; and the thick and stronger sort serves to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a> upon, and to make sails for their canoes, &c. Among other useful utensils, they have various sorts of baskets, some made of the same materials as their mats, and others of the twisted fibres of cocoa-nuts. These are not only durable, but beautiful, being generally composed of different colours, and studded with beads made of shells or bones. They have many little nick-nacks among them, which show that they neither want <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> to design, nor skill to execute, whatever they take in hand. Their <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a> implements are much the same as in the other islands; here was purchased a fish-<a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NET">net</a> made like our casting nets, knit of very firm though slender threads. Notwithstanding their friendly disposition, those people have very formidable weapons; some of their spears have many barbs, and must be very dangerous weapons when they take effect. A large flat shell or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>-plate was purchased, made of a roundish bone, white and polished like <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a>, about 18 inches in diameter, which appeared to have belonged to an animal of the whale tribe.

AMULET

Pages 176-178

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARM">charm</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> preservative against mischief, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WITCHCRAFT">witchcraft</a>, or diseases. Amulets were made of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, metal, simples, animals, and in a word of every thing that imagination suggested. Sometimes they consisted of words, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>, and sentences, ranged in a particular order, and engraved upon wood, &c. and worn about the neck, or some other <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the body. See Abracadabra. At other times they were neither written nor engraved; but prepared with many superstitious ceremonies, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> regard being usually paid to the influence of the stars. The Arabians have given to this <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of amulet the name of Talisman. All nations have been fond of amulets: the Jews were extremely superstitious in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of them, to drive drive away diseases; and the Mishna forbids them, unless received from an approved <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> who had cured at least three persons before by the same means. Among the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> of the early times, amulets were made of the wood of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>, or ribbands with a text of Scripture written in them, as preservatives against diseases. Notwithstanding the progress of learning and refinement, there is not any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, even at this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, where they do not believe in some charm or other. The pope is supposed to have the virtue of making amulets, which he exercises in the consecrating of Agnus Dei's, &c. The sponge which has wiped his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, was formerly in great veneration as a preservative from wounds, and from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> itself: on this account it was sent with great solemnity by Gregory II. to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Aquitain. Amulets are now much fallen from the repute they were anciently in; yet the great Mr Boyle alleges them as an instance of the ingress of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> effluvia into the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>, in order to show the great porosity of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> body. He adds, that he is persuaded some of these external medicines do answer; for that he himself, having been once subject to bleed at the nose, and reduced to use several remedies to check it, found the moss of a dead man's skull, though only applied so as to touch the skin till the moss was warm thereby, the most effectual of any. The same Mr Boyle shows how the effluvia, even of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a> amulets, may, in course of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, pervade the pores of a living animal; by supposing an agreement between the pores of the skin and the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of the corpuses. Bellini has attempted to demonstrate the possibility of the thing in his last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPOSITIONS">propositions</a> De Febribus; and the like is done by Dr Wainwright, Dr Keill, &c. AMURATH or AMURAT I. the fourth <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> of the Turks, and one of the greatest princes of the Ottoman empire, succeeded Solyman in 1390. He took from the Greeks <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GALLIPOLI">Gallipoli</a> in Thrace, and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ADRIANOPLE">Adrianople</a>, which last he chose for the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of his residence. He defeated the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of Bulgaria, conquered Misnia, chastised his rebellious bashaws, and is said to have gained 36 battles. This prince, in order to form a body of devoted troops that might serve as the immediate guards of his person and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, appointed his officers to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEIZE">seize</a> annually, as the imperial <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, the fifth part of the Christian youth taken in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. These, after being instructed in the Mahometan <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, inured to obedience by severe <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a>, and trained to warlike exercises, were formed into a body distinguished by the name of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JANIZARIES">Janizaries</a>, or New <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">Soldiers</a>. Every sentiment which enthusiasm can inspire, every mark of distinction that the favour of the prince could confer, were employed in order to animate this body with martial ardour, and with a consciousness of its own pre-eminence. The Janizaries soon became the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> strength and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a> of the Ottoman armies, and were distinguished above all the troops whose duty it was to attend on the person of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SULTAN">sultan</a>.—At length the death of Lazarus, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESPOT">despot</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVIA">Servia</a>, who had endeavoured in vain to stop the progress of Amurath's arms, touched Milo, one of his servants, in so sensible a manner, that, in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a>, he stabbed the sultan in the midst of his troops, and killed him upon the spot, A.D. 1389, after he had reigned 23 years. AMURATH II. the 10th emperor of the Turks, was the eldest son of Mahomet I. and succeeded his father in 1421. He besieged Constantinople and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELGRADE">Belgrade</a> without success; but he took Thessalonica from the Venetians, and compelled the prince of Bosnia and John Castriot prince of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBANIA">Albania</a> to pay him tribute. He obliged the latter to send his three sons as hostages; among whom was George, celebrated in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> by the name of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCANDERBEG">Scanderbeg</a>. John Hunniades defeated Amurath's troops, and obliged him to make peace with the Christian princes in 1442. These princes afterwards breaking the peace, Amurath defeated them in the famous <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of Varna, November 10, 1444, which proved so fatal to the Christians, and in which Ladislaus <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a> was killed. He afterwards defeated Hunniades, and killed above 20,000 of his men; but George Castriot, better known by the name of Scanderbeg, being re-established in the estates of his father, defeated the Turks several times, and obliged Amurath to raise the siege of Croia, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of Albania. Amurath died, chagrined with his ill success, and infirm with <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, February 11, 1451, at Adrianople. It is observed to this prince's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, that he always kept his treaties with the greatest fidelity. AMURATH IV. surnamed the Valiant, was the son of Achmet I. and in the year 1622, at the age of 13, succeeded his uncle Mustapha. <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAGDAD">Bagdad</a> fell into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the Persians, and several other disastrous events clouded the commencement of his reign. The pacha of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ERZERUM">Erzerum</a> had raised the standard of rebellion in the former reign; and, continuing his opposition, he overran many of the provinces of Lesser <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>. But the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> talents of the sultan were soon roused to exertion; and, making peace with Germany, he hastened with a formidable <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> to regain Bagdad. But new rebellions in his Asiatic dominions, and several other causes, prevented him from recovering the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>. The Spahis also rebelled at home, and several viziers were slain during the tumults of the Porte. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> dispositions of the young monarch were ill adapted to his situation, and extremely destructive to his people. It is reported, that a flash of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a> rushing into his chamber during the darkness of the night, strongly impaired his reason, and produced a violence and intemperance of character which remained to the end of his days. It was therefore nothing more than reasonable to expect that his policy should be variable and inconstant; it appears, however, that he actively resisted the foes who pressed upon his dominions from different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a> of Bagdad being still his favourite object, in the year 1637, he again marched against it; and after 30 days of unremitting assault, with the expense of much blood, he took possession of the city. By pushing his men forward to the attack by the point of the scimitar, and by slaughtering 30,000 Persians in cold blood after their surrender, he displayed the brutal ferocity of his disposition. One person alone is reported to have moved his obdurate heart on the present occasion. A famous player upon the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HARP">harp</a> entreated those who were sent to massacre him, to allow him to speak to the sultan previous to his death. Informed who he was, the sultan requested him to give a specimen of his skill in his profession; with this he readily complied, and touched his harp so melodiously, and sung sung in such pathetic strains the lamentations on the tragedy of Bagdad, intermixed with the praises of Amurath, that the hard heart of the cruel monarch being at length softened, he melted into tears, and saved both the musician and the remaining inhabitants. The loss sustained by the Persians at this time, so reduced their military strength, that they were unable for a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> to attack the Ottoman empire. The violence of Amurath soon enfeebled his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>; and the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of his debaucheries and excesses were obvious even in the prime of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. At the age of 31, he fell a victim to an excess of reveling in the feast of Bairam, in the year 1640. Beholding his end approaching, he is reported to have given orders to assassinate his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>, in order to secure the throne for his favourite Mustapha; but the affection of his mother prevented the cruel mandate from being carried into effect. The manners and amorous adventures of this monarch have afforded materials for numerous Turkish descriptions full of extravagance, singularity, and cruelty. He surpassed all his predecessors in the abominable vice of intoxication, and even violated the established laws of the country, by issuing an edict permitting the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a> and use of wine. But, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it was not sufficient to violate the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>, he also opposed himself to the common usage of the country, by shutting up the coffeehouses, and prohibiting opium and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a> upon the pain of death. The wanton cruelty of this prince was almost unexampled. During his hours of dissipation, he would rush forth into the streets with a drawn <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> in his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and cut in pieces all the unhappy persons who chanced to be in his way. Nay, even in his calmest moments, he often discharged arrows from his upper windows at the innocent passengers as they went along. In short, to such extravagance did his cruelty extend, that the very name of Amurath carried terror along with it, and the opium-chewers fell into fits upon the simple mention thereof. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of persons that fell victims to his cruelty during a reign of 17 years, amounted to no less than 14,000; among whom were many officers of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> power and distinction in the state. The meanness of his dispositions, however, manifested themselves in his descending to familiarities with his favourites, and even joining in the meanest services. He also displayed a singular humour in making marriages between old men and girls, and young men and women of fourscore. It may, however, on the whole, be asserted, that if he had not been intoxicated with wine and power, the qualities of his mind and body might have rendered him a more respectable member of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>. He was very remarkable for swiftness of foot and dexterity in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> the bow. The reverses of fortune made small <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> on his mind, and he pursued with resolute firmness any object in which he seriously engaged. Dissembling, avaricious, and blasphemous, he gave full <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a>, that his moral qualities were greatly depraved. (Mod. Un. Hist. Gen. Biog.) AMYCLÆ, a city of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LACONIA">Laconia</a>, distant about 18 miles from the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a>, founded by Amyclas the son of Lacedæmon, and famed afterwards for the birth of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASTOR">Castor</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLLUX">Pollux</a> the sons of Tyndarus, eighth king of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SPARTA">Sparta</a>. It was afterwards famed for sending a considerable colony of its own inhabitants into Upper <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALABRIA">Calabria</a>, who built there a city which they called by the same name. This last city was situated between Cajeta and Terracina, and gave its name to the neighbouring <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. According to Pliny and Solinus, the territory of Amyclæ was so infested with vipers and other <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERPENTS">serpents</a>, that the inhabitants were obliged to abandon their dwellings and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> elsewhere. Among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> poets, the Amyclæ, or inhabitants of this city, obtained the epithet of taciti, "silent." The reason of this was, either because it was built by the Lacedæmonians, who, as they followed the doctrine of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYTHAGORAS">Pythagoras</a>, were always inculcating the precept of silence, and thence called taciti; or because of a law which obtained in this place, forbidding any one, under severe penalties, to mention the approach of an enemy. Before this law was made, the city was daily alarmed by false reports, as if the enemy had been already at the gates. From terrors of this kind the above-mentioned law indeed delivered them; but, in the end, it proved the ruin of the city: for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DORIANS">Dorians</a> appearing unexpectedly under the walls, no one ventured to transgress the law; so that the city was easily taken. They reduced it to an inconsiderable <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAMLET">hamlet</a>; in which, however, were seen some of the remains of its ancient <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a>. One of the finest buildings that escaped the common ruin, was the temple and statue of Alexandra, whom the inhabitants pretended to be the same with <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASSANDRA">Cassandra</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Priam.

AMYLACEOUS

Pages 178-178

from amyllum, "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STARCH">starch</a>;" a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> applied to the fine flour of farinaceous seeds, in which consists their nutritive <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">Bread</a>.

AMYNTA

Pages 178-178

in literary <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a beautiful pastoral <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMEDY">comedy</a>, composed by Tasso; the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODEL">model</a> of all dramatic pieces wherein shepherds are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTORS">actors</a>. The Pastor Fido, and Filii de Sciro, are only copies of this excellent piece.

AMYNTOR

Pages 178-178

aquvte, formed of the verb aquv, I defend <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> avenge, properly denotes a person who defends or vindicates a cause. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, Mr Toland entitles his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILTON">Milton</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, Amyntor, as being a vindication of that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, against Mr Blackhall and others, who had <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> him with questioning the authority of some of the books of the New <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, and declaring his doubt that several pieces under the name of Christ and his Apostles, received now by the whole Christian <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, were supposititious.

AMYOT

Pages 178-179

JAMES, bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AUXERRE">Auxerre</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> almoner of France, was born of an obscure family at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MELUN">Melun</a>, the 30th of October 1514, and studied <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Le Moine. He was naturally dull and heavy; but diligence and application made amends for these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> defects. He left Paris at the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 23; and went to <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOURGES">Bourges</a> with the Sieur Colin, who had the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a> of St <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBROSE">Ambrose</a> in that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>. At the recommendation of this <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABBOT">abbot</a>, a secretary of state took Amyot into his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> to be <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a> to his children. The great improvements they made under his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> induced the secretary to recommend him to the Princess Margaret duchess of Berry, only sister of Francis I. and by means of this recommendation Amyot was made public professor of Greek and Latin in the university of Bourges. It was during this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> he translated into French the "Amours of Theagines and Chariclea," which Francis I. was so pleased with, that he conferred upon him the abbey of Bellosane. He also translated Plutarch's Lives, which he dedicated to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>; and afterwards undertook that of Plutarch's Morals, which he ended in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> IX., and dedicated to that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>. Charles conferred upon him the abbey of St Cornelius de Compiègne, and made him the great almoner of France and bishop of Auxerre. He died in 1593, aged 79.

AMYRALDISM

Pages 179-179

a name given by some writers to the doctrine of universal <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">grace</a>, as explained and asserted by Amyraldus, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Moses Amyrauld, and others his followers, among the reformed in France, towards the middle of the 17th century. This doctrine principally consisted of the following particulars, viz. that God desires the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> of all men, and none are excluded by a divine <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DECREE">decree</a>; that none can obtain <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALVATION">salvation</a> without <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> in Christ; that God refuses to none the power of believing, though he does not <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> to all his assistance, that they may improve this power to saving purposes; and that many perish through their own fault. Those who embraced this doctrine were called Universalists; though it is evident they rendered grace universal in words, but partial in reality, and are chargeable with greater inconsistencies than the Supralapsarians.

AMYRAULT

Pages 179-179

Moses, an eminent French Protestant divine, born at Bourgueil in Touraine in 1566. He studied at <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAUMUR">Saumur</a>, where he was chosen professor of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>; and his learned works gained him the esteem of Catholics as well as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>, particularly of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Richelieu, who consulted him on a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of reuniting their churches, which, however, as may well be supposed, came to nothing. He published a piece in which he attempted to explain the mystery of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREDESTINATION">predestination</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">grace</a>, which occasioned a controversy between him and some other divines. He also wrote, An Apology for the Protestants; a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARAPHRASE">Paraphrase</a> on the New <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>; and several other books. This eminent divine died in 1664. AMYRIS. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ANA

Pages 179-179

in matters of literature, a Latin termination, adopted into the titles of several books in other languages.—<a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANAS">Anas</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> books in ana, are collections of the memorable sayings of persons of learning and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a>; much the same with what we otherwise called <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>-talk. Wolfius has given the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of books in ana, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREFACE">preface</a> to the Casauboniana. He there observes, that though such titles be new, the thing itself is very old; that Xenophon's books of the deeds and sayings of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOCRATES">Socrates</a>, as well as the dialogues of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a>, are Socraticana; that the aphorisms of the philosophers collected by <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIOGENES">Diogenes</a> Laërtius, the sentences of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYTHAGORAS">Pythagoras</a> and those of Epictetus, the works of Athenaeus, Stobeus, and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> others, are so many anas. Even the Gemara of the Jews, with several other oriental writings, according to Wolfius, properly belong to the same class. To this head of ana may likewise be referred the Orphica, the Pythagoræa, Æsopica, Pyrrhonea, &c. Scaliger was the first piece that appeared with a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> in Ana. It was composed by Isan de Vassan, a young Champanois, recommended to Jos. Scaliger by Casaubon. Being much with Scaliger, who was daily visited by the men of learning at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>, De Vassan wrote <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> whatever things of any moment he heard Scaliger say. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> was not printed till many years after at <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENEVA">Geneva</a> in 1666. Patin. Let. 431.—Soon after came the Perroniana, Thuana, Naudéana, Patineana, Sorberiana, Menagiana, Anti-Menagiana, Furetiana, Chevreana, Leibnitziana, Arlequiniana, Poggiana, &c. See ANA, Supplement.

ANABAPTISTS

Pages 179-181

a name which has been indiscriminately applied to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> of very different principles and practices; though many of them object to the denomination, and hold nothing in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a>, besides the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a> ought always to be performed by immersion, and not administered before the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a>. The word Anabaptist is compounded of ἀνα, "new," and βάπτισμα, "a baptist;" and in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> the Novatians, the Cataphrygians, and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DONATISTS">Donatists</a>, may be considered as a kind of Anabaptists in the earlier ages, though not then denoted by this name; for they contended, that those Christians of the Catholic <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> who joined themselves to their respective parties should be rebaptized. But we must not class under the same denomination those <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, who, in the third century, maintained, that baptism administered by those whom they called heretics was not valid, and therefore that such of them as returned into their churches ought to be rebaptized. Nor do the English and Dutch Baptists consider the denomination as at all applicable to their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a>: by whom the baptism appointed by Christ is held to be "nothing short of immersion upon a personal profession of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>;" of which profession <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INFANTS">infants</a> being incapable, and sprinkling being no adequate symbol of the thing included, the baptizing of proselytes to their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a>, who in their infancy had undergone the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> of sprinkling, cannot, it is urged, be interpreted a repetition of the baptismal ordinance. Anabaptists, in a strict and proper sense, appear to be those who not only rebaptize, when they arrive at an adult age, persons that were baptized in their infancy, but also, as often as any person comes from one of their sects to another, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> as often as any one is excluded from their communion and again received into the bosom of the church, they baptize him. And such were many of the German Baptists. But the single opinion common to all the sects to which the name of Anabaptists has been indiscriminately applied, is that of the invalidity of infant baptism, in whatever way administered: And hence the general denomination of Antipedobaptists; which included Anabaptists, Baptists, Mennonites, Waterlandians, &c. as distinguished by their respective peculiarities; though Anabaptists seems to have been adopted by most writers as the general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a>. To the above peculiar notion concerning the baptismal sacrament, the Anabaptists added principles of a different <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, depending upon certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> which they entertained concerning a perfect church establishment, pure in its members, and free from the institutions of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> policy. The Anabaptists appear to have made little noise, or to have been little noticed, before the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the reformation in Germany. The most prudent and rational <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of them considered it possible, by human <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>, industry, and vigilance, to purify the church from the contagion of the wicked, provided the manners and spirit of the primitive Christians could but recover their lost <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> and lustre; and seeing the attempts of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUTHER">Luther</a>, seconded by several persons of eminent piety, prove so successful, they hoped that the happy <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> was arrived in which the restoration of the church to purity was to be accomplished, under the divine protection, by the labours and counsels of pious and eminent men. Others, far from being satisfied with the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of reformation proposed by Luther, looked upon it as much beneath the sublimity of their views; and consequently undertook a more perfect reformation, or, to express more properly their visionary enterprise, they proposed to found a new church, entirely spiritual, and truly divine. This sect was soon joined by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> numbers, and (as usually happens in sudden revolutions of this nature) by many persons, whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> and capacities were very different, though their views seemed to turn upon the same object. Their progress was rapid; for, in a very short space of time, their discourses, visions, and predictions, excited commotions in a great part of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, and drew into their communion a prodigious multitude, whose <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> rendered them easy victims to the illusions of enthusiasm. The most pernicious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACTION">faction</a> of all those which composed this motley multitude, was that which pretended that the founders of the new and perfect church, already mentioned, were under the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of a divine impulse, and were armed against all opposition by the power of working <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a>. It was this faction that, in the year 1521, began their fanatical <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, under the guidance of Munzer, Stübner, Storch, &c. These persons were disciples of Luther; but well knowing that their opinions were such as would receive no sanction from him, they availed themselves of his absence to disseminate them in Wittenburg, and had the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> to overreach the piety of Melanchthon. Their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> purpose was to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> over the populace, and to form a considerable party. To effect this, says Bayle, they were industrious and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a>, each in his own way. Storch wanting knowledge, boasted of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSPIRATION">inspiration</a>; and Stübner, who had both genius and erudition, laboured at commodious explications of Scripture. Not content with discrediting the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of Rome, and decrying the authority of consistories, they taught, That among Christians, who had the precepts of the gospel to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a>, and the Spirit of God to guide them, the office of magistracy was not only unnecessary, but an unlawful encroachment on their spiritual <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>; that the distinctions occasioned by birth, or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>, or wealth, being contrary to the spirit of the gospel, which considers all men as equal, should be entirely abolished; that all Christians, throwing their possessions into one common stock, should live together in that state of equality which becomes members of the same family; that as neither the laws of nature nor the precepts of the New <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a> had placed any restraint upon men with regard to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of wives which they might marry, they should <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> that liberty which God himself had granted to the patriarchs. They employed at first the various arts of persuasion in order to propagate their doctrine. They preached, exhorted, admonished, and reasoned, in a manner that seemed proper to impress the multitude; and related a great number of visions and revelations with which they pretended to have been favoured from above. But when they <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> that these methods of making proselytes were not attended with such rapid success as they fondly expected, and that the ministry of Luther and other eminent reformers was detrimental to their cause, they then had recourse to more expeditious <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a>, and madly attempted to propagate their fanatical doctrine by force of arms. Munzer and his associates, in the year 1523, put themselves at the head of a numerous <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, composed for the most part of the peasants of Swabia, Thuringia, Franconia, and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>; and declared <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> against all laws, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, and magistrates of every kind, under the chimerical <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRETEXT">pretext</a> that Christ was now to take the reins of civil and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> government into his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, and to rule alone over the nations. But this seditious crowd was routed and dispersed, without much difficulty, by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> of Saxony and other princes; and Munzer their <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RING">ring</a>-leader ignominiously put to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, and his factious counsellors scattered abroad in different places. Many of his followers, however, survived and propagated their opinions through Germany, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>. In the year 1533, a party of them settled at <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUNSTER">Munster</a> under the direction of two Anabaptist prophets, John Matthias a baker of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HAARLEM">Haarlem</a>, and John Bockholdt a journeyman taylor of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>. Having made themselves masters of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, they deposed the magistrates, confiscated the estates of such as had escaped, and deposited the wealth they amassed together in a public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a> for common use. They made preparations of every kind for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of the city; and sent out emissaries to the Anabaptists in the Low Countries, inviting them to assemble at Munster, which was now dignified with the name of Mount <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SION">Sion</a>, that from hence they might be deputed to reduce all the nations of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> under their dominion. Matthias, who was the first in command, was soon cut off in an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of frenzy by the bishop of Munster's army; and was succeeded by Bockholdt, who was proclaimed by a special designation of Heaven, as he pretended, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Sion, and invested with legislative powers like those of Moses. The extravagancies of Bockholdt were too numerous to be recited: it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be sufficient to add, that the city of Munster was taken after a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> siege and an obstinate resistance; and Bockholdt, the mock monarch, was punished with a most painful and ignominious death. It must, however, be acknowledged, that the true rise of the numerous insurrections of this period ought not to be attributed to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> opinions. The first insurgents groaned under the most grievous oppressions; they took up arms principally in defence of their civil liberties; and of the commotions that took <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, the Anabaptist leaders above mentioned seem rather to have availed themselves, than to have been the prime movers. See the article REFORMATION.—That a great part of the main body, indeed, consisted of Anabaptists, seems indisputable; and whatever fanaticism existed among them would naturally be called forth or be inflamed by the situations that occurred, and run riot in its wildest shapes. At the same time it appears from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, that a great part also consisted of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ROMAN_CATHOLICS">Roman Catholics</a>, and a still greater of persons who had scarcely any religious principles at all. Indeed, when we read of the vast numbers that were concerned in those insurrections, of whom it is reported that 100,000 fell by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, it appears reasonable to conclude that a great majority of them were not Anabaptists. Before concluding this article, it must be remarked, that the Baptists or Mennonites in England and Holland are to be considered in a very different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> from the enthusiasts we have been describing: And it appears equally uncandid and invidious, to trace up their distinguishing sentiment, as some of their adversaries have done, to those obnoxious characters, and there to stop, in order as it were to associate with it the ideas of turbulence and fanaticism, with which it certainly has no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> connection. Their coincidence with some of those oppressed and infatuated people in denying baptism to infants, is acknowledged by the Baptists; but they disavow the practice which the appellation of Anabaptists implies; and their doctrines seem referable to a more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and respectable origin. They appear supported by history in considering themselves as the descendants of the Waldenses, who were so grievously oppressed and persecuted by the despotic heads of the Roman <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HIERARCHY">hierarchy</a>; and they profess an equal aversion to all principles of rebellion on one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and to all suggestions of fanaticism on the other. See Baptists. The denomination of Mennonites, by which they are distinguished in Holland, they derive from Menno, the famous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> who latterly gave consistence and stability to their sect. See Mennonites.

ANABASII

Pages 181-181

in antiquity, were couriers who were sent on horseback <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARIOTS">chariots</a>, with dispatches of importance. ANABASIS. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ANABATHRA

Pages 181-181

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> writers, denotes a kind of steps <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LADDER">ladder</a> whereby to ascend to some eminence. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> we read of the anabathra of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-THEATRES">theatres</a>, pulpits, &c. Anabathra appears to have been sometimes also applied to ranges of seats rising gradually over each other. ANABATHRA is more particularly applied to a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> blocks raised by the highway sides, to assist travellers in mounting or alighting, before the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of stirrups was invented. The first author of this contrivance among the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> was C. Gracchus <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> of Tiberius.

ANABLEPS

Pages 181-181

in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a>, the trivial name of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of cobitis. See Cobitis.

ANABOA

Pages 181-181

a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> situated near the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Loango in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 9°. N. Lat. 1°. Here are several fertile valleys, which produce plenty of bananas, oranges, pine apples, lemons, citrons, tamarinds, cocoa nuts, &c. together with vast quantities of cotton. In this island are two <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, which being continually covered with <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a>, occasion frequent rains. ANABOLÆUM, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Anabole, in antiquity, a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> or upper coat, worn over the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUNICA">tunica</a>.

ANABOLESUS

Pages 181-181

in antiquity, an appellation given Anabolesus to grooms of the stable, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> equerries, who assisted their masters in mounting their horses. As the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> had no stirrups, or instruments that are now in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> for mounting a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, they either jumped upon his back, or were aided in mounting by anabolesi.

ANACALYPTERIA

Pages 181-181

according to Suidas, were presents made to the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIDE">bride</a> by her husband's relations and friends, when she first uncovered her <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> and showed herself to men. These presents were also called επανάληψις: for, among the Greeks, virgins before <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> were under strict confinement, being rarely permitted to appear in public, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONVERSE">converse</a> with the other <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEX">sex</a>; and when allowed that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, wore a veil over their faces, termed Καλυπτήριον, or Καλυπτήριον, which was not left off in the presence of men till the third <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> after marriage; whence, according to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HESYCHIUS">Hesychius</a>, this day was also called anacalypserion.

ANACAMPSEROS

Pages 181-181

in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, a synonyme of the portulaca and several other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>.

ANACAMPTERIA

Pages 181-181

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> antiquity, a kind of little edifices adjacent to the churches, designed for the entertainment of strangers and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> persons.

ANACAMPTIC

Pages 181-181

a name applied by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> to that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPTICS">optics</a> which treats of reflection, being the same with what is now called <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CATOPTRICS">CATOPTRICS</a>.

ANACARDIUM

Pages 181-181
or CASHEW-NUT TREE. See Botany Index. ANACEPHALÆOSIS, in Rhetoric, the same with Recapitulation. See Recapitulation.

ANACHARSIS

Pages 181-182

a Scythian <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, who lived about 600 years before Christ. His father was one of the chiefs of his <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, and married a woman of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>. Instructed in the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> by his mother, he caught the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a> for Grecian literature, and prevailed upon the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> to intrust him with an embassy to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>. Arrived in that renowned <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, he was introduced to Solon by one of his own countrymen, named Foxaris; and it is reported, that when he came to the door of Solon, he requested a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> to inform his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, that Anacharsis a Scythian was at the door, and was desirous of being received as his friend and guest. Solon is said to have returned for answer, that "friendships are best formed at home." To this the Scythian philosopher replied, "then let Solon, who is at home, make me his friend and receive me into his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>." Solon was so astonished at the propriety of this reply, that he gave him admittance; and, finding him upon farther acquaintance worthy of his confidence, he honoured him with his friendship. From such a well qualified master, Anacharsis rapidly acquired a knowledge of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> of Greece, and the literature then in circulation.
