By the influence of Solon he was introduced to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> of Athens, and was the first stranger who was honoured with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of citizen by the Athenians. After he had resided several years at Athens, he travelled through different countries in quest of knowledge, and then returned to his native <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> inflamed with the desire of instructing them in the laws and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> of the Greeks. But his countrymen were not prepared to profit by his instructions; and while he was performing sacrifice to the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> Cybele, correspondent to a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOW">vow</a> which he had made on his his way home, he was slain by an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARROW">arrow</a>, said to have proceeded from the king's own <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. Thus fell the Scythian philosopher a victim to the folly and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> of his countrymen, who wantonly rejected the wisdom and learning of Greece. The energetic manner in which he was accustomed to express himself, gave birth to the proverbial saying, "Scythian eloquence." Although the potter's wheel was invented in the days of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>, some have inaccurately ascribed its <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> to Anacharsis. The following ingenious sayings may be mentioned as a specimen of his genius. "The best way of teaching a youth sobriety, is to set before his eyes a drunken <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>. The vine bears three sorts of fruit; the first <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> intoxication, the third remorse. An ape is by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> ridiculous; man by art and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a>. An Athenian of bad morals reproached him with being a Scythian: to him he replied, 'My country may be a disgrace to me, but you are a disgrace to your country.' Some suppose, that the epistles which bear his name are spurious. (Gen. Biog.)"

ANACHORET

Pages 182-182

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, denotes a hermit, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> solitary monk, who retires from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> of mankind into some <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DESERT">desert</a>, with a view to avoid the temptations of the world, and to be more at leisure for meditation and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a>. Such were Paul, Anthony, and Hilarian, the first founders of monastic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALESTINE">Palestine</a>. Anachorets, among the Greeks, consist principally of monks, who retire to caves or cells, with the leave of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABBOT">abbot</a>, and an allowance from the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a>; or who, weary of the fatigues of the monastery, purchase a spot of ground, to which they retreat, never appearing in the monastery unless on solemn occasions.

ANACHRONISM

Pages 182-182

in matters of literature, an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ERROR">error</a> with respect to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">chronology</a>, whereby an event is placed earlier than it really happened. The word is compounded of ἀνω, "higher," and χρόνος, "<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>." Such is that of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>, who placed Dido in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a> at the time of Æneas, though in reality she did not come there till 300 years after the taking of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">Troy</a>.—An error on the other side, whereby a fact is placed later and lower than it should be, is called a parachronism.

ANACLASTIC GLASSES

Pages 182-182

a kind of sonorous phials <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> glasses, chiefly made in Germany, which have the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of being <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLEXIBLE">flexible</a>, and emitting a vehement noise by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> breath.—They are also called vexing glasses by the Germans (exziter glaser), on account of the fright and disturbance they occasion by their resiliency. The anaclastic glasses are a low kind of phials with flat bellies, resembling <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INVERTED">inverted</a> funnels, whose bottoms are very thin, scarce surpassing the thickness of an onion peel: this bottom is not quite flat, but a little convex. But upon applying the mouth to the orifice, and gently inspiring, or as it were sucking out the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>, the bottom gives way with a prodigious crack, and the convex becomes concave. On the contrary, upon expiring or breathing gently into the orifice of the same glass, the bottom with no less noise <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENDS">bends</a> back to its former <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and becomes gibbous as before.—The anaclastic glasses first taken notice of were in the castle of Goldbach; where one of the academists <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">Nature</a> Curiosorum, having seen and made experiments on them, published a piece express on their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> and phenomena. They are all made of a fine <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> glass. It is to be observed, 1. That <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the anaclastic bottom be concave at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSPIRATION">inspiration</a>, it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> burst; and the like will happen if it be convex at the anacreon, time of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPIRATION">expiration</a>. 2. A strong breath will have the same effect even under the contrary circumstances.

ANACLASTICS

Pages 182-182

that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPTICS">optics</a> which considers the refraction of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, and is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called Dioptries. See Dioptries.

ANACLETERIA

Pages 182-182

in antiquity, a solemn festival celebrated by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> when their kings <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> princes came of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, and assumed the reins of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. It is so called, because <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCLAMATION">proclamation</a> being made of this event to the people, they went to salute their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> during the anacleria, and to congratulate him upon his new <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>.

ANACLETICUM

Pages 182-182

in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> art of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, a particular blast of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRUMPET">trumpet</a>, whereby the fearful and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">flying</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> were rallied, and recalled to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a>.

ANACLINOPALE

Pages 182-182

Ανακλινοπάλη, in antiquity, a kind of wrestling, wherein the champions threw themselves voluntarily on the ground, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a> by pinching, biting, scratching, and other methods of offence. The Anaclinopale was contradistinguished from the Orthapale, wherein the champions stood erect. In the Anaclinopale, the weaker combatants sometimes gained the victory.

ANACLINTERIA

Pages 182-182

in antiquity, a kind of pillows on the dining <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a>, whereon the guests used to lean. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> tricliniary beds had four pillows, one at the head, another at the feet, a third at the back, and a fourth at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>. That on which the head lay, was properly called by the Greeks ανακλινόνυξ <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> ανακλινός; by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> fulcrum, sometimes pluteus.

ANACOLLEMA

Pages 182-182

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of astringent powders, applied by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> to the head, to prevent delusions on the eyes.

ANACONDIO

Pages 182-182

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, is a name given in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of Ceylon to a very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and terrible snake, which often devours the unfortunate traveller alive, and is itself accounted excellent and delicious fare. It is probably the Boa Constrictor.

ANACREON

Pages 182-183

a Greek poet, born at Teos, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IONIA">Ionia</a>, flourished about 532 years before the Christian era. Polycrates, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAMOS">Samos</a>, invited him to his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, and made him share with him in his business and his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>. He had a delicate <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a>, as may be judged from the inexpressible beauties and graces that shine in his works: but he was fond of pleasure, was of an amorous disposition, and addicted to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRUNKENNESS">drunkenness</a>: yet, notwithstanding his debaucheries, he lived to the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 85; when, we are told, he was choked by a grapestone which stuck in his throat as he was regaling on some new wine. There is but a small <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of Anacreon's works that remain: for, besides his odes and epigrams, he composed elegies, hymns, and iambics. His poems which are extant were rescued from oblivion by Henry Stephens, and are universally admired. The verses of Anacreon are sweeter, says Scaliger, than <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>. His <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> excellence, says Madame Dacier, lay in imitating <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, and in following reason; so that he presented to the mind no images but what were noble and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a>. The odes of Anacreon, says Rapin, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIN">pin</a>; are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, beauties, and perpetual graces; it is familiar to him to write what is natural, and to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, he having an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> so delicate, so easy and graceful, that among all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> there is nothing comparable to the method he took, nor to that kind of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> he followed. He flows soft and easy, every where diffusing the joy and indolence of his mind through his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>, and tuning his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HARP">harp</a> to the smooth and pleasant temper of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>. But none has given a juster character of his writings than the God of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">Love</a>, as taught to speak by Mr Cowley: All thy verse is softer far Than the downy feathers are Of my wings, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> of my arrows, Of my mother's doves and sparrows: Graceful, cleanly, smooth, or round, All with Venus' girdle bound.

ANACREONTIC VERSE

Pages 183-183

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>, so called from its being much used by the poet Anacreon. It consists of three feet and a half, usually spondees and iambuses, and sometimes anapests: Such is that of Horace, Lydia, die per omnes.

ANACRISIS

Pages 183-183

among civilians, an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVESTIGATION">investigation</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, interrogation of witnesses, and inquiry made into any fact, especially by torture.

ANACROSIS

Pages 183-183

in antiquity, denotes a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the Pythian song, wherein the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a> and Python is described.—The anacrosis was the first part, and contained the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> to the fight. ANACYCLUS. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. ANADAVADÆA, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a>, a barbarous name of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALAUDA">alauda</a>. See ALAUDA, Ornithology Index.

ANADEMA

Pages 183-183

among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, denotes an ornament of the head, wherewith victors at the sacred games had their <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a> bound.

ANADIPLOSIS

Pages 183-183

in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">Rhetoric</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">Poetry</a>, a repetition of the last word of a line, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> clause of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a>, in the beginning of the next: thus, Pierides, vos hæc faciétis maxima Gallo: Galla, cujus amor, &c. Et matutinis acrecula vocibus instat, Vocibus instat, et assiduas jacit ore querelas.

ANADROMUS

Pages 183-183

among ichthyologists, a name given to such fishes as go from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> to the fresh <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> at stated seasons, and return back again; such as the salmon, &c. See SALMO.

ANADUOMENE VENUS

Pages 183-183

in the Grecian <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">Mythology</a>, answered to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a> Venus in the Roman, and was the appellation given to one of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> deities of the sea. The most celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> in all antiquity was that of this <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APELLES">Apelles</a>; and the famous Venus of Medicis is a Sea Venus. ANÆDEIA, in antiquity, a denomination given to a silver stool placed in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AREOPAGUS">Areopagus</a>, on which the defendant, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> person accused, was seated for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a>. The word is Greek, ἀναιδεία, which imports imprudence; but according to Junius's correction, it should rather be ἀναιδεία, q. d. innocence. The plaintiff or accuser was placed on an opposite stool called ἅρβης, or injury; here he proposed three questions to the party accused, to which positive answers were to be given. The first, Are you guilty of this fact? The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, How did you commit the fact? The third, Who were your accomplices? ANÆSTHESIA, signifies a privation of the senses.

ANAGNIA

Pages 183-183

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of Latium, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the Hernici; which, after a faint resistance, submitting to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, was admitted to the freedom of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, yet without the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of suffrage, (Livy). It was afterwards a colony of Drusus Caesar, and walled round, and its territory assigned to the veterans, (Frontinus). Here Antony married Cleopatra, and divorced <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OCTAVIA">Octavia</a>. Now Anagni, 36 miles to the east of Rome. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 13. 45. N. Lat. 42. 48.

ANAGNOSTA

Pages 183-183
or ANAGNOSTES, in antiquity, a kind of literary servant, retained in the families of persons of distinction, whose chief business was to read to them during meals, or at any other time when they were at leisure. Cornelius Nepos relates of Atticus, that he had always an anagnostes at his meals. He never supped without reading; so that the minds of his guests were no less agreeably entertained than their appetites. The same custom, Eginhard observes, was kept up by Charlemagne, who at table had the histories and acts of ancient kings read to him. This custom seems to have been a relick of that of the ancient Greeks, who had the praises of great men and heroes sung to them while at table. The ancient monks and clergy kept up the like usage, as we are informed by St Augustin.*

ANAGOGICAL

Pages 183-183

signifies mysterious, transporting; and is used to express whatever elevates the mind, not only to the knowledge of divine things, but of divine things in the next <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. This word is seldom used, but with regard to the different senses of the Scripture. The anagogical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> is, when the sacred text is explained with regard to eternal life, the point which <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> should have in view: for example, the rest of the Sabbath, in the anagogical sense, signifies the repose of everlasting <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a>.

ANAGOGY

Pages 183-183

in a more particular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, denotes the application of the types and allegories of the Old <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a> to subjects of the New; thus called, because the veil being here drawn, what before was hidden is exposed to open sight.

ANAGRAM

Pages 183-184

in matters of literature, a transposition of the letters of some name, whereby a new word is formed, either to the advantage <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> disadvantage of the person or thing to which the name belongs. Thus the anagram of Galenus in angelus; that of Logica, caligo; that of Alstedius, sedulitas; that of Lorraine is alerion, on which account it was that the family of Lorraine took alerions for their armoury.—Calvin, in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of his Institutions, printed at Strasburgh in 1539, calls himself Alcuinus, which is the anagram of Calvinus, and the name of an eminently learned person in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLEMAGNE">Charlemagne</a>, who contributed greatly to the restoration of learning in that <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. Those who adhere strictly to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-DEFINITION">definition</a> of an anagram, take no other <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> than that of omitting or retaining the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> H at <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>; whereas others make no scruple to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> E for AE, V for W, S for Z, and C for K: and vice versa. Besides anagrams formed as above, we meet with another kind in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> writers, made by dividing a single word into several; thus, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SUS">sus</a> tinea mus, are formed out of the word sustineamus. Anagrams are sometimes also made out of several words: such as that on the question put by Pilate to our Saviour, Quid est veritas? whereof we have this admirable anagram, viz. Est vir qui adeat. The Cabbalists among the Jews are professed anagrammatists; the third <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of their art, which they call themur, i.e. "changing," being nothing but the art of making anagrams, or finding hidden and mystical meanings in names; which they do by changing, transposing, and differently combining the letters of those names. Thus, of נֹחַ the letters of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOAH">Noah</a>'s name, they make נָחַר <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">grace</a>; of מְשֶׁה the Messiah, they make נֵבוֹ he shall rejoice.

ANAGRAMMATIST

Pages 184-184

a maker <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> composer of anagrams. Thomas Billon, a Provencal, was a celebrated anagrammatist, and retained by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIII. with a pension of 1200 livres, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of anagrammatist to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>.

ANAGROS

Pages 184-184

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">Commerce</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> for grain used in some cities in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, particularly at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEVILLE">Seville</a>; 45 anagros equal about 10½ <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>.

ANAGYRIS

Pages 184-184
or ANAGYRUS, in Ancient Geography, the name of a place in Attica, of the tribe Erechtheis, where a fetid plant, called Anagyris, probably the same with the foregoing, grew in great plenty, (Dioscorides, Pliny, Stephanus); and the more it was handled, the stronger it smelled; hence commovere anagyrim or (anagyrum), is to bring a misfortune on one's self, (Aristophanes).

ANAK

Pages 184-184

the father of the Anakims, was the son of Arba, who gave his name to Kirjath-arba, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HEBRON">Hebron</a>, (Josh. xiv. 15.). Anak had three sons, Sheshai, Ahiman, and Talmai, (chap. xv. 14. and Numb. xiii. 22.), who, as well as their father, were giants, and who, with their posterity, all terrible for their fierceness and extraordinary stature, were called the Anakims; in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> of whom the Hebrews, who were sent to view the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANAAN">Canaan</a>, reported that they were but as grasshoppers, Numb. xiii. ult. Caleb, assisted by the tribe of Judah, took Kirjath-arba, and destroyed the Anakims (Judges i. 20. and Josh. xv. 14.) in the year of the world 2559.

ANALECTA

Pages 184-184

Analects, in a literary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, is used to denote a collection of small pieces; as, essays, remarks, &c.

ANALEMMA

Pages 184-184

denotes likewise an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> wood, upon which this kind of projection is drawn, with a horizon or cursor fitted to it, wherein the solstitial colure, and all circles <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to it, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be concentric circles; all circles oblique to the eye will be ellipses; and all circles whose planes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through the eye, will be <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of this instrument is to show the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> astronomical problems: which it will do, though not very exactly, unless it be very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>.

ANALOGY

Pages 184-185

in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">Philosophy</a>, a certain relation and agreement between two <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> more things, which in other respects are entirely different. There is likewise an analogy between things that have some conformity or resemblance to one another; for example, between animals and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>; but the analogy is still stronger between two different <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of certain animals. Analogy enters much into all our reasoning, and serves to explain and illustrate. A <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of our philosophy, indeed, has no other foundation than analogy. It is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> to mankind to judge of things less known, by some similitude, real or imaginary, between them and things more familiar or better known. And where the things compared have really a great similitude in their <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, when there is reason to think that they are subject to the same laws, there may be a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> in conclusions drawn from analogy. Thus we may observe a very great similitude between this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> which we inhabit, and the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SATURN">Saturn</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARS">Mars</a>, Venus, and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a>. They all revolve round the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, as the earth does, although at different distances, and in different periods. They borrow all their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> from the sun, as the earth does. Several of them are known to revolve round their axis like the earth, and, by that means, must have a like succession of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> and night. Some of them have moons, that serve to give them light in the absence of the sun, as our <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a> does to us. They are all, in their motions, subject to the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GRAVITATION">gravitation</a> as the earth is. From all this similitude, it is not unreasonable to think, that those planets may, like our earth, be the habitation of various orders of living creatures. There is some probability in this conclusion from analogy. But it ought to be observed, that, as this kind of reasoning Analogy reasoning can afford only probable <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> at best; so, unless great caution be used, we are apt to be led into <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ERROR">error</a> by it. To give an instance of this: Anatomists, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> ages, seldom dissected <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> bodies; but very often the bodies of those <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUADRUPEDS">quadrupeds</a> whose internal structure was thought to approach nearest to that of the human body. <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">Modern</a> anatomists have discovered many mistakes the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> were led into, by their conceiving a greater similitude between the structure of men and of some beasts than there is in reality. Perhaps no author has made a more <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> and a more happy <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of this <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of reasoning, than Bishop <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTLER">Butler</a> in his Analogy of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">Religion</a>, Natural and Revealed, to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">Constitution</a> and Course of Nature. In that excellent <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, the author does not ground any of the truths of religion upon analogy, as their proper evidence. He only makes use of analogy to answer objections against them. When objections are made against the truths of religion, which may be made with equal strength against what we know to be true in the course of nature, such objections can have no <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>. Analogical reasoning, therefore, may be of excellent use in answering objections against truths which have other evidence. It may likewise give a greater or a less degree of probability in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> where we can find no other evidence. But all arguments drawn from analogy are still the weaker, the greater disparity there is between the things compared; and therefore must be weakest of all when we compare body with mind, because there are no two things in nature more unlike. There is no subject in which men have always been so prone to form their notions by analogies of this kind, as in what relates to the mind. We form an early acquaintance with material things by means of our senses, and are bred up in a constant familiarity with them. Hence we are apt to <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> all things by them; and to ascribe to things most remote from <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> the qualities that belong to material things. It is for this reason that mankind have, in all ages, been so prone to conceive the mind itself to be some subtle kind of matter; that they have been disposed to ascribe human <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> and human organs not only to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGELS">angels</a>, but even to the Deity. To illustrate more fully that analogical reasoning from a supposed similitude of mind to body, which appears to be the most fruitful source of error with regard to the operations of our minds, the following instance may be given. When a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> is urged by contrary motives, those on one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> inciting him to do some <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, those on the other to forbear it; he deliberates about it, and at last resolves to do it, or not to do it. The contrary motives are here compared to the weights in the opposite scales of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a>; and there is not perhaps any instance that can be named of a more striking analogy between body and mind. Hence the phrases of weighing motives, of deliberating upon actions, are <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> to all languages. From this analogy, some philosophers draw very important conclusions. They say, that as the balance cannot incline to one side more than the other when the opposite weights are equal, so a man cannot possibly determine himself <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the motives on both <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> are equal; and as the balance must necessarily turn to that side which has most weight, so the man must necessarily be determined to that hand where the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a> is strongest. And on this foundation some of the schoolmen maintained, that if a hungry ass were placed between two bundles of hay equally inviting, the beast must stand still and starve to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, being unable to turn to either, because there are equal motives to both. This is an instance of that analogical reasoning, which, it is conceived, ought never to be trusted; for the analogy between a balance and a man deliberating, though one of the strongest that can be found between matter and mind, is too weak to support any argument. A piece of dead inactive matter, and an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> intelligent being, are things very unlike; and because the one would remain at rest in a certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, it does not follow that the other would be inactive in a case somewhat similar. The argument is no better than this, that because a dead animal moves only as it is pushed, and if pushed with equal force in contrary directions, must remain at rest; therefore the same thing must happen to a living animal: for surely the similitude between a dead animal and a living is as great as that between a balance and a man.

ANALYTIC

Pages 187-187
or **ANALYTICAL**, something that belongs to, or partakes of, the nature of analysis.—Thus we say, an analytical demonstration, analytical process, analytical table or scheme, analytical method of investigation, &c. The analytic method stands opposed to the synthetic. In ef="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural philosophy, as in mathematics, the investigation of difficult things by the analytic method ought to precede the method of composition. This analysis consists in making experiments and observations, and in drawing general conclusions therefrom by induction; and admitting of no objections against the conclusions, but such as are drawn from experiments, and other certain truths: and though the reasoning from experiments and observations by induction be no demonstration of general conclusions, yet it is the best method of reasoning which the nature of things admits of; and may be esteemed so much the stronger, as the induction is more general; and, if no exception occur from phenomena, the conclusion may be pronounced general. By this way of analysis, we may proceed from compounds to their ingredients; from motions to the forces producing them; and in general from effects to their causes, and from particular causes to more general ones, until we arrive at those which are the most general. This is the analytic method, according to the illustrious Newton. The synthetic method consists in assuming the causes discovered and received as principles: and by them explaining the phenomena proceeding from them, and proving the explanation. See **SYNTHESIS**.

ANALYTICS

Pages 187-187

(*Analytica*), the science and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALYSIS">analysis</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> advantage of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a> above the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> is in point of analytics. Pappus, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREFACE">preface</a> to his seventh book of Mathematical Collections, enumerates the authors on the ancient analytics; being Euclid, in his *<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATA">Data</a>* and *Porismata*; Apollonius, *de Sectione Rationis*, and in his *Conics*; Aristaenus, *de Locis Solidis*; and Eratosthenes, *de Meditis Proportionalibus*. But the ancient analytics were very different from the modern. To the modern analytics principally belongs <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALGEBRA">algebra</a>; an historical account of which, with the several authors thereon, see under the article **ALGEBRA**.

ANAMABOA

Pages 187-187

a populous town in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Fantin, in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUINEA">Guinea</a>. The natives are generally <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> cheats, and must be carefully looked after in dealing with them, and their <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> well examined, for it is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> adulterated. It lies under the cannon of the English castle. The landing is pretty difficult on account of the rocks; and therefore those that come here to trade are forced to go ashore in canoes. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> here is very proper to make bricks: the oysters, when burnt, afford good lime; and there is <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> in great abundance; so that here are all the materials for <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> at Anamaboa is full of hills, beginning at a good distance from the town, and affording a very pleasant prospect. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> corn and palm-wine are in great plenty. They have a green fruit called *papas*, as big as a small melon, and which has a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> like <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAULIFLOWER">cauliflower</a>. Anamaboa is much frequented by the English ships and others for corn and slaves, which last are sometimes to be had in great numbers. The English fort is built on the foundation of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> old <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, which subsisted entire in 1679. It is a large edifice, flanked by two towers, and fortified towards the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> with two bastions: the whole of brick and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> cemented with lime. It stands upon a rock at the distance of 30 paces from the sea. It is mounted with 12 pieces of cannon and 12 paterooses; and defended by a garrison of 12 whites and 18 blacks, under the command of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACTOR">factor</a>. The natives treat the garrison of this fort with great insolence, insomuch as often to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLOCK">block</a> them up, and frequently, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they dislike the governor, send him off in a canoe to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">Coast</a> with marks of the utmost contempt. Far from being able to oppose them, the English are glad to obtain their favour with presents. In 1701, they declared <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> against the English; and having assembled in a tumultuous manner before the fort, they set fire to the exterior buildings, and went on with their outrages, till they were dispersed by a discharge of the cannon from the batteries. The night following the English took their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a>, by setting fire to the town of Anamaboa: and thus hostilities <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> for 20 days, till at last the natives were obliged to sue for peace. This fort was abandoned in 1733; but has been resumed by the English, who have continued in it ever since.

ANAMELECH

Pages 187-187

an idol of the Sepharvaites, who are said in Scripture to have burned their children in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of Adrammelech and Anamelech.—These idols probably signified the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a>. Some of the rabbins represent Anamelech under the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MULE">mule</a>, others under that of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUAIL">quail</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> pheasant.

ANAMIM

Pages 187-187

the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> son of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MIZRAIM">Mizraim</a> (Gen. x. 14.) Ananim, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we may <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> the paraphrast <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JONATHAN">Jonathan</a> the son of Uzziel, peopled the Mareotic; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENTAPOLIS">Pentapolis</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CYRENE">Cyrene</a>, according to the paraphrast of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>. Bocchart is of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that these Anamins were the people that dwelt in the parts adjacent to the temple of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMMON">Ammon</a>, and in the Nasamotitis. Calmet thinks the Amanians and Garamantins to be descended from Ananim.

ANAMORPHOSIS

Pages 187-187

in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol8.html#article-PERSPECTIVE">perspective</a> drawings, is a deformed <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> distorted <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTRAIT">portrait</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, generally confused and unintelligible to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> unassisted view; but when seen at a certain distance and height, or as reflected from a plain or curved mirror, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> appear regular and in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> proportion. See **<a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPTICS">OPTICS</a>** (the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>), and **PERSPECTIVE**.

ANANAS

Pages 187-187

in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, the trivial name of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of bromelia. See **BROMELIA**, Botany <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ANANCITIS

Pages 187-187

in antiquity, a kind of figured <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, otherwise called *synochitis*, celebrated for its magical virtue of raising the shadows of the infernal gods.

ANANIAS

Pages 187-187

a Saducee, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> of the Jews, who put to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> St James the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> of our <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>, and was deposed by Agrippa.

ANANISABTA

Pages 187-187
or **ANANISAPTA**, a magical word frequently found inscribed on coins and other amulets, supposed to have a virtue of preserving the wearer from the plague. **ANAPÆST**, in ancient poetry, a foot consisting of two short syllables and one long: Such is the word *scopulos*. It is just the reverse of the dactyl. **ANAPÆSTIC VERSES**, those consisting wholly or chiefly of anapests.

ANAPHAE

Pages 187-188

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> spontaneously emerging out of the Cretan <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, near Thera (Pliny, Strabo); now called Nansio. Its name is from the sudden appearance of the new <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a> to the Argonauts in a storm (Apollonius). Anaphaeus, an epithet of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a>, who was worshipped there. Anaphæi, the people.

ANAPHORA

Pages 188-188

among physicians, the throwing off purulent <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> by the mouth.

ANAPHRODISIA

Pages 188-188

signifies <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMPOTENCE">impotence</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> want of power to procreate. See IMPOTENCE.

ANAPLORETICS

Pages 188-188

medicines that promote the growth <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANULATION">granulation</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> in wounds, ulcers, &c.

ANARCHI

Pages 188-188

(Αναρχοι), in antiquity, a name given by the Athenians to four supernumerary days in their year, during which they had no magistrates. The Attic year was divided into 10 parts, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of tribes, to whom the presidency of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> fell by turns. Each <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> consisted of 35 days; what remained after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPIRATION">expiration</a> of these, to make the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUNAR">lunar</a> year complete, which according to their computation consisted of 354 days, were employed in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREATION">creation</a> of magistrates, and called αναρχοι ἀρχαι, and αναρχοι ἀρχαι.

ANARCHY

Pages 188-188

the want of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> in a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, where no supreme authority is lodged either in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other rulers; but the people live at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, and all things are in confusion. The word is derived from the Greek privative α and αξιον, command, principality. Anarchy is supposed to have reigned after the deluge, before the foundation of monarchies. We still find it to obtain in several parts, particularly of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>. Anarchy is also applied to certain troublesome and disorderly periods, even in governments otherwise regular. In England, the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Cromwell and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a>'s restoration is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> represented as an anarchy. Every <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> produced a new scheme or form of government. Enthusiasts talked of nothing but annulling all the laws, abolishing all writings, records, and registers, and bringing all men to the primitive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a>. No <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> nation was more subject to anarchies than <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>; where every <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> between the death of one king and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> of another was a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> disorder, so that it was a proverb among that people, Poland is governed by confusion. The Jewish <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> presents numerous instances of anarchies in that state, usually denoted by this phrase, that in those days there was no king in Israel, but every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> did that which was <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> in his own eyes; which is a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> of an anarchy. ANARRHICAS. See <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">ICHTHYOLOGY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ANARROPIA

Pages 188-188

among physicians, a tendency of the humours to the head <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> superior parts.

ANAS

Pages 188-188

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a river of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> rising in the territory of Laminium in the Hither Spain, and now spreading into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>, again restraining its waters, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a>, burrowing itself entirely in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, is pleased often to reappear. It pours into the Atlantic (Pliny). Now Guadiana, rising in the south-east of New Castile, in a district <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called Campo de Montiel, not far from the mountain Cousuegra, from the lakes called las Logunas de Guadiana, and then it is called Rio Roydera; and, after a course of six leagues, burying itself in the earth for a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a>, it then rises up again from three lakes, called los Ojos de Guadiana, near the village Villa Harta, five leagues to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALATRAVA">Calatrava</a>, and directs its course westward through New Castile, by Medelin, Merida, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BADAJOZ">Badajoz</a>, where it begins to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEND">bend</a> its course southwards, between <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANDALUSIA">Andalusia</a>, falling into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CADIZ">Cadiz</a> near <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AYAMONTE">Ayamonte</a>. ANAS. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">ORNITHOLOGY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ANASARCA

Pages 188-188

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DROPSY">dropsy</a>. See MEDICINE <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. ANASSER. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> Index.

ANASSUS

Pages 188-188
or ANAXUS, in Ancient Geography, a river in the territory of Venice, (Pliny); now the Piave, which rising from the mountains of Tyrol, not far from the borders of Carinthia, runs from north to south, through the territories of Cadorna, Belluno, Feltre, and, after running from west to east, through Trevigi, falls into the Adriatic, 13 miles to the south-east of Venice. ANASTATICA. See BOTANY Index.

ANASTASIS

Pages 188-190

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> among <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> physicians, for a rising up to go to stool. It also signifies the passage of any humour, when expelled from one <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a>, and obliged to remove to another. ANASTASIUS I., <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> of the east, succeeded Zeno in the year 491, and was inaugurated that same year on April the 11th. The Manicheans and Arias were greatly in hopes of being supported by the new emperor; the former because his mother was their friend, and favoured their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a>; the latter because the emperor's uncle was of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> Anastasius did not persecute them (as we do not find he ever did), yet it does not appear that he supported either of these sects. But in order to maintain the peace of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, upon which the tranquillity of the state very much depends, he declared, that such <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other clergymen who should disturb the public tranquillity, by maintaining with too much <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> either side of the question for or against the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHALCEDON">Chalcedon</a>, should be deprived of their benefices. Accordingly, the disputes concerning Eutychianism running to a very <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> height, and Euphemius being deeply concerned in them, the emperor expelled him from his see, and chose Macedonius in his stead. The hatred which the different parties entertained against one another occasioned often such tumults and seditions at Constantinople as threatened the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of the emperor himself; who, to keep the people in awe, ordered that the governor of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> should be present at all church assemblies and public processions. This was so much the more necessary, because these tumults were chiefly occasioned by a kind of doxology or short <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HYMN">hymn</a> which used to be sung at divine <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. This doxology consisted only of the following words, ἀγαπεῖς ὁ Θεός, ἀγαπεῖς ἐκεῖνος, ἀγαπεῖς ἄλλους, that is, "Holy God, holy the powerful, holy the immortal;" for which reason it was Anastasius, called Ἅγιος Ἅγιοις, Trisagius, "three times holy;" because the word holy was therein three times repeated. The orthodox used to sing that hymn without any addition, or by adding only to it, Ἡ τριάς ἡ ἁγίας, ἐχεῖν ἡμῖν, i.e. "Holy Trinity, have mercy upon us?" But <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> the Puller, bishop of Antioch, pretended to add these words to it, viz. ὁ ἀναστατωτὸς ἡμῶν, i.e. "who hast been crucified for us;" and as it was supposed that the first holy related to the Father, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> to the Son, the third to the Holy Ghost, the adding these words, who hast been crucified for us, seemed to insinuate that the whole consubstantial Trinity had suffered; for which reason the orthodox were resolved not to admit this addition. Anastasius desiring to have these fatal words added to that hymn whenever it should be sung at Constantinople, this occasioned a terrible sedition in the city, as though the very fundamentals of Christianity had been overthrown. Macedonius and his clergy are said to have raised that sedition, which came to such a height, that the emperor himself was obliged to come, without his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> on his head, and in a very humble manner, to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CIRCUS">circus</a>, where he declared to the people that he was very willing to quit the imperial throne; but he told them at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, that they could not all enjoy the sovereign power, which does not admit of a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PARTNERSHIP">partnership</a>: and that one person still must govern them if he resigned the crown. This discourse had such a power over the raging multitude, that, as if they had been divinely inspired, they immediately requested the emperor to take up his crown, promising that they would be quiet and obedient for the future. Anastasius is by the Popish writers represented as a great persecutor of the orthodox, because he banished and deprived Euphemius and Macedonius; but they should prove that these two prelates had been unjustly banished, which is a very hard task. As to his civil <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, it is confessed that at the beginning of his reign he showed himself a very good <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>: he eased the people of a very heavy tax called Chrysargyrum, under which they had groaned for a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> time; he prohibited the fighting with wild beasts; he raised several buildings; and avoided being involved in dangerous wars as much as lay in his power. Anastasius reigned 27 years three months and three days, or, according to F. Pagi, wanting three days; and died <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> the 10th, A.C. 518, in the 88th year of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. Anastasius II., whose proper name was Artemius, was in the year 713 elevated to the throne of Constantinople, from the low station of a secretary, by the free <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> and Roman people. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> talents, improved by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> and daily exertion, enabled him to manage with great <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a> the affairs of the empire during the time that he was secretary to his predecessor Philippicus. The Saracens had made inroads upon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASIA_MINOR"><a class="</a>xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINOR">Minor</a>, in the beginning of his reign; but he sent a strong <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> to the frontiers of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a> for its protection, under the command of Leo the Isaurian, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of great <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>. These enemies of the empire also meditated the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of taking Constantinople; but the vigilance of Anastasius defeated their purpose, by providing a formidable naval force, repairing and strengthening the walls of the city, and by forcing all the inhabitants either to provide themselves with <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> for three years, or instantly to depart from the city. Disappointed in their design, the Anastasius' enemy's fleet sailed to Phoenicia, and the imperial fleet assembled at <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RHODES">Rhodes</a> to watch the motions of the enemy. But the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> of the emperor received a severe check from the conduct of the sailors, who raised a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUTINY">mutiny</a>, and slew their <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a> for no other cause but his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> endeavours to maintain proper <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> in the fleet. Justly dreading severe <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>, the seamen raised the standard of rebellion, declared Anastasius unworthy to reign, and conferred the purple upon one Theodosius, a person of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> birth. Informed of this sedition, Anastasius fled from his tottering throne to Nice. The new emperor hastened to besiege Constantinople, which, after a feeble <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of six months, he reduced to his subjection. The late emperor being assured of his life, abandoned his claim to the crown, assumed the character of a monk, and was banished to Thessalonica, having worn the purple only during the space of two years. Having, however, prevailed upon the Bulgarians to espouse his cause, he laid aside the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> of the monk for that of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WARRIOR">warrior</a>, and, in the year 719, in the time of the emperor Leo, he resumed his claim to the throne. A numerous army of these barbarians hastened to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>; but, being unable to reduce it, they delivered up the unhappy Anastasius to the emperor, who put him to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> along with his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> associates. (Anc. Un. Hist.) Anastasius, surnamed Bibliothecarius, a Roman <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABBOT">abbot</a>, library-keeper of the Vatican, and one of the most learned men of the ninth century, assisted in 869 at the fourth general council, the acts and canons of which he translated from the Greek into Latin. He also composed the lives of several popes, and other works; the best edition of which is that of the Vatican. Anastatika, the rose of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERICHO">Jericho</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANASTOMOSIS">Anastomosis</a>, in Anatomy, the opening of the mouths of vessels, in order to discharge their contained <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a>. It is likewise used for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> of two vessels at their extremities; as the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INOCULATION">inoculation</a> of a vein with a vein, of an artery with an artery, or of an artery with a vein. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANASTOMATICS">Anastomatics</a>, medicines supposed to have the power of opening the mouths of the vessels, and promoting the circulation; such as deobstruent, cathartic, and sudorific medicines. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANASTROPHE">Anastrophe</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">Rhetoric</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>, denote the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVERSION">inversion</a> of the natural order of the words; such is, saxa per et scopulos, for per saxa et scopulos. Anasus, or Ansis, in Ancient <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, now the Ens, a river of Germany, which rises on the borders of the territory of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALZBURG">Salzburg</a>; then separating Upper Stiria from Upper <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>, and washing the town of Ens, falls, at the distance of a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a> below it, into the Danube, in a course from south to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANATHEMA">Anathema</a>, among <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> writers, imports whatever is set apart, separated, or divided; but is most usually meant to express the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> off a person from the privileges of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a> with the faithful. The anathema differs from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXCOMMUNICATION">excommunication</a> in the circumstances of being attended with curses and execrations. It was practised in the primitive church against notorious offenders; and the form of that pronounced Anathema, pronounced by Synecius against one Andronicus is as follows: "Let no church of God be open to Andronicus, but let every sanctuary be shut against him. I admonish both private men and magistrates to receive him neither under their <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> nor to their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>; and priests more especially, that they neither <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONVERSE">converse</a> with him living, nor attend his funeral when dead." Several councils also have pronounced anathemas against such as they thought corrupted the purity of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>; and their decisions have been conceived in the following form: *St quis dixerit, &c. anathema sit.* There are two kinds of anathemas, the one judiciary and the other abjuratory. The former can only be denounced by a council, a pope, or a bishop; the latter makes a part of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> of abjuration, the convert being obliged to anathematize the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERESY">heresy</a> he abjures. Anathema, in heathen antiquity, was an offering or present made to some deity, and hung up in the temple. Whenever a person left off his employment, it was usual to dedicate the tools to the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> deity of the trade. Persons too who had escaped from imminent danger, as shipwreck and the like, or had met with any other remarkable instance of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a>, seldom failed to testify their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a> by some present of this kind.

ANATOCISM

Pages 190-190

Anatocismus, an usurious <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a>, wherein the interests arising from the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> sum are added to the principal itself, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> exacted upon the whole. The word is originally Greek, but used by Cicero in Latin; whence it has descended into most other languages. It comes from the preposition ἀνά, which in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> signifies repetition <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> duplication, and ὀφείλειν, usury. Anatocism is what we properly call interest upon interest, or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> interest. This is the worst kind of usury, and has been severely condemned by the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>, as well as by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> laws of most other countries. See INTEREST. ANATOLIA. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATOLIA">NATOLIA</a>.

Every point of their body seems independently to attract nourishment, and independently to possess the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSATION">sensation</a>; hence the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRRITABILITY">irritability</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> power of vitality and of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-REPRODUCTION">reproduction</a>, which we find in these animals. For propagation, they need only be cut in pieces, and do not require a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEX">sex</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> organs of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a> to preserve the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>: They may be divided into two orders; the first of which, as <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> a resemblance to both animals and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, may be properly called zoophytes; and the last, as resembling both plants and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, may be called lithophytes. Into the cartilages of the 5th, 6th, and 7th ribs, and the edge of the cartilago ensiformis (u). Use. To compress the fore part of the abdomen, and to bend the trunk forwards. 5. Pyramidalis (v). Origin. From the anterior and upper part of the pubis. Insertion. Into the linea alba and inner edge of the rectus, commonly about two inches above the pubis. Use. To assist the lower portion of the rectus. Muscles at the fore part of the thorax, 1. Pectoralis major. Origin. From the cartilaginous ends of the 5th and 6th ribs; the sternum, and anterior part of the clavicle. Insertion. Into the upper and inner part of the os humeri (w). Use. To draw the arm forwards, or obliquely forwards. 2. Subclavius. Origin. From the cartilage of the first rib. Insertion. Into the under surface of the clavicle. Use. To move the clavicle forwards and downwards, and to assist in raising the first rib. 3. Pectoralis minor (x). Origin. From the upper edges of the 3d, 4th, and 5th ribs. Insertion. Into the coracoid process of the scapula. Use. To move the scapula forwards and downwards, or to elevate the ribs. 4. Serratus magnus. Origin. From the eight superior ribs. Insertion. Into the basis of the scapula. Use. To bring the scapula forwards. That concur in forming the thorax, 1. Diaphragma (y). Origin. From the transverse processes of the last cervical, and the eleven upper dorsal vertebrae. Insertion. Into the upper side of each rib, near its tuberosity. Use. To move the ribs upwards and outwards. 2. Levatores costarum. Origin. From the lower edge of each upper rib. Insertion. Into the superior edge of each lower rib. Use. To elevate the ribs. 3. Intercostales externi. Origin. From the lower edge of each upper rib. Insertion. Into the superior edge of each lower rib. Use. To elevate the ribs. 4. Intercostales interni (a). Origin. From the lower edge of each upper rib. Insertion. Into the superior edge of each lower rib. Use. To elevate the ribs. 5. Sterno-costales. (u) The fibres of the rectus are generally divided by three tendinous intersections. The two upper thirds of this muscle, passing between the tendinous layers of the obliquus internus, are enclosed as it were in a sheath: but at its lower part we find it immediately contiguous to the peritoneum, the inferior portion of the tendon of the transversalis passing over the rectus, and adhering to the interior layer of the obliquus internus. (v) This muscle is sometimes wanting. (w) The fibres of this muscle pass towards the axilla in a folding manner, and with those of the latissimus dorsi form the arm-pit. (x) This and some other muscles derive their name of serratus, from their arising by a number of tendinous or fleshy digitations, resembling the teeth of a saw (terra). (y) For a description of the diaphragm, see Chap. IV. Sect. IV. (a) The origin, insertion, and use of the internal intercostals, are similar to those of the external. The reader, however, will be pleased to observe, that the intercostales externi occupy the spaces between the ribs only from the spine to their cartilages; from thence to the sternum, there being only a thin membrane, which is spread over the intercostales interni; and that the latter, on the contrary, extend only from the sternum to the angles of each rib. The fibres of the external muscles run obliquely forwards; those of the internal obliquely backwards. This difference in the direction of their fibres induced Galen to suppose that they were intended for different uses; that the external intercostals, for instance, serve to elevate, and the internal ones to depress the ribs. Fallopius seems to have been the first who ventured to dispute the truth of this doctrine, which has since been revived by Boyle. Muscles at the back part of the neck and trunk, 1. Trapezius (c), or cucullaris. From the middle of os occipitis, and the spinous processes of the two inferior cervical, and of all the dorsal vertebrae. Into the posterior half of the clavicle, part of the acromion, and the spine of the scapula. To move the scapula. 2. Rhomboideus (E). From the spinous processes of the three lowermost cervical, and of all the dorsal vertebrae. Into the basis of the scapula. To move the scapula upwards and backwards. 3. Latissimus dorsi. From part of the spine of the os ilium, the spinous processes of the os sacrum and lumbar vertebrae, and of six or eight of the dorsal vertebrae; also from the four inferior false ribs near their cartilages. Into the os humeri, at the inner edge of the groove for lodging the long head of the biceps muscle. To draw the os humeri downwards and backwards, and to roll it upon its axis. 4. Serratus inferior posticus. From the spinous processes of the two lowermost dorsal, and of three of the lumbar vertebrae. Into the lower edges of the three or four lowermost ribs near their cartilages. To draw the ribs outwards, downwards, and backwards. 5. Levator scapulae. From the transverse processes of the four uppermost vertebrae colli. Into the upper angle of the scapula. To move the scapula forwards and upwards. 6. Serratus superior posticus. From the lower part of the ligamentum colli, the spinous processes of the lowermost cervical vertebra, and of the two superior dorsal vertebrae. Into the 2d, 3d, and 4th ribs. To expand the thorax. 7. Splenius Boyle, and more lately still by Hamberger, whose theoretical arguments on this subject have been clearly refuted by the experiments of Haller. (B) These consist of four, and sometimes five distinct muscles on each side. Vesalius, and after him Douglas and Albinus, consider them as forming a single muscle, which, on account of its shape, they name triangularis. Verheyen, Winiford, and Haller, more properly describe them as so many separate muscles, which, on account of their origin and insertion, they name sternocostales. (c) So named by Riolanus, from τεκτονικός, on account of its quadrilateral shape. Columbus and others give it the name of cucullaris, from its resemblance to a monk's hood. (D) The tendinous fibres of this muscle, united with those of its fellow in the nape of the neck, form what is called the ligamentum colli. (E) This muscle consists of two distinct portions, which are described as separate muscles by Albinus, under the names of rhomboideus minor and rhomboideus major. ###

anatomical writers. There are some who contend, that it is separated in the substance of the liver, from whence it passes into the gall-bladder through particular vessels. In deer, and in some other quadrupeds, as well as in several birds and fishes, there is an evident communication, by means of particular vessels, between the liver and the gall-bladder. Bianchi, Window, and others, have asserted the existence of such vessels in the human subject, and named them *hepatico-cystic ducts*; but it is certain that no such ducts exist.—In obstructions of the cystic duct, the gall-bladder has been found shrivelled and empty: so that we may consider the gall-bladder as a reservoir of hepatic bile; and that it is an established fact, that the whole of the bile contained in the gall-bladder is derived from the liver; that it passes from the hepatic or the cystic duct, and from that to the gall-bladder. The difference in the colour, consistence, and taste of the bile, is merely the consequence of stagnation and absorption. When the stomach is distended with aliment, this reservoir undergoes a certain degree of compression, and the bile passes out into the intestinal canal; and in the efforts to vomit, the gall-bladder seems to be constantly affected, and at such times discharges itself of its contents. Sometimes (c) The ancients, who were not acquainted with the real use of the liver, considered the bile as an excrementitious and useless fluid. Sometimes the bile concretes in the gall-bladder, so as to form what are called gall-stones (d). When these concretions pass into the cystic duct, they sometimes occasion exquisite pain, by distending the canal in their way to the duodenum; and by lodging in the ductus choledochus communis, and obstructing the course of the bile, this fluid will be absorbed, and by being carried back into the circulation occasion a temporary jaundice. Sect. X. Of the Spleen.
