The spleen is a soft and spongy viscus, of a bluish colour, and about five or six fingers breadth in length, and three in width, situated in the left hypochondrium, between the stomach and the false ribs. That side of it which is placed on the side of the ribs is convex; and the other, which is turned towards the stomach, is concave. The splenic artery, which is a branch from the celiac, supplies this viscus with blood, and a vein of the same name carries it back into the vena portae. Its nerves are derived from a particular plexus called the splenic, which is formed by branches of the intercostal nerve, and by the eighth pair, or par vagum. The ancients, who supposed two sorts of bile, considered the spleen as the receptacle of what they called atra bilis. Havers, who wrote professedly on the bones, determined its use to be that of secreting the synovia; and the late Mr Hewson imagined, that it concurred with the thymus and lymphatic glands of the body in forming the red globules of the blood. All those opinions seem to be equally fanciful. The want of an excretory duct has occasioned the real use of this viscus to be still doubtful. Perhaps the blood undergoes some change in it, which may assist in the preparation of the bile. This is the opinion of the generality of modern physiologists; and the great quantity of blood with which it is supplied, together with the course of its veins into the vena portae, seem to render this notion probable. Sect. XI. Of the Glandulae Renales, Kidneys, and Ureters. The glandulae renales, which were by the ancients supposed to secrete the atra bilis, and by them named caput atrabiliarum, are two flat bodies of an irregular figure, one on each side between the kidney and the aorta. In the fetus they are as large as the kidneys: but they do not increase afterwards in proportion to those parts; and in adults and old people they are generally found shrivelled, and much wasted. They have their arteries and veins. Their arteries usually arise from the splenic or the emulgent, and sometimes from the aorta; and their veins go to the neighbouring veins, or to the vena cava. Their nerves are branches of the intercostal. The use of these parts is not yet perfectly known. In the fetus the secretion of urine must be in a very small quantity, and a part of the blood may perhaps then pass through these channels, which in the adult is carried to the kidneys to supply the matter of urine. The kidneys are two in number, situated one on the right and the other on the left side in the lumbar region, between the last false rib and the os ilium, by the sides of the vertebrae. Each kidney in its figure resembles a sort of bean, which from its shape is called kidney bean. The concave part of each kidney is turned towards the aorta and vena cava ascendens. They are surrounded by a good deal of fat, and receive a coat from the peritoneum; and when this is removed, a very fine membrane is found investing their substance and the vessels which ramify through them. Each kidney has a considerable artery and vein, which are called the emulgent. The artery is a branch from the aorta, and the vein passes into the vena cava. Their nerves, which everywhere accompany the blood vessels, arise from a considerable plexus, which is derived from the intercostal. In each kidney, which in the adult is of a pretty firm texture, there are three substances to be distinguished (e). The outer part is glandular or cortical, beyond this is the vascular or tubular substance, and the inner part is papillary or membranous. It is in the cortical part of the kidney that the secretion is carried on; the urine being there received from the minute extremities of the capillary arteries, is conveyed out of this cortical substance by an infinite number of very small cylindrical canals or excretory vessels, which constitute the tubular part. These tubes, as they approach the inner substance of the kidney, gradually unite together; and thus forming larger canals, at length terminate in ten or twelve little protuberances called papillae, the orifices of which may be seen without the assistance of glasses. These papillae open into a small cavity or reservoir called the pelvis of the kidney, and formed by a distinct membranous bag which embraces the papillae. From this pelvis the urine is conveyed through a membranous canal which passes out from the hollow side of the kidney, a little below the blood-vessels, and is called ureter. The ureters are each about as large as a common writing pen. They are somewhat curved in their course from the kidneys, like the letter J, and at length terminate in the posterior and almost inferior part of the bladder, at some distance from each other. They pass into the bladder in the same manner as the ductus choledochus communis passes into the intestinum duodenum, not by a direct passage, but by an oblique course. (d) These concretions sometimes remain in the gall-bladder without causing any uneasiness. Dr Heberden relates, that a gall-stone, weighing two drachms, was found in the gall-bladder of Lord Bath, though he had never complained of the jaundice, or of any disorder which he could attribute to that cause. Med. Trans., vol. ii. (e) The kidneys in the fetus are distinctly lobulated; but in the adult they become perfectly firm, smooth, and regular. course between the two coats; so that the discharge of urine into the bladder is promoted, whilst its return is prevented. Nor does this mode of structure prevent the passage of fluids only from the bladder into the ureters, but likewise air—for air thrown into the bladder inflates it, and it continues to be distended if a ligature is passed round its neck; which seems to prove sufficiently that it cannot pass into the ureters. **Sect. XII. Of the Urinary Bladder.** The urinary bladder is a membranous and muscular bag of an oblong roundish shape, situated in the pelvis, between the os pubis and intestinum rectum in men, and between the os pubis and uterus in women. Its upper and widest part is usually called the bottom, its narrower part the neck of the bladder; the former is only covered by the peritoneum. The bladder is formed of three coats, connected together by means of cellular membrane. The external or peritoneal, is only a partial one, covering the upper and back part of the bladder. The middle, or muscular coat, is composed of irritable, and of course muscular fibres, which are most collected around the neck of the bladder, but not so as to form a distinct muscle or sphincter, as the generality of anatomists have hitherto supposed. The inner coat, though much smoother, has been said to resemble the villous tunic of the intestines, and like that is provided with a mucus, which defends it against the acrimony of the urine. It will easily be conceived, from what has been said, that the kidneys are two glandular bodies, through which a saline and excrementitious fluid called urine is constantly filtering from the mass of blood. While only a small quantity of urine is collected in the bladder, it excites no kind of uneasiness; but when a greater quantity is accumulated, so that the bladder is distended in a certain degree, it excites in us a certain sensation, which brings on as if were a voluntary contraction of the bladder to promote its discharge.—But this contraction is not effected by the muscular fibres of the bladder alone: for all the abdominal muscles contract in obedience to our will, and press downwards all the viscera of the lower belly; and these powers being united, at length overcome the resistance of the fibres surrounding the neck of the bladder, which dilates and affords a passage to the urine through the urethra. The frequency of this evacuation depends on the quantity of urine secreted; on the degree of acrimony it possesses; on the size of the bladder, and on its degree of sensibility. The urine varies much in its colour and contents. These varieties depend on age, sex, climate, diet, and other circumstances. In infants it is generally a clear watery fluid, without smell or taste. As we advance in life, it acquires more colour and smell, and becomes more impregnated with salts. In old people it becomes still more acid and fetid. In a healthy state it is nearly of a straw colour.—After being kept for some time, it deposits a tartarous matter, which is found to be composed chiefly of earth and salt, and soon incrusts the sides of the vessel in which it is contained. While this separation is taking place, appearances like minute fibres or threads of a whitish colour, may be seen in the middle of the urine, and an oily scum observed floating on its surface. So that the most common appearances of the urine are sufficient to ascertain that it is a watery substance, impregnated with earthy, saline, and oily particles. The urine is not always voided of the same colour and consistence; for these are found to depend on the proportion of its watery part to that of its other constituent principles.—Its colour and degree of fluidity seem to depend on the quantity of saline and inflammable particles contained in it: so that an increased proportion of those parts will constantly give the urine a higher colour, and add to the quantity of sediment. The variety in the appearances of the urine depends on the nature and quantity of solid and fluid aliment we take in; and it is likewise occasioned by the different state of the urinary vessels, by which we mean the channels through which it is separated from the blood, and conveyed through the pelvis into the ureters. The causes of calculous concretion in the urinary passages, are to be looked for in the natural constitution of the body, mode of life, &c. It having been observed, that after drinking any light wine or Spa water, it very soon passes off by urine, it has been supposed by some, that the urine is not altogether conveyed to the bladder by the ordinary course of circulation, but that there must certainly exist some other shorter means of communication, perhaps by certain vessels between the stomach and the bladder, or by a retrograde motion in the lymphatics. But it is certain, that if we open the belly of a dog, press out the urine from the bladder, pass a ligature round the emulsified arteries, and then sew up the abdomen, and give him even the most diuretic liquor to drink, the stomach and other channels will be distended with it, but not a drop of urine will be found to have passed into the bladder; or the same thing happens when a ligature is thrown round the two ureters. This experiment then seems to be a sufficient proof, that all the urine we evacuate is conveyed to the kidneys through the emulsified arteries, in the manner we have described.—It is true, that wine and other liquors promote a speedy evacuation of urine: but the discharge seems to be merely the effect of the stimulus they occasion; by which the bladder and urinary parts are solicited to a more copious discharge of the urine, which was before in the body, and not immediately of that which was last drank; and this increased discharge, if the supply is kept up, will continue: nor will this appear wonderful, if we consider the great capacity of the vessels that go to the kidneys; the constant supply of fresh blood that is essential to health; and the rapidity with which it is incessantly circulated through the heart to all parts of the body. **Sect. XIII. Of Digestion.** We are now proceeding to speak of digestion, which seems to be introduced in this place with propriety, after a description of the abdominal viscera, the greater part of which contribute to this function. By digestion is to be understood, the changes the aliment undergoes The mouth, of which every body has a general knowledge, is the cavity between the two jaws, formed anteriorly and laterally by the lips, teeth, and cheeks, and terminating posteriorly in the throat. The lips and cheeks are made up of fat and muscles, covered by the cuticle, which is continued over the whole inner surface of the mouth, like a fine and delicate membrane.—Besides this membrane, the inside of the mouth is furnished with a spongy and very vascular substance called the gum, by means of which the teeth are secured in their sockets. A similar substance covers the roof of the mouth, and forms what is called the velum pendulum palati, which is fixed to the extremity of the arch formed by the os maxillaria and os palati, and terminates in a soft, small, and conical body, named uvula; which appears, as it were, suspended from the middle of the arch over the basis of the tongue. The velum pendulum palati performs the office of a valve between the cavity of the mouth and the pharynx, being moved by several muscles (r). The tongue is composed of several muscles (c) which enable it to perform a variety of motions for the articulation of the voice; for the purposes of mastication; and for conveying the aliment into the pharynx. Its upper part is covered with papillae, which constitute the organ of taste, and are easily to be distinguished; it is covered by the same membrane that lines the inside of the mouth, and which makes at its inferior part towards its basis a reduplication called frenum. Posteriorly, under the velum palati, and at the basis of the tongue, is the pharynx; which is the beginning of the oesophagus, stretched out every way, so as to resemble the top of a funnel, through which the aliment passes into the stomach. The mouth has a communication with the nostrils at its posterior and upper part; with the ears, by the Eustachian tubes; with the lungs, by means of the larynx; and with the stomach, by means of the oesophagus. The pharynx is constantly moistened by a fluid, secreted by two considerable glands called the tonsils, one on each side of the velum palati. These glands, from their supposed resemblance to almonds, have likewise been called amygdalur. The mouth is moistened by a considerable quantity of saliva. This fluid is derived from the parotid glands; a name which by its etymology points out their situation to be near the ears. They are two in number, one on each side under the os maxillae; and they are of the conglomerate kind; being formed of many smaller glands, each of which sends out a very small excretory duct, which unites with the rest, to form one common channel, that runs over the cheek, and piercing the buccinator muscle, opens into the mouth on each side, by an orifice into which a bristle may be easily introduced. Vol. II. Part I. Besides these, the maxillary glands, which are placed near the inner surface of the angle of the lower jaw on each side; the sublingual glands, which are situated at the root of the tongue; the glands of the palate, which are seated in the velum palati; and those of the cheeks, lips, &c., together with many other less considerable ones,—pour the saliva into the mouth through their several excretory ducts. The saliva, like all the other humours of the body, is found to be different in different people; but in general, it is a limpid and insipid fluid, without smell in healthy subjects; and these properties would seem to prove, that it contains very few saline or inflammable particles. The uses of the saliva seem to be to moisten and lubricate the mouth, and to assist in reducing the aliment into a soft pulp before it is conveyed into the stomach. The variety of functions which are constantly performed by the living body, must necessarily occasion a continual waste and dissipation of its several parts. A great quantity is every day thrown off by the inflexible perspiration and other discharges; and were not these losses constantly recruited by a fresh supply of chyle, the body would soon effect its own dissolution. But nature has very wisely favoured us with organs fitted to produce such a supply; and has at the same time endowed us with the sensations of hunger and thirst, that our attention may not be diverted from the necessary business of nutrition. The sensation of hunger is universally known; but it would perhaps be difficult to describe it perfectly in words. It may, however, be defined to be a certain uneasy sensation in the stomach, which induces us to wish for solid food; and which likewise serves to point out the proper quantity, and time for taking it. In describing the stomach, mention was made of the gastric juice, as everywhere lubricating its inner coat. This humour mixes itself with the aliment in the stomach, and helps to prepare it for its passage into the intestines; but when the stomach is perfectly empty, this same fluid irritates the coats of the stomach itself, and produces the sensation of hunger. A certain proportion of liquid aliment is required to assist in the process of digestion, and to afford that moisture to the body, of which there is such a constant dissipation. Thirst induces us to take this necessary supply of drink; and the seat of this sensation is in the tongue, fauces, and oesophagus, which from their great sensibility are required to be kept moist: for though the fauces are naturally moistened by the mucous and salivary juices; yet the blood, when deprived of its watery part, or rendered acrimonious by any natural causes, never fails particularly to affect these parts, and the whole alimentary canal, and to occasion thirst.—This is the common effect of fevers and of hard labour, by both which too much of the watery part of the blood is dissipated. It has been observed, that the aliment undergoes --- (f) These are the circumflexus palati, levator palati mollis, palato-pharyngeus, constrictor isthmi faucium, and azygos uvulae. (c) These are, the genio-glossus, hyo-glossus, lingualis, and stylo-glossus.

ANATOMY

Pages 281-291

anatomy was formerly, as we have shewn in the history, much more cultivated than that of the human body; but when the prejudices of bigotry and ignorance subsided, and allowed human dissection to be more freely exercised, the study of this species of anatomy was almost entirely neglected. Of late, however, it has attracted the attention of several of the most eminent naturalists and anatomists, particularly of Monro, Hunter, Vieq d'Azyr, and Cuvier, from whose labours it has received considerable improvement, and has attained a degree of accuracy and an extent of application, which render it an object of inquiry highly interesting to the philosopher and the physician. Many advantages are derived from the study of comparative anatomy. First, It furnishes us with a sufficient knowledge of the several parts of animals, to prevent our being imposed on by those authors who have described and delineated many organs from brutes as belonging to the human body. That this is of importance, is evinced by examining the works of some of the earliest and greatest masters of anatomy, who, for want of human subjects, have often taken their descriptions from other animals; Galen is notoriously faulty in this respect, and the great Vesalius, though he justly reproved Galen, has fallen into the same error, as is plain from his delineations of the kidneys, the uterus, the muscles of the eye, and other parts. Nor is antiquity only chargeable with this, since in Willis's *Anatomia Cerebri* (the plates of which were verified by that accurate anatomist Dr Lower) there are several of the figures taken from different brutes, especially from the dog, besides what he acknowledges for such. Secondly, It helps us to understand several passages in the ancient writers on medicine, especially Hippocrates and Galen, who have taken many of their descriptions from brutes, and reasoned from them. Thirdly, It affords one of the best assistants and most certain guides in the study of natural history; and the

ANAXAGORAS

Pages 356-357

an eminent <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> of antiquity, was born in the first year of the 70th Olympiad, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 500 years before Christ. In <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of the eminent talents of this philosopher he obtained the appellation of Mind. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYTHAGORAS">Pythagoras</a> represents philosophers as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> spectators of the affairs of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and who, neglecting all other pursuits, devote their exertions to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVESTIGATION">investigation</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, and the search after <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>. According to this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-DEFINITION">definition</a> of a philosopher, Anaxagoras strictly merited the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> appellation; for though he was of a respectable <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a>, and possessed of a considerable fortune, yet he relinquished both, so that, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of Cicero, he might " give himself wholly to the divine pleasures of learning and inquiry." The sons of wealth, and the lovers of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> probably unite in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIDICULE">ridicule</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> upon him by the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> in which he lived, even "that he philosophized very foolishly;" but the mind of Anaxagoras disregarded their scorn, and persevered in his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>; and although the reader may hesitate in giving applause to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> who deprives <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> of the benefits of his social <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TALENT">talent</a>, yet the eager thirst of his mind after knowledge is entitled to becoming <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a>. Leaving his lands to be cultivated and enjoyed by his friends, Anaxagoras placed himself under the care of Anaximenes the Milesian. About the age of twenty he went to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a> and entered upon the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, where he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> 30 years. Some suppose that he was the first <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of the Ionian school, founded by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THALES">Thales</a> a teacher of philosophy in Athens. When Anaxagoras assumed the character of a public teacher of philosophy, he quickly rose to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> eminence, and produced many famous scholars, among whom were <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EURIPIDES">Euripides</a> the tragedian, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERICLES">Pericles</a> the statesman, and the renowned <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOCRATES">Socrates</a>. This philosopher contented himself with serving the republic in his own station, without interfering in any of the public affairs of the state. Both by the principles of wisdom which he inspired into the minds of the Athenian youth, and also by his daily advice in the most important affairs, particularly in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of Pericles, he was of singular <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. But neither the friendship of the famous Pericles, nor his own general disinterestedness of character, nor his immense stores of learning, could <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARD">ward</a> off the shafts of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a>. Cleo accused him of impiety, and the introduction of new opinions concerning the gods, because he taught that the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> was a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, or an inanimate fiery substance. By this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> he was said to rob the sun of his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>, because in the popular opinion he was deemed <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a>, one of the greatest deities. But although Cleo made <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> the avowed cause of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACCUSATION">accusation</a> of Anaxagoras, it is highly probable that civil causes chiefly operated towards his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONDEMNATION">condemnation</a>. It is, however, abundantly evident, that he did not hesitate to expose the vulgar superstitions on several occasions; but the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> is not sufficient which pretends to prove that he was condemned for teaching the doctrine of a supreme intelligence, the creator of this world. His judges condemned him to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>; but Pericles appearing in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> was changed from that of death to banishment and a pecuniary fine. It is reported, that when one of his friends regretted his exile, he replied: "It is not I who have lost the Athenians, but the Athenians who have lost me." Whilst a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of vanity appears in this sentiment, it nevertheless informs posterity with what calmness of mind he endured the changes of fortune. But other sayings tend more fully to unfold his character. During the course of a lecture one <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, he was interrupted with the unpleasant news of the death of a son; he calmly replied, "I knew that I begat him mortal." When he received the sentence of condemnation, he consoled himself by this consideration: "Nature," ture, (said he) <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> ago pronounced the same sentence against me." Expelled from Athens, Anaxagoras passed the remainder of his days at <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-LAMPSACUS">Lampsacus</a>, teaching philosophy in the school of his deceased <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> Anaximenes, until the infirmities of nature terminated his useful life in the year 428 before Christ. Before his death his friends inquired <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they should carry his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> to his native <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>; he returned for answer, that this was quite "unnecessary, the way to the regions below is everywhere alike open." When the magistrates of Lampsacus sent a message to him before his death, requesting to know in what manner he wished them to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>, he said, "Only let the day of my death be annually kept as a holiday by the boys in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> of Lampsacus." This was complied with, and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> remained even in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIOGENES">Diogenes</a> Laertius. This <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> philosopher died at the advanced age of 72, and the inhabitants of Lampsacus erected a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> over his remains, with the following epitaph. Ἐνδιάδες, πλησίον ἀκραῖον ἐν τῷ πέρατι πέρατος Οὐχὶ μόνον ἡμῶν, καὶ τοῦ Ἀναξαγόρου. This tomb great Anaxagoras confines, Whose mind explor'd the paths of heavenly <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>. It is also reported, that there was an altar erected to his memory, upon which were <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSCRIBED">inscribed</a> the words Truth and Mind. Many fabulous reports are narrated concerning this philosopher, of which it appears unnecessary to take any particular notice; and Diogenes Laertius has collected with little care and judgment, after an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> of more than 700 years, the remains concerning this philosopher, which were scattered through various writings. With no small degree of diffidence then the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEN">pen</a> must record a summary of his doctrine collected from such unsatisfactory information; especially since his biographer himself has given full <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> both of his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> and negligence, and as the whole narrative abounds with chronological contradictions and other inconsistencies. It appears, however, that in the midst of some extravagant conceptions Anaxagoras held opinions which indicate a considerable acquaintance with the laws of nature. His idea of the heavens appears to have been, that they were a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> vault, originally composed of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, elevated from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> by the violent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the ambient æther, inflamed by its <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, and by the rapid circular motion of the heavens fixed in their respective places. The testimonies of several writers, among which is that of the respectable Xenophon, unite in proving that he considered the sun to be a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> fiery stone; and Xenophon introduces Socrates as refuting that doctrine, and delivering an unfavourable opinion concerning his other writings. From his perceiving that the rainbow is the effect of the reflection of the solar rays from a dark cloud, and that <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> is produced by the rarefaction, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> by the percussion of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>, Anaxagoras seems to have paid considerable <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to the phenomena of nature. He must have had some knowledge of the nature of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a>, and the doctrine of eclipses, if, according to report, he could predict a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> and darkness at noonday. Our information is more correct concerning his opinions of the principles of nature and the origin of things. He imagined that in nature there are as many kinds of principles as there are <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> bodies, and that the peculiar form of the primary particles of which any body is composed, is the same with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of the compound body itself. For instance, he supposed that a piece of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> is composed of small particles which are themselves gold, and a bone of a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of small bones; thus, according to Anaxagoras, bodies of every kind are <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATED">generated</a> from similar particles. That <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of his system is more agreeable to reason which explains the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> principle in nature. According to Diogenes Laertius, Anaxagoras taught, that "the universe consists of small bodies composed of similar parts, and that mind is the beginning of motion." "He was the first, (says the same writer,) who superadded mind to <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, opening his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> in this pleasing and sublime language: 'All things were confused; then came mind, and disposed them in order.'" <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a> informs us that this philosopher taught the existence of a disposing mind, the cause of all things. Anaxagoras, according to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>, taught that mind was "the cause of the world, and of all order; and that while all things else are compounded, this alone is pure and unmixed;" and that "he ascribes to this principle two powers, to know and to move, saying, that mind put the universe into motion." Cicero expressly asserts, that Anaxagoras was the first who taught, that "the arrangement and order of all things was contrived and accomplished by the understanding and power of an infinite mind." (Gen. Biog.)

ANAXARCHUS

Pages 357-357

a Grecian <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, who lived under <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> of Macedon and Alexander, was born in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABDERA">Abdera</a>, and belonged to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a> generally known by the name of the Eleatic. He is said to have been conducted in the progress of his early studies by the skilful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of Dionenes of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SMYRNA">Smyrna</a> and Metrodorus of Chios. He had the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to be a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a> of Alexander; and a few anecdotes transmitted to posterity concerning him render it evident that he treated him with the usual freedom of a friend. This philosopher candidly checked the vain <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> of Alexander (when elated with <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a> he aspired to the honours of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>), by pointing to his finger when it bled, saying, "See the blood of a mortal, not of a god." It is likewise reported, that, on another occasion, while indulging immoderately at a banquet, he repeated a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EURIPIDES">Euripides</a>, reminding Alexander of his mortality. It is, however, to be regretted, that the fidelity of the philosopher was wanting at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> when the mind of Alexander was tortured with remorse at having slain his friend <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLITUS">Clitus</a>; for it is reported that he, on that occasion, endeavoured to soothe the agitated mind of Alexander, by saying, that "kings, like the gods, could do no wrong." It is reported that Nicocreon, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Cyprus, exposed him to the torture of being pounded in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MORTAR">mortar</a>, and that he endured this torture with incredible <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATIENCE">patience</a>; but as the same fact is reported of Zeno the Eleatic, there is reason to suppose that it is fabulous; and it may be added, that this narrative is inconsistent with the general character of Anaxarchus, who, on account of his easy and peaceable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, received the appellation of "The Fortunate." (Gen. Biog.)

ANAXIMANDER

Pages 357-358

ANAXIMANDER, a famous Greek <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, born at <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILETUS">Miletus</a> in the 42d Olympiad, in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Polycrates <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAMOS">Samos</a>. He was the first who publicly taught <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, and wrote upon philosophical subjects. He carried his researches into <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> very far for the time in which he lived. It is said, that he discovered the obliquity of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZODIAC">zodiac</a>, was the first who published a geographical <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, invented the gnomon, and set up the first <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIAL">dial</a> in an open <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> at Lacedemon. He taught, that infinity of things was the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> and universal element; that this infinite always preserved its unity, but that its parts underwent changes; that all things came from it; and that all were about to return into it. According to all appearance, he meant by this obscure and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDETERMINATE">indeterminate</a> principle the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHAOS">chaos</a> of the other philosophers. He asserted, that there is an infinity of worlds; that the stars are composed of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> and fire, which are carried in their spheres, and that these spheres are gods; and that the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> is placed in the midst of the universe, as in a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> centre. He added, that infinite worlds were the product of infinity, and that corruption proceeded from separation.

ANAXIMANDRIANS

Pages 358-358

in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, the followers of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANAXIMANDER">Anaximander</a>, the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> of the philosophical <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ATHEISTS">atheists</a>, who admitted of no other substance in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> but <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>.

ANAXIMENES

Pages 358-358

a Greek historian and rhetorician, was born at <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-LAMPSACUS">Lampsacus</a> about 580 years before Christ. <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIOGENES">Diogenes</a>, the Cynic, laid the principles of erudition in the mind of this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>. Some writers ascribe to him, "A Treatise on the Principles of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">Rhetoric</a>," which bears the name of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>; and it is reported that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> of Macedon invited him to his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> to instruct his son Alexander in that science. Alexander was attended in his expedition against <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a> by this learned <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> and many other eminent men. The inhabitants of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, which had the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to give him birth, having espoused the cause of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DARIUS">Darius</a>, upon Alexander's conquering them, they entreated their countryman Anaximenes to intercede with Alexander in their behalf. He humanely undertook to interpose for them; but the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> being informed of his intention, as soon as he came into his presence, swore that he would <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> him nothing that he should ask. He instantly replied, "I entreat you to destroy Lampsacus, to burn its <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>, and to sell the inhabitants for slaves." Alexander, struck with this dexterous reply, kept his word, and saved the city. Another pleasing anecdote is related of Anaximenes. For some unrecorded cause, he being displeased with the historian Theopompus, in order to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> himself, wrote a severe satire against the Spartans and Thebans, in a stile exactly similar to that of Theopompus, and under his name addressed it to the Athenians. Theopompus was generally believed to be the author of that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, and consequently it brought upon him the odium and indignation of all <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>. Whilst this <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> afforded an illustrious <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of the strength of his talents, it afforded an equal <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of his heart. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of Philip, of Alexander, and likewise twelve books on the early history of Greece, were the productions of his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEN">pen</a>, but are now unfortunately lost. (Gen. Biog.)

ANAZARBUS

Pages 358-358

ANAZARBA (Stephanus); a town of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CILICIA">Cilicia</a>, on the river Pyramus, the birthplace of Dioscorides, and of the poet Oppian. It was sometimes called Cesarea, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> either of Augustus <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> of Tiberius. The inhabitants are called Anazarbeni (Pliny), and on coins Anazarbeis after the Greek idiom. It was destroyed by a dreadful earthquake in the year 525, along with several other important cities: but they were all repaired at a vast expense by the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Justin; who was so much affected with their misfortune, that putting off the diadem and purple, he appeared for several days in sack-cloth.

ANBERTKEND

Pages 358-358

in the eastern <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, a celebrated book of the Brachmans, wherein the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> are contained. The word in its literal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> denotes the cistern wherein is the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. The anbertkend is divided into 50 beths <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> discourses, each of which consists of 10 chapters. It has been translated from the original Indian into Arabic, under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Morat al Maani, q. d. "the marrow of intelligence."

ANCARANO

Pages 358-358

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the marquisate of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCONA">Ancona</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 14. 54. N. Lat. 42. 48.

ANCASTER

Pages 358-358

a town of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LINCOLNSHIRE">Lincolnshire</a>, situated in W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 30. N. Lat. 52. 30. It gives <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> to the noble family of Bertie.

ANCENIS

Pages 358-358

a town of France in the department of the Lower <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOIRE">Loire</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1. 9. N. Lat. 47. 20.

ANCESTORS

Pages 358-359

those from whom a person is descended in a straight line. The word is derived from the Latin ancestor, contracted from antecessor, q. d. "goer before." Most nations have paid honours to their ancestors. It was properly the departed souls of their forefathers that the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> worshipped under the denominations of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LARES">lares</a>, lemures, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a> gods. Hence the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> tombs were a kind of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rather altars, whereon oblations were made by the kindred of the deceased. The Russians have still their anniversary feasts in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of their ancestors, which they call roditi sabbot, q. d. "kinsfolk's sabbath;" wherein they make formal visits to the dead in their graves, and carry them <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>, eatables, and presents of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> other kinds. They interrogate them, with loud lamentable cries, what they are doing; how they spend their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; what it is they want; and the like. The Quojas, a people of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, offer sacrifices of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a> and wine to their ancestors before ever they undertake any considerable <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a>. The anniversaries of their Ancestors, their deaths are always kept by their families with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> solemnity. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> invokes the souls of his father and mother to make trade flourish and the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHASE">chase</a> succeed. The Chinese seem to have distinguished themselves above all other nations in the veneration they bear their ancestors. By the laws of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONFUCIUS">Confucius</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the duty which children owe their parents consists in worshipping them when dead. This <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, which makes a considerable part of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> of the Chinese, is said to have been instituted by the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Kun, the fifth in order from the foundation of that ancient empire. Bibl. Un. tom. vii. The Chinese have both a solemn and ordinary worship which they pay their ancestors. The former is held regularly twice a year, viz. in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> and autumn, with much pomp. A person who was present at it gives the following account of the ceremonies on that occasion: The sacrifices were made in a chapel well adorned, where there were six altars furnished with censers, tapers, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>. There were three ministers, and behind them two young acolites. The three former went with a profound silence, and frequent genuflexions, towards the five altars, pouring out wine: afterwards they drew near to the sixth, and when they came to the foot of the altar, half bowed <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, they said their prayers with a low <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>. That being finished, the three ministers went to the altar; the officiating <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> took up a vessel full of wine, and drank; then he lifted up the head of a deer or goat; after which, taking fire from the altar, they all lighted a bit of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>: and the minister of the ceremonies <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> towards the people, said with a loud voice, That he gave them thanks in the name of their ancestors for having so well honoured them; and in recompense he promised them, on their part, a plentiful <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HARVEST">harvest</a>, a fruitful issue, good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, and a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and all those advantages that are most pleasing to men. The Chinese give their ancestors another simpler and more private worship. To this end they have in their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> a niche or hollow <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, where they put the names of their deceased fathers, and make prayers and offerings of perfumes and spices to them at certain times, with bowing, &c. They do the like at their tombs. The Jews settled in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a> are said to worship their ancestors like the heathens, and with the same ceremonies, except that they offer not swines <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>. Near their synagogue they have a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALL">hall</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of ancestors, wherein are niches for <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABRAHAM">Abraham</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a>, &c. The Jesuits also conformed, and were permitted by their general to conform to this and many other superstitious customs of the Chinese. There is one peculiarity of another kind, wherein the Chinese show their regard for their ancestors; in proportion as any of their descendants are preferred to a higher <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, their dead ancestors are at the same time preferred and ennobled with them. The kings Ven Van, Veu Van, and Chen Cum, who were descended from vassal kings, when they mounted the imperial throne, raised their ancestors from the vassal or depending state wherein these had lived to the dignity of emperors; so that the same honours were for the future rendered them as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they had been emperors of China. The same example was followed by the subsequent kings, and now obtains among the Ancestors grandees and literati: all now worship their ancestors, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> which they themselves hold in the world. If the son be a mandarin, and the father only a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a>, the latter is buried as a doctor, but sacrificed to as a mandarin. The like holds in degradations, where the condition of the fathers is that of their sons.

ANCHE

Pages 365-365

a small town of France, in Picardy, with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of a marquisate, seated on a little river of the same name. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2. 45. N. Lat. 49. 59.

ANCHILOPS

Pages 359-359

ἀγκυλα, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRACTION">contraction</a>, and ὄψ, eye, in Medicine, denotes an abscess, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> collection of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, between the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> of the eye and the nose. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> suffered to remain too <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, or unskilfully managed, it degenerates, the stagnating humours corrupt, and an ulcer is produced. When the tumour is broke, and the tears flow involuntarily, whilst the os lachrymale is not carious, it is an argylops; but when the ulcer is of a long standing, deep, fetid, and the os lachrymale becomes carious, it is a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISTULA">fistula</a>. The cure is by restriction and excision, tying it at the root on the glandula lachrymalis, and, when ready, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> it off. See <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ANCHISES

Pages 359-359

in fabulous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a Trojan <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, descended from Dardanus, and the son of Capys. Venus made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> to him in the form of a beautiful <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NYMPH">nymph</a>; and bore him Æneas, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>’s Æneid.

ANCHOR

Pages 359-364

a heavy, strong, crooked <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, dropped from a ship into the bottom of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, to retain her in a convenient station in a harbour, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> river. The most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> anchors are said to have been of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>; and sometimes of wood, to which a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> was usually fixed. In some places, baskets full of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, and sacks filled with sand, were employed for the same <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>. All these were let <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> by cords into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, and by their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> stayed the course of the ship. Afterwards they were composed of iron, and furnished with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>, which being fastened to the bottom of the sea, preserved the vessel immovable; whence adors and dentes are frequently taken for anchors in the Greek and Latin poets. At first there was only one tooth, whence anchors were called ἀγκυλοποιοι; but in a short <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> was added by Eupalamus, or Anacharsis the Scythian <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>. The anchors with two teeth were called μυρδεροι or μυρδεραι; and from ancient monuments appear to have been much the same with those used in our days, only the transverse piece of wood upon the handles (the stock) is wanting in all of them. Every ship had several anchors; one of which, surpassing all the rest in bigness and strength, was peculiarly termed ἱσχυρα, or sacra, and was never used but in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> danger; whence sacram anchoram solvere, is proverbially applied to such as are forced to their last refuge. The anchors now made are contrived so as to sink into the ground as soon as they reach it, and to hold a great strain before they can be loosened or dislodged from their station. They are composed of a shank, a stock, a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RING">ring</a>, and two arms with their flukes. The stock, which is a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> piece of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> fixed across the shank, serves to guide the flukes in a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> perpendicular to the surface of the ground: so that, one of them sinks into it by its own weight as soon as it falls, and is still preserved steadily in that position by the stock. stock, which, altogether with the shank, lies flat on the bottom. In this situation it must necessarily sustain a great effort before it can be dragged through the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> horizontally. Indeed this can only be effected by the violence of the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> or tide, or both of them, sometimes increased by the turbulence of the sea, and acting upon the ship so as to stretch the cable to its utmost tension, which accordingly may dislodge the anchor from its <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a>, especially <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the ground be soft and oozy, or rocky. When the anchor is thus displaced, it is said, in the sea phrase, to come home. That the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of this useful instrument may be more clearly understood, let us suppose a long massy beam of iron erected perpendicularly, b, at the lower end of which are two arms, d e, of equal thickness with the beam (usually called the shank), only that they <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TAPER">taper</a> towards the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a>, which are elevated above the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANE">plane</a> at an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> of 30 degrees, or inclined to the shank at an angle of 60 degrees; on the upper <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of each arm (in this position) is a fluke or thick plate of iron, g h, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> shaped like an isosceles triangle whose base reaches inwards to the middle of the arm. On the upper end of the shank is fixed the stock transversed with the flukes; the stock is a long beam of oak, f, in two parts, strongly bolted and hooped together with iron rings. See also No. 2. <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">Close</a> above the stock is the ring a, to which the cable is fastened or bent; the ring is curiously covered with a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of pieces of short rope, which are twisted about it so as to form a very thick texture or covering called the puddlening, and used to preserve the cable from being fretted or chafed by the iron. Every ship has, or ought to have, three <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> anchors, with a cable to each, viz. the sheet, maitresse-ancre (which is the anchora sacra of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>); the best bower, second ancres; and small bower, ancres d'afourche, so called from their usual situation on the ship's bows. There are besides smaller anchors, for removing a ship from <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> to place in a harbour or river, where there may not be room or wind for sailing; these are the stream anchor, ancres de tone; the kedge and grappling, grapin: this last, however, is chiefly designed for boats. Method of Making Anchors. The goodness of the anchor is a point of great importance. Great care is therefore to be taken, that the metal it is made of be neither too soft nor too brittle; the latter rendering it liable to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a>, and the former to straighten. The shank, arms, and flukes, are first forged separately; then the hole is made at one end of the shank for the ring, which being also previously forged, is put into the hole of the shank, and the two ends shut together. After which the arms are shut to the shank one after the other, and the anchor is finished. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">Proof</a> is made of anchors by raising them to a great height, and then letting them <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> again on a kind of iron <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLOCK">block</a> placed across for the purpose. To try whether the flukes <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> turn to the bottom and take hold of the ground, they place the anchor on an even surface, with the end of one of the flukes, and one of the ends of the stock resting on the surface: in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> the anchor turns, and the point of the fluke rises upwards, the anchor is good. In England, France, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, anchors are made of forged iron; but in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> they are sometimes made of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, and likewise in several parts of the South sea. For the proportions of anchors, according to Manwaring, the shank is to be thrice the length of one of the flukes, and half the length of the beam. According to Aubin, the length of the anchor is to be four-tenths of the greatest breadth of the ship; so that the shank, e.g.r. of an anchor in a vessel 30 feet wide, is to be 12 feet long. When the shank is, for instance, eight feet long, the two arms are to be <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> feet long, measuring them according to their curvity. As to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of curvity given the arms, there is no rule for it; the workmen are here left to their own <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a>. The latter writer observes, that the anchor of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> heavy vessel is smaller in proportion than that of a lesser and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> one. The reason he gives is, that though the sea employs an equal force against a small vessel as against a great one, supposing the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of wood upon which the water acts to be equal in both, yet the little vessel, by reason of its superior lightness, does not make so much resistance as the greater; the defect whereof must be supplied by the weight of the anchor. From these and other hydrostatic principles, the following <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> has been formed; wherein is shown, by means of the ship's breadth within, how many feet the beam or shank ought to be long, giving it four-tenths or two-fifths of the ship's breadth within: by which proportion might be regulated the length of the other parts of the anchor. In this table is represented likewise the weight an anchor ought to be for a ship from eight feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> to 45, increasing by one foot's breadth; supposing that all anchors are similar, or that their weights are as the cubes of the lengths of the shanks. | Breadth of the Vessel | Length of the Anchor | Feet | Pounds | |-----------------------|---------------------|------|--------| | 8 | 3 | 33 | | | 9 | 3 | 47 | | | 10 | 4 | 64 | | | 11 | 4 | 84 | | | 12 | 4 | 110 | | | 13 | 5 | 140 | | | 14 | 5 | 175 | | | 15 | 6 | 216 | | | 16 | 6 | 262 | | | 17 | 6 | 314 | | | 18 | 7 | 373 | | | 19 | 7 | 439 | | | 20 | 8 | 512 | | | 21 | 8 | 592 | | | 22 | 8 | 681 | | | 23 | 9 | 778 | | | 24 | 9 | 884 | | | 25 | 10 | 1000 | | | 26 | 10 | 1124 | | | 27 | 10 | 1259 | | | 28 | 11 | 1405 | | | 29 | 11 | 1562 | | | 30 | 12 | 1728 | | | 31 | 12 | 1906 | | M. Bouguer, in his *Traité de Navire*, directs to take the length of the shank in inches, and to divide the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUBE">cube</a> of it by 1160 for the weight. The reason is obvious; because the quotient of the cube of 201 inches, which is the length of an anchor weighing 7000lb, divided by the weight, is 1160; and therefore, by the rule of three, this will be a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> divisor for the cube of any length, and a single operation will suffice. The same author gives the following dimensions of the several parts of an anchor. The two arms generally form the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> of a circle, whose centre is three-eighths of the shank from the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERTEX">vertex</a>, or point where it is fixed to the shank; and each arm is equal to the same length, or the radius; so that the two arms together make an arch of 120 degrees; the flukes are half the length of the arms, and their breadth two-fifths of the said length. With respect to the thickness, the circumference at the throat, or vertex of the shank, is generally made about a fifth part of its length, and the small end two-thirds of the throat; the small end of the arms of the flukes, three-fourths of the circumference of the shank at the throat. These dimensions should be greater when the iron is of a bad <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, especially if <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> iron is used instead of forged iron. See Anchor Supplement. At Anchor, the situation of a ship which rides by her anchor in a road or haven, &c. Plate XXXII. fig. r. No. 3, represents the fore part of a ship as riding in this situation. See also <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUOY">Buoy</a>-Rope. To fish the Anchor, to draw up the flukes upon the ship's side after it is catted. See the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> Davit and Fish. To steer the ship to her Anchor, is to steer the ship's head towards the place where the anchor lies when they are heaving the cable into the ship; that the cable may thereby enter the hause with less resistance, and the ship advance towards the anchor with greater facility. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCHOR_GROUND">Anchor-Ground</a>, is a bottom which is neither too deep, too shallow, nor rocky; as in the first the cable bears too nearly perpendicular, and is thereby apt to jerk the anchor out of the ground; in the second, the ship's bottom is apt to strike at low water, or when the sea runs <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, by which she is exposed to the danger of sinking; and in the third, the anchor is liable to hood the broken and pointed ends of rocks, and tear away its flukes, whilst the cable, from the same cause, is constantly in danger of being cut through as it rubs on their edges. Anchor, in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, is a sort of carving somewhat resembling an anchor. It is commonly placed as part of the enrichment of the boultings of capitals of the Tuscan, Doric, and Ionic orders, and also of the boultings of bed <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOULDINGS">mouldings</a> of the Doric, Ionic, and Corinthian cornices, anchors and eggs being carved alternately through the whole <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>. Anchors, in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, are emblems of hope, and are taken for such in a spiritual as well as a temporal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>. Anchorage, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, is a duty upon ships for the use of the port or harbour where they cast anchor. Anchovy, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a>, the English name of the clupea encrasicolus. See Clupea, Ichthyology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Anchovy-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEAR">Pear</a>. See Grias. Anchusa, Alkanet or Bugloss. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> Index. Anchyloblepharon. See Anchyloblepharon. Anchylops. See Anchilops. Anchylosis. See Ankylosis. Ancient, or Antient, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> applied to things which existed long ago; thus we say, ancient nations, ancient customs, &c. See Antiquities. Ancient, sometimes denotes elderly, or of long standing, in opposition to young, or new; thus we say, an ancient barrister, ancient buildings. Ancient, in a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> sense, denotes either the ensign or colours. Ancient, in ships of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, the streamer or <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAG">flag</a> borne in the stern. Ancient demesne, in English Law, is a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TENURE">tenure</a>, whereby all manors belonging to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> in William the Conqueror's and St Edward's time were held. The numbers, names, &c. hereof were entered by the Conqueror, in a book called Domesday Book, yet remaining in the Exchequer; so that such lands as by that book appeared to have belonged to the crown at that time, are called ancient demesne.—The tenants in ancient demesne are of two sorts; one who hold their lands frankly by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a>; the other by copy of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>-roll, or by the verge, at the will of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a>, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANOR">manor</a>.—The advantages of this tenure are, 1. That tenants holding by charter cannot be rightfully impleaded out of their manor; and, when they are, they may abate the writ, by pleading the tenure. 2. They are free from toll for all things relating to their livelihood and husbandry; nor can be impannelled on any inquest.—These tenants held originally by ploughing the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>, plashing his hedges, and the like <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, for the maintenance of his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a>; and it was on this account that such liberties were given them, for which they may have writs of monasterium to such as take the duties of tolls, &c.—No lands are to be accounted ancient demesne, but such as are held in socage. Whether land be ancient demesne or not, shall be tried by the book of Domesday. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTY">Ancienty</a>, in some ancient statutes, is used for eldership or seniority. The elder sister can demand no more Ancillon, more than her other <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SISTERS">sisters</a>, beside the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> mesne, by reason of her ancieney. This word is used in the statute of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, 14 Henry III.

ANCILLON

Pages 364-364
David, a minister of the reformed church at Metz, where he was born the 17th of March 1617. He studied from the ninth or tenth year of his age in the Jesuits college, where he gave such proofs of his genius, that the heads of the society tried every means to draw him over to their religion and party; but he continued firm against their attacks. He went to Geneva in 1633; and studied divinity under Spanheim, Diodati, and Tronchin, who conceived a very great esteem for him. He left Geneva in April 1641, and offered himself to the synod of Charenton in order to take upon him the office of a minister: his abilities were greatly admired by the examiners, and the whole assembly were so highly pleased with him, that they gave him the church of Meaux, the most considerable then unprovided for. Here he acquired a vast reputation for his learning, eloquence, and virtue, and was even highly respected by those of the Roman Catholic communion. He returned to his own country in the year 1653, where he remained till the revocation of the edict of Nantes in 1685. He returned to Francfort after this fatal blow; and having preached in the French church at Hanau, the whole congregation were so edified by it, that they immediately called together the heads of the families, in order to propose that he might be invited to accept of being minister there. The proposition was agreed to; and he began the exercise of his ministry in that church about the end of the year 1685. His preaching made so great a noise at Hanau, that the professors of divinity, and the German and Dutch ministers, attended his sermons frequently: the count of Hanau himself, who had never before been seen in the French church, came thither to hear Mr Ancillon; they came from the neighbouring parts, and even from Francfort; people who understood nothing of French flocked together with great eagerness, and said, they loved to see him speak. This occasioned a great jealousy in the two other ministers; which tended to make his situation uneasy. He therefore went to Berlin; where he met with a kind reception from his highness the elector, and was made minister of the city. Here he had the pleasure of seeing his eldest son made judge and director of the French in the same city, and his other son rewarded with a pension, and entertained at the university of Francfort upon the Oder. He had likewise the satisfaction of seeing his brother made judge of all the French in the states of Brandenburg; and Mr Cayart his son-in-law, engineer to his electoral highness. He enjoyed these agreeable circumstances, and several others, till his death, which happened at Berlin the 3rd of September 1692, when he was 75 years of age.—Mr Ancillon having got a considerable fortune by marriage, was enabled thereby to gratify his passion for books; his library was accordingly very curious and large, and he increased it every day with all that appeared new and important in the republic of letters, so that at last it was one of the noblest collections in the hands of a private person in the kingdom. He published a book, in quarto, in which the whole dispute concerning Traditions is fully examined: he also wrote an apology for Luther, Zuinglius, Calvin, and Beza, and several other pieces.

ANCLAM

Pages 364-364

a strong town of Germany, in the circle of Upper <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Pomerania, remarkable for its excellent pastures. It is seated on the river Peene. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 14. 5. N. Lat. 54. 10.

ANCONA

Pages 364-364

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-port town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the marquisate of that name, and the see of a bishop. It was formerly the finest port in all Italy, being built by the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Trajan, about the year 115; but was almost ruined, and its trade lost: however, it has again begun to revive. Its harbour is the best in all the pope's dominions. The town lies round it on two hills; one of which is at the point of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> St Syriaco, from whence there is a delightful prospect. On the other stands the citadel, which commands the town and harbour. The streets of this <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> are narrow and uneven; and the public and private buildings inferior to those of the other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> in Italy. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> is a low dark structure; and though the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a> is covered with fine marble, the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a> has neither <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> nor regularity. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of St Dominic, and that of the Franciscans, have each an excellent <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> by Titian. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a>, where the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> meet, is a handsome <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> portico, in which is an equestrian statue of Trajan, who first built the port. At the four corners are four other <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a>. The triumphal <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> of Trajan remains almost entire, with its inscription. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> people in this town are a little particular and fantastical in their dress, but the better sort follow the French <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a>. It is a great thoroughfare from the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of Italy to Loreto; which renders <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> very dear. The tide does not rise here above a foot, and near the Mediterranean it is scarce visible. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 13. 35. N. Lat. 43. 36.

ANCONES

Pages 364-364

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, the corners <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> quoins of walls, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> beams, or rafters.—Vitruvius calls the consoles by the same name.

ANCONY

Pages 364-365
