in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>-works, a piece of half-wrought iron, of about three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of 100 <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>, and of the shape of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a> in the middle, but rude and unwrought at the ends. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> for bringing the iron to this state is this: They first melt off a piece from a sow of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> iron, of the proper size; this they hammer at the forge into a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of two feet <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> shape, which they call a bloom; when this is done, they send it to the finery; where, after two <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> three heats and workings, they bring it to this <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, and call it an ancony. The middle <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> out at the finery, is about three feet long, and of the shape and thickness the whole is to be; this is then sent to the chafery, and there the ends are wrought to the shape of the middle, and the whole made into a bar. See ANC ANCORARUM urbs (Αγροτιπόλις), a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> in the Nomos Aphroditopolites, towards the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RED_SEA"><a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">Red</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>; so called because there was in the neighbourhood a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARRY">quarry</a>, in which they hewed stone anchors (<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>) before iron anchors came to be used. The gentilitial name is Ancyropolis (Stephanus).

ANCOURT

Pages 365-365

FLORENT CARTON D', an eminent French <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTOR">actor</a> and dramatic writer, was born at Fontainebleau, October 1661. He studied in the Jesuits <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> under Father de la Rue; who, discovering in him a remarkable vivacity and capacity for learning, was extremely desirous of engaging him in their order; but Ancourt's aversion to a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> rendered all his efforts ineffectual. After he had gone through a course of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, he applied himself to the civil <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>, and was admitted advocate at 17 years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. But falling in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> with an actress, he was induced to go upon the stage, and he married her. As he had all the qualifications necessary for the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>, he soon greatly distinguished himself; and not being satisfied with the applause only of an actor, he began to write pieces for the stage; many of which had such prodigious success, that most of the players grew rich from the profits of them. His merits in this way procured him a very favourable reception at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIV. showed him many marks of his favour. His sprightly conversation and polite behaviour made his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> agreeable to all the men of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> both at court and in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, and the most considerable persons were extremely pleased to have him at their houses. Having taken a journey to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUNKIRK">Dunkirk</a>, to see his eldest <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> who lived there, he took the opportunity of paying his compliments to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BAVARIA">Bavaria</a>, who was then at <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRUSSELS">Brussels</a>: this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> received him with the utmost civility; and having detained him a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, dismissed him with a present of a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIAMOND">diamond</a> valued at 1000 pistoles: he likewise rewarded him in a very generous manner, when, upon his coming to Paris, Ancourt composed an entertainment for his diversion. Ancourt began at length to grow weary of the theatre, which he quitted in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LENT">Lent</a> 1718, and retired to his estate of Courcelles le Roy, in Berry, where he applied himself wholly to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>, and composed a translation of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a>'s Psalms in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>, and a sacred tragedy, which were never printed. He died the 6th of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1726, being 65 years of age.—The plays which he wrote are 52 in all; most of which were printed separately at the time when they were first represented: They were afterwards collected into five volumes, then into <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a>, and at last into <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a>. This last edition is most complete.

ANCUS MARTIUS

Pages 365-365

the fourth <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, succeeded Tullus Hostilius, 639 years before Christ. He defeated the Latins, subdued the Fide-nates, conquered the Sabines, Volsci, and Veientines, enlarged Rome by joining to it Mount Janiculum, and made the harbour of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OSTIA">Ostia</a>. He died about 615 years before the Christian era.

ANCYCLE

Pages 365-365

in antiquity, a kind of shield that fell, as was pretended, from heaven, in the reign of Numa Pompilius; at which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, likewise, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> was heard declaring that Rome should be mistress of the world as <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> as she should preserve this holy buckler. It was kept with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> care in the temple of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARS">Mars</a>, under the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of twelve priests; and lest any should attempt to steal it, eleven others were made so like, as not to be distinguished from the sacred one. These ancylia were carried in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESSION">procession</a> every year round the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Rome.

ANCYLOBLEPHARON

Pages 365-365

(from ἀγκυλος, bent, and βλέφαρος, an eyelid); a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> of the eye, which closes the eyelids. Sometimes the eyelids grow together, and also to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUNICA">tunica</a> albuginea of the eye, from carelessness when there is an ulcer in these parts. Both these <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> are called ancyloblepharon by the Greeks. This disorder must be distinguished from that coalition of the eyelids which happens from viscid <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> gluing them together. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COHESION">cohesion</a> is on the corner, the sight is inevitably lost. This hath sometimes happened in the small pox. If there is only a growing together of the eyelids, they may be separated with the specillum, and pledgets kept between them to prevent their reunion. If the eyelids adhere to the eye, they are to be separated by a fine edged <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a>; and their reunion is to be prevented by a proper <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of injections, and lint placed between them, after <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIPPING">dipping</a> it in some proper liniment. ANCYLOGLOSSUM (from ἀγκυλος, crooked, and γλώσσα, the tongue); a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRACTION">contraction</a> of the ligaments of the tongue. Some have this imperfection from their birth, others from some disease. In the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, the membrane which supports the tongue is too short <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> too hard; in the latter, an ulcer under the tongue, healing and forming a cicatrix, is sometimes the cause: These speak with some difficulty. The ancy-loglossi by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> are late before they speak; but when they begin, they soon speak properly. These we call tongue-tied. Mauriceau says, that in this case it is a small membranous production, which extends from the frenulum to the tip of the tongue, that hinders the child from sucking, &c. He justly condemns the cruel practice among nurses, of tearing this membrane with their nails; for thus ulcers are sometimes formed, which are of difficult cure: he advises to snip it with scissors in two or three places, taking care not to extend the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of the scissors so far as the frenulum. The instances rarely occur which require any kind of assistance; for if the child can thrust the tip of its tongue to the outer edge of its lip, this disease does not exist; and if the tongue is not greatly restrained, the frenulum <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> stretch by the child's sucking and crying.

ANCYLOSIS

Pages 365-365

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>, implies a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISTORTION">distortion</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> stiffness of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a>, caused by a settlement of the humours, or a distension of the nerves; and therefore remedies of a mollifying and relaxing <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> are required.

ANCYRA

Pages 365-366

the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GALATIA">Galatia</a>, (Livy, Pliny, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>); at no <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> distance from the river <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALYS">Halys</a>, (Livy): said to be built by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIDAS">Midas</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHRYGIA">Phrygia</a>, and to take its name from an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCHOR">anchor</a> found there (Pausanias). It was greatly improved by Augustus, deem- ANCYSTRUM. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. ANDABATÆ, in antiquity, a sort of gladiators, who, mounted on horseback <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARIOTS">chariots</a>, fought hoodwinked, having a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HELMET">helmet</a> that covered their eyes.

ANDALUSIA

Pages 366-366

is the most western <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, having <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESTREMADURA">Estremadura</a> and La Mancha on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>; the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANADA">Granada</a>, the straits of Gibraltar, and the ocean, on the east and south; and on the west, the kingdom of Algarva in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>, from which it is separated by the river Guadiana. It is about 182 miles <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and 150 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> cities and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> are <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEVILLE">Seville</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, Baeza, Gibraltar, Cordova, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CADIZ">Cadiz</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1823/vol0.html#article-MEDINA_SIDONIA">Medina Sidonia</a>, Jaen, Port St <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>, &c. It is the best, most fruitful, and the richest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of all Spain. There is good <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>, a fertile <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, and a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> fit for <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> in 1787 amounted to 738,153. New Andalusia, a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of the province of Terra Firma in South <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, whose boundaries cannot be well ascertained, as the Spaniards pretend a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to countries in which they have never established any settlements. According to the most reasonable limits, it extends in length 500 miles from north to south, and about 270 in breadth from east to west. The interior <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is woody and mountainous, variegated with fine valleys that yield corn and pasturage. The produce of the country consists chiefly in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DYEING">dyeing</a> drugs, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUMS">gums</a>, medicinal roots, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRAZIL">brazil</a> wood, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>, and some valuable <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>. To this province also belonged five valuable <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEARL">pearl</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FISHERIES">fisheries</a>. The capital of New Andalusia is Comana, Cumana, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> New Corduba, situated in N. Lat. 10°, about <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> miles from the north sea. Here the Spaniards laid the foundation of a town in the year 1520. The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> is strong by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, and fortified by a castle capable of making a vigorous defense. The country is better known under the name of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUIANA">Guiana</a>. The revolution which began there in 1810 is not yet terminated. ANDAMAN or ANDEMAN <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">Islands</a>, in the East Indies, situated about 80 leagues distant from Tanasseron on the coast of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIAM">Siam</a>. They are but little known. The East <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a> ships sometimes touch at them, and are supplied by the natives with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>, herbs, and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>. The inhabitants are by some represented as a harmless inoffensive <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of men, and by others as cannibals. E. Long. 92°. N. Lat. from 10° to 15°.

ANDANTE

Pages 366-366

in Music, signifies a movement moderately slow, between <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LARGO">largo</a> and allegro.

ANDECAVI

Pages 366-366

(Tacitus); <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANDEGAVI">ANDEGAVI</a>, (Pliny); <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANDES">ANDES</a>, (Cæsar); ANDI, (Lucan): A people of Gallia Celtica, having the Turones to the east, the Namnetes to the west, the Pictones to the south, and the Auverci Conomani to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>: now Anjou.

ANDEGAVI

Pages 366-366
or ANDEGAVUS, a town of Gallia Celtica, (Pliny, Ptolemy;) now Angiers. Called Andecavi, (Tacitus). W. Long. 30°. N. Lat. 47°. 30'.

ANDELY

Pages 366-366

a town of Normandy in France, parted in two by a paved causeway. Here is a fountain to which pilgrims flock from all parts, to be cured of their disorders, on the feast <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> of the saint to which it is dedicated. It is 20 miles south-east of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROUEN">Rouen</a>, and 40 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1°. 30'. Lat. 49°. 20'.

ANDENA

Pages 366-366

in old writings, denotes the swath made in the mowing of hay, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> as much ground as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> could stride over at once.

ANDEOL

Pages 366-366

SAINT, a town of France, in the department of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOZERE">Lozere</a>, five miles south of St Viviers, whose bishop formerly resided there. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2°. 50'. N. Lat. 44°. 24'.

ANDERAB

Pages 366-366

the most southern <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Balkh, possessed by the Usbeck Tartars. It is very rich and populous, but a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of no <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> strength. The neighbouring <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> yield excellent quarries of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAPIS">lapis</a> lazuli, in which the Bukhars drive a great trade with <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>.—This city is situated at the foot of the mountains dividing northern India, and the Persian dominions, from Great Bukharia. As there is no other way of crossing these mountains but by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> through this city, all travellers with goods must pay 4 per cent. On this account the khan of Balkh maintains a good <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> in the place.

ANDERNACHT

Pages 366-366

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of the Lower <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>, belonging to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>. It is situated in a plain on the river Rhine; and is fortified with a wall, castle, and bulwarks. It has a trade in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> jugs and pitchers, which are sent to the mineral waters at Dunchstein. There are three monasteries here, and several churches. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 7°. 4'. N. Lat. 50°. 27'.

ANDERO

Pages 366-366

SAINT, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> port town in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-BISCAY">Biscay</a>, in Old Castile, seated on a small <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a>. It is a trading town, and contains about 700 houses, two <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> churches, and four monasteries. Here the Spaniards build and lay up some of their men of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3°. 45'. N. Lat. 43°. 20'.

ANDERSON

Pages 366-369

Sir EDMUND, a younger son of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Scotch family settled in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LINCOLNSHIRE">Lincolnshire</a>. He was sometime a student of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LINCOLN">Lincoln</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>; and removed from thence to the Inner Temple, where he applied himself diligently to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>, and became a barrister. In the ninth of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a> he was both <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LENT">Lent</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">Summer</a> reader, and in the 16th <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> reader. He was appointed her majesty's serjeant at law in the 19th year of her reign; and some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> after, one of the justices of the assize. In 1582 he was made <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-COMMON_PLEAS"><a class="xr</a>ef" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> pleas, and in the year following was knighted. He held his office to the end of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, died in the year 1605, and was buried at Eyeworth in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEDFORDSHIRE">Bedfordshire</a>. He was an able but punctilious lawyer; a scourge to the Puritans; and a strenuous supporter of the established <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. His works are, 1. Reports of many <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> argued and adjudged in the time of Queen Elizabeth in the common <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENCH">bench</a>. Lond. 1644, fol. 2. Resolutions and judgements on the cases and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> agitated in all courts of Westminster, in the latter end of the reign of Queen Elizabeth. Published by John Goldsborough, Esq. Lond. 1655, 4to. Besides these, there is a manuscript copy of his readings still in being. Anderson, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADAM">Adam</a>, a native of Scotland, was <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> to the reverend James Anderson, D.D., editor of the Diplomata Scotiae and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> Genealogies, many years since minister of the Scots Presbyterian church in Anderson, in Swallow-street, Piccadilly, and well known in those days among the people of that persuasion resident in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> by the name of Bishop Anderson, a learned but imprudent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, who lost a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> in the fatal year 1720. He married, and had issue a son, and a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> who was the wife of an officer in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>. Adam Anderson was for 40 years a clerk in the South-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>; and at length arrived at his acmé there, being appointed chief clerk of the Stock and New <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANNUITIES">Annuities</a>, which office he retained till his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. He was appointed one of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TRUSTEES">trustees</a> for establishing the colony of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEORGIA">Georgia</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>; and was also one of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of assistants of the Scots corporation in London. The time of the publication of his "Historical and Chronological Deduction of Trade and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">Commerce</a>," a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> replete with useful information, was about the year 1762. He was thrice married; and by the first wife he had issue a daughter. She was, like him, tall and graceful; and her <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> has been thought to have some resemblance to that of the ever-living countess of Desmond, given in Mr Pennant's first Tour in Scotland. Mr Anderson died at his house in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">Red</a>-Lion street, Clerkenwell, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 10, 1775. He had a good library of books, which were sold by his widow, who survived him several years, and died in 1781. Anderson, Alexander, a Scottish mathematician. See Supplement. Anderson, Dr James, an eminent agricultural writer. See Supplement. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANDES">Andes</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> chain of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> in South America, which running from the most northern part of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERU">Peru</a> to the straits of Magellan, between 3000 and 4000 miles, are the longest and most remarkable in the world. The Spaniards call them the Cordillera de los Andes. They form two ridges, the lowermost of which is overspread with woods and groves, and the uppermost covered with everlasting snow. Those who have been at the top, affirm, that the sky is always serene and bright; the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a> and piercing; and yet so thin, that they were scarce able to breathe, and the respiration was much quicker than ordinary; and this is attended with retching and vomiting; which, however, has been considered by some as merely accidental. When they looked downwards, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> was hid by the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a> that hovered on the mountain sides. The mountains <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> mentioned, which have been frequently ascended, are much inferior in height to many others in this enormous chain. The following is the account given of the mountain called Pichincha, by the mathematicians sent by the kings of France and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> to make observations in relation to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. Soon after our artists arrived at Quito, they determined to continue the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of the triangles for measuring an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> of the meridian to the south of that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>: the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> accordingly divided themselves into two bodies, consisting of French and Spaniards, and each retired to the part assigned them. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DON">Don</a> George Juan and M. Godin, who were at the head of one party, went to the mountain of Pamamarca; while M. Bouguer, de la Condamine, and Don Ulloa, together with their assistants, climbed up to the highest summit of Pichincha. Both parties suffered extremely, as well from the severity of the cold as from the impetuosity of the winds, which on these heights blow with incessant violence; difficulties the more painful, as they had been little used to such sensations. Thus in the torrid zone, nearly under the equinoctial, where it is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> to suppose they had most to fear from the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, their greatest pain was caused by the excessiveness of the cold. Their first scheme for shelter and lodging in these uncomfortable regions, was to pitch a field-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TENT">tent</a> for each company; but on Pichincha this could not be done from the narrowness of the summit; they were therefore obliged to be contented with a hut so small that they could hardly all creep into it. Nor <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> this appear strange, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the reader considers the bad disposition and smallness of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, it being one of the loftiest crags of a rocky mountain, 100 fathoms above the highest part of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DESERT">desert</a> of Pichincha. Such was the situation of their mansion, which, like all the other adjacent parts, soon became covered with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ICE">ice</a> and snow. The ascent up this stupendous rock, from the base <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the place where the mules could come, to their habitation was so craggy as only to be climbed on foot; and to perform it cost them four hours continual labour and pain, from the violent efforts of the body, and the subtlety of the air; the latter being such as to render respiration difficult. The strange manner of living to which our artists were reduced during the time they were employed in a geometrical <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MENSURATION">mensuration</a> of some degrees of the meridian, may not perhaps prove unentertaining to the reader; and therefore the following account is given as a specimen of it. The desert of Pichincha, both with regard to the operations performed there and its inconveniences, differing very little from others, an idea may be very easily formed of the fatigues, hardships, and dangers, to which they were continually exposed during the time they were prosecuting the enterprise, with the conduct of which they had been honoured. The principal <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between the several deserts consisted in their greater or lesser distance from places where they could procure <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>; and in the inclemency of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, which was proportionate to the height of the mountains, and the season of the year. They generally kept within their hut. Indeed they were obliged to do this, both on account of the intenseness of the cold, the violence of the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, and their being continually involved in so thick a fog, that an object at six or eight paces was hardly discernible. When the fog cleared up, the clouds by their gravity moved nearer to the surface of the earth, and on all sides surrounded the mountains to a vast distance, representing the sea, with their rock like an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the centre of it. When this happened, they heard the horrid noises of the tempests, which then discharged themselves on Quito and the neighbouring country. They <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> the lightnings issue from the clouds, and heard the thunders roll far beneath them; and whilst the lower parts were involved in tempests of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>, they enjoyed a delightful serenity; the wind was abated, the sky clear, and the enlivening rays of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> moderated the severity of the cold. But their circumstances were very different when the clouds rose; their thickness rendered respiration difficult; the snow and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIL">hail</a> fell continually; and the wind returned with all Andes all its violence; so that it was impossible entirely to overcome the fears of being, together with their hut, blown <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the precipice, on whose edge it was built, or of being buried under it by the daily accumulations of ice and snow. The wind was often so violent in these regions, that its velocity dazzled the sight, whilst their fears were increased from the dreadful concussions of the precipice, caused by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> of enormous fragments of rocks. These crashes were the more alarming, as no other noises are heard in these deserts; and during the night, their rest, which they so greatly wanted, was frequently disturbed by such sudden sounds. When the weather was anything fair with them, and the clouds gathered about some of the other mountains which had a connection with their observations, so that they could not make all the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> they desired of this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> of good weather, they left their hut to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> themselves. Sometimes they descended to some small distance; and at others, amused themselves with rolling <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> fragments of rocks down the precipice; and these frequently required the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> strength of them all, though they often saw the same effected by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> force of the wind. But they always took care in their excursions not to go so far out, but that on the least appearance of the clouds gathering about their cottage, which often happened very suddenly, they could regain their shelter. The door of their hut was fastened with thongs of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, and on the inside not the smallest crevice was left unstopped; besides which, it was very compactly covered with straw: but notwithstanding all their care, the wind penetrated through. The days were often little better than the nights; and all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> they enjoyed was that of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAMP">lamp</a> or two, which they kept continually <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a>. Though their hut was small, and crowded with inhabitants, besides the heat of the lamps; yet the intensity of the cold was such, that every one of them was obliged to have a chafing-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DISH">dish</a> of coals. These precautions would have rendered the rigour of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> supportable, had not the imminent danger of perishing by being blown down the precipice roused them, every time it snowed, to encounter the severity of the outward air, and sally out with shovels to free the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> of their hut from the masses of snow which were gathering on it. Nor would it, without this precaution, have been able to support the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>. They were not indeed without servants and Indians; but these were so benumbed with the cold, that it was with great difficulty they could get them out of a small tent, where they kept a continual fire. So that all our artists could obtain from them was to take their turns in this labour; and even then they went very unwillingly about it, and consequently performed it slowly. It may easily be conceived what this company suffered from the asperities of such a climate. Their feet were swelled, and so tender, that they could not even bear the heat; and walking was attended with <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> pain. Their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> were covered with chilblains; their lips swelled and chopped; so that every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> in speaking, or the like, drew blood; consequently they were obliged to strict taciturnity, and little disposed to laugh, as, by causing an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENSION">extension</a> of the lips, it produced such fissures as were very painful for two or three days after. Their common food in this inhospitable region was Andes, a little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a> boiled with some <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> or fowl procured from Quito; and, instead of fluid <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, their pot was filled with ice. They had the same resource with regard to what they drank; and while they were eating, every one was obliged to keep his plate over a chafing-dish of coals, to prevent his provisions from freezing. The same was done with regard to the water. At first they imagined the drinking strong liquors would diffuse a heat through the body, and consequently render it less sensible of the painful sharpness of the cold; but, to their surprise, they felt no manner of strength in such liquors, nor were they any greater preservative against the cold than common water. At the same time, they found it impossible to keep the Indians together. On their first feeling of the climate, their thoughts were immediately turned on deserting their masters. The first instance they had of this kind was so unexpected, that had not one, of a better disposition than the rest, staid and acquainted them of their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, it might have proved of very bad <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>. The affair was this: There being on the top of the rock no room for pitching a tent for the Indians, they used every evening to retire to a cave at the foot of the mountain; where, besides a natural diminution of the cold, they could keep a continual fire; and consequently enjoyed more comfortable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> than their masters. Before they withdrew at night, they fastened on the outside the door of the hut, which was so low that it was impossible to go in or out without stooping; and as every night the hail and snow which had fallen formed a wall against the door, it was the business of one or two of the Indians to come early and remove this obstruction. For though the negro servants were lodged in a little tent, their hands and feet were so covered with chilblains, that they would rather have suffered themselves to have been killed than move. The Indians therefore came constantly up to despatch this work betwixt <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> and ten in the morning; but they had not been there above four or five days, when they were not a little alarmed to see ten, eleven, and twelve o'clock come, without any news of their labourers; when they were relieved by the honest <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> mentioned above, who had withstood the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-SEDUCTION">seduction</a> of his countrymen, and informed his masters of the desertion of the four others. As soon as the snow was cleared away from the door, they despatched the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> to the corregidor of Quito, who with equal despatch sent other Indians, threatening to chastise them severely if they were wanting in their duty. But the fear of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> was not sufficient to induce them to support the rigour of this situation; for within two days they deserted. The corregidor therefore, to prevent any other inconvenience, sent four Indians under the care of an alcade, and gave orders for their being relieved every fourth <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>. Twenty-three tedious days our artists spent on this rock, viz. to the sixth of September; and even without any possibility of finishing their observations of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a>: for when it was fair and clear weather with them, the others, on whose summits the signals which formed the triangles for measuring the degrees of the meridian, were hid in the clouds; and when those were clear, Pichincha was involved in clouds. It was therefore necessary to erect their signals in a lower situation, and and in a more favourable region. This, however, did not produce any change in their habitation till the beginning of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a>; when, having finished the observations which particularly concerned Pichincha, they proceeded to others; but with no abatement either of inconveniences, cold, or fatigue; for the places where they made their observations being necessarily on the highest parts of the deserts, the only respite in which they enjoyed some little ease was during the short interval of passing from one to the other. In all their stations subsequent to that on Pichincha, during their fatiguing mensuration of the degrees of the meridian, each company lodged in a field-tent, which, though small, they found less inconvenient than the hut on Pichincha; though at the same time they had more trouble, being oftener obliged to clear it from the snow, as the weight of it would otherwise have demolished the tent. At first, indeed, they pitched it in the most sheltered places; but on taking a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> that the tents themselves should serve for signals, to prevent the inconvenience of having others of wood, they removed them to a more exposed situation, where the impetuosity of the winds sometimes tore up the piquets, and blew them down. Though this mountain is famous for its great height, it is considerably lower than the mountain of Cotopaxi: but it is impossible to conceive the coldness of the summit of the last-mentioned mountain from that felt on this; since it must exceed every idea that can be formed by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> mind, though they are both seated in the midst of the torrid zone. In all this range of mountains, there is said to be a constant inferior boundary, beyond which the snow never melts: this boundary, in the midst of the torrid zone, is said by some to be 2434 fathoms above the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> of the sea; by others, only 2400 fathoms. The snow indeed falls much lower, but then it is subject to be melted the very same day. According to Humboldt, there are in the Andes 40 volcanoes or burning mountains, which throw out fire and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a> with a terrible noise. The height of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIMBORAZO">Chimborazo</a>, said to be the highest peak of the Andes, has been determined by geometrical calculations to be 20,282 feet. Humboldt, who visited this region in 1802, found the height of the volcanic cone of Tunguragua to be 16,500 feet; the summit of Pichincha 15,840 feet; that of Antisana 19,150 feet. The dreadful volcano of Cotopaxi is only 260 feet lower than this last. Such is the climate on these mountains, that the region adapted to the growth of all kinds of European grain is between 6000 and 9000 feet above the level of the sea. The limit of perpetual congelation under the equator, has been fixed by Humboldt at 15,700 feet. On the declivity of the Andes, at the height of from 3000 to 5000 feet, there reigns a perpetual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> temperature, which never varies more than <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> or nine degrees of Fahrenheit. The Andes give birth to a vast <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, some of which are very large. Some hurry along with a prodigious rapidity; while others form beautiful cascades, or run through holes in rocks, which look like bridges of a stupendous height. There is a public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> through the mountains, 1000 miles in length, part of which runs from Quito to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSCO">Cusco</a>. See ANDES, Supplement.

ANDES

Pages 369-369

a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAMLET">hamlet</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANTUA">Mantua</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, the birthplace of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>. Hence the epithet Andinus (Silvus Italicus). Now called Pietola, two miles to the west of Mantua. ANDETRIUM; ANDRETUM (Strabo); ANDERCRIUM, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> ANDRECUM (<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>): An inland town of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DALMATIA">Dalmatia</a>. The genuine name is Andetrium (Inscription). It is described as situated near <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALONA">Salona</a>, on a naturally strong and inaccessible rock, surrounded with deep valleys, with rapid torrents; from which it appears to be the citadel now called Clissa. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 17° 46'. N. Lat. 43° 20'.

ANDEUSE

Pages 369-369

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUEDOC">Languedoc</a> in France, situated in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3° 40', and N. Lat. 43° 45'. ANDOMADUNUM; ANDOMATUNUM (<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>); and ANTEMATUNUM (Antonine); CIVITAS LINGONUM (Tacitus): A city of Gallia <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELGICA">Belgica</a>; now <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGRES">Langres</a> in Champagne, situated on an eminence (which seems to justify the termination danum), on the borders of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BURGUNDY">Burgundy</a>, at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARNE">Marne</a>. Tacitus calls an inhabitant Lingon. E. Long. 5° 22'. N. Lat. 48° 0'.

ANDOVER

Pages 369-369

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> market town in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HAMPSHIRE">Hampshire</a>, which is situated on a branch of the river Test. It has several inns, which afford good accommodation for travellers; and has a market on Saturday, well stocked with <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>. It is governed by a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAILIFF">bailiff</a>, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STEWARD">steward</a>, a recorder, ten approved men, and twenty-two <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> burgesses, who yearly choose the bailiff. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">Population</a> 3205 in 1811. The living is a vicarage valued at £171. 4s. 4d. in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s books. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 0° 56'. N. Lat. 51° 22'.

ANDRADA

Pages 369-369

DIEGO DE PAYVA D', <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> ANDRADIUS, a learned Portuguese, born at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COIMBRA">Coimbra</a>, who distinguished himself at the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRENT">Trent</a>, where <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> Sebastian sent him as one of his divines. There is scarce any Catholic author who has been more quoted by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a> than he, because he maintained some opinions a little extravagant concerning the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALVATION">salvation</a> of the Heathens. Andrada was esteemed an excellent preacher. His sermons were published in three parts, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> of which was translated into Spanish by Benedict de <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALCORAN">Alcoran</a>. Many encomiums have been bestowed upon Andrada. Osorius, in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREFACE">preface</a> to the "Orthodox Explanations of Andradius," gives him the character of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a>, vast application, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> knowledge in the languages, with all the zeal and eloquence necessary to a good preacher; and Rosweidus says, that he brought to the council of Trent the understanding of a most profound divine, and the eloquence of a consummate orator.

ANDRAPODISMUS

Pages 369-369

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> writers, the selling of persons for slaves. Hence also andrapodistes, a dealer in slaves, more particularly a kidnapper, who steals men <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> children to sell them; a crime for which the Thessalians were noted.

ANDRAPODOCAPELI

Pages 369-370

in antiquity, a kind of dealers in slaves. The Andrapodocapeli had a particular <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> for taking off moles and the like disfigurements on the faces of the slaves they kept for <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a>, by rubbing them with bran. At <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, several places in the forum were appointed for the sale of slaves. Upon the first <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> of every <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> called Ἀνδραποδοκαπελῆς brought them into the market, and exposed them to sale; the crier standing upon a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> erected for that purpose, called the people together.

ANDREA

Pages 370-370

Sr., a small village on the Malabar <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> in the East Indies, founded originally by the Por- tuguese. It takes its name from a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> dedicated to St Andrew, and served by the priests of St Tho- mas.—On the shore of St Andrea, about half a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> out in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, lies Mud-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> which few in the world can <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a>. It is open to the wide ocean, and has neither <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> nor <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> the force of the billows, which come rolling with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> violence from all parts, in the south-west monsoons; but on this bank of mud they lose themselves in a moment; and ships <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> on it as secure as in the best harbour, without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> disturbance. It reaches about a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a> along shore, and has been observed to shift its place from the northward about three miles in 30 years. From St Andrea to Kranganor, about twelve leagues to the south, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> has the bad <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of causing swellings in the legs of those who drink it constantly. Some it affects in one leg, and some in both. It causes no pain, but itching; nor does the swelled leg seem heavier to the owner than the small one, though some have been seen a yard in circumfe- rence at the ankle. The Roman legends impute the cause of this distemper (for which no preventive or cure hath been hitherto found) to a curse laid by St Thomas upon his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MURDERERS">murderers</a> and their posterity; though, according to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> themselves, St Thomas was killed by the Tillinga priests at Meliapour, on the coast of Coromandel, about 400 miles distant, and where the natives have not this distemper.

ANDREAS

Pages 370-371

John, was born a Mahometan, at Xati- va in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VALENCIA">Valencia</a>, and succeeded his fa- ther in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of alfaqui of that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>. He was enlightened with the knowledge of the Christian reli- gion by being present at a sermon in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Valencia on the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASSUMPTION">Assumption</a> of the Blessed Virgin, in the year 1487. Upon this he desired to be baptized; and, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of the calling of St John and St Andrew, he received the name John Andreas. "Having received holy orders (says he), and from an alfaqui and a slave of Lucifer, become a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> and minister of Christ; I began, like St Paul, to preach and publish the contrary of what I had erroneously be- lieved and asserted; and, with the assistance of Al- mighty God, I converted at first a great many souls of the Moors, who were in danger of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HELL">hell</a>, and under the dominion of Lucifer, and conducted them into the way of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALVATION">salvation</a>. After this, I was sent for by the most catholic princes <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> Ferdinand and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> Isabella, in order to preach in Grenada to the Moors of that kingdom, which their majesties had conquered: by God's blessing on my preaching, an infinite <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of Moors were brought to abjure Mahomet, and to turn to Christ. A little after this, I was made a canon by their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">grace</a>; and sent for again by the most Christian Queen Isabella to Arragon, that I might be employed in the conversion of the Moors of those kingdoms, who still persisted in their errors, to the great contempt and dishonour of our crucified Saviour, and the prodigious loss and danger of all Christian princes. But this ex- cellent and pious <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of her majesty was rendered ineffectual by her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>." At the desire of Martin Garcia, bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARCELONA">Barcelona</a>, he undertook to trans- late from the Arabic, into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of Arragon, the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> of the Moors; and after having finished this undertaking, he composed his famous <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of The Confusion of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">Sect</a> of Mahumed; it contains twelve chapters, chapters, wherein he has collected the fabulous stories, impostures, forgeries, brutalities, follies, obscenities, absurdities, impossibilities, lies, and contradictions, which Mahomet, in order to deceive the simple people, has dispersed in the writings of that sect, and especially in the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALCORAN">Alcoran</a>, which, as he says, was revealed to him in one night by an angel, in the city of Meke; though in another <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> he contradicts himself, and affirms that he was 20 years in composing it. Andreas tells us, he wrote this work, that not only the learned amongst <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, but even the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> people, might know the different <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a> and doctrine of the Moors; and on the one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> might laugh and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIDICULE">ridicule</a> such insolent and brutal notions, and on the other might lament their <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol2.html#article-BLINDNESS">blindness</a> and dangerous condition. This book, which was published at first in Spanish, has been translated into several languages; all those who write against the Mahometans quote it very much.

ANDREINI

Pages 371-371

ISABELLA, a native of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PADUA">Padua</a>, was an excellent poetess, and one of the best comedians in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, towards the beginning of the 17th century. The Intenti of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PAVIA">Pavia</a> thought they did their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> by admitting her a member of it; and she, in acknowledgement of this honour, never forgot to mention amongst her titles that of Academica Infanta; her titles were these, "Isabella Andreini, comica, gelosa, academica infanta, detta l'accessa." She was also a woman of extraordinary <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>: which, added to a fine <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>, made her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARM">charm</a> both the eyes and ears of the audience. She died of a miscarriage, at Lyons, the 10th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1604, in the 42nd year of her <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. Her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> being a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of general concern and lamentation, there were many Latin and Italian elegies printed to her <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>: several of these pieces were placed before her poems in the edition of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a>, in 1605. Besides her sonnets, madrigals, songs, and eclogues, there is a pastoral of hers entitled Myrtila, and letters, printed at <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> in 1610. She sung extremely well, played admirably on several instruments, understood the French and Spanish languages, and was not unacquainted with <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>.

ANDRELINUS

Pages 371-371

PUBLIUS FAUSTUS, born at Forli in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. He was <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> professor of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> in the university of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XII. of France made him his poet laureat; and Erasmus tells us he was likewise poet to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>. His <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEN">pen</a> was not wholly employed in making verses; for he wrote also moral and proverbial letters in prose, which were printed several times. His poems which are chiefly in Latin, are inserted in vol. i. of the Delicie Poetarum Italorum. M. de la Monnoire tells us, "that Andrelinus, when he was about 22 years old, received the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of laurel: That his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> verses, divided into four Books, entitled Livia, from the name of his mistress, were esteemed so fine by the Roman Academy, that they adjudged the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a> of the Latin elegy to the author." He died in 1518. This author's manner of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> was not very exemplary; yet he was so fortunate, says Erasmus, that though he took the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of rallying the divines, he was never brought into trouble about it.

ANDREW

Pages 371-371
or Knights of St ANDREW, an order of knights, more usually called the order of the Thistle. See THISTLE. Knights of St ANDREW, is also an order instituted by Peter the Great of Muscovy in 1668; the badge of which is a golden medal; on one side whereof is represented St Andrew's cross, with these words, Cazar Pierre monarque de tout le Russie. This medal, being fastened to a blue ribbon, is suspended from the right shoulder. St ANDREW'S Cross, one in form of the letter X. See CROSS. St ANDREW'S Day, a festival of the Christian church, celebrated on the 30th of November, in honour of the apostle St Andrew.

ANDREW'S

Pages 371-375

Sr, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIFESHIRE">Fifeshire</a> in Scotland, once the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a> of the Pictish <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, lying in W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2. 25. N. Lat. 56. 18. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> we may <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEGEND">legend</a>, St Andrew's owes its origin to a singular accident. St Regulus (<a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Rule, as he is likewise called), a Greek of Achaia, was warned by a vision to leave his native <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and visit <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBION">Albion</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> placed in the remotest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the world; and to take with him the arm-bone, three fingers, and three toes, of St Andrew. He obeyed, and set sail with his companions, but had a very tempestuous passage. After being tossed for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> on a stormy <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, he was at last shipwrecked on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Otholania, in the territories of Her gustus <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of the Picts, in the year 370. On hear- Andrew's, ing of the arrival of the strangers, with their precious relics, the king immediately gave orders for their reception, afterwards presenting the saint with his own <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> near it the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, which still bears the name of St Regulus. At this time the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> was styled Mucross, or the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> of boars: all round was forest, and the lands bestowed on the saint were called Byrehid. The boars equalled in size the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Erymanthian; as a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of which, two tusks, each sixteen inches long and four thick, were chained to the altar of St Andrew's. St Regulus changed the name to Kilrymont; and established here the first Christian priests of the country, called Culdees. The church was supreme in the kingdom of the Picts; Ungus having granted to God and St Andrew, that it should be the head and mother of all the churches in his dominion. He also directed that the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> of St Andrew should become the badge of the country. In 518, after the conquest of the Picts, he removed the episcopal see to St Andrew's, and the bishop was styled maximus Sotorum episcopus. In 1441, it was erected into an archbishopric by Sextus IV. at the intercession of James III. In 1616, the priory was suppressed; and, in 1617, the power of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> was transferred to eight <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of St Leonard's <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, the archdeacon, the vicars of St Andrew's, Leuchars, and Cupar. This see contained the greatest part of the shire of Fife, with a part of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERTH">Perth</a>, Forfar, and Kincairdine shires, and a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of parishes, churches, and chapels in other dioceses. The town of St Andrew's was erected into a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> borough by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a> I. in the year 1140, and its privileges afterwards confirmed. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a> of Malcolm II. is preserved in the tolbooth; and appears written on a bit of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARCHMENT">parchment</a>, but the contents equally valid with what would at this time require whole skins. Here also are kept the silver keys of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>; which, for form's sake, are delivered to the king, if he should visit the place, or to a victorious enemy, in token of submission. In this place, likewise, is to be seen the monstrous axe which, in 1646, took off the heads of Sir Robert Spotswood and other distinguished loyalists. The town underwent a siege in 1337; at which time it was possessed by the English and other partizans of Baliol; but the loyalists, under the earls of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> and Fife, made themselves masters of it in three weeks, by the help of their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTERING">battering</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MACHINES">machines</a>. St Andrew's is now greatly reduced in the number of its inhabitants. In 1811 they were about 3300. It is impossible to ascertain the sum when it was the seat of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIMATE">primate</a>; all that can be known is, that during the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of its splendour, there were between sixty and seventy <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-BAKERS">bakers</a>; but now <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> or ten are sufficient for the place. It is a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a> in circuit, and contains three principal streets. On entering the west port, a well built street, straight, and of a vast length and breadth, appears; but so grass-grown, and presenting such a dreary solitude, that it forms the perfect idea of having been laid waste by the pestilence. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> of St Andrew's was founded by Bishop Arnold in 1161, but did not attain its full magnificence till 1318. Its length from east to west was 370 feet; that of the transept, 322. But though this vast pile was 157 years in building, John Knox, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1559, effected its demolition in a single <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>; and so effectually has it been destroyed, that nothing now remains but part of the east and west ends, and of the south side. Near the east end is the chapel of St Regulus; the tower of which is a lofty equilateral triangle, of 20 feet each side, and 103 feet <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>; the body of the chapel remains, but the two side chapels are ruined. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a> of the windows and doors are round, and some even more than semicircles; an undoubted proof of their antiquity. The priory was founded by Alexander I. in 1122; and the monks (canons regular of St Augustine) were brought from Scone in 1140, by Robert bishop of this see. By an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">Parliament</a>, in the time of James I., the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> had precedence of all abbots and priors, and on the days of festival wore a mitre and all episcopal ornaments. Dependent on this priory were those of Lochleven, Portmoak, Monimusk, the isle of May, and Pittenweem, each originally a seat of the Culdees. The revenues of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> were vast, viz. in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> 2237l. 2s. 10½d.; 38 chalders 1 boll 3 firlots of wheat; 132 ch. 7 bolls of bear; 114 ch. 3 bolls 1 peck of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAL">meal</a>; 151 ch. 10 bolls 1 <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIRLOT">firlot</a> 1 peck and a half of oats; 3 ch. 7 bolls of pease and beans; 480 acres of land also belonged to it. Nothing remains of the priory except the walls of the precinct, which show its vast <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>. In one part is a most artless gateway, formed only of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>. This enclosure begins near the cathedral, and extends to the shore. The other <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> houses were, one of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMINICANS">Dominicans</a> founded in 1274, by Bishop Wishart; another of Observantines, founded by Bishop Kennedy, and finished by his successor Patrick Graham in 1478; and, according to some, the Carmelites had a fourth. Immediately above the harbour stood the collegiate church of Kirk-heugh, originally founded by Constantine III. who, retiring from the world, became here a Culdee. From its having been first built on a rock, it was styled, Propositura Sanctae MARIE de rupe. On the east side of the city are the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> remains of the castle, on a rock overlooking the sea. This fortress was founded in 1481, by Bishop Trail, who was buried near the high altar of the cathedral, with this singular epitaph: Hic fuit ecclesia directa columna, fenestra <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-LUCIDA">Lucida</a>, thuribulum redolens, campana sonora. The castle was the residence of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Beaton; who, after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of George Wishart, apprehending some danger, caused it to be fortified so strongly as to be at that time deemed impregnable. In this fortress, however, he was surprised and assassinated by Norman Lesly with 15 others. They seized on the gate of the castle early in the morning of May 29, 1546; it having been left open for the workmen who were finishing the fortifications: and having placed sentinels at the door of the cardinal's apartment, they awakened his numerous domestics one by one; and, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> them out of the castle, they, without violence, tumult, or offering an injury to any other person, inflicted on Beaton the death he justly merited. The conspirators were immediately besieged in this castle by the regent, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARRAN">Arran</a>; and notwithstanding they had acquired no greater strength than 150 men, they resisted all his efforts for five months. This, however, was owing to Andrew's, the unskilfulness of the besiegers more than to the strength of the place or the valour of the besieged; for in 1547 the castle was reduced and demolished. The entrance of it is still to be seen; and the window is shown, out of which it is said the cardinal leaned to glut his eyes with the cruel martyrdom of George Wishart, who was burnt on a spot beneath. In the church of St Salvator is a most beautiful <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> of Bishop Kennedy, who died, an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to his family, in 1466. The Gothic <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> is uncommonly elegant. Within the tomb were discovered six magnificent maces, which had been concealed here in troublesome times. One was given to each of the other three Scotch <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a>, and three are preserved here. In the top is represented our Saviour; around are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGELS">angels</a>, with the instruments of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>. With these are shown some silver arrows, with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> silver plates affixed to them, on which are <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSCRIBED">inscribed</a> the arms and names of the noble youth, victors in the annual competitions in the generous art of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHERY">archery</a>, which were dropt but a few years ago; and golf is now the reigning <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAME">game</a>. That sport, and foot-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a>, were formerly prohibited, as useless and unprofitable to the public; and at all weapon schawings, or reviews of the people, it was ordered, that fute-ball and golfe be utterly cryed <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, and that bowe-markes be made at ilk <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> kirk, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of batts and schutting be used; and that ilk <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> schute <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEX">sex</a> shottes at least, under the paine to be raiped upon them that cummes not, at least twa pennyes to be given to them that cummis to the bowmarkes to drink. The celebrated university of this city was founded in 1411, by Bishop Wardlaw. It consisted once of three colleges. 1. St Salvator's, founded in 1458, by Bishop Kennedy. This is a handsome building, with a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> or quadrangle within: on one side is the church, on another the library; the third contains apartments for students: the fourth is unfinished. 2. St Leonard's college was founded by Prior Hepburn, in 1522. This is now united with the last, and the buildings sold, and converted into private houses. 3. The new, or St <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>'s college, was established by Archbishop <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAMILTON">Hamilton</a> in 1552; but the house was built by James and David Bethune, or Beaton, who did not live to complete it. This is said to have been the site of a schola illustris long before the establishment even of the university, where several eminent clergymen taught, gratis, the sciences and languages. But it was called the new college, because of its late erection into a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> college by the archbishop. The university is governed by a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a>, an office originally designed to be perpetually vested in the archbishop of St Andrews; but since the Reformation, he is elected by the two principals, and the professors of both the colleges. The rector is the next great officer; to whose care are committed the privileges, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a>, and statutes of the university. The colleges have their rectors, and professors of different sciences, who are indefatigable in their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to the instruction of the students, and to that essential article their morals. The place possesses several very great advantages respecting the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> of youth. The <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> is pure and salubrious; the place for <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a>, dry and extensive; the exercises themselves are healthy and innocent. The university is fixed in a peninsulated country; remote from all <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> with the world, the haunt of dissipation.
