From the smallness of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, every student's character is perfectly known. No little irregularity can be committed, but it is instantly discovered and checked: vice cannot attain a head in this place, for the incorrigible are never permitted to remain the corrupters of the rest. The trade of St Andrew's was once very considerable. So late as the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I, this place had thirty or forty trading vessels, and carried on a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERRING">herring</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> fishery, by means of busses, in deep <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>; which <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FISHERIES">fisheries</a> had for ages been the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> source of their commerce, wealth, and splendour. After the death of the king, this whole coast, and St Andrew's in particular, became a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a>, plunder, and rapine: every town suffered in proportion to its magnitude and opulence. Nor were those hypocritical ruffians satisfied with the shipping, merchandise, plate, cattle, and whatever came within their sight; they also laid the whole coast under contribution. St Andrew's was required to pay 1000l.; but the inhabitants not being able to raise that sum after being thus plundered, the general compounded for 500l. which was raised by a loan at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>, and hath remained a burden upon the corporation, it is believed, ever since. The harbour is <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a>, guarded by piers, with a narrow entrance, to give shelter to vessels from the violence of a very heavy sea, by the encroachments of which it has suffered much. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> this city might in former times possess, are now reduced to one, that of golf balls; which, trifling as it may seem, maintains a great number of people. It is, however, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> fatal to the artists; for the balls are made by stuffing a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of feathers into a leathern <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, by help of an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> rod, with a wooden handle, pressed against the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>, which seldom fails to bring on a consumption. Andrews, Lancelot, bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINCHESTER">Winchester</a>, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> in 1555, and educated at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>. After several preferments, he was made bishop, first of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHICHESTER">Chichester</a>, then of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELY">Ely</a>, and, in 1610, was raised to the see of Winchester. This very learned prelate, who was distinguished by his piety, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a>, and integrity, may be justly ranked with the best preachers and completest scholars of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>; he appeared to much greater advantage in the pulpit than he does now in his works, which abound with Latin quotations and trivial witticisms. His sermons, though full of puns, were suited to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> of the times in which he lived, and were consequently greatly admired. He was a man of polite manners and lively conversation; and could quote Greek and Latin authors, or even pun, with King James. There is a pleasant story related of him in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of Waller the poet. When that <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> was young, he had the curiosity to go to court, and stood in the circle to see King James dine; where, among other <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>, there sat at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> two bishops, Neale and Andrews. The king proposed aloud this question, Whether he might not take his subjects money when he needed it, without all this formality of parliament? Neale replied, "God forbid you should not; for you are the breath of our nostrils." Whereupon the king turned, and said to the bishop of Winchester, "Well, my <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a>, what Andrews say you?" "Sir (replied the bishop), I have no skill to judge of parliamentary <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>." The king answered, "No put-offs, my lord; answer me presently." "Then, Sir (said he), I think it lawful for you to take my <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Neale's money, for he offers it." Mr Wal-ler says, the company was pleased with this answer, but the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a> of it seemed to affect the king; for a certain lord coming soon after, his majesty cried out, "O, my lord, they say you lig with my lady." "No, Sir (says his lordship, in confusion), but I like her company because she has so much wit." "Why then (says the king) do not you lig with my lord of Winchester there?" This great prelate was in no less reputation and esteem with King Charles I. than he had been with his predecessors. He died at Winchester house in Southwark, September 27. 1626, in the 71st year of his age; and was buried in the parish church of St Saviour's, where his executors erected to him a very fair monument of marble and alabaster, on which is an elegant inscription, in Latin, written by one of his chaplains. <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILTON">Milton</a> also, at 17 years of age, wrote a beautiful elegy on his death, in the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. Bishop Andrews had, 1. A share in the translation of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENTATEUCH">Pentateuch</a>, and the historical books from Joshua to the first book of Chronicles exclusively. He also wrote, 2. Tortura Torri, in answer to a work of Cardinal Bel-larmine, in which that cardinal assumes the name of Matthew Tortus. 3. A <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MANUAL">Manual</a> of Private Devotions; and, 4. A Manual of Directions for the Visitation of the Sick; besides the Sermons and Tracts, in English and Latin, published after his death. Andrews, James Pettit, a late English writer. See Supplement. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANDRIA">Andria</a>, in Grecian antiquity, public entertainments first instituted by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINOS">Minos</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a>, and, after his example, appointed by <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LYCURGUS">Lycurgus</a> at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SPARTA">Sparta</a>, at which a whole city or a tribe assisted. They were managed with the utmost frugality; and persons of all ages were admitted. Andria, a city and a bishop's see in the territory of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARI">Bari</a>, in the kingdom of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>. It is pretty large, well peopled, and seated in a spacious plain, four miles from the Adriatic coast. E. Long. 17.4. N. Lat. 41.15. Andriscus, a man of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTRACTION">extraction</a>, who pretended to be the son of Perseus last king of Macedon, took upon him the name of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a>, for which reason he was called Pseudo-Philippus, the False Philip. After a complete victory over Juventus, the Roman prætor sent against him, he assumed kingly power, but exercised it with vast cruelty. At last, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> obliged him to fly into Thrace, where he was betrayed and delivered into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of Metellus. This victory gained <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MACEDONIA">Macedonia</a> once more into the power of the Romans, and to Metellus the name of Macedonicus, but cost the Romans 25,000 men. Andriscus adorned the triumph of Metellus, walking in chains before the general's chariot. Androas, or Androdamas, among ancient naturalists, a kind of pyrite, to which they attributed certain magical virtues. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANDROGEUS">Androgeus</a>, in fabulous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, the son of Minos king of Crete, was murdered by the Athenian youth and those of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEGARA">Megara</a>, who envied his being always victor at the Attic games. But Minos having taken <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a> and Megara, obliged the inhabitants to send him an annual tribute of seven young men and as many virgins, to be devoured by the Minotaur; but <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THESEUS">Theseus</a> delivered them from that tribute. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANDROGYNES">Androgynes</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> History, a name given to those living creatures which, by a monstrous formation of their generative parts, seem (for it is only seeming) to unite in themselves the two sexes, that of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MALE">male</a> and of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a>. This lusus naturæ, this defect, or perhaps redundancy, in the animal structure, is described by medical authors in the following manner: "There is a depravation in the structure of the parts intended by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> for propagation, when, besides those concealed parts that are found necessary for the discharge of prolific functions, the pudenda of the other sex likewise appear. This monstrous production of nature is diversified in four different ways; of which three appear in males and one in females. In men, the female pudendum, clothed with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, sometimes appears contiguous to the perineum; at other times, in the middle of the scrotum; at other times, which constitutes the third diversity, through that part itself which in the midst of the scrotum exhibits the form of a pudendum, urine is emitted. Near that part which is the test of puberty, and above the pudendum, even in females, the masculine genitals appear in some conspicuous in all their three forms, one resembling the veretrum or yard, the other like the two testicles: but for the most part it happens, that, of the two instruments of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a>, one is feeble and inert; and it is extremely rare that both are found sufficiently valid and proper for feats of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a>: nay, even in a great many, both these members are deficient and impotent, so that they can perform the office neither of a male nor of a female." With respect to them, it appears, from a collation of all the circumstances which have been observed by naturalists worthy of credit, that there is no such thing as a perfect androgyne, or real hermaphrodite; that is to say, a living creature, which, by its unnatural, or rather preternatural structure, possesses the genuine powers of both sexes, in such a manner as to be qualified for performing the functions of either with success: the irregularity of their fabrication almost always consists in something superfluous added to one of the two sexes, which gives it the appearance of the other, without bestowing the real and characteristical distinction; and every hermaphrodite is almost always a very woman. Since this monstrous <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXHIBITION">exhibition</a> of nature is not such as to abrogate the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> or destroy the character of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> amongst <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> beings, this involuntary misfortune implies no <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to deprive those upon whom it is inflicted by nature of the privileges natural to every citizen; and as this deficiency is no more infectious than any other corporeal mutilation, it is not easy to see why <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> should be prohibited to one of these unhappy beings, merely on account of its equivocal appearance, which acts in the character of its prevailing sex. If such a creature, by the defect of its <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a>, should be barren, this does not infer any right of dissolving the marriage which it may have contracted, more than the same sterility proceeding from any cause whether known or unknown, if his or her consort should not on that account require a divorce. It is only the licentious abuse either of one or the other sex which can be subjected to the animadversion of the <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol18.html#article-POLICE">police</a>. See HERMAPHRODITE. Such are the sentiments of the authors of the French Encyclopédie. After all, we cannot forbear to add that from such <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HETEROGENEOUS">heterogeneous</a> matches nature seems to recoil with innate and inextinguishable horror. Nor are any of these invincible aversions implanted in our frame without a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FINAL">final</a> cause worthy of its Author. We would gladly ask these free-thinking gentlemen, In cases where the sexes are so unnaturally confounded, how the police can, by its most severe and rigorous animadversions, either detect or prevent those licentious abuses against which they remonstrate? Since, therefore, an evil so baneful to human society could no otherwise be prevented than by the sanction of Nature against such horrible conjunctions, the instinctive antipathy which they inspire was highly worthy of her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> and purity.

ANDROGYNES

Pages 375-375

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">mythology</a>, creatures of whom, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FABLE">fable</a>, each individual possessed the powers and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> of both sexes, having two heads, four arms, and two feet. The word itself is compounded of two Greek radical words; ἀνήρ, in genitive ἀνδρός, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MALE">male</a>; and γυνή, a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a>. Many of the rabbinical writers pretend, that <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADAM">Adam</a> was created <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a>, one body being male, the other female, which in their origin not being essentially joined, God afterwards did nothing but separate them. The gods, says <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a> in his Banquet, had formed the structure of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> round, with two bodies and two sexes. This fantastic being, possessing in itself the whole <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> system, was endowed with a gigantic force, which rendered it insolent, insomuch that it resolved to make <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> against the gods. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>, exasperated, was going to destroy it; but, sorry at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to annihilate the human <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a>, he satisfied himself with debilitating this double being, by disjoining the male from the female, and leaving each half to subsist with its own powers alone. He assigned to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a> the task of repolishing these two half bodies, and of extending their skins so that the whole surface might be covered. Apollo obeyed, and fastened it at the umbilicus: <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> this half should still rebel, it was once more to be subdivided by another <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECTION">section</a>, which would only leave it one of the parts of which it was then constituted; and even this fourth of a man was to be annihilated, if it should persist in its obstinacy and mischief. The idea of these androgynes might well be borrowed from a passage in Moses, where that historian of the birth and infancy of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, describes Adam as calling <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVE">Eve</a> bone of his bone and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> of his flesh. However this may be, the fable of Plato has been used with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> ingenuity by a French poet, who has been rendered almost as conspicuous by his misfortunes as by his verses. With the ancient <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, he attributes the propensity which attracts one of the sexes towards the other, to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> ardour which each half of the androgynes feels for reunion; and their inconstancy, to the difficulty which each of the separated parts encounters in its efforts to recover its proper and original half. If a woman appears to us amiable, we instantly imagine her to be that moiety with whom we should only have constituted one whole, had it not been for the insolence of our original double-sexed progenitor: The heart, with fond credulity impress'd, Tells us the half is found, and hopes for rest; But 'tis our curse, that sad <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> shows, We neither find our half, nor <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> repose.

ANDROGYNOUS

Pages 375-375

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZOOLOGY">Zoology</a>, an appellation given to animals which have both the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MALE">male</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEX">sex</a> in the same individual.—In <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> is applied to such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> as bear both male and female <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> on the same root.

ANDROIDES

Pages 375-377

in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICS">Mechanics</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, which, by certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other movements, is capable of performing some of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> motions of a living <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>. The motions of the human body are more complicated, and consequently more difficult to be imitated, than those of any other creature; whence the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of an androides, in such a manner as to imitate any of these actions with tolerable exactness, is justly supposed to indicate a greater skill in mechanics than any other piece of workmanship whatever. A very remarkable figure of this kind appeared in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, in the year 1738. It represented a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLUTE">flute</a>-player, and was capable of performing many different pieces of music on the German flute; which, considering the difficulty of blowing that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>, the different contractions of the lips necessary to produce the distinctions between the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> and low notes, and the complicated motions of the fingers, must appear truly wonderful. This machine was the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of M. Vaucanson, member of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> Academy of Sciences; and a particular <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of it was published in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a> of the Academy for that year. The figure itself was about five feet and a half in height, situated at the end of an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> rock, and placed upon a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> pedestal four feet and a half high and three and a half <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> entered the body by three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a> separated one from the other. It was conveyed to them by <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of bellows, three of which were placed above and six below. These were made to expand and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> regularly in succession by means of an axis of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STEEL">steel</a> turned round by some clockwork. On this axis were different protuberances at proper distances, to which were fixed cords thrown over pulleys, and terminating in the upper boards of the bellows, so that, as the axis turned, these boards were alternately raised and let <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>. A contrivance was also used to prevent the disagreeable hissing fluttering noise usually attending the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of bellows. This was by making the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CORD">cord</a>, by which the bellows was moved, press, in its <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a>, upon one end of a smaller <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEVER">lever</a>, the other end of which ascending forced open the small leathern <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VALVE">valve</a> that admitted the air, and kept it so, till, the cord being relaxed by the descent of the upper board, the lever fell, and the air was forced out. Thus the bellows performed their functions constantly without the least hissing, or other noise, by which it could be judged in what manner the air was conveyed to the machine. The upper boards of three of the pairs of bellows were pressed down by a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of four pounds, that of three others by a weight of two pounds, Androides, and those of the three remaining ones by nothing but their own weight. The three tubes, by which the air entered, terminated in three small reservoirs in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a> of the figure. There they united, and, ascending towards the throat, formed the cavity of the mouth, which terminated in two small lips adapted in some <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> to perform their proper functions. Within this cavity also was a small moveable tongue; which, by its play, at proper periods, admitted the air, or intercepted its passage to the flute. The fingers, lips, and tongue, received their proper directions by means of a steel <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CYLINDER">cylinder</a> turned by clockwork. It was divided into 15 equal parts, which by means of pegs pressing upon the ends of 15 different levers, caused the other extremities to ascend. <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">Seven</a> of these levers directed the fingers, having wires and chains affixed to their ascending extremities, which being attached to the fingers, caused them ascend in proportion as the other extremity was pressed down by the motion of the cylinder, and vice versa. Thus the ascent or descent of one end of a lever produced a similar ascent or descent in the corresponding finger, by which one of the holes of the flute was occasionally opened or stopped, as by a living performer. Three of the levers served to regulate the ingress of the air, being contrived so as to open and shut, by means of valves, the three reservoirs of air above mentioned, so that more or less strength might be given, and a higher or lower <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOTE">note</a> produced as occasion required. The lips were, by a similar mechanism, directed by four levers, one of which opened them, to give the air a freer passage; the other contracted them; the third drew them backward; and the fourth pushed them forward. The lips were projected upon that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the flute which receives the air; and, by the different motions already mentioned, modified the tone in a proper manner. The remaining lever was employed in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the tongue, which it easily moved so as to shut or open the mouth of the flute. Thus we see how all the motions necessary for a German flute player could be performed by this machine; but a considerable difficulty still remains, namely, how to regulate these motions properly, and make each of them follow in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> succession. This, however, was effected by the following simple method. The extremity of the axis of the cylinder was terminated on the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> side by an endless screw, consisting of twelve threads, each placed at the distance of a line and a half from the other. Above this screw was fixed a piece of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, and in it a steel pivot, which, falling in between the threads of the screw, obliged the cylinder to follow the threads, and, instead of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> directly round, it was continually pushed to one side. Hence, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a lever was moved, by a peg placed on the cylinder, in any one revolution, it could not be moved by the same peg in the succeeding revolution, because the peg would have moved a line and a half beyond it by the lateral motion of the cylinder. Thus, by an artificial disposition of those pegs in different parts of the cylinder, the statue was made, by the successive elevation of the proper levers, to exhibit all the different motions of a flute-player, to the admiration of every one who <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> it. The construction of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MACHINES">machines</a> capable of imitating even the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> actions of the human body, show Androides exquisite skill; but what shall we say of one capable, not only of imitating actions of this kind, but of acting as <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> circumstances require, as though it were endowed with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> and reason? This, nevertheless, has been done. M. de Kempelen, a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRESBURG">Presburg</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>, excited by the performances of M. de Vaucanson, at first endeavoured to imitate them, and at last far excelled them. This gentleman constructed an androides capable of playing at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHESS">chess</a>!—Every one who is in the least acquainted with this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAME">game</a> must know, that it is so far from being mechanically performed, as to require a greater exertion of the judgment and rational faculties than is sufficient to accomplish many matters of greater importance. An attempt, therefore, to make a wooden chess-player, must appear as ridiculous as to make a wooden preacher or counsellor of state. That this machine really was made, however, the public have had ocular demonstration. The inventor came over to <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> in 1783, where he remained above a year with his automaton. It is a figure as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> as life, in a Turkish dress, sitting behind a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, with doors of three feet and a half in length, two in depth, and two and a half in height. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> on which it sits is fixed to the table, which runs on four <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHEELS">wheels</a>. The automaton leans its right arm on the table, and in its left <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> holds a pipe; with this hand it plays after the pipe is removed. A chess board of 18 inches is fixed before it. This table or rather cupboard, contains wheels, levers, cylinders, and other pieces of mechanism; all which are publicly displayed. The vestments of the automaton are then lifted over its head, and the body is seen full of similar wheels and levers. There is a little door in its thigh, which is likewise opened; and with this, and the table also open, and the automaton uncovered, the whole is wheeled about the room. The doors are then shut, and the automaton is ready to play; and it always takes the first move. At every motion the wheels are heard; the image moves its head, and looks over every part of the chess board. When it checks the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>, it shakes its head twice, and thrice in giving check to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>. It likewise shakes its head when a false move is made, replaces the piece, and makes its own move; by which means the adversary loses one. M. de Kempelen remarks as the most surprising circumstance attending his automaton, that it had been exhibited at Presburg, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIENNA">Vienna</a>, Paris, and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, to thousands, many of whom were mathematicians and chess-players, and yet the secret by which he governed the motion of its arm was never discovered. He prided himself solely in the construction of the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-MECHANICAL_POWERS">mechanical powers</a>, by which the arm could perform ten or twelve moves. It then required to be wound up like a watch, after which it was capable of continuing the same <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of motions. The automaton could not play unless M. de Kempelen or his substitute was near it to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> its moves. A small square box, during the game, was frequently consulted by the exhibitor; and herein consisted the secret, which he said he could in a moment communicate. He who could <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> M. de Kempelen was, of course, certain of conquering the automaton. It was made in 1769. His own account of it was: "C'est "Androidees" C'est une bagatelle qui n'est pas sans mérite du côté du mécanisme : mais les effets n'en paraissent si merveilleux que par la hardiesse de l'idée, et par l'heureux choix des moyens employés pour faire illusion." The strongest and best armed loadstone was allowed to be placed on the machine by any of the spectators. As the inventor of this admirable piece of mechanism hath not yet thought proper to communicate to the public the means by which it is actuated, it is in vain for any, except those who are exquisitely skilled in mechanics, to form conjectures concerning them.—Many other curious imitations of the human body, as well as that of other animals, have been exhibited, though none of them equal to the last mentioned one. See the article AUTOMATON.

ANDROLEPSY

Pages 377-377

in Grecian antiquity, an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> allowed by the Athenians against such as protected persons guilty of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a>. The relations of the deceased were empowered to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEIZE">seize</a> three men in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> whither the malefactor had fled, till he were either surrendered, or satisfaction made some way or other for the murder.

ANDROMACHE

Pages 377-377

the wife of the valiant Hector, the mother of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTYANAX">Astyanax</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Eetion <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Thebes in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CILICIA">Cilicia</a>. After the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Hector and the destruction of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">Troy</a>, she married Pyrrhus; and afterwards Helenus the son of Priam, with whom she reigned over <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of Epirus.

ANDROMEDA

Pages 377-377

the name of a celebrated tragedy of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EURIPIDES">Euripides</a>, admired by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> above all the other compositions of that poet, but now lost. It was the representation of this play, in a hot <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, that occasioned that epidemic fever, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> phrensy, for which the Abderites are often mentioned, wherein they walked about the streets, rehearsing verses, and acting parts of this piece. See <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABDERA">ABDERA</a>.

ANDRON

Pages 377-377

in Grecian antiquity, denotes the apartment in houses designed for the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of men; in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> it stands opposed to Gynaeceum.—The Greeks also gave their dining-rooms the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of andron, because the women had no admittance to feasts with the men.

ANDRONA

Pages 377-379

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> writers, denotes a street, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> public <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, where people met and conversed together. In some writers, androna is more expressly used for the space between two houses; in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, the Greeks also <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> andragoge, for the way or passage between two apartments. ANDRONA is also used, in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> writers, for that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> in churches destined for the men. Anciently it was the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> for the men and women to have separate apartments in places of worship, where they performed their devotions asunder; which method is still Androna, religiously observed in the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. The andgor, or androna, was in the southern side of the church, and the women's apartment on the northern. ANDRONICUS I. COMNENUS, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> of the East, was the son of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a>, and grandson of Alexius Comnenus. Naturally endowed with a vigorous <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> of body, and a firm mind, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a>, temperate, martial, and eloquent, he shines as one of the most conspicuous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. Following the bent of his inclination, he attended the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> in their retreat; but in their <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a> through <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASIA_MINOR"><a class="</a>xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINOR">Minor</a>, wandering into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, he fell into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of some Turkish huntsmen, was carried to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SULTAN">sultan</a>, and remained his prisoner. But regaining his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, both his virtues and vices soon recommended him to the favour of his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUSIN">cousin</a> Manuel, the reigning emperor. The vicious heart of Andronicus manifested itself clearly in maintaining a licentious correspondence with Eudocia the emperor's niece, while the emperor himself lived in public <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-INCEST">incest</a> with her sister Theodora. His martial spirit gained him a considerable command in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CILICIA">Cilicia</a>, where he laid siege to Mopsuestia: but by a successful sally of the enemy, he was obliged to raise the siege, and retire in considerable disorder. Inflamed with a desire of revenging the infamy of their sister in his blood, the brothers of Eudocia made an unsuccessful attempt to assassinate Andronicus at midnight in his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TENT">tent</a>; but being providentially awakened, he defended himself with surprising bravery, forced his way through his enemies, and escaped in safety. Afterwards engaging in a treasonable correspondence, with the emperor of Germany and the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>, he was arrested, and thrown into confinement. He remained in this state about twelve years, and after several repeated attempts to escape, he at last effectuated his purpose, and fled for refuge to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Russia. The cunning of Andronicus soon found means to regain his favour with the emperor Manuel; for having exerted all his influence, he succeeded in obtaining the Russian <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, to engage to join his troops with those of Manuel, in the invasion of Hungary. Accordingly, on account of his important <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, he obtained a free <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a> from the emperor, and after an expedition to the Danube, returned with him to Constantinople. He again fell under the displeasure of the emperor, by refusing to take an oath of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLEGIANCE">allegiance</a> to the prince of Hungary, his intended son-in-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>, and consequently presumptive heir to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, and was thereupon returned to his former command in Cilicia. While residing here, his powerful <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> captivated the heart of Philippa, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of the Latin prince of Antioch, and sister to the empress <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARIA">Maria</a>; and in her <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>, he spent his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> in all the amusements that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> could afford, till the emperor's resentment put a stop to their correspondence. Thus circumstanced, he collected a band of adventurers, and undertook a pilgrimage to the holy <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>, where by his insinuating turn of mind, he so far succeeded in gaining the favour of the king and clergy, as to be invested with the lordship of Berytus on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Phoenicia. In this neighbourhood, Theodora the beautiful widow of Baldwin, king of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>, and nearly allied in blood to him, resided. The personal accomplishments and address of Andronicus captivated her heart, and she became... came the third victim to his artful <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-SEDUCTION">seduction</a>, and lived publicly as his concubine. Still pursued by the emperor with unabating resentment, he was forced to take refuge in Damascus, and then in several other places in the east, till at length he settled in Asia Minor. While residing here, he made frequent incursions into the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Trebizond, and seldom returned without success. After several occurrences, Theodora was made captive, by the governor of Trebizond, along with her two children, and sent to Constantinople: upon which Andronicus implored and obtained pardon. He acted the affected penitent in such a manner, that he again ingratiated himself into the favours both of the church and state: but was sent to dwell at Oenoë, a town situated on the Euxine coast. In the year 1177 Manuel died, and was succeeded by his son Alexius II. a youth about twelve or fourteen years of age, without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>, by which the ambition of Andronicus was again called into <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a>. A civil <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> having been occasioned, by the misconduct of the empress in Constantinople, the public mind was directed towards Andronicus, as the only person whose <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> and accomplishments could restore the public tranquillity. Incited by the patriarchs and patricians, he marched towards Constantinople, which he entered, took possession of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, confined the empress, consigned her minister to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, assumed the office of protector, put to death many persons of distinction, tried and executed the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>, on a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of corresponding with the king of Hungary, and vowed fidelity to the young emperor upon his coronation, at the same time teaching the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of an experienced ruler, to assure the evils that threatened the empire; upon which his adherents called out "<a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a> live Alexius and Andronicus, Roman emperors." While he affected reluctance, he was elevated to a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PARTNERSHIP">partnership</a> in the empire. This conjunction of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> power was soon dissolved, by the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> of the unfortunate Alexius. The body of the deceased being brought into his presence, striking it with his foot, he said, "Thy father was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNAVE">knave</a>, thy mother a whore, and thyself a fool." Having arrived at the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of sole emperor, A.D. 1183, he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to sway the sceptre, with a mixture of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> and bounty towards his subjects at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, but those whom he feared or hated he governed with the most cruel tyranny. The noble families that were either cut off, or exiled by him, were all allied to the Comneni. Some of these were engaged in revolt; and the public calamity was heightened, by an invasion of the Sicilians, in which they took and sacked Thessalonica. A rival without merit, and a people without arms, at last overthrew his throne. A descendant from the first Alexius, in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> line, named Isaac Angelus, being singled out by Andronicus, as a victim to his cruelty, he with courage and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> defended his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> and liberty, slew his executioner, fled to the church of St Sophia, and there took refuge with several of his friends. Isaac was instantly raised by the populace, from a sanctuary to a throne. When this event took place, Andronicus was absent from Constantinople; but he no sooner heard of it, than he with the utmost speed returned. Upon his arrival there, he found himself deserted by all, and was seized, and dragged in chains before the new emperor. All the eloquence he displayed was of no avail; for Isaac delivered him into the hands of those whom he had injured, and for the space of three days, he endured with uncommon <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATIENCE">patience</a>, all the insults and torments that were inflicted upon him. In the midst of these he would frequently cry out, "<a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> have mercy upon me," and, "why <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> you bruise a broken reed." At last, two friendly or furious Italians, plunging their swords into his body, put a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> to his life. His death, in the 73rd year of his age, terminated the dynasty of the Comneni. (Gen. Biog.) Andronicus of Cyrrhus, an Athenian astronomer, built at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a> an octagon tower, with figures carved on each side, representing the eight <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> winds. A <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> Triton at the summit, with a rod in its <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, turned round by the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, pointed to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> from whence it blew. From this <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODEL">model</a> is derived the custom of placing weathercocks on steeples. Androphagi, in Ancient <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, the name of a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> whose country, according to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a>, was adjacent to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SCYTHIA">Scythia</a>. Their name, compounded of two Greek words, signifies <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>-eaters. Herodotus does not inform us whether their manner of subsisting corresponded with their name: whether they were so <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> as to eat <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>. See the article Anthrophagi. They are represented, however, as the most barbarous and fierce of all nations. They were not governed by laws; the care of their cattle was their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> employment. Their dress was like that of the Scythians; and they had a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> peculiar to themselves. Andropogon, or Man's-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARD">Beard</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANDROS">Andros</a>, one of the ancient Cyclades, lying between <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TENEDOS">Tenedos</a> and Euboea: being one <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a> distant from the former, and ten from the latter. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> gave it various names, viz. Cauros, Lasia, Nonagria, Epagris, Antandros, and Hydrusia. The name of Andros it received from one Andreas, appointed, according to Diodorus Siculus, by Rhadamantus, one of the generals, to govern the Cyclades, after they had of their own <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACCORD">accord</a> submitted to him. As to the name of Antandros, the same author tells us, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASCANIUS">Ascanius</a> the son of Æneas, being taken prisoner by the Pelasgians, gave them this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> for his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RANSOM">ransom</a>, which on that account was called Antandros, or "delivered for one man." The name of Hydrusia it obtained in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> with other places well supplied with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. It had formerly a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOTE">note</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> the same name, and situated very advantageously on the brow of a hill, which commanded the whole coast. In this city, according to Strabo and Pliny, stood a famous temple dedicated to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a>. Near this temple, Mutianus, as quoted by Pliny, tells us, there was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> called the gift of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>; the water of which had the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> of wine in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a>, during the feast of Bacchus, which lasted <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> days. The same author adds, that the waters, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> carried to a place whence the temple could not be seen, lost their miraculous taste. Pausanias makes no mention of this spring; but says, that, during the feast of Bacchus, wine flowed, or was at least by the Andrians believed to flow, from the temple of that god. The priests, no doubt, found their account in keeping up this <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a>, by conveying, through secret conduits, a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of wine into the temple. The Andrians were the first of all the islanders who joined joined the Persians at the time <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-XERXES">Xerxes</a> invaded <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>; and therefore Themistocles, after the victory at <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALAMIS">Salamis</a>, resolved to attack the city of Andros, and oblige the inhabitants to pay large contributions for the maintenance of his fleet. Having landed his men on the island, he sent heralds to the magistrates, acquainting them, that the Athenians were coming against them with two powerful divinities, persuasion and force; and therefore they must part with their <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> by fair means or foul. The Andrians replied, That they likewise had two mighty deities who were very fond of their island, viz. poverty and impossibility; and therefore could give no money. Themistocles, not satisfied with this answer, laid siege to the town; which he probably made himself <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of and destroyed, as we are informed by Plutarch, that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERICLES">Pericles</a>, a few years after, sent thither a colony of 250 Athenians. It was, however, soon retaken by the Persians; and, on the overthrow of that empire by Alexander the Great, submitted to him, along with the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>. On his death it sided with Antigonus, who was driven out by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>. The successors of the last mentioned prince held it till the time of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>; when Attalus, king of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERGAMUS">Pergamus</a>, besieged the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a> at the head of a Roman army; and, having taken it, was by them put in possession of the whole island. Upon the death of Attalus the republic claimed this island, as well as his other dominions, in virtue of his last will. Andros is now subject to the Turks; and contains a town of the same name, with a great many villages. It is the most fruitful island in all the Archipelago, and yields a great quantity of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>. There are said to be about 12,000 inhabitants, besides those of the villages Arni and Amoldeos, who are about two hundred, have a different language and customs, and are called Albanois. There are seven monasteries, a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of churches, and a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> for the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> of the Roman Catholic persuasion; but most of the inhabitants are of the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a>. The Jesuits had a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> and a church in this island; but they were forced to quit them long ago. Here are some delightful valleys; but the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> is bad, and the water of the city worse. The women would be agreeable enough, if it was not for their dress, which is very unbecoming; for they stuff out their clothes without the least regard to their shape: but the Albanese women make a much better appearance. The peasants make wicker-baskets, wherewith they supply the greatest part of the Archipelago. They have all sorts of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAME">game</a> in the woods and mountains, but know not how to take them for want of guns. Their principal food is goats flesh; for there is no fish to be met with on their coasts. When they are sick, they are obliged to let the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> take its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> course, having neither physician nor surgeon on the island. A cadi, assisted by a few of the principal persons of the island, has the management of civil affairs, and his residence is in the castle: an aga, who presides over the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> force, lives in a tower without the city. About two miles from the present town are still to be seen the ruins of a strong wall, with the fragments of many columns, chapters, bases, broken <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a>, and several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a>, some of which mention the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> and people of Andros, and the priests of Bacchus; from which it is probable that this was the site of the ancient city. E. Long. 25. 30. N. Lat. 37. 50. Andros, in Ancient Geography, an island in the Irish <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> (Pliny), called Hedros by Ptolemy. Now Bardsey, distant about a mile from the coast of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>. ANDROSACE. See Botany Index.

ANDRUM

Pages 379-379

a kind of hydrocele, to which the people of Malabar are very subject.—Its origin is derived from the bad <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> waters, impregnated with certain salts, the source of most other diseases that affect the Malabrians. Its signs, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> symptoms, are an erysipelas of the scrotum, returning every new <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a>, by which the lymphatics, being eroded, pour a serous saline humour into its cavity. The andrum is incurable; those once seized with it have it for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; but it is not dangerous nor very troublesome to those used to it; though sometimes it degenerates into an hydrosarcocele. The method of prevention is by a heap of sand fetched from a river of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> Mangatti, and strewed in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WELLS">wells</a>. This is practised by the rich. As to the cure, they have only a palliative one; which is by incision, or tapping, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> off the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> from the scrotum, once in a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> or two.

ANDUXAR

Pages 379-379

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANDALUSIA">Andalusia</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, situated on the Guadalquivir. It is defended by a good castle, and contains about 14,000 inhabitants. It is adorned with handsome churches and several <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> houses, and inhabited by many families of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> about it abounds in corn, wine, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>, and fruit of all sorts; and the inhabitants carry on a considerable trade in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 4. 2. N. Lat. 37. 45.

ANDUZE

Pages 379-379

a town of France, in the department of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARD">Gard</a>, seated on the river Gardon. It carries on a considerable trade in serges and woollen cloth. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3. 42. N. Lat. 43. 39.

ANECDOTE

Pages 379-379

(Anecdota), a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> used by some authors for the titles of Secret Histories: but it more properly denotes a relation of detached and interesting particulars. The word is Greek, ἀνεκδότης, q. d. things not yet known <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> hitherto kept secret. Procopius gives this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> to a book which he published against <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTINIAN">Justinian</a> and his wife Theodora; and he seems to be the only person among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> who has represented princes such as they are in their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> relation.—Varillas has published Anecdotes of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">House</a> of Medicis. ANECDOTES is also an appellation given to such works of the ancients as have not yet been published. In which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, M. Muratori gives the name Anecdota Graeca to several writings of the Greek fathers, found in the <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol13.html#article-LIBRARIES">libraries</a>, and first published by him.—F. Martene has given a Thesaurus Anecdotarum Novus, in folio, 5 vols.

ANEMOMETER

Pages 379-380

ANEMOMETER, in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICS">Mechanics</a>, implies a machine for measuring the force and velocity of the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>. Various <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MACHINES">machines</a> of this kind have been invented at different times, and by different persons. The following has been often experienced, and found to answer the intention. An open frame of wood, ABCDEFGHI*, is supported by the shaft <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> arbor I. In the two <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>-pieces HK, LM, is moved a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a> axis QM, by means of the four sails ah, cm, Of, gh, exposed to the wind in a proper manner. Upon this axis is fixed a cone of wood, MNO; upon which, as the sails move round, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> R, or S, is raised by a string round its superficies, proceeding from the smaller to the larger end NO. Upon this larger end or base of the cone, is fixed a rocket-wheel k, in whose <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> the click X falls, to prevent any retrograde <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> from the depending weight. The structure of this machine sufficiently shows that it may be accommodated to estimate the variable force of the wind; because the force of the weight <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> continually increase as the string advances on the conical surface, by acting at a greater distance from the axis of motion; consequently, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> such a weight be added on the smaller <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> M, as will <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> keep the machine in equilibrium in the weakest wind, the weight to be raised, as the wind becomes stronger, will be increased in proportion, and the diameter of the cone NO may be so <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> to that of the smaller end at M, that the strongest wind shall but just raise the weight at the greater end. If, for example, the diameter of the axis be to that of the base of the cone NO as 1 to 28; then, if S be a weight of one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> at M on the axis, it will be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> to 28 pounds when raised to the greater end; if therefore, when the wind is weakest, it supports one pound on the axis, it must be 28 times as strong as to raise the weight to the base of the cone. If therefore a line or <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a> of 28 equal parts be drawn on the side of the cone, the strength of the wind will be indicated by that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> on which the string rests.

ANEMOSCOPE

Pages 380-381

a machine that shows either the course <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> velocity of the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>. (See also the article Wind-Gauge). The machine which shows the course of the wind, or from what point of the compass it blows, consists of an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">index</a> moving upon an upright circular plate, like the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIAL">dial</a> of a clock, on which the 32 <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of the compass are drawn instead of the hours. The index, which points to the divisions on the dial, is turned by a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a> axis, having a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUNDLE">trundle</a>-head at its <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> extremity. This trundle-head is moved by a cog-wheel on a perpendicular axis; on the top of which a vane is fixed, that moves with the course of the wind, and puts the whole machine in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>. The whole contrivance is extremely simple; and nothing required in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a>, but that the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of cogs in the wheel, and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROUNDS">rounds</a> in the trundle-head, be equal; because it is necessary, that, when the vane moves entirely round, the index of the dial also make a complete revolution.—An anemoscope of this kind is placed in one of the turrets of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>’s <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>. The anemoscope, calculated for indicating the force or velocity of the wind is the same with what most writers call an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANEMOMETER">anemometer</a>; and we have accordingly described one of those <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MACHINES">machines</a> under that article. We shall here add another, contrived by the late Mr Pickering, and published in the Philosophical Transactions, No 473. This anemoscope is a machine four feet and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, consisting of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> and weighty pedestal, a pillar fastened into it, and an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> axis of about half an inch diameter fastened into the pillar. Upon this axis turns a wooden tube; at the top of which is placed a vane, of the same materials, 21 inches <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, consisting of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUADRANT">quadrant</a>, graduated, and shod with an iron rim, notched to each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>; and a counterpoise of wood, as in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, on the other. Through the centre of the quadrant runs an iron <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIN">pin</a>, upon which are fastened two small round pieces of wood, which serve as moveable radii to describe the degrees upon the quadrant, and as handles to a velum or sail, whose pane is one foot <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, made of canvas, stretched upon four battens, and painted. On the upper batten, next to the shod rim of the quadrant, is a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> which catches at every notch corresponding to each degree, as the wind shall, by pressing against the sail, raise it up; and prevents the falling back of the sail, upon lessening of the force of the wind. At the bottom of the wooden tube, is an iron index, which moves round a circular piece of wood fastened to the top of the pillar on the pedestal, on which are described the 32 points of the compass. The figure of this machine is given on Plate XXXIII. fig. 3, where a is the pedestal; b, the pillar on which the iron axis is fitted; c, the circle or wood, on which are described the 32 points of the compass; e, the wooden tube upon its axis; f, the velum; g, the graduated quadrant; h, the counterpoise of the vane. The adjoining figure represents the velum, which takes off: a is the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANE">plane</a> of the velum; b, the spring; cc, the wooden radii; dd, the holes through which the pin in the centre of the quadrant goes. Its uses are the following. 1. Having a circular motion round the iron axis, and being furnished with a vane at top, and index at the bottom, when once you have fixed the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a> points, described on the round piece of wood on the pillar, to the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of the heavens, it gives a faithful account of that quarter from which the wind blows. 2. By having a velum or sail elevated by the wind along the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> of the quadrant to a height <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPORTIONAL">proportional</a> to the power of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLUMN">column</a> of wind pressing against it, the relative force of the wind, and its comparative power, at any two times of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a>, may be accurately taken. 3. By having a spring fitted to the notches of the iron with which the quadrant is shod, the velum is prevented from returning back upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> of the wind; and the machine gives the force to the highest blast, since the last <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of examination, without the trouble of watching it. The ingenious contriver of this machine tells us, that he carefully examined what dependence may be had upon it, during the storms of February 1743-4, and found that it answered exceedingly well; for that, in such winds as the sailors call violent storms, the machine had six degrees to spare for a more violent gust, before it comes to a horizontal position. It is certainly tainly to be depended upon in ordinary <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, the velum being hung so tenderly as to feel the most gentle breeze. There is however reason to fear, that the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPOSING">exposing</a> the anemoscope to all winds for a continuance, must disorder it, especially <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> blasts and squalls. It may not therefore be amiss, in violent weather, for the observer to take the tube with its vane and velum in his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, in order to know the force of the wind; and when he has finished his observations, to carry the machine into the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, till the violence of the storm is abated, when it may be placed in its former situation.

ANEURISM

Pages 381-381

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>, a throbbing tumor, distended with blood, and formed by a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DILATATION">dilatation</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rupture of an artery. See SURGERY <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ANGARI

Pages 381-381
or ANGARII, in antiquity, denote public couriers, appointed for the carrying of messages. The ancient Persians, Budaeus observes, had their ἀγγεῖον διακοπής; which was a set of couriers on horseback, posted at certain stages or distances, always in readiness to receive the dispatches from one, and forward them to another, with wonderful celerity, answering to what the moderns call posts, q.d. positi, as being posted at certain places or stages. The angari were also called by the Persians astanda; by the Greeks ἀποστάσιον, on account of the long journeys they made in one day, which, according to Suidas, amounted not to less than 1500 stadia.

ANGARIA

Pages 381-381

in Roman antiquity, a kind of public <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> imposed on the provincials, which consisted in providing horses and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRIAGES">carriages</a> for the conveyance of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> stores and other public burdens. It is sometimes also used for a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>, posted for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. In a more general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> it is used for any kind of oppression, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> services performed through compulsion.

ANGAZYA

Pages 381-381

one of the Comora <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, lying between the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> end of Madagascar and the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Zangezur in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, from Lat. 10° to 15° S. It is inhabited by Moors, who trade with <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> parts of the continent, in cattle, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, and other commodities of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>; which they <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a> for callicoes and other cotton cloths. The houses here are built of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, and lime made of calcined oyster shells; with which the walls and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> are plastered in a very elegant manner. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of Angazya is a pure aristocracy; the island being subject to ten lords, who have all the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SULTAN">Sultan</a>. The people are very careful of their women; never permitting strangers to see them, without permission from a sultan, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> an order which the stranger brings with him. Many of them read and write Arabic with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> facility; and some even understand Portuguese, which they learn from their intercourse with <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOZAMBIQUE">Mozambique</a>, whither they trade in vessels of 40 tons burden.

ANGEIOTOMY

Pages 381-381

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>, implies the opening a vein <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> artery, as in bleeding; and consequently includes both arteriotomy and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHLEBOTOMY">phlebotomy</a>.

ANGEL

Pages 381-385

a spiritual intelligent substance, the first in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> among created beings. The word angel is Greek, and signifies a messenger: the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> אֵלֶּה signifies the same thing. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGELS">angels</a> are in Daniel (chap. iv. ver. 13, &c.) called וְאֵלֶּה, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> watchers, from their vigilance: for the same reason they are, in the remains we have of the prophecy attributed to Enoch, named Eggregori; which word imports the same in Greek. Angels, therefore, in the proper signification of the word, do not import the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of any being, but only the office to which they are appointed, especially by way of message or intercourse between God and his creatures; in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> they are called the ministers of God, who do his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, and ministering spirits sent forth to minister for them who shall be heirs of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALVATION">salvation</a>. That there are such beings as we call angels, that is, certain permanent substances, invisible and imperceptible to our senses, endowed with understanding and power superior to that of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> nature, created by God, and subject to him as the Supreme Being; ministering to his divine <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">providence</a> in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of the world by his appointment, and more especially attending the affairs of mankind; is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> so fully attested by Scripture, that it cannot be doubted. Nay, the existence of such invisible beings was generally acknowledged by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> heathens, though under different appellations: the Greeks called them demons; and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> genii, or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LARES">lares</a>. Epicurus seems to have been the only one among the old philosophers who absolutely rejected them. Indeed, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a> of middle intelligences influencing the affairs of the world, and serving as ministers or interpreters between God and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, is as extensive as the belief of a God; having never, so far as we know, been called in question by those who had any <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> at all. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREATION">creation</a> of angels is not indeed expressly mentioned by Moses in the first of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GENESIS">Genesis</a>, yet it is generally considered by judicious expositors as implied.
