These, however, have preserved their conquests, and for some time they allowed the natives to choose a king for themselves, or rather they chose him for them, as we have already noticed. These Low state kings enjoyed only a mere shadow of royalty; their whole <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a> consisting in being allowed to breed the Porpeacocks, and adorn themselves with their feathers, which was forbidden to their subjects under pain of perpetual slavery. The last of these kings was named Ngola Sedesio, who disliking an empty name of royalty, revolted from the Portuguese, and carried on a long war with them; but being at last defeated and killed, his head was cut off, salted, and sent to Lisbon in pickle. After this the Portuguese seem not to have thought it safe to trust their Angolic subjects even with the name of a king of their own, but have vested the power entirely in their viceroy; but, as to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of his dominions, and how matters stand between him and that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of Angolic princes who have preserved their liberty, we are entirely in the dark. When in its greatest splendour, the kingdom of Angola contained the following provinces: Chessama, Sumbi, Benguela, Rimba, Sieta, High and Low Benbea, Temba, Oacco, Cabezzo, Lubolo, Loanda, Bengo, Danda, Mosiche, Higher and Lower Ilamba, Oraij, and Embacca. The provinces conquered by the Portuguese during the wars above mentioned were, Danda, Mosiche, Bengo, the Higher and Lower Ilamba, Oraij, Embacca, Benguela, Sieta, Cabezzo, Lubolo, and Oacco. The principal rivers are those already mentioned, viz. the Danda and Coanza. The Coanza is large, deep, and rapid. It empties itself into the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATLANTIC_OCEAN">Atlantic ocean</a> about latitude $9^\circ 25'$ south, twelve leagues south of Loanda the capital of the kingdom. It is navigable for 150 miles, and abounds with variety of fish. It forms several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, has some cataracts, and one in particular which bears its name. As for its source, and the length of ground it crosses from east to west before it comes to the Portuguese settlements, it is absolutely unknown, as well as the countries through which it runs. Its mouth, which runs between the capes Palmerino and Lego, is above a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> wide; the northern shore is the deepest, and along which the vessels sail. The fall of this river into the ocean is so rapid, that the sea appears quite muddy for two or three leagues below it. Its mouth is not easily perceived from the open sea, by reason of an island quite covered with high trees which lies just before it. The two principal islands formed by this river are called Massander and Motchiamia. The one is six leagues long, and about two miles <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>: it is very fertile in maize, millet, and some other grains, which are reaped at three different seasons of the year. It produces likewise vast quantities of manhioe, a root of which they make a coarse kind of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAL">meal</a>, which serves instead of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>. Here also grow great numbers of palm and other fruit trees of various kinds. The island of Motchiamia is four or five miles long, and one in breadth, mostly plain, and producing variety of roots and herbs. It likewise abounds in cattle; and there were formerly five or six Portuguese families settled upon it, who drove a considerable trade in those commodities, and likewise in slaves. Concerning the river Danda we know little or nothing: only, that though its mouth is not above 70 or 80 miles distant from that of the Coanza, yet their distance grows so considerably wider as you penetrate further into the inlands, as to be much above twice if not thrice that space; though how much, is not exactly known. The manners, religion, and dress, &c. of the inhabitants, are much the same with the Congoose. See Congo. Angola <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEA">Pea</a>, or Pigeon pea. See Cyttisus, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGON">Angon</a>, in the ancient <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> art, a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JAVELIN">javelin</a> used by the French. They darted it at a considerable distance. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> head of this weapon resembled a fleur-de-luce. It is the opinion of some writers, that the arms of France are not fleurs-de-luce, but the iron point of the angon or javelin of the ancient French. Angor, among ancient physicians, a concentration of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>: the consequence of which is a pain of the head, palpitation, and sadness. Angot, a province or kingdom of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABYSSINIA">Abyssinia</a>, formerly rich and fertile, but almost ruined by the Gallas, a wandering nation in the internal parts of Africa, who dispossessed the Abyssinian monarchs of all that was worth possessing. Angoulesme, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of France, the capital of the former <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGOUMOIS">Angoumois</a>, now the department of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARENTE">Charente</a>, and the see of a bishop. It is seated on the top of a hill, surrounded with rocks, at the foot of which runs the river Charente. The inhabitants are said to be about 8000, and have a considerable trade in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, which they manufacture. E. Long. 0. 14. N. Lat. 45. 39. Angoumois, formerly a province of France, now a district, bounded on the north by Poitou, on the east by Limosin and Marche, on the south by Perigord, and on the west by Saintonge. Through this province run the rivers Touvre and Charente. This last is full of excellent fish; and though it often overflows its banks, it is so far from doing any damage, that it greatly enriches the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>. The Touvre is full of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TROUT">trout</a>. The air is generally warmer than at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, though the country is hilly. The soil produces plenty of wheat, rye, oats, Spanish corn, saffron, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAPES">grapes</a>, and all sorts of fruits. Here are several iron <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>, which yield a very good sort of iron. Angoura, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGORA">Angora</a>, or Angori, a city of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, in Anatolia, formerly called Ancyra, and still full of remarkable antiquities, which are so many marks of its ancient magnificence. It is at present one of the best cities in Anatolia; its streets are full of pillars and old marbles, among which are some of porphyry and jasper. The greatest part of the pillars are smooth and cylindrical; some are channelled spirally; but the most singular are oval, with plate bands before and behind from the top to the bottom of the pedestal. The houses are now made of clay, which is sometimes intermixed with fine pieces of marble. The walls of the city are low, with very mean <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BATTLEMENTS">battlements</a>. The masonry of the walls is intermixed with pillars, architraves, capitals, and other ancient fragments, especially that of the towers and gates. The castle of Angora has a triple enclosure; and the walls are of large pieces of white marble, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> much like porphyry. The basha of Angora has about 30 purses income; and there are here about 300 <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JANIZARIES">janizaries</a>, under the command of a sardar. The Turks are said to be 40,000, the Armenians 4000 or 5000, and the Greeks 600. The Armenians have <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> churches, besides a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a>, and the Greeks two. They breed the finest goats in the world; and their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, which is of a dazzling white, is almost as fine as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> inches in length: it is worked into very fine stuffs, particularly <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBLET">camblet</a>. All the inhabitants are employed in this manufacture. Several large <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARAVANS">caravans</a> pass through this city to different places. E. Long. 32. 5. N. Lat. 39. 30. See Ancyra. Angoy, a kingdom of Loango in Africa, bound- ed on the north by Cacongo, and on the south by Congo; from the former of which it is separated by the river Cabinda, and from the latter by the river Zaire. It is but of small extent; being only a vassal province of Cacongo, till the mani or prince, who had married a Portuguese's daughter, was persuaded by his father-in-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> to make himself independent. This he effected at a favourable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNCTURE">juncture</a>, the king of Loango having but just before revolted from the king of Congo, and the king of Cacongo from the new king of Loango. The country is full of woods and thickets; and has no towns of any <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOTE">note</a>, except one called Bomangoy, situated on the north <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the Zaire, and not far from its mouth. Its chief port is Cabinda, called also Kabenda, or Cubenda, situated on the mouth of a river of the same name, about five leagues north of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> Palmerino, on the north side of the Zaire's mouth. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> is very commodious for trade, or wooding and watering along the shore. It is flat and marshy in some places; but ascends gradually about three miles inland, and then forms itself into a ridge of hills. On the ascent of these is situated a town belonging to the father-in-law of the king above mentioned, where he constantly kept a stock of wood ready cut, to sell to foreign ships at an easy rate. From these wood piles, southwest along the bay, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> scattered a number of fishermen's huts, on each side a small fresh-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> river which falls into the bay; and thence all the water for ships is brought in casks to the mouth of the river, which is so shallow, that even at full <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a> it can only be entered by a yawl carrying a cask or two. The town stands on the round point of the bay looking to the westward; and the English have a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACTORY">factory</a> on the south-west of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a>. The country round the bay is mostly barren; owing chiefly to the laziness of the inhabitants, which often occasions a scarcity of provisions. The wild beasts swarm so in the woods, that they destroy all the tame kinds; so there are no cattle bred here but hogs. From the woods in this country some monkeys have been brought away which in shape and stature resembled the human <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>. Civet cats abound here in great plenty, and parrots may be bought for three or four ordinary knives. The coasts abound so with oysters, that the sailors quickly load their boats with them; they being found lying in great heaps like small rocks. The natives follow the occupation of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a> more than any other. They fish both in the sea and in the rivers, making use of drag nets, which have long canes fixed at equal distances, instead of corks, to show when any fish is caught. These nets are made of a peculiar kind of root, which, after being beaten, may be spun like <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>. The dress of the inhabitants is the same with that of the Congolese. They allow polygamy, and the best beloved wife hath the command of the rest; but is no less liable to be turned out, if she proves unfaithful. The ladies of the blood-royal have the privilege of choosing their husbands out of any, even the meanest rank; and have even the power of life and death over them; as likewise over their paramours, if any of them are caught tripping: but the husbands are by no means entitled to expect the same fidelity from their royal ladies. Women of the lower rank are obliged, when they receive a stranger, to admit him for a night or two into their embraces. This obliged the missionaries, who traveled through this country, to give notice of their approach to any of their houses, that none of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> sex might enter within their doors.—Their religion consists chiefly in a variety of superstitious customs; such as powdering their public and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> idols with the dust of a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> wood, on the first day of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a>, and paying a kind of worship to that planet. If, on that night, it happens to shine clear and bright, they cry out, "Thus may I renew my life as thou dost;" but if the air is cloudy, they imagine the moon hath lost her virtue, and pay her no respect. We do not hear of their offering any sacrifices to their idols; though they commonly consult them about the success of their enterprises, thefts, or such like. The king of Congo still styles himself sovereign of Angoy; but the king of this little state pays neither tribute nor homage to any foreign power.

ANGRA

Pages 403-404

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TERCERA">Tercera</a>, one of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AZORES">Azores</a>; the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, not only of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, but of all the rest, and the residence of the governor. It is seated on the south side, near the middle of the longest diameter of the island, on the edge of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. The harbour is the only tolerable one in the whole island, being equally secured against storms and the efforts of an enemy. It is of the form of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRESCENT">crescent</a>; the extremities of which are defended by two <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> rocks, that run so far into the sea as to render the entrance narrow, and easily covered by the batteries on each side. From this harbour the town is said to derive its name, the word Angra signifying a creek, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> station for shipping; and this is the only convenient one among all the Azores. The opening of the port is from the east to the south-west; and, according to Frezier, it is not above four <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CABLES">cables</a> length in breadth, and not two of good bottom. Here ships may ride in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> safety during the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>; but as soon as the winter begins, the storms are so furious, that the only safety for shipping is the putting to sea with all possible expedition. Happily, however, these storms are preceded by infallible signs, with which <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> has made the inhabitants perfectly well acquainted. On these occasions the Pico, a high mountain in another of the Azores, is overcast with thick <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a>, and grows exceedingly dark; but what they look upon as the most certain sign is the fluttering and chirping of flocks of birds round the city for some days before the storm begins. The town is the see of a bishop, under the jurisdiction of the archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LISBON">Lisbon</a>. It hath five parishes, a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>, four monasteries, as many nunneries, besides an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INQUISITION">inquisition</a> and bishop's <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, which extends its jurisdiction over all the Azores, Flores, and Corvo. It is surrounded by a wall and a dry ditch, and is defended by a castle rendered famous by the imprisonment of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> Alphonso by his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> in 1668. Of late the fortifications have been much neglected. Though most of the public and private buildings have a good appearance externally, they are but indifferently furnished within; but for this poverty the Portuguese excuse themselves, by saying, that too much furniture would prove inconvenient in so warm a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>. At Angra are kept the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> magazines for anchors, cables, sails, and other stores for the royal <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a>, or occasionally for merchantmen in great distress. All ma- Angivarii ritime affairs are under the inspection of an officer called Desembergrador, who hath subordinate officers and pilots for conducting ships into the harbour, or to proper watering places. The English, French, and Dutch, have each a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a> residing here, though the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> of any of these nations with the Azores is very inconsiderable.

ANGRIVARII

Pages 404-404

(Tacitus): a people of Germany situated between the Weser and the Ems, and eastward reaching beyond the Weser, as far as the Cherusci, on which side they raised a rampart (Tacitus); to the south, having the Tubantes on the Ems, and on the Weser where it <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENDS">bends</a> to the forest Bacemis; to the west, the Ems and the confines of the Bructeri; and to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, the territory of the Angrivarii lay between the Chamavi and Ansibarri. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a> places them between the Cauchi and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-SUEVI">Suevi</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Catti. Supposed now to contain a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Schaumburg, the half of the bishopric or principality of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINDEN">Minden</a> to the south, the greatest part of the bishopric of Osnaburg, the north part of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of Teclenburg, and a part of the county of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAVENSBURG">Ravensburg</a>. A trace of the name of the people still remains in the appellation Energyn, a small town in the county of Ravensburg.

ANGUILLA

Pages 404-404

one of the West <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARIBBEE_ISLANDS">Caribbee <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, lying in about 18° 15' N. Lat. It has its name from its snake-like form; and is about ten leagues in length and three in breadth. It was first discovered by the English in 1650, when it was filled with alligators and other noxious animals; but they, finding the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> fruitful, and proper for raising <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a> and corn, settled a colony on it, and imported live cattle, which have since multiplied exceedingly. But the colony not being settled under any public encouragement, each planter laboured for himself, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> became a prey to every rapacious invader, which disheartened the inhabitants so much, that all industry was lost among them. Their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> sufferings were from a party of wild Irish, who landed here after the Revolution, and treated them worse than any of the French pirates who had attacked them before. The people of Barbadoes, and other English Caribbees, knowing the value of the soil, several of them removed to Anguilla, where they remained for many years, and even carried on a profitable trade, though without any <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> either civil or <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a>. In 1745, their <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITIA">militia</a>, though not exceeding 100 men, defended a breastwork against 1000 French who came to attack them; and at last obliged them to retire with the loss of 150 men, besides carrying off some of their arms and colours as trophies of their victory. Since that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the inhabitants have subsisted mostly by farming; though they still plant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>, and the island is said to be capable of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> improvements.

ANGUINUM OVUM

Pages 404-404

a fabulous kind of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGG">egg</a>, said to be produced by the saliva of a cluster of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERPENTS">serpents</a>, and possessed of certain magical virtues. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a> in respect to these was very prevalent among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Britons, and there still remains a strong <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a> of it in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>. The account Pliny * gives of it is as follows: Præterea est ovorum genus in magna Galliarum fama, omissum Graecis. Angues innumere "ri æstato convoluti, salivis faucium corporumque spumis artifici complexu glomerantur; anguinum appellatur. Druidæ sibilis id dicunt in sublime jactari, sagoque oportere intercipi, ne tellurem attingat; profugere raptem equo: serpentes enim inseguiri, donec arceantur amnis alicujus interventu."—Of which the following may serve as a translation: from Mason's Caractacus; the person speaking, a Druid.) But tell me yet From the grot of charms and spells, Where our matron sister dwells, Brennus, has thy holy <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> Safely brought the Druid wand, And the potent <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADDER">Adder</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, Gender'd 'fore th' autumnal <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a>? When, in undulating twine, The foaming snakes prolific join; When they hiss, and when they bear Their wond'rous egg aloft in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>: Thence before to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a>, The Druid in his hallow'd pall Receives the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a>, And instant flies, Follow'd by th' envenom'd brood, 'Till he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> the crystal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a>. This wond'rous egg seems to be nothing more than a bead of glass, used by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRUIDS">Druids</a> as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARM">charm</a> to impose on the vulgar, whom they taught to believe, that the possessor would be fortunate in all his attempts, and that it would <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> the favour of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a>. Our <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> Druidesses (says Mr Pennant, from whom we extract) give much the same account of the ovum anguinum, glain naidr, as the Welsh call it, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the adder gem, as the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> does; but seem not to have so exalted an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of its powers, using it only to assist children in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>, or to cure the chincough, or to drive away an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGUE">ague</a>. These beads are of a very rich blue <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>; some plain, others streaked. For their <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, see Plate XXXVI. fig. 22, No 1, 2, 3.

ANGUIS

Pages 404-404
or SNAKE, in Zoology, a genus belonging to the order of amphibia serpentes. See OPHIOLOGY Index.

ANGULLIFORM

Pages 404-404

an appellation given by zoologists, not only to the different <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of eels, but to other animals resembling them in shape. ANGUINA. See Tricosanthes.

ANGUS

Pages 404-404

a district of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Forsfar in Scotland. It was an earldom belonging to the Douglas, now extinct.

ANGUSTICLAVIA

Pages 404-404

in Roman antiquity, a tunic embroidered with little purple studs. It was worn by the Roman knights, as the laticlavia was by the senators.

ANHALT

Pages 404-405

a principality of Germany, in the circle of Upper <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>, is a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> narrow tract, situated for the most <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> betwixt the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-ELBE">Elbe</a> and Saal, about 90 miles in length from east to west, but of unequal breadth, the greatest being on the east side, which is but 35 miles. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of Anhalt, from whence the electors of Saxony and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRANDENBURG">Brandenburg</a> are said to derive their original, is a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> family. The best genealogists deduce their origin from Berenthobaldus, who made <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> upon the Thuringians in the sixth century; it has produced many princes who make a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> in the German <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>. story. Joachim Ernest, who died in 1586, left five sons, who divided the principality among them. All of them having children, and being of equal authority, they unanimously agreed to submit to the eldest of the family, who has the supreme <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, which is Anhalt Dessau. The others are, Anhalt <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BERNBURG">Bernburg</a>, Anhalt Schaumburg, Anhalt Coethen, and Anhalt Zerbst. The last house became extinct in 1793. The three houses of Dessau, Bernburg, and Coethen, have votes in the new German diet, established in 1814. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of all the principalities in 1815, was 123,000; the revenue about 113,000l. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a>. The tax on lands is four per cent, which, rating them at 20 years purchase, is not quite one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHILLING">shilling</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a>. Upon an emergency the subjects are able to raise half a million dollars extraordinary. The <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> in these little states are not so numerous in proportion to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> as in Saxony, but better peopled. It is bounded on the south by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Mansfeld, on the west by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HALBERSTADT">Halberstadt</a>, on the east by the duchy of Saxony, and on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the duchy of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MAGDEBURG">Magdeburg</a>. It abounds in corn, and is watered by the Sadle and Mulda; its <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> trade is in beer.

ANHELATIO

Pages 405-405
or ANHELITUS, among physicians, a shortness of breath. ANHINGA. See Ornithology Index.

ANHOLT

Pages 405-405

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUTLAND">Jutland</a>, lying in the Categat, eight miles from the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Jutland, ten from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZEALAND">Zealand</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>. It is dangerous for seamen, for which reason there is a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-LIGHTHOUSE">lighthouse</a>.

ANIMA

Pages 405-405

among chemists, denotes the volatile <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> spirituous parts of bodies. ANIMA Hepatis, is a name by which some call sal martis, or <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, on account of its supposed efficacy in diseases of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVER">liver</a>. ANIMA Mundi, a certain pure ethereal substance or spirit, diffused, according to many of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> philosophers, through the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of the world, informing, actuating, and uniting the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> parts thereof into one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a>, perfect, organical, and vital body or animal. <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a> treats at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> of the ἀρχαὶ τῶν ὕλης, in his Timaeus; and is even supposed to be the author of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOGMA">dogma</a>; yet are interpreters much at a loss about his meaning. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>, however, taking it in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> and obvious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, strenuously opposes it. The <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> Platonists explain their <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>'s anima mundi by a certain universal ethereal spirit, which in the heavens exists perfectly pure, as retaining its proper <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>; but on <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> pervading elementary bodies, and intimately mixing with all the minute atoms thereof, it assumes somewhat of their nature, and becomes of a peculiar kind.—So the poet: Spiritus intus alit, totosque infusa per artus Mens agitat molem; et magno se corpore miscet. They add, that this anima mundi, which more immediately resides in the celestial regions as its proper seat, moves and governs the heavens in such a manner, as that the heavens themselves first received their existence from the fecundity of the same spirit: for that this anima, in being the primary source of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, everywhere breathed a spirit like itself, by virtue whereof various kinds of things were framed conformable to the divine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a>. ANIMA Saturni, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> powder obtained by pouring distilled <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a> on <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LITHARGE">litharge</a>; of considerable <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> in enamelling. See Enamel.

ANIMADVERSION

Pages 405-405

in matters of literature, is used to signify, sometimes correction, sometimes remarks upon a book, &c. and sometimes a serious consideration upon any point.

ANIMAL

Pages 405-410

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, an organized and living body, which is also endowed with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSATION">sensation</a>; thus, minerals are said to grow <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> increase, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> to grow and live, but animals alone to have sensation. It is this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of sensation alone that can be deemed the essential characteristic of an animal; and by which the animal and vegetable kingdoms seem to be so essentially separated, that we cannot even imagine the least approximation of the one to the other. Those naturalists, indeed, who have supposed the distinction between animals and vegetables to consist in anything else than what we have already mentioned, have found themselves greatly embarrassed; and have generally agreed, that it was extremely difficult, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not impossible, to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> the boundaries between the animal and vegetable kingdoms. But this difficulty <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be easily seen to arise from their taking the characteristic marks of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ANIMAL_KINGDOM">animal <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> from something that was evidently <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> to both. Thus Boerhaave attempted... tempted to distinguish an animal from a vegetable, by the former having a mouth, which the latter has not: but here, as the mouth of an animal is only the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> by which nourishment is conveyed to its body, it is evident that this can be no essential distinction, because vegetables also require nourishment, and have instruments proper for conveying it into their bodies; and where the end is the same, a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> in the means can never be essential. The fixing the difference in an animal's having a gula, stomach, and intestines, as is done by Dr Tyson, is as little to the purpose. The power of moving from one <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> to another, hath by many been thought to constitute their difference; and indeed, in most <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, it is the obvious mark by which we distinguish an animal from a vegetable: but <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Kames hath given several very curious instances of the locomotive power of plants; some of which, as he says, would do <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to an animal. "Upon the slightest touch, the sensitive plant shrinks back and folds up its leaves, similar to a snail; which on the slightest touch retires within its shell. A new <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of the sensitive plant hath been lately discovered. See Dionaea. If a fly perch upon one of its flower leaves, it closes instantly, and crushes the insect to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. There is not an article in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a> more admirable than a contrivance, visible in many plants, to take advantage of good <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, and to protect themselves against bad. They open and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> and leaves in different circumstances; some close before sunset, some after; some open to receive <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>, some close to avoid it. The petals of many flowers expand in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>; but <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> at night, or on the approach of rain. After the seeds are fecundated, the petals no longer contract. All the trefoils may serve as a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAROMETER">barometer</a> to the husbandman; they always contract their leaves on an impending storm. Some plants follow the sun, others turn from it. Many plants, on the sun's recess, vary the position of their leaves, which is styled the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a> of plants. A singular plant was lately discovered in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENGAL">Bengal</a>. Its leaves are in continual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> all <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>; but when night approaches, they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> from an erect posture to rest. "A plant has a power of directing its roots for procuring food. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> whortleberry, a low evergreen plant, grows naturally on the tops of our highest hills, among <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a> and gravel. This shrub was planted in an edging to a rich border, under a fruit wall. In two or three years, it overran the adjoining deep-laid gravel walk; and seemed to fly from the border, in which not a single runner appeared. An effort to come at food in a bad situation, is extremely remarkable in the following instance: Among the ruins of Newabbey, formerly a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GALLOWAY">Galloway</a>, there grows on the top of a wall a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANE">plane</a> tree about 20 feet <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>. Straightened for nourishment in that barren situation, it several years ago directed roots down the side of the wall, till they reached the ground ten feet below; and now the nourishment it afforded to those roots during the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of their descending is amply repaid, having every year since that time made vigorous shoots. From the top of the wall to the surface of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, these roots have not thrown out a single <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIBRE">fibre</a>; but are now united in a single root. "Plants, when forced from their natural position, are endowed with a power to restore themselves, A hop plant, twisting round a stick, directs its course from south to west, as the sun does. Untwist it, and tie it in the opposite <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>; it dies. Leave it loose in the wrong direction: it recovers its natural direction in a single night. Twist a branch of a tree so as to invert its leaves, and fix it in that position: if left in any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> loose, it untwists itself gradually, till the leaves be restored to their natural position. What better can an animal do for its welfare? A root of a tree, meeting with a ditch in its progress, is laid open to the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>. What follows? It alters its course like a rational being, dips into the ground, surrounds the ditch, rises on the opposite side to its wonted distance from the surface, and then proceeds in its original direction. Lay a wet sponge near a root laid open to the air; the root will <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> its course to the sponge. Change the place of the sponge: the root varies its direction. Thrust a pole into the ground at a moderate distance from a scandent plant: the plant directs its course to the pole, lays hold of it, and rises on it to its natural height. A honeysuckle proceeds in its course, till it be too long for supporting its <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>; and then strengthens itself by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SHOOTING">shooting</a> into a spiral. If it meet with another plant of the same kind, they coalesce for mutual support; the one screwing to the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>, the other to the left. If a honeysuckle twig meets with a dead branch, it screws from the right to the left. The claspers of a briony shoot into a spiral, and lay hold of whatever comes in their way for support. If, after completing a spiral of three <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROUNDS">rounds</a>, they meet with nothing, they try again by altering their course." By comparing these and other instances of seeming voluntary motion in plants, with that share of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> wherewith some of the inferior kinds of animals are endowed, we can scarce hesitate at ascribing the superiority to the former; that is, putting sensation out of the question. Mussels, for instance, are fixed to one place as much as plants are; nor have they any power of motion, besides that of opening and shutting their shells: and in this respect they have no superiority over the motion of the sensitive plant; nor doth their <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> discover more sagacity, or even so much as the roots of the plane tree mentioned by Lord Kames. Mr Buffon, who seems to be desirous of confounding the animal and vegetable kingdoms, denies sensation to be any essential distinction. "Sensation (says he) more essentially distinguishes animals from vegetables: but sensation is a complex idea, and requires some explication. For if sensation implied no more than motion consequent upon a stroke or an impulse, the sensitive plant enjoys this power. But if, by sensation, we <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> of perceiving and comparing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a>, it is uncertain whether brute animals are endowed with it. If it should be allowed to dogs, elephants, &c. whose actions seem to proceed from motives similar to those by which men are actuated, it must be denied to many species of animals, particularly to those which appear not to possess the faculty of progressive motion. If the sensation of an oyster, for example, differed only in degree from that of a dog; why do we not ascribe the same sensation to vegetables, though in a degree still inferior? This distinction, therefore, between the animal and vegetable, is neither sufficiently general nor determined." "From this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVESTIGATION">investigation</a> we are led to conclude, that there is no <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> and essential distinction between the animal and vegetable kingdoms; but that <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> proceeds, by imperceptible degrees, from the most perfect to the most imperfect animal, and from that to the vegetables; and the fresh <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> polypus may be regarded as the last of animals and the first of plants." It were to be wished, that philosophers would on some occasions consider, that a subject may be dark as well on account of their inability to see, as when it really affords no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>. Our author boldly concludes, that there is no essential difference between a plant and an animal, because we ascribe sensation to an oyster, and none to the sensitive plant; but we ought to remember, that though we cannot perceive a distinction, it may nevertheless exist. Before Mr Buffon, therefore, had concluded in this manner, he ought to have proved that some vegetables were endowed with sensation. It is no doubt, however, as much incumbent on those who take the contrary side of the question, to prove that vegetables are not endowed with sensation, as it was incumbent on Mr Buffon to have proved that they are. But a little <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> will show us, that the difficulty here proceeds entirely from our inability to see the principle of sensation. We perceive this principle in ourselves, but no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> can perceive it in another. Why then does every individual of mankind conclude that his neighbour has the same sensations with himself? It can only be from <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANALOGY">analogy</a>. Every man perceives his neighbour formed in a manner similar to himself; he acts in a similar manner on similar occasions, &c. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">Just</a> so it is with brute animals. It is no more doubtful that they have sensations, than that we have them ourselves. If a man is wounded with a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a>, for instance, he expresses a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of pain, and endeavours to avoid a repetition of the injury. Wound a dog in the same manner, he will also express a sense of pain; and, if you offer to strike him again, will endeavour to escape, before he feels the stroke. To conclude here, that the action of the dog proceeded from a principle different from that of the man, would be absurd and unphilosophical to the last degree. We must further take notice, that there are sensations essentially distinct from one another; and in proportion as an animal is endowed with more or fewer of these different senses, it is more or less perfect as an animal; but, as long as one of them remains, it makes not the least approach to the vegetable kingdom; and, when they are all taken away, is so far from becoming a vegetable, that it is only a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of dead <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>. The senses of a perfect animal, for instance, are five in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>. Take away one of them, suppose sight; he becomes then a less perfect animal, but is as unlike a vegetable as before. Suppose him next deprived of hearing; his resemblance to a vegetable would be as little as before; because a vegetable can neither feel, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, nor smell, and we suppose him still to enjoy these three senses. Let us, lastly, suppose him endowed only with the sense of feeling, which, however, seems to include that of taste, and he is no more a vegetable than formerly, but only an imperfect animal. If this sense is then taken away, we connect him not with the vegetable kingdom, but with what Mr. Buffon calls brute matter. It is to this kingdom, and not to the vegetable, that animals plainly approximate as they descend. Indeed, to suppose an approximation between the vegetable and animal kingdoms, is very absurd: for, at that rate, the most imperfect animal ought to be the most perfect plant; but we observe no such thing. All animals, from the highest to the lowest, are possessed of vegetable life; and that, as far as we can perceive, in an equal degree, whether the animal life is perfect or imperfect; nor doth there seem to be the smallest connexion between the highest degree of vegetation and the lowest degree of sensation. Though all animals, therefore, are possessed of vegetable life, these two seem to be as perfectly distinct and incommensurate to one another as any two things we can possibly imagine. The power of vegetation, for instance, is as perfect in an onion or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEEK">leek</a>, as in a dog, an elephant, or a man; and yet, though you threaten a leek or an onion ever so much, it pays no regard to your words, as a dog would do; nor, though you wound it, does it avoid a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> stroke. It is this principle of self-preservation in all animals, which, being the most powerful one in their nature, is generally taken, and with very good reason, as the true characteristic of animal life. This principle is undoubtedly a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of sensation; and as it is never observed to take place in vegetables, we have a right to say that the foundation of it, namely sensation, belongs not to them. There is no animal, which makes any motion in consequence of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> impulse where danger is threatened, but what puts itself in a posture of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>; but no vegetable whatsoever does so. A muscle, when it is touched, immediately shuts its shell; and as this action puts it in a state of defence, we conclude that it proceeded from the principle of self-preservation. When the sensitive plant contracts from a touch, it is no more in a state of defence than before; for whatever would have destroyed it in its expanded state, will also do it in its contracted state. We conclude, therefore, that the motion of the sensitive plant proceeds only from a certain property called by physicians <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRRITABILITY">irritability</a>; and which, though our bodies possess it in an eminent degree, is a characteristic neither of animal nor vegetable life, but belongs to us in common with brute matter. It is certain that an electrified <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a> thread shows a much greater variety of motions than any sensitive plant. If a bit of silk thread is dropt on an electrified metal plate, it immediately erects itself; spreads out the small fibres like arms; and, if not detained, will fly off. If a finger is brought near it, the thread seems greedily to catch at it. If a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANDLE">candle</a> approaches, it clasps close to the plate, as if afraid of it.—Why do we not conclude that the thread in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> is really afraid of the candle? For this plain reason, That its seeming flight is not to get away from the candle, but to get towards the electrified metal; and, if allowed to remain there, will suffer itself to be burnt without offering to stir.—The sensitive plant, in like manner, after it has contracted, will suffer itself to be cut in pieces, without making the least effort to escape. The case is not so with the meanest animal. A hedgehog, when alarmed, draws its body together, and expands its prickles, thereby putting itself in a posture of defence. Throw it into water; and the same principle of self-preservation... Animal preservation prompts it to expand its body and swim. A snail, when touched, withdraws itself into its shell; but if a little quicklime is sprinkled upon it, so that its shell is no longer a place of safety, it is thrown into agonies, and endeavours to avail itself of its locomotive power in order to escape the danger. In mussels and oysters, indeed, we cannot observe this principle of self-preservation so strongly, as nature has deprived them of the power of progressive motion: but, as we observe them constantly to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> the means which nature has given them for self-preservation, we can have no reason to think that they are destitute of that principle upon which it is founded. But there is no need of arguments drawn from the inferior <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREATION">creation</a>. We ourselves are possessed both of the animal and vegetable life, and certainly must know whether there is any connection between vegetation and sensation, or not.—We are conscious that we exist; that we hear, see, &c.: but of our vegetation we are absolutely unconscious. We feel a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, for instance, in gratifying the calls of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HUNGER">hunger</a> and thirst; but of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> by which our aliment is formed into chyle, the chyle mixed with the blood, the circulation of that fluid, and the separation of all the humours from it, we are altogether ignorant. If we then, who are more perfect than other vegetables, are utterly insensible of our own vegetable life, why should we imagine that the less perfect vegetables are sensible of it? To illustrate our reasoning here by an example.—The direction of the roots of the plane tree mentioned by Lord Kames, shows as much sagacity, if we are to look only to the outward action, as can be observed in any motion of the most perfect animal whatever; nevertheless, we have not the least suspicion, either that the tree <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> the ground at a distance, or that it was informed of its being there by the rest of its roots. If a wound is made in the body of a man, and a loss of substance is to be repaired, the same sagacity will be observed in the arrangement of the fibres, not only as if they were animated, but they will dispose of themselves seemingly with a degree of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> far superior to what we have any idea of; yet this is done without our having the least knowledge either how it is done, or of its being done at all. We have therefore in ourselves a demonstration, that vegetable life acts without knowing what it does: and if vegetables are ignorant of their most sagacious actions, why should we suspect that they have a sensation, let it be ever so obscure, of any of their inferior ones, such as contracting from a touch, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> towards the sun, or advancing to meet a pole. Thus we may easily give Mr Buffon a reason why we ascribe sensation to an oyster, and none to a vegetable; namely, because we perceive the vegetable do nothing but what is also performed in our own bodies, without our having the least sensation of it; whereas on oyster puts itself in a defensive posture on the approach of danger; and this being an action similar to our own upon a like occasion, we conclude that it proceeds from the same principle of sensation. Here it may also be observed, that though the inferior animals are deficient in the number, they are by no means so in the acuteness of their sensations; on the contrary, though a mussel or an oyster is probably endowed with no other sense than that of feeling, yet this sense is so exquisite, that it will contract upon the slightest touch, such as we would be altogether insensible of. As to that power of contractility, or irritability, which is observed in some plants; our solids have it, when deprived both of vegetable and animal life: for a muscle, cut out of a living body, will continue to contract, if it is irritated by pricking it, after it has neither sensation nor vegetation. A very good moral reason may also be adduced why we do not believe vegetables to be endowed with sensation.—Had they been so, we must suppose them to suffer pain when they are cut or destroyed; and, if so, what an unhappy state must they be in, who have not the least power to avoid the injuries daily offered them! In fact, the goodness of the Deity is very conspicuous in not giving to vegetables the same sensations as to animals; and, as he hath given them no means of defence, though we had not been told it by himself, we might have known that he gave them for food for animals; and, in this case, to have endowed them with sensation would have been a piece of cruelty. Though animals without number prey upon one another, yet all of them have some means of defence; from whence we may justly conclude, that their mutual destruction was not an original appointment of the Creator, but what he foresaw would happen in a course of time, and which he therefore gave every one of them some means of guarding against. It may no doubt be here objected, that the giving some means of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SELF_DEFENCE">self-defence</a> to every animal cannot be reckoned a sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> that it was not the original <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of the Creator that they should be destroyed, seeing these means are not always effectual for their preservation. This objection, however, cannot be completely obviated without a solution of the question concerning the origin of evil among the works of a perfectly good Being. But whatever difficulty there may be in solving this question, it is certain, that, as some means of self-defence is given to every animal, it has been the original design of the Creator, that in all cases one species of animals should not be destroyed at the pleasure of any other species; and as no means of self-defence is given to any vegetable, it is plain that they have been destined for a prey to every species of animals that had access to them. Philosophers have insisted much on the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of one animal's devouring another, that there might be room sufficient for all; but this, so far from being a system worthy of the divine wisdom, seems to us to be a reflection upon it, as if the Author of nature could not have found means to preserve the life of one <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of his creatures, without the destruction and misery of the rest. The sacred writings leave us at no loss to see how this carnivorous disposition came in; and, in the next world, this piece of perfection (as the sanguinary philosophers above mentioned would have it to be) seems to be left out; for there, it is said, "They shall not hurt nor destroy; the lion shall eat straw like the ox, and there shall be no more pain." When speaking of the food of plants, we took occasion to mention a certain power totally different from that of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTRACTION">attraction</a> or repulsion, by which the food of a plant, after it was attracted, or otherwise brought to it, was assimilated to its substance. This power, which we there distinguish by the name of transmutation, belongs longs in a more eminent degree to animals. The alimentary substance is changed into two kinds of matter: (1.) An excrementitious one, which passes off through the intestines; and (2.) A fluid, which is the direct pabulum of the animal. Different substances, however, are not equally changeable by this process. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> stomach is not capable of acting upon any animal substance till it has lost its vital principle: the stomachs of some animals cannot <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> upon creatures of their own species: some have an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPARATUS">apparatus</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRINDING">grinding</a> their food after it is swallowed, &c. and there are no animals but what are subject to death by taking certain substances into their stomach. Some substances also, though they resist the action of the stomach, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> unchanged into the system, produce no bad effects. Thus, madder will turn the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> of animals red; <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-RHUBARB">rhubarb</a> will communicate its purgative nature to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILK">milk</a>, and its deep <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> to the urine.—All these changes, however, seem to belong to the vegetative part of our system: for as every one of them are performed without our knowledge of the manner how; and not only so, but while we are absolutely unconscious of their being done; we can have no reason to suppose, that the animal life, properly so called, is at all connected with them, any farther than as they are at present the means of preserving the creature alive, and making the connexion betwixt the principle of life and this visible creation. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> and classing of animals make a considerable part of Natural History, known by the name of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZOOLOGY">Zoology</a>. Animal, used adjectively, denotes any thing belonging to, or partaking of, the nature of animals. Thus, animal actions, those that are peculiar to animals; such are sensation and muscular motion. Animal-Flower, in Zoology, a name given to several species of animals belonging to the genus <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-ACTINIA">Actinia</a> of Linnæus. They have likewise been distinguished by the names of Urtica Marina, or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>-nettle, from their supposed property of stinging; and Sea-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ANEMONE">anemone</a>, from their claws or tentacles being disposed in regular circles, and tinged with a variety of bright lively colours, resembling the petals of some of our most beautiful flowers. As to one species particularly, mentioned by Abbé Dicquemarre, (Phil. Trans. for 1773, art. 37.) the purest <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, carmine, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ULTRAMARINE">ultramarine</a>, are said to be scarce sufficient to express their brilliancy. The bodies of some of them are hemispherical, of others cylindrical, and of others shaped like a fig. Their substance likewise differs: some are stiff and gelatinous, others fleshy and muscular; but all of them are capable of altering their <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> when they extend their bodies and claws in search of food. They are found on many of the rocky coasts of the West <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, and likewise on some parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of England. They have only one opening, which is in the centre of the uppermost part of the animal; round this are placed rows of fleshy claws; this opening is the mouth of the animal, and is capable of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENSION">extension</a>. The animals themselves, though exceedingly voracious, will bear long fasting. They may be preserved alive a whole year, or perhaps longer, in a vessel of sea-water, without any visible food; but, when food is presented, one of them will successively devour two mussels in their shells, or even swallow a whole crab as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> as a hen's <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGG">egg</a>. In a day or two the crab-shell is voided at the mouth, perfectly cleared of all the meat. The mussel shells are likewise discharged whole, with the two shells joined together, but entirely empty, so that not the least particle of fish is to be perceived on opening them. An anemone of one species will even swallow an individual of another species; but after retaining it ten or twelve hours, will throw it up alive and uninjured. Through this opening also it produces its young ones alive, already furnished with little claws, which, as soon as they fix themselves, they begin to extend in search of food. One of the extremities of the sea-anemone resembles, as we have said, the outward leaves of that flower; while its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMBS">limbs</a> are not unlike the shag or inner part of it. By the other extremity it fixes itself, as by a sucker, to the rocks or stones lying in the sand; but it is not totally deprived of the power of progressive motion, as it can shift its situation, though very slowly. A particular species of animal-flowers has been found in some of the islands ceded to <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> at the last <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of peace with France; and the following account of them was published in the Philosophical Transactions, vol. lvii., by Mr Ellis, in a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to Lord Hillsborough. "This <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> animal, which is of a tender fleshy substance, consists of many tubular bodies swelling gently towards the upper part, and ending like a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BULB">bulb</a> or very small onion: on the top of each is its mouth, surrounded by one or two rows of tentacles, or claws, which when contracted look like circles of beads. "The lower part of all these bodies has a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> with a firm fleshy wrinkled tube, which sticks fast to the rocks, and sends forth other fleshy tubes, which creep along them in various directions. These are full of different sizes of these remarkable animals, which rise up irregularly in groups near to one another. "This adhering tube, that secures them fast to the rock, or shelly bottom, is worthy of our notice. The knobs that we observe, are formed in several parts of it by its insinuating itself into the inequalities of the coral rock, or by grasping pieces of shells, part of which still remain in it, with the fleshy substance grown over them. "This shows us the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTINCT">instinct</a> of nature, that directs these animals to preserve themselves from the violence of the waves, not unlike the anchoring of mussels, by their fine silken filaments that end in suckers; or rather like the shelly basis of the serpula, or worm shell, the tree oyster, and the slipper barnacle, &c. whose bases conform to the shape of whatever substance they fix themselves to, grasping it fast with their testaceous claws, to withstand the fury of a storm. "When we view the inside of this animal dissected lengthwise, we find like a little tube leading from the mouth to the stomach, from whence there rise eight wrinkled small guts, in a circular order, with a yellowish soft substance in them; these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEND">bend</a> over in the form of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a> towards the lower part of the bulb, from whence they may be traced downwards, to the narrow part of the upright tube, till they come to the fleshy adhering tube, where some of them may be perceived entering into a papilla, or the beginning of an animal of the like kind, most probably to convey it nourishment." Animal nourishment till it is provided with claws; the remaining part of these slender gills is <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> on in the fleshy tube, without doubt, for the same purpose of producing and supporting more young ones from the same common <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARENT">parent</a>. "The many longitudinal figures that we discover lying <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to each other, on the inside of the semi-transparent skin, are all inserted in the several claws round the animal's mouth, and are plainly the tendons of the muscles for moving and directing the claws at the will of the animal; they may be likewise traced down to the adhering tube. "As this specimen has been preserved in spirits, the colour of the animal, when living, cannot be certainly known; it is at present of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> yellowish <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>. "With regard to its name, it may be called Actinia sociata, or the Cluster Animal flower." The Abbé Diequemarre, by many curious though cruel experiments, related to the Phil. Trans. for 1773, has shown that these animals possess, in a most extraordinary degree, the power of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-REPRODUCTION">reproduction</a>; so that scarce anything more is necessary to produce as many sea anemones as we please, than to cut a single one into as many pieces. A sea anemone being cut in two by a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECTION">section</a> through the body, that part, where the limbs and mouth are placed, ate a piece of a mussel offered to it soon after the operation, and continued to feed and grow daily for three months after. The food sometimes passed through the animal; but was generally thrown up again, considerably changed, as in the perfect sea anemone. In about two months, two rows of limbs were perceived growing out of the part where the incision was made. On offering food to this new mouth, it was laid hold of and eaten; and the limbs continually increasing, the animal gradually became as perfect as those which had never been cut. In some instances, however, he found that, when one of these creatures was cut through, new limbs would be produced from the cut place, those at the mouth remaining as before: so that a monstrous animal was the consequence, having two mouths, and feeding at both ends. Having put some of them into a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAN">pan</a> of water, set over a slow fire, he found that they lost their life at 30 degrees of Reaumur's thermometer. To avoid the imputation of cruelty in these experiments, the author argues the favourable consequences that have attended his operations on the sea anemones which have been so fortunate as to fall into his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>; as he hath not only multiplied their existence, but also renewed their youth; which last, he adds, "is surely no small advantage." In Hughes's Natural History of Barbadoes, an account is also given of several species of animal-flowers. They are there described as only found in a basin in one particular cave; and of the most remarkable species mentioned by him we have the following description. "In the middle of the basin, there is a fixed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, or rock, which is always under water. Round its sides, at different depths, seldom exceeding 18 inches, are seen, at all times of the year, issuing out of little holes, certain substances that have the appearance of fine radiated flowers, of a pale yellow, or a bright straw colour, slightly tinged with green, having a circular border of thick set petals, about the size of, and much resembling, those of a single garden marigold, except that the whole of this seeming flower is narrower at the discus, or setting-on of the leaves, than any flower of that kind. "I have attempted to pluck one of these from the rock, to which they are always fixed; but never could effect it: for as soon as my fingers came within two or three inches of it, it would immediately contract, close together its yellow border, and shrink back into the hole of the rock; but if left undisturbed for about four minutes, it would come gradually in sight, expanding, though at first very cautiously, its seeming leaves, till it last it appeared in its former bloom. However, it would again recoil, with a surprising quickness when my <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> came within a small distance of it. Having tried the same experiment by attempting to touch it with my <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANE">cane</a>, and a small slender rod, the effect was the same. "Though I could not by any means contrive to take or pluck from the rock one of these animals entire; yet I once cut off (with a knife which I had held for a long time out of sight, near the mouth of a hole out of which one of these animals appeared) two of these seeming leaves. These, when out of the water, retained their shape and colour; but, being composed of a membrane-like substance, surprisingly thin, it soon shrivelled up, and decayed." The reproductive power of the Barbadoes animal-flower is prodigious. Many people coming to see these strange creatures, and occasioning some inconvenience to a person through whose grounds they were obliged to pass, he resolved to destroy the objects of their curiosity, and, that he might do so effectually, caused all the holes out of which they appeared, to be carefully bored and drilled with an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> instrument, so that we cannot suppose but their bodies must have been entirely crushed to a pulp: nevertheless, they again appeared in a few weeks from the very same places. Plate XXXIV. fig. 1. represents the actinia sociata, or clustered animal-flower, described by Mr Ellis, with its radical tube adhering to a rock: (a) One of the animals stretching out its claws. Fig. 2. A perpendicular dissection of one of the bodies, to show the gullet, intestines, stomach, and fibres or tendons that move the claws: (a) A young one arising out of the adhering tube. Fig. 3. The actinia aster, or animal-flower of the newly ceded islands. Fig. 4. The actinia anemone, or sea anemone from the same place. Fig. 5. The under part of the same by which it adheres to the rocks. Fig. 6. The actinia helianthus, or sea sun-flower, from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DITTO">ditto</a>. Fig. 7. The under part of the same. Fig. 8. The actinia dianthus, or sea carnation, from the rocks at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HASTINGS">Hastings</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUSSEX">Sussex</a>. This animal adheres by its tail, or sucker, to the upper part of the projecting rocks opposite to the town; and, when the tide is out, has the appearance of a long white fig; this is the form of it when put into a glass of sea water. It is introduced here as a new variety of this animal not yet described. Animal Food. See Food. Animal Economy. This subject is explained under Anatomy. Animal <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGNETISM">Magnetism</a>. See Magnetism. Animal Spirit. See Nervous Fluid.
