As to the word death, a state of misery which is as bad, or worse than death, may properly enough be called by that name; and thus the punishment of wicked men after the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> of judgment is in the book of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVELATION">Revelation</a> frequently called the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> death. Some Christian writers allow a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> time of the most terrible torments of sinners; and after that suppose that there shall be an utter end of their being. Of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> Irenæus appears to have been; who, according to M. du <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIN">Pin</a>, taught that the souls, at least of the wicked, would not subsist eternally; but that, after having undergone their torments for a certain period, they would at last cease to be at all. But Tillemont, Petit, Didier, and others, endeavour to defend Irenæus from this imputation, as being too favourable to the wicked. It has been much disputed among divines, whether, at the consummation of all things, this earth is to be annihilated, or only purified, and fitted for the habitation of some new order of beings. Gerard in his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">Common</a> Places, and Hakewil in his Apology, contend earnestly for a total abolition or annihilation. Ray, Calmet, and others, think the system of renovation or restitution more probable, and more consonant to Scripture, reason, and antiquity. The fathers who have treated on the question are divided; some holding that the universe shall not be annihilated, but only its <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> changed; others asserting, that the substance of it shall be destroyed. How widely have the sentiments of mankind differed as to the possibility and impossibility of annihilation! According to some, nothing so difficult; it requires the infinite power of the Creator to effect it: some go further, and seem to put it out of the power of God himself. According to others nothing so easy: Existence is a state of violence; all things are continually endeavouring to return to their primitive nothing; it requires no power at all; it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> do itself; nay, what is more, it requires an infinite power to prevent it. Many authors consider preservation as a continual <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-REPRODUCTION">reproduction</a> of a thing, which, subsisting no longer of itself, would every moment return into nothing. Gassendi on the contrary asserts, that the world may indeed be annihilated by the same power which first created it, but that to continue it there is no occasion for any power of preservation. Some divines, of which number the learned Bishop <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> seems to be, hold annihilation for the greatest of all evils, worse than even the utmost torments of hell flames; whilst others, with some of the eastern philosophers, acknowledge annihilation for the ultimate pitch of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> nature is capable of; that sovereign good, that <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> beatitude, so long vainly sought for by the philosophers, is found here. No wonder it had been so long concealed; for who would have thought of looking for the summum bonum, where others have placed the sum of misery? The said prelate proposes it as a question, Whether suffering eternal torments be a greater evil than not existing? He thinks it highly probable, that the damned will... will be such fools, that feeling their own misery in the most exquisite <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, they will rather applaud their own conduct, and choose to be, and to be what they are, rather than not to be at all; fond of their condition, however wretched, like people enraged, they will persist in their former sentiments without opening their eyes to their folly, and persevere by way of indignation and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a>. Mr Bayle refutes him on this head; but might, one would think, have saved himself the trouble. The Talapoin hold it the supreme degree of happiness to have the soul totally annihilated, and freed from the burden and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a> of transmigrations. They speak of three Talapoins, who, after a great number of transmigrations, became gods; and when arrived at this state, procured this further reward of their merit, to be annihilated. The ultimate reward of the highest perfection man can arrive at is neuropean, or annihilation; which at length is granted to those who are perfectly pure and good, after their souls have wandered many thousand years through various bodies.

ANNIVERSARY

Pages 435-435

the annual return of any remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>. Anniversary days, in old times, more particularly denoted those days in which an office was yearly performed for the souls of the deceased, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the martyrdom of the saints was yearly celebrated in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>.

ANNOBON

Pages 435-435

a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Loango, belonging to the Portuguese. It lies in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 5. 10. S. Lat. 1. 50. and receives its name from being discovered on New-year's-<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>. According to Pyrard, it is about five <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> six French leagues in compass; but Baudrand says, it is ten leagues round. Here are two <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, the tops of which being continually covered with <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a>, occasion frequent rains. On the south-east of the island are two rocks; one of which is low, and upon a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> with the surface of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>; the other higher and larger, but both dangerous in the night to shipping; but between them the channel is deep and clear. These rocks are inhabited by vast numbers of birds, so tame, that the sailors frequently catch them with their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. On the same side of the island is a convenient watering <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> at the foot of a rivulet, which tumbles from the mountains <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to a valley covered with <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CITRON">citron</a> trees, &c. and affording a pleasant and refreshing <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a>; but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west side is difficult and dangerous, though most frequented by ships who have no intention of touching upon the continent. In either place it is difficult to take in a sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, on account of the violent breaking of the sea, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> intrenchment erected by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEGROES">negroes</a>, from which they annoy all strangers that attempt to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>. The true road for shipping lies on the north-east side, where they may <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCHOR">anchor</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a>, ten, thirteen, or sixteen fathoms, on a fine sand <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to the land, opposite to the village where the negroes have thrown up their intrenchments. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> is wholesome, and the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> clear and serene for the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the year. Every part of the island is watered by pleasant brooks and fresh water <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a>, which, however, at the new and full moons, or in all high <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIDES">tides</a>, acquire a brackishness. The banks of every rivulet are covered with palms, whence the inhabitants extract their wine by incision. Here are a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of fertile valleys, which produce <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> corn, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>, millet, yams, potatoes, &c. and afford pasture for abundance of oxen, sheep, goats, &c. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POULTRY">Poultry</a> and fish also abound here: but the only mercantile production is cotton, which is esteemed equal in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> to any produced in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, though the quantity is small. In the year 1655, the Dutch <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a> Matelief found 200 negroes, and two Portuguese, on Annobon, most of them able to bear arms, expert in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of them, and trained up in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a>. La Croix says, it has a town opposite to the road that contains above 100 houses, the whole surrounded by a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARAPET">parapet</a>. Most of their dwellings are <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANE">cane</a> huts. In the whole island there is not a single <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> built of stone, and only two of wood, which belong to the Portuguese. All the inhabitants are meanly clothed; the women go bareheaded, and have also the upper part of the body naked, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a> being defended by a piece of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> wrapt under their stomach, and falling down in the form of a petticoat, or wide apron, to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNEES">knees</a>. As to the men, they wear only a linen girdle round the loins, with a small flap before. The women carry their children on their backs, and suckle them over the shoulder. All the inhabitants are subject to the Portuguese governor, who is the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> person in the island; at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> that the negroes have their own chief subordinate to him. They are all rigid Catholics, having either been compelled or persuaded by the arguments of the Portuguese to embrace that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>; and, like all other converts, they are bigotted in proportion to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOVELTY">novelty</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a>, and their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> of the true tenets. ANNO Domini, i.e. the year of our <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>; the computation of time from our Saviour's incarnation.

ANNOMINATION

Pages 435-435

in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">Rhetoric</a>, the same with what is otherwise called paranomasia. See PARONOMASTIA.

ANNONA

Pages 435-435

the Custard Apple. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. ANNONÆ PRÆFECTUS, in antiquity, an extraordinary <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a>, whose business it was to prevent a scarcity of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>, and to regulate the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> and fineness of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>.

ANNONAY

Pages 435-435

a small town of France, in the department of Ardeche, formerly Upper Vivarais, scated on the river Deunre. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 4. 52. N. Lat. 45. 15.

ANNOT

Pages 435-435

a small <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of Provence in France. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 7. 0. N. Lat. 44. 4.

ANNOTATION

Pages 435-435

in matters of literature, a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIEF">brief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMENTARY">commentary</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> remark, upon a book or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, in order to clear up some passage, or draw some conclusion from it. ANNOTTA. See ANOTTA.

ANNUAL

Pages 435-436

in a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, an appellation given to whatever returns every year, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> is always performed within that space of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. ANNUAL <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">Motion</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">Earth</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">ASTRONOMY</a>. ANNUAL Leaves, are such leaves as come up afresh in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>; and perish in winter. These stand opposed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVERGREENS">Evergreens</a>. ANNUAL <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">Plants</a>, called also simply annuals, are such as only live their year, i.e., come up in the spring and die again in the autumn; and accordingly are to be recruited every year. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ANNUALRENT">ANNUALRENT</a> is used, in Scots <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, to denote a yearly profit due by a debtor in a sum of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> to a creditor for the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of it. <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">Right</a> of ANNUALRENT, in Scots Law, the original method of burdening lands with a yearly payment for the loan of money, before the taking of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> for money was allowed by statute.

ANNUEL OF NORWAY

Pages 436-436

of which mention is made in the acts of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> James III., was an annual payment of a hundred merks <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a>, which the kings of Scotland were obliged to pay to the kings of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWAY">Norway</a>, in satisfaction for some pretensions which the latter had to the Scottish <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, by virtue of a conveyance made thereof by Malcolm Kenmore, who usurped the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> after his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>'s decease. This annuel was first established in 1266: in consideration whereof the Norwegians renounced all <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> to the succession to the isles of Scotland. It was paid till the year 1468, when the annuel, with all its arrears, was renounced in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> between King James III. and Margaret <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Christian I., king of Norway, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>.

ANNUITY

Pages 436-443

a sum of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, payable yearly, half-yearly, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> quarterly, to continue a certain <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of years, for ever, or for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. An annuity is said to be in arrear, when it continues unpaid after it falls due. And an annuity is said to be in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVERSION">reversion</a>, when the purchaser, upon paying the price, does not immediately enter upon possession; the annuity not commencing till some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> after. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">Interest</a> on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANNUITIES">annuities</a> may be computed either in the way of simple or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> interest. But compound interest being found most equitable, both for buyer and seller, the computation by simple interest is universally disused. I. Annuities for a certain time. Problem 1. Annuity, rate, and time, given; to find the amount, or sum of yearly payments, and interest. Rule. Make 1 the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> of a geometrical <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a>, and the amount of £1. for a year the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> ratio; continue this series to as many terms as there are years in the question, and the sum of this series is the amount of £1. annuity for the given years; which, multiplied by the given annuity, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> produce the amount sought. Example. An annuity of 40l. payable yearly, is forborne and unpaid till the end of 5 years: What will then be due, reckoning compound interest at 5 per cent. on all the payments then in arrear? \[ \begin{align*} 1 & : 1.05 : 1.1025 : 1.157625 : 1.21550625 \\ & \text{whose sum is } 5.25563125; \text{ and } 5.25563125 \times 40 = 210.2525 = 221l. os. 6d. \text{ the amount sought.} \end{align*} \] The amount may also be found thus: Multiply the given annuity by the amount of £1. for a year; to the product add the given annuity, and the sum is the amount in two years; which multiply by the amount of £1. for a year; to the product add the given annuity, and the sum is the amount in 3 years, &c. The former question wrought in this manner follows: | 40 am. in 1 year | 126.1 am. in 3 years | |-----------------|---------------------| | 1.05 | 1.05 | | 42.00 | 132.405 | | 40 | 40 | | 82 am. in 2 years | 172.405 am. in 4 years | | 1.05 | 1.05 | | 86.10 | 181.02525 | | 40 | 40 | | 126.1 am. in 3 years | 221.02525 am. in 5 years | <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the given time be years and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>, find the amount for the whole years, as above: then find the amount of £1. for the given quarters; by which multiply the amount for the whole years; and to the product add such a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the annuity as the given quarters are of a year. If the given annuity be payable half yearly, or quarterly, find the amount of £1. for half a year or a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>; by which find the amount for the several half-years or quarters, in the same manner as the amount for the several years is found above. Prob. 2. Annuity, rate, and time given; to find the present worth, or sum of money that will purchase the annuity. Rule. Find the amount of the given annuity by the former problem; and then, by compound interest, find the present worth of this amount, as the sum due at the end of the given time. Exampl. What is the present worth of an annuity of 40l. to continue 5 years, discounting at 5 per cent. compound interest? By the former problem, the amount of the given annuity for 5 years, at 5 per cent. is 221.02525; and by compound interest, the amount of £1. for 5 years, at 5 per cent. is 1.2762815625. And, 1.2762815625 \times 221.02525000 = 173.179 = 173l. 3s. 7d. the present worth sought. The present worth may be also found thus: By compound interest, find the present worth of each year by itself, and the sum of these is the present worth sought. The former example done in this way follows: \[ \begin{align*} 1.2762815625 & \times 40.000000000 = (31.3410) \\ 1.21550625 & \times 40.0000000 = (32.9080) \\ 1.157625 & \times 40.0000 = (34.5535) \\ 1.1025 & \times 40.000 = (36.2811) \\ 1.05 & \times 40.0 = (38.0952) \end{align*} \] Present worth = 173.1788 If the annuity to be purchased be in reversion, find first the present worth of the annuity, as commencing immediately, by any of the methods taught above; and, then, by compound interest, find the present worth of that present worth, rebating for the time in reversion; and this last present worth is the answer.] Annuity. **Examp.** What is the present worth of a yearly pension or rent of £75, to continue 4 years, but not to commence till three years hence, discounting at 5 per cent.? \[ \begin{align*} 0.05 : 1 : : 75 : 1500 \\ 1.05 \times 1.05 \times 1.05 \times 1.05 = 1.21550625 \\ 1.21550625 \times 1500 = 1823.25371 \\ 1500 \\ 1234.05371 \\ \end{align*} \] 265.94629, present worth of the annuity, if it was to commence immediately. \[ \begin{align*} 1.05 \times 1.05 \times 1.05 \times 1.05 = 1.157625 \\ L. s. d. \\ 1.157625 \times 265.94629 = 299.7344 = 229 \text{ } 8 \frac{1}{4} \\ \end{align*} \] **Prob. 3.** Present worth, rate, and time given; to find the annuity. **Rule.** By the preceding problem, find the present worth of 1l. annuity for the rate and time given; and then say, As the present worth thus found to 1l. annuity, so the present worth given to its annuity; that is, divide the given present worth by that of 1l. annuity. **Examp.** What annuity, to continue 5 years, will 173l. 3s. 7d. purchase, allowing compound interest at 5 per cent.? \[ \begin{align*} 0.05 : 1 : : 1 : 20l. \\ 1.05 \times 1.05 \times 1.05 \times 1.05 \times 1.05 = 1.2762815625 \\ 1.2762815625 \times 20 = 25.525625 \\ 20 \\ 15.6705 \\ \end{align*} \] 4.3295 present worth of 1l. annuity. 4.3295 \times 173.179 = 740l. annuity. Ans. II. Annuities for ever, or freehold Estates. In freehold estates, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called annuities in fee-simple, the things chiefly to be considered are, 1. The annuity or yearly rent. 2. The price or present worth. 3. The rate of interest. The questions that usually occur on this head will <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> under one or other of the following problems. **Prob. 1.** Annuity and rate of interest given, to find the price. As the rate of 1l. to 1l. so the rent to the price. **Examp.** The yearly rent of a small estate is 40l. What is it worth in ready money, computing interest at 3\(\frac{1}{2}\) per cent.? As \(0.035 : 1 : : 40 : 1142.857142 = L.1142 \text{ } 17 \text{ } 1\frac{1}{2}\). **Prob. 2.** Price and rate of interest given, to find the rent or annuity. As 1l. to its rate, so the price to the rent. **Examp.** A <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> purchases an estate for 4000l. and has 4\(\frac{1}{2}\) per cent for his money: Required the rent. As 1 : 0.045 : : 4000 : 1 : 180l. rent sought. **Prob. 3.** Price and rent given, to find the rate of interest. As the price to the rent, so 1 to the rate. **Examp.** An estate of 180l. yearly rent is bought for 4000l.: What rate of interest has the purchaser for his money? As 4000 : 180l. : : 1 : 0.045 rate sought. **Prob. 4.** The rate of interest given, to find how many years purchase an estate is worth. Divide 1 by the rate, and the quot is the number of years purchase the estate is worth. **Examp.** A gentleman is willing to purchase an estate, provided he can have 2\(\frac{1}{2}\) per cent. for his money: How many years purchase may he offer? 0.025 \times 1000 = 40 years purchase. Ans. **Prob. 5.** The number of years purchase, at which an estate is bought or sold, given; to find the rate of interest. Divide 1 by the number of years purchase, and the quot is the rate of interest. **Examp.** A gentleman gives 40 years purchase for an estate: What interest has he for his money? 40 \times 0.025 = rate sought. The computations hitherto are all performed by a single <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> or multiplication, and it will scarcely be perceived that the operations are conducted by the rules of compound interest; but when a reversion occurs, recourse must be had to tables of annuities on compound interest. **Prob. 6.** The rate of interest, and the rent of a freehold estate in reversion, given; to find the present worth or value of the reversion. By Prob. 1. find the price or present worth of the estate, as if possession was to commence presently; and then, by the Tables, find the present value of the given annuity, or rent, for the years <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> to the commencement; subtract this value from the former value, and the remainder is the value of the reversion. **Examp.** A has the possession of an estate of 130l. per annum, to continue 20 years; B has the reversion of the same estate, from that time for ever: What is the value of the estate, what the value of the 20 years possession, and what the value of the reversion, reckoning compound interest at six per cent.? By Prob. 1. 0.06 \times 130.00 = 2166.6666 value of the estate. By Tables 1491.0896 val. of the possession. 675.5770 val. of the reversion. **Prob. 7.** The price or value of a reversion, the time prior to the commencement, and rate of interest, given, to find the annuity or rent. By the Tables, find the amount of the price of the reversion for the years prior to the commencement; and then by Prob. 3. find the annuity which that amount will purchase. **Examp.** The reversion of a freehold estate, to commence 20 years hence, is bought for 675.577l. compound interest being allowed at 6 per cent.: Required the annuity or rent? By the Tables the amount of 675.577l. \(L.\) for 20 years, at 6 per cent. is 2166\(\frac{1}{2}\). By Prob. 2. 2166\(\frac{1}{2}\) \times 0.06 = 130.0 rent sought. III. Life Annuities. The value of annuities for life is determined from observations made on the bills of mortality. Dr. Halley, Mr Simpson, and Mons. de Moivre, are gentlemen of distinguished merit in calculations of this kind. Dr Halley had recourse to the bills of mortality at Breslaw, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SILESIA">Silesia</a>, as a proper standard for the other parts of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, being a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> pretty central, at a distance from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, and not much crowded with traffickers or foreigners. He pitches upon 1000 persons all born in one year, and observes how many of these were alive every year, from their birth to the extinction of the last, and consequently how many died each year, as in the first of the following Tables; which is well adapted to Europe in general. But in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> there is observed to be a greater disparity in the births and burials than in any other place, owing probably to the vast <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> of people thither, in the way of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, from all parts of the known world. Mr Simpson, therefore, in order to have a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> particularly suited to this populous city, pitches upon 1280 persons all born in the same year, and records the number remaining alive each year till none were in life. It may not be improper, however, to observe, that however perfect tables of this sort may be in themselves, and however well adapted to any particular <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>, yet the conclusions deduced from them must always be uncertain, being nothing more than probabilities, or conjectures drawn from the usual <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> life. And the practice of buying and selling annuities on lives, by rules founded on such principles, may be justly considered as a sort of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOTTERY">lottery</a> or chance <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, in which the parties concerned must often be deceived. But as estimates and computations of this kind are now become fashionable, we shall subjoin some <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIEF">brief</a> account of such as appear most material. href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> of the continuance or extinction of human life is estimated as follows. 1. The probability that a person of a given age shall live a certain number of years, is measured by the proportion which the number of persons living at the proposed age has to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between the said number and the number of persons living at the given age. Thus, if it be demanded, what chance a person of 40 years has to live <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years longer? from 445, the number of persons living at 40 years of age in Dr Halley's table, subtract 377, the number of persons living at 47 years of age, and the remainder 68 is the number of persons that died during these seven years; and the probability or chance that the person in the question shall live these 7 years is as 377 to 68, or nearly as 5½ to 1. But, by Mr Simpson's table, the chance is something less than that of 4 to 1. 2. If the year to which a person of a given age has an equal chance of arriving before he dies, be required, it may be found thus: Find half the number of persons living at the given age in the tables, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLUMN">column</a> of age you have the year required. Thus, if the question be put with respect to a person of 30 years of age, the number of that age in Dr Halley's table is 531, the half whereof is 265, which is found in the table between 57 and 58 years; so that a person of 30 years has an equal chance of living between 27 and 28 years longer. 3. By the tables, the premium of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSURANCE">insurance</a> upon lives may in some <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> be regulated. Thus, Thus, the chance that a person of 25 years has to live another year, is, by Dr Hallely’s table, as 80 to 1; but the chance that a person of 50 years has to live a year longer is only 30 to 1; and, consequently, the premium for insuring the former ought to be to the premium for insuring the latter for one year, as 30 to 80, or as 3 to 8. Prob. I. To find the value of an annuity of £1. for the life of a single person of any given age. Mons. de Moivre, by observing the decrease of the probabilities of life, as exhibited in the table, composed an algebraic theorem or canon, for computing the value of any annuity for life; which canon we here lay <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> by way of Rule. Find the complement of life; and, by the tables, find the value of £1. annuity for the years denoted by the said complement; multiply this value by the amount of £1. for a year, and divide the product by the complement of life; then subtract the quotient from 1; divide the remainder by the interest of £1. for a year; and this last quotient will be the value of the annuity sought, or, in other words, the number of years purchase the annuity is worth. Exampl. But yet those who sell annuities have generally one and a half or two years more value, than specified in the table, from purchasers whose age is 20 years or upwards. Annuities of this sort are commonly bought or sold at so many years purchase: and the value assigned in the table may be so reckoned. Thus the value of an annuity of one pound for an age of 50 years, at 3 per cent. interest, is 12.51; that is, 12l. 10s. or twelve and a half years purchase. The marginal figures on the left of the column of age serve to shorten the table, and signify, that the value of an annuity for the age denoted by them is the same with the value of an annuity for the age denoted by the numbers before which they stand. Thus the value of an annuity for the age of 9 and 10 years is the same; and the value of an annuity for the age of 6 and 14, for the age of 3 and 24, &c., is the same. The further <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the table will appear in the questions and problems following. QUEST. 1. A person of 50 years would purchase an annuity for life of 200l.: What ready money ought he to pay, reckoning interest at 4½ per cent.? L. By the table the value of 1l. is 10.8 Multiply by 200 Value to be paid in ready money, 2164.00 Ans. QUEST. 2. A young merchant marries a widow lady of 40 years of age, with a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINTURE">jointure</a> of 300l. a-year, and wants to dispose of the jointure for ready money: What sum ought he to receive, reckoning interest at 3½ per cent.? L. By the table, the value of 1l. is 13.98 Value to be received in ready money, 4194.00 Ans. PROB. 2. To find the value of any annuity for the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> continuance of two lives; one life failing, the annuity to cease. Here there are two <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, according as the ages of the two persons are equal or unequal. 1. If the two persons be of the same age, work by the following RULE. Take the value of any one of the lives from the table; multiply this value by the interest of 1l. for a year; subtract the product from 2; divide the foresaid value by the remainder; and the quot will be the value of 1l. annuity, or the number of years purchase sought. EXAMP. What is the value of 100l. annuity for the joint lives of two persons, of the age of 30 years each, reckoning interest at 4 per cent.? By the table, one life of years is 14.68 Multiply by .04 Subtract the product 587.2 From 2.0000 Remains 1.4128 And 1.4128)14.68(10.39 value of 1l. annuity. And 10.39 X 100 = 1039 the value sought. 2. If the two persons are of different ages, work as directed in the following RULE. Take the values of the two lives from the table; multiply them into one another, calling the result the first product; then multiply the said first product by the interest of 1l. for a year, calling the result the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> product; add the values of the two lives, and from their sum subtract the second product; divide the first product by the remainder, and the quot will be the value of 1l. annuity, or the number of years purchase sought. EXAMP. What is the value of 70l. annuity for the joint lives of two persons, whereof one is 40 and the other 50 years of age, reckoning interest at 5 per cent.? By the table, the value of 40 years is 11.83 And the value of 50 years is 10.35 First product, 122.4405 Multiply by .05 Second product, 6.122025 Sum of the two lives, 22.180000 Second product deduct, 6.122025 Remainder, 16.057975 And 16.057975)122.4405(7.62 value of 1l. annuity. 533.40 value sought. PROB. 3. To find the value of an annuity upon the longest of two lives; that is, to continue so <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> as either of the persons is in life. RULE. From the sum of the values of the single lives subtract the value of the joint lives, and the remainder will be the value sought. EXAMP. What is the value of an annuity of 1l. upon the longest of two lives, the one person being 30, and the other 40 years of age, interest at 4 per cent.? By the table, 30 years is 14.68 40 years is 13.20 Value of their joint lives, by Prob. 2, 27.88 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">Case</a> 2, is 9.62 Value sought, 18.26 If the annuity be any other than 1l., multiply the answer found as above by the given annuity. The reader probably may wish that the reason of the rules, which, it must be owned, are intricate, had been assigned: but this could not be done without entering deeper into the subject than was practicable in this place. See Chances. See also Annuities, Supplement. Annuities. Annuities, Borrowing upon; one of the methods employed by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> for raising supplies. Of this there are two methods; that of borrowing upon annuities for terms of years, and that of borrowing upon annuities for lives. During the reigns of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> William and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> sums were frequently borrowed upon annuities for terms of years, which were sometimes longer and sometimes shorter. In 1693, an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> was passed for borrowing one million upon an annuity of 14 per cent. or of 142,000l. a year for 16 years. In 1691, an act was passed for borrowing a million upon annuities for lives, upon terms which in the present times would appear very advantageous. But the subscription was not filled up. In the following year the deficiency was made good by borrowing upon annuities for lives at 14 per cent. or at a little more than seven years purchase. In 1695, the persons who had purchased those annuities were allowed to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a> them for others of 96 years, upon paying into the exchequer 63 pounds in the hundred; that is, the difference between 14 per cent. for life, and 14 per cent. for 96 years, was sold for 63 pounds, or for four and a half years purchase. Such was the supposed instability of government, that even these terms procured few purchasers. In the reign of Queen Anne, money was upon different occasions borrowed both upon annuities for lives and upon annuities for terms of 32, of 89, of 98, and of 99 years. In 1719, the proprietors of the annuities for 32 years were induced to accept in lieu of them South Sea stock to the amount of eleven and a half years purchase of the annuities, together with an additional <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of stock equal to the arrears which happened then to be due upon them. In 1720, the greater part of the other annuities for terms of years both long and short were subscribed into the same <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FUND">fund</a>. The long annuities at that time amounted to 666,821l. 8s. 3½d. a year. On the 5th of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1775, the remainder of them, or what was not subscribed at that time, amounted only to 136,453l. 12s. 8d. During the two wars which began in 1739, and in 1755, little money was borrowed either upon annuities for terms of years, or upon those for lives. An annuity for 98 or 99 years, however, is worth nearly as much money as a perpetuity, and should, therefore, one might think, be a fund for borrowing nearly as much. But those who, in order to make family settlements, and to provide for remote futurity, buy into the public stocks, would not care to purchase into one of which the value was continually diminishing; and such people make a very considerable proportion both of the proprietors and purchasers of stock. An annuity for a long term of years, therefore, though its intrinsic value may be very nearly the same with that of a perpetual annuity, will not find nearly the same number of purchasers. The subscribers to a new loan, who <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> generally to sell their subscription as soon as possible, prefer greatly a perpetual annuity redeemable by <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, to an irredeemable annuity for a long term of years of only equal amount. The value of the former may be supposed always the same, or very nearly the same; and it makes, therefore, a more convenient transferable stock than the latter. During the two last-mentioned wars, annuities, either for terms of years or for lives, were seldom granted but as premiums to the subscribers to a new loan, over and above the redeemable annuity to interest upon the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> of which the loan was supposed to be made. They were granted, not as the proper fund upon which the money was borrowed; but as an additional encouragement to the lender. Annuities for lives have occasionally been granted in two different ways; either upon separate lives, or upon lots of lives, which in French are called Tontines, from the name of their inventor. When annuities are granted upon separate lives, the death of every individual annuitant disburdens the public revenue so far as it was affected by his annuity. When annuities are granted upon tontines, the liberation of the public revenue does not commence till the death of all the annuitants comprehended in one <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">lot</a>, which may sometimes consist of twenty or thirty persons, of whom the survivors succeed to the annuities of all those who die before them; the last survivor succeeding to the annuities of the whole lot. Upon the same revenue more money can always be raised by tontines than by annuities for separate lives. An annuity, with a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of survivorship, is really worth more than an equal annuity for a separate life; and from the confidence which every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> naturally has in his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a>, the principle upon which is founded the success of all lotteries, such an annuity generally sells for something more than it is worth. In countries where it is usual for government to raise money by granting annuities, tontines are upon this account generally preferred to annuities for separate lives. The expedient which will raise most money, is almost always preferred to that which is likely to bring about in the speediest manner the liberation of the public revenue. In France a much greater proportion of the public debts consists in annuities for lives than in England. According to a memoir presented by the parliament of Bordeaux to the king in 1764, the whole public debt of France is estimated at twenty-four hundred millions of livres; of which the capital, for which annuities for lives had been granted, is supposed to amount to three hundred millions, the eighth part of the whole public debt. The annuities themselves are computed to amount to thirty millions a-year, the fourth part of one hundred and twenty millions, the supposed interest of that whole debt. It is not the different degrees of anxiety in the two governments of France and England for the liberation of the public revenue, which occasions this difference in their respective <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of borrowing; it arises altogether from the different views and interests of the lenders. In <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, the seat of government being in the greatest mercantile city in the world, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> are generally the people who advance money to government. By advancing it they do not mean to diminish, but on the contrary, to increase their mercantile capitals; and unless they expected to sell with some profit their share in the subscription for a new loan, they never would subscribe. But if by advancing their money they were to purchase, instead of perpetual annuities, annuities for lives only, whether their own or those of other people, they would not always be so likely to sell them with a profit. Annuities upon their own lives they would always sell with loss; because no man will give for an annuity upon the life. Annuities life of another whose age and state are nearly the same with his own, the same price which he would give for one upon his own. An annuity upon the life of a third person, indeed, is no doubt, of equal value to the buyer and the seller; but its real value begins to diminish from the moment it is granted, and continues to do so more and more as long as it subsists. It can never, therefore, make so convenient a transferable stock as a perpetual annuity, of which the real value may be supposed always the same, or very nearly the same. In France, before the revolution, the seat of government not being in a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> mercantile city, merchants did not make so great a proportion of the people who advance money to government. The people concerned in the finances, the farmers general, the receivers of the taxes which were not in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARM">farm</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-BANKERS">bankers</a>, &c. made the greater part of those who advance their money in all public exigencies. Such people were commonly men of mean birth, but of great wealth, and frequently of great <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a>. They were too proud to marry their equals, and women of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> disdained to marry them. They frequently resolved, therefore, to live bachelors; and having neither any families of their own, nor much regard for those of their relations, whom they were not always very fond of acknowledging, they desired only to live in splendour during their own time, and were not unwilling that their fortune should end with themselves. The number of rich people, besides, who were either averse to marry, or whose condition of life rendered it either improper or inconvenient for them to do so, was much greater in France than in England. To such people, who had little or no care for posterity, nothing could be more convenient than to exchange their capital for a revenue, which is to last just as long, and no longer, than they wish it to do.

ANNUITY OF TEINDS

Pages 443-443

in Scots <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, a certain proportion of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TEINDS">teinds</a> of erected benefices formerly payable to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, but now gone into disuse.

ANNULAR

Pages 443-443

in a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, something in the form of, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> resembling a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RING">ring</a>. It is also a peculiar denomination of the fourth finger, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called the ring finger.

ANNULET

Pages 443-443

a little circle, born as a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> in coats of arms, as also added to them as a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a>. Among the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> it represented <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>. It also denotes strength and eternity, by reason of its circular form.

ANNULLING

Pages 443-443

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> sometimes used for canceling <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> making void a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEED">deed</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a>, or the like.

ANNULOSA

Pages 443-443

a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYPE">type</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ANIMAL_KINGDOM">animal <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, comprehending five classes; see Supplement.

ANNUNCIADA

Pages 443-443

Annuntiada, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Annunciata, an order of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHTHOOD">knighthood</a> in Savoy, first instituted by Amadeus I. in the year 1409: their collar was of 15 links, interwoven one with another, in form of a true lover's knot: and the motto, F. E. R. T. signifying, Fortitudo ejus Rhodum tenuit. Amadeus VIII. gave the name Annunciada to this order, which was formerly known by that of the knot of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a>; changing at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the image of St Maurice <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> of Savoy, which hung at the collar, for that of the Virgin <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>; and instead of the motto above mentioned, substituting the words of the angel's salutation. ANNUNCIADA is also the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of several <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> orders, instituted at different times, and at different places, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the annunciation. See the next article.

ANNUNCIATION

Pages 443-443

is likewise a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> given by the Jews to a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSOVER">passover</a>.

ANNUNCIATOR

Pages 443-443

the name of an officer in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Constantinople. It was his business to inform the people of the festivals that were to be celebrated.

ANODYNE

Pages 443-443

from α privative, and ἀδωρον, doleo; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> α neg. and ἀδωρον, pain), a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> applied to medicines which ease pain, and procure <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a>. They are divided into three sorts, viz. 1. Paregorics, or such as assuage pain. 2. Hypnotics, or such as relieve by procuring sleep. 3. Narcotics, or such as ease the patient by stupifying him. Opiates and narcotics destroy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSATION">sensation</a>. Some hypnotics and paregorics, as nitre, camphor, &c. procure ease and sleep by removing the offending cause. Camphor is said to be the best anodyne in nervous <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> and at the decline of fevers. The doses of these medicines are generally regulated by the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PULSE">pulse</a>.

ANOINTERS

Pages 443-443

a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a> in some parts of England, so called from the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> they used of anointing all persons before they admitted them into their <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. They founded their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of anointing upon the fifth of James, ver. 14, and 15.

ANOLYMPIADES

Pages 443-444

in antiquity, a name given by the Elians to those Olympic games which had been celebrated under the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the Pisaeans and Arcadians. The Elians claimed the sole <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of managing the Olympic games, in which they sometimes Anolympiad was celebrated by order of the Arcadians, by whom the Elians were at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> reduced very low; this, as well as those managed by the inhabitants of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PISA">Pisa</a>, they called ἀνολυμπιάδες, that is, "unlawful Olympiads;" and left them out of their annals, wherein the names of their victors and other occurrences were registered. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANOMALISTICAL_YEAR">ANOMALISTICAL year</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, the time that the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> takes to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through her orbit: it is also called the Periodical Year. The space of time belonging to this year is greater than the tropical year, on account of the precession of the equinoxes. See Astronomy.

ANOMALOUS

Pages 444-444

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> applied to whatever is <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> deviates from the rule observed by other things of the like <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. ANOMALOUS Verbs, in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>, such as are not conjugated conformably to the paradigm of their conjugation. They are found in all languages. In Latin, the verb lego is the paradigm of the third conjugation; and runs thus, lego, legis, legit: by the same rule it should be fero, feris, fert; but we say, fero, fers, fert: fero, then, is an anomalous verb. In English the irregularity relates often to the preter tense and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSIVE">passive</a> participle; for example, give, were it formed according to rule, would make gived in the preter tense and passive participle; whereas, in the former, it makes gave, and in the latter given.

ANOMALY

Pages 444-444

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, an irregularity in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a>, whereby they deviate from the aphelion <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> apogee.

ANOMOEANS

Pages 444-444

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, the name by which the pure <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARIANS">Arians</a> were called in the fourth century, in contradistinction to the Semi-Arians. The word is formed from the Greek ἀνόμοιος, different, dissimilar: For the pure Arians asserted, that the Son was of a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> different from, and in nothing like, that of the Father: whereas the Semi-Arians acknowledged a likeness of nature in the Son; at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> that they denied, with the pure Arians, the consubstantiality of the Word. The Semi-Arians condemned the Anomoeans in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SELEUCIA">Seleucia</a>; and the Anomoeans in their turn condemned the Semi-Arians in the councils of Constantinople and Antioch, erasing the word ὁμόων, like, out of the Formula of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIMINI">Rimini</a> and that of Constantinople.

ANOMORHOMBIDIA

Pages 444-444

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, the name of a genus of spars; the word is derived from the Greek ἀνομοῦς, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a>, and ῥόμβος, a rhomboidal <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>. The bodies of this genus are pellucid crystalline spars of no determinate <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> regular <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> form, but always breaking into regularly rhomboidal masses; easily fissile, and composed of plates running both horizontally and perpendicularly through the masses, but cleaving more readily and evenly in a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a>, than in a perpendicular <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>; the plates being ever composed of irregular arrangements of rhomboidal concretions. Of this genus there are five known <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>. 1. A <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, bright, and shattery one; found in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> quantities in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DERBYSHIRE">Derbyshire</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>. 2. A <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILK">milk</a>-white, opaque, and shattery one, found in some parts of France, and very plentifully in Germany, and sometimes in Wales and Scotland, and in the hills of Yorkshire. 3. A hard, dull, and snow-white one, found in some of the mines in Derbyshire, and in many of our northern counties. 4. A hard, gray, and pellucid one, found in the lead mines of Yorkshire, and very <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> in Germany. And, 5. A pellucid and colourless one; this is found in the lead mines of Derbyshire and Yorkshire. All these in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> have the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> refraction of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICELAND">Iceland</a> crystal. See ICELAND Crystal. ANONIS. See ONONIS, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ANONYMOUS

Pages 444-444

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>. The sending anonymous letters demanding <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, &c. is felony by the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">Act</a>, 9 Geo. I. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. xxii.

ANOREXIA

Pages 444-445

ANOREXY, (from ἀ <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEGATIVE">negative</a>, and ἐσθίειν, appetite): a want of appetite, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a loathing of food. The disorder is either original or symptomatic. When it is original, its causes are bad diet, too free drinking, voraciousness, &c.: In which <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, a vomit or two of ipecacuanha may be taken; and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEMPERANCE">temperance</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> but cordial nourishing diet, and daily <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> persisted. persisted in, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> generally effect a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a>. But it is more frequently a symptom of some other disorder; and then the cure depends on the removal of the original one.

ANOSSI

Pages 445-446

a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Madagascar, lying between Lat. 23° 18' and 26° 0' S. It is watered by many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, most of which run into the Franchere, Ramevate, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Immour, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> of which is in a mountain called Manghaze, and discharges itself into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> in Lat. 25° 18' S. The mouth of this river is often stopped, and the course to the sea interrupted, unless kept open by the overflows of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> rains and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIDES">tides</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> runs <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> one <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> above the mouth, particularly in a free <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> with the sea. A lake, called Ambou, is formed at the mouth, half a league wide, with depth sufficient for any ship <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the mouth of the river was kept open. Next in bigness to the Franchere, is the Manghasia, which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> from a mountain called Sidiva, and empties itself into the sea, where <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> ships may ride at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCHOR">anchor</a>. Crocodiles breed in these and all the other rivers of the island. Between the two rivers above mentioned lies <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> St Romain, half a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a> distant from the mouth of the Franchere, and which runs from the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west six or <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> leagues into the sea. When the cape is passed the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> forms a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>, in the shape of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>, which extends to the mouth of a river called Dian Panouge or Pitorah. In the middle of this bay the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> runs out, and almost forms a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> called Thorangare. Fort Dauphin lies to the north of this peninsula, and Port Dauphin over against it. This province has several other peninsulas and small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> belonging to it. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is beautiful; abounds in fruit trees; is fertile in pastures for cattle; and, if carefully cultivated, would produce all the necessaries of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. It is surrounded by high <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, which are covered with woods and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHRUBS">shrubs</a>; but, about four miles distant from Fort Dauphin, the adjacent hills are quite destitute of verdure. The French often dug in this neighbourhood, expecting to meet with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver, particularly in one mountain where several springs flow near each other and empty themselves into a neighbouring river. In this river they found several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a> and heaps intermixed with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> clay, with a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> spangles shining like silver, which they carefully pounded and washed, but without effect. About 60 yards above these springs the grass, and every sort of vegetable, appears half dried and yellow, from a metallic sulphur, which gives that aspect; but the top of the mountain is covered with a fresh and beautiful verdure. It is said that the Portuguese found gold at the foot of this mountain on the north side, but that the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> they had dug was filled up by the chiefs of the country after the Portuguese had been driven out. The province of Anossi is inhabited by three different sorts of whites, and four sorts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEGROES">negroes</a>. The whites are distinguished by the names of Rohandrians, Anacandrians, and Ondzatsi. The whites are distinguished from the negroes by the general names of Rafferamini or Rahimini; and the Rohandrians are distinguished above the other whites. When they proceed to an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> of a sovereign, whom they call Om-piandrian, or Dian Bahouache, he is chosen from the Rohandrian <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a>. Next to him the others hold the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of princes, and are honoured as such by all the rest of the subjects. The Anacandrians are descendants of the chiefs, but who have degenerated, and are accounted the bastards of princes, or those who are descended from a Rohandrian and any inferior white or black woman. These are likewise called by the name of Ontempassemaca, or people from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> parts of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECCA">Mecca</a>, from whence, they say, came the Rohandrians. Both the Rohandrians and Anacandrians wear <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, which hangs <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> in curls; and enjoy the privilege of killing beasts. The Ondzatsi, or lowest class of whites, are descended from the bastards of the Anacandrians. These are all fishermen, and are allowed to kill no land animal except a chicken. The four classes of negroes are named Voadziri, Lohavohits, Ontsoa and Ondveves. The Voadziri, the most powerful and the richest, are masters of several villages; and descended from the original lords of the country. They enjoy the privilege of killing beasts, when at a distance from the whites, and no Rohandrian or Anacandrian in the village. The Lohavohits are descendants from the Voadziri, and also lords; but with this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a>, that the one commands a whole district, and the jurisdiction of the others extends only to their own village and family. They are also permitted to kill those beasts they intend to eat, when at a distance from the whites. The Ontsoa are next to the Lohavohits, and are their near relations. The Ondveves are the lowest of all, being originally slaves by father and mother. The Voadziri, Lohavohits, and Ontsoa, enjoy the privilege of submitting themselves, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of their <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>, to any <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> they please. In return for such homage, the new lord makes them a present, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of which he becomes heir to all their possessions. Hence the lower classes both of whites and blacks, when death approaches, are under the greatest concern and anguish of mind, well knowing that their lords <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> not fail to deprive their children of every thing they possess. The Ondveves have not the same <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> with the others; but, in times of famine, the chiefs are obliged to supply them with necessaries; which if they fail to do, they have the liberty of submitting themselves to new masters. The inhabitants of this province have no <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>, and very little appearance of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>; only they keep up a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of immolating beasts upon particular occasions, as in sickness, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTING">planting</a> yams or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>, on assemblies, &c. They offer the first born beast to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVIL">devil</a> and to God, naming the devil first, in this manner, Dianbilis Aminhanhabare, or "Lord Devil and God."—There are several <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> on the river Franchere; and near this river the Portuguese had a fort built upon a steep rock, and several buildings below, with enclosures, which furnished all sorts of necessaries for their subsistence; but they were all massacred by the natives. This province seems originally to have been inhabited by negroes. The whites or Rafferamini settled in it about 200 years ago, and conquered the negroes. But they themselves were conquered by the French, though under the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of a king whom they honoured as a god. In 1642, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Rivault obtained permission to establish a colony in this <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the island; and accordingly he took possession of it in the name of the king of France, in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of September, that same year. Anossi, year. The French landed 200 men, well armed, and provided with store of ammunition and other necessaries for <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> a fort, which they immediately set about; but no sooner did the natives observe their intention, than they used their utmost art to prevent their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> from taking effect. This created a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, in which the French were victors; and, the natives becoming in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> much better reconciled to them, they intermarried, and lived up and down in several towns at some distance from one another, not above five or six in a place. This tranquillity lasted for some years; but at last the natives, growing jealous, resolved to free themselves from a foreign yoke; and accordingly formed a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSPIRACY">conspiracy</a> to cut off all the French in one <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>; which they soon after effected, not leaving a single person alive. In 1644 the above-mentioned Fort Dauphin was erected in Lat. 25° 6' S. Many buildings were erected, behind the fort, adjoining to the governor's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, with great enclosures that produced every sort of fruit and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KITCHEN">kitchen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERB">herb</a>. In 1656 it was accidentally destroyed by fire; but was soon after repaired, and still continues, notwithstanding the catastrophe above mentioned, and its garrison carries on frequent wars with the natives.

ANOTTA

Pages 446-446
or ARNOTTA, in dyeing, an elegant red colour, formed from the pellicles or pulp of the seeds of the Bixa, a tree common in South America. It is also called Terra Orleansa, and Roucou. The manner of making anotta is as follows: The red seeds, cleared from the pods, are steeped in water for seven or eight days, or longer, till the liquor begins to ferment; then strongly stirred, stamped with wooden paddles and beaters, to promote the separation of the red skins; this process is repeated several times, till the seeds are left white. The liquor, passed through close cane sieves, is pretty thick, of a deep red colour, and a very ill smell; in boiling, it throws up its colouring matter to the surface in form of scum, which is afterwards boiled down by itself to a due consistence, and made up while soft into balls. The anotta commonly met with among us, is moderately hard and dry, of a brown colour on the outside, and a dull red within. It is difficultly acted upon by water, and tinges the liquor only of a pale brownish yellow colour. It very readily dissolves in rectified spirit of wine; and communicates a high orange or yellowish red. Hence it is used as an ingredient in varnishes, for giving more or less of an orange cast to the simple colours. Alkaline salts render it perfectly soluble in boiling water, without altering its colour. Wool or silk boiled in the solution acquires a deep, but not a very durable, orange dye. Its colour is not changed by alum or by acids, any more than by alkalies: but when imbibed in cloth, it is discharged by soap, and destroyed by exposure to the air. It is said to be an antidote to the poisonous juice of manioc or cassava.—Labat informs us, that the Indians prepare anotta greatly superior to that which is brought to us, of a bright shining red colour, almost equal to carmine: that, for this purpose, instead of steeping and fermenting the seeds in water, they rub them with the hand, previously dipped in oil, till the pellicles come off, and are reduced into a clear paste; which is scraped off from the hands with a knife, and laid on a clean leaf in the shade to dry. De Laet, in his notes on Maygrave's href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural History of Brazil, mentions also two kinds of anotta; one of a permanent crimson colour, used as a fucus or paint for the face; and another which gives a colour inclining more to that of saffron. This last, which is our anotta, he supposes to be a mixture of the first sort with certain resinous matters, and with the juice of the root of the tree. The wax or pulp in which the seeds are enclosed is a cool agreeable rich cordial, and has been long in use among the Indians and Spaniards in America, who still mix it with their chocolate, both to heighten the flavour and raise the colour. It is said to be a successful remedy in bloody fluxes. The roots have much the same properties with the wax.

ANOUT

Pages 446-446

a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the Schagerrack, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a> which has <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWAY">Norway</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUTLAND">Jutland</a> on the west, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of Zeeland on the south. It lies in 13° O. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. and 56° 36' N. Lat.

ANQUETIL DU FERRON

Pages 446-446

A. H. an eminent French oriental scholar. See Supplement. ANSÆ, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, implies the parts of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SATURN">Saturn</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RING">ring</a> projecting beyond the disk of the planet.—The word is Latin, and properly signifies handles; these parts of the ring appearing like handles to the body of the planet.

ANSARIANS

Pages 446-447

a people of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, so called in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, but styled in De l'<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">Isle</a>'s maps Ensarians, and in those of D'Anville, Nassaris. The territory occupied by these Ansaria is that chain of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> which extends from Antakia to the rivulet called Nahr-el-Kabir, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> River. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of their origin, though little known, is yet instructive. The following account is from the Bibliothèque Orientale of Assemani, a writer who has drawn his materials from the best authorities. "In the year of the Greeks, 1202 (A.D. 891), there lived at the village of Nasar, in the environs of Koufa, an old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, who, from his fastings, his continual prayers, and his poverty, passed for a saint. Several of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> people declaring themselves his partizans, he selected from among them twelve disciples to propagate his doctrine. But the commandant of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, alarmed at his proceedings, seized the old man, and confined him in prison. In this reverse of fortune, his situation excited the pity of a girl who was slave to the gaoler, and she determined to give him his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>. An opportunity soon offered to effect her <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>. One <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> when the gaoler was gone to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a> intoxicated, and in a profound <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a>, she gently took the keys from under his pillow, and after opening the door to the old man, returned them to their place unperceived by her <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>: the next day when the gaoler went to visit his prisoner, he was extremely astonished at finding he had made his escape, and the more so since he could perceive no marks of violence. He therefore judiciously concluded he had been delivered by an angel, and eagerly spread the report, to avoid the reprehension he merited: the old man, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, asserted the same thing to his disciples, and preached his doctrines with more earnestness than ever.
