He even wrote a book, in which, among other things, he says, 'I such a one, of the village of Nasar, have seen Christ who is the word of God, who is Ahmad, son of Mohammed, son of Hanafa, of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALI">Ali</a>; who Ansarians who also is Gabriel: and he said to me, Thou art he who readeth (with understanding); thou art the man who speakest <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>; thou art the camel which preserveth the faithful from wrath; thou art the beast which carrieth their burden; thou art the (Holy) Spirit, and John, the son of Zachary. Go, and preach to men that they make four genuflections in praying; two before the rising of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, and two before his setting, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> their faces towards <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>: and let them say, three times, God Almighty! God Most <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">High</a>! God Most Great! Let them observe only the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> and third festival; let them fast but two days annually; let them not wash the prepuce, nor drink beer, but as much wine as they think proper; and lastly, let them abstain from the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> of carnivorous animals.' This old man, passing into Syria, propagated his opinions among the lower orders of the country people, numbers of whom believed in him: And after a few years he went away, and nobody ever knew what became of him." Such was the origin of these Ansarians, who are, for the most <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a>, inhabitants of the mountains before mentioned. The Ansaria are divided into several tribes or sects; among which are distinguished the Shamsia, or adorers of the sun; the Kelbia, or worshippers of the dog; and the Kadmosia, who are said to pay a particular homage to that part in women which corresponds to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIAPUS">priapus</a>. Many of the Ansaria believe in the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METEMPSYCHOSIS">metempsychosis</a>; others reject the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMMORTALITY">immortality</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>; and in general, in that civil and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> anarchy, that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> and rudeness which prevail among them, these peasants adopt what opinions they think proper, following the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a> they like best, and frequently attaching themselves to none. Their country is divided into three <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> districts, farmed by the chiefs called Mokaddamim. Their tribute is paid to the pacha of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIPOLI">Tripoli</a>, from whom they annually receive their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a>. Their mountains are in general not so steep as those of Lebanon, and consequently are better adapted to cultivation; but they are also more exposed to the Turks; and hence, doubtless, it happens, that with greater plenty of corn, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>, wines, and olives, they are more thinly inhabited than those of their neighbours the Maronites and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRUSES">Druses</a>.

ANSELM

Pages 447-447

archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a>, in the reigns of William Rufus and Henry I. He was born in the year 1033, at Aost, a town in Savoy at the foot of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALPS">Alps</a>. He became a monk in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a> of Bec in Normandy; of which he was afterwards chosen <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a>, and then <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABBOT">abbot</a>. In the year 1092, he was invited over to England by Hugh <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHESTER">Chester</a>; and in the year following was prevailed on, as we are told, with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> difficulty, to accept the archbishopric of Canterbury. He enjoined celibacy on the clergy; for which he was banished by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> Rufus, but recalled by Henry at his coming to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>. He refused to consecrate such <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> as were invested by the king, according to Pope Urban's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DECREE">decree</a>; flatly denying it to be the king's <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREROGATIVE">prerogative</a>: for this he was outed again; till, the pope and king agreeing, he was recalled in 1107. In short, from the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> of his consecration to that of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, he was continually employed in fighting the prerogative of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> against that of the crown; and for that purpose spent much of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> in travelling backwards and forwards between England and Rome, for the advice and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLINESS">holiness</a>. At the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARI">Bari</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, the pope being puzzled by the arguments of the Greeks against the Holy Ghost's proceeding from the Father, he called upon Anselm, who was present, and he discussed their objections with great applause. Priests call him a resolute saint; to other people he appears to have been an obstinate and insolent <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>. He wrought many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we believe the author of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, both before and after his death, which happened at Canterbury, in the 76th year of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, anno 1109. He was canonized in the reign of Henry VII. Anselm, though we may disregard him as a saint, deserves to be remembered as one of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> revivers of literature, after three centuries of profound <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a>. His works have been printed in different years, and at different places, viz. Nuremb. 1491. <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> 1544 and 1549. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> 1549. <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOGNE">Cologne</a> 1573 and 1612. Lyons 1630. But the best is that of Father Gerberon, printed at Paris 1675. It is divided into three parts; the first contains dogmatical tracts, and is entitled Mologia; the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> contains practical and devotional tracts; the third <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> consists of letters, in four books.

ANSER

Pages 447-447

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, a small <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STAR">star</a>, of the fifth <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> sixth magnitude, in the milky way, between the swan and eagle, first brought into order by Hevelius.

ANSERES

Pages 447-447

the name which Linnaeus gives to his third order of birds. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">ORNITHOLOGY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ANSIBARII

Pages 447-448
or ANSIVARI, an ancient people of Germany, situated somewhere in the neighbourhood of the Chauci. All we know of their history is, that, in the reign of the emperor Nero, they were driven from their own possessions by the Chauci. Being then in a forlorn condition, they took possession of some uninhabited lands, which had been used as pasture for the horses of the Roman soldiers. They were led by one Boiocalus, a man of great valour, and of known fidelity to the Romans. He remonstrated to the Romans, who objected to their taking possession of these lands, That the territory in dispute was large; and requested, that it might be allowed to an unhappy people driven from their own habitations: that, at the same time, wide tracts might be retained for the horses and cattle of the soldiers to graze in; that it was inconsistent with humanity to famish men in order to feed beasts, &c.: and at last, lifting up his eyes to heaven, he asked the celestial luminaries how they could behold a desolate soil, and if they would not more justly let loose the sea to swallow up usurpers, who had engrossed the whole earth? To this the Roman commander, Avitus, replied, That the weakest must submit to the strongest; and that since the gods, to whom they had appealed, had left the sovereign judgment to the Romans, they were resolved to suffer no other judges than themselves. To Boiocalus himself, however, he privately offered lands as a reward for his long attachment to the Romans; but this offer the brave German rejected, as a price for betraying Ansibarii, betraying his people: adding, "A place to live in we may want, but a place to die in we cannot." The Ansibarii now invited the neighbouring nations to join them against the Romans; but they, dreading the power of that nation, refused to give them any assistance; upon which they applied to the neighbouring nations, begging leave to settle in their territories; but being everywhere driven out as enemies and intruders, these unhappy people were reduced to wander up and down till every one of them perished.

ANSIKO

Pages 448-448

a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, bounded on the west by the river Umbre which runs into the Zaire, the kingdom of Wangua, and the Amboes who border on Loango; on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, by some deserts of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUBIA">Nubia</a>; and on the south, by Songo and Sonda, provinces of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGO">Congo</a>. Here are <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> numbers of wild beasts, as lions, rhinoceroses, &c., and many <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Ansiko, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the great Macoco, commands 13 kingdoms, and is esteemed the most powerful monarch in Africa. The inhabitants of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGOLA">Angola</a> have a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a>, that this is the proper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of the Giagas, who came originally from Sierra Leon, and overran, like a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TORRENT">torrent</a>, the whole <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> as far as <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENGUELA">Benguela</a>; that, being weakened by numerous battles, and unable to force the defiles in order to return to Sierra Leon, they arrived on the borders of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONOMOTAPA">Monomotapa</a>, where being defeated, they were forced to remain in the provinces of Ansiko. Be this as it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a>, the Ansikans yield not in the least to the Giagas in fierceness and barbarity. They are so accustomed to the eating of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>, that it is asserted they have <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a> where it is publicly sold, and that there are no other graves for the dead than the bellies of the living. They try the courage of their prisoners of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SHOOTING">shooting</a> at them as at marks, directing their arrows above or around their heads; and whoever discovers the least signs of fear, is immediately devoured without remedy. Those who appear intrepid and resolute, have their noses and ears bored, and two fore <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> of the upper jaw drawn. They are then improved in barbarity, by accustoming them to the most horrid cruelties. The Ansikans are neat, well proportioned, and strong; wandering about from <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> to place, without either sowing or reaping. They are dreaded for their <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> brutality, and never traded with by the Europeans. Their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> is barbarous, and difficult to be learned, even by the inhabitants of Congo. The most distinguished among them wear <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> caps of Portuguese velvet; the lower ranks go naked from the waist upwards; and, to preserve their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, anoint their bodies with a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of pounded <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SANDAL">sandal</a> wood and palm <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>. Their arms are <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> axes, and small but very strong bows, adorned with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERPENTS">serpents</a> skins. Their strings are made of supple and tender shoots of trees, that will not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a>, and their arrows of hard and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> wood. These people, who kill birds <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">flying</a>, shoot with such surprising swiftness, that they can discharge 28 arrows from the bow before the first falls to the ground. With equal dexterity they manage their battle axes; one end of which is sharpened and cuts like a wedge, and the other flattened like a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALLET">mallet</a>, with a handle set between, about half the length of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, rounded at the end like an apple, and covered with the skin of a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SERPENT">serpent</a>.—The current <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> in this country is the zimbis or shell, which is fished for, and passes among several African nations.—Ansiko. They worship the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> as their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> deity; whom they represent by the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a> by that of a woman. They have also an infinite <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of inferior deities, each individual having a particular idol whom he addresses on certain occasions.

ANSLO

Pages 448-448

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> port town of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWAY">Norway</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Aggerhys, with a bishop's see. The supreme <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> is held here for Norway. It is seated on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of the same name. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 10° 14'. N. Lat. 50° 24'.

ANSON

Pages 448-450

GEORGE, a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> whose merit and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a>, as a naval commander, exalted him to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>. He was the son of William Anson, Esq. of Huckborough, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STAFFORDSHIRE">Staffordshire</a>; and, showing an early inclination for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, received a suitable <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>. The first command he enjoyed was that of the Weasel sloop, in 1722; but the most memorable <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and the foundation of his future good fortune, took <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> on his receiving the command of five ships, a sloop, and two victuallers, equipped to annoy the Spaniards in the South seas, and to co-operate with <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADMIRAL">Admiral</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-VERNON">Vernon</a> across the isthmus of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DARIEN">Darien</a>; an expedition the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> object of which failed by the unaccountable delay in fitting him out. He sailed, however, in Sept. 1740; doubled <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORN">Horn</a> in a dangerous season; lost most of his men by the scurvy; and with only one remaining ship, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CENTURION">Centurion</a>, crossed the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PACIFIC_OCEAN">Pacific ocean</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> no considerable national advantage resulted from this voyage, Commodore Anson made his own fortune, and enriched his surviving companions, by the capture of a rich galleon on her passage from <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACAPULCO">Acapulco</a> to Manila; with which he returned home round the Cape of Good Hope. If he was lucky in meeting this galleon, he was no less fortunate in escaping a French fleet then cruising in the Channel, by sailing through it during a fog. He arrived at Spithead in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1744. In a short <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> after his return, he was appointed rear-admiral of the blue, and one of the lords of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADMIRALTY">admiralty</a>. In April 1745, he was made rear-admiral of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, and the following year vice-admiral of the blue; at which time he was chosen to represent the borough of Heydon in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. In 1747, being on board the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> George of 90 guns, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> with Admiral Warren, and 12 other ships, he intercepted, off Cape <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FINISTERRE">Finisterre</a>, a powerful fleet, bound from France to the East and West Indies; when, by his valour and conduct, he again enriched himself and his officers, and at the same time strengthened the British <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a>, by taking six men of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> and four East Indiamen, not one of them escaping. The French admiral, M. Jonquiere, on presenting his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> to the conqueror, said, Monsieur, vous avez vaincu l'Invincible, et la Gloire vous <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUIT">suit</a>: "Sir, you have conquered the Invincible, and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">Glory</a> follows you;" pointing to the ships, named the Invincible and the Glory, he had taken. For his signal services, his late majesty created him baron of Soberton in Hants. The same year he was appointed vice-admiral of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>; and, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Sir John Norris, was made vice-admiral of England. In 1748 he was made admiral of the blue; he was afterwards appointed first <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> of the admiralty, and was at length made admiral and commander in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of his majesty's fleet; in which rank rank he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a>, with a very short <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a>, until his death; and the last <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> he performed was to convey <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> Charlotte to England. He died in June 1762. No performance ever met with a more favourable reception, than the account of Anson's Voyage round the World. Though it is printed under the name of his chaplain, it was composed under his lordship's own inspection, and from the materials he himself furnished, by Mr Benjamin Robins. Anspach, Marquisate of, a small territory of Franconia, in Germany, bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the bishoprics of Wartsburg and Bamberg, which last likewise lies to the west; by the earldoms of Holach and Oeting, with the bishopric of Aichstet, on the south; and the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALATINATE">palatinate</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BAVARIA">Bavaria</a> and the territory of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUREMBERG">Nuremberg</a> on the east. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is fruitful, and interspersed with woods, which render it agreeable for hunting. Besides the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> Anspach, which is the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, the chief <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> are Kreglin, Swasbach, and Kreilshiem. Since 1806 it belongs to Bavaria. Anspach is a small but pretty town, very well built, and has several churches. It is walled round, but has no other fortifications. In the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> there is a remarkable cabinet of curiosities. It is situated on a river of the same name. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 10° 42'. N. Lat. 49° 14'. Anspessades, in the French armies, a kind of inferior officer in the foot, below the corporals, but above the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> sentinels. There are usually four <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> five of them in a company. Anstruther, Easter and Wester, two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> boroughs of Scotland, situated on the south-east <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Fife, containing about 1300 inhabitants in 1811. W. Long. 2° 45'. N. Lat. 56° 12'. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANT">Ant</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZOOLOGY">Zoology</a>. See Formica and Termes. See also the article Ant in the Supplement. Ant-Bear, or Ant-eater, in Zoology. See Myrmecophaga. Ant-eggs, a name popularly given to a kind of little white balls found in the banks or nests of ants, ordinarily supposed to be the ova of this insect. Late naturalists have observed that these are not properly the ants eggs, but the young brood themselves in their first state; they are so many little vermiculi wrapped up in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FILM">film</a> or skin, composed of a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, which they spin out of themselves as silk <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORMS">worms</a> and caterpillars do. At first they are hardly observed to stir; but, after a few days continuance, they exhibit a feeble <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of flexion and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENSION">extension</a>; and begin to look yellowish and hairy, shaped like small maggots, in which shape they grow up till they are almost as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> as ants. When they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> their metamorphosis, and appear in their proper shape, they have a small <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> speck on them <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to the anus of the enclosed ant, which M. Leeuwenhoek probably enough imagines to be the faeces voided by it. Dr Edward <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> opened several of these vulgarly reputed eggs; in some of which he found only a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-MAGGOT">maggot</a> in the circumstances above described; while in another the maggot had begun to put on the shape of an ant about the head, having two little <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> specks, where the eyes were to be. In others, a further progress was observed, the included maggots being furnished with every thing to complete the shape of an ant, but wholly transparent, the eyes only excepted, which were as black as bugles. Lastly, in others he took out very perfect and complete ants, which immediately crept about among the rest. These supposed ants eggs are brought up every morning in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> near the top of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a>, where they are lodged all the warm <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, within reach of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>'s influence. At night, or if it be cool, or like to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>, they carry them <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to a greater depth; so that you may dig a foot deep e'er you come at them. The true ants eggs are the white substance, which, upon opening their banks, appears to the eye like the scatterings of fine white <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, but very soft and tender. Examined by a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MICROSCOPE">microscope</a>, it is found to consist of several pure white appearances, in distinct membranes, all figured like the lesser sort of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIRD">bird</a>'s eggs, and as clear as a fish's bladder. The same substance is found in the bodies of the ants themselves. On this spawn, when emitted, they <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> in multitudes, to brood, till in some time it is turned into little vermicules as small as mites, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called ants eggs. Ant-Hills, are little hillocks of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, which the ants throw up for their habitation and the breeding of their young. They are a very great mischief to dry pastures, not only by wasting so much <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> as they cover, but by hindering the scythe in mowing the grass, and yielding a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> hungry food pernicious to cattle. The manner of destroying them is to cut them into four parts from the top, and then dig into them so deep as to take out the core below, so that, when the turf is laid down again, it may lie somewhat lower than the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> of the rest of the land: by this means it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be better than the rest of the land, and this will prevent the ants from returning to the same place, which otherwise they would certainly do. The earth that is taken out must be scattered to as great a distance every way as may be, otherwise they will collect it together, and make another hill <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> by. The proper time for doing this is winter; and if the places be left open, the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FROST">frost</a> and rains of that time of the year will destroy the rest: but in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> care must be taken that they are covered up early enough in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, otherwise they will be less fertile in grass than the other places. In <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HERTFORDSHIRE">Hertfordshire</a> they <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> a particular kind of spade for this purpose. It is very sharp, and formed at the top into the shape of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRESCENT">crescent</a>, so that the whole edge makes up more than three-fourths of a circle; this cuts in every part, and does the business very quickly and effectually. Others use the same instruments that they do for <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOLE">mole</a>-hills. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">Human</a> dung is a better remedy than all these, as is proved by experiment; for it will kill great numbers of them, and drive all the rest away, if only a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of it be put into their hills. Acid of Ants, an acid produced by distilling millions of these insects, either without addition, or with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. It resembles <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a> in many respects; but differs from it in forming crystals with <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGNESIA">magnesia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZINC">zinc</a>. Its attractions are not yet determined, but are supposed to coincide with those of vinegar. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANTA">Anta</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> pilaster, placed at the corners of buildings. Anta, or Ante, a small <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">Gold</a> coast of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, extending about ten leagues in length.—The country is covered with large trees, among which stand a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of fine villages. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is exceedingly rich, and the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> of the country beautiful. <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> is also much more salubrious than in other places of the Gold coast; it being observed by all writers, that the number of deaths here bears no proportion to that on any other part on the coasts of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUINEA">Guinea</a>. This country contains the following villages, which deserve a particular <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> on account of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> they drive; viz. Bouvirey, Tokorari, Sukoua, and Sama; for which, see those <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>.—Formerly Anta was potent and populous, inhabited by a bold and rapacious people, who greatly annoyed the Europeans by their frequent incursions; but by continual wars with their neighbours they are now greatly enfeebled, and the country in a manner depopulated. The spirit of the few remaining inhabitants is fled; they are desponding, dispirited and abject, seeking protection from the Dutch and other Europeans who have forts on this coast, and looking upon them as their best friends.

ANTACIDS

Pages 450-450

in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHARMACY">Pharmacy</a>, an appellation given to all medicines proper to correct acid <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> sour humours. Under the class of Antacids come, 1. Absorbents; as chalk, coral, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-shells, haematites, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STEEL">steel</a> filings. 2. Obtundents; as oils and fats. 3. Immutants; as lixivious salts and soaps.

ANTAEUS

Pages 450-450

in fabulous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a giant of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBYA">Libya</a>, son of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEPTUNE">Neptune</a> and Terra. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGNING">Designing</a> to build a temple to his father, of men's skulls, he slew all he met; but <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a> fighting him, and perceiving the assistance he received from his mother, (for by a touch of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> he refreshed himself when weary), lifted him up from the ground and squeezed him to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. Antaeus was <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MAURITANIA">Mauritania</a>; and from several circumstances, with which we are supplied by various authors, it appears extremely probable that he was the same person with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATLAS">Atlas</a>: they were both of them the sons of Neptune, who reigned over Mauritania, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMIDIA">Numidia</a>, and a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of Libya; as may be naturally inferred from his having such particular marks of distinction conferred upon him by the inhabitants of those regions. They both ruled with <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> power over a great part of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, particularly Tingitana. Hercules defeated and slew Antaeus in the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> wherein he took the Libyan world from Atlas; both Atlas and Antaeus invaded <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, and contended with Hercules in the wars with the gods, and were both vanquished by him. Antaeus, as well as Atlas, was famed for his knowledge in the celestial sciences: from whence we may fairly conclude them to have been the same king of Mauritania. Antaeus, in his wars with Hercules, who commanded an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of Egyptians and Ethiopians, behaved with great bravery and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a>. Receiving <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> reinforcements of Libyan troops, he cut off vast numbers of Hercules's men; but that celebrated commander having at last intercepted a strong body of Mauritanian <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Libyan forces sent to the relief of Antaeus, gave him a total overthrow, wherein both he and the best part of his forces were put to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>. This decisive <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> put Hercules in possession of Libya and Mauritania, and consequently of all the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RICHES">riches</a> in those kingdoms; hence arose the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FABLE">fable</a> that Hercules finding Antaeus, a giant of an enormous size, with whom he was engaged in single <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a>, to receive fresh strength as often as he touched his mother earth when thrown upon her, at last lifted him up in the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> and squeezed him to death. Hence likewise may be deduced the fable, intimating, that Hercules took Atlas's globe upon his own shoulders, overcame the dragon that guarded the orchards of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HESPERIDES">Hesperides</a>, and made himself <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of all the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> fruit. The golden apples, so frequently mentioned by the old mythologists, were the treasures that fell into Hercules's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> upon Antaeus's defeat, the Greeks giving the Oriental word ἀργυροί riches, the signification annexed to their own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a>, μακάρια, apples. After the most diligent and impartial <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> of all the different hypotheses of historians and chronologers, relating to Atlas and Antaeus, we find none so little clogged with difficulties as that of Sir <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Newton. According to that illustrious author, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMMON">Ammon</a>, the father of Sesac, was the first king of Libya, or that vast tract extending from the borders of Egypt to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATLANTIC_OCEAN">Atlantic ocean</a>; the conquest of which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> was effected by Sesac in his father's lifetime. Neptune afterwards excited the Libyans to a rebellion against Sesac; slew him, and then invaded Egypt under the command of Atlas or Antaeus, the son of Neptune, Sesac's <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a>. Not <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> after, Hercules, the general of Thebais and Ethiopia for the gods or great men of Egypt, reduced a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the whole continent of Libya, having overthrown and slain Antaeus near a town in Thebais, from that event called Antea or Anteopolis: this, we say, is the notion advanced by Sir Isaac Newton, who endevours to prove, that the first <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REDUCTION">reduction</a> of Libya by Sesac happened a little above a thousand years before the birth of Christ, as the last by Hercules did some few years after.

ANTAGOGUE

Pages 450-450

in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">Rhetoric</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> by which, when the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACCUSATION">accusation</a> of the adversary is unanswerable, we load him with the same <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other crimes.

ANTAGONIST

Pages 450-450

denotes an adversary, especially in speaking of combats and games. ANTAGONIST Muscles, in Anatomy, those which have opposite functions; as flexors and extensors, abductors, and adductors, &c.

ANTANACLASIS

Pages 450-450

in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">Rhetoric</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> which repeats the same word, but in a different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>; as dum vivimus vivamus.

ANTANDROS

Pages 450-450

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSIA">Mysia</a>, on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, at the foot of Mount <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of Mount Ida, (Strabo, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>): it was a town of the Leleges, (Strabo); anciently called Edonis, then Ginneris, (Pliny, Stephanus). It takes its name from Antandros, a general of the Æolians: it is now called S. Dimitri.

ANTAPHRODISIACS

Pages 450-450

in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHARMACY">Pharmacy</a>, medicines proper to diminish the semen, and consequently extinguish <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> lessen all desires of venery.

ANTARCTIC

Pages 450-450

in a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, denotes something opposite to the northern <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> arctic pole. Hence antarctic circle is one of the lesser circles of the sphere, and distant only $23^\circ 30'$ from the south pole, which is likewise called antarctic for the same reason.

ANTARES

Pages 450-450

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, the name of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STAR">star</a> of the first magnitude, called also the scorpion's heart. Its <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a> is $60^\circ 13' 14''$ of Sagittarius; and its latitude $43^\circ 51' 26''$ south.

ANTAVARE

Pages 450-451

a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Madagascar, lying about $21^\circ 30'$ S. Lat. and bounded by the the province and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">cape</a> of Manousi. The greatest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of it is watered by the river Mananzari, whose source is in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of Ambohitsmene.

ANTEAMBULONES

Pages 451-451

in Roman antiquity, servants who went before persons of distinction to clear the way before them. They used this formula, *<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">Date</a> locum domino meo*, i.e. "Make room <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> way for my <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>."

ANTECEDENCE

Pages 451-451

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, an apparent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of a planet towards the west, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> contrary to the order of the signs.

ANTECEDENT

Pages 451-451

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">Mathematics</a>, is the first of two terms of a ratio, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> that which is compared with the other.

ANTECESSOR

Pages 451-451

one that goes before. It was an appellation given to those who excelled in any science. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTINIAN">Justinian</a> applied it particularly to professors of civil <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>; and, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a> of France, the teachers of law take the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> *antecessors* in all their theses.

ANTECURSORES

Pages 451-451

in the Roman armies, a party of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> detached before, partly to get intelligence, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>, &c., and partly to choose a proper <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> to encamp in. These were otherwise called *antecessores*, and by the Greeks *prodromi*.

ANTEDATE

Pages 451-451

among lawyers, a spurious <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> false <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">date</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> to the true date of a bond, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BILL">bill</a>, or the like.

ANTEDILUVIAN

Pages 451-451

in a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, implies something that existed before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a>. **ANTEDILUVIAN World**: the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> as it existed before the flood. See EARTH.

ANTEDILUVIANS

Pages 451-468

a general name for all mankind who lived before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a>, and so includes the whole of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADAM">Adam</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOAH">Noah</a> and his family. As Moses has not set <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the particular <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of any transaction before the flood, except only the years of the father's <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> wherein the several descendants of Adam in the line of Seth were begotten, and the length of their several lives; it has been the business of chronologers to endeavour to fix the years of the lives and deaths of those patriarchs, and the distance of time from the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREATION">creation</a> to the deluge. In this there could be little difficulty, were there no varieties in the several copies we now have of Moses's writings; which are, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a>, the Samaritan, and the Greek version of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEPTUAGINT">Septuagint</a>; but as these differ very considerably from one another, learned men are much divided in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> concerning the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">chronology</a> of the first ages of the world; some preferring one copy, and some another. That the reader may the better judge of the variations in the three copies in this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, they are exhibited in the following <a class="xref" 583 | | Jared, Methuselah, and Lamech die | 1307 | The Flood, 847 720 653 600 To the varieties exhibited in the two last tables, others might be added, by admitting the various readings of some numbers in the Samaritan and Septuagint: for as to the Hebrew copies, there is here a constant agreement among them. The manuscript from which the Samaritan Pentateuch was published, agrees exactly with the Samaritan numbers given by Eusebius. But St Jerome tells us, that in his time, there were some Samaritan copies which make Methuselah 187 years old at the birth of Lamech, and Lamech 182 at the birth of Noah, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> as the Hebrew does. Now <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> these numbers be approved as the true original numbers, the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> from the creation to the flood will be 1556 years; differing from the Hebrew computation but 100 years in the age of Jared at the birth of Enoch; and if this last be allowed to be a mistake of the transcriber, by his dropping a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> 62 instead of 162, as has been suspected, the Samaritan will be perfectly reconciled with the Hebrew, and all <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between them vanish. Scaliger, on the authority of an old Samaritan <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRONICLE">chronicle</a>, having at the end a table of the years of the patriarchs to the time of Moses, would correct two of the Samaritan numbers in Eusebius; viz. instead of 65, the age of Mahalaleel when he begat Jared, he thinks it should be 75; and instead of 67, the age of Methuselah when he begat Lamech, he would have it 77. By which alterations he reckons 20 years more to the flood than Eusebius and the manuscript; that is, 1327. But, as he acknowledges the table, whereon he grounds these corrections, contains some <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> absurdities, it seems unreasonable to oppose it to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> authority of Eusebius and the Samaritan manuscript. As to the Septuagint, in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> editions of that version, the age of Methuselah at the birth of Lamech is 167; and consequently the sum of this period, according to them, is no more than 2242. But, in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, Methuselah will outlive the flood 14 years; and we may well wonder, with Eusebius, where he was preserved. To obviate this objection, we are told, that, in some copies, Methuselah is said to have lived but 782 (not 802) years after the birth of Lamech, and no more than 949 in all. But the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIAN">Alexandrian</a> manuscript entirely takes away the difficulty, by giving the same number in this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> with the Hebrew. Pezron is of opinion, that the age of Lamech, at the birth of Noah, should be but 182, as it is both in the Hebrew and in Josephus, supposing, with St Austin, that the present number is the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ERROR">error</a> of the scribe who first copied the original Septuagint manuscript in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>'s library. So that he computes 2256 years to the flood. And, if this correction be admitted, and one more mentioned also by St Austin, viz. that Lamech lived 595 years after the birth of Noah, and not 565, as in the present copies, there will then remain no other difference between the Septuagint and the Hebrew than 600 years added to the ages of the six patriarchs when they begat their sons, and Methuselah will, conformably to the Hebrew and Samaritan, die in the year of the flood. Having premised this chronological view, we shall proceed to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the antediluvian patriarchs. Of the great progenitor we are told, that "the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Of Adam God took the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> and put him into the garden," in Paradise. These words plainly indicate, that Adam was not created within the precincts of Paradise; and it is afterwards said, upon his being turned out of the garden, "He..." Adam was doubtless created in the prime of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, with all his powers and faculties in the highest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of strength and vigour. His body would be graceful, and well proportioned; while his countenance was comely, and glowed with all the lustre of youthful innocence. The poet thus describes our first parents: Adam the goodliest man, of men since born His sons; the fairest of her daughters <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVE">Eve</a>. —for in their looks divine The image of their glorious Maker shone. <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILTON">MILTON</a>. Many have entertained an opinion (as mentioned under the article ADAM), that our first <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARENT">parent</a> was created an adept in knowledge and in science, a consummate <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, and an accomplished divine. But the very reverse of this must be true, providing we give <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> to the account which Moses gives of him. If Adam was created with intuitive knowledge, for what end was he endowed with the senses of a man, through which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> might be conveyed to his mind, and make him capable of such improvements as arise from <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> and observation? And if he originally possessed such a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FUND">fund</a> of valuable knowledge, why had he such an ardent thirst for an unwarrantable portion of more, and for the sake of this additional pittance forfeited his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> and life? Besides, if Adam was at first all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> and knowledge, and was soon after reduced to a state of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> and error, this transition would make a retrograde in the system of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, quite dissimilar to that uniformity which obtains throughout the whole of the divine <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> and economy. Moses introduces our first parents into life in the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> manner, as having capacities to acquire knowledge, senses to receive impressions from objects round them, and a sufficient degree of reason to form a judgment of the things perceived; yet all these faculties can only be considered as so many instruments, by the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of which they might be enabled to discharge the duties of their future life. The following <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTRAIT">portrait</a> of our first progenitor when he first came into life, drawn by the inimitable <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a> of Buffon, is extremely beautiful, while it is dissonant from no <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the Mosaic history. "Let us suppose a man in the same situation with him who first received existence; a man whose organs were perfectly formed, but who was equally new to himself, and to every object which surrounded him. Were he to give a history of his thoughts, and of the manner in which he received impressions, he might give some such information as this. I remember the moment when my existence commenced. It was a moment replete with joy, with amazement and anxiety. I neither knew what I was, where I was, nor whence I came. I opened my eyes. But what an amazing increase of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSATION">sensation</a>! The light, the celestial vault, the verdure of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, the transparency of the waters, gave <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANIMATION">animation</a> to my spirits, and conveyed pleasures which exceed the powers of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>. At first I believed that all these objects existed within me, and formed a part of myself. When, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> mine eyes to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, his splendour overpowered me. I voluntarily shut out the light, and felt a small degree of pain. During this moment of darkness, I imagined that I had lost the greatest part of my being. I was then roused with a variety of sounds. The singing of birds and the murmuring breezes formed a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONCERT">concert</a>, which excited most sweet and enchanting emotions. I listened, and was convinced that these harmonious sounds existed within me.—I made a step forwards; and afterwards renewing my <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, I walked with my <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> turned towards the heavens; till I struck against a palm tree, and felt some degree of pain. Seized with terror, I ventured to lay my <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> upon the object, and perceived it to be a being distinct from myself, because it did not, like touching my own body, give me a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> sensation. I resolved then to feel every object I <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a>, and had a strong desire to touch the sun; but stretching out my <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> to embrace the heavens, they met without any intermediate object. All objects appeared to me equally near; and it was not till after many trials that I learned to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> my eye as a guide to my hand. At last the train of my ideas was interrupted, and I lost the consciousness of my existence. My <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a> was profound; but having no <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of measuring time, I knew nothing of its <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>. When I awakened, I was astonished to find by my side another form, perfectly similar to my own. I conceived it to be another self; and instead of losing by my sleep, I imagined myself to be double. I ventured to lay my hand upon this new being. With rapture and astonishment I perceived that it was not myself, but something much more glorious and desirable." This philosophical detail coincides with the opinion that, excepting what portions of knowledge Adam might acquire by the exercise of his senses, his Maker taught him every thing that was necessary for his comfort and subsistence. But before the Almighty gave any instructions to our first parents, we must suppose he inspired them with the knowledge of the meaning of every word which they heard him speak; otherwise it would have been impossible that he could have had any such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> with them. The words which they heard and were made to understand, being imprinted upon their memories, would serve as the foundation of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, which they would afterwards increase and enlarge as new objects began to multiply, and hence give rise to new terms and definitions. One of the first <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LESSONS">lessons</a> taught to Adam by his infallible <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTOR">Director</a>, would be the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of food for the support of his life. Accordingly Moses informs us, that for this purpose a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> was made him to eat of every tree of the garden, excepting one. At the same time it was made known to him, in what manner he was to repair the decays of nature, namely, by eating of the tree of life. Then, in order to qualify him for social intercourse, he was ordered to exercise his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> of speech, by giving names to different creatures. The author of the book of Ecclesiasticus says of our first parents, "They received the use of the five operations of the Lord; and in the sixth he imparted to them understanding; and in the seventh, speech to interpret the cogitations thereof." The meaning cannot be, that he gave them every word they were to pronounce, more than every idea which their senses were to convey to their understanding. Our talents, and the exercise of them, may be both said to be given us of God; but whatever capacities we receive from him, it is supposed that we ourselves must improve them, before we can attain to any acquirements whatever. Although Adam had heard and understood the words of God, yet Moses does not give the least hint that he ever attempted to speak before this time. For if he had, as some imagine, innate knowledge and proper terms for every thing presented to him, what occasion was there to bring animals before him to see what names he would impose upon them? Some writers have endeavoured to turn into <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIDICULE">ridicule</a> the whole of this transaction, and have asked, how could all creatures upon earth appear at one time before Adam? not only one, but many days would have elapsed before he could give each a name. But this objection arises from not understanding the words of Moses. What our translators render, to see what he would call them, is in the original, to see what name he would call it. "And whatsoever Adam called it (viz. the living creature), that was the name of it." The meaning seems to be no more than this: God brought a few creatures to Adam, to make him try to name them; and whatever he called any of them, that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to be its name. And no doubt he would denominate every animal before him, from its <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> appearance, from its size, its <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> its <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>: And in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of time, he would give names to all those creatures which <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a> brought within his view, or with which he became afterwards acquainted. The next thing in which God instructed Adam, though probably in a trance or vision, was his near <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVELATION">revelation</a> to Eve, as being a part of his own body. This piece of knowledge was imparted to him, in order to cement the greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> and affection between the two during the remaining period of their lives. These, according to Moses, are all the transactions in which our first parents were interested during their abode in paradise, till they lost their innocence, and forfeited the enjoyments of their happy situation. And nothing can be more evident, than that the instructions which they received bespoke the infantile state of their minds; though there is no doubt but further and higher dispensations of knowledge would have been communicated to them, as they became able to bear them, and had their minds matured by experience and reflection. How <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> our first parents retained their innocence, we are nowhere told. Many assert that they fell on the very first <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> of their creation. But Moses mentions so many transactions on that day, as must have engrossed the whole of their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>, and prevented them from falling into such temptations as arise from indolence and want of reflection. Besides, if, in such circumstances as they were placed, they could not refrain from an open violation of the Divine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> for the space of one day, it would bespeak a deceitfulness of heart in them greater than in most of their posterity. It is somewhat singular, that many of the great trials recorded in sacred writing were limited to 40 days; which in prophetic style is sometimes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> to 40 years. This appears from the history of Moses, of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELI">Eli</a>-jah, of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINEVEH">Nineveh</a>, and of the Jewish <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> after the death of Christ. And, what is very remarkable, he, of whom Adam was a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYPE">type</a>, was tempted 40 days in the wilderness. Agreeable to this part of the Divine economy, perhaps the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> of our first parents lasted so long. However, that they remained for a considerable time in the garden, appears highly probable from this consideration, that their indulgent Creator, who had manifested his tender concern for them while innocent, and extended his mercy to them when fallen, would never have turned them out of paradise, and sent them into an uncultivated world, before they had acquired the arts of living, and were capable of providing against the vicissitudes of their future <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">lot</a>. The particulars of this memorable transaction are considered under the article <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">FALL</a>. Moses gives us no farther account of Adam's life after leaving the garden, but that he begat some children, and died at such an age. Yet we have no reason to doubt, but the venerable patriarch ever after led a life of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENITENCE">penitence</a>, and of the strictest piety. The various communications which he had enjoyed with his Maker in paradise, and which were probably renewed to him after his fall, could not fail to make the deepest impressions upon his mind. The gracious respite he had met with, from the execution of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> denounced against him, would make him cautious of offending for the time to come; lest the next violation of the Divine authority should put an end to his existence. The cherubim and flaming <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, or the devouring <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a>, on the east of Eden (which might continue <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> all his life) would be to him what the vestiges of the ark were to Noah and his sons, an awful memorial of the danger of incurring the Divine displeasure. Besides, his worldly comforts being in a great <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> withdrawn, his mind would be naturally disposed for relishing those pleasures which flow from piety and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. The first thing which we hear of Adam in his new situation was, that he knew Eve his wife, and she conceived and bare <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAIN">Cain</a>. Afterwards, we are told, she bare <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABEL">Abel</a>. When the brothers were grown up, they betook themselves to distinct employments; the former to husbandry, and the latter to the keeping of sheep. Their inward dispositions were still more different; Cain being wicked and avaricious, but Abel just and virtuous. In process of time they brought their respective offerings to God; Cain of the fruit of the ground, and Abel of the firstlings of his flock: but they met with very different success; for God accepted the offering of Abel, but Cain's he did not accept; the consequences of which are related under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> ABEL and CAIN. Soon after the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> of Abel, his loss was made up to his parents in another son they had, whom Eve named Seth, that is "appointed;" because he was appointed instead of Abel whom Cain slew. As the whole progeny of Adam, of whom we have any mention in Scripture, were the descendants of Cain and Seth, it may be proper to give the following Genealogical The sacred historian, confining himself chiefly to the line of Seth, from whence Noah was descended, has acquainted us with very few particulars relating to that of Cain: nor can we thus form any conjectures how long he or any of his descendants lived. All we know is, that Lamech, the fifth in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> from him, married two wives, Adah and Zillah, the first known instance of polygamy; that by the former he had two sons, Jabal, who was the first that dwelt in tents, and fed cattle, and Jubal, the inventor of music; and by the other, a son named Tubal-Cain, who found out the art of forging and working <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-METALS">metals</a>. Zillah likewise brought him a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> named Naamah, supposed to have invented <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPINNING">spinning</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEAVING">weaving</a>: and we are told that, on some occasion or other, Lamech made a speech to his wives, the explication of which has greatly puzzled the interpreters. See LAMECH. Moses proceeds to tell us, that Seth had a son born to him called Enos, and that then began men to call upon the name of the Lord. Commentators give as three different senses of these words. Some think the words should be rendered, Then men profaned in calling on the name of the Lord; and that even Enos arrogated to himself a power as if he had been a god. But this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> seems harsh and unnatural. There is nothing more unlikely, than that Adam’s grandchildren, who lived under his own eye, would so soon shake off parental authority, and apostatize from the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a> and worship of the one true God. Others think, that though men had hitherto worshipped God in private, yet they now instituted public assemblies, met in larger <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a> for solemn and social worship, and introduced liturgies and forms for more effectually paying their homage to the Almighty. This indeed is a very natural comment from those who place religion in modes and set forms of worship. But it is scarcely credible, that Adam and his family had never met together to worship God till now, when we are told that Cain and Abel, and probably both their families along with them, brought their offerings to the Lord; this they no doubt did every Sabbath day. Others, therefore, put a more consistent interpretation upon the words, namely, namely, that men now called themselves by the name of the Lord. The meaning of which is, that about this period, the family of Seth, who adhered to God and his worship, began to give themselves a denomination, expressive of their relation and regards to him. They distinguished themselves from the irreligious family of Cain, and assumed the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of the sons or children of God; which designation was afterwards applied to them by Moses; it was even used after the flood, and adopted by the writers of the New <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>. Of the three next descendants of Seth, Cainan, Mahalaleel, and Jared, and of Methuselah and Lamech, the grandfather and father of Noah, Moses has recorded no more than their several ages. The oriental authors commend them, as they do Seth and Enoch, for their piety, and the salutary injunctions they left behind them, forbidding their children all intercourse with the race of cursed Cain. Enoch the son of Jared, and father of Methuselah, was a person of most extraordinary piety, walking with God, as the Scripture expresses it, for at least the last three hundred years of his life; as a reward for which exemplary behaviour in so corrupt an age, he was taken up by God into heaven, without tasting death. See Enoch. Moses afterwards informs us, When men began to multiply, i.e., when the earth was filled with inhabitants, and tribes formerly living remote began to approach nearer to one another, Daughters were born unto them: meaning in greater abundance than formerly; which seems to hint, that at this period there were considerably more females than males born into the world. Some think that Moses, being now about to mention the wickedness of the Antediluvians, introduces the posterity of Cain as being the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> cause of their corruption; and that he styles them men and daughters of men, because they were sensual and earthly; in which sense the word men is sometimes used in the Scriptures. The sons of God saw the daughters of men that they were fair; and they took them wives of all that they chose. These words have given rise to many absurd and ridiculous comments both of Jews and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>. There are two meanings affixed to them, which may be mentioned as the most probable. Whenever the name of God is added to any thing, it not only denotes God's being the efficient cause, but it heightens and increases its usual meaning. For which reason any thing that is excellent in its kind, or uncommonly lofty and magnificent, was by the Jews said to be of God, or of the Lord. Thus the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGELS">angels</a> are called the sons of God. And Adam being created with a nobler image than any other creature, is said to be made in the image of God. The cedars of Lebanon are called the cedars of the Lord; and great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, the mountains of God. Therefore by the sons of God in this place are meant men of great opulence, power, and authority. And by way of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRAST">contrast</a>, the historian introduces those of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> circumstances in life, and calls them the daughters of men. The words thus explained, are not an unlikely <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of that dissolute age. The great and mighty in this world are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> most addicted to sensual gratifications, because they have so many incentives to inflame their passions, and so few restraints to curb them; and, instead of using their power to punish and discountenance vice, are too often the greatest examples and promoters of lasciviousness and debauchery. Thus, these sons of God, these great men, when they happened to meet with the daughters of their inferiors, gazed upon them as fit objects to gratify their lust; and from among these they took to themselves, in a forcible manner, wives, or (as it may be rendered) concubines, of all that they chose, whether married or unmarried, without ever asking their consent. No wonder, then, that the earth should be filled with violence, when the highest <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of men were above the restraint of law, of reason, and religion, and not only oppressed the poor, but with impunity treated them and their children in such a base and cruel manner. But there are other writers who cannot relish the above opinion; because they think it a harsh and unnatural <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a>, to call great and powerful persons the sons of God, and all mean and plebeian women the daughters of men. Besides, the text does not say, that the sons of God offered any violence to these inferior women; but that they saw that they were fair, and made choice of them for wives. And wherein is the heinousness of the offence, if men of a superior rank marry their inferiors, especially when an excess of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> apologizes for their choice? Or why should a few unequal matches be reckoned among the causes of bringing upon the world an universal destruction? For these reasons many are of opinion, that the descendants of Seth, who were styled the sons of God on account of Mila, their near relation to him, saw the daughters of men, i.e., the impious progeny of Cain, and by intermarriages became associated with them; and surrendering to those enchantresses their hearts and their freedom, they surrendered at the same time their virtue and their religion. From this union proceeded effects similar to what has happened ever since. When a pure <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> mixest with a profane, the better principles of the one become soon tainted by the evil practices of the other; which verifies the old adage, Evil communication corrupts good manners. Thus it appears, that the great source of universal degeneracy was owing to the posterity of Seth mingling with the progeny of Cain, in opposition to what their pious fathers had strictly <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> them. It is afterwards said, There were giants in the earth in those days: and also after that, when the sons of God came in unto the daughters of men, and they bare children to them, the same became mighty men, which were of old men of renown. Translators are not agreed about the meaning of the word giants. Some render the word, violent and cruel men; others, men who fall upon and rush forward, as a robber does upon his prey: the meaning then is, that they were not more remarkable for their strength and stature, than for their violence and cruelty. In <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUTHER">Luther</a>'s German translation of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a>, this word is rendered tyrants. It is generally agreed, that in the first ages of the world, men were of a gigantic stature; though Moses does not mention them as giants till after the union of the families of Seth and Cain, when men used their superiority in bodily strength for the purposes of gratifying their unhallowed passions. At this period of the world, and long after, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> power and bodily strength went hand and hand together. Antediluvian. Whoever was able to encounter and kill a fierce and dangerous wild beast, and clear the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of noxious animals, or who was able in the day of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> to destroy most of his enemies, was looked up to by the rest of his companions as the fittest to be their leader and commander. Thus Nimrod, from being a mighty hunter, became a great <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>, and, grasping at power, was never satisfied till every obstacle to his ambition was removed.
