a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> song performed in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> by choristers, who sang alternately. It was used to denote both psalms and hymns, when performed in this manner. But, at present, anthem is used in a more confined <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, being applied to certain <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> taken out of the Scriptures, and adapted to a particular solemnity. Anthems were first introduced in the reformed service of the English church, in the beginning of the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>.

ANTHERA

Pages 469-469

in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the stamen which is fixed on the top of the filamentum, within the corolla; it contains the pollen <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> fine dust, which, when mature, it emits for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMPREGNATION">impregnation</a> of the plant, according to Linnæus. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APEX">Apex</a> of Ray, Tournef. and Rivin.; Capsula staminis, of Malpighi.

ANTHESPHORIA

Pages 469-469

in antiquity, a Sicilian festival instituted in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of Proserpine. The word is derived from the Greek ἀνθος, flower, and φέρω, I carry; because that <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> was forced away by Pluto when she was gathering <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> in the fields. Yet Festus does not ascribe the feast to Proserpine; but says it was thus called by reason ears of corn were carried on this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> to the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>.—Anthesphoria seems to be the same thing with the florissertum of the Latins, and answers to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HARVEST">harvest</a>-home among us.

ANTHESTERIA

Pages 469-469

in antiquity, was a feast celebrated by the Athenians in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a>. The most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> derivation of the word is from the Greek ἀνθος (flōs), a flower, it being the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> at this feast to offer garlands of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> to Bacchus. The antheustria lasted three days, the 11th, 12th, and 13th of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a>; each of which had a name suited to the proper office of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>. The first day of the feast was called παράγωγα, i.e. opening of the vessels, because on this day they tapped the vessels, and tasted the wine. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> day they called κόσμος, congiī, the name of a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> containing the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of 10 pounds; on this they drank the wine prepared the day before. Anthesteria. The third day they called χυλοποιί, kettles: on this day they boiled all sorts of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PULSE">pulse</a> in kettles; which however they were not allowed to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, as being offered to <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a>.

ANTHESTERION

Pages 469-469

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">chronology</a>, the sixth <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of the Athenian year. It contained 29 days; and answered to the latter <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of our November and beginning of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a>. The Macedonians called it dasion <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> desion. It had its name from the festival anthesteria kept in it. ANTHISTIRIA. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ANTHOLOGION

Pages 469-469

the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> book used in the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. It is divided into 12 months, containing the offices sung throughout the year, on the festivals of our Saviour, the Virgin, and other remarkable saints.

ANTHOLOGY

Pages 469-469

a discourse of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> of beautiful <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> from any authors.—It is also the name given to a collection of epigrams taken from several Greek poets.

ANTHONY

Pages 469-470
or Knights of St Anthony, a military order, instituted by Albert duke of Bavaria, Holland, and Zealand, when he designed to make war against the Turks in 1382. The knights wore a collar of gold; ANT Anthony gold made in form of a hermit's girdle, from which hung a stick cut like a crutch, with a little bell, as they are represented in St Anthony's pictures. St Anthony also gives the denomination to an order of religious founded in France about the year 1295, to take care of those afflicted with St Anthony's fire; (see the next article).—It is said, that, in some places, these monks assume to themselves a power of giving, as well as removing, the ignis sacer, or erysipelas; a power which stands them in great stead for keeping the poor people in subjection, and extorting alms. To avoid the menaces of these monks, the country people present them every year with a fat hog a piece. Some prelates endeavoured to persuade Pope Paul III. to abolish the order; questuarios istos sancti Anthonii, qui decipiunt rusticos et simplices, eosque innumeris superstitionibus implicant, de medio tollendos esse. But they subsist, notwithstanding, to this day, in several places. St Anthony's Fire, a name properly given to the erysipelas. Apparently it took this denomination, as those afflicted with it made their peculiar application to St Anthony of Padua for a cure. It is known, that anciently particular diseases had their peculiar saints; thus, in the ophthalmia, persons had recourse to St Lucia; in the toothach, to St Apollonia; in the hydrophobia, to St Hubert, &c.

ANTHORA

Pages 470-470

the trivial name of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of aconitum. See ACONITUM, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ANTHORISMUS

Pages 470-470

in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">Rhetoric</a>, denotes a contrary <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-DEFINITION">definition</a> of a thing from that given by the adverse party.—Thus, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the plaintiff urge, that to take anything away from another without his knowledge or consent, is a theft; this is called ἀγορεύειν, or definition. If the defendant reply, that to take a thing away from another without his knowledge or consent, provided it be done with <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> to return it to him again, is not theft; this is an ἀποδιάγονος.

ANTHRACIS

Pages 470-470

Anthracias, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Anthracitis, names promiscuously used by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> naturalists for very different fossils, viz. the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARBUNCLE">carbuncle</a>, hæmatites, and a kind of asteria. See Carbuncle, &c.

ANTHRACOCIS

Pages 470-470

in Medicine, a corrosive scaly ulcer either in the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BULB">bulb</a> of the eye <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the eyelids.

ANTHRAX

Pages 470-470

a Greek <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a>, literally signifying a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> coal, used by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> to denote a gem, as well as a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>, more generally known by the name of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARBUNCLE">carbuncle</a>. ANTHRAX is sometimes also used for lithanthrax <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> pit coal.

ANTHROPOGLOTTUS

Pages 470-470

among zoologists, an appellation given to such animals as have tongues resembling that of mankind, particularly to the parrot kind.

ANTHROPOGRAPHY

Pages 470-470

denotes the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> body, its parts, structure, &c. See Anatomy. ANTHROPOLATRÆ, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, an appellation given to the Nestorians, on account of their worshipping Christ, notwithstanding that they believed him to be a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>.

ANTHROPOLATRIA

Pages 470-470

the paying divine honours to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>; supposed to be the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> kind of idolatry.

ANTHROPOLITES

Pages 470-471

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> denoting petrifications of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> body, as those of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUADRUPEDS">quadrupeds</a> are called zoolites. It has been doubted whether any real human petrifications ever occur, and whether those which have been supposed such were not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> lusus naturae. But the generality of naturalists best versed in this branch assure us of real anthropolites being sometimes found. And indeed, as it is universally admitted that the zoolites are frequently seen, what <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEGATIVE">negative</a> argument therefore can be brought against the existence of the others? Are not the component parts of the human body nearly similar to those of the brute <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREATION">creation</a>? Consequently, correspondent <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> may be subject to, and acquire, the like accidental changes, wherever the same power <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> causes concur to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> upon either object. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the former are not so <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a>, it may be accounted for, in some <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, by reflecting that human bodies are generally deposited in select and appropriate places; whereas the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> of animals are deposited everywhere, and falling into various beds of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, at a greater or less depth, there is more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> of their encountering the petrifying <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGENT">agent</a>. Could we <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> some authors who have treated on this subject, they <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> tell us of entire bodies and skeletons that were found petrified. One in particular, discovered at <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIX">Aix</a> in Provence, anno 1583, in a rocky cliff, the cerebrum whereof, when struck against a piece of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STEEL">steel</a>, produced sparks, the bones being at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> friable. The reports of Happel and Kircher are too absurd for <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a>. Van Helmont's strange relations, together with those of Jean à Costa, must also be rejected as fabulous. Scheuhzer has published an engraved <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, which he calls the Antediluvian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>: how far it is authentic, it would be rash to say. It is, however, asserted by many respectable writers on <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, that whole skeletons petrified have been brought to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> from certain old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>, which remained closed up and disused for several centuries. These indeed are acknowledged to be very rare. Yet it is a known fact, that detached parts (osteoliths) are sometimes found, especially in situations where either the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, or both, have been observed to possess a strong petroscent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>. The human vertebre, fragments or portions of the tibia, and even the whole cranium itself, have been seen in an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> state of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETRIFICATION">petrification</a>. Some of these are said to appear vitriolated or mineralized. As to the petrified bones of pretended giants, they are more probably real zoolites, the bones of the larger animals. All these bones are found in various states, and under different appearances. Some are only indurated; others calcined, vitriolated, or mineralized; some, again, are simply incrusted; whilst others have been proved completely petrified. Notwithstanding what is here advanced, it may be granted that a positive lusus naturae, in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, is repeatedly mistaken for a real petrification. They are, however, distinguishable at all times by an experienced naturalist; particularly by the two following rules: First, We may determine that fossil a lusus naturae, which, on a strict <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a>, is observed to deviate in any material <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> from the true res analogica existens. Secondly, By the same parity of reasoning, these fossil shells <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANT">ANT</a> shells are to be esteemed certain petrifications, and genuine Antediluvian reliquiae, in which, on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> with their analogues, collected from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, there appears an exact conformity in size and figure. This comparative observation will hold good for all fossils; that is, such as present themselves either under the animal or vegetable form. It is nevertheless worthy of notice, that all testaceous fossils are not petrified; since some kinds of them have been found in beds of sand, which retained their original perfect shape and quality, but at the same time they proved very brittle, indeed scarcely <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> the most gentle touch. Shells of this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> are always dissoluble by <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACIDS">acids</a>, in contradistinction to the petrified or calcareous fossil shells, whose <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> it is to resist the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of such like menstrua. See further the article PETRIFICATION.

ANTHROPOLOGY

Pages 471-471

among divines, denotes that manner of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>, by which the inspired writers <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> parts and passions to God.

ANTHROPOMANCY

Pages 471-471

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVINATION">divination</a>, performed by inspecting the entrails of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> creature.

ANTHROPOMORPHA

Pages 471-471

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> formerly given to the primates of that class of animals which have the greatest resemblance to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> kind.

ANTHROPOMORPHISM

Pages 471-471

among <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> writers, denotes the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERESY">heresy</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ERROR">error</a> of the Anthropomorphites. See the next article.

ANTHROPOMORPHITES

Pages 471-471

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">Church</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> heretics, who, taking every thing spoken of God in Scripture in a literal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, particularly that passage of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GENESIS">Genesis</a> in which it is said, God made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> after his own image, maintained that God had a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> shape. They are likewise called Audeans, from Audeus their leader.

ANTHROPOMORPHOUS

Pages 471-471

something that bears the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> resemblance of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>. Naturalists give instances of anthropomorphic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, anthropomorphic minerals, &c. These generally come under the class of what they call lusus naturae, or monsters.

ANTHROPOPATHY

Pages 471-471

a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> by which some <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> is ascribed to God, which properly belongs only to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>.

ANTHROPOPHAGI

Pages 471-472

(of ἀνθρώπος, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, and φάγω, to eat, Men-eaters). That there have been, in almost all ages of the world, nations who have followed this barbarous practice, we have abundance of testimonies. The Cyclops, the Lestrygons, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCYLLA">Scylla</a>, are all represented in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>, as Anthropeophagi, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> man-eaters; and the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> phantoms, Circe, and the Sirens, first bewitched with a show of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, and then destroyed. This, like the other parts of Homer's <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, had a foundation in the manners of the times preceding his own. It was still, in many places, the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> spoken of by <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORPHEUS">Orpheus</a>. When men devour'd each other like the beasts, Gorging on <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>. According to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a>, among the Essedonian Scythians, when a man's father died, the neighbours brought several beasts, which they killed, mixed up their flesh with that of the deceased, and made a feast. Among the Massagetæ when any person grew old, they killed him and ate his flesh; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he died of sickness, they buried him, esteeming him unhappy. The same author also assures us, that several nations in the Indies killed all their old people and their sick, to feed on their flesh: he adds, that persons in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> were sometimes accused of being sick, to afford a pretence for devouring them. According to Sextus Empiricus, the first laws that were made, were for the preventing of this barbarous practice, which the Greek writers represent as universal before the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Orpheus. Of the practice of anthropophagy in later times, we have the testimonies of all the Romish missionaries who have visited the internal parts of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, and even some parts of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>. Herrera speaks of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, furnished wholly with human flesh, for the better sort of people. Marcus Paulus speaks of the like in his time, in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Concha towards Quinsay, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Zapengit; others, of the great <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JAVA">Java</a>; Barbosa, of the kingdom of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIAM">Siam</a> and island of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMATRA">Sumatra</a>; others, of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENGAL">Bengal</a>, of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of the Samogitians, &c. The philosophers <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIOGENES">Diogenes</a>, Chrysippus, and Zeno, followed by the whole <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of Stoics, affirmed, that there was nothing unnatural in the eating of human flesh; and that it was very reasonable to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> dead bodies for food, rather than to give them a prey to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORMS">worms</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUTREFACTION">putrefaction</a>. In order to make the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a>, however, whether there was any real repugnancy in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> to the feeding of an animal with the flesh of its own <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, Leonardus Floroventius fed a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HOG">hog</a> with hog's flesh, and a dog with dog's flesh; upon which he found the bristles of the hog to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> off, and the dog to become full of ulcers. When <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a> was discovered, this practice was found to be almost universal, insomuch that several authors have supposed it to be occasioned through a want of other food, or through the indolence of the people to seek for it; though others ascribe its origin to a spirit of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a>. It appears pretty certain from Dr Hawkesworth's account of the Voyages to the South seas, that the inhabitants of the island of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-NEW_ZEALAND">New <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZEALAND">Zealand</a>, a country unfurnished with the necessaries of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, eat the bodies of their enemies. It appears also to be very probable, that both the wars and anthropophagy of these savages, take their rise and owe their continuance to irresistible <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a>, and the dreadful alternative of destroying each other by violence, or of perishing by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HUNGER">hunger</a>. See vol. iii. p. 447, et seq. and vol. ii. p. 389, &c. Mr Marsden also informs us, that this horrible <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> is practised by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BATTAS">Battas</a>, a people in the island of Sumatra. "They do not eat human flesh (says he) as a means of satisfying the cravings of nature, owing to a deficiency of other food; nor is it sought after as a glutinous delicacy, as it would seem among the New Zealanders. The Battas eat it as a species of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a>; as a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of showing their detestation of crimes, by an ignominious <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>; and as a horrid indication of revenge and insult to their unfortunate enemies. The objects of this barbarous repast are the prisoners taken in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, and offenders convicted and condemned for <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> crimes. Persons of the former..." former <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> may be ransomed or exchanged, for which they often wait a considerable time; and the latter suffer only when their friends cannot redeem them by the customary fine of twenty beenchanghs, or eighty dollars. These are tried by the people of the tribe where the fact was committed, but cannot be executed till their own particular raja or <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> has been acquainted with the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a>; who, when he acknowledges the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> of the intended punishment, sends a cloth to cover the delinquent's head, together with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DISH">dish</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> and lemons. The unhappy object, whether prisoner of war or malefactor, is then tied to a stake: the people assembled throw their lances at him from a certain distance; and when mortally wounded, they run up to him, as if in a transport of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>; cut pieces from the body with their knives; dip them in the dish of salt and lemon juice; slightly broil them over a fire prepared for the purpose; and swallow the morsels with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> enthusiasm. Sometimes (I presume according to the degree of their animosity and resentment) the whole is devoured; and instances have been known, where, with barbarity still aggravated, they tear the flesh from the carcass with their mouths. To such a depth of depravity may man be plunged, when neither <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> nor <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> enlighten his steps! All that can be said in extenuation of the horror of this diabolical ceremony is, that no view appears to be entertained of torturing the sufferers; of increasing or lengthening out the pangs of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>: the whole fury is directed against the corpse, warm indeed with the remains of life, but past the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSATION">sensation</a> of pain. I have found a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> in regard to their eating the bodies of their enemies slain in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>. Some persons <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> resident there, and acquainted with their proceedings, assert that it is not customary; but as one or two particular instances have been given by other people, it is <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> to conclude, that it sometimes takes <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, though not generally. It was supposed to be with this intent, that Raja Neabin maintained a long conflict for the body of Mr Nairne, a most respectable <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> and valuable <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">Company</a>, who fell in an attack upon the campong of that chief, in the year 1775." It may be said, that whether the dead body of an enemy be eaten or buried, is a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> perfectly indifferent. But whatever the practice of eating human flesh may be in itself, it certainly is relatively, and in its consequences, most pernicious. It manifestly tends to eradicate a principle, which is the chief security of human life, and more frequently restrains the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> of the murderer, than the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of duty or the dread of punishment. Even if this horrid practice originates from hunger, still it must be perpetuated from revenge. Death must lose much of its horror among those who are accustomed to eat the dead; and where there is little horror at the sight of death, there must be less repugnance to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a>. See some further observations on this subject, equally just and ingenious, by Dr Hawkesworth, ut supra.

ANTHROPOPHAGIA

Pages 472-472

the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> of eating <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>. This is pretended by some to be the effect of a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>, which leads people affected with it to eat every thing alike. Some choose only to consider it as a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICA">PICA</a>. The annals of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a> furnish an extraordinary instance of anthropophagy. A Milanese woman named <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>, from a depraved appetite, like what women with child, and those whose phlegmenses are obstructed, frequently <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>, had an invincible inclination to human flesh, of which she Antichris made provision by enticing children into her <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, where she killed and salted them: a discovery of which having been made, she was broken on the wheel and burnt in 1519.

ANTHROPOSOCPIA

Pages 472-472

from ἀνθρώπος, and σκοπεῖν, I consider, the art of judging <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> discovering a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s character, disposition, passions, and inclinations, from the lineaments of his body. In which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, anthroposcopy seems of somewhat greater <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> than physiognomy or metoposcopy. Otto has published an Anthroposcopy, sive judicium hominis de homine ex lineamentis externis.

ANTHUS

Pages 472-472

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a>, a synonyme of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of loxia. See LOXIA, ORNITHOLOGY <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ANTHYPOPHORA

Pages 472-472

in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">Rhetoric</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of speech; being the counterpart of an hypophora. See HYPOPHORA.

ANTI

Pages 472-472

in matters of literature, is a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> given to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> pieces written by way of answer to others, whose names are usually annexed to the anti. See the Anti of M. Baillet; and the Anti-Baillet of M. Menage: there are also Anti-Menagiani, &c. Caesar the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DICTATOR">dictator</a> wrote two books by way of answer to what had been objected to him by Cato, which he called Anti-Catones; these are mentioned by Juvenal, Cicero, &c. Vives assures us, he had seen Caesar's Anti-Catones in an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> library.

ANTIBACCHIUS

Pages 472-472

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, a foot consisting of three syllables, the two first <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and the last one short; such is the word ambré.

ANTIBES

Pages 472-472

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> port town of France, in the department of Var, with a strong castle. Its territory produces excellent fruit; and the town stands opposite to Nice, in the Mediterranean. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 7° 9' N. Lat. 43° 42'.

ANTICHAMBER

Pages 472-472

an outer chamber for strangers to wait in, till the person to be spoken with is at leisure.

ANTICHRIST

Pages 472-473

among <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> writers, denotes a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> adversary of Christianity, who is to appear upon the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> towards the end of the world. We have demonstrations, disputations, and proofs, in great order and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, both that the pope is, and that he is not, Antichrist. F. Calmet is very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> in describing the father and mother of Antichrist, his tribe and pedigree, his wars and conquests, his achievements against Gog, Magog, &c. Some <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> at Constantinople, others at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>, others at <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOSCOW">Moscow</a>, and some few at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>; but the generality at Rome, though these last are divided Antichrist, vided. Grotius and some others suppose Rome Pagan to have been the seat of Antichrist: most of the Lutheran and reformed doctors contend earnestly for Rome Christian under the papal <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HIERARCHY">hierarchy</a>. In fact, the point having been maturely debated at the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAP">Gap</a>, held in 1603, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> was taken thereupon, to insert an article in the Confession of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">Faith</a>, whereby the pope is formally declared to be Antichrist.—Pope Clement VIII. was stung to the quick with this decision; and even <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> Henry IV. of France was not a little mortified, to be thus declared, as he said, an imp of Antichrist. M. le Clerc holds, that the rebel Jews and their leader Simon, whose <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> is given by Josephus, are to be reputed as the true Antichrist. Lightfoot and Vanderhart rather apply this character to the Jewish Sanhedrim. Hippolitus and others held that the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVIL">devil</a> himself was the true Antichrist; that he was to be incarnate, and make his appearance in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> shape before the consummation of all things. Others among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> held that Antichrist was to be born of a virgin by some prolific power imparted to her by the devil. A <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> writer* of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEX">sex</a>, whom many hold for a saint, has improved on this sentiment; maintaining that Antichrist is to be begotten by the devil on the body of a witch by means of the semen of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> caught in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> of a certain crime, and conveyed, &c. Hunnius and some others, to secure Antichrist to the pope (notwithstanding that this latter seemed excluded by not being of the tribe of Dan), have broke in upon the unity of Antichrist, and assert that there is to be both an eastern and a western Antichrist. Father Malvenda, a Jesuit, hath published a large <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> entitled Antichristo, in which this subject is amply discussed. It consists of thirteen books. In the first he relates all the opinions of the fathers with regard to Antichrist. In the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, he speaks of the times when he shall appear; and shows, that all the fathers who supposed Antichrist to be near at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, judged the world was near its <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>. In the third, he discourses of his origin and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>; and shows that he is to be a Jew of the tribe of Dan: this he founds on the authority of the fathers; on the passage in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GENESIS">Genesis</a> xlix. 17, Dan shall be a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SERPENT">serpent</a> by the way, &c.; on that of Jeremiah viii. 16, where it is said, The armies of Dan shall devour the earth; and on Rev. vii., where St John, enumerating all the tribes of Israel, makes no mention of that of Dan. In the fourth and fifth books he treats of the signs of Antichrist. In the sixth, of his reign and wars. In the seventh, of his vices. In the eighth, of his doctrine and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a>. In the ninth, of his persecutions: and in the rest, of the coming of Enoch and Elias, the conversion of the Jews, the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Antichrist, after he has reigned three years and a half. See also Louman on the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVELATION">Revelation</a>. How endless are conjectures! Some of the Jews, we are told, actually took Cromwell for the Christ; while some others have laboured to prove him Antichrist himself. Pfaffius assures us he <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> a folio book in the Bodleian library, written on purpose to demonstrate this latter position. Upon the whole, the Antichrist mentioned by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APOSTLE">apostle</a> John, 1 Ep. ii. 18, and more particularly described in the book of Revelation, seems evidently to be the same with the Man of Sin, &c. characterized by St Paul in his Second Epistle to the Thessalonians, ch. ii. And the entire <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> literally applies to the excesses of papal power. Had the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of private judgment, says an excellent writer, been always adopted and maintained, Antichrist could never have been; and when that sacred right comes to be universally asserted, and men follow the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> of their own reason and consciences, Antichrist can be no more.

ANTICHRISTIANISM

Pages 473-473

a state <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> in persons or principles, which denominates them antichristian, or opposite to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Christ. M. Jurieu takes the idea of the unity of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> to have been the source of Anticrhistianism. Had not mankind been infatuated with this, they would never have stood in such awe of the anathemas of Rome. It is on this the popes erected their monarchical power. ANTICHRISTIANS properly denote the followers or worshippers of Antichrist. Antichristians are more particularly understood of those who set up or believe a false Christ or Messiah.

ANTICHTHONES

Pages 473-473

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, an appellation given to the inhabitants of opposite hemispheres.

ANTICITY

Pages 489-489

Y signifies <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> ages past <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> ago. Thus, we say, the heroes of antiquity, &c. ANTICITY is also used to denote the works or monuments of antiquity. See ANTIQUITIES.

ANTICITY LIKEWISE

Pages 489-489

Y likewise expresses the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of a thing; and in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> we say, the antiquity of a family, the antiquity of a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>.

ANTICOR

Pages 473-473
or ANTICOEUR, among Farriers, an inflammation in a horse's throat, being the same with the quinsy in mankind. See FARRIERY.

ANTICOSTE

Pages 473-473

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BARREN_ISLAND">barren <a cla</a>ss="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> lying in the mouth of the river St Lawrence, in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 64. 16. N. Lat. 49. 40.

ANTICYRA

Pages 473-474

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHOCIS">Phocis</a>, on the Corinthian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>, opposite to Cirrha, lying to the west on the same bay. The Phoeceans seizing the temple of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DELPHI">Delphi</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, called the sacred, commenced, and lasted ten years; when <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a>, father of Alexander the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>, avenged the god by destroying many of the cities of the pillagers. Anticyra was one of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>. It was again taken and subverted by Attlius a Roman general in the war with the Macedonians. It afterwards became famous for its hellebore. That drug was the root of a plant, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> produce of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROCKY_MOUNTAINS">rocky <a class=</a>"xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> above the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, and of two kinds, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, which had a purgative <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, which was an emetic. Sick persons resorted to Anticyra to take the medicine, which was prepared there by a peculiar and very excellent recipe: Hence the adage, Naviget Anticyram, (Horace). By the port in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> century was a temple of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEPTUNE">Neptune</a>, not <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, built with selected <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, and the inside white-washed: the statue of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>. The agora <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> market-<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> was adorned with images of the same metal; and above it was a well with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, sheltered from the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> by a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> supported by columns. A little higher was a monument formed with such stones as occurred, and designed, it was said, for the sons of Iphitus. One of these, Schedius, was killed by Hector, while fighting for the body of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATROCLUS">Patroclus</a>, but his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> were transported to Anticyra; where his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> died after his return from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">Troy</a>. About two stadia or a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a> distant was a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> rock, a portion of the mountain, on which a temple of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIANA">Diana</a> stood; the image bigger than a large woman, and made by Praxiteles. The walls and other edifices at Anticyra were probably erected, like the temple of Neptune, with stones or pebbles. The site is now called Asprosytia, or The White Houses; and some traces of the buildings from which it was so named remain. The port is landlocked, and frequented by vessels for corn. Some paces up from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> is a fountain.

ANTIDICOMARIANITES

Pages 474-474
ancient heretics who pretended that the Holy Virgin did not preserve a perpetual virginity, but that she had several children by Joseph after our Saviour's birth. Their opinion was grounded on some expressions of our Saviour, wherein he mentions his brothers and his sisters; and of St Matthew, where he says, that Joseph knew not Mary till she had brought forth her first-born son. The Antidicomarianites were the disciples of Helvidius and Jo- vinian, who appeared in Rome toward the close of the fourth century.

ANTIDORON

Pages 474-474

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">Ecclesiastical</a> Writers, a name given by the Greeks to the consecrated <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>, out of which the middle <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a>, marked with the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>, where-in the consecration resides, being taken away by the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>, the remainder is distributed after <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASS">mass</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a>. On the sides of the antidoron are impressed the words <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christus vicit. The word is formed from δόρον, donum, "a gift," as being given away loco muneris, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a>. The antidoron is also called panis presanctificatus. Some supposed the antidoron to be distributed in lieu of the sacrament, to such as were prevented from attending in person at the celebration; and thence derive the origin of the word, the eucharist being denominated doron, "gift," by way of eminence.

ANTIDOSIS

Pages 474-474

in antiquity, denotes an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a> of estates, practised by the Greeks on certain occasions with peculiar ceremonies, and first instituted by Solon. When a person was nominated to an office, the ex-pence of which he was not able to support, he had recourse to the antidosis: that is, he was to seek some other citizen of better substance than himself, who was free from this, and other offices; in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> the former was excised. In case the person thus substituted denied himself to be the richest, they were to exchange estates, after this manner; the doors of their houses were <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> shut up and sealed, that nothing might be conveyed away: then both took an oath to make a faithful discovery of all their effects, except what lay in the silver <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>, which by the laws was excused from all imposts: accordingly, within three days, a full discovery and exchange of estates was made.

ANTIDOTE

Pages 474-474

among physicians, a remedy taken to prevent, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> to cure, the effects of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POISON">poison</a>, &c. ANTIENT. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ANCIENT</a>.

ANTIGONEA

Pages 474-476
or ANTIGONIA, in Ancient Geography, a town of Bithynia, so called from Antigonus, the son of Philip, and afterwards called Nicea (Strabo, Stephanus). Another of Epirus, to the north of the Montes Ceramii, opposite to the city of Oricum (Polybius, Ptolemy). A third of Arcadia, namely Mantinea, so called in honour of King Antigonus, (Plutarch, Pausanias). A fourth in Macedonia, in the territory of Mygdonia (Pliny, Ptolemy). A fifth in the territory of Chalcidice, in Macedonia, on the east side of the Sinus Thermaicus (Livy). A sixth of Antigonea Syria, built by Antigonus, not far from Antioch, on the Orontes (Stephanus); but soon after destroyed by Seleucus, who removed the inhabitants to Seleucia, a town built by him (Diodorus Siculus). A seventh of Troas, called Alexandria in Pliny's time. ANTIGONUS I, one of the captains of Alexander the Great, was the son of Philip a Macedonian nobleman. After Alexander's death, a division of the provinces taking place, Pamphylia, Lycia, and Phrygia Major fell to his share. But Perdiccas, well acquainted with his ambitious spirit and great abilities, determined to divest him of his government, and laid plans for his life, by bringing various accusations against him. Antigonus, aware of the danger, retired with his son Demetrius into Greece, where he obtained the favour and protection of Antipater; and in a short time Perdiccas dying, a new division taking place, he was invested not only with the government of the former provinces, but also with that of Lycaonia. He was likewise entrusted with the command of the Macedonian household troops, and upon Eumenes being declared a public enemy, he received orders to prosecute the war against him with the utmost vigour. On the commencement of this war, Eumenes suffered a total overthrow, and was obliged to retire with only 600 brave followers to a castle situated on an inaccessible rock, where he might rest in safety from all the assaults of Antigonus. In the interval, his friends assembling a new army for his relief, were routed by Antigonus, who now began to exhibit the great projects of his ambition. Polysperchon succeeding to the tutorship of the young king of Macedon after Antipater's death, Antigonus resolved to set himself up as lord of all Asia. On account of the great power of Eumenes, he greatly desired to gain him over to his interest; but that faithful commander effecting his escape from the fortress where he was closely blockaded, raised an army, and was appointed the royal general in Asia. The governors in Upper Asia co-operating with him, he succeeded in several engagements against Antigonus, but was at last delivered up to him through treachery, and put to death. Upon this, the governors of Upper Asia yielded to Antigonus. Those whom he suspected, he either sacrificed to his resentment or displaced them from their offices. Then seizing upon all the treasures at Susa, he directed his march towards Babylon, of which city Seleucus was governor. Seleucus fled to Ptolemy, and entered into a league with him, together with Lysimachus and Cassander, with the intention of giving a check to the exorbitant power of Antigonus, who, notwithstanding this, made a successful attempt upon the provinces of Syria and Phenicia. Yet these provinces were soon after recovered by Ptolemy, who defeated his son Demetrius, while he himself was employed in repelling Cassander, who had made rapid progress in Lesser Asia. They were again taken by Antigonus, and he being flushed with his success, planned an expedition against the Nabathæan Arabs, dwelling in the deserts adjacent to Judea; but on the first enterprise against the town of Petra, his general Athenæus, with almost all his troops, was cut to pieces by the Arabs. Antigonus then sent his son against them, who returned after forcing them to reasonable terms. Demetrius then Antigonus then expelled Seleucus from Babylon, and success attending his arms wherever he went, the confederates were obliged to make a treaty with Antigonus, in which it was stipulated, that he should remain in possession of all Asia, but that the Greek cities should continue in possession of their liberty. This agreement was soon violated, under the pretence that garrisons had been placed in some of these cities by Antigonus. At first Ptolemy made a successful descent in Lesser Asia and on several of the islands of the Archipelago; but he was at length defeated by the successful arms of Demetrius in a sea-fight, who also took the island of Cyprus, with many prisoners. On this victory Antigonus was so elated that he assumed the title of king, and bestowed the same upon his son; and from that time, B.C. 306, his reign in Asia; and that of Ptolemy in Egypt, and of the other captains of Alexander in their respective governments, properly commence. Irritated at the hostile conduct of Ptolemy, Antigonus prepared a numerous army and a formidable fleet, and having taken the command of the army, he gave the command of the fleet to Demetrius, and hastened to attack him in his own dominions. After enduring the severest hardships, they met in the vicinity of Mount Cassius; but Ptolemy acted with such valour and address that Demetrius could gain no advantage over him; and after several fruitless attempts, he abandoned the undertaking. He next attempted the reduction of Rhodes, but meeting with obstinate resistance, he was obliged to make a treaty upon the best terms that he could, having been called to join Antigonus against Cassander, who at this time had formed a confederacy with Seleucus and Lysimachus. When Demetrius united his forces with those of Antigonus, they advanced to Phrygia, and having met the enemy at Ipsus, a decisive battle was fought, in which Antigonus fell, in the 84th year of his age, B.C. 301. Ardent in his passions, Antigonus frequently used improper means for their gratification; but as a soldier he was sagacious, active, brave, and fortunate. An insatiable ambition, however, the general passion of great men, proved a strong stimulus to all his actions; but with these blemishes better qualities were blended in his character. The violence and temerity of youth were tempered by the clemency and moderation of advanced life, and he endeavoured to conciliate the affections of those whom force had subjected to his power. In matters of private concern he was strictly just; for when his brother wished him to listen to a cause in private where he was concerned, he exclaimed, "No, my dear brother, I will hear it in the open court of justice, because I mean to do justice." When flattered with the title of god, he replied, "My chamberlain well knows the contrary;" and similar philosophical sentiments would frequently drop from his lips. He apologized for the rigour of his taxes by saying, "Alexander reaped Asia, but I only glean it." He shone with peculiar lustre in domestic retirement. Notwithstanding the strong ambition of his son Demetrius, he continued in perfect harmony both with him and all his family. The son had a full share of the authority of the father; and one day saluting his son upon his return from hunting in the presence of some ambassadors, he desired them to tell their masters upon what terms he lived with his son. (Gen. Biog.) Antigonus Gonatus, son of Demetrius Poliorcetes, Antigonus was the grandson of the former Antigonus. His character was eminently distinguished by humanity and mildness of disposition. When he besieged Thebes under the command of his father, he strongly remonstrated against the loss of so many lives for such an insignificant object. Filial affection was so powerful in his mind, that when his father was taken prisoner by Seleucus, he generously offered himself in his stead, and being rejected, he wore deep mourning, and refrained from all festivals and amusements during his father's imprisonment. Informed of his death, all the floods of sorrow burst from his tender heart, and sailing with a fleet to meet his ashes, he received them with all the demonstrations of filial sensibility and dutiful respect. By the death of his father he became master of all the European dominions of Demetrius, together with the kingdom of Macedon and various other cities in Greece. The Gauls invading his country, he defeated and expelled them, but was soon after routed by Pyrrhus king of Epirus. Some time after, however, Pyrrhus was slain at Argos; and when his head was brought him by his son, he expressed the highest displeasure, and throwing his robe over it, he gave orders to search for his body, and to inter the same with all funeral honours. With singular kindness, also, he treated Helenus, the son of that unfortunate king, who fell into his hands by the fortune of war. In the evening of his reign, he so cultivated the arts of peace, and so conciliated the minds of his subjects, that he secured their affections both to himself and his descendants. The taking of the citadel of Corinth by intrigue was the meanest action of his reign, but he improved that event in maintaining the freedom of the small states of Greece, and in increasing his own dominions. The Achaeans, and Aratus their famous chief, vigorously opposed his measures, and at length recovered Corinth; but Antigonus was so inclined to peace, that notwithstanding this event, he pursued his wonted plan, and left his kingdom in peace about the 80th year of his life, and the 44th of his reign, B.C. 243; and Demetrius II., his son, next ascended the throne. (Gen. Biog.) Antigraphus, in antiquity, an officer of Athens, who kept a counterpart of the apodecti, or chief treasurer's accounts, to prevent mistakes, and keep them from being falsified. Antigraphus is also used, in middle-age writers, for a secretary or chancellor. He is thus called, according to the old glossarists, on account of his writing answers to the letters sent to his master. The antigraphus is sometimes also called archigraphus; and his dignity antigraphia or archigraphia. Antigraphus is also used in Isidorus for one of the notes of sentences which is placed with a dot to denote diversity of sense in the translations. Antigraphus is also applied in ecclesiastical writers to an abbreviator of the papal letters. In which sense the word is used by Pope Gregory the Great in his register. Of late days the office of antigraphus consists in making minutes of bulls from the petitions agreed to by his holiness, and renewing the bulls after engrossing. Antigua, one of the Antilles or Caribbee islands, situated 20 leagues east of St Christopher's, in Antigua W. Long. 61° 45' and N. Lat. 17° 6'. It is about 52 miles in circumference, and is reckoned the largest of all the British leeward islands. This island having no rivers, and but few springs, or such as are brackish, the inhabitants are obliged to preserve the rain water in cisterns. The air here is not so wholesome as in the neighbouring islands, and it is more subject to hurricanes; but it has excellent harbours, particularly English Harbour, which is capable of receiving the largest man of war in the navy. Here is also a dock yard, supplied with all stores and conveniences for repairing and careening ships. The principal trade, however, is carried on in the harbour of St John's, the capital, situated in the north-west part of the island, and which has water sufficiently deep for merchant vessels. The island contains 59,838 acres of land, of which about 34,000 are appropriated to the growth of sugar, including those which are annexed as pasture grounds. The other staples are cotton, wool, and tobacco. This island was first attempted to be settled by Sir Thomas Warner, about the same time with St Christopher's and Nevis: but no establishment then took place. It was afterwards granted by Charles II. to Lord Willoughby, then governor of Barbadoes, who settled a colony upon it in the space of a few years. In a short time, but by what means is not evident, it became again the public property. It raises at present about 16,000 hogsheads of sugar, which was at first of a very bad quality, unfit for the English market; but the planters have greatly improved their staple since, and it is now as good as in any of the other islands. It has continued unmolested in all the late wars with France. It is divided into five parishes, St John's Town, Falmouth, Porham, Bridge Town, and St Peter's. According to returns in 1817 the number of white inhabitants was 2102, exclusive of troops, of free people of colour 1747, of free blacks 438, and of slaves 31,452. The slaves had increased 1170 since 1807, when the slave trade was abolished.

ANTIGUGLER

Pages 476-476

is a crooked tube of metal, so bent as easily to be introduced into the necks of bottles, and used in decanting liquors, without disturbing them. For this purpose the bottle should be a little inclined, and about half a spoonful of the liquor poured out, so as to admit an equal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>; let one end of the bent tube be stopped with the finger, whilst the other is thrust into the body of the liquor near to the bubble of air already admitted. When the finger is taken off, the bottle <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> have vent, and the liquor will run out steadily and undisturbed.

ANTIHECTICUM POTERII

Pages 476-476

the name of a medicine formerly much celebrated, but now laid aside in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> practice.

ANTILIBANUS

Pages 476-476

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a mountain of Coelosyria, which bounds it on the south, running <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> with Libanus: they both begin a little above the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, Libanus near Tripolis, Antilibanus at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIDON">Sidon</a>: and both terminate near the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a>, which run to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of Damascus, and the mountains of Traconitis, and there end in other mountains, (Strabo). The Scripture, making no distinction between Libanus and Antilibanus, calls them by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> name Lebanon.

ANTILOGARITHM

Pages 476-476

the complement of the logarithm of a sine, tangent, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECANT">secant</a>; or the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of that logarithm from the logarithm of 90 degrees.

ANTILOGY

Pages 476-476

in matters of literature, an inconsistency between two <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> more <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> of the same book. ANTILOPE. See Capra.

ANTIMENSIA

Pages 476-476

a kind of consecrated <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>-cloth, occasionally used in the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, in places where there is no proper altar. F. Goar observes, that in regard the Greeks had but few consecrated churches, and that consecrated altars are not things easy to be removed, that church has, for many ages, made <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of certain consecrated stuffs <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> linens, called antimensia, to serve the purposes thereof. Antimensia, in the Greek church, answers to the altare portabile, or portable altar in the Latin church. They are both only of late <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a>, though Habertus would have them as old as St <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASIL">Basil</a>. But Durant and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BONA">Bona</a> do not pretend to find them in any author before the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Bede and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLEMAGNE">Charlemagne</a>. Antimensia is also applied to other tables, used in offices of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, besides those whereon the eucharist is administered: such, e.g., are those whereon the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOST">host</a> is exposed, &c. The origin of the antimensia is described by Meursius: when the bishop had consecrated a church, the cloth which had been spread on the ground and over the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a> table, was torn in pieces, and distributed among the priests, who carried each a fragment away, to serve to cover the tables in their churches and chapels. Not that it was necessary that such cloths should be laid on all tables; but only on those which either were not consecrated, or at least whose consecration was doubted of.

ANTIMERIA

Pages 476-476

in a more restrained <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, is a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> where the noun is repeated instead of the pronoun. The antimeria is frequent in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a>, and is sometimes retained in our version of the Old <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a> accordingly: e.g., Hear my <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>, ye wives of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAMECH">Lamech</a>, for my wives, Gen. iv. 23.

ANTIMETABOLE

Pages 476-476

in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">Rhetoric</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> which sets two things in opposition to each other. The word is Greek, compounded of ἀντί against, and μεταβολή from μεταβάλλω, I shift <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> transfer, i.e. shifting, or setting two things over-against each other. This figure is twice exemplified in an apophthegm of Musonius; which, on account of its excellence, is called aurum monitum, the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> maxim or precept. Αἱ τι πράξεις καλῶν μετὰ ποιη, ὅτι ποῖος εἰχεῖται, τὸ δὲ παν- λοῦ μετεῖ. Αἱ τι πράξεις αἰσχρῶν μετὰ ἐδόθη, τὸ μὴ ποῖος εἰχεῖται, τὸ δὲ αἰσχρῶν μετεῖ. In English thus: "Allowing the performance of an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> to be attended with labour; the labour is soon over, but the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> immortal: whereas, should even <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> wait on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> of what is dishonourable, the pleasure is soon gone, but the dishonour eternal."

ANTIMETATHESIS

Pages 476-477

ANTIMETATHESIS, in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">Rhetoric</a>, is the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVERSION">inversion</a> of the parts <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> members of an antithesis. Such is that of Cicero in Verrem, lib. iv. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 52. "Compare this peace with that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>; the arrival of this governor with the victory of that general; his profligate troops with the invincible <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of the other; the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a> of the former with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEMPERANCE">temperance</a> of the latter: you <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> say, that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRACUSE">Syracuse</a> was founded by him who took it; and taken by him, who held it when founded."

ANTIMONY

Pages 477-478

a blackish mineral substance, staining the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, full of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, shining, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEEDLE">needle</a>-like strix, hard, brittle, and considerably heavy. It is found in different parts of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, as <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>, Transylvania, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>, France, and England; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> by itself, intermixed with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> and stony matters. Sometimes it is blended with the richer ores of silver, and renders the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTRACTION">extraction</a> of that metal difficult by volatilizing a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the silver, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of the miners, robbing the ore. See <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METALLURGY">METALLURGY</a>, for the different operations. Antimony is the stibium of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>; by the Greeks called ῥυμα. The reason of its <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> denomination, antimony, is usually referred to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASIL">Basil</a> Valentine, a German monk; who, as the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a> relates, having thrown some of it to the hogs, observed, that after purging them violently, they immediately grew fat upon it. This made him think, that by giving his fellow monks a like dose, they would be the better for it. The experiment, however, succeeded so ill, that they all died of it: and the medicine thenceforward was called antimony, q. d. anti-monk. Uses. Antimony at first was of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> only in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of paint. Scripture describes it to us as a sort of paint, with which the women blackened their eyebrows. Jezebel, understanding that Jehu was to enter <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAMARIA">Samaria</a>, painted her eyes with antimony; or, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a>, "put her eyes in antimony." As <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> eyes were thought the finest, they of both sexes, who were careful of their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, rubbed their eyes, eyelids, and round their eyes, with a needle dipped in a box of paint made of antimony, with a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of blackening them.—At this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, the women of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BABYLONIA">Babylonia</a>, anoint and blacken themselves about the eyes; and both men and women put black upon their eyes in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DESERT">desert</a>, to preserve them from the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> and the piercing of its rays. M. Darvieux tells us, that the Arabian women border their eyes with a black <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> made of tutty, which the Arabians call rebel. They draw a line of this kind of blacking without the corner of their eyes, to make them appear larger. Isaiah, in his enumeration of the several ornaments belonging to the daughters of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SION">Sion</a>, has not forgot the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEEDLES">needles</a> which they made <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> their eyes and eyelids. Nor has this practice escaped the lash of Juvenal: Ille supercilium madida fuligine tinctum Obliqua producit acu, pingitique trementes Attollens oculos. <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EZEKIEL">Ezekiel</a>, discovering the irregularities of the Jewish <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> under the idea of a debauched woman, says, Antimony, that she bathed and perfumed herself, and that she anointed her eyes with antimony. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOB">Job</a> shows sufficiently how much antimony was in esteem, by calling one of his daughters a vessel of antimony, or a box to put paint in, cornu stibii. The author of the book of Enoch says, that before the deluge the angel Azleel taught young women the art of painting themselves. Tertullian and St Cyprian have declaimed very warmly against this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of painting the eyes and eyebrows, which was much practised in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a> even by the men: Inunge oculos tuos non stibio diaboli, sed collyrio Christi, says St Cyprian. Pliny, speaking of the Roman ladies, says, that they painted their very eyes: Tanta est decoris affectatio, ut tingantur oculi quoque. <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SARDANAPALUS">Sardanapalus</a> painted his eyes and eyebrows. Josephus reproaches the seditious with the same, who assumed the name of zealots, and made themselves masters of the temple of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>. The modern uses of antimony are very numerous and important. It is a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> ingredient in specula or <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> concaves, serving to give the composition a finer texture. It makes a part in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELL">bell</a> metal, and renders the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> more clear. It is mingled with tin, to make it more hard, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, and sounding; and with <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, in the casting of printers letters, to render them more smooth and firm. It is also a general help in the melting of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-METALS">metals</a>, and especially in casting of cannon-balls. It is likewise made use of for purifying and heightening the colour of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHEMISTRY">CHEMISTRY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. For a long <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> this mineral was esteemed poisonous. In 1566, its use was prohibited in France by an edict of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>; and in 1609, one Besnier was expelled the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> for having given it. The edict was repealed in 1659; antimony having a few years before been received into the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of purgatives. In 1668, a new edict came forth, forbidding its use by any but doctors of the faculty. It is now universally allowed, that pure antimony in its crude state has no noxious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, and that though many of its preparations are most virulently emetic and cathartic, yet, by a slight <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> or addition, they lose their virulence, and become mild in their operation. The virtues of antimony in the diseases of animals are greatly extolled. Pigs that have the measles are at all times recovered by it, which proves it a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> purifier of the blood.
