Horses who have running heels that cannot be cured by the common methods used by the farriers, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> generally be cured by this medicine in a little time. The manner of using it is this: Mix one drachm with every feeding of oats which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> has in a morning. It is best put together in one <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, buried under a few oats; and the horse's head being withheld a little, and then let go <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> against that place, he will take it all in at a mouthful. Some horses do not dislike it; others obstinately refuse it, but to these it may be easily given in balls. The virtues of this drug in fattening cattle have been thought imaginary, but experiment proves it to be a real <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>. A horse that is lean and scabby, and not to be fatted by any other means, will become fat on taking a dose of antimony every morning for two months together. A boar fed for brawn, and having an ounce of anti- Antimony given him every morning, will become fat a fortnight sooner than others put into the style at the same time, and fed in the same manner, but without the antimony. ANTINOE. See ENFINE.

ANTINOEIA

Pages 478-478

in antiquity, annual sacrifices, and quinquennial games, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of Antinous the Bithynian. They were instituted at the command of Adrian, the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>, at Mantinea, in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCADIA">Arcadia</a>, where Antinous was honoured with a temple and divine worship.

ANTINOMIANS

Pages 478-478

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, certain heretics who maintain the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> of no <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> obligation under the gospel-dispensation, or who hold doctrines that clearly supersede the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of good works and a virtuous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. The Antinomians took their origin from John Agricola about the year 1538; who taught that the law is no ways necessary under the gospel; that good works do not promote our <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALVATION">salvation</a>, nor ill ones hinder it; that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REPENTANCE">repentance</a> is not to be preached from the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECALOGUE">decalogue</a>, but only from the gospel. This <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a> sprung up in England during the protectorate of Oliver Cromwell, and extended their system of libertinism much farther than Agricola the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUTHER">Luther</a>. Some of their teachers expressly maintained, that as the elect cannot <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">grace</a>, nor forfeit the Divine favour, the wicked actions they commit are not really sinful, nor are to be considered as instances of their violation of the divine law; and that consequently they have no occasion either to confess their sins, or to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> them off by repentance. According to them, it is one of the essential and distinctive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> of the elect, that they cannot do any thing which is either displeasing to God or prohibited by the law.—Luther, Rutherford, Schluselburg, Sedgwick, Gataker, Witsius, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">Ball</a>, Williams, &c. have written refutations; Crisp, Richardson, Saltmarsh, &c. defences, of the Antinomians; Wigandus, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> between <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> Antinomians. The doctrine of Agricola was in itself obscure, and perhaps represented worse than it really was by Luther, who wrote with acrimony against him, and first styled him and his followers Antinomians. Agricola stood on his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>, and complained that opinions were imputed to him which he did not hold. Nicholas Amsdorf fell under the same odious name and imputation, and seems to have been treated more unfairly than even Agricola himself. It is rather hard to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> upon a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> all the opinions that may be inferred from things that have hastily dropped from him, when he himself disavows such inferences.

ANTINOUS

Pages 478-478

the favourite of Adrian, was born at Bithynia in Bithynia. His <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> engaged the heart of Adrian in such a manner, that there never was a more boundless and extravagant <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> than that of this <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> towards this youth. After his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, the emperor ordered divine honours to be paid him; and he also erected a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of his name. See ENFINE.

ANTIOCH

Pages 478-480

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, situated on the river <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORONTES">Orontes</a>, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 36° 5' N. Lat. 36° 10'. It was built by Seleucus Nicator, founder of the Syro-Macedonian empire, who made it his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>. It stood on the above-mentioned river, about 25 miles from the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where it empties itself into the Mediterranean; being equally distant from Constantinople and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, that is, about 700 miles from each. Antioch, Seleucus called it Antioch, from his father's name, according to some; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> from that of his son, according to others. He built 16 other cities <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> the same name; of which one, situated in Pisidia, is probably that where the name of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> was first given to the followers of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ. But that situated on the Orontes by far eclipsed, not only all the others of this name, but all the cities built by Seleucus. Antigonos, not long before, had founded a city in that neighbourhood, which from his own name he had called Antigonia, and designed it for the capital of his empire: but it was razed to the ground by Seleucus, who employed the materials in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> his <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a>, and also transplanted the inhabitants thither. The city of Antioch was afterwards known by the name of Tetrapolis, being divided as it were into four cities, each of them being surrounded with its proper wall, besides a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> one which enclosed them all. The first of these cities was built by Seleucus Nicator, as already mentioned; the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> by those who flocked thither on its being made the capital of the Syro-Macedonian empire; the third by Seleucus Callinicus; and the fourth by Antiochus Epiphanes.—About four or five miles distant, stood a place called <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAPHNE">Daphne</a>, which was nevertheless reckoned a suburb of Antioch. Here Seleucus planted a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROVE">grove</a>, and in the middle of it built a temple which he consecrated to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIANA">Diana</a>, making the whole an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASYLUM">asylum</a>. To this place the inhabitants of Antioch resorted for their pleasures and diversions; whereby it became at last so infamous, that "to live after the manner of Daphne" was used as a proverb to express the most voluptuous and dissolute way of living. Here Lucius Verus, the colleague of M. Aurelius, chose to take up his residence, instead of marching against the Parthians; while his general Cassius forbade by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCLAMATION">proclamation</a> any of his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> to enter or even go near the place. In short, so remarkable was Daphne of old, that the metropolis itself was distinguished by it, and called Antioch near Daphne. Though Antioch <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to be, as Pliny calls it, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> of the East, for near 1600 years; yet scarce any city mentioned in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> hath undergone such calamities, both from the attacks of its enemies, and its being naturally subject to earthquakes. The first disaster mentioned in history which befell the Antiochians happened about 145 years before Christ. Being at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> very much disaffected to the person and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of Demetrius their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>, they were continually raising tumults and seditions; insomuch that he found himself at last obliged to solicit assistance from the Jews; and was furnished by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JONATHAN">Jonathan</a>, one of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MACCABEES">Maccabees</a>, with 3000 men; by which reinforcement, believing himself sufficiently strong to reduce the mutineers by force, he ordered them immediately to deliver up their arms. This unexpected order caused a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> uproar in the city. The inhabitants ran to arms, and invested the king's <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of 120,000, with a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> to put him to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. All the Jews hastened to his relief, fell upon the rebels, killed 100,000 of them, and set fire to the city. On the destruction of the Syrian empire by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, Antioch submitted to them as well as the other cities of that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, and continued for a long time under their dominion. About the year 115, in the reign of the the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Trajan, it was almost entirely ruined by one of the most dreadful earthquakes mentioned in history. Trajan himself happened to be there at that time, being returned from an expedition against the Parthians; so that the city was then full of troops, and strangers come from all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> either out of curiosity or upon business and embassies: the calamity was by this means felt almost in every <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of the Roman empire. The earthquake was preceded by violent claps of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a>, unusual winds, and a dreadful noise under ground. The shock was so terrible, that great numbers of houses were overturned, and others tossed to and fro like a ship at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. Those who happened to be in their houses were for the most <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> buried under their ruins: those who were walking in the streets or in the squares, were, by the violence of the shock, dashed against each other, and most of them either killed or dangerously wounded. This earthquake continued, with some small intermission, for many days and nights; so that vast numbers perished. The most violent shock, according to the Acts of St Ignatius, was on a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUNDAY">Sunday</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 23. By this Trajan was much hurt, but escaped through a window. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DION">Dion</a> Cassius pretends, that he was taken out of the window by one who exceeded the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> size in tallness. The same historian adds, that Mount Lison, which stood at a small distance from the city, bowed its head and threatened to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> upon it: that other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> fell; that new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> appeared, and others that had flowed before forsook their course and vanished. When the earthquake ceased, a woman was heard crying under the ruins; which being immediately removed, she was found with a living child in her arms. Search was made for others; but none was found alive, except one child which continued sucking its dead mother. No doubt, Trajan, who was an eye-witness of this terrible calamity, would contribute largely towards the re-establishment of Antioch in its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> splendour. Its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a>, however, did not continue long; for in 155, it was almost entirely burnt by accidental fire; when it was again restored by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANTONINUS_PIUS">Antoninus Pius</a>. In 176 or 177, the inhabitants having sided with Cassius, the above-mentioned Roman general, who had revolted from M. Aurelius, that emperor published a severe edict against them, deprived them of all their privileges, suppressed their public assemblies, and took from them the shows and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SPECTACLES">spectacles</a> to which they were greatly addicted: but his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGER">anger</a> being soon appeased, he restored them to their former condition, and even condescended to visit their city. In 194, having sided with <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NIGER">Niger</a> against Severus, the latter deprived them of all their privileges, and subjected Antioch as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> village to Laodicea; but, however, pardoned them the next year, at the entreaties of his eldest son, then a child. When the power of the Roman empire began to decline, Antioch became the bone of contention between them and the eastern nations; and, accordingly, on the breaking out of a Persian <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, it was almost always sure to suffer. In 242, it was taken and plundered by Sapor; and, though he was defeated by Gordian, it underwent the same misfortune in the time of Valerian, about 18 years after; and after the defeat and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTIVITY">captivity</a> of Valerian, being taken by the Persian monarch a third time, he not only plundered it, but levelled all the public buildings with the ground. The Persians, however, being soon driven out, this unfortunate city continued free from any remarkable calamity till about the time of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of the Roman empire by Constantine in 331. It was then afflicted with so grievous a famine, that a bushel of wheat was sold for 400 pieces of silver. During this grievous distress, Constantine sent to the bishop 30,000 bushels of corn; besides an incredible <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of all kinds of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>, to be distributed among the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICS">ecclesiastics</a>, widows, orphans, &c. In the year 347, Constantine II. caused a harbour to be made at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SELEUCIA">Seleucia</a>, for the convenience of Antioch. This was effected at an immense expense; the mouth of the Orontes, where the port was made, being full of sands and rocks. When the emperor Julian set out on his expedition against the Persians, he made a long stay at Antioch; during which time, many of the Roman provinces were afflicted with a famine, but which raged more violently at Antioch than in other places. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> writers of those times say, that this famine followed Julian from place to place; and as he continued longer at Antioch than any other city, it raged more violently there than anywhere else. To remedy this evil, Julian fixed the price of corn: by which means the famine was greatly increased, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> conveying their corn privately to other places, so that this metropolis was reduced to a most deplorable situation. In 381, in the reign of Theodosius the Great, Antioch was again visited by a famine, accompanied by a grievous <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAGUE">plague</a>. The latter soon ceased: but, the famine still continuing, the bishop, Libanius, applied to Icarius, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">count</a> of the East, requesting him by some means or other to relieve the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a>, who had flocked from all parts to the metropolis, and were daily perishing in great numbers; but to this Icarius gave no other answer, than that they were abhorred and justly punished by the gods. This inhuman answer raised great disturbances; which, however, were terminated without bloodshed. In 387, Theodosius, finding his exchequer quite drained, and being obliged to be at an extraordinary expense in celebrating the fifth year of the reign of his son Arcadius, and the tenth of his own, an extraordinary tax was laid upon all the people in the empire. Most of the cities submitted willingly to this: but the people of Antioch, complaining of it as an unreasonable oppression, crowded to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of Flavianus, their bishop, as soon as the edict was published, to implore his protection. Being unable to find him, they returned to the forum; and would have torn the governor in pieces, had not the officers who attended him kept back with great difficulty the enraged multitude, till he made his escape. Upon this, they broke some of the emperor's <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a>, and dragged others through the city, uttering the most injurious and abusive expressions against him and his whole family. They were, however, dispersed by a body of archers, who, by wounding only two of the rabble, struck terror into all the rest. The governor proceeded against the offenders with the utmost cruelty; <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPOSING">exposing</a> some to wild beasts in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> others alive. He did not spare even the children, who had insulted the emperor's statues; and caused several persons to be executed, who had been only spectators of the disorder. In the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time a report was spread, that a body of troops was at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, with orders to plunder the city. Antioch, city, and put all to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, without distinction of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEX">sex</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>; upon which the citizens abandoned their dwellings in the utmost terror and confusion, retiring to the neighbouring mountains with their wives and families. As the report proved groundless, some of them returned; but the greater part dreading the cruelty of the governor, and the displeasure of the emperor, continued in their retreats. To those who returned, St Chrysostom preached some homilies, which have reached our times, and are greatly admired; and which are said by St Chrysostom himself, as well as some <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> writers, to have had a considerable effect in reforming the lives of this licentious and dissolute people. On hearing the news of this tumult, Theodosius was so much enraged, that he commanded the city to be destroyed, and its inhabitants to be put to the sword without distinction; but this order was revoked before it could be put into execution, and he contented himself with a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> similar to that inflicted by Severus above mentioned. He appointed judges to punish the offenders; who proceeded with such severity, and condemned such numbers, that the city was thrown into the utmost consternation. On this occasion St Chrysostom and the hermits, who were very numerous in the neighbourhood, exerted all their eloquence in behalf of the unhappy people, and obtained a respite for those who had been condemned. They next proceeded to draw up a memorial to the emperor in favour of the citizens in general; and being joined by Flavianus, at last obtained a general <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a>, and had the city restored to all its former privileges. In the year 458, Antioch was almost entirely ruined by an earthquake, which happened on the 14th of September; scarce a single house being left standing in the most beautiful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of the city. The like misfortune it experienced in 529, during the reign of the emperor Justin; and in 15 years after, being taken by Cosroes king of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, that insulting and haughty monarch gave it up to his soldiers, who put all they met to the sword. The king himself seized on all the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver vessels belonging to the great <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>; and caused all the valuable statues, pictures, &c. to be taken down and conveyed to Persia, while his soldiers carried off everything else. The city being thus completely plundered, Cosroes ordered his men to set fire to it; which was accordingly done so effectually, that none of the buildings even without the walls escaped. Such of the inhabitants as escaped slaughter were carried into Persia and sold as slaves. Notwithstanding so many and so great calamities, the city of Antioch soon recovered its wonted splendour; but in a short time underwent its usual fate, being almost entirely destroyed by an earthquake in 587, by which 30,000 persons lost their lives. In 634, it fell into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the Saracens, who kept possession of it till the year 858, when it was surprised by one Burtzas, and again annexed to the Roman empire. The Romans continued masters of it for some time, till the civil dissensions in the empire gave the Turks an opportunity of seizing upon it as well as the whole kingdom of Syria. From them it was again taken by the Crusaders in 1098. In 1262, it was again taken by Bibaris <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SULTAN">sultan</a> of Egypt, who put a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FINAL">final</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> to its <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a>. Antioch, now called Antakia, is a ruinous town, whose houses, built with mud and straw, and narrow and miry streets, exhibit every appearance of misery and wretchedness. These houses are situated on the southern <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the Orontes, at the extremity of an old decayed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>: they are covered to the south by a mountain; upon the slope of which is a wall, built by the Crusaders. The distance between the present town and this mountain may be about 400 yards, which space is occupied by gardens and heaps of rubbish, but presents nothing interesting. Notwithstanding the unpolished manners of its inhabitants, Antioch was better calculated than <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEPPO">Aleppo</a> to be the emporium of the Europeans. By clearing the mouth of the Orontes, which is six leagues lower down, boats might have been towed up that river, though they could not have sailed up, as Pococke has asserted; its current being too rapid. The natives, who never knew the name Orontes, call it, on account of the swiftness of its stream, El aasi, that is, the rebel. Its breadth at Antioch, is about forty paces. <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">Seven</a> leagues above that town it passes by a lake abounding in fish, and especially in eels. A great quantity of these are salted every year, but not sufficient for the numerous fasts of the Greek Christians. It is to be remembered, we no longer hear at Antioch, either of the Grove, or Daphne, or of the voluptuous scenes of which it was the theatre. The plain of Antioch, though the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> of it is excellent, is uncultivated, and abandoned to the Turcomans; but the hills on the side of the Orontes, particularly opposite Serkin, abound in plantations of figs and olives, vines, and mulberry trees, which, a thing uncommon in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a>, are planted in quincunx, and exhibit a landscape worthy our finest provinces. Seleucus Nicator, who founded Antioch, built also at the mouth of the Orontes, on the northern bank, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and well fortified city, which bore his name, but of which at present not a single habitation remains; nothing is to be seen but heaps of rubbish, and works in the adjacent rock, which prove that this was once a place of very considerable importance. In the sea also may be perceived the traces of two piers, which are indications of an ancient port, now choked up. The inhabitants of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> go thither to fish, and call the name of the place Souaidia.

ANTIOCHETTA

Pages 480-480

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, in Caramanis, with a bishop's see, over against the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Cyprus. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 32. 15. N. Lat. 36. 20.

ANTIOCHIA

Pages 480-481

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASSYRIA">Assyria</a>, situated between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Tigris and Tondadotus (Pliny).—Another of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARIA">Caria</a>, on the Meander; called also Pythopolis, Athymbra, and Nyssa, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Nysa, (Stephanus): but Strabo says, that Nysa was near Tralles.—A third of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CILICIA">Cilicia</a> Trachea, on Mount Craigus (<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>).—A fourth called Epidaphnes, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, distinguished from cities of the same name, either by its situation on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORONTES">Orontes</a>, by which it was divided, or by its <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROXIMITY">proximity</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAPHNE">Daphne</a> (see Antiochia).—A fifth Antiochia, a town of Comagene, on the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUPHRATES">Euphrates</a> (Pliny).—A sixth of Lydia Tralles, so called (Pliny).—A seventh, of Margiana (Strabo, Pliny, Ptolemy), on the river Margus, taking its name from Antiochus, son of Seleucus, who rebuilt it, and walled it round, being before called <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>, from from Alexander the founder, and surnamed Syria; in compass seventy stadia; whither Orodus carried the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, after the defeat of Crassus (Pliny).—An eighth, in Mesopotamia, on the lake Calirhoe, the old name of Edessa (Pliny).—A ninth Antiochia, on the river Mygdonius, in Mesopotamia, situated at the foot of Mount Masius, and is the same with Nisibis (Strabo, Plutarch). It was the bulwark and frontier town of the Romans against the Parthians and Persians, till given up to the Persians, by Jovinian, by an ignominious peace (Ammian, Eutropius).—A tenth Antiochia, was that situated in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of Pisidia (Luke, Ptolemy, Strabo): it was a Roman colony, with the appellation Caesarea. There is an Antiochia at Mount Taurus, mentioned by Ptolemy, but by no other author. ANTIOCHIAN <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a> or Academy, a name given to the fifth academy, or branch of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACADEMIES">Academies</a>. It took the denomination from its being founded by Antiochus, a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> with Cicero.—The Antiochian academy succeeded the Philonian. As to point of doctrine, the philosophers of this sect appear to have restored that of the ancient academy, except that in the article of the criterion of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>. Antiochus was really a Stoic, and only nominally an Academic. Antiochian Epoch, a method of computing <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCLAMATION">proclamation</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> granted the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Antioch about the time of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHARSALIA">Pharsalia</a>.

ANTIOCHUS

Pages 481-481

the name of several kings of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>. See that article. Antiochus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASCALON">Ascalon</a>, a celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of Philo of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LARISSA">Larissa</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of Cicero, and the friend of Lucullus and Brutus. He was founder of a fifth academy: but, instead of attacking other sects, he set himself <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to reconcile them together, particularly the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of the Stoics with that of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> academy.

ANTIOPE

Pages 481-481

in fabulous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, the wife of Licus, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Thebes, who, being deflowered by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> in the form of a satyr, brought forth Amphion and Zethus.—Another Antiope was <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMAZONS">Amazons</a>; and, with the assistance of the Scythians, invaded the Athenians; and was vanquished by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THESEUS">Theseus</a>. ANTIPÆDOBAPTISTS, (derived from ἀντι, against, παιδί, child, and βαπτίζω, baptize, whence βαπτιστής), is a distinguishing denomination given to those who object to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INFANTS">infants</a>; because they say infants are incapable of being instructed, and of making that profession of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> which entitles them to this ordinance, and an admission into <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANABAPTISTS">Anabaptists</a> and Baptists.

ANTIPAROS

Pages 481-484

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the Archipelago, opposite to Paros, from which it is separated by a strait about <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> miles over. It is the Olearies <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Oliaros, mentioned by Strabo, Pliny, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>, Ovid, &c.; and was, according to Heracles Ponticus, as quoted by Stephanus, first peopled by a Phoenician colony from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIDON">Sidon</a>. According to Mr Tournefort's account, it is about 16 miles in circumference, produces a little wine and cotton, with as much corn as is necessary for the maintenance of 60 or 70 families, who live together in a village at one end of the island, and are mostly Maltese and French corsairs. The island is remarkable for a subterraneous cavern or grotto, accounted one of the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> curiosities in the world. It was first discovered in the last century by one Magni an Italian traveller, who has given us the following account: "Having been informed (says he) by the natives of Paros, that in the little island of Antiparos, which lies about two miles from the former, a gigantic statue was to be seen at the mouth of a cavern in that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, it was resolved that we (the French <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a> and himself) should pay it a visit. In pursuance of this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a>, after we had landed on the island, and walked about four miles through the midst of beautiful plains and sloping woodlands, we at length came to a little hill, in the side of which yawned a most horrid cavern, that, with its gloom, at first struck us with terror, and almost repressed curiosity. Recovering the first surprise, however, we entered boldly; and had not proceeded above 20 paces, when the supposed statue of the giant presented itself to our view. We quickly perceived, that what the ignorant natives had been terrified at as a giant, was nothing more than a sparry concretion, formed by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> dropping from the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> of the cave, and by degrees hardening into a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> that their fears had formed into a monster. Incited by this extraordinary appearance, we were induced to proceed still further, in quest of new adventures in this subterranean abode. As we proceeded, new wonders offered themselves; the spars, formed into trees and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHRUBS">shrubs</a>, presented a kind of petrified <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROVE">grove</a>; some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, some green; and all receding in due <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol8.html#article-PERSPECTIVE">perspective</a>. They struck us with the more amazement, as we knew them to be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> productions of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, who, hitherto in solitude, had, in her playful moments, dressed the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> for her own amusement. "But we had as yet seen but a few of the wonders of the place, and we were introduced as yet only into the portico of this amazing temple. In one corner of this half-illuminated recess, there appeared an opening of about three feet wide, which seemed to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> to a place totally dark, and that one of the natives assured us contained nothing more than a reservoir of water. Upon this we tried, by throwing <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, which rumbling along the sides of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> seemed at last quashed in a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a> of water. In order, however, to be more certain, we sent in a Levantine mariner, who, by the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> of a good reward, with a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAMBEAU">flambeau</a> in his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, ventured into this narrow aperture. After continuing within it for about a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>, he returned, carrying some beautiful pieces of white <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAR">spar</a> in his hand, which art could neither imitate nor equal. Upon being informed by him that the place was full of these beautiful incrustations, I ventured in once more with him, for about 50 paces, anxiously and cautiously descending by a steep and dangerous way. Finding, however, that we came to a precipice which led into a spacious <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMPHITHEATRE">amphitheatre</a>, if I may so call it, still deeper than any other <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a>, we returned; and being provided with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LADDER">ladder</a>, flambeaux, and other things to expedite our descent, our whole <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> by man, ventured into the same opening, and, descending one after another, we at last <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> ourselves all together in the most magnificent part of the cavern. "Our candles being now all lighted up, and the whole place completely illuminated, never could the eye be presented with a more glittering or a more magnifi- cent scene. The roof all hung with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> icicles, transparent as glass, yet solid as marble. The eye could scarce reach the lofty and noble ceiling; the sides were regularly formed with spars; and the whole presented the idea of a magnificent <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>, illuminated with an immense profusion of lights. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a> consisted of solid marble; and in several places, magnificent columns, thrones, altars, and other objects, appeared, as if nature had designed to mock the curiosities of art. Our voices, upon speaking or singing, were redoubled to an astonishing loudness; and upon the firing of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUN">gun</a>, the noise and reverberations were almost deafening. In the midst of this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> amphitheatre rose a concretion of about 15 feet <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, that, in some <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, resembled an altar; from which, taking the hint, we caused <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASS">mass</a> to be celebrated there. The beautiful columns that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> up round the altar, appeared like candlesticks; and many other natural objects represented the customary ornaments of this sacrament. "Below even this spacious grotto, there seemed another cavern; down which I ventured with my former mariner, and descended about 50 paces by means of a rope. I at last arrived at a small spot of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> ground, where the bottom appeared different from that of the amphitheatre, being composed of soft clay, yielding to the pressure, and in which I thrust a stick to about six feet deep. In this, however, as above, numbers of the most beautiful crystals were formed; one of which, particularly resembled a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>. Upon our egress from this amazing cavern, we perceived a Greek inscription upon a rock at the mouth; but so obliterated by time, that we could not read it. It seemed to import, that one Antipater, in the time of Alexander, had come thither; but whether he penetrated into the depths of the cavern, he does not think fit to inform us." From this account Mr Tournefort's differs considerably. Mr Magni mentions only one descent or precipice from the entry of the cave to the grotto, or most magnificent part; Mr Tournefort says that there were many very dangerous precipices and rugged ways, through which they were obliged to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> sometimes on their back, and sometimes on their belly, but gives no particular account of his journey till he come to the grand cavern. This indeed he describes very pompously; but as by it he evidently wants to support a favourite <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a>, namely, the vegetation of stones, perhaps the particulars are not altogether to be depended upon. He informs us, that, at the entry into the cavern, he met with a Greek inscription almost effaced, containing a good <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of proper names; and that there was a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a> among the inhabitants, that these were the names of those who had conspired against Alexander the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>, and having missed their aim, had taken refuge in this grotto. The most particular account, however, of this famous grotto that hath hitherto been published, appeared in the British <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGAZINE">Magazine</a>, in a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> signed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> Saunders, and dated Feb. 24. 1746-7; which, as it is very particular, and seems to bear sufficient marks of authenticity, we shall here insert. "Its entrance lies in the side of a rock, about two miles from the seashore; and is a spacious and very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a>, formed of rough craggy rocks, overhung with brambles and a great many climbing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, that give it a gloominess which is very awful and agreeable. Our surgeon, myself, and four passengers, attended by six guides Antiperos, with lighted torches, entered this cavern about eight o'clock in the morning in the middle of August last. We had not gone 20 yards in this cavity when we lost all sight of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>: but our guides going before us with light, we entered into a low narrow kind of alley, surrounded every way with stones all glittering like diamonds by the light of our torches; the whole being covered and lined throughout with small crystals, which gave a thousand various colours by their different reflections. The alley grows lower and narrower as one goes on, till at length one can scarce get along it. At the end of this passage we were each of us presented with a rope, to tie about our middles; which when we had done, our guides led us to the brink of a most horrible precipice. The descent into this was quite steep, and the place all dark and gloomy. We could see nothing, in short, but some of our guides with torches in a miserable dark place, at a vast distance below us. The dreadful depth of this place, and the horror of the descent through a miserable darkness into it, made me look back to the lane of diamonds, if I may so call it, through which we had <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> passed; and I could not but think I was leaving heaven, to descend into the infernal regions. The hope of something fine at my journey's end tempted me, however, to trust myself to the rope and my guides at the top, to let myself down. After about two minutes dangling in this posture, not without much pain as well as terror, I found myself safe, however, at the bottom; and our friends all soon followed the example. When we had congratulated here with one another on our safe descent; I was inquiring where the grotto, as they called it, was. Our guides, shaking their heads, told us, we had a great way to that yet: and led us forward about 30 yards under a roof of ragged rocks, in a scene of terrible darkness, and at a vast depth from the surface of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, to the brink of another precipice much deeper and more terrible than the former. Two of the guides went down here with their torches first; and by their light we could see, that this passage was not so perpendicular indeed as the other, but lay in a very steep slant, with a very slippery rock for the bottom; vast pieces of rough rugged rocks jutting out in many places on the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> hand, in the descent, and forcing the guides sometimes to climb over, sometimes to creep under them, and sometimes to round them; and on the left, a thousand dark caverns, like so many monstrous <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WELLS">wells</a>, ready, if a foot should slip, to swallow them up for ever. We stood on the edge to see these people with their lights descend before us; and were amazed and terrified to see them continue descending till they seemed at a monstrous and most frightful depth. When they were at the bottom, however, they hollaed to us; and we, trembling and quaking, began to descend after them. We had not gone 30 feet down, when we came to a place where the rock was perfectly perpendicular; and a vast cavern seemed to open its mouth to swallow us up on one side, while a wall of rugged rock threatened to tear us to pieces on the other. I was quite disheartened at this terrible prospect, and declared I would go back; but our guides assured us there was no danger; and the rest of the company resolving to see the bottom now they were come so far, I would not leave them: so on we went to a corner where there Antiparos there was placed an old slippery and rotten ladder, which hung down <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to the rock; and down this, one after another, we at length all descended. When we had got to the bottom of this, we found ourselves at the entrance of another passage, which was terrible enough indeed; but in this there was not wanting something of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>. This was a wide and gradual descent; at the entrance of which one of our guides seated himself on his breech, and began to slide down, telling us we must do the same. We could discover, by the light of his torch, that this passage was one of the noblest vaults in the world. It is about <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> feet high, seven wide, and has for its bottom a fine green glossy marble. The walls and arch of the roof of this being as smooth and even in most places as if wrought by art, and made of a fine glistening <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> and white <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANITE">granite</a>, supported here and there with columns of a deep blood-red shining porphyry, made, with the reflection of the lights, an appearance not to be conceived. This passage is at least 40 yards <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>; and of so steep a descent, that one has enough to do, when seated on one's breech not to descend too quickly. Our guides, that we kept with us, could here keep on each side of us; and, what with the prodigious <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a> and beauty of the place, our easy travelling through it, and the diversion of our now and then running over one another whether we would or not; this was much the pleasantest part of our journey. When we had entered this passage, I imagined we should at the bottom join the two guides we had first set down; but alas! when we were got there we found ourselves only at the mouth of another precipice, down which we descended by a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> ladder not much better than the former. I could have admired this place also, would my terror have suffered me; but the dread of falling, kept all my thoughts employed during my descent. I could not but observe, however, as my companions were coming down after me, that the wall, if I may so call it, which the ladder hung by, was one mass of blood-red marble, covered with white sprigs of rock crystal as long as my finger, and making, with the glow of the purple from behind, one <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> immense sheet of amethysts. From the foot of this ladder we slid on our bellies through another shallow vault of polished green and white marble, about 20 feet; and at the bottom of this joined our guides. Here we all got together once again, and drank some rum, to give us courage before we proceeded any farther. After this short refreshment, we proceeded by a strait, but somewhat slanting passage, of a rough, hard, and somewhat coarse <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, full of a thousand strange figures of snakes rolled round, and looking as if alive; but in reality as <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a> and hard as the rest of the stone, and nothing but some of the stone itself in that shape. We walked pretty easily along this descent for near 200 yards; where we saw two pillars seemingly made to support the roof from falling in; but in reality it was no such thing; for they were very brittle, and made of a fine glittering <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> marble. When we had passed these about 200 yards, we found ourselves at the brink of another very terrible precipice: but this our guides assured us was the last; and there being a very good ladder to go down by, we readily ventured. At the bottom of this steep wall, as I may call it, we found ourselves for some way upon plain even ground; but, after about 40 yards walking, were presented by our guides with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a> again; which Antiparos, we fastened about our middles, though not to be swung down by, but only for fear of danger, as there are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a> and deep waters all the way from hence on the left hand. With this caution, however, we entered the last alley; and horrible <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> it was indeed to get through it. All was perfectly horrid and dismal here. The sides and roof of the passage were all of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> stone; and the rocks in our way were in some places so steep, that we were forced to <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> all along on our backs, and slide down; and so rough, that they cut our clothes, and bruised us miserably in passing. Over our heads, there was nothing but ragged black rocks, some of them looking as if they were every moment ready to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> in upon us; and, on our left <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, the light of our guides torches shewed us continually the surfaces of dirty and miserably looking lakes of water. If I had heartily repented of my expedition often before, here I assure you I was all in a cold sweat, and fairly gave myself over for lost; heartily cursing all the travellers that had written of this place, that they had described it so as to tempt people to see it, and never told us of the horrors that lay in the way. In the midst of all these reflections, and in the very dismallest part of all the cavern, on a sudden we had lost four of our six guides. What was my terror on this sight! The place was a thousand times darker and more terrible for want of their torches; and I expected no other but every moment to follow them into some of these lakes, into which I doubted not but they were fallen. The remaining two guides said all they could indeed, to cheer us up; and told us we should see the other four again soon, and that we were near the end of our journey. I do not know what effect this might have upon the rest of my companions; but I assure you I believed no part of the speech but the last, which I expected every moment to find fulfilled in some pond or precipice. Our passage was by this time become very narrow, and we were obliged to crawl on all-fours over rugged rocks; when in an instant, and in the midst of these melancholy apprehensions, I heard a little hissing noise, and saw myself in utter, and not to be described, darkness. Our guides called indeed cheerfully to us, and told us that they had accidentally dropped their torches into a puddle of water, but we should soon come to the rest of them, and they would light them again; and told us there was no danger, and we had nothing to do but to crawl forward. I cannot say but I was amazed at the courage of these people; who were in a place where, I thought, four of them had already perished, and from whence we could none of us ever escape; and determined to lie down and die where I was. Words cannot describe the horror or the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> darkness of the place. One of our guides, however, perceiving that I did not advance, came up to me, and clapping his hand firmly over my eyes, dragged me a few paces forward. While I was in this strange condition, expecting every moment <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> in a thousand shapes, and trembling to think what the guide meant by this rough proceeding, he lifted me at once over a great stone, set me down on my feet, and took his hand from before my eyes. What words can describe at that instant my astonishment and transport! Instead of darkness and despair, all was splendour and magnificence before me: our guides all appeared about us: the place was illuminated by 50 torches. Antiparos, torches, and the guides all welcomed me into the grotto of Antiparos. The four that were first missing, I now found had only given us the slip, to get the torches lighted up before we came; and the other two had put out their lights on purpose, to make us enter out of utter darkness into this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PAVILION">pavilion</a> of splendour and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a>. I am now come to the proper business of this letter: which was to describe this grotto. But I must confess to you that words cannot do it. The amazing beauties of the place, the eye that sees them only can conceive. The best account I can give you, however, pray accept of. "The people told us, the depth of this place was 485 yards; the grotto, in which we now were, is a cavern of 120 yards wide, and 113 long, and seems about 60 yards high in most places. These <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> differ something from the accounts travellers in general give us; but you may depend upon them as exact, for I took them with my own hand. Imagine then with yourself, an immense arch like this, almost all over lined with fine and bright crystallized white marble, and illuminated with 50 torches; and you <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> then have some faint idea of the place I had the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> to spend three hours in. This, however, is but a faint <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of its beauties. The roof, which is a fine vaulted arch, is hung all over with icicles of white shining marble, some of them ten feet long, and as thick as one's middle at the root; and among these hang a thousand festoons of leaves and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, of the same substance; but so very glittering, that there is no <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> to look up at them. The sides of the arch are planted with seeming trees of the same white marble, rising in rows one above another, and often enclosing the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of the icicles. From these trees there are also hung festoons, tied as it were from one to another in vast quantities; and in some places among them there seem <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> of marble winding through them in a thousand meanders. All these things are only made, in a long course of years, from the dropping of water, but really look like trees and brooks turned to marble. The floor we trod upon was rough and uneven, with crystals of all colours growing irregularly out of it, red, blue, green, and some of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> yellow. These were all shaped like pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALTPETRE">saltpetre</a>; but so hard, that they cut our shoes; among these, here and there, are placed icicles of the same white shining marble with those above, and seeming to have fallen down from the roof and fixed there; only the big end of these is to the floor. To all these our guides had tied torches, two or three to a pillar, and kept continually <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEATING">beating</a> them, to make them burn bright. You may guess what a glare of splendour and beauty must be the effect of this illumination, among such rocks and columns of marble. All round the lower part of the sides of the arch are a thousand white masses of marble, in the shape of oak trees. Mr Tournefort compares them to cauliflowers, but I should as soon compare them to toadstools. In short, they are large enough to enclose, in many places, a piece of ground big enough for a bedchamber. One of these chambers has a fair white curtain, whiter than satin, of the same marble, stretched all over the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a> of it. In this we all cut our names, and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">date</a> of the year, as a great many people have done before us. In a course of years afterwards, the stone blisters out like this white marble over the letters. Mr Tournefort thinks the rock grows like oaks or apple trees for this reason; but I remember I saw some of the finest cockle and muscle shells, in the rock thereabouts, that ever I saw in my <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. I wonder whether he thinks they grow there too. Besides, if this rock grows so fast, the cavern ought to be all grown up by this time; and yet, according to his measures and mine, the cavern seems on the other hand to be turned larger since. Indeed, all that I can gather from his account of this glorious place is, that he had drank a bottle or two too much before he went down into it."

ANTIPAS HEROD

Pages 484-484
or HEROD-ANTIPAS, the son of Herod the Great, by one of his wives called Cleopatra, a native of Jerusalem. Herod the Great, in his first will, appointed Antipas his successor in the kingdom; but afterwards, altering that will, he named his son Archelaus his successor, giving to Antipas the title only of tetrarch of Galilee and Persea. Antipas took a great deal of pains in adorning and fortifying the principal places of his dominions. He married the daughter of Aretas king of Arabia; whom he divorced about the year of Christ 33, to marry his sister-in-law Herodias, wife to his brother Phillip, who was still living. St John the Baptist exclaiming continually against this incest, was taken into custody by order of Antipas, and imprisoned in the castle of Macherus, (Mat. xiv. 3, 4. Mark i. 14. vi. 17, 18. Luke iii. 19, 20.) Josephus says, that Antipas caused St John to be laid hold of, because he drew too great a concourse of people after him; and that he was afraid lest he should make use of the authority which he had acquired over the minds and affections of the people, to induce them to revolt. But the evangelists, who were better informed than Josephus, as being eye witnesses of what passed, and acquainted in a particular manner with St John and his disciples, assure us that the true reason of imprisoning St John was the aversion which Herod and Herodias had conceived against him for the liberty he had used in censuring their scandalous marriage. The virtue and holiness of St John were such, that even Herod feared and respected him; but his passion for Herodias had prevailed with him to have killed that prophet, had he not been restrained by his apprehensions of the people, who esteemed John the Baptist as a prophet. (Mat. xiv. 5, 6.) One day, however, while the king was celebrating the festival of his birth, with the principal persons of his court, the daughter of Herodias danced before him; and pleased him so well, that he promised with an oath to give her whatever she should ask of him. By her mother's advice she asked the head of John the Baptist: upon which the king commanded John to be beheaded in prison, and the head to be given her. Aretas, king of Arabia, to revenge the affront which Herod had offered to his daughter, declared war against him, and overcame him in a very obstinate engagement. Herod being afterwards detected as a party in Sejanus's conspiracy, was banished by the emperor Caius to Lyons in Gaul; whither Herodias accompanied him. This Antipas is the Herod who, being at Jerusalem at the time of our Saviour's passion (Luke xxiii. 11.), ridiculed him, by dressing him in a white robe, and directing him to be conducted back to Pilate, as a mock king, whose ambition gave him no umbrage. The time when Antipas died is not known; however, it is certain

ANTIPATER

Pages 485-485

Cælius, a Roman historian, who wrote a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the Punic <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, much valued by Cicero. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Adrian preferred him to Sallust. ANTIPATER of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIDON">Sidon</a>, a Stoic <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, and likewise a poet, commended by Cicero and Seneca: he flourished about the 171st Olympiad. We have several of his epigrams in the Anthologia.

ANTIPATHY

Pages 485-486

in Physiology, is formed from the two Greek words, ἀντί contrary, and πάθος <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>. Literally taken, the word signifies incompatibility: but for the most <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> antipathy is not used to signify such incompatibilities as are merely physical; it is reserved to express the aversion which an animated <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> sensitive being feels at the real or ideal presence of particular objects. In this point of view, which is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> in which we at present consider the term, antipathy, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, signifies "a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> horror and detestation, an insuperable hatred, an involuntary aversion, which a sensitive being feels for some other object, whatever it is, though the person who feels this abhorrence is entirely ignorant of its cause, and can by no means account for it. Such is, they say, the natural and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECIPROCAL">reciprocal</a> hostility between the salamander and the tortoise; between the toad and the weasel; or between sheep and wolves. Such is, the invincible aversion of particular persons against cats, mice, spiders, &c.: a prepossession which is sometimes so violent, as to make them faint at the sight of these animals. Of these and a thousand other antipathies, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> naturalists, the schoolmen, and the vulgar, form so many legends; and relate them as certain facts, that they may demand an explication of them from the philosophers. But these sages begin with investigating whether such antipathies actually exist or not. To explore the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> without <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a>, we shall find it necessary to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSTRACT">abstract</a> from the subjects of this disquisition, 1. All such antipathies as are not ascertained; as that which is supposed to be felt by hens at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> of a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HARP">harp</a> whose strings are made of a fox's bowels, between the salamander and tortoise, and between the weasel and the toad. Nothing is less confirmed, or rather nothing is more false, than these facts, with which vulgar credulity and astonishment are amused and actuated: and though some of these antipathies should be ascertained, this would be no <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> that the animals which feel them are not acquainted with their causes, according to their <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> and proportion of knowledge; in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be no longer the antipathy which we have defined. 2. We must abstract those antipathies which can be extinguished or resumed at <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>; those fictitious aversions, which certain persons feel, or pretend to feel, with affected <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIRS">airs</a>, that they may appear more precise and finical, or singularly and prodigiously elegant; that they may seem to have qualities so exquisitely fine, as require to be treated with peculiar delicacy. One who bestows any <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> on the subject, would be astonished to find how many of these chimerical aversions there are, which are pretended, and passed upon the world by those who affect them as natural and unconquerable. 3. When we abstract those aversions the causes of which are known and evident; we shall be surprised after our deduction of those pretended antipathies from the general sum, how small, how inconsiderable, is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of those which are conformable to our <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-DEFINITION">definition</a>. Will any one pretend to call by the name of antipathy, those real, innate, and incontestable aversions which prevail between sheep and wolves? Their cause is obvious; the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WOLF">wolf</a> devours the sheep, and subsists upon his victims; and every animal naturally flies with terror from pain or destruction; sheep ought therefore to regard wolves with horror, which for their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NUTRITION">nutrition</a> tear and mangle the unresisting prey. From principles similar to this, arises that aversion which numbers of people feel against <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERPENTS">serpents</a>; against small animals, such as reptiles in general, and the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of insects. During the credulous and susceptible <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of infancy, pains have been taken to impress on our minds the frightful idea that they are venomous; that their bite is mortal; that their sting is dangerous, productive of tormenting inflammations or tumours, and sometimes fatal: they have been represented to us as ugly and sordid; as being, for that reason, pernicious to those who touch them; as poisoning those who have the misfortune to swallow them. These horrible prepossessions are industriously inculcated from our infancy; they are sometimes attended and supported by dismal tales, which are greedily imbibed, and indelibly engraved on our memories. It has been taught us both by precept and example, when others at their approach have assumed in our view the appearance of detestation and even of terror, that we should fly from them, that we should not touch them. Is it then wonderful (<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> our false impressions as to this subject have been corrected neither by future reflections nor experiments) that we should entertain, during our whole lives, an aversion for these objects, even when we have forgot the admonitions, the conversations, and examples, which have taught us to believe and apprehend them as noxious beings? and in proportion to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSIBILITY">sensibility</a> of our frame, in proportion as our nerves are irritable, our emotions at the sight of what we fear will be more violent, especially if they anticipate Antipathy, our <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPECTATION">expectation</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEIZE">seize</a> us unprepared, though our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> of what we have to fear from them are the most confused and indistinct imaginable. To explain these facts, is it necessary to fly to the exploded subterfuge of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OCCULT">occult</a> qualities inherent in bodies, to latent relations productive of antipathies, of which no person could ever form an idea? It is often sufficient to influence a person who had formerly no aversion for an object, if he lives with some other associate who gives himself up to such capricious panics; the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> is insensibly contracted to be agitated with disagreeable emotions at the presence of an object which had been formerly beheld with indifference and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a> blood. I was acquainted (says the author of the article Antipathy in the French Encyclopédie) with a person of a very sound understanding, whom <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a> by no means terrified; nay, to whom the spectacle appeared magnificent and the sound majestic: yet to a mind thus seemingly fortified against the infectious terror, no more was necessary than spending the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> with a friend in whom the appearance of lightning excited the strongest emotions, and whom the remotest clap of thunder affected with extravagant paroxysms, to become timid in excess at the approach of thunder; nor could he ever afterwards surmount the fear which it inspired. The frightful stories of dogs and cats, which have killed their masters, or which have given them mortal wounds, are more than sufficient to inspire a timorous person with aversion against these animals; and if the olfactory nerves of such a person be delicate, he will immediately discover the smell of them in a chamber: disturbed by the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPREHENSION">apprehension</a> which these effluvia excite in his mind, he gives himself up to the most violent uneasiness, which is tranquillized when he is assured that the animal is no longer in the room. If by chance, in the search which is made to calm the uneasiness of this timorous person, one of these creatures should at last be discovered, every one presently exclaims, A miracle; and admits the reality of antipathies into his creed; whilst all this is nothing but the effect of a childish fear, founded on certain confused and exaggerated ideas of the hazard which one may run with these animals. The antipathy which some people entertain against eels, though they are eaten by others with pleasure, arises from nothing but the fear of serpents, to which these fishes are in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> similar. There are likewise other antipathies which do not originate in the imagination, but arise from some natural incongruity; such as we often remark in children, for particular kinds of victuals, with which their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> is not offended, but which their stomachs cannot digest, and which are therefore disgorged as soon as swallowed. To what then are those antipathies of which we have heard so much reducible? Either to legendary tales; or to aversions against objects which we believe dangerous; or to a childish terror of imaginary perils; or to a disrelish, of which the cause is disguised; or to a ridiculous affectation of delicacy; or to an infirmity of the stomach; in a word, to a real or pretended reluctance for things which are either invested, or supposed to be invested, with qualities hurtful to us. Too much care cannot be taken in preventing, or regulating, the antipathies of children; in familiarizing them with objects of every kind; in discovering to them, without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMOTION">emotion</a>, such as are dangerous; in teaching them the means of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> and security, or the methods of escaping their noxious influence: and, when the rational powers are matured by <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, in reflecting on the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of those objects which we fear, in ascertaining what has been told concerning their qualities, or in vigorously operating upon our own dispositions to overcome those vain repugnancies which we may feel. See Sympathy, which is the opposite of Antipathy. Antipathy, in Ethics, hatred, aversion, repugnancy. Hatred is entertained against persons; aversion, and antipathy indiscriminately, against persons or things; and repugnancy against actions alone. Hatred is more voluntary than aversion, antipathy, or repugnancy. These last have greater <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFFINITY">affinity</a> with the animal <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>. The causes of antipathy are less known than those of aversion. Repugnancy is less permanent than either the one or the other. We hate a vicious character; we feel aversion to its exertions: we are affected with antipathy for certain persons at first sight; there are some affairs which we transact with repugnancy.—Hatred calumniates; aversion keeps us at a distance from certain persons: antipathy makes us detest them; repugnancy hinders us from imitating them. Antipatris (Acts xxiii. 31), a town of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALESTINE">Palestine</a>, anciently called Caphar Saba, according to Josephus, but named Antipatris by Herod the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of his father Antipater. It was situated in a pleasant valley near the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, in the way from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a> to Caesarea. Josephus places it at about the distance of seventeen miles from Joppa. Antipelargia, among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>, whereby children are obliged to furnish necessaries to their aged parents. The ciconia, or stork, is a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIRD">bird</a> famous for the care it takes of its parents when grown old. Hence, in some Latin writers, this is rendered lex ciconiaria, or the stork's law. Antiphonary, Antiphonarium, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> book, which contained all the invitatories, responsories, collects, and whatever else was sung or said in the choir, except the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LESSONS">lessons</a>. This is otherwise called responsorium, from the responses therein contained. The author of the Roman antiphony was Pope Gregory the Great. We also find mention of nocturnal and diurnal antiphonaries, for the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the daily and nightly offices; summer and winter antiphonaries; also antiphonaries for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> churches, &c. By the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCIAL">provincial</a> constitutions of Archbishop Winchelsey, made at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MERTON">Merton</a>, A.D. 1305, it is required that one of these should be found in every <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> within the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a>. The use of these, and many other popish books, was forbid by the 3d and 4th of Edward VI. c. 10. Antiphony, the answer made by one choir to another, when the psalm or anthem is sung between two.
