ANTIPHONY SOMETIMES

Pages 486-488

y sometimes denotes a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of psalmody, wherein the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a> being divided into two parts, repeat the psalms, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> for verse, alternately. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, antiphony stands contradistinguished from symphony, where the whole congregation sings together. Antiphony differs from responsorium, because in this latter the verse is only spoken by one person, where- Antiphony as in the former, the verses are sung by the two choirs alternately. The original of antiphonal singing in the western churches is referred to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of St <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBROSE">Ambrose</a>, about the year 374. That father is said to have first introduced it into the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of the eastern church, where it appears to be of greater antiquity, though as to the time of its <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a>, authors are not agreed; it was most probably introduced at Antioch, between the year of Christ 347 and 356. Antiphony is also used to denote the words given out at the beginning of the psalm, to which both the choirs are to accommodate their singing. Antiphony, in a more <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> sense, denotes a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> made of several verses extracted out of different psalms, adapted to express the mystery solemnized on the occasion. Antipodes, in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a name given to those inhabitants of the globe that live diametrically opposite to each other. The word is Greek, and compounded of αντί, opposite, and πόδες, a foot; because their feet are opposite to each other. The antipodes <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> under opposite meridians and opposite parallels; in the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of latitude, but of opposite denominations, one being <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> and the other south. They have nearly the same degree of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, days and nights of equal length, but in opposite seasons. It is noon to one when midnight to the other; and the longest <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> with the one is the shortest with the other. <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a> is esteemed the first who thought it possible that the antipodes subsisted, and is looked upon as the inventor of the word. As this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> apprehended the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> to be spherical, he had only one step to make to conclude the existence of the antipodes. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, in general, treated this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> with the highest contempt; never being able to conceive how men and trees could subsist suspended in the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> with their feet upwards, for so they apprehended they must be in the other hemisphere. They never reflected that these terms upwards and downwards are merely relative; and signify only nearer to, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> farther from, the centre of the earth, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> centre to which all heavy bodies gravitate; and that, therefore, our antipodes have not their feet upwards and head downwards any more than ourselves; because they, like us, have their feet nearer the centre of the earth, and their heads farther from it. To have the head downwards and feet upwards, is to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> the body in a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of gravity tending from the feet to the head: but this cannot be supposed with regard to the antipodes; for they, like us, tend toward the centre of the earth, in a direction from head to foot. Antipolis, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> Geography, now <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTIBES">Antibes</a>, on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Provence, a colony of the Massilians, near the river Verus, in Gallia Narbonensis (Livy), three leagues to the west of Nice. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 7° 9'. N. Lat. 43° 42'. Antiquary, among Roman lawyers, properly denotes the rejecting of a new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>, or refusing to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> it. In which sense, antiquating differs from abrogating; as the latter imports the annulling an old law, the former the rejecting a new one. Antiquary is also used for a law's growing obsolete, or into disuse, either by <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> or non-observance. Antiquarii, a name given to copiers of old Antiquarii books. After the decline of learning among the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, and when many <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> houses were erected, learning was chiefly in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the clergy; the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of whom were regulars, and lived in monasteries. In these houses were many industrious men who were continually employed in making new copies of old books, either for the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> or for their own emolument. These <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> monks were distinguished by the name of Antiquarii. They deprived the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> librarii, or common scriptores, of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of their business, so that these found it difficult to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> a subsistence for themselves and families. This put them upon finding out more expeditious methods of transcribing books. They formed the letters smaller, and made use of more jugations and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABBREVIATIONS">abbreviations</a> than had been usual. They proceeded in this manner till the letters became exceedingly small; the abbreviations were very numerous, and extremely difficult to be read. This in some <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> accounts for the great variety of hands in the species of writing called Modern Gothic. When a number of copies were to be made of the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, it was usual to employ several persons at the same time in writing it; each person, except him who wrote the first skin, began where his fellow was to leave off. Antiquary, a person who studies and searches after monuments and remains of antiquity; as old medals, books, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a>, sculptures, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a>; and, in general, all curious pieces that may afford any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> into antiquity. In the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> cities of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, there were persons of distinction called antiquaries, whose business it was to show strangers the antiquities of the place, to explain the ancient inscriptions, and to give them all the assistance they could in this way of learning.—Pausanias calls these antiquaries Εγκύρων. The Sicilians call them mystagogi. There was an ancient <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of antiquaries erected in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a> by Ollamh Fodhla, 700 years before Christ, for composing a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>: And to this, say the Irish historians, it is owing that the history and antiquities of that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> may be traced back beyond those of most other nations. There is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> of antiquaries in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, and another in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, incorporated by the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a>. See Society. Antiquary is also used by ancient writers for the keeper of the antiquarium or cabinet of antiquities. The officer is otherwise called archivota, or antiquary of a king, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, a state or the like. Henry VIII. gave John Leland the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of his antiquary; a title which, says the author of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, nobody ever enjoyed besides himself. But the restriction, we suppose, was only intended to be understood in respect of the kings of England. M. Schott, we find, had the title of antiquary to the king of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>; P. Pedruzzi, that of antiquary of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Parma; M. Galland resided some time in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> under the title of antiquary of the king of France.—The university of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a> have still their antiquary, under the denomination of custos archivorum.—The kings of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a> have been at great expenses in order to illustrate the antiquity of their country, having established an academy of antiquaries with this single view.—The office Antiquary of the ancient Irish antiquaries was to preserve the genealogies of the kings of Ireland, to correct the regal tables of succession, and deliver <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the pedigree of every collateral branch of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> family.

ANTIQUE

Pages 488-488

in a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, something that is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>; but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> is chiefly used by sculptors, painters, and architects, to denote such pieces of their different arts as were made by the ancient Greeks and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>. Thus we say, an antique bust, an antique statue, &c. Antique is something contradistinguished from ancient, which signifies a less <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of antiquity. Thus antique <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a> is frequently distinguished from ancient architecture.

ANTIQUITIES

Pages 488-489

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> implying all testimonies, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> authentic accounts, that have come <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to us, of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> nations. <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACON">Bacon</a> calls antiquities the wrecks of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, or such particulars as industrious and learned persons have collected from genealogies, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a>, monuments, coins, names, etymologies, archives, instruments, fragments of history, &c. Antiquities form a very extensive science, including "an historical knowledge of the edifices, magistrates, offices, habiliments, manners, customs, ceremonies, worship, and other objects worthy of curiosity, of all the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> ancient nations of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>." This science is not a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> curiosity, but is indispensable to the theologian; who ought to be thoroughly acquainted with the antiquities of the Jews, to enable him properly to explain numberless <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> in the Old and New Testaments; to the lawyer, who, without the knowledge of the antiquities of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a> and Rome, can never well understand and properly apply the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the Roman laws; to the physician and the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, that they may have a complete knowledge of the history and principles of the physic and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>; to the critic, that he may be able to understand and interpret ancient authors; to the orator and poet; who <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be thereby enabled to ornament their writings with numberless images, allusions, comparisons, &c. Antiquities are divided into sacred and profane, into public and private, universal and particular, &c. It is true, that the antiquaries (especially such as are infected with a spirit of pedantry, and the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of these is <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a>) frequently carry their inquiries too far, and employ themselves in laborious researches after learned trifles; but the abuse of a science ought never to make us neglect the applying it to rational and useful purposes. Many antiquaries also restrain their learned labours to the eclaircissement of the antiquities of Greece and Rome: but this field is far too confined, and by no means contains the whole of this science, seeing it properly includes the antiquities of the Jews, Egyptians, Persians, Phoenicians, Carthaginians, Hetruscans, Germans, and, in general, all those principal nations mentioned in ancient history: so far as any accounts of them are come down to us. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> to the general subjects above-mentioned we add the particular <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of antiques, of the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASS">bass</a>-reliefs, and the precious relics of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, camaieus, medals, &c. it is easy to conceive that antiquities form a science very extensive and very complicated, and with which only a very small acquaintance could have been attainable by any one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, if our predecessors had not prepared the way for us; if they had not left us such inestimable works as those of Gronovius, Gravius, Montfaucon, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">Count</a> Caylus, Winckelman, the Hebraic antiquities of D. Iken of Bremen, the Grecian antiquities of Brunnings, the Roman antiquities of Nieuport, and especially that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> which is entitled Bibliographia Antiquaria Joh. Alberti Fabricii, professor at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAMBURG">Hamburg</a>, &c. &c. Nor must we here forget that very valuable work, with which our countryman Mr Robert Wood has lately enriched this science, and which is so well known, and so justly esteemed by all true connoisseurs, under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of the Ruins of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALMYRA">Palmyra</a>, and those of Bualbec. It is by this work that we are fully convinced of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a> and magnificence, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> and elegance, of the buildings of the ancients. We here see that the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of these matters is not all owing to the Greeks, but that there were other nations who served them as models. For though many of the edifices of Palmyra are to be attributed to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Aurelian, and to Odenatus and his wife Zenobia, who reigned there about the year 264, yet there are found at the same <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> ruins of buildings that appear to be of far greater antiquity, and that are not less beautiful. The ancient Persepolis is sufficient to prove this assertion. When we duly reflect on all these matters, and especially if we attempt to acquire any knowledge of this science, we shall soon be convinced that it but ill becomes a petit-maitre to laugh at a learned antiquary. The knowledge of those monuments of the ancients, the works of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a>, statuary, graving, painting, &c., which they call antiques, requires a strict <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> with regard to the matter itself on which the art has been exercised; as the wax, clay, wood, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a> of every kind, marble, flint, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRONZE">bronze</a>, and every sort of metal. We should begin by learning on what matter each ancient <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> principally worked, and in which of the fine arts they excelled: For the matter itself, as the different sorts of marble, compositions of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-METALS">metals</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of precious stones, serve frequently to characterize the true antique, and to discover the counterfeit. The connoisseurs pretend also to know, by certain distinct <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> and execution of a work of art, the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> and nation where it was made. They find, moreover, in the invention and execution, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of excellence which <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> artists are not able to imitate. Now, though we ought to allow, in general, the great merit of the ancients in the polite arts, we should not, however, suffer our admiration to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> us into a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLIND">blind</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>. There are pieces of antiquity of every sort, which have come down to us; some that are perfectly excellent: and others so wretched, that the meanest among modern artists would not acknowledge them. The mixture of the good and bad has taken place in all subjects, at all times and in all nations. The misfortune is, that most of our great antiquaries have been so little skilled in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGNING">designing</a> as scarcely to know how to draw a circle with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPASSES">compasses</a>. It is <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a>, therefore, which frequently directs them to give the palm to the ancients, rather than a judgment directed by a knowledge of the art. That character of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> which they find so marvellous in the works of antiquity, is often nothing more than a mere chimera. They pretend that the artists of our days constantly exaggerate their expressions; that a modern <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a> has the appearance of a man distracted with intoxication; that a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a> seems to be animated with the spirit of a fury; and so of the rest. But let them not decide too hastily. Almost all the antique figures are totally void of all spirit of expression; we are forced to guess at their characters. Every <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> expression requires, moreover, to be somewhat exaggerated. A statue or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTRAIT">portrait</a> is an inanimate <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>; and must therefore have a very different effect from one which, being endowed with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, has the muscles constantly in play, and where the continual change of the features, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the eyes, and the looks more or less lively, easily and clearly express the passions and sentiments. Whereas, in a figure, that is the produce of art, the delicate touches, that should express the passions, are lost to the eyes of the spectators: they must therefore be struck by strong bold characters, which can affect them at the first glance of the eye. A very moderate <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a> is sensible, at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, that he is not to give his figures extravagant expressions, or to place them in distorted attitudes.

ANTIRRHINUM

Pages 489-489

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a promontory at the mouth of the Corinthian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>, where it is scarce a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, and where it separates Ætolia from the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PELOPONNESUS">Peloponnesus</a>; so called from its opposite situation to Rhium in Peloponnesus (Pliny): both are now called the Dardanelles of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEPANTO">Lepanto</a>.

ANTISABBATARIANS

Pages 489-489

a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a> who oppose the observance of the Christian sabbath. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> principle of the Antisabbatarians is, that the Jewish sabbath was only of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CEREMONIAL">ceremonial</a>, not moral obligation; and consequently is abolished by the coming of Christ.

ANTISAGOGUE

Pages 489-489

in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">Rhetoric</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> differing little from that called concession. The following passage from Cicero is an instance of it: Difficilis ratio belli gerendi; at plena fidei, plena pietatis: et si dicas, magnus labor, multa pericula proponuntur; at gloria ex his immortalis est consecutura. See CONCESSION.

ANTISCIL

Pages 489-489

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, people who live on different sides of the equator, whose shadows at noon are projected opposite ways. Thus the people of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> are Antiscii to those of the south: the one projecting their shadows at noon towards the north pole, and the other towards the south pole.

ANTISEPTICS

Pages 489-490

an appellation given to such substances as resist <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUTREFACTION">putrefaction</a>. We have some curious experiments in relation to antiseptic substances by Dr. Pringle, who has ascertained their several virtues. Thus, in order to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> the antiseptic virtue of salts, he compared it with that of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>; which being one of the weakest, he supposes equal to unity, and expresses the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPORTIONAL">proportional</a> strength of the rest by higher numbers, as in the following <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>. | Salts, their antiseptic virtue. | |--------------------------------| | Sca salt | 1 | | Sal gemmae | 1+ | | Tartar vitriolated | 2 | | Spiritus Mindereri | 2 | | Tartarus solubilis | 2 | | Sal diureticus | 2+ | | Crude sal ammoniac | 3 | | Saline mixture | 3 | | Nitre | 4+ | | Salt of hartshorn | 4+ | | Salt of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMWOOD">wormwood</a> | 4+ | | <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BORAX">Borax</a> | 12+ | | Salt of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBER">amber</a> | 20+ | | <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">Alum</a> | 30+ | In this table the proportions are marked in integral numbers: only to some there is added the sign +, to show, that those salts are possessed of a stronger antiseptic virtue than the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> in the table expresses, by some fractions: unless in the three last, where the same sign imports that the salt may be stronger by some units. Some resinous and other substances even exceed the antiseptic virtues of the neutral salts; thus <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYRRH">myrrh</a>, asafoetida, terra japonica, and aloes, are at least 12 times more antiseptic than sea salt. Two grains of camphor are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> to 60 grains of that salt. An infusion of a few grains of Virginian snake-root, in powder, exceeds 12 times its <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of sea salt. Chamomile <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> have nearly the same extraordinary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>. The Jesuits bark has it also. Besides these, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEPPER">pepper</a>, ginger, saffron, contrayerva root, are 12 times more antiseptic than sea salt. Dried sage, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-RHUBARB">rhubarb</a>, the root of the wild valerian, mint, angelica, ground ivy, senna, green <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEA">tea</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> roses, wormwood, mustard, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> radish, were likewise found more antiseptic than the standard. To the class of antiseptic medicines may likewise be added fermented liquors, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACIDS">acids</a>, spirits, and even those <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> called anti-acids, and erroneously supposed hasteners of putrefaction, particularly horse radish. Now vegetables, possessing this virtue, are the more valuable, in that being usually free of acrimony, they may be taken in much greater quantities than either spirits, acids, resins, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> even the neutral salts. Antiseptics are prescribed in all putrid, malignant, and pestilential <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>. It is to be remarked, however, that different kinds of them are to be given in different diseases, and even in different stages of the same <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>. Thus, the bark is a specific in gangrene, when the vessels are relaxed, and the blood resolved or disposed to putrefaction; but <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> fail, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the vessels are too full, or the blood be too thick. With the same caution is the bark to be used in wounds, viz. chiefly in cases of absorbed <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, when it infects the humours, and brings on a hectic fever. By the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> antiseptic virtue of alum, the bark, and other astringents, it should seem, that astriction had no small share in the cure of putrid disorders; and, indeed, the very <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of putrefaction consists in a separation or disunion of the parts. But as astringents are improper to be administered in many cases, contrayer- Antiseptics va root, snake root, camphor, &c. may supply their <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>; which, though highly antiseptic, have very little, or any, of an astringent quality.

ANTISPASMODICS

Pages 490-490

are medicines proper for the cure of spasms and convulsions. Opium, balsam of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERU">Peru</a>, and the essential oils of many vegetables, are the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> in this class of medicines. Opium excels, for its immediate effects. Peruvian balsam, in many instances, produces more lasting benefit than opium, and sometimes succeeds where opium fails. As antispasmodics, the essential oils differ from this opium, that they <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> more on a particular <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> than on the system in general, and have no soporific effect. Some medicines remove spasms by immediate contact, as asses <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILK">milk</a>, cream, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> of almonds; others by repelling <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, as <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAS">gas</a>, sulphur, nitre, sal ammoniac, &c. And where the strictures are produced by inanition and a defect of vital heat, spasms are removed by those medicines that restore the vis vitae, such as valerian, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASTOR">castor</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSK">musk</a>, &c.

ANTISTASIS

Pages 490-490

in Oratory, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> from the consideration that, had it been omitted, worse would have ensued. This is called by Latin writers comparativum argumentum; such, e.g. would be the general's defence who had made an inglorious <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITULATION">capitulation</a>, That, without it, the whole <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> must have perished.

ANTISTHENES

Pages 490-490

a Greek <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, and founder of the Cynics. He was born at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, and passed the former <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> as a soldier. Having afterwards been an attendant at the lectures of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOCRATES">Socrates</a>, he was principally charmed with those exhortations of that <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> philosopher, which persuaded to frugality, to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEMPERANCE">temperance</a>, and to moderation; these Antisthenes was resolved to practise by carrying every precept to its utmost <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>. Permitting therefore his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARD">beard</a> to grow, he went about the streets in a thread-bare coat, scarcely to be distinguished from a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> beggar. He prided himself upon the most rigid virtue, and thought himself obliged to attack the vicious wherever he found them. This gave him some reputation in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>; but it may be supposed, that, in a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> so very luxurious as Athens, he had more enemies than disciples. His <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> consisted rather in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> than speculation: it was therefore his constant maxim, That to be virtuous was to be happy, and that all virtue consisted in action; that the wise <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> should live for himself, contented in all situations, and happy alone in the consciousness of his own virtue. He acknowledged nothing to be good but what was <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a>; and asserted, that virtue might be acquired by practice. Laertius tells us there were 10 tomes of his works; and he has given us many of his apophthegms. ANTISTOCHÉON, in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>, the using one <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> instead of another: as oll for illi.

ANTISTROPHE

Pages 490-490

among lyric poets, that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of a song and dance in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, which was performed before the altar, in returning from west to east; in opposition to strophe. See STROPHE and ODE. ANTITACTÆ, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a branch of Gnostics, who held, that God was good and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a>, but Antitactæ that a creature had created evil; and consequently that it is our duty to oppose this author of evil, in order to avenge God of his adversary.

ANTITHENAR

Pages 490-490

in Anatomy, a name given to the adductor indicis. See ANATOMY, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">Table</a> of the Muscles.

ANTITHESIS

Pages 490-490

in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">Rhetoric</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRAST">contrast</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> opposition of words or sentiments. Such is that of Cicero, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> Catilinarian: "On one side stands <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a>, on the other impudence; on one fidelity, on the other deceit; here piety, there sacrilege; here continency, there lust, &c." Such also is that of Augustus to some seditious young men, Audite, juvenes, senem, quem juvenem senes audire. Such again is that of Seneca: Curæ levæs loquuntur, ingentes stupent. And that of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>: Plectere si nequeo superos, Acheronta movebo. St Augustine, Seneca, Salvian, and many other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> writers, seem greatly to affect antitheses; but among the moderns they are generally decried. Desmaertz represents them as the favourites of young writers. The following is an example of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> antithesis. Though gentle, yet not dull; Strong, without rage; without o'erflowing, full. ANTITHESIS is sometimes used for controversy. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, we meet with antithetic method, antithetic discourses, &c. Marcion composed a volume of Antitheses, or contrarieties and oppositions between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> and the gospel.

ANTITRAGUS MUSCULUS

Pages 490-490

in Anatomy, a muscle of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-EAR">ear</a>. See ANATOMY, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">Table</a> of the Muscles.

ANTITRINITARIANS

Pages 490-490

those who deny the trinity, and teach that there are not three persons in the Godhead. Thus the Samosatenians, who do not believe the distinction of persons in God; the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARIANS">Arians</a>, who deny the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> of the Word, and the Macedonians, who deny that of the Holy Spirit, are all properly Antitrinitarians. Among the moderns, Antitrinitarians are particularly understood of Socinians, called also Unitarians. The Bibliotheca Antitrinitariorum, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Antitrinitarian Library, is a posthumous <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of Christopher Sandius, an eminent Antitrinitarian; wherein he gives a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIST">list</a>, digested in order of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, of all the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-SOCINIAN">Socinian</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> Antitrinitarian authors, with a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIEF">brief</a> account of their lives, and a catalogue of their works. See UNITARIAN.

ANTITYPE

Pages 491-491

among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Greek fathers, and in the Greek liturgy, is also applied to the symbols of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> and wine in the sacrament. Hence it hath been argued, by many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>, that the Greeks do not really believe the doctrine of transubstantiation; because they call the bread and wine antitypes, ὑπάρχει, q.d. figures, similitudes; and this even after the consecration.

ANTIUM

Pages 491-491

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the Volsci, (Livy); situated on the Tuscan <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, yet without a harbour, because they had a neighbouring <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAMLET">hamlet</a> called Ceno, with a harbour, (Strabo). The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> gained their first reputation in naval affairs against the Antiates; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of whose ships they conveyed into the arsenal of Rome, and part they burnt; and with their beaks <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rostra adorned the pulpit erected in the forum, thence called Rostra, (Livy, Florus). Here stood a famous temple of Fortune, (Horace). Addison says, there were two Fortuna worshipped at Antium.—It is now extinct, but the name still remains in the Capo d'Anzo.

ANTIVARI

Pages 491-491

a strong town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DALMATIA">Dalmatia</a>, a Greek archbishop's see, and subject to the Turks. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 19. 15. N. Lat. 42. 20. ANTIVIRGILIAN husbandry, an appellation given to Mr Tull's new method of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>-hoeing husbandry. See <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">AGRICULTURE</a>.

ANTLER

Pages 491-491

among sportsmen, a start <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> branch of a deer's attire. Brow Antler, denotes the branch next the head; and, Bes Antler, the branch next above the brow antler.

ANTLIA

Pages 491-491

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> machine, supposed to be the same with our <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUMP">pump</a>. Hence the phrase in antliam condemnari, according to the critics, denotes a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> whereby criminals were condemned to drain ponds, ditches, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the like.

ANTOEICI

Pages 491-491

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, those inhabitants of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> who live under the same meridian, and at the same distance from the equator: the one toward the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, and the other toward the south. Hence they have the same <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a>: and their latitude is also the same, but of a different denomination. They are in the same <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEMICIRCLE">semicircle</a> of the meridian, but in opposite parallels. They have precisely the same hours of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> and night, but opposite seasons; and the night of the one is always equal to the day of the other.

ANTOINE

Pages 491-491

a town of France, in Dauphiny, in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIENNE">Vienne</a>, with a celebrated <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a>. It is seated among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, 13 miles east of Lyons. Antoine E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 5. 26. N. Lat. 45. 43.

ANTONA

Pages 491-491

(Tacitus); a river of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, which Camden supposes to be a faulty <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> for Avona <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Aufona, (the Avon).

ANTONACUM

Pages 491-491

Antonnacum, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Antunnacum, a town of the Treviri; now Andernach, below <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COBLENZ">Coblenz</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 7. 5. N. Lat. 50. 25.

ANTONIA

Pages 491-491

Saint, a town of France, in the department of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT_AND_GARONNE"><a class="xref"</a> href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">Lot</a> and Garonne, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of Rhôdez, whose fortifications are demolished. It is seated on the river Aveyron. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 0. 55. N. Lat. 44. 10. ANTONIAN waters, medicinal waters of Germany, very pleasant to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, and esteemed good in many chronic and hypochondriac <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>. See TONSTEIN.

ANTONIANO

Pages 491-495

Silvio, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> learning, who raised himself from a low condition by his merit, was born at Rome in the year 1540. When he was but ten years old, he could make verses upon any subject proposed to him; and these so excellent, though pronounced extempore, that even a man of genius could not compose the like without a good <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> and pains. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FERRARA">Ferrara</a> coming to Rome, to congratulate Marcellus II. upon his being raised to the pontificate, was so charmed with the genius of Antoniano, that he carried him to Ferrara, where he provided able masters to instruct him in all the sciences. From thence he was sent for by Pius IV. who made him professor of the belles lettres in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> at Rome. Antoniano filled this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> with so much reputation, that, on the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> when he began to explain the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORATION">oration</a>, pro Marco Marcello, he had a vast crowd of auditors, and among these no less than 25 cardinals. He was afterwards chosen rector of the college; and after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Pius IV. being seized with a spirit of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>, he joined himself to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> Neri, and accepted the office of secretary to the sacred college, offered him by Pius V. which he executed for 25 years with the reputation of an honest and able man. He refused a bishopric which Gregory XIV. would have given him; but he accepted the office of secretary to the briefs, offered him by Clement VIII. who made him his chamberlain, and afterwards a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a>. Antoniano killed himself by too great fatigue: for he spent whole nights in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> letters; which brought on a sickness, whereof he died, in the 63rd year of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. He wrote with such ease and fluency, that he never almost made any blot <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rasure; and it is said of him, that he preserved the flower of his virginity during his whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. ANTONIDES Vander Goes, John, an eminent Dutch poet, born at Goes in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZEALAND">Zealand</a>, the 3d of April 1647. His parents were <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANABAPTISTS">Anabaptists</a>, people of good character, but of low circumstances. They went to live at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a> when Antonides was about four years old; Antonides, old; and, in the ninth year of his age, he began his studies, under the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HADRIAN">Hadrian</a> Junius and James Cocceius. Antonides took great <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> the Latin poets, and carefully compared them with Grotius, Heinsius, &c. By this means he acquired a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, and enriched his mind with noble <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a>. He first attempted to translate some pieces of Ovid, Horace, and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>; and, having formed his taste on these excellent models, he at length undertook one of the most difficult tasks in poetry, to write a tragedy: This was entitled Traszel, or, The invasion of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>. Antonides, however, was so modest, as not to permit it to be published. Vondel, who was then engaged in a dramatic piece, which was taken also from some event that happened in China, read Antonides's tragedy; and was so well pleased with it, that he declared, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the author would not print it, he would take some <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> out of it, and make <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of them in his own tragedy. He accordingly did so; and it was reckoned much to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of Antonides, to have written what might be adopted by so great a poet as Vondel was acknowledged to be by all good judges. Upon the conclusion of the peace between Great <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, in the year 1674, Antonides wrote a piece, entitled Bellona aan band, i.e. "Bellona chained;" a very elegant poem, consisting of several hundred verses. He next wrote an ingenious heroic poem, which he entitled The River Y (the river on which Amsterdam is built). Antonides's parents had bred him up an apothecary; but his remarkable genius for poetry soon gained him the esteem and friendship of several persons of distinction; and particularly of Mr Buisero, one of the lords of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADMIRALTY">admiralty</a> at Amsterdam, and a great lover of poetry, who sent him at his expense to pursue his studies at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>, where he remained till he took his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of physic, and then his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> gave him a place in the admiralty. In 1678, Antonides married Susanna Bermans, a minister's <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>, who had also a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TALENT">talent</a> for poetry. His <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> was celebrated by several eminent poets, particularly by the famous <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> Francius, professor of eloquence, who composed some Latin verses on the occasion. After marriage, he did not much indulge his poetie genius; and within a few years he fell into a consumption, of which he died on the 18th September 1684, being then but thirty-<a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years and a few months old. He is esteemed the most eminent Dutch poet after Vondel. His works have been printed several times, having been collected by Father Antony Tansz. The last edition was printed by Nicholas Ten Hoom, at Amsterdam, in the year 1714, in 4to, under the direction of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a> Van Hoogstraaten, one of the masters of the Latin school of that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, who added to it also the life of the poet. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANTONINUS_PIUS">ANTONINUS Pius</a>, a celebrated Roman <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>, was born A.D. 86, at Lanuvium in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. Distinguished for eminence of character, his family had <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> maintained the honour of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NISMES">Nismes</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAUL">Gaul</a>, from whence they had descended. Both his father and grandfather had held the office of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARIUS">Arius</a> Antoninus, his maternal grandfather, by his amiable disposition and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of literature, had acquired an eminent character, and was very intimate with Pliny the younger. Under him the young Titus after his father's death completed his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>. His Antoninus, character on arriving at the age of maturity, manifested itself in the most promising manner. To an improved understanding, a virtuous heart, a mild and dignified character, and a noble eloquence, he joined a happy physiognomy. Simple in his taste, and guided by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEMPERANCE">temperance</a> in all his actions and sentiments, he was entirely free from all affectation and pomposity. In the year 120, among the many public honours which his birth and connexions gave him a claim to, he was elevated to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> of consul, and was afterwards appointed by Adrian to be one of the four consuls, betwixt whom the supreme power of Italy was divided. Becoming in his turn proconsul of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, he acquitted himself with such reputation that he even excelled his grandfather Arius who had formerly enjoyed that high trust. Returning from Asia he was not only received into the favour, but likewise the confidence and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of Adrian, and was always disposed to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> with lenity. He married Amia Faustina, the daughter of Annius Verus, whose character was far from being untaxed with reproach; but his lenient disposition induced him to avoid public scandal, and he behaved towards his aged father-in-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> with the most becoming respect. Two sons and two daughters were the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of this marriage. The sons died when they were young, and the eldest daughter, who was married to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAMIA">Lamia</a> Sylvanus, died when Titus proceeded towards his Asiatic <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. Faustina the youngest married Marcus Aurelius, who was afterwards emperor. After the death of Verus, Adrian resolving to adopt Antoninus, he was induced to accept of the succession to so important a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> as the Roman empire, although with a considerable degree of reluctance, and was accordingly nominated by Adrian in February 25, A.D. 138, in the presence of the council of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> senators, who at the same time created him his colleague in performing the proconsular and tribunitial duties. Extending his plans of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADOPTION">adoption</a> still farther, Adrian caused Antoninus adopt the son of Verus, then seven years of age, and Marcus Annius, afterwards named Aurelius, then seventeen years of age, a relation of Adrian's, and nephew to his own wife. The dutiful and merited <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> which Antoninus bestowed on Adrian during the last months of his illness, gives a very high idea of his character. On <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 10, A.D. 138, he succeeded to the empire amidst the universal acclamations of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> and people, who anticipated in his well tried virtues that <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> which a good and wise sovereign is able to bestow upon his subjects. The Roman world enjoyed such tranquillity under his reign that it affords few materials for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>; yet it is to be regretted that Capitolinus is the only historian from whom any <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> information can be received concerning this peaceful <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, and he is none of the most perspicuous. It however appears that the usual honours and titles, together with the addition of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SURNAME">surname</a> of Pius, which both his conduct and zeal in defending and honouring the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of his predecessor united to suggest, were willingly conferred upon him by the senate. In the beginning of his reign there were several conspiracies formed against him, but this only afforded him an instance of signalizing his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLEMENCY">clemency</a>, which he did in the most striking manner. Although he was unable to prevent <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> from taking its due course... Antoninus, course against the ringleaders, he prohibited all <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVESTIGATION">investigation</a> after their accomplices, and took the son of Attillus, one of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> conspirators, under his protection. Various commotions were raised in several parts of the empire; but by the vigilance of his lieutenants, these were easily quelled. The incursions of the Brigantes in Britain were restrained, and a new wall which was built to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of that of Adrian, from the mouth of the Esk to that of Tweed, and which was called the Wall of Antoninus, was fixed as the boundary of the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> in Britain. The reign of Antoninus upon the whole was singularly peaceful, and realized a saying of Scipio, "That he preferred saving the life of one citizen, to destroying a thousand enemies." A desire of promoting the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of his people, of protecting them from oppression, of administering justice through every corner of the realm, and of being instrumental to the happiness and peace of his government, influenced all his proceedings. He delighted greatly in laying before the senate the motives of all his actions; and in his manner of living and conversing he employed the same prudential economy and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> of equality, which had so distinguished his predecessors Trajan and Adrian. On account of the sweetness of his temper he bore with firmness many indignities offered him; and under his reign the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of informers was entirely extinguished, and condemnations and confiscations were very rare. The various public calamities which occurred in his time were all relieved by him with the greatest benevolence. He avoided as much as possible laying any burthens upon his people, and on this account made few journeys through his dominions. He was frugal in the use of the public revenues, but profuse in his own patrimony, a great economist, devoid of avarice, and very liberal towards works of ornament and utility, and even towards gratifying the pleasure of his people. A temple in honour of Adrian in Rome, and perhaps the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMPHITHEATRE">amphitheatre</a> and aqueduct at Nismes, were his chief buildings. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JURISPRUDENCE">Jurisprudence</a> was to this emperor, like that of his predecessor, an interesting subject for improvement; and several decrees which he issued, display his commendable spirit of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EQUITY">equity</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of this equity was, that Antoninus acquired a reputation and fame which no <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> achievements could have conferred; and his friendship was courted by the neighbouring princes. There is scarcely a blot to be found to tarnish his character; and frugality, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a>, and harmless amusement <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to employ his private hours. It may perhaps be admitted that he was too indulgent towards an unworthy wife, and that the divine honours he bestowed on her memory were not merited by her conduct. In the management of his complicated business, he was exact to such a degree that it was even ridiculed by some; but he found the daily advantage of this accuracy. The growing virtue of Marcus Aurelius soon drew his attention after he ascended the throne, and having given him his daughter in marriage, he declared him Caesar. Nor was he mistaken in his choice; for Aurelius acted with the utmost fidelity and affection amid all the honours that he continued to confer upon him. Enjoying this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> share of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> bliss, in the 74th year of his life he was seized with a fever at his favourite <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> seat of Loriga. Convinced of his approaching fate, he convened the principal officers of the state, and confirmed his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> of Aurelius, and gave him the imperial ensigns. A delirium ensued, in an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> of which he gave the watchword Æquanimitas, and calmly resigned his breath in the 23d year of his reign. His ashes were consigned to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> of Adrian, and divine honours paid to his memory. He was universally regretted, and succeeding emperors bore his name as a badge of honour. The senate and his successor erected a sculptured pillar to his memory, which is still shown to strangers as one of the chief ornaments of Rome. (Gen. Bieg.) Antoninus Philosophus, Marcus Aurelius, the Roman emperor, born at Rome, the 26th of April, in the 121st year of the Christian era. He was called by several names till he was admitted into the Aurelian family, when he took that of Marcus Aurelius Antoninus. Hadrian, upon the death of Cejonius Commodus, turned his eyes upon Marcus Aurelius; but, as he was not then 18 years of age, and consequently too young for so important a station, he fixed upon Antoninus Pius, whom he adopted, upon condition that he should likewise adopt Marcus Aurelius. The year after this adoption, Hadrian appointed him questor, though he had not yet attained the age prescribed by the law. After the death of Hadrian, Aurelius married Faustina, the daughter of Antoninus Pius, by whom he had several children. In the year 139, he was invested with new honours by the emperor Pius, in which he behaved in such a manner as endeared him to that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> and the whole people. Upon the death of Pius, which happened in the year 161, he was obliged by the senate to take upon him the government; in the management of which he took Lucius Verus as his colleague. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DION">Dion</a> Cassius says, that the reason of doing this was, that he might have leisure to pursue his studies, and on account of his ill state of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>; Lucius being of a strong vigorous <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, and consequently more fit for the fatigues of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. The same day he took upon him the name of Antoninus, which he gave likewise to Verus his colleague, and betrothed his daughter Lucilla to him. The two emperors went afterwards to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>; where, after having performed the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FUNERAL_RITES">funeral <a cl</a>ass="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a> of Pius, they pronounced each of them a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PANEGYRIC">panegyric</a> to his memory. They discharged the government in a very <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMICABLE">amicable</a> manner. It is said that, soon after Antoninus had performed the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOTHEOSIS">apotheosis</a> of Pius, petitions were presented to him by the Pagan priests, philosophers, and governors of provinces, in order to excite him to persecute the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>; which he rejected with indignation, and interposed his authority for their protection, by writing a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> of Asia, then held at Ephesus (A). The happiness which the empire began to enjoy under these two emperors was interrupted, in the year 162, by a dreadful inundation of the Tiber, which (A) Eusebius has preserved this letter, Hist. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-ECCLES">Eccles</a>. lib. iv. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 13, but he falsely ascribes it to Antoninus Pius, whereas it was wrote by Marcus Antoninus, as Valerius makes it appear in his annotations on Eusebius. Antoninus, which destroyed a vast <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of cattle, and occasioned a famine at Rome. This calamity was followed by the Parthian war; and at the same time the Catti ravaged Germany and Rhaetia. Lucius Verus went in person to oppose the Parthians; and Antoninus continued at Rome, where his presence was necessary. During this war with the Parthians, about the year 163 or 164, Antoninus sent his daughter Lucilla to Verus, she having been betrothed to him in marriage, and attended her as far as Brundusium: he intended to have conducted her to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>; but it having been insinuated by some persons, that his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of going into the east was to claim the honour of having finished the Parthian war, he returned to Rome. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> having gained a victory over the Parthians, who were obliged to abandon Mesopotamia, the two emperors triumphed over them at Rome in the year 166; and were honoured with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Fathers of their country. This year was fatal, on account of a terrible pestilence which spread itself over the whole world, and a famine under which Rome laboured: it was likewise in this year that the Marcomanni, and many other people of Germany, took up arms against the Romans; but the two emperors having marched in person against them, obliged the Germans to sue for peace. The war, however, was renewed the year following, and the two emperors marched again in person; but Lucius Verus was seized with an apoplectic fit, and died at Altinum. The Romans were now defeated with great slaughter; and the emperor, not choosing to burden his subjects with new taxes, exposed to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a> the furniture of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver plate belonging to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, and his wife's rich garments embroidered with gold, and a curious collection of pearls, which Adrian had purchased during his long progress through the provinces of the empire, and was called Adrian's cabinet. In the year 170, Antoninus made vast preparations against the Germans, and carried on the war with great vigour. During this war, in 174, a very extraordinary event is said to have happened, which, according to Dion Cassius, was as follows: Antoninus's <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> being blocked up by the Quadi, in a very disadvantageous place, where there was no possibility of procuring <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>; in this situation, being worn out with fatigue and wounds, oppressed with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> and thirst, and incapable of retiring or engaging the enemy, in an instant the sky was covered with <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a>, and there fell a vast <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>: the Roman army were about to quench their thirst, when the enemy came upon them with such fury, that they must certainly have been defeated, had it not been for a shower of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIL">hail</a>, accompanied with a storm of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a>, which fell upon the enemy, without the least annoyance to the Antonine Romans, who by this means gained the victory (B). In 175, Antoninus made a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> with several nations of Germany. Soon after, Avidius Cassius, governor of Syria, revolted from the emperor: this insurrection, however, was put an end to by the death of Cassius, who was killed by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CENTURION">centurion</a> named Anthony. Antoninus behaved with great lenity towards those who had been engaged in Cassius's party; he would not put to death, nor imprison, nor even sit in judgment himself upon any of the senators engaged in this revolt; but he referred them to the senate, fixing a day for their appearance, as if it had been only a civil affair. He wrote also to the senate, desiring them to act with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDULGENCE">indulgence</a> rather than severity; nor to shed the blood of any senator or person of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, or of any other person whatsoever; but to allow this honour to his reign, that, even under the misfortune of a rebellion, none had lost their lives, except in the first heat of the tumult. In 176, Antoninus visited Syria and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>: the kings of those countries, and ambassadors also from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARTHIA">Parthia</a>, came to visit him. He staid several days at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SMYRNA">Smyrna</a>; and, after he had settled the affairs of the east, went to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, on which city he conferred several honours, and appointed public professors there. From thence he returned to Rome with his son Commodus, whom he chose consul for the year following, though he was then but 16 years of age, having obtained a dispensation for that purpose. On the 27th of September, the same year, he gave him the title of Imperator; and on the 23d of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a>, he entered Rome in triumph, with Commodus, on account of the victories gained over the Germans. Dion Cassius tells us, that he remitted all the debts which were due to himself and the public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a> during 46 years, from the time that Hadrian had granted the same favour, and burnt all the writings relating to these debts. He applied himself likewise to correct many enormities, and introduced several excellent regulations. In the year 179, he left Rome with his son Commodus, in order to go against the Marcomanni, and other barbarous nations; and the year following gained a considerable victory over them, and would, in all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a>, have entirely subdued them in a very short time, had he not been taken with an illness, which carried him off on the 17th of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 180, in the 59th year of his age, and 19th of his reign. The whole empire regretted the loss of so valuable a prince, and paid the greatest regard to his memory: he was ranked amongst the gods, and almost every person had a statue of him in their houses. His book of meditations has been much admired by the best judges. (B) The Pagans, as well as Christians, according to Mr Tillement (p. 621, art xvi.), have acknowledged the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of this prodigy, but have greatly differed as to the cause of such a miraculous event; the former ascribing it, some to one magician and some to another: In Antoninus's pillar, the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> is ascribed to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>, the god of rain and thunder. But the Christians affirmed, that God granted this favour at the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a> of the Christian <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> in the Roman army, who are said to have composed the twelfth or Melitene legion; and, as a mark of distinction, we are told that they received the title of the Thundering legion, from Antoninus (Euseb. Eccles. Hist. lib. v. cap. 5.). Mr Moyle, in the letters published in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> volume of his works, has endeavoured to explode this story of the Thundering Legion; which occasioned Mr Whiston to publish an answer, in 1726, entitled, Of the Thundering Legion; or, Of the miraculous deliverance of Marcus Antoninus and his army, upon the prayers of the Christians. ANTONINE'S <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLUMN">COLUMN</a>. See COLUMN.

ANTONINUS'S WALL

Pages 495-496

the name of the third rampart <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> that had been built or repaired by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> against the incursions of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> Britons. It is called by the people in the neighbourhood, Graham's Dyke; from the notion that one Graham, or Grimos, first made a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREACH">breach</a> in it after the retreat of the Romans out of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. The first <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARRIER">barrier</a> erected by the Romans was the chain of forts made by Agricola* from the frith of Forth to that of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLYDE">Clyde</a>, in the year 81, to protect his conquest from the inroads of the Caledonians. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> was the vallum, or dyke, flung up by Adrian† in the year 121. It terminated on the western side of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> at Axclodunum, or Brugh, on the Solway sands, and was supposed to have reached no further than Pons Aelii, or <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEWCASTLE">Newcastle</a>, on the eastern. But from an inscription lately discovered, it appears to have extended as far as the wall of Severus‡. This rampart of Adrian's was situated much farther south than Agricola's chain; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> to the north having been either, according to some authors, recovered by the native Britons after the departure of Agricola; or, according to others, voluntarily slighted by Adrian. However, this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of Adrian's did not <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> continue to be the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> boundary of the Roman territories to the north in Britain. For <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANTONINUS_PIUS">Antoninus Pius</a>, the adopted son and immediate successor of Adrian, having, by his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a> Lollius Urbicus, recovered the country once conquered by Agricola, commanded another rampart to be erected between the friths of Forth and Clyde, in the track where Agricola had formerly built his chain of forts. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a> which have been found in or near the ruins of this wall, or rampart, to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of Antoninus Pius, leave us no room to doubt its having been built by his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> and command. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the fragment of a Roman pillar with an inscription, now in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> library of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, belonged to this work, as it is generally supposed to have done, it fixes the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">date</a> of its execution to the third consulship of Antoninus, which was A.D. 149, only 25 years after that of Adrian, of which this seems to have been an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a>. This wall or rampart, as some imagine, reached from Caer-ridden on the frith of Forth to Old Kirkpatrick on the Clyde; or, as others think, from Kinniel on the east to Dunglass on the west. These different suppositions hardly make a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> in the length of this work, which, from several actual mensurations, appears to have been 37 English or 40 Roman miles. Capitolinus, in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of Antoninus Pius, directly affirms, that the wall which that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> built in Britain was of turf. This in the main is unquestionably true; though it is evident (from the vestiges of it still remaining, which not very many years ago were dug up and examined for near a mile together) that the foundation was of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>. Mr Camden also tells us, from the papers of one Mr Anthony Pont, that the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> rampart was faced with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> stone, to prevent the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> from falling into the ditch. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> parts of this work were as follows: 1. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> and deep ditch, whose dimensions cannot now be discovered with certainty and exactness, though Mr Pont says, it was 12 feet wide. 2. The principal wall or rampart was about 12 feet thick at the foundation, but its original height cannot now be determined. This wall was situated on the south brink of the ditch. 3.
