A <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> way on the south side of the principal wall, well paved, and raised a little above the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> of the ground. This work, as well as that of Adrian, was defended by garrisons placed in forts and stations along the line of it. The number of these forts or stations, whose vestiges were visible in Mr Pont's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, was 18, situated at about the distance of two miles from each other. In the intervals between the forts, there were turrets or watch towers. But the number of these, and their distance from each other, cannot now be discovered. It is not a little surprising, that though it is now more than 1600 years since this work was finished, and more than 1300 since it was slighted, we can yet discover from authentic monuments, which are still remaining, by what particular bodies of Roman troops almost every <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of it was executed. This discovery is made from inscriptions upon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, which were originally built into the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> of the wall, and have been found in or near its ruins, and are carefully preserved. The number of stones with inscriptions of this kind now extant, is 11; of which six may be seen at one view in the college of Glasgow, one in the college of Aberdeen, one in the college of Edinburgh, one in the collection of Baron Clerk, one at Cochnoch <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, and one at Calder house. From these inscriptions it appears in general, that this great work was executed by the second legion, the vexillation of the sixth legion and of the twentieth legion, and one cohort of auxiliaries. If these corps were all complete, they would make in all a body of 7800 men. Some of these inscriptions have suffered greatly by the injuries of time and other accidents; so that we cannot discover from them, with <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> certainty, how many paces of this work were executed by each of these bodies of troops. The sum of the certain and probable information contained in these inscriptions, as it is collected by the learned and illustrious Mr <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HORSLEY">Horsley</a>, stands thus: | Paces | |-------| | The second legion built | 11,603 | | The vexillation of the sixth legion | 7411 | | The vexillation of the twentieth legion | 7801 | | All certain | 26,815 | | The vexillation of the twentieth legion, the monument certain, and the number probable | 3411 | | The same vexillation, on a plain monument, no number visible, supposed | 3500 | | The sixth legion, a monument, but no number, supposed | 3000 | | Cohors prima Cugernorum | 3000 | Total | 39,726 | or 39 miles 726 paces, nearly the whole length of the wall. It would have been both useful and agreeable to have known how long time these troops were employed in the execution of this great work. But of this we have no information. Neither do we know what particular bodies of troops were in garrison in the several forts and stations along the line of this wall, because these garrisons were withdrawn before the Notitia Imperii was written. Though we cannot discover exactly how many years this... Antonio, this wall of the emperor Antonius <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to be the boundary of the Roman territories in Britain, yet we know with certainty that it was not very long. For we are told by an author of undoubted <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a>, that, in the reign of Commodus, A.D. 180, "he had wars with several foreign nations, but none so dangerous as that of Britain. For the people of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, having passed the wall which divided them from the Romans, attacked them, and cut them to pieces."

ANTONIO

Pages 496-496

ST, a Dutch fort in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AXIM">Axim</a>, on the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">Gold</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>. It stands on a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> rock, which projects into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> in form of a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a>; and is so environed by rocks and dangerous shoals, as to be inaccessible to an enemy but by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>, where it is fortified by a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARAPET">parapet</a>, drawbridge, and two batteries of heavy cannon. Besides this it has a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTERY">battery</a> towards the sea. The three batteries consist of 24 cannon. Its form is triangular; the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> is neat, strong, and commodious for the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, that being but small, on account of the narrowness of the rock on which it is built. The garrison is usually composed of 25 <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> men, and an equal <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEGROES">negroes</a>, under the command of a serjeant. It is maintained at the expence of the West <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">Company</a>; and when well stored with <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>, is capable of making a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> against any number of negroes. It is, however, as well as all other forts on this coast, liable to inconveniences from the heavy and continual rains, which damage the walls, and render frequent reparations necessary. This obliges the Dutch always to keep ready a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of lime <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> cement made of calcined oyster shells, of which the coast produces <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> numbers. This settlement was first founded by the Portuguese during the reign of Emanuel. They fixed it first upon a small point; where, finding themselves insecure, they built the fort where it now stands. They were driven out by the Dutch in 1641; and upon the conclusion of a peace with the States General, the fort remained by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the Dutch West India Company, who have kept possession of it ever since.

ANTONIUS

Pages 496-497

MARCUS, a famous Roman orator. While he filled the office of praetor, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a> fell to his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">lot</a>, and he cleared the seas of the pirates which infested that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a>. He was made <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a> with A. Posthumus <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBINUS">Albinus</a>, in the year of Rome 653; when he opposed the turbulent designs of Sextus Titus, tribune of the people, with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> and success. Some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> after, he was made governor of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CILICIA">Cilicia</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of proconsul; where he performed so many great exploits, that he obtained the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of a triumph. We cannot omit observing, that in order to improve his great <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TALENT">talent</a> for eloquence, he became a scholar to the greatest men at <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RHODES">Rhodes</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, in his way to Cilicia, and when on his return to Rome. Soon after he was appointed censor; which office he discharged with great reputation, having carried his cause before the people, against Marcus Duronius, who had preferred an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACCUSATION">accusation</a> of bribery against him, in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> for Antonius's having erased his name out of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIST">list</a> of senators, which this wise censor had done, because Duronius, when tribune of the people, had abrogated a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> Octavius, and finding Octavius was become publicly his enemy, Antonius entered into a confederacy with Sextus Pompeius, who was still <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of Sicily. He then went into <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in order to fight Octavius; but Fulvia, who had been the author and promoter of this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, dying, Octavius and Antonius came to an agreement. One of the conditions of this new peace was, that they should together attack Pompey, though the former had lately made an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> with him. Antonius then married <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OCTAVIA">Octavia</a>, sister of Octavius, as a pledge of their renewed friendship: but returned soon after to his beloved Cleopatra, and again lived with her in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>. Octavius took hold of this pretence to inveigh against him, and begin the war again. At last they engaged in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> fight at <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIUM">Actium</a>, in which Octavius gained a complete victory; which was followed by the deaths both of Antonius and Cleopatra. The infatuated Antonius fell upon his own <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>; and Cleopatra stung herself to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> with an asp, as was supposed, to avoid gracing the victor's triumph at Rome.

ANTONOMASIA

Pages 497-497

a form of speech, in which, for a proper name, is put the name of some <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, office, profession, science <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> trade; or when a proper name is put in the room of an appellative. Thus a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> is called his majesty; a nobleman, his lordship. We say the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> instead of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>, and the orator for Cicero: Thus a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> is called by the name of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, a German, an Italian; and a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a> man is called a Cato, and a wise man a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a>.

ANTOSIANDRIANS

Pages 497-497

a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of rigid Lutherans, who oppose the doctrine of Osiander relating to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTIFICATION">justification</a>. These are otherwise denominated Osiandro-mastigtes.—The Antosianandrians deny that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> is made <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a>, with that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> wherewith God himself is just; that is, they assert, that he is not made essentially, but only imputatively, just; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a>, that he is not really made just, but only pronounced so.

ANTRIM

Pages 497-498

the most northerly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>. It is bounded by that of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">Down</a> on the south-east, that of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDONDERRY">Londonderry</a> on the west, from which it is separated by the river Bann, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMAGH">Armagh</a> on the south, St George's channel on the east, and the Deucaliedonian ocean on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>. Its greatest length is about 46 miles, its greatest breadth about 27; and it contains 972 <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 622,959 English acres. Though the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is much encumbered with bogs and marshes, yet it enjoys a pretty good <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>; and it is well peopled, chiefly with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>. Where it is free from bogs the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is fruitful. It sends five members to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, two for the shire, and one for each of the three <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELFAST">Belfast</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRICKFERGUS">Carrickfergus</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LISBURN">Lisburn</a>. Certain narrow valleys, called glyns, beginning here, and running a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> way along the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, belonged formerly to the Bissets, noblemen of Scotland, who having been obliged to quit that country for having assassinated Patrick <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Athole upon a private quarrel, came hither, and had a great estate bestowed upon them by Henry III. of England; of which in the reign of Edward II. a part was forfeited by the rebellion of Hugh, then <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of the family. Another tract near this, called the Route, belonged anciently to the Macguillers, but now to the McDonnels, earls of Antrim. Upon the coast of this county are the promontories called by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>, Robogdium, Vennicinium and Boravum, now Fair Foreland, Ramshead, and St Helen's head. The river also, styled by the same author Vida, and now Croada, runs through this county.—Here, also is the remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> curiosity called the Giant's Causeway, for a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of which see that article. See Antrim, Supplement. Antrim, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> town of the county of Antrim, in Ireland, seated at the north end of the lake Lough Neagh, about six miles from the mouth of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>, having a good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> before it, with a pier near the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, within which vessels <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> dry at low <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. It was anciently a borough of great <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>, as appears from the mayor's being <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a> of a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of coast, as well in Down as in this county; the corporation enjoying the customs paid by all vessels within those bounds, the creeks of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANGOR">Bangor</a> and Belfast only excepted. This <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANT">grant</a>, however, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> repurchased, and thereupon transferred the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CUSTOM_HOUSE"><a class="xr</a>ef" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> to Belfast, to which town it is now much inferior as well in size as in trade. It is, however, still a place of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOTE">note</a>, and formerly sent two members to the Irish house of commons. It gives the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of earl to the noble family of M'Donnel.—At Antrim is a seat, with noble demesnes, and beautiful and highly cultivated lands, of the earl of Massareene. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 6. 26. N. Lat. 54. 45.

ANTRUM

Pages 498-498

among Anatomists, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> used to denote several cavities of the body: as the antrum highmorianum, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> that in the maxillary or jaw bone; antrum pylori, or that at the bottom of the pylorus, &c.

ANTWERP

Pages 498-500

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Brabant, in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, formerly <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the marquisate of Antwerp, otherwise called the marquisate of the holy Roman empire, situated in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 4. 15. N. Lat. 51. 12. It lies in a low marshy ground on the Scheld, 24 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRUSSELS">Brussels</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>. It is the third city in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> in Brabant, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and well built, containing 22 squares, and above 200 streets, all straight and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, especially that called the Merc, in which six coaches can go abreast. Most of the houses are of freestone, and have an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> of antiquity, being <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, with courts before and gardens behind. At the head of the Merc is a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRUCIFIX">crucifix</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> thirty-three feet high. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> dedicated to the Virgin <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>, the stadhhouse, and the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a>, are magnificent structures: the latter is the first <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> of that kind in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, and on its <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODEL">model</a> the exchanges of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a> are built. Its pillars are all of blue marble, and carved, but all in a different manner. The exchange cost the city 300,000 crowns. Antwerp, towards the end of the fifteenth century, was one of the most celebrated <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> that ever existed. The Scheld, on which it stands, being 20 feet deep at low <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and rising 20 feet more at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a>, ships of the greatest burden came up to the quays, as in the river <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a> at London; but when the United Provinces formed themselves into a free state, after having shaken off the yoke of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, they got the entire command of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a> of the Scheld; which ruined the trade of Antwerp, and transferred it to Amsterdam. This made the inhabitants turn their heads to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, jewelling, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BANKING">banking</a>, which they have <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> success and reputation; for at Antwerp bills of exchange may be negotiated for any sum to any <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of Europe; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> Antwerp <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>'s wars, two brothers of the name of De Koning, paid the one the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of France, and the other that of the confederates. Besides, here is a fine manufacture of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TAPESTRY">tapestry</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LACE">lace</a>; and, for the promoting of trade, an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSURANCE">insurance</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> has been erected. This city was the see of a bishop, who, as <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABBOT">abbot</a> of St Bernard, was the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> prelate in Brabant. The bishopric was of great <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, and the cathedral a most noble pile, with one of the finest steeples in the world. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> V. when he made his entry into Antwerp, said it ought to be put in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, and showed only once a year for a rarity. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANSE">hanse</a> towns, built when the city was in its flourishing condition, is a stately building, with magazines above for dry goods, and cellars below for wet, and in the middle story were 300 lodging rooms for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>; but now it is turned to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> barrack. There is a market here, called the Friday's Market, because it is held every Friday, where all sorts of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a> goods, pictures, and jewels, are sold by auction. No city in the Netherlands has so many and so fine churches as this. Many of them, particularly the cathedral and Jesuits <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, are adorned with paintings, by Sir <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> Paul Rubens, who was a native of this city; and by Quintin Massyes, who is said to have been a blacksmith; but having fallen in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> with a painter's <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>, and been told by her father, when he asked her of him in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>, that he would have none but a painter for his son-in-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>, he went to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> painting, and, in a few years, returned so eminent in his new profession, that he found no difficulty in obtaining the father's consent. He is interred at the entry of the cathedral, where his effigy is put up, with an inscription, signifying, that conjugal love made an A-pelles of a blacksmith. The above mentioned Jesuits church is extremely magnificent, and the chapel of the Virgin, joining to it, still more so. Among the cloisters the most remarkable are, the noble and rich <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a> of St Michael, on the banks of the Scheld, the apartments of which are truly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a>, and in which sovereign princes were often lodged; and the English nunnery, of the order of St Teresa, the nuns of which never wore <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, nor ate <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>, and lay upon straw: the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GRATES">grates</a> of the convent are so dismal, that it looks like a prison. As to the fortifications of the city, it is environed with a fine wall, planted with rows of trees on each side, with walks between, broad enough for two coaches to go abreast, being also defended by a very strong, large, regular citadel, in form of a pentagon, erected by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Alva in 1568, which commands the town and the neighbouring <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. The magistracy of this city is chosen only out of the several patrician families; and consists of two burgomasters and 18 chevins, besides inferior magistrates. Among the privileges granted to it by its princes, there is one by which every person born in it is a citizen, though both his father and mother were foreigners. In 1583, Antwerp underwent a remarkable siege by the duke of Parma. It was then the most wealthy city in the Netherlands, and had long been the object of his designs; but the difficulties attending the enterprise obliged him to postpone it for a considerable time. In order to succeed, it was necessary to cut off the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> communication of the city with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, Ghent, and all places above and below Antwerp on the Scheld. To effect this, he laid siege to Liskenhousk and Tillo, places of the utmost <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> to the security and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> of the city: both were obstinately defended; and the siege of the latter was raised, after it had been carried on for three months; however, the duke gained several other posts on the river, where he built forts, and greatly annoyed the shipping and trade of the city. He next laid siege to Dendermonde, in order to cut off the communication with Ghent, in which he succeeded by the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REDUCTION">reduction</a> of the town. His next attempt was on Vilvorde: this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> he took by assault, and thereby cut off the communication with Brussels. Finding, however, this method of hemming in the city tedious, and ineffectual while an opening to the mouth of the river remained, he formed a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of building a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> across the Scheld, the extremities of which were to be defended by strong forts and outworks. He began with collecting great quantities of wood at Callo and Fort St <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a>, where he intended the bridge should be built; but his project was for some time retarded by the Antwerpers, who broke <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the dykes, overflowed the whole country, and carried off his magazines by the inundation. Not discouraged by this loss, he applied himself diligently to repair it, and with incredible expedition cut a canal from Steken to Callo, by which he carried off the waters. He then set to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> upon the bridge, and finished it in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> months, without any interruption from the Zealanders. During the building of this bridge, Aldegonde, governor of Antwerp, proposed to build a fort on Couvensteyn dyke, in order to secure that important <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a>, and then <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> down the dyke when the bridge was near finished: but he was violently opposed by certain citizens; who apprehended that their lands and villas would be destroyed by the inundation. This unseasonable opposition, with the negligence of the magistrates, who, because the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a> were high, had not laid in a sufficient stock of corn, occasioned the loss of the city. However, in despite of all the duke of Parma's precaution, the Zealanders found means to throw in a convoy of corn; but the citizens, knowing they would not run the risk of carrying it back again, so cheapened the price, that these bold traders refused ever to bring their goods again to so bad a market. The Antwerpers, having thus through avarice brought on their ruin, began in a short time to suffer by famine; they then pressed the Zealanders to attempt something for their relief, but it was now too late. While the magistrates were deliberating on some means for destroying the bridge, which they might have prevented from being ever completed, one Ginebelli, a Mantuan engineer, offered his services, undertaking at a certain expense to blow it into the air. Even in this extremity the expense was grudged: but <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> at last overcame this obstacle; Ginebelli was furnished with two large vessels, a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of small boats, and every thing necessary. He formed the two large vessels into fire ships, which he set adrift with the stream, deceiving the enemy by means of false fires lighted up in the fleet of small boats. The train of one of the fire ships was expended before the time expected, and she blew up with a terrible <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPLOSION">explosion</a>, but with little damage to the bridge. The other was more successful, carrying off all the Antwerp outworks, setting fire to the whole bridge, and burying above 300 <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> in the ruins it made. The bridge however, was repaired, and the Antwerpers were soon reduced to the greatest straits, and obliged to surrender. It is said that the city of Amsterdam had obstructed every <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> for the relief of Antwerp, hoping to profit by its destruction. By a stipulation between Spain and Holland at the peace of Westphalia in 1648, the navigation of the Scheld was closed. The emperor <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> made an attempt to break this agreement in 1785, but did not succeed. At length, when the place fell into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the French in 1792, the navigation of the river was declared open. Subsequent to this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, docks and store-houses were built, and the port improved. It was surrendered to the allies in 1814, after the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITULATION">capitulation</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, and now begins to revive. It contains at present 61,800 inhabitants. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANUBIS">Anubis</a>, a symbolical deity of the Egyptians, was regarded as the faithful <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OSIRIS">Osiris</a> and of Isis. <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">Temples</a> and priests were consecrated to him, and his image was borne in all <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> ceremonies. Cynopolis, the present Minieh, situated in the Lower Thebais, was built in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of Anubis. The temple wherein he was worshipped no longer subsists. The priests celebrated his festivals there with great pomp, and consecrated the dog to him as his living representation. "Anubis (says Strabo) is the city of dogs, the capital of the Cynopolitan prefecture. These animals are fed there on sacred aliments, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> has decreed them a worship." An event, however, related by Plutarch, brought them into considerable discredit with the people. Cambyses having slain the god <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APIS">Apis</a>, and thrown his body into a field, all animals respected it except the dogs, which alone ate of his flesh. This impiety diminished the popular veneration for them. Cynopolis was not the only city which burned incense on the altars of Anubis. He had chapels in almost all the temples. On solemnities, his image always accompanied those of Isis and Osiris. Rome having adopted the ceremonies of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, the emperor Commodus, to celebrate the Isiac feasts, shaved his head, and himself carried the god Anubis. The statue of this god was either of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASSIVE">massive</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> gilt, as well as the attributes that accompanied him. Anubis signifies gilded. The denomination was mysterious; and the Egyptian priests, it would seem, had not given it without reason. The signification of this emblematical deity is thus explained by Plutarch: "The circle which touches and separates the two hemispheres, and which is the cause of this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a>, receiving the name of horizon, is called Anubis. He is represented under the form of a dog, because that animal watches day and night." St Clemens of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>, who was well informed in the mystic <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a> of the Egyptians, favours this explication. The two dogs, says he, (the two Anubes) are the symbols of two hemispheres which environ the terrestrial globe. He adds in another place: Others pretend that these animals, the faithful guardians of men, indicate the tropics, which <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> on the south and on the north like porters. According to the former of these interpretations, the priests, regarding Anubis as the horizon, gilded his statue; to mark, that this circle, receiving the first rays of the sun, appears sparkling with brightness on his rising, and that at his setting he reflects his last rays upon the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. They said, in their sacred fables, that Anubis was the son of Osiris, but illegitimate. In fact, he only gives to the earth a borrowed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>; and cannot be esteemed, like <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORUS">Horus</a>, as the father of the day, or as the legitimate offspring of Osiris. It may be added, that the visible horizon <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> with the sun, is his inseparable companion. In the latter of these explications, where Anubis represents the tropics, he is also the faithful <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUARDIAN">guardian</a> of Isis and Osiris. In fact, the course of the sun and of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a> is contained between the circles wherein the solstices are performed. They neither deviate to the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> nor left. These limits assigned by the Author of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> might therefore, in hieroglyphic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, be represented by a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> with the head of a dog, who seemed to oppose the passage on the side of the two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a>. The other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, notwithstanding, seems more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a>, and to be more analogous to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> of the priests. Upon the whole, it is reasonable to imagine, that Anubis at first was only a symbolical image, invented by astronomers to give a sensible <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> of their discoveries; that afterwards, the people, accustomed to see it in their temples, which were the depositaries of science, adored it as a deity; and that the priests favoured their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> by connecting it with their religion. The worship of Anubis introduced, that of the dog became his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMBLEM">emblem</a>. Almost all the gods of the Gentiles have originated in this manner.

ANVIL

Pages 500-500

a smith's utensil, serving to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> on to be hammered <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> forged. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> or uppermost <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the anvil, must be very flat and smooth, without flaws, and so hard that a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FILE">file</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> not touch it. At one end there is sometimes a pike, bickern or beak-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, for the rounding of hollow work. The whole is usually mounted on a firm wooden <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLOCK">block</a>.—Forged anvils are better than those of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> work, and the best have the upper part made of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STEEL">steel</a>. Locksmiths have a smaller kind of anvil called the stake, which is used for setting small <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a> work straight. See ANVIL, Supplement.

ANVILLE

Pages 500-500

Jean B. B. D., a celebrated French geographer. See Supplement.

ANXUR

Pages 500-500

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the Volsci, in Latium; called Tarracina, by the Greeks and Latins; Now Terracina; situated on an eminence (Livy, Horace, Sil. Italicus). Anxurias, a citizen of Anxur (Livy). And the epithet Anxurus, a name of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>, worshipped without a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARD">beard</a> at Anxur (<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>). Though others read Axuras, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Axyras, without a razor. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 14. 5. Lat. 41. 18.

AONIDES

Pages 500-500

in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">Mythology</a>, one of the many appellations of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSES">muses</a>; so called from Aonia, a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOEOTIA">Boeotia</a>.

AORASIA

Pages 500-500

in Antiquity, the invisibility of the gods. The word is Greek, ἀορασία, and derived from αὐράσια, priv. and ἰδεῖν, to see. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> with regard to the appearance of the gods to men, was that they never showed themselves <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> to face, but were known from their backs as they withdrew. <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEPTUNE">Neptune</a> assumed the form of Calchas to speak to the two Ajaxes; but they knew him not till he turned his back to leave them, and discovered the god by his majestic step as he went from them. Venus appeared to Æneas in the character of a huntress; but her son knew her not till she departed from him: her <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> was then betrayed by her radiant head, her flowing robe, and her majestic pace.

AORIST

Pages 500-500

among grammarians, a tense peculiar to the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, comprehending all the tenses; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rather, expressing <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> in an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDETERMINATE">indeterminate</a> manner, without any regard to past, present, and future.

AORISTIA

Pages 500-500

in the sceptic <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, denotes that state of the mind wherein we neither assert nor deny anything positively, but only speak of things as seeming <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> appearing to us in such a manner. The aorista is one of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> or terms of scepticism, to which the philosophers of that denomination had continual recourse by way of explication, or subterfuge. Their adversaries, the dogmatists, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> them with dogmatizing, and asserting the principles and positions of their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a> to be true and certain.

AORNUS

Pages 500-501

a very <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> rock of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, having its name from its extraordinary height, as being above the flight of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIRD">bird</a>. Its circuit was about 25 miles, its height 11 furlongs, and the way leading up to the top <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> and narrow. At the bottom, on one side, ran the river <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDUS">Indus</a>; on the top was a fine plain, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of which was covered with a thick wood; the rest arable <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>, with a fountain furnishing abundance of excellent <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. This rock was taken by Alexander the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>, in whose <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> there was a report that <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a> had attempted it in vain; however, according to Arrian, this report was without foundation. It is probable indeed, that it was raised after the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> was taken, in order to magnify Alexander's exploit. While the Macedonian monarch was preparing all things necessary for the siege, an old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> with his two sons, who had <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> lived in a cave near the summit, came and offered to show him a private way of ascending. This being readily accepted, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>, with a considerable body of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>-armed troops, was despatched with them, with orders, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> they succeeded, to intrench themselves strongly upon the rock, in the wood to which the old man was to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> them, before they ventured to attack the Indians. Ptolemy exactly executed his orders; and gave notice, by a lighted torch set upon a pole, that he had got safely up. Upon this, Alexander gave immediate orders for a body of troops to attempt the passage by which the rock was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> ascended; but they were repulsed with great slaughter. He then sent an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> with letters to Ptolemy, desiring him, the next time an attack was made by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> way, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> upon the enemy behind; but in the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time, those who defended the rock attacked Ptolemy with great vigour; but were at last repulsed, though with much difficulty: but the next <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, when Alexander renewed the attack, though Ptolemy attacked the Indians in the rear, the Macedonians were repulsed on both sides. At last, the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> perceiving that the strength of the Indians lay in the straitness and declivity of the way by which they were attacked, caused a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of trees to be felled, and with them filled the cavities between the plain on which... which the Indians were encamped and the highest of his own advanced posts. The Indians at first derided his undertaking; but at length perceiving the ardour with which the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> was carried on, and having felt the effects of the missile weapons of the Macedonians, they sent deputies to propose terms of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITULATION">capitulation</a>. Alexander suspecting that their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> was only to amuse him till they made their escape, withdrew his troops from the avenues. As soon as he knew the Indians were descended, he, with 700 of Ptolemy's light-armed foot, took possession of the deserted rock, and then made a signal for his forces to fall upon the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">flying</a> Indians. They, setting up a loud shout, so terrified the fugitives, that numbers of them fell from the rocks and precipices, and were dashed to pieces, while the greatest part of the remainder were cut off in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a>.

AORTA

Pages 501-501

in Anatomy, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> artery which rises immediately from the left ventricle of the heart, and is from thence distributed to all parts of the body. It is divided into two <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> trunks, distinguished by the epithets ascending and descending. See ANATOMY.

AOUSTA

Pages 501-501
or AOST, a town of Italy, in Piedmont, and capital of the duchy of the same name, a bishop's see, and subject to the king of Sardinia. It is remarkable for several monuments of the Romans, and for the birth of Anselm archbishop of Canterbury. It is seated at the foot of the Alps, on the river Doria. E. Long. 7. 33. N. Lat. 45. 58. Aousta, a territory of Piedmont, with the title of a duchy. It is a valley 30 miles in length, and extends from the pass of St Martin's, near the frontiers of Yvree, to St Bernard. It abounds in pastures, and all sorts of fruits. The capital is of the same name.

AOUTA

Pages 501-501

the name of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> mulberry tree at Otaheite in the South <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, from which a cloth is manufactured that is worn by the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> inhabitants. See the article BARK.

APACHES

Pages 501-501

a people of New <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEXICO">Mexico</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>. They are brave, resolute, and warlike, fond of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, and the invertebrate enemies of tyranny and oppression. Of this disposition the Spaniards had fatal <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> towards the end of the last century, when they revolted against the Catholic <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>, massacred several of his officers, and committed the greatest devastations. Ever since, they have remained the allies, not the subjects of the Spaniards; and the viceroy of Mexico has been obliged to maintain a more formidable garrison, and a greater <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of troops. APÆDUSIA, denotes <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> unskilfulness in what relates to learning and the sciences. Hence also persons uninstructed and illiterate are called apædeute. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> apædeute was particularly used among the French in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Huet; when the men of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> were divided into two factions, one called by way of reproach apædeute, and the others erudit. The apædeute are represented by Huet as persons who, finding themselves either incapable or unwilling to undergo a severe course of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> in order to become truly learned, conspire to deify learning, and turn the knowledge of antiquity into <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIDICULE">ridicule</a>, thus making a merit of their own incapacity. The apædeute in effect were the men of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>; the eruditi the men of study. The apædeute in every thing preferred the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> writers to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>, to supersede the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of studying the latter. The eruditi derided the moderns, and valued themselves wholly on their acquaintance with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>. APAGOGÉ, in Logic. See <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABDUCTION">ABDUCTION</a>. APAGOGÉ, in the Athenian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>, the carrying a criminal taken in the fact to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the accuser was not able to bring him to the magistrate, it was usual to take the magistrate along with him to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> where the criminal lay concealed, or defended himself. APAGOGÉ, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">Mathematics</a>, is sometimes used to denote a progress or passage from one proposition to another; when the first having been once demonstrated, is afterwards employed in the proving of others.

APAGOGICAL DEMONSTRATION

Pages 501-501

an indirect way of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a>, by showing the absurdity of the contrary.

APALACHIAN MOUNTAINS

Pages 501-501

more properly called the Alleghany <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">Mountains</a>, have their southern beginning in the latitude of 34°, extending northerly through the United States, and running nearly <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> with the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> to the latitude of 41° <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>. The length of the chain is about 800 miles. Their height is not <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a>, being in general not above 3000 feet. Their summits, in many <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, form a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> line, neither broken by transverse fissures, nor elevated into peaks. They include properly three <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> four distinct ridges, the westmost of which is called Laurel Mountain, and the eastmost Blue Mountain; and they thus cover a space of a hundred miles in breadth. Between these ridges the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is generally excellent. The valleys are wide, and not steep, and the hills are often wooded to their summits. These mountains divide the United States like a backbone, and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> the course of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> on the one side to the sea, and on the other to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MISSISSIPPI">Mississippi</a>. Chestnuts and small oaks are the trees that principally grow on these mountains, with some chinkapin* and Fagus other small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHRUBS">shrubs</a>. The grass is thin, mixed with vetch and small pease; and in some places there is very little vegetable appearance. The rocks of the Appalachian mountains are mostly of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> grey <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>; some are of a coarse-grained marble like alabaster; others of a metallic lustre: some pieces are in the form of slate, and brittle; others in lumps, and hard; and some appear with spangles, or covered over with innumerable small shining specks, like silver. These frequently appear at the roots of trees when blown <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>. The different spars are found mostly on the highest and steepest parts of the hills, where there is little grass and few trees; but the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the soil between the rocks is generally a dark <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a>-coloured kind of mould, and shallow.

APAMEA

Pages 501-502
or APAMIA, the name of several ancient cities. 1. One of Bithynia, formerly called Myrlea, from Myrus, general of the Colophonians: destroyed by Philip, father of Perseus; and given to his ally Prusias, who rebuilt it, and called it Apamea, from the name of his queen Apama (Strabo). Stephanus says, that Nicomedes Epiphanes, son of Prusias, called it after his mother; and that it had its ancient name from Myrlea, an Amazon. The Romans led a colony thither (Strabo); APA Apamea bo); called Colonia Apamena (Pliny, Appian). The gentilisit name is Apamaeus and Apamenus (Trajan in a letter to Pliny). 2. Another Apamea, called Cibotus, of Phrygia, at some distance from the Meander (Agathodemon); but by a coin of Tiberius, on the Meander. The name is from Apame, mother of Antiochus Soter, the founder, and the daughter of Artabazos (Strabo). The rise, or at least the increase, of Apamea, was owing to the ruins of Celene. The inhabitants were called Apamienses; and, though inland, were worshippers of Neptune. The reason, it has been conjectured, was, that they had suffered often from earthquakes, of which he was the supposed author. Mithridates gave a hundred talents towards the restoration of the city; which, it is said, had likewise been overthrown in the time of Alexander. Their tribute money was remitted to them for five years on the same account under the emperor Tiberius. The subterraneous passage of the Lyens and the other streams, showed that the ground had many cavities; and these, it has been surmised, rendered the region very liable to be shaken. 3. A third, on the confines of Parthia and Media, surnamed Raphane (Strabo, Pliny). 4. A fourth Apamea, a town of Mesene, an island in the Tigris (Pliny, Ammian); where a branch of the Euphrates, called the Royal River, falls into the Tigris (Ptolemy). 5. A fifth in Mesopotamia, on the other side of the Euphrates, opposite to Zeugma on this side, both founded by Seleucus, and joined by a bridge, from which the latter takes its name (Pliny, Isidor. Characenus). 6. A sixth Apamea, now Famia, also in Syria, below the confluence of the Orontes and Marsyas; a strong city, and situated in a peninsula, formed by the Orontes and a lake. "It is here (says Strabo) that the Seleucidae had established the school and nursery of their cavalry." The soil of the neighbourhood, abounding in pasturage, fed no less than 30,000 mares, 300 stallions, and 500 elephants; instead of which, the marshes of Famia at present scarcely afford a few buffaloes and sheep. To the veteran soldiers of Alexander, who here reposed after their victories, have succeeded wretched peasants, who live in perpetual dread of the oppressions of the Turks and the inroads of the Arabs. Apamea was also the ancient name of Pella, in the Decapolis.

APANAGE

Pages 502-502
or APPENNAGE, in the French customs, lands assigned by a sovereign for the subsistence of his younger sons, which revert to the crown upon the failure of male issue in that branch to which the lands are granted.

APANOMIA

Pages 502-502

a town of Santorin, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the Mediterranean <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, called in this <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> by some the sea of Candia. It has a spacious harbour, in the form of a half <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a>; but the bottom is so deep, that ships cannot <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCHOR">anchor</a> there. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 25° 59'. N. Lat. 36° 18'.

APANTHROPY

Pages 502-502

in Medicine, denotes a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of solitude, and aversion for the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of mankind. Apanthropy is by some reckoned among the symptoms, by others among the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> degrees of melancholy; and also passes for an ill indication in leucophlegmatic <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>.

APARINE

Pages 502-502

in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, a synonyme of the urticaria and several other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>.

APARITHMESIS

Pages 502-502

in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">Rhetoric</a>, denotes the answer to the protasis <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> proposition itself. Thus, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the protasis be, Appellandi tempus non erat,—the aparithmesis is, At teum anno plus vixi.

APARTISMENUUS

Pages 502-502

in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, an appellation given to a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>, which comprehended an entire <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> in itself. This is sometimes also written apartemenus, i.e. suspended, as not needing any following verse.

APATHY

Pages 502-502

among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> philosophers, implied an utter privation of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>, and an insensibility of pain. The word is compounded of a priv. and aube, affection. The Stoics affected an entire apathy; they considered it as the highest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> to enjoy a perfect calmness <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> tranquillity of mind, incapable of being ruffled by either <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> or pain. In the first ages of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> adopted the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> apathy, to express a contempt of all earthly concerns; a state of mortification, such as the gospel prescribes. Clemens Alexandrinus, in particular, brought it exceedingly in vogue; thinking hereby to draw the philosophers to Christianity, who aspired after such a sublime pitch of virtue. Quietism is only apathy disguised under the appearance of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>.

APATURIA

Pages 502-502

in antiquity, a solemn feast celebrated by the Athenians in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a>. The word is usually derived from apaturi, fraud. It is said to have been instituted in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of a fraudulent victory obtained by Melanthus, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, over Xanthus, king of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOEOTIA">Boeotia</a>, in a single <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a>, which they agreed upon, to put an end to a debate between them relating to the frontiers of their countries. Hence Budaeus calls it festum deceptoris, "the feast of deceit." Other authors give a different <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ETYMOLOGY">etymology</a> of this feast: They tell us, that the young Athenians were not admitted into the tribes on the third <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> of the apaturia, till their fathers had first sworn that they were their own children; and that till that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, they were supposed, in some <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, to be without fathers, apaturi; whence the feast, say they, took its name. Xenophon, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, informs us, that the relations and friends met on this occasion, and joined with the fathers of the young people who were to be received into the tribes; and that from this <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> the feast took its name; that in apaturia, the a, far from being a privative, being here a conjunctive, signifies the same thing with ovs, together. This feast lasted four days: the first day, those of the same tribe made merry together; and this they called deoptia. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> day, which they called anaepovis, they sacrificed to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a>. The third day, which they called xepovis, such of their young men and maids as were of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> were admitted into their tribes. The fourth day they called eviS.

APAULIA

Pages 502-503

in antiquity, the third <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> solemnity. It was thus called because the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIDE">bride</a>, returning to her father's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, did apavlovivai tu ryvpoiv, lodge apart from the bridegroom. Some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> have the apaulia to have been the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> day of the marriage, viz. that whereon the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> was performed; thus called by way of contradistinction from the first day, which was called pevoula. On the day called ἀπαυλία (whenever that was), the bride presented her bridegroom with a garment called ἀπαυλία.

APAUME

Pages 524-524

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, denotes one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> extended, with the full palm appearing, and the thumb and fingers at full length.

APE

Pages 503-503

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZOOLOGY">Zoology</a>, the general English name of a very numerous <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of animals, the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of which is given at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> under the article SIMIA; comprehending Apes, properly so called, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> such as want tails; and Monkeys and Baboons, or such as have tails, the former <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and the other short, ones. See SIMIA. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a> APE, a name given by Steller to a marine animal which he <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, and is thus described *. "The head appeared like that of a dog, with sharp and upright ears, large eyes, and with both lips bearded: the body round and conoid; the thickest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> near the head; the tail forked; the upper lobe the longest: the body covered with thick <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, gray on the back, reddish on the belly. It seemed destitute of feet. It was extremely wanton, and played a multitude of monkey tricks. It sometimes swam on one side, sometimes on the other side of the ship, and gazed at it with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> admiration. It made so near an approach to the vessel, as almost to be touched with a pole; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> anybody moved, it instantly retired. It would often stand erect for a considerable space, with one-third of its body above <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>; then dart beneath the ship, and appear on the other side; and repeat the same thirty times together. It would frequently arise with a sea plant, not unlike the bottle gourd, toss it up, and catch it in its mouth, playing with it numberless fantastic tricks.

APELYTES

Pages 503-503

Christian heretics in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> century, who affirmed that Christ received a body from the four elements, which at his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> he rendered back to the world, and so ascended into heaven without a body.

APENE

Pages 504-504

in antiquity, a kind of chariot wherein the images of the gods were carried in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESSION">procession</a> on certain days, attended with a solemn pomp, songs, hymns, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DANCING">dancing</a>, &c. It was very rich, made sometimes of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> of silver itself, and variously decorated.

APENNINUS

Pages 504-504

now the Apennine; a mountain, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> ridge of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, running through the middle of Apennium; <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, from <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west to south-west, for 700 miles, in the form of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRESCENT">crescent</a> (Pliny); beginning at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALPS">Alps</a> in Liguria, or the Rivieri di <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENOA">Genoa</a>; and terminating at the strait of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MESSANA">Messana</a>, or at <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REGGIO">Reggio</a>, and the promontory Leucopetra; and separating, as by a back or ridge, the Adriatic from the Tuscan <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> (Pliny, Strabo, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>, Polybius, Vitruvius). This mountain, though <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, is greatly short of the height of the Alps. Its name is Celtic, signifying a high mountain.

APENRADE

Pages 504-504

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a> in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Sleswick, seated at the bottom of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> in the Baltic <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, between Flensbourg and Hadaschleben. It is 25 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> from Sleswick. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 9. 28. N. Lat. 55. 4.

APENZEL

Pages 504-504

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTON">canton</a> of the same name, seated on the river Chus, E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 9. 1. N. Lat. 47. 31. The canton itself, which was allied to the others in 1513, consists only of three <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> four valleys; having the town and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a> of St <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GALL">Gall</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Toggenburg on the west; the lordship of Sax in the canton of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZURICH">Zurich</a>, and that of Gams in the canton of Schweitz, on the south; and the Rheinthal, or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>-valley, on the east. Its greatest length is about thirty miles, and its breadth about twenty. It yields good pasturage, and consequently is not destitute of cattle, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILK">milk</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a>, or cheese. Considerable quantities also of wheat, rye, barley, oats, beans, pease, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>, and wine, are produced in it: besides a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of fruit, wood, and turf; with mineral waters, and warm <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a>. There are many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> in the canton, the highest of which is that called the Hohesantis, or the Hohe Mesmer, which commands a prospect of a prodigious <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>. There are also several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>. The inhabitants, who are partly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>, and partly <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ROMAN_CATHOLICS">Roman Catholics</a>, subsist chiefly by their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, crape, fustian, and thread, or by <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLEACHING">bleaching</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a> of their cattle, butter, cheese, horses, wood, and coal. Of the twenty-three parishes in the canton, four are Popish, and nineteen Protestant. Before the Reformation, the inhabitants were subject to the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABBOT">abbot</a> of St Gall; but they then shook off his yoke, and united themselves with the other cantons: after that, however, there were violent animosities between the Papists and Protestants, the former continually persecuting the latter, till at last, in 1587, by the mediation of the other cantons, the two parties came to an accommodation, by which certain districts were assigned to each party, whereas before they lived promiscuously together: and though these two divisions now constitute but one canton, yet each forms a distinct <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a> or free state, sending its particular representatives to the diets of the confederacy, and having its separate councils and officers. In spirituals, the Papists are subject to the bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSTANCE">Constance</a>, but the Protestants to their own consistory. The canton contains altogether 326 <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles, and 55,414 inhabitants.

APEPSIA

Pages 504-505

(from α <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEGATIVE">negative</a>, and πεπλω, to digest), indigestion. Abstemiousness and excess are alike causes of indigestion. An over-distension of the stomach may in some <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> injure its proper tone; and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> fasting, by inducing a bad <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> in the juices secered into the stomach, renders it feeble, and generates <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>. Hard drinking, and any of the causes of an anorexia, also injure digestion. The columbo root is said to be particularly useful when the stomach is languid, the appetite defective, digestion with difficulty carried on, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> when a nausea with flatulency attends. It is prescribed in substance, with any grateful aromatic, or infused in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MADEIRA">Madeira</a> wine, now and then interposing gentle doses of the tincture of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-RHUBARB">rhubarb</a>. A mixture of mustard seed with the columbo root is of admirable utility in complaints of this kind; particularly where acidity and flatulence prevail much in the prime vis.

APERIENTS

Pages 505-505

in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">Materia Medica</a>, an appellation given to such medicines as facilitate the circulation of the humours by removing obstructions. The five aperient roots of the shops are, smalage, fennel, asparagus, parsley, and butchers <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROOM">broom</a>.

APERTURE

Pages 505-505

in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPTICS">Optics</a>, a round hole in a turned bit of wood <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> plate of tin, placed within the side of a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TELESCOPE">telescope</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MICROSCOPE">microscope</a>, near to the object glass, by means of which more rays are admitted, and a more distinct appearance of the object is obtained.

APERTURES

Pages 505-505
or Apertions, in Architecture, are used to signify doors, windows, &c.

APETALOSE

Pages 505-505
or APETALOUS, among botanists, an appellation given to such plants as have no flower leaves.

APHACA

Pages 505-505

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, the name of a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, situated between <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HELIOPOLIS">Heliopolis</a> and Byblus, near Lebanon; infamous for a temple of Venus, called Aphacitis, near which was a lake, round which fire usually burst forth, and its waters were so heavy, that bodies floated on them. The temple was destroyed by Constantine, as being a school of incontinence, (Eusebius). The name is of Syriac origin, signifying embraces. APHÆRESIS, in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> by which a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYLLABLE">syllable</a> is cut off from the beginning of a word. Thus eiconia, by aphæresis, is written <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONIA">conia</a>; contemnere, temnere; omittere, mittere, &c. A like retrenchment at the end of a word is called APOCOPE. APHÆRESIS, in Medicine, denotes a necessary taking away or removal of something that is noxious.—In <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURGERY">surgery</a>, it signifies an operation whereby something superfluous is taken away.

APHEK

Pages 505-505

the name of several cities mentioned in Scripture. 1. Aphek, in the tribe of Judah, where the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILISTINES">Philistines</a> encamped when the ark was brought from Shiloh, which was taken by them in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, 1 Sam. iv. 1, 2, &c. It is thought to be the same with Aphekah mentioned in Josh. xv. 53. 2. Aphek in the valley of Jezreel, where the Philistines encamped while <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAUL">Saul</a> and his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> were near Jezreel, upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of Gilboa, Sam. xxix. 1, &c. 3. Aphek, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> belonging to the tribe of Asher, near the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of the Sidonians; (Josh. xix. 30, and xiii. 4.). 4. Aphek, a city of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, one of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> in Benhadad's <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, near which the battle was fought between Ahab and Benhadad, wherein the Syrians were worsted; and whereof, as they retreated with precipitation into the city, the walls fell upon them, and crushed in pieces 27,000 (1 Kings xx. 26, et seq.).
