This city lay between <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HELIOPOLIS">Heliopolis</a> and Byblus.

APHELIUM

Pages 505-505
or APHELION, in Astronomy, is that point in any planet's orbit, in which it is farther distant from the sun, being that end of the greater axis of the elliptical orbit of the planet most remote from the focus where the sun is.

APHIASIA

Pages 505-505

(from α, and φω, "I speak,") in the sceptic <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, denotes a state of doubt, wherein a person not knowing what to determine on, it is best for him to be silent. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, aphasia stands opposed to phasis, under which are included both assertion and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEGATION">negation</a>.

APHION

Pages 505-505

KARAHISSART, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATOLIA">Natolia</a>, in Asiatic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a>; it is named Aphion, because it produces a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of opium, called aphion by the Turks. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 30. 26. N. Lat. 38. 35.

APHIS

Pages 505-508

the Puceron, VINE-FRETTER, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> PLANT-LOUSE. See Entomology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Linnaeus enumerates 33 <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of the aphis, all of them inhabitants of particular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, from which their trivial names are taken; as aphis ribi, ulmi, rose, &c. And he adds, that there seems to be a greater variety of plants producing aphides than there are different sorts of this insect. But some late observers have been able to distinguish more than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> the above <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of species; and it is probable that many more remain still to be added, as many of the same kind of plants are found to support two or three quite different sorts of aphides. Thus the plum tree has two sorts very distinct from each other; one of a yellowish green, with a round short body; the other of a bluish green, as it were enamelled with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, and the shape more <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a>. On the gooseberry bush and currant the same aphides may be found; but each of these is inhabited by two very different species: the one being of a dusky green, with a short plump body; the other of paler green, the body more <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TAPER">taper</a>, and transversely wrinkled. The rose tree, again, supports not less than three distinct species: the largest is of a deep green, having <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> legs of a brownish <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a>, with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a> of a very dark <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>, as also are the horns and antennae; a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> sort is of a paler green, has much shorter legs, and a more flat body; the third sort is of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>, its body transversely wrinkled, and is most frequently on the sweet-briar. The extraordinary <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of these insects has for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> past justly excited the wonder and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> of naturalists. They were long ranked among the animals which had been classed with the true <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANDROGYNES">androgynes</a> spoken of by Mr Breynius; for having never been catched copulating, it was hastily concluded that they multiplied without <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPULATION">copulation</a>. This, however, was but a doubt, or at best a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> surmise; but this surmise was believed and adopted by Mr Reaumur; and though he supported it by some observations peculiar to himself, the question remained still undecided, till Mr <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BONNET">Bonnet</a> seemed to have cleared it up in the affirmative, by taking and shutting up a young aphid at the instant of its birth, in the most perfect solitude, which yet brought forth in his sight 95 young ones. The same experiment being made on one of the individuals of this family, that had been tried with its <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>, the new hermit soon multiplied like its <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARENT">parent</a>; and one of this third <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a>, in like manner brought up in solitude, proved no less fruitful than the former. Repeated experiments, in this respect, as far as the fifth or sixth generation, all uniformly presenting the observer with fecund virgins, were communicated to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> Academy of Sciences; when an unforeseen and very strange suspicion, imparted by Mr Trembley to Mr Bonnet engaged him anew in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of still more painful experiments than the foregoing. In a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> which that celebrated observer wrote to him from the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAGUE">Hague</a>, the 27th <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1741, he thus expresses himself: "I formed, since the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of November, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of rearing several generations of solitary pace- rons, in order to see <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they would all equally bring forth young. In <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> so remote from usual circumstances, it is allowed to try all sorts of means; and I argued with myself, Who knows but that one copula- tion might serve for several generations?" This "who knows," to be sure, was next to avouching nothing; but as it came from Mr Trembley, it was sufficient to persuade Mr Bonnet that he had not gone far enough in his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVESTIGATION">investigation</a>. If the fecundity of aphides was owing to the secret copulation suggested by Mr Trem- bley; this copulation served at least five or more succes- sive generations. Mr Bonnet therefore reared to the amount of the tenth generation of solitary aphides, and had the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATIENCE">patience</a> to keep an account of the days and hours of the births of each generation. In short it was discovered, That they are really distinguished by sexes: That there are males and females amongst them, whose amours are the least equivocal of any in the world: that the males are produced only in the tenth generation, and are but few in number: that these, soon arriving at their full growth, copulate with the females: that the virtue of this copulation serves for ten generations: that all these generations, except the first, (from the fecundated eggs), are produced vi- viparous; and all the individuals are females, except those of the last generation, among whom, as we have already observed, some males make their appearance to lay the foundation of a fresh series.—These circum- stances have been confirmed by other naturalists. In particular we have a curious and accurate detail of them by Dr Richardson of Rippon, in the Philosophi- cal Transactions, vol. xi. art. 22, an extract of which we shall here insert, in order to give the reader as full an insight into the nature of these singular insects, as can be done by a mere detail of facts in themselves ut- terly unaccountable. "The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> variety of species which occur in the insects now under consideration, may make an inquiry into their particular nature seem not a little perplexed; having them, however, skilfully reduced under their pro- per genus, the difficulty is by this means considerably diminished. All the insects comprehended under any distinct genus, we may reasonably suppose to partake of one general nature; and, by diligently examining any of the particular species, may thence <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> some insight into the nature of all the rest. With this view I have chosen, out of the various sorts of aphides, the largest of those found on the rose tree; not only as its size makes it the more conspicuous, but as there are few others of so long a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>. This sort appearing early in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, continues late in the autumn; while several are limited to a much shorter <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a>, in conformity to the different trees and plants from whence they draw their nourishment. 1. "If at the beginning of February the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> happens to be so warm as to make the buds of the rose tree swell and appear green; small aphides are frequently to be found upon them, not larger than the young ones in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> when first produced. But there being no old ones to be found at this time of the year, which in summer I had observed to be viviparous, I was formerly not a little perplexed by such appearances, and almost induced to give <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> to the old doctrine of equivocal generation. That the same kind of animal should at one time of the year be viviparous, and at another time oviparous, was an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> I could then by no means entertain. This, however, frequent observa- tion has at last convinced me to be fact; having found those aphides which appear early in the spring, to proceed from small <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> oval eggs, which were deposited on the last year's shoots in autumn; though when it happens that the insects make too early an appearance, I have observed the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> to suffer from the sharp weather that usually succeeds, by which means the rose trees are some years in a manner freed from them. "Those which withstand the severity of the weather seldom come to their full growth before the month of April; at which time they usually begin to breed, after twice casting off their exuviae or outward covering. It appears then that they are all females, which produce each of them a very numerous progeny, and that without having intercourse with any <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MALE">male</a> insect. As I observed before, they are viviparous; and what is equally uncommon, the young ones all come into the world backwards. When they first come from the pa- rent they are enveloped by a thin membrane, having in this situation the appearance of an oval <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGG">egg</a>; which, I apprehend, must have induced Reaumur to suspect that the eggs discovered by Bonnet were nothing more than mere abortions. These egg-like appearances <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AD">ad</a>- here by one extremity to the mother; while the young ones contained in them extend the other; by that means gradually <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> the ruptured membrane over the head and body to the hind feet. During this ope- ration, and for some time after, by means of some- thing glutinous, the fore part of the head adheres to the vent of the parent. Being thus suspended in the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>, it soon frees itself from the membrane in which it was confined, and after its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMBS">limbs</a> are a little strengthened, is set <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> on some tender shoot, and then left to provide for itself. 2. "In the spring months, there appear on the rose trees but two generations of aphides, including those which immediately proceed from the last year's eggs; the warmth of the summer adds so much to their ferti- lity, lity, that no less than five generations succeed one another in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a>. One is produced in May, which casts off its covering; while the months of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> each supply two more, which cast off their coverings three or four times, according to the different warmth of the season. The frequent change of the outward covering is the more extraordinary, as it is the oftener repeated when the insects come the soonest to their growth; which I have sometimes observed to happen in ten days, where warmth and plenty of nourishment have mutually conspired. From which considerations I am thoroughly convinced that these various coverings are not connate with the insect; but that they are, like the scarf skin, successively produced. "Early in the month of June, some of the third generation which were produced about the middle of May, after casting off their last covering, discover four erect wings, much longer than their bodies; and the same is observable in all the succeeding generations, which are produced during the summer months; without, however, distinguishing any diversity of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEX">sex</a>, as is usual in several other kinds of insects. For some time before the aphides come to their full growth, it is easy to discover which of them <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> have wings, by a remarkable fullness of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>, which, in the others, is hardly to be distinguished from the body. When the last covering is rejected, the wings, which were before folded up in a very narrow compass, gradually extend themselves in a most surprising manner, till their dimensions are at last very considerable. But these winged ones have the peculiarity, that the number of them does not seem so much to depend on their original structure, as on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of the nourishment with which they are supplied; it being frequently observed, that those on a succulent shoot have few or none with wings among them, while others of the same generation, on a less tender branch, are most of them winged; as if only the first <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of wings were composed in the former, while nature thought proper to expand them in the latter, that they might be more at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to supply their wants. "The increase of these insects in the summer time is so very great, that, by wounding and exhausting the tender shoots, they would frequently suppress all vegetation, had they not many enemies which restrain them. To enumerate the variety of other insects that in their worm and fly state are constantly destroying them, would exceed the bounds of the present design: there is one, however, so singular in the manner of executing its purpose, that I cannot <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> by it without some further notice. This is a very small black ichneumon fly, with a slender body and very long antennae, which darts its pointed tail into the bodies of the aphides, at the same time depositing an egg in each. This egg produces a worm which feeds upon the containing insect till it attains its full growth; when it is usually changed to that kind of fly from whence it came. In this, however, it is sometimes prevented by another sort of small black fly, which wounds this worm through its <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEARL">pearl</a>-like habitation; and by laying one of its eggs therein, instead of the former fly, produces its own likeness. I must, however, further observe, notwithstanding these insects have many enemies, they are not without friends; if we may consider those as such who are very officious in their attendance, for the good things they expect to to reap thereby. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANT">ant</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEE">bee</a> are both of this kind, collecting the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONEY">honey</a> in which the aphides abound: but with this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a>, that the ants are constant visitors, the bee only when <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> are scarce. To which let me also add, that the ants will suck in the delicious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NECTAR">nectar</a> while the aphides are in the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of discharging it from the anus; but the bees only collect it from the leaves on which this honey <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DEW">dew</a> has fallen. 3. "In the autumn I find three more generations of aphides to be produced; two of which make their appearance in the month of August, and the third usually appears before the middle of September. As the two first differ in no respect from those which we meet with in summer, it would be wasting time to dwell any longer upon them; but the third differing greatly from all the rest, demands our giving it a more serious attention. Though all the aphides which have hitherto appeared were females, in this tenth generation are found several male insects; not that they are by any means so numerous as the females, being only produced by a small number of the former generation. To which I must further add, that I have observed those which produced males, previously to have produced a number of females; which in all respects resembling those already described, I shall decline taking into any further consideration. "The females have at first altogether the same appearance with those of the former generations; but in a few days their <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> changes from a green to a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>, which is gradually converted into an <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a> colour before they come to their full growth. They differ likewise in another respect, at least from those which occur in the summer, that all those yellow females are without wings. The male insects are, however, still more remarkable; their outward appearance readily distinguishing them from the females of this and of all other generations. When first produced, they are not of a green colour like the rest, but of a reddish brown; and have afterwards, when they begin to thicken about the breast, a dark line along the middle of the back. These male insects come to their full growth in about three weeks time, and then cast off their last covering; the whole insect being, after this operation, of a bright yellow colour, the wings only excepted. But after this they soon change to a darker yellow; and in a few hours to a very dark brown; if we except the body, which is something <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> coloured, and has a reddish cast. They are of the winged sort; and the wings, which are white at first, soon become transparent, and at length appear like very fine black <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAUZE">gauze</a>. "The males no sooner come to maturity than they copulate with the females; in which act they are readily discovered, as they remain in conjunction for a considerable time, and are not easily disturbed. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> between them continues the whole month of October, and may be observed at all times of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, though I have found it most frequent about noon; especially when the weather is moderately warm, and the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> overcast. The females, in a day or two after their intercourse with the males, I have observed to lay their eggs; which they usually do near the buds, when they are left to their own choice. Where there are a number crowded together, they of course inter- fere with each other: in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> they will frequently deposite their eggs on other parts of the branches, or even on the spines with which they are beset." These insects are found in great numbers not only on the stems and leaves, but even upon roots of many trees and plants. Those trees that are most loaded with the insects, as already observed, suffer greatly from them. The plant-<a class="xref" href="../1823/vol0.html#article-LICE">lice</a> thrust their sharp-pointed rostrum into the substance of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a> to draw out their sustenance, which warps the stems and leaves, and occasions in the latter cavities underneath, and swellings above; nay, even in some, a kind of hollow <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GALL">gall</a> filled with insects, as is often seen upon elm leaves. It appears astonishing that the slight puncture of so small an animal should so greatly disfigure a plant; but it must be remembered, that plant-lice always live in numerous associations, which increase visibly by the prodigious fruitfulness of those insects; so that although each puncture be slight, yet the number of them is so great, so reiterated, that it is no longer a wonder the leaves should be disfigured. Lovers of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARDENING">gardening</a> and plants are extremely anxious to free and cleanse their trees from this vermine; but their care often proves unavailing, the insect is so fruitful that it soon produces a fresh colony. The best and surest method of extirpating it is to put on the trees infested with them some larva of the plant-louse lion, or aphidivorous flies; for those voracious larvae destroy every day a great number of the insects, and that with so much the more facility, as the latter remain quiet and motionless in the neighbourhood of those dangerous enemies, who range over heaps of plant-lice, which they gradually waste and diminish.

APHLASTUM

Pages 508-508

in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>, a wooden ornament, shaped like a plume of feathers, fastened on the goose's <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> swan's neck used by the ancient Greeks in the heads of their ships. The aplastum had much the same office and effect in a ship that the crest had on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HELMET">helmet</a>. It seems also to have had this further <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, viz. by the waving of a party-coloured ribbon fastened to it, to indicate from what <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> blew.

APHONIA

Pages 508-508

among physicians, signifies a suppression <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> total loss of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>. It is never a primary <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>; but a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of many different disorders. The cure is to be effected by removing the disorder from whence the aphonia proceeds.

APHORISM

Pages 508-508

a maxim <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> principle of a science; or a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> which comprehends a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> in a few words. The word comes from \(\alpha\phiορισμός\), I separate; q.d. a choice or select sentence. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> is chiefly used in medicine and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>. We say the aphorisms of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HIPPOCRATES">Hippocrates</a>, of Sanctorius, of Boerhaave, &c., aphorisms of the civil law, &c.

APHRACTI

Pages 508-508

in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> art, denotes open vessels, without decks <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HATCHES">hatches</a>, furnished only at head and stern with <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> planks, whereon the men stood to fight.

APHRODISIA

Pages 508-508

in antiquity, festivals kept in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of Venus, the most remarkable of which was that celebrated by the Cyprians. At this solemnity several mysterious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a> were practised: all who were initiated to them offered a piece of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> to Venus as a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HARLOT">harlot</a>, and received as a token of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a>'s favour a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, and a \(\varphiαλλος\); the former, because salt is a concretion of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, to which Venus was thought <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APHRODITE">Aphrodite</a> to owe her birth; the latter, because she was the goddess of wantonness.

APHRODISIACS

Pages 508-508

among physicians, medicines which were supposed to increase the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of semen, and create an inclination to venery. APHRODITA. See <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HELMINTHOLOGY">HELMINTHOLOGY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

APHRODITE

Pages 508-508

in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">Mythology</a>, a name of Venus, derived from \(\alpha\phiορισμός\), <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FROTH">froth</a>; because, according to the poets, Venus is supposed to have been produced from the froth <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> foam of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>.

APHRONITRE

Pages 508-508

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, a name given by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> to a particular kind of natrum.

APHTHAE

Pages 508-508

in Medicine, small, round, and superficial ulcers arising in the mouth. See MEDICINE <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. APITHARTODOCETÆ, a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a>, sworn enemies of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHALCEDON">Chalcedon</a>. The word is derived from \(\alpha\phiορισμός\), incorruptible, and \(\deltaοξα\), I imagine; and was given them, because they imagined the body of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ was incorruptible and impassible, and not capable of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. They arose among the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUTYCHIANS">Eutychians</a>, and made their appearance in the year 535.

APIARY

Pages 508-508

a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where bees are kept. See the article <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEE">BEE</a>. See also APIARY, SUPPLEMENT.

APIASTER

Pages 508-508

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a>, the trivial name of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of the merops. See MEROPS, ORNITHOLOGY <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

APICES

Pages 508-508

in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, the same with ANTHERÆ. APICIUS. There were at Rome three of that name, famous for their gluttony. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> is the most celebrated of the three. He lived under Tiberius, spent immense sums on his belly, and invented <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> sorts of cakes which bore his name. He kept as it were a school of gluttony at Rome. After having spent two millions and a half in entertainments, finding himself very much in debt, he examined into the state of his affairs; and seeing that he had but 2,500,000 livres remaining, he poisoned himself, out of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPREHENSION">apprehension</a> of starving with such a sum. He had prostituted himself when very young to Sejanus.

APINA

Pages 508-508
or Apinae, a town of Apulia, built by Diomedes, as was also Trice (Pliny). Apinae and Tricea is a proverbial saying for things trifling and of no value (Martial); and Apinarii was the appellation for triffers or bullions, (Trebellius Pollio).

APION

Pages 508-508

a famous grammarian, born in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, was a professor at Rome in the reign of Tiberius. He had all the arrogance of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> pedant, and amused himself with difficult and insignificant inquiries. One of his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> works are his Antiquities of Egypt.

APIS

Pages 508-511

in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">Mythology</a>, a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> worshipped by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Egyptians at <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMPHIS">Memphis</a>. It was an ox, having certain exterior marks; in which animal the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OSIRIS">Osiris</a> was supposed to subsist. The animal had the preference to all others, as being the symbol of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a>, the improvement of which that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> had so much at heart. According to several learned writers on the Egyptian <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, Apis was only a symbolical deity. "Among the animals consecrated to ancient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a> (says <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMMIANUS_MARCELLINUS">Ammianus Marcellinus</a>), Mnevis and Apis are the most celebrated; the first is an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMBLEM">emblem</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a>..." cond of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a>." Porphyry tells us, that Apis bore the characteristic signs of the two stars; and Macrobius, who confirms this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, adds, that he was equally consecrated to them both. This bull, become the object of public <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADORATION">adoration</a>, it may be supposed, could not be born like other animals; accordingly the priests published that his origin was celestial. "An Apis is seldom born," says Pomponius Mela.) He is not produced by the ordinary laws of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a>. The Egyptians say he owes his birth to celestial fire." Plutarch explains this passage: "The priests pretend that the moon diffuses a generative influence, and as soon as a cow which takes the bull is struck by it, she conceives an Apis. Accordingly we discover in him the signs of that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STAR">star</a>. Such were the fables industriously spread by those who presided over the divine institutions. The vulgar, to whom this emblematical deity presaged abundance, received them eagerly, and implicitly believed them. Pliny has described the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> which distinguished this sacred bull: "A <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> spot, resembling a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRESCENT">crescent</a>, on the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> side, and a lump under the tongue, were the distinguishing marks of Apis." When a cow, therefore, which was thought to be struck with the rays of the moon, produced a calf, the sacred guides went to examine it, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they found it conformable to this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>, they announced to the people the birth of Apis, and fecundity. "Immediately (says Ælian) they built a temple to the new god, facing the rising sun, according to the precepts of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a>, where they nourished him with <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILK">milk</a> for four months. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> expired, the priests repaired in pomp to his habitation, and saluted him by the name of Apis. They then placed him in a vessel magnificently decorated, covered with rich <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TAPESTRY">tapestry</a>, and resplendent with <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, and conducted him to Nilopolis, singing hymns, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> perfumes. There they kept him for forty days. During this space of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, women alone had permission to see him, and saluted him in a particular manner. After the inauguration of the god, in this <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, he was conveyed to Memphis with the same retinue, followed by an innumerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of boats sumptuously decked out. There they completed the ceremonies of his inauguration, and he became sacred to all the world. Apis was superbly lodged, and the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where he lay was mystically called the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a>. Strabo having visited his <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, thus describes it: "The edifice where Apis is kept, is situated near the temple of Vulcan. He is fed in a sacred apartment, before which is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> in which they keep the cow that produced him, occupies one of its sides. Sometimes, to satisfy the curiosity of strangers, they make him go out into this court. One may see him at all times through a window; but the priests produce him also to public view." Once a year (says Solinus) they present a heifer to him, and the same <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> they kill her. A bull, born in so marvellous a manner, must be possessed of supernatural knowledge. Accordingly the priests published, that he predicted future events by gestures, by motions, and other ways, which they construed according to their fancy. "Apis (says Pliny) has two <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a> called Beds, which served as an augury for the people. When they come to consult him, if he enters into a particular one, it is a favourable <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRESAGE">presage</a>, and fatal if he passes into the other. He gives answers to individuals by taking food from their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. He refused that offered him by Germanicus, who died soon after." It would be unjust to conclude, that this respectable writer gave <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> to such auguries. He relates the opinion of the Egyptians, and contents himself with citing facts without offering his judgment. Such was the installation of Apis. His anniversary was always celebrated for <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> days. The people assembled to offer sacrifices to him, and what is extraordinary, oxen were immolated on the occasion. This solemnity did not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> without prodigies. Ammianus Marcellinus, who has collected the testimonies of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, relates them in these words: "During the seven days in which the priests of Memphis celebrate the birth of Apis, the crocodiles forget their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> ferocity, become gentle, and do no harm to anybody." This bull, however, so honoured, must not exceed a mysterious term fixed for his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. "Apis (says Pliny) cannot live beyond a certain <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of years. When he has attained that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> they drown him in the fountain of the priests; for it is not permitted, adds Ammianus Marcellinus, to let him prolong his life beyond the period prescribed for him by the sacred books." When this event happened, he was embalmed, and privately let <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> into the subterraneous places destined for that purpose. In this circumstance, the priests announced that Apis had disappeared; but when he died a natural <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, before this period arrived, they proclaimed his death, and solemnly conveyed his body to the temple of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERAPIS">Serapis</a>. "At Memphis was an ancient temple of Serapis which strangers were forbidden to approach, and where the priests themselves only entered when Apis was interred. It was then (says Plutarch) that they opened the gates called Lethe and Cocytus (of oblivion and lamentation), which made a harsh and piercing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOUND">sound</a>." Ammianus Marcellinus, and Solinus, paint with great energy the general despair of the Egyptians, who with cries and lamentations demanded another Apis from heaven. According to Plutarch, the term prescribed for the life of Apis was 25 years; which number marked a period of the sun and of the moon, and the bull was consecrated to these two bodies. Syncellus, in his Chronography, when he comes down to the 32d <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHARAOH">Pharaoh</a>, called Aseth, says, "before Aseth, the solar year consisted of 360 days. This prince added five to complete its course. In his reign a calf was placed amongst the gods, and named Apis." And in the Bibliotheca of Fabricius we have the following passage: "It was customary to inaugurate the kings of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> at Memphis, in the temple of Apis. They were here first initiated in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a>, and were religiously invested; after which they were permitted to bear the yoke of the god through the town to a place called the Sanctuary, the entrance of which was prohibited to the profane. There they were obliged to swear that they would neither insert months nor days in the year, and that it should remain composed of 365 days, as had been established by the ancients." From these facts, Mr Savary, in his Letters on Egypt, infers, that Apis was the tutelar divinity of the new form given to the solar year, and of the cycle of 25 years, discovered at the same same time. This deity, besides, had a marked relation to the swelling of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NILE">Nile</a>, as is testified by a great number of historians. The new moon which followed the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> solstice, was the era of this phenomenon, on which the eyes of every body were fixed: And Pliny speaks as follows on this subject: "Apis had on his right side a white mark, representing the crescent: This mark (continues Ælian) indicated the commencement of the inundation." If Apis possessed the characteristic signs which proved his divine origin, he promised fertility and abundance of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. It seems demonstrated, therefore, Mr Savary adds, that this sacred bull, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUARDIAN">guardian</a> of the solar year of 365 days, was also regarded as the genius who presided over the overflowing of the river. The priests, by fixing the course of his life to 25 years, and by making the installation of a new Apis concur with the renewal of the period above mentioned, had probably perceived, as the result of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> meteorological observations, that this revolution always brought about abundant seasons. Nothing was better calculated to procure a favourable reception of this emblematical deity from the people, since his birth was a presage to them of a happy inundation, and of all the treasures of teeming <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. The solemnity of his inauguration was called Apparition. That which was renewed every year towards the 12th <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 13th of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> Payn, which corresponds with the 17th or 18th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a>, was called the birth of Apis. It was a time of rejoicing, which Ælian describes in the following manner: "What festivals! what sacrifices take place in Egypt at the commencement of the inundation! It is then that all the people celebrate the birth of Apis. It would be tedious to describe the dances, the rejoicings, the shows, the banquets, to which the Egyptians abandon themselves on this occasion, and impossible to express the intoxication of joy which breaks forth in all the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>." These observations Mr Savary thinks further confirmed by the name of this respectable bull; Apis, in the Egyptian tongue, signifying number, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>. This epithet perfectly characterizes an animal established as the guardian of the solar year, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYPE">type</a> of the cycle of 25 years, and the presage of a favourable inundation. Monsieur Huet, bishop of Avranches, has endeavoured to prove that Apis was a symbolical image of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRIARCH">patriarch</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a>, and has supported his opinion with all his erudition. Dr Bryant apprehends that the name of Apis was an Egyptian term for a father; that it referred to the patriarch <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOAH">Noah</a>; and that the crescent which was usually marked on the side of the animal, was a representation of the ark. Apis, or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEE">Bee</a>. See Entomology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>, and Bee. Apium, Parsley. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> Index. Apivorous, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a>, a synonyme of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of falco. See Falco, Ornithology Index. Apluda. See Botany Index. Apobatana, the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a> of Media, and where the kings kept their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a> (Isiodorus Characenus); supposed to be the same with <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECBATANA">Ecbatana</a>. Apobateron, in antiquity, a valedictory speech or poem made by a person on departing out of own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and addressed to his friends or relations. Apoabathra, a place near <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SESTOS">Sestos</a> (Strabo); the landing place where <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-XERXES">Xerxes</a>'s ships were frozen and stuck in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ICE">ice</a> (<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUSTATHIUS">Eustathius</a>). Apocalypse, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVELATION">Revelation</a>, the name of one of the sacred books of the New <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, containing revelations concerning several important doctrines of Christianity. The word is Greek, and derived from ἀποκαλύπτω, to reveal or discover. This book, according to Irenæus, was written about the year 96 of Christ, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATMOS">Patmos</a>, whither St John had been banished by the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Domitian. But Sir <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Newton places the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> of it earlier, viz. in the time of Nero. Some <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> this book to the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a>-heretic Cerinthus: but the ancients unanimously ascribed it to John, the son of Zebedee, and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> of James; whom the Greek fathers called the Divine, by way of eminence, to distinguish him from the other evangelists. This book has not, at all times, been esteemed canonical. There were many churches in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, as St Jerome informs us, which did not receive it: neither is it in the catalogue of canonical books prepared by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of Laodicea, nor in that of St Cyril of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>: but Justin, Irenæus, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORIGEN">Origen</a>, Cyprian, Clemens of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>, Tertullian, and all the fathers of the fourth, fifth, and the following centuries, quote the Revelation as a book then acknowledged to be canonical. The Alogians, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MARCIONITES">Marcionites</a>, Cerdonians, and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUTHER">Luther</a> himself, rejected this book: but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a> have forsaken Luther in this particular; and Beza has strongly maintained against his objections, that the Apocalypse is authentic and canonical. The Apocalypse consists of twenty-two chapters. The three first are an instruction to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> of the seven churches of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASIA_MINOR"><a class="</a>xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINOR">Minor</a>. The fifteen following chapters contain the persecutions which the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> was to suffer from the Jews, heretics, and Roman emperors. Next St John prophesies of the vengeance of God, which he <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> against those persecutors, against the Roman empire, and the city of Rome; which, as the Protestants suppose, he describes under the name of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BABYLON">Babylon</a> the great whore, seated upon seven hills. In the last place, the 19th, 20th, 21st, and 22d chapters, describe the triumph of the church over its enemies, the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> of the Lamb, and the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> of the church triumphant. "It is a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of this prophecy (says Sir Isaac Newton), that it should not be understood before the last <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of the world; and therefore it makes for the credit of the prophecy, that it is not yet understood. The folly of interpreters has been to foretel times and things by this prophecy, as if God designed to make them prophets. By this rashness they have not only exposed themselves, but brought the prophecy also into contempt. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of God was much otherwise: He gave this and the prophecies of the Old Testament, not to gratify men's curiosities, by enabling them to foreknow things; but that, after they were fulfilled, they might be interpreted by the events; and his own <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">providence</a>, not the interpreters, be then manifested thereby to the world. And there is already so much of the prophecy fulfilled, that as many as will take pains Apocalypse pains in this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a>, may see sufficient instances of God's providence. There have been several other works published under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Apocalypse. Sozomen mentions a book used in the churches of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALESTINE">Palestine</a>, called the Apocalypse or Revelation of St <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>. He also mentions an Apocalypse of St Paul; which the Coptic retain to this day. Eusebius also speaks of both these Apocalypses. St Epiphanius mentions an Apocalypse of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADAM">Adam</a>; Nicephorus, an Apocalypse of Esdras; Gratian and Cedrenus, an Apocalypse of Moses, another of St Thomas, and another of St Stephen; St Jerome, an Apocalypse of Elias. Porphyry, in his life of Plotin, makes mention of the Apocalypse or Revelations of Zoroaster, Zostrian, Nicothaeus, Allogenes, &c.

APOCOPE

Pages 511-511

among grammarians, a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> which cuts off a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYLLABLE">syllable</a> from the end of a word; as ingenii for ingeni.

APOCRISARIUS

Pages 511-511

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> antiquity, a sort of resident in an imperial <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, in the name of a foreign <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> bishop, whose office was to negotiate, as proctor at the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, in all ecclesiastical causes in which his principals might be concerned. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> of the office seems to have been in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Constantine, or not <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> after, when, the emperors being become <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, foreign churches had more occasions to promote their suits at court than formerly. However, we find it established by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> in the time of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTINIAN">Justinian</a>. In <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of this officer, almost every <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> had its Apocrisarius, or resident, in the imperial city. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of Apocrisary became at length appropriated to the pope's <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGENT">agent</a>, or munio, as he is now called; who resided at Constantinople, to receive the pope's despatches, and the emperor's answers. The word is formed from ἀποκριναι, to answer.

APOCRYPHA

Pages 511-511
or APOCRYPHAL BOOKS, such books as are not admitted into the canon of Scripture, being either not acknowledged as divine, or considered as spurious. The word is Greek; and derived from από, and κρύπτω, to hide or conceal. When the Jews published their sacred books, they gave the appellations of canonical and divine only to such as they then made public; such as were still retained in their archives they called apocryphal, for no other reason but because they were not public; so that they might be really sacred and divine, though not promulgated as such. Thus, in respect of the Bible, all books were called apocryphal which were not inserted in the Jewish canon of Scripture. Vossius observes, that, with regard to the sacred books, none are to be accounted apocryphal, except such as had neither been admitted into the synagogue nor the church, so as to be added to the canon, and read in public. The Protestants do not only reckon those books to be apocryphal which are esteemed such in the church of Rome, as the prayer of Manasses king of Judah, the third and fourth books of Esdras, St Barnabas's epistle, the book of Hermos, the addition at the end of Job, and the 151st psalm; but also Tobit, Judith, Esther, the book of Wisdom, Jesus the son of Sirach, Baruch the prophet, the Song of the Three Children, Apocrypha the History of Susannah, the History of Bel and the Dragon, and the first and second books of the Maccabees. It is now pretended that these books were not received by the Jews, or so much as known to them. None of the writers of the New Testament cite or mention them; neither Philo nor Josephus speak of them. The Christian church was for some ages an utter stranger to these books. Origen, Athanasius, Hilary, Cyril of Jerusalem, and all the orthodox writers, who have given catalogues of the canonical books of Scripture, unanimously concur in rejecting these out of the canon. And for the New Testament, they are divided in their opinions, whether the epistle to the Hebrews, the epistle of St James, and the second epistle of St Peter, the second and third epistles of St John, the epistle of St Jude, and the Revelation, are to be acknowledged as canonical or not. The Protestants acknowledge such books of Scripture only to be canonical as were so esteemed to be in the first ages of the church; such as are cited by the earliest writers among the Christians as of divine authority, and after the most diligent inquiry were received and so judged to be by the council of Laodicea. The several epistles above mentioned, and the book of Revelation, whatever the sentiments of some particular persons are or may have been of them, are allowed by all the reformed churches to be parts of the canon of the New Testament. The apocryphal books, however, according to the sixth article of the church of England, are to be read for example of life and instruction of manners; but it doth not apply them to establish any doctrine. APOCYNUM. See DOGS-BANE, BOTANY Index. APODECTÆ, in antiquity, a denomination given to ten general receivers appointed by the Athenians to receive the public revenues, taxes, debts, and the like. The apodectæ had also a power to decide controversies arising in relation to money and taxes, all but those of the most difficult nature and highest concern, which were reserved to the courts of judicature. APODECTÆI, in the Athenian government, officers appointed to see that the measures of corn were just.

APODES

Pages 511-511

in the Linnean system, the name of the first order of fishes, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> those which have no belly fins. See <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

APODICTICAL

Pages 511-511

among philosophers, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> importing a demonstrative <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> systematical method of teaching.

APODOSIS

Pages 511-511

in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">Rhetoric</a>, makes the third <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of a complete exordium, being properly the application <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> restriction of the protasis. The apodosis is the same with what is otherwise called axiosis; and stands opposed to protasis: e.g., protasis, all branches of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> are necessary for a student; eatesene, so that, without these, he can never make any considerable <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>;

APODYTERIUM

Pages 511-512

in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a>, the apartments where persons dressed and undressed.

APOGEE

Pages 512-512

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, that point in the orbit of a planet which is at the greatest distance from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. The apogee of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> is that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-EARTH_S">earth's</a> orbit which is at the greatest distance from the sun; and consequently the sun's apogee, and the earth's aphelion, are one and the same point.

APOGGIATURA

Pages 527-527

in Music, a small <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOTE">note</a> inserted by the practical musician, between two others, at some distance.

APOLIDES

Pages 512-512

in antiquity, those condemned for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> to the public works, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> exiled into some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, and thus divested of the privileges of Roman citizens.

APOLLINARIAN GAMES

Pages 512-512

in Roman antiquity, were instituted in the year of Rome 542. The occasion was a kind of oracle delivered by the prophet Marcus after the fatal <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> at Cannae, declaring that to expel the enemy, and cure the people of an infectious <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> which then prevailed, sacred games were to be annually performed in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a>; the prætor to have the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of them, and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMVIRI">decemviri</a> to offer sacrifices after the Grecian rite. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> ordered that this oracle should be observed the rather, because another of the same Marcus, wherein he had foretold the overthrow at Cannae, had come true; for this reason, they gave the prætor 12,000 asses out of the public cash to defray the solemnity. There were sacrificed an ox to Apollo, as also two <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> goats, and a cow to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LATONA">Latona</a>; all with their horns gilt. Apollo had also a collection made for him, besides what the people who were spectators gave voluntarily. The first prætor by whom they were held was P. Cornelius Sylla. For some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> they were moveable <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> indistinct; but at length were fixed, under P. Licinius Varus, to the fifth of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>, and made perpetual. The men, who were spectators at these games, wore garlands on their heads; the women performed their devotions in the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a> at the same time, and at last they caroused together in the vestibules of their houses, the doors standing open. The Apollinarian games were merely scencical; and at first only observed with singing, piping, and other sorts of music; but afterwards there were also introduced all manner of mountebank tricks, dances, and the like: yet so as that they still remained scencical; no chariot races, wrestling, or the like laborious exercises of the body, being ever practised at them.

APOLLINARIANS

Pages 512-512

APOLLINARISTS, called also by Epiphanius Dimaritæ, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> heretics, who denied the proper <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> of Christ, and maintained that the body which he assumed was endowed with a sensitive, and not a rational, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>, but that the Divine <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">Nature</a> supplied the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of the intellectual principle in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>. This <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a> derived its name from Apollinaris, bishop of Laodicea, in the fourth century. The Apollinarians have been <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with other opinions, such as, the Millenarian and Sabellian, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRE_EXISTENCE">pre-existence</a> of the body of Christ, and the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> of his Deity; but <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> writers are not agreed with respect to these and other particulars. Their doctrine was first condemned by a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a> in the year 362, and afterwards in a more formal manner by a council at Rome in 375; and by another council in 378, which deposed Apollinaris from his bishopric. Notwithstanding all, his doctrine spread through most of the churches of the east: and his followers were subdivided into various sects. In 388, The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Theodosius enacted a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>, forbidding them to hold assemblies, to have any <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICS">ecclesiastics</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>, or to dwell in cities. The rigorous execution of this law, in concurrence with the decrees of different councils, reduced them to a very small <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, and their doctrine had no <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>.

APOLLINARIS

Pages 512-512
CAIUS SULPICIUS, a very learned grammarian, born at Carthage, lived in the 2d century, under the Antonines; he is supposed to be the author of the verses which are prefixed to the comedies of Terence, and contain the arguments of them. He had for his successor in the profession of grammar Helvius Pertinax, who had been his scholar, and was at last emperor.

APOLLINARIS SIDONIUS

Pages 512-512
CAIUS LOLLIUS, an eminent Christian writer and bishop in the 5th century, was born of a noble family in France. He was educated under the best masters, and made a prodigious progress in the several arts and sciences, but particularly in poetry and polite literature. After he had left the schools, he applied himself to the profession of war. He married Papianilla, the daughter of Avitus, who was consul, and afterwards emperor, by whom he had three children. But Majorianus in the year 457 having deprived Avitus of the empire, and taken the city of Lyons, in which our author resided, Apollinaris fell into the hands of the enemy. However, the reputation of his learning softened Majorianus's resentment, so that he treated him with the utmost civility, in return for which Apollinaris composed a panegyric in his honour; which was so highly applauded, that he had a statue erected to him at Rome, and was honoured with the title of Count. In the year 467 the emperor Anthemius rewarded him for the panegyric which he had written in honour of him, by raising him to the post of governor of Rome, and afterwards to the dignity of a patrician and senator, and erecting a statue to him. But he soon quitted these secular employments for the service of the church. The bishopric of Clermont being vacant in 472 by the death of Eparchus, Apollinaris, who was then only a layman, was chosen to succeed him without any interest or solicitation on his part, in which see he acted with the greatest integrity. Clermont being besieged by the Goths, he animated the people to the defence of that city, and would never consent to the surrender of it; so that, when it was taken about the year 480, he was obliged to retire; but he was soon restored by Evagrius king of the Goths, and continued to govern the church as he had done before. He died in peace the 21st of August 487; and his festival is still observed in the church of Clermont, where his memory is held in great veneration. He is esteemed the most elegant writer of his age, both in prose and verse. He wrote a great many little pieces; but preserved none but those which he thought were worthy of being continued down to posterity. He collected himself the nine books which we have remaining of his letters. His chief pieces in poetry are the three panegyrics upon the emperors Avitus, Majorianus, and Anthemius. The rest of them are a collection of poems addressed to his friends upon particular subjects. His letters contain a variety of particulars relating to polite literature and profane history.

APOLLINARIUS

Pages 512-513

Claudius, a learned bishop of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HIERAPOLIS">Hierapolis</a>, who, about the year 170, presented to Marcus Aurelius an excellent Apology for the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>. APOLLINARIUS the Younger, thus called to distinguish him from his father, called Apollinaris the Elder, was at first lector <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> reader of Laodicea, and afterwards bishop of that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>. He was universally esteemed the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, both for learning and piety, and a most accurate and nervous defender of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> against all its enemies: but notwithstanding this, on his advancing some opinions that were not approved, he was anathematized as an heretic by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> general <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of Constantinople in 381.

APOLLO

Pages 513-515

in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">Mythology</a>, a Pagan deity worshipped by the Greeks and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>. Cicero mentions four of this name: the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> of whom was the son of Vulcan; the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> a son of Corybas, and born in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a>; the third an Arcadian, called Nomian, from his being a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEGISLATOR">legislator</a>; and the last, to whom the greatest <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> is ascribed, the son of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LATONA">Latona</a>. Apollo had a variety of other names, either derived from his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> attributes, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> places where he was worshipped. He was called the Healer, from his enlivening warmth and cheering influence; Pæan, from the pestilential heats: to signify the former, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> placed the Graces on his <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>; and for the latter, a bow and arrows in his left: Nomius, or the shepherd, from his fertilizing the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and thence sustaining the animal <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREATION">creation</a>: Delius, from his rendering all things manifest: Pythius, from his victory over Python; Lycias, Phobus, and Phaneta, from his purity and splendour. As Apollo is almost always confounded by the Greeks with the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, it is no wonder that he should be dignified with so many attributes. It was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> for the most glorious object in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, whose influence is felt by all creation, and seen by every animated <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of it, to be adored as the fountain of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. The power of healing diseases being chiefly given by the ancients to medicinal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> and vegetable productions, it was natural to exalt into a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>, the visible cause of their growth. Hence he was also styled the God of Physic; and that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> heat which cheers and invigorates all nature, being transferred from the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> body to the mind, gave rise to the idea of all mental effervescence coming from this god; hence, likewise, poets, prophets, and musicians, are said to be Numine afflati, inspired by Apollo. Whether Apollo was ever a real personage, or only the great luminary, many have doubted. Indeed, Vossius has taken great pains to prove this god to be only a metaphorical being, and that there never was any other Apollo than the sun. "He was styled the Son of Jupiter (says this author), because that god was reckoned by the ancients the author of the world. His mother was called Latona, a name which signifies hidden; because, before the sun was created, all things were wrapped up in the obscurity of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHAOS">chaos</a>. He is always represented as beardless and youthful, because the sun never grows old or decays. And what else can his bows and arrows imply, but his piercing beams?" And he adds, that all the ceremonies which were performed to his honour, had a manifest relation to the great source of light which he represented. Whence (he concludes) it is in vain to seek for any other divinity than the sun, which was adored under the name of Apollo." However, though this be in general true, yet it does appear, from many <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> in ancient authors, that there was some illustrious personage named Apollo, who, after his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOTHEOSIS">apotheosis</a>, was taken for the sun; as <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OSIRIS">Osiris</a> and Orus in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, whose existence cannot be called in question, were, after their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, confounded with the sun, of which they became the symbols, either from the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> and splendour of their reigns, or from a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a> that their souls had taken up their residence in that luminary. Of the four <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLOS">Apollos</a> mentioned by Cicero, it appears that the three last were Greeks, and the first an Egyptian; who, according to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a>, was the son of Osiris and Isis, and called Orus. Pausanias is of the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> as Herodotus, and ranks Apollo among the Egyptian divinities. The testimony of Diodorus Siculus is still more express; for in speaking of Isis, after saying that she had invented the practice of medicine, he adds, that she taught this art to her son Orus, named Apollo, who was the last of the gods that reigned in Egypt. It is easy to trace almost all the Grecian fables and mythologies from Egypt. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the Apollo of the Greeks was said to be the son of Jupiter, it was because Orus the Apollo of the Egyptians had Osiris for his father, whom the Greeks confounded with Jupiter. If the Greek Apollo was reckoned the god of eloquence, music, medicine, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, the reason was, that Osiris, who was the symbol of the sun among the Egyptians, as well as his son Orus, had there taught those liberal arts. If the Greek Apollo was the god and conductor of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSES">Muses</a>, it was because Osiris carried with him in his expedition to the Indies singing women and musicians. This <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> might be carried on still further; but enough has been said to prove that the true Apollo was that of Egypt. To the other perfections of this divinity the poets have added <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">grace</a>, and the art of captivating the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-EAR">ear</a> and the heart, no less by the sweetness of his eloquence, than by the melodious sounds of his lyre. However, with all these accomplishments, he had not the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TALENT">talent</a> of captivating the fair with whose charms he was enamoured. But the amours and other adventures related of this god during his residence on earth, are too numerous, and too well known, to be inserted here. His musical contests, however, being more connected with the nature of this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, must not be wholly unnoticed. To begin, therefore, with the dispute which he had with <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAN">Pan</a>, that was left to the arbitration of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIDAS">Midas</a>. Pan, who thought he excelled in playing the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLUTE">flute</a>, offered to prove that it was an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> superior to the lyre of Apollo. The challenge was accepted; and Midas, who was appointed the umpire in this contest, deciding in favour of Pan, was rewarded by Apollo, according to the poets, with the ears of an ass for his stupidity.—This fiction seems founded upon <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>. Midas, according to Pausanias, was the son of Gordius and Cybele; and reigned in the Greater <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHRYGIA">Phrygia</a>, as we learn from Strabo. He was possessed of such great <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RICHES">riches</a>, and such an inordinate desire of increasing them by the most contemptible parsimony, Apollo that, according to the poets, he converted whatever he touched into <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>. However, his talent for accumulation did not extend to the acquirement of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> and knowledge in the fine arts; and, perhaps, his dulness and inattention to these provoked some musical poets to invent the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FABLE">fable</a> of his decision in favour of Pan against Apollo. The scholiast upon <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOPHANES">Aristophanes</a>, to explain the fiction of his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> ears, says, that it was designed to intimate that he kept spies in all parts of his dominions. Marsyas, another player on the flute, was still more unfortunate than either Pan or his admirer Midas. This Marsyas, having engaged in a musical dispute with Apollo, chose the people of Nisa for judges. Apollo played at first a simple <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> upon his instrument; but Marsyas, taking up his pipe, struck the audience so much by the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOVELTY">novelty</a> of its tone, and the art of his performance, that he seemed to be heard with more <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> than his rival. Having agreed upon a second <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> of skill, it is said that the performance of Apollo, by accompanying the lyre with his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>, was allowed greatly to excel that of Marsyas upon the flute alone.
