Marsyas, with indignation, protested against the decision of the judges; urging that he had not been fairly vanquished according to the rules stipulated, because the dispute was concerning the excellence of their several instruments, not their voices; and that it was wholly unjust to employ two arts against one. Apollo denied that he had taken any unfair advantages of his antagonist, since Marsyas had employed both his mouth and fingers in performing upon his instrument; so that, if he was denied the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of his mouth, he would be still more disqualified for the contention. The judges approved of Apollo's reasoning, and ordered a third trial. Marsyas was again vanquished; and Apollo, inflamed by the violence of the dispute, flayed him alive for his presumption. See Marsyas. Pausanias relates a circumstance concerning this contest, that had been omitted by Diodorus, which is, that Apollo accepted the challenge from Marsyas, upon condition that the victor should use the vanquished as he pleased. Diodorus informs us, that Apollo soon repenting of the cruelty with which he had treated Marsyas, broke the strings of the lyre, and by that means put a stop, for a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, to any further progress in the practice of that new instrument. The next incident to be mentioned in the history of Apollo is his defeat of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SERPENT">serpent</a> Python. The waters of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEUCALION">Deucalion</a>'s deluge, says Ovid, which had overflowed the earth, left a slime from whence sprung innumerable monsters; and among others the serpent Python, which made great havoc in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> about <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARNASSUS">Parnassus</a>. Apollo, armed with his darts, put him to death; which, physically explained, implies, that the heat of the sun having dissipated the noxious steams, these monsters soon disappeared: or if this fable be referred to history, the serpent was a robber, who haunting the country about <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DELPHOS">Delphos</a>, and very much infesting those who came hither to sacrifice; a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, who bore the name of Apollo, or one of the priests of that god, put him to death. This event gave rise to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> of the Pythian games, so frequently mentioned in the Grecian history; and it was from the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEGEND">legend</a> of Apollo's victory over the Python that the god himself acquired the name of Pythius, and his priestess that of Pythia. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Delphos, where the famous <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-ORACLES">oracles</a> were so long delivered, was frequently styled Pytho. As Apollo was the god of the fine arts, those who cultivated them were called his sons. Of this <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> was Philammon of Delphos, whom the poets and mythologists make the twin-<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> of Autolycus, by the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NYMPH">nymph</a> Chione, and Apollo and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a>. It is pretended that both these divinities were favoured by the nymph on the same <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, and that their sires were known from their different talents. Philammon, a great poet and musician, was reported to be the offspring of the god who presides over those arts; and Autolycus, from the craftiness and subtlety of his disposition, was said to have sprung from Mercury, god of theft and fraud. Philammon is one of the first, after Apollo, upon fabulous record, as a vocal performer, who accompanied himself with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> of the lyre: his son was the celebrated Thamyris. See Thamyris. There can be no doubt but that Apollo was more generally revered in the Pagan world than any other deity; having, in almost every region of it, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>, oracles, and festivals, as innumerable as his attributes: the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WOLF">wolf</a> and hawk were consecrated to him, as symbols of his piercing eyes; the crow and the raven, because these birds were supposed to have by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTINCT">instinct</a> the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> of prediction; the laurel, from a persuasion that those who slept with some branches of that tree under their heads received certain vapours, which enabled them to prophecy. The cock was consecrated to him, because by his crowing he announces the rising of the sun; and the grasshopper on account of his singing faculty, which was supposed to do honour to the god of music. Most of the ancient poets have celebrated this tuneful insect, but none better than Anacreon, Ode xliii. <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a> says that the grasshopper sings all <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> without food, like those men who, dedicating themselves to the Muses, forget the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> concerns of life. The swan was regarded by the ancients as a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIRD">bird</a> sacred to Apollo in two capacities; first, as being, like the crow and raven, gifted with the spirit of prediction; and, secondly, for his extraordinary vocal powers. The sweetness of his song, especially at the approach of death, was not only extolled by all the poets of antiquity, but by historians, philosophers, and sages; and to call a great writer the swan of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, was a full acknowledgement of his sovereignty. Thus Horace calls <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PINDAR">Pindar</a> the Theban swan. Plutarch, who was himself a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> of Apollo, impressed with the highest respect and veneration for him and for music, in his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIALOGUE">dialogue</a> upon that art, makes one of his interlocutors say, that an <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> so useful and charming could never have been the work of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, but must have originated from some god, such as Apollo, the inventor of the flute and lyre, improperly attributed to Hyagnis, Marsyas, Olympus, and others; and the proofs he urges in support of this assertion, show, if not its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, at least that it was the common and received opinion. All dances and sacrifices, says he, used in honour of Apollo, Apollo, are performed to the sound of flutes: the statue of this god at Delos, erected in the time of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>, had in its right hand a bow; and on the left stood the three Graces, who were furnished with three kinds of instruments, the lyre, the flute, and the syrinx. The youth also who carries the laurel of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-TEMPE">Tempe</a> to Delphos, is accompanied by one playing on the flute; and the sacred presents formerly sent to Delos by the Hyperboreans, were conducted thither to the sound of lyres, flutes, and shepherds <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a>. He supports these facts by the testimonies of the poets Alceus, Alcman, and Corinna. It seems as if the account of Apollo could not be concluded by any thing that is left to offer on the subject, so properly, as by part of the celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HYMN">hymn</a> of Callimachus, which during many ages was performed and heard by the most polished people on the globe with the utmost <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> zeal, at the festivals instituted to this god. Ha! how the laurel, great Apollo's tree, And all the cavern, shakes! Far off, far off, The man that is unhallow'd: for the god Approaches. Hark! he knocks; the gates Feel the glad impulse, and the sever'd bars Submissive clink against their brazen portals. Why do the Delian palms incline their boughs, Self-mov'd; and hovering swans, their throats releas'd From native silence, carol sounds harmonious? Begin, young men, the hymn: let all your harps <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">Break</a> their inglorious silence; and the dance, In mystic numbers trod, explain the music. But first, by ardent pray'r and clear <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LUSTRATION">lustration</a>, Purge the contagious spots of human weakness: Impure, no mortal can behold Apollo. So may you flourish, favour'd by the god, In youth with happy nuptials, and in age With silver hairs, and fair <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> of children; So lay foundations for aspiring cities, And bless your spreading colonies increase. Pay sacred reverence to Apollo's song; Lest wrathful the far-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SHOOTING">shooting</a> god emit His fatal arrows. Silent nature stands: And seas subside, obedient to the sound Of Io! Io Pæan! nor <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DARES">dares</a> Thetis Longer bewail her lov'd <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACHILLES">Achilles</a>' death. For Phœbus was his foe. Nor must sad Niobe In fruitless sorrow persevere, or weep, Ev'n thro' the Phrygian marble. Hapless mother! Whose fondness could compare her mortal offspring To those which fair Latona bore to Jove. Io! again repeat ye, Io Pæan! Recite Apollo's praise till night draws on, The ditty still unfinish'd; and the day Unequal to the godhead's attributes Various, and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> copious of your songs. Sublime at Jove's right hand Apollo sits, And thence distributes honour, gracious <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>, And theme of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> perpetual. From his robe Flows light ineffable! his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HARP">harp</a>, his quiver, And Lactian bow, are gold: with <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> sandals His feet are shod. How rich! how beautiful! Beneath his steps the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> min'ral rises; And earth reveals her treasures. Youth and beauty Eternal deck his cheek; from his fair head Perfumes distil their sweets; and cheerful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, His dutous handmaid, through the air improv'd With lavish hand diffuses scents ambrosial. The spearman's arm by thee, great god, directed, Sends forth a certain wound. The laurel'd bard, Inspir'd by thee, composes verse immortal. Taught by thy art divine, the sage physician Eludes the urn, and chains or exiles death. Perpetual fires shine hallow'd on thy altars, When annual the Carnean feast is held; The warlike Libyans, clad in armour, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> The dance; with clanging swords and shields they <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> The dreadful <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>: In the chorus join Their women; <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>, but beautiful: such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a> To thee well pleasing. The monstrous Python Durst tempt thy wrath in vain; for dead he fell, To thy great strength and golden arms unequal, Io! while thy unerring hand elanc'd Another and another dart, the people Joyfully repeated Io! Io Pæan! Elance the dart, Apollo; for the safety And health of man, gracious thy mother bore thee! APOLLO Belvidere, ranked the first in the first class of ancient <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a>, and so called from having been placed in the Belvidere of the Vatican at Rome by Pope Julius II., where it remained for 300 years, and till Rome was taken and plundered by the French in 1797. This celebrated statue was found in the ruins of ancient Antium about the end of the 15th century. The <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a> is unknown. The excellence of this statue, which has attracted universal admiration, consists in the elegance and sublimity of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>. Beside this, there are many ancient statues referred to the first which are distinguished by peculiar beauties.

APOLLODORUS

Pages 515-516

a celebrated painter of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, about 408 years before the birth of Christ, was the first who invented the art of mingling colours, and of expressing the lights and shades. He was admired also for his judicious choice of subjects, and for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> and strength of colouring surpassed all the masters that went before him. He excelled likewise in statuary. APOLLODORUS the Athenian, a famous grammarian, the son of Asclepiades and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of Aristarchus. He wrote many works not now extant; but his most famous production was his Bibliotheca, concerning the origin of the gods. This <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> consisted of 24 books, but only three are now in being. Several other pieces of his are to be found in Fabricius's Bibliotheca Graeca. There were various other persons of this name. Scipio Testi, a Neapolitan, has written a treatise of the Apolodoruses, which was printed at Rome in 1555; and Dr Thomas <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-GALE">Gale</a> published a work of the same kind in 1675.

APOLLONIA

Pages 516-516

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a promontory of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, upon the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUINEA">Guinea</a>, near the mouth of the river Mancu.

APOLLONIUS

Pages 516-516

a Pythagorean <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, born at Tyana in Cappadocia, about the beginning of the first century. At 16 years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> he became a strict observer of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYTHAGORAS">Pythagoras</a>’s rules, renouncing wine, women, and all sorts of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>; not wearing shoes, letting his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> grow, and wearing nothing but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>. He soon after set up for a reformer of mankind, and chose his habitation in a temple of Æsculapius, where he is said to have performed many wonderful cures. Philostratus has wrote the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of Apollonius, in which there are numberless fabulous stories recounted of him. We are told that he went five years without speaking; and yet, during this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, that he stopped many seditions in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CILICIA">Cilicia</a> and Pamphylia; that he travelled, and set up for a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEGISLATOR">legislator</a>; and that he gave out he understood all languages, without having ever learned them: that he could tell the thoughts of men, and understood the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-ORACLES">oracles</a> which birds gave by their singing. The Heathens were fond of opposing the pretended <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a> of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> to those of our Saviour; and by a treatise which Eusebius wrote against one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIEROCLES">Hierocles</a>, we find that the drift of the latter, in the treatise which Eusebius refutes, seems to have been to draw a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> betwixt <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ and Apollonius, in which he gives the preference to this philosopher. M. du <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIN">Pin</a> has wrote a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONFUTATION">confutation</a> of Philostratus’s life of Apollonius. Apollonius wrote some works, viz. four books of Judicial Astrology; a treatise upon the Sacrifices, showing what was proper to be offered to each deity; and a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of letters; all of which are now lost.

APOLLOS

Pages 516-517

in Scripture <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a Jew of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>, who came to Ephesus during the absence of St Paul, who was gone to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a> (Acts xviii. 24.). Apollos was an eloquent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, and well versed in the Scriptures; and as he spoke with zeal and fervour, he taught diligently the things of God; but knowing only the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a> of John, he was no more than a catechumen, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> one of the lowest order of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, and did not as yet distinctly know the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a> of the Christian doctrine. However, he knew that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ Christ was the Messiah, and declared himself openly to be his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a>. When therefore he was come to Ephesus, he began to speak boldly in the synagogue, and to show that Jesus was the Christ. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AQUILA">Aquila</a> and Priscilla having heard him, took him home with them; instructed him more fully in the ways of God; and baptized him, probably in the name of Jesus Christ. Some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> after this he had a mind to go into Achaia; and the brethren having exhorted him to undertake this journey, they wrote to the disciples, desiring them to receive him. He arrived at Corinth; and was there very useful in convincing the Jews out of the Scriptures, and demonstrated to them that Jesus was the Christ. Thus he watered what St Paul had planted in this <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> (1 Cor. iii. 6.); but the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> fondness which his disciples had for his person had like to have produced a schism; some saying, I am of Paul; others, I am of Apollos; I am of Cephas." However, this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a>, which St Paul speaks of in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> last quoted, did not prevent that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APOSTLE">apostle</a> and Apollos from being closely united by the bands of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a>. Apollos hearing that the apostle was at Ephesus, went to meet him, and was there when St Paul wrote the first epistle to the Corinthians; wherein he testifies that he had earnestly entreated Apollos to return to Corinth, but hitherto had not been able to prevail with him; that nevertheless, he gave him room to hope that he would go when he had an opportunity. St Jerome says, that Apollos was so dissatisfied with the division which had happened upon his account at Corinth, that he retired into <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a> with Zena, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>; and that this disturbance having been appeased by the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> which St Paul wrote to the Corinthians, Apollos returned to this city, and was bishop thereof. The Greeks make him bishop of Duras; others say, he was bishop of Iconium in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHRYGIA">Phrygia</a>; and others, that he was bishop of Caesarea.

APOLLYON

Pages 517-517

a Greek word that signifies the destroyer, and answers to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> Abaddon. St John in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVELATION">Revelation</a> (ix. 11.) says, that an angel having opened the bottomless pit, a thick <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a> issued out of it; and with this smoke locusts, like horses, prepared for <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, and commanded by the angel of the bottomless pit, called in Hebrew Abaddon, but in the Greek Apollyon.

APOLOGETIC

Pages 517-517

APOLOGETICAL, something said <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> written, by way of excuse or apology, for any <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> or person. The Apologetic of Tertullian is a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> full of strength and spirit. He there vindicates the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> from all that had been objected to them; particularly from the abominable crimes said to be perpetrated at their meetings, and their want of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> and fidelity to their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. The ground of this last <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACCUSATION">accusation</a> was, their refusing to take the accustomed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OATHS">oaths</a>, and swear by the tutelar gods of the empire.—Tertullian addresses his Apologetic to the magistrates of Rome, the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Severus being then absent.

APOLOGUE

Pages 517-517

in matters of literature, an ingenious method of conveying instruction by means of a feigned relation called a moral <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FABLE">fable</a>. The only <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between a parable and an apologue is, that the former, being drawn from what passes among mankind, requires <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NARRATION">narration</a>; whereas the apologue, being taken from the supposed actions of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUTES">brutes</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> even of things inanimate, is not tied <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the strict rules of probability. Aesop's fables are a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODEL">model</a> of this kind of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>.

APOLOGY

Pages 517-517

a Greek <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a>, literally importing an excuse <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of some person or <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a>.

APOMELI

Pages 517-517

among <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> physicians, a decoction of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONEY">honey</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a>, much used as a detergent, promoter of stool, urine, &c.

APOMYOS DEUS

Pages 517-517

in the Heathen <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">mythology</a>, a name under which <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> was worshipped at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIS">Elis</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a> as well as Jupiter at the Olympic games. These deities were supplicated under this name, to destroy <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> drive away the vast <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of flies which always attended at the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> sacrifices; and in those who accompanied the Olympic games, the first was always to the Apomos, or Myiagrus Deus, that he might drive away the flies from the rest. The usual sacrifice was a bull.

APONEUROSIS

Pages 517-517

among physicians, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> sometimes used to denote the expansion of a nerve <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> tendon in the manner of a membrane; sometimes for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> off a nerve; and, finally, for the tendon itself.

APONO

Pages 517-518
PETER D', one of the most famous philosophers and physicians of his age, born in the year 1350, in a village about four miles from Padua. He studied some time at Paris, and was there promoted to the degree of doctor in philosophy and physic. When he came to practise as a physician, he is said to have insisted on very large sums for his visits: we are not told what he demanded for the visits he made in the place of his residence; but it is affirmed that he would not attend the sick in any other place under 150 florins a-day; and when he was sent for by Pope Honorius IV., he demanded 400 ducats for each day's attendance. He was suspected of magie, and prosecuted by the Inquisition on that account. "The common opinion of almost all authors (says Naude) is, that he was the greatest magician of his age; that he had acquired the knowledge of the seven liberal arts, by means of the seven familiar spirits, which he kept enclosed in a crystal; and that he had the dexterity to make the money he had spent come back into his purse." The same author adds, that he died before the process against him was finished, being then in the 80th year of his age; and that, after his death, they ordered him to be burnt in effigy, in the public place of the city of Padua; designing thereby to strike a fear into others of incurring the like punishment, and to suppress the reading three books which he had wrote; the first being the Heptameron, which is printed at the end of the first volume of Agrrippa's work; the second, that which is called by Trithemius Elucidareum necromanticum Petri de Albano; and the last, that which is entitled by the same author, Liber experimentorum mirabilium de annulis secundum xxviii. mansiones lunae. His body being secretly taken up by his friends, escaped the vigilance of the inquisitors, who would have burnt it. It was removed several times, and was at last placed in the church of St Augustin, without an epitaph or any mark of honour. The most remarkable book which Apono wrote, was that which procured him the surname of Conciliator; he wrote also a piece entitled De medicina omnimoda. There is a story told of him, that, having no well in his house, he caused his neighbour's to be carried into the street by devils, when. when he heard they had forbidden his maid fetching water thence. He had much better (says Mr Bayle) have employed the devils to make a well in his own house, and have stopped up his neighbour's; or, at least, transported it into his house, rather than into the street. APONOGETON. See Botany Index.

APONUS

Pages 518-518

a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAMLET">hamlet</a> near Patavium, with warm <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a>. It was the birthplace of Livy, (Martial;) and is now called <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBANO">Albano</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 10. N. Lat. 45. 15.

APOPEMPTIC

Pages 518-518

in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HYMN">hymn</a> addressed to a stranger on his departure from a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> to his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> had certain holidays, wherein they took leave of the gods with apopemptic songs, as supposing them returning each to his own country. The deities having the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRONAGE">patronage</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> places, it was but <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> to divide their presence, and allow some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to each. Hence it was, that among the Delians and Milesians we find feasts of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a>, and among the Argians feasts of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIANA">Diana</a>, called Epidemiea, as supposing these deities then more peculiarly resident among them. On the last <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> of the feast they dismissed them, following them to the altars with apopemptic hymns.

APOPHASIS

Pages 518-518

a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">Rhetoric</a>, by which the orator, speaking ironically, seems to wave what he would plainly insinuate; as, Neither <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> I mention those things; which, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> I should, you notwithstanding could neither confute, nor speak against them.

APOPHLEGMATIZANTS

Pages 518-518

in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHARMACY">Pharmacy</a>, medicines proper to clear the head from superfluous phlegm, whether by spitting <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> by the nose.

APOPHYGE

Pages 518-518

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, a concave <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RING">ring</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLUMN">column</a>, lying above or below the flat member. The French call it le conge d'en bas or d'en haut: the Italians, cavo di basso or di sopra; and also il vivo di basso. The apophyge originally was no more than the ring, or ferril, at first fixed on the extremities of wooden pillars, to keep them from splitting; which afterwards was imitated in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>.

APOPHYSIS

Pages 518-518

in Anatomy, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> protuberance of a bone. See Anatomy.

APOPLEXY

Pages 518-518

a distemper in which the patient is suddenly deprived of all his senses, and of voluntary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>. See Medicine <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

APOPTHHEGM

Pages 518-518

a short, sententious, and instructive remark, pronounced by a person of distinguished character. Such is that of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CYRUS">Cyrus</a>: He is unworthy to be a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a>, who is not better than his subjects. <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">Or</a> this: He, that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> not take care of his own business, will be forced to take care of that of others. Or that of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTAXERXES">Artaxerxes</a> Mnemon, when reduced to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HUNGER">hunger</a> by the loss of his baggage: How much <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> have I hitherto lived a stranger to? Or that of Cato, Homines nihil agendo discunt <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MALE">male</a> agere. Or, finally, that of Augustus, Festina lente. The apophthegms of Plutarch are well known.

APORIA

Pages 518-518

is a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">Rhetoric</a>, by which the speaker shows, that he doubts where to begin for the multitude of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> what to say in some strange and ambiguous thing; and doth, as it were, argue the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> with himself. Thus Cicero says, Whether he took them from his fellows more impudently, gave them to a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HARLOT">harlot</a> more lasciviously, removed them from the Roman people more wickedly, or altered them more presumptuously, I cannot well declare.

APORON

Pages 518-518
or APORIME, a problem difficult to resolve, and which has never been resolved, though it be not, in itself, impossible. The word is derived from ἀπορέω, which signifies something very difficult, and impracticable; being formed from the privative a, and πορέω, passage. Such we conceive the quadrature of the circle; the duplicature of the cube; the trisection of an angle, &c. When a question was proposed to any of the Greek philosophers, especially of the sect of Academists; if he could not give a solution, his answer was ἀπορέω, I cannot see through it.—This word is also used by some law writers for an inexplicable speech or discourse.

APOSFRAGISMA

Pages 518-518

(from ἀπο, and φραγμός, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEAL">seal</a>), in antiquity, the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> of a seal. It was forbid among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> to have the figure or image of God on their rings and seals. To this purpose the precept of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYTHAGORAS">Pythagoras</a>, Ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ εἰσελθε μὴ προσφραγίσθητε! But in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, this was little regarded; it was usual enough to have the figures of Egyptian and other deities, as well as of heroes, monsters, friends, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>, and even <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUTES">brutes</a>, on their dactyls or <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RING">ring</a>-seals. Thus Caesar had the image of Venus, Pollio of Alexander, Augustus of the Sphinx, Pompey of a frog, Lentulus of his grandfather, &c.

APOSIOPESIS

Pages 518-518

in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">Rhetoric</a>, otherwise called reticency and suppression; a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, by which a person really speaks of a thing, at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> that he makes a show as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he would say nothing of it. The word comes from ἀποσιωπάω, I am silent.—It is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> used to denote the same with <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELLIPSIS">ELLIPSIS</a>. Jul. Scaliger distinguishes them. The latter, according to him, being only the suppression of a word; as me, me; adsum qui feci; the former, the omitting to relate some <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a>; as, Dixerat, atque illam media inter talia ferro Collapsam adspicunt. where the poet does not mention how Dido killed herself.—This figure is of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> to keep up the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a> and sublimity of a discourse.

APOSTATA CAPIENDO

Pages 519-519

in the English <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, a writ that formerly lay against a person who, having entered into some order of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a>, broke out again, and wandered up and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>.

APOSTATE

Pages 519-519

one who deserts his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. Among the Romanists, it signifies a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> who, without a legal dispensation, forsakes a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> order of which he had made profession. **A POSTERIORI**, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> demonstration **à posteriori**. See **DEMONSTRATION**.

APOSTII

Pages 519-521

in matters of literature, the same with a marginal <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOTE">note</a>. **APPOSTLE** properly signifies a messenger <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> person sent by another upon some business; and hence, by way of eminence, denotes one of the disciples commissioned by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ to preach the gospel. Our blessed <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> selected twelve out of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of his disciples to be invested with the apostleship. Their names were Simon <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>, Andrew, James the greater, John, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a>, Bartholomew, Thomas, Matthew, James the less, Jude, surnamed Lebbeus or Thaddeus, Simon the Canaanite, and Judas Iscariot. Of these, Simon, Andrew, James the greater, and John, were fishermen; and Matthew a publican, or receiver of the public revenue; of what profession the rest were, we are not told in Scripture: though it is probable they were fishermen. There are various conjectures as to the reason of our Saviour's making choice of twelve apostles. The most probable is, that it might be in allusion to the twelve patriarchs, as the founders of their several tribes; or to the twelve <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> heads or rulers of those tribes, of which the body of the Jewish <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> consisted. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> seems to be countenanced by what our Saviour tells his apostles, that "when the Son of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> shall sit on the throne of his <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a>, they also shall sit upon twelve thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel." Our Lord's first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> to his apostles was in the third year of his public ministry, about eight months after their solemn <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a>; at which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> he sent them out by two and two. They were to make no provision of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> for their subsistence in their journey, but to expect it from those to whom they preached. They were to declare, that the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of heaven, or the Messiah, was at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>; and to confirm their doctrine by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a>. They were to avoid going either to the Gentiles or to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAMARITANS">Samaritans</a>, and to confine their preaching to the people of Israel. In obedience to their <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">Master</a>, the apostles went into all the parts of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALESTINE">Palestine</a> inhabited by the Jews, preaching the gospel, and working miracles. The evangelical <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> is silent as to the particular circumstances attending this first preaching of the apostles; and only informs us, that they returned, and told their Master of all that they had done. Their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> commission, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> before our Lord's ascension into heaven, was of a more extensive and particular <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. They were now not to confine their preaching to the Jews, but to "go and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost." Accordingly they began publicly, after our Lord's ascension, to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> the office of their ministry, working miracles daily in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of their mission, and making <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> numbers of converts to the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>. This alarmed the Jewish Sanhedrim; whereupon the apostles were apprehended, and being examined before the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> and elders, were commanded not to preach any more in the name of Christ. But this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INJUNCTION">injunction</a> did not terrify them from persisting in the duty of their calling; for they <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> daily, in the temple, and in private houses, teaching, and preaching the gospel. After the apostles had exercised their ministry for twelve years in Palestine, they resolved to disperse themselves in different parts of the world, and agreed to determine by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">lot</a> what parts each should take. According to this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a>, St Peter went into Pontus, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GALATIA">Galatia</a>, and those other provinces of the Lesser <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>. St Andrew had the vast northern countries of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SCYTHIA">Scythia</a> and Sogdiana allotted to his portion. St John's was partly the same with Peter's, namely the Lesser Asia. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APOSTLE">Apostle</a>. St Philip had the Upper Asia assigned to him, with some parts of Scythia and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLCHIS">Colchis</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a> Felix fell to St Bartholomew's share. St Matthew preached in Chaldea, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARTHIA">Parthia</a>. St Thomas preached likewise in Parthia; as also to the Hyrcanians, Bactrians, and Indians. St James the less continued in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>, of which <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> he was bishop. St Simon had for his portion <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CYRENE">Cyrene</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBYA">Libya</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MAURITANIA">Mauritania</a>; St Jude, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a> and Mesopotamia; and St Matthias, who was chosen in the room of the traitor Judas, Cappadocia and Colchis. Thus, by the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DISPERSION">dispersion</a> of the apostles, Christianity was very early planted in a great many parts of the world. We have but very short and imperfect accounts of their travels and actions. In order to qualify the apostles for the arduous task of converting the world to the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, they were, in the first <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, miraculously enabled to speak the languages of the several nations to whom they were to preach; and, in the second place, were endowed with the power of working miracles, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONFIRMATION">confirmation</a> of the doctrines they taught; gifts which were unnecessary, and therefore ceased, in the after ages of the church, when Christianity came to be established by the civil power. St Paul is frequently called the apostle, by way of eminence; and the apostle of the Gentiles, because his ministry was chiefly made <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of for the conversion of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENTILE">Gentile</a> world, as that of St Peter was for the Jews, who is therefore styled the apostle of the circumcision. The several apostles are usually represented with their respective badges or attributes; St Peter with the keys; St Paul with a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>; St Andrew with a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> or saltier; St James <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINOR">minor</a> with a fuller's pole; St John with a cup, and a winged <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SERPENT">serpent</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">flying</a> from it; St Bartholomew with a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a>; St Philip with a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STAFF">staff</a>, whose upper end is formed into a cross; St Thomas with a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANCE">lance</a>; St Matthew with a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HATCHET">hatchet</a>; St Matthias with a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> axe; St James <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">major</a> with a pilgrim's staff and a gourd bottle; St Simon with a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a>; and St Jude with a club. This appellation was also given to the ordinary travelling ministers of the church.—Thus St Paul, in the Epistle to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, xvii. 7, says, "Salute Andronicus and Junia, my kinsmen and fellow prisoners, who are of note among the apostles." It was likewise a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> given to those sent by the churches to carry their alms to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> of other churches. This usage they borrowed from the synagogues, who called those whom they sent on this message by the same name; and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FUNCTION">function</a> or office itself ἀποστόλος, apostle, q.d. mission. Thus St Paul, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> to the Philippians, tells them that Epaphroditus their apostle had ministered to his wants, ch. ii. 25. The appellation is given in like manner to those persons who first planted the Christian faith in any place. Thus Dionysius of Corinth is called the apostle of France; Xavier, the apostle of the Indies, &c. In the East Indies the Jesuit missionaries are also called apostles. Apostle is also used among the Jews for a kind of officer anciently sent into the several parts and provinces in their jurisdiction, by way of visitor or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMISSARY">commissary</a>, to see that the laws were duly observed, and to receive the moneys collected for the reparation of the temple, and the tribute payable to the Romans. Apostle. The Theodosian code, lib. 14. De Judaeis, calls those apostoli, qui <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AD">ad</a> exigendum aurum atque argentum, à patriarcha certo tempore diriguntur. Julian the apostate remitted the Jews the apostle, ἐπισκόπος; that is, as he himself explains it, the tribute they had been accustomed to send him. These apostles were a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> below the officers of the synagogue called patriarchs, and received their commissions from them. Some authors observe, that St Paul had borne this office; and that it is this he alludes to in the beginning of the epistle to the Galatians; as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he had said, Paul, no longer an apostle of the synagogue, nor sent thereby to maintain the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> of Moses, but now an apostle and envoy of Jesus Christ, &c. St Jerome, though he does not believe that St Paul had been an apostle of this kind, yet imagines that he alludes to it in the passage just cited. Apostle, in the Greek liturgy, is particularly used for a book containing the epistles of St Paul, printed in the order wherein they are to be read in churches, through the course of the year. Another book of the like kind, containing the Gospels, is called Εὐαγγέλιον, Gospel.—The apostle, of late days, has also contained the other canonical epistles, the Acts of the Apostles, and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVELATION">Revelation</a>. Hence it is also called Acts of the Apostles, Πράξεις Ἀποστόλων; that being the first book in it. Apostle is also thought by many to have been the original name for <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>, before the denomination bishop was appropriated to their order. Thus Theodoret says expressly, the same persons are anciently called promiscuously both bishops and presbyters, whilst those who are now called bishops were called apostles. In the arsenal of Bremen, there are twelve pieces of cannon called the Twelve Apostles, on a supposition that the whole world must be convinced, and acquiesce in the preaching of such apostles. Apostles Creed: a formula, or summary of the Christian faith, drawn up, according to Ruffinus, by the apostles themselves: who, during their stay at Jerusalem, soon after the Lord's ascension, agreed upon this creed, as a rule of faith, and as a word of distinction by which they were to know friends from foes. Baronius, and some other authors, conjecture, that they did not compose it till the second year of the reign of Claudius, a little before their dispersion. As to their manner of composing it, some fancy, that each apostle pronounced his article, which is the reason of its being called symbolum <a class="xref" href="../1823/vol0.html#article-APOSTOLICUM">apostolicum</a>, it being made up of sentences jointly contributed, after the manner of persons paying each their club (symbolum), or share of a reckoning. But there are reasons which may induce us to question whether the apostles composed any such creed as this. For, first, Neither St Luke in the Acts, nor any other <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> writer before the 5th century, make any mention of an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> of the apostles in order to the composing of a creed. Secondly, The fathers of the three first centuries, in disputing against the heretics, endeavoured to prove that the doctrine contained in this creed was the same which the apostles taught; but they never pretend that the apostles composed it. Thirdly, If the apostles had made this creed, it would have been the same in all churches, and in all ages; and and all authors would have cited it after the same manner. But the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> is quite otherwise. In the second and third ages of the church, there were as many creeds as authors, and one and the same author sets <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the creed after a different manner in several places of his works; which is an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> that there was not at that time any creed which was reputed to be the apostles. In the fourth century Ruffinus compares together the three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> creeds of the churches of Aquileia, Rome, and the East, which differ very considerably in the terms. Besides, these creeds differed not only in the terms and expressions, but even in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>, some of which were omitted in one or other of them; such as those of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> into <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HELL">hell</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a> of the saints, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> everlasting. From these reasons it may be gathered, that though this creed may be said to be that of the apostles in regard to the doctrines contained therein, yet it is not to be referred to them as the authors and first composers of it. Who was the true author of it, is not easy to determine; though its great antiquity may be inferred from hence, that the whole form, as it now stands in the English liturgy, is to be found in the works of St <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBROSE">Ambrose</a> and Ruffinus, the former of whom flourished in the third century, and the latter in the fourth century. The primitive <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, in regard they always concealed this and their other <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a>, did not publicly recite the creed, except at the times of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a>; which, unless in case of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a>, were only in Easter and Whitsuntide. The constant repeating of it was not introduced into the church till the end of the fifth century; about which time Petrus Gnapheus, bishop of Antioch, prescribed the recital of it every time divine <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> was performed.

APOSTOLARE

Pages 521-521

APOSTOLICARE, apostolizing, in some middle <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> writers, denotes the being preferred to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of pope.

APOSTOLATE

Pages 521-521

in a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, is used for mission. In this sense, Olearius has a discourse concerning the apostolate of Christ.

APOSTOLATE MORE PROPERLY

Pages 521-521

E more properly denotes the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> office of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APOSTLE">apostle</a> of Christ; but it is also used, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> writers, for the office of a bishop. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> we meet with several letters, petitions, requests, &c. directed to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>, under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of your apostolate, or apostolatus vester. But as the title <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-APOSTOLICUS">apostolicus</a> had been appropriated to the pope, so that of apostolate, became at length restrained to the sole dignity of the popedom. Every bishop's see was anciently dignified with the title of sedes apostolica, an apostolical see, which is now the peculiar denomination of the see of Rome.

APOSTOLI

Pages 521-521

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, denote those letters missive which are demanded in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a>.

APOSTOLIANS

Pages 521-521

a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of the Mennonites, which first sprung up in the year 1663, and derived its name from Apostool, one of the Mennonite ministers at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a>. They concurred with them in doctrine, and admitted to their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a> those only who professed to believe all the sentiments which are contained in their public confession of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>.

APOSTOLIC

Pages 521-521

in the primitive <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, was an appellation given to all such churches as were founded by the apostles; and even to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> of those churches, as being the reputed successors of the apostles.—These were confined to four, viz. Rome, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>, Antioch, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>. In after times, other churches assumed the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, on account, principally, of the conformity of their doctrine with that of the churches which were apostolical by foundation, and because all bishops held themselves successors of the apostles, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> acted in their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> with the authority of apostles. The first <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> apostolical is attributed to bishops as such, is in a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> of Clovis to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORLEANS">Orleans</a>, held in 511, though that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> does not there expressly denominate them apostolical (but apostolica sede dignissima) highly worthy of the apostolical see. In 581, Guntram calls the bishops, met at the council of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MACON">Macon</a>, apostolical pontiffs, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOSTOLICI">apostolici</a> pontifices. In progress of time, the bishop of Rome growing in power above the rest, and the three patriarchates of Alexandria, Antioch, and Jerusalem, falling into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the Saracens, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> apostolical was restrained to the pope and his church alone. Though some of the popes, and St Gregory the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>, not contented to hold the title by this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TENURE">tenure</a>, began at length to insist, that it belonged to them by another and peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>, as being the successors of St <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>. The council of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHEIMS">Rheims</a> in 1049 declared that the pope was the sole apostolical <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIMATE">primate</a> of the universal church. And hence a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of apostolicals; apostolical see, apostolical nuncio, apostolical notary, apostolical <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIEF">brief</a>, apostolical chamber, apostolical <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VICAR">vicar</a>, &c. APOSTOLICAL Constitutions. See <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">Constitution</a>. APOSTOLICAL Traditions. See <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">Tradition</a>. APOSTOLICAL Fathers is an appellation usually given to the writers of the first century who employed their pens in the cause of Christianity. Of these writers, Cotelerius, and after him Le Clerc, have published a collection in two volumes, accompanied both with their own annotations and the remarks of other learned men.

APOSTOLICI

Pages 521-522
or APOSTOLICS, was a name assumed by three different sects, on account of their pretending to imitate the manner and practice of the apostles. The first apostolici, otherwise called Apotactici and Apotactici, rose out of the Encratitae and Cathari in the third century. They made profession of abstaining from marriage, and the use of wine, flesh, money, &c. Gerhard Sagarelli was the founder of the second sect; he obliged his followers to go from place to place as the apostles did, to wander about clothed in white, with long beards, dishevelled hair, and bare heads, accompanied with women, whom they called their spiritual sisters. They likewise renounced all kinds of property and possessions, inveighed against the growing corruption of the church of Rome, predicted its overthrow, and the establishment of a purer church on its ruins. Sagarelli was burnt alive at Parma in the year 1300, and was afterwards succeeded by Dulcinus, who added to the character of an apostle those of a prophet and a general, and carried on a bloody Apostolici and dreadful war for the space of more than two years against Reynerius, bishop of Vercelli; he was at length defeated, and put to death in a barbarous manner in the year 1307. Nevertheless, the sect subsisted in France, Germany, and in other countries, till the beginning of the 15th century, when it was totally extirpated under the pontificate of Boniface IX. The other branch of apostolici was of the twelfth century. These also condemned marriage, preferring celibacy, and calling themselves the chaste brethren and sisters; though each was allowed a spiritual sister, with whom he lived in a domestic relation; and on this account they have been charged with concubinage: they held it unlawful to take an oath; they set aside the use of baptism; and in many things imitated the Manichees. Bernard wrote against this sect of apostolici. APOSTOLICUM is a peculiar name given to a kind of song or hymn, anciently used in churches. The apostolicum is mentioned by Greg. Thaumaturgus as used in his time. Vossius understands it as spoken of the apostles creed: Suicer thinks this impossible, for that this creed was then unknown in the churches of the east.

APOSTROPHE

Pages 522-522

in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">Rhetoric</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> by which a person who is either absent <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> dead is addressed as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he were present and attentive to us. This figure is, in boldness, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> lower than the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> to personified objects (see PERSONIFICATION); since it requires a less effort of imagination to suppose persons present who are dead or absent, than to imitate insensible beings and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> our discourse to them. The poems of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OSSIAN">Ossian</a> abound with the most beautiful instances of this figure. "Weep on the rocks of roaring winds, O Maid of Inistore! <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEND">Bend</a> thy fair head over the waves, thou fairer than the ghost of the hills when it moves in a sunbeam at noon over the silence of Morven! He is fallen! Thy youth is low: <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> beneath the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> of Cuchullin!"

APOTASY

Pages 518-519

the abandoning the true <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. The primitive Christian <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> distinguished several kinds of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APOSTASY">apostasy</a>. The first, of those who went over entirely from Christianity to Judaism; the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, of those who mingled Judaism and Christianity together; and the third, of those who complied so far with the Jews, as to communicate with them in many of their unlawful practices, without making a formal profession of their religion. But the fourth sort was of those who, after having been some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, voluntarily relapsed into Paganism. The perversion of a Christian to Judaism, Paganism, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other false religion, was punished by the emperors Constantius and Julian with confiscation of goods; to which the emperors Theodosius and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-VALENTINIAN">Valentinian</a> added <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> the apostate endeavoured to pervert others to the same iniquity: A punishment too severe for any temporal laws to inflict; and yet the zeal of our <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a> imported it into this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; for we find by Bracton, that in his time apostates were to be burnt to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. Doubtless the preservation of Christianity, as a national religion, is, abstracted from its own intrinsic <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, of the utmost <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> to the civil state: which a single instance <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> sufficiently demonstrate. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a> of a future state of rewards and punishments, the entertaining <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> of the moral attributes of the supreme Being, and a firm persuasion that he superintends and will finally compensate every <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> (all which are clearly revealed in the doctrines, and forcibly inculcated by the precepts, of our Saviour Christ), these are the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> foundation of all judicial <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OATHS">oaths</a>: which call God to witness the truth of those facts, which perhaps may be only known to him and the party attesting; all moral <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> therefore, all confidence in human veracity, must be weakened by apostasy, and overthrown by total <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INFIDELITY">infidelity</a>. Wherefore all affronts to Christianity, or endeavours to depreciate its efficacy, in those who have once professed it, are highly deserving of censure. But yet the loss of life is a heavier penalty than the offence, taken in a civil <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, deserves; and, taken in a spiritual light, our laws have no jurisdiction over it. This punishment, therefore, has <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> ago become obsolete; and the offence of apostasy was, for a long time, the object only of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> courts, which corrected the offender pro salute animae. But about the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of the last century, the civil liberties to which we were then restored being used as a cloak of maliciousness, and the most horrid doctrine subversive of all religion being publicly avowed both in discourse and writings, it was thought necessary again for the civil power to interpose, by not admitting those miscreants to the privileges of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, who maintained such principles as destroyed all moral obligation. To this end it was enacted, by statute 9 and 10 William III. c. 32. That <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> any person educated in, or having made profession of the Christian religion, shall, by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a>, teaching, or advised speaking, deny the Christian religion to be true, or the holy Scriptures to be of divine authority, he shall, upon the first offence, be rendered incapable to hold any office, or <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of trust; and, for the second, be rendered incapable of bringing any action, or of being <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUARDIAN">guardian</a>, executor, legatee, or purchaser of lands, and shall suffer three years imprisonment without bail. To give room, however, for <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REPENTANCE">repentance</a>, if, within four months after the first conviction, the delinquent will in open <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> publicly renounce his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ERROR">error</a>, he is discharged for that once from all disabilities.

APOTEICHISMUS

Pages 522-522

in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> art, a kind of line of circumvallation drawn round a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in order to besiege it. This was also called periapteichismus. The first thing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> went about, when they designed to lay <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> siege to a place, was the apoteichismus; which sometimes consisted of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> wall <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rampart, raised of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>; the innermost to prevent sudden salies from the town, the outermost to keep off foreign enemies from coming to the relief of the besieged. This answered to what are called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTER">counter</a>-vallation and circumvallation among the moderns.

APOTHECARY

Pages 522-522

Apothecarius, in writers of the middle <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, denotes a shop-keeper <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> warehouse-keeper. APOTHECARIIUS is also used to denote a store-keeper, or officer appointed to have the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGAZINE">magazine</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANARY">granary</a>, &c. In which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> apothecarii is sometimes rendered by horcarit and rationarii.

APOTHEOSIS

Pages 522-523

in antiquity, a heathen <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a>, whereby their emperors and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> men were placed among the gods. The word is derived from ἀπό, and θεός, God. After the apotheosis which they also called deification and consecration, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>, altars, and images were erected to the new deity; sacrifices, &c. were offered, and colleges of priests instituted. It was one of the doctrines of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYTHAGORAS">Pythagoras</a>, which he had borrowed from the Chaldees, that virtuous persons after their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> were raised into the order of the gods. And hence the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> deified all the inventors of things useful to mankind; and those who had done any important services to the commonwealth. Tiberius proposed to the Roman <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> the apotheosis of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ, as is related by Eusebius, Tertullian, and Chrysostom. Juvenal rallying the frequent apotheoses, introduces <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATLAS">Atlas</a>, complaining that he was ready to sink under the burden of so many new gods as were every <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> added to the heavens. Seneca ridicules the apotheosis of Claudius with admirable humour. The ceremony, according to Herodian's <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPARATUS">APPARATUS</a> was as follows: After the body of the deceased had been burnt with the usual solemnities, an image of wax, exactly resembling him, was placed on an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a> couch, where it lay for <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> days, attended by the senate and ladies of the highest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOURNING">mourning</a>; and then the young senators and knights bore the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a> of state through the Via Sacra to the old forum, and from thence to the Campus Martius, where it was deposited upon an edifice built in form of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYRAMID">pyramid</a>. The bed being thus placed amidst a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of spices and other combustibles, and the knights having made a solemn <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESSION">procession</a> round the pile, the new <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>, with a torch in his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, set fire to it, whilst an eagle, let fly from the top of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, and mounting in the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> with a firebrand, was supposed to convey the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> of the deceased to heaven; and thenceforward he was ranked among the gods. We often meet with the consecration <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> apotheosis of emperors represented on medals: where we see the pyramids of several stories, each growing less and less; we see also the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EAGLES">eagles</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">flying</a> away with the souls of the deceased emperors. A gem in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSEUM">museum</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRANDENBURG">Brandenburg</a> represents the apotheosis of Julius Caesar, mounted upon the celestial globe, and holding a helm in his hand, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he were now the governor of heaven, as before of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. See Deification.

APOTHERAPIA

Pages 523-523

(from ἀποθεραπεύω, I cure), in Physic, properly denotes a complete <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> finished cure. APOTHERAPIA is also used in the gymnastic art, for the last <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of all regular <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a>, viz. friction, or uncation with <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, before as well as after <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATHING">bathing</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of this was partly to cleanse the skin from any filth or dust it might have contracted during the exercise, and partly to remove weariness.

APOTOME

Pages 523-523

in Music, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between a greater and a lesser semi-tone; expressed by the ratio, $128 : 125$. APOTROPÆ, (from ἀποτρέπω, I avert), in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, verses composed for averting the wrath of incensed deities; and the deities invoked for averting any threatened misfortune were called Apotrepeans; they were also called Alexiavi, from ἀλέξω, I drive away; and Averrunci from averrunco, which denotes the same.

APOTROPE

Pages 522-522

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRACTION">contraction</a> of a word by the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMA">comma</a>: as call'd for called, tho' for though. APOTACTITÆ, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> APOTACTICI, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a>, who affecting to follow the evangelical counsels of poverty, and the examples of the apostles and primitive <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, renounced all their effects and possessions. It does not appear that they gave into any errors during their first state; some <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> writers assure us they had <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> holy virgins and martyrs under the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a> of Dioclesian in the fourth century; but they afterwards fell into the opinions of the Encratitae, and taught that the renouncing of all <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RICHES">riches</a> was not only a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of counsel and advice, but of precept and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a>. And hence the sixth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> in the Theodosian code joins the Apotactitæ with the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EUNOMIANS">Eunomians</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARIANS">Arians</a>.

APPARATUS

Pages 523-523

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> used to denote a complete set of instruments, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other utensils, belonging to any <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a> or machine.
