APPARATUS is frequently used for the operation of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>. For this there are three sorts of apparatus, viz. the small, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> apparatus. See <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>. APPARATUS is also used as a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of several books composed in form of catalogues, bibliothecas, dictionaries, &c. for the ease and conveniency of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a>. The apparatus to Cicero is a kind of concordance, or collection of Ciceronian phrases, &c. The apparatus sacer of Possevin, is a collection of all kinds of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> authors, printed in 1611, in three volumes.—Glossaries, comments, &c. are also frequently called apparatuses.

APPARENT

Pages 523-523

among mathematicians and astronomers, denotes things as they appear to us, in contradistinction from real <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> true; thus we say, the apparent diameter, distance, magnitude, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, &c. of bodies. APPARENT Heir, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>. No inheritance can vest, nor can any person be the actual complete heir of another, till the ancestor is previously dead. Nemo est heres viventis. Before that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the person who is next in the line of succession is called an heir apparent, or heir presumptive. Heirs apparent are such, whose <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of inheritance is indefeasible, provided they outlive the ancestor; as the eldest son or his issue, who must by the course of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> law be heirs to the father whenever he happens to die. Heirs presumptive are such, who, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the ancestor should die immediately, would in the present circumstances of things be his heirs; but whose right of inheritance may be defeated by the contingency of some nearer heir being born; as a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>, or nephew, whose presumptive succession may be destroyed by the birth of a child; or <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>, whose present hopes may be hereafter cut off by the birth of a son. Nay, even if the estate hath descended, by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of the owner, to such brother, or nephew, or daughter, in the former <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, the estate shall be divested, and taken away by the birth of a posthumous child; and, in the latter, it shall also be totally divested by the birth of a posthumous son.

APPARITION

Pages 523-524

in a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, denotes simply the appearance of a thing. In a more limited sense, it is used for a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SPECTRE">spectre</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> ghost. Several instances of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APPARITIONS">apparitions</a> occur in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a>; that of Samuel, raised by the witch of Endor, has occasioned <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> disputes. We find great controversies among authors, in relation to the reality, the existence or non-existence, the possibility or impossibility, of apparitions. The Chaldeans, the Jews, and other nations, have been the steady assertors of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a> of apparitions. The denial of spirits and apparitions is by some made one of the marks of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INFIDELITY">infidelity</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not of atheism. Many of the apparitions we are told of in writers, are doubtless <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> delusions of the sense; many others are fictitious, contrived merely to amuse, or answer some purpose. Apparitions, it is certain, are <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MACHINES">machines</a> that on occasion have been of good <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> both to generals, to ministers of state, to priests, and others. Partial darkness, or obscurity, are the most powerful means by which the sight is deceived: night is therefore the proper season for apparitions. Indeed the state of the mind, at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, prepares it for the admission of these delusions of the imagination. The fear and caution which must be observed in the night; the opportunity it affords for ambuscades and assassinations; depriving us of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> off many pleasing trains of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a>, which objects in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> never fail to introduce, are all circumstances of terror: and perhaps, on the whole, so much of our <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> depends upon our senses, that the deprivation of any one may be attended with proportionable horror and uneasiness. The notions entertained by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> respecting the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>, may receive some illustration from these principles. In dark or twilight, the imagination frequently transforms Apparition an inanimate body into a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>; on approaching, the same appearance is not to be found; hence they sometimes fancied they <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> their <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>; but not finding the reality, distinguished these illusions by the name of shades. Many of these fabulous narrations might originate from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DREAMS">dreams</a>. There are times of slumber when we are not sensible of being asleep. On this principle, Hobbes has ingeniously accounted for the spectre which is said to have appeared to Brutus. "We read," says he, "of M. Brutus, that at Philippi, the night before he gave <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> to Augustus Caesar, he saw a fearful apparition, which is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> related by historians as a vision; but, considering the circumstances, one may easily judge it to have been but a short dream. For sitting in his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TENT">tent</a>, pensive, and troubled with the horror of his rash <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a>, it was not hard for him, slumbering in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, to dream of that which most affrighted him; which fear, as by degrees it made him wake, so it must needs make the apparition by degrees to vanish: and having no assurance that he slept, he could have no cause to think it a dream, or any thing but a vision."—The well known story told by Clarendon, of the apparition of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUCKINGHAM">Buckingham</a>'s father, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> admit of a similar solution. There was no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> so much the subject of conversation as the duke; and from the corruptness of his character, he was very likely to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> a sacrifice to the enthusiasm of the times. Sir George Villiers is said to have appeared to the man at midnight: therefore there is the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> that the man was asleep; and the dream affrighting him, made a strong <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a>, and was likely to be repeated.

APPARITOR

Pages 524-524

among the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> to comprehend all attendants of judges and magistrates appointed to receive and execute their orders. Apparitor, in England, is a messenger that serves the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of a spiritual <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a beadle in a university who carries the mace.

APPEAL

Pages 524-525

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">Common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, denotes an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACCUSATION">accusation</a> by a private subject against another for some heinous crime; demanding <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> on account of the particular injury suffered, rather than for the offence against the public. This private <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a>, for the punishment of public crimes, had probably its original in those times, when a private pecuniary satisfaction, called a weregild, was constantly paid to the party injured, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> his relations, to expiate enormous offences. This was a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> derived to the English, in common with other northern nations, from their <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Germans; among whom, according to Tacitus, laitur homicidium certo armentorum ac pecorum numero; recipitque satisfactionem universa <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOMUS">domus</a>. In the same manner, by the Irish Brehon law, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a>, the brehon or judge was used to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> between the murderer and the friends of the deceased who prosecuted him, by causing the malefactor to give unto them, or to the child or wife of him that was slain, a recompense which they called an eriach. And thus we find in the Anglo-Saxon laws (particularly those of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> Athelstan) the several weregilds for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOMICIDE">homicide</a> established in progressive order, from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of the ceorl or <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEASANT">peasant</a>, up to that of the king himself. And in the laws of Henry I. we have an account of what other offences were redeemable by weregild, and what were not so. As, therefore, during the continuance of this custom, a process was certainly given for recovering the weregild by the party to whom it was due; it seems that, when these offences by degrees grew no longer redeemable, the private process was still <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a>, in order to ensure the infliction of punishment upon the offender, though the party injured was allowed no pecuniary compensation for the offence. But though appeals were thus, in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of prosecutions for some atrocious injury, committed more immediately against an individual, yet it also was anciently permitted, that any subject might appeal another subject of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREASON">treason</a>, either in the courts of common law, or in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, or (for treasons committed beyond the seas) in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of the high <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTABLE">constable</a> and marshal. The cognizance of appeals in the latter still continues in force; and so late as 1631, there was a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> awarded in the court of chivalry, on such an appeal of treason: but that in the first was virtually abolished by the statutes 5 Edw. III. c. 9, and 2 Edw. III. c. 24, and in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> expressly, by statute 1 Hen. IV. c. 14. So that the only appeals now in force, for things done within the realm, are appeals of felony and mayhem. An appeal of felony may be brought for crimes committed either against the parties themselves or their relations. The crimes against the parties themselves are larceny, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAPE">rape</a>, and arson. And for these, as well as for mayhem, the persons robbed, ravished, maimed, or whose houses are burnt, may institute this private process. The only crime against one's relation, for which an appeal can be brought, is that of killing him, by either murder or manslaughter. But this cannot be brought by every relation; but only by the wife for the death of her husband, or by the heir <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MALE">male</a> for the death of his ancestor; which heirship was also confined by an ordinance of Henry I. to the four nearest degrees of blood. It is given to the wife on account of the loss of her husband; therefore, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> she marries again, before or pending her appeal, it is lost and gone; or, if she marries after judgment, she shall not demand execution. The heir, as was said, must also be heir male, and such a one as was the next heir by the course of the common law at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the killing of the ancestor. But this rule has three exceptions: 1. If the person killed leaves an innocent wife, she only and not the heir, shall have the appeal. 2. If there be no wife, and the heir be accused of the murder, the person, who next to him would have been heir male, shall bring the appeal. 3. If the wife kills her husband, the heir may appeal her of the death. And, by the statute of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GLOUCESTER">Gloucester</a>, cesser, 6 Edw. I. c. 9, all appeals of death must be sued within a year and a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> after the completion of the felony by the death of the party: which seems to be only declaratory of the old common law; for in the Gothic constitutions we find the same "præscriptio annalis, quæ currit adversus actorem, si de homicida ei non constat intra annum a cede facta, nec quenquam interca arguat et accusat." These appeals may be brought previous to any <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDICTMENT">indictment</a>; and, if the appellee be acquitted thereon, he cannot afterwards be indicted for the same offence. In like manner as by the old Gothic <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, if any offender gained a verdict in his favour, when prosecuted by the party injured, he was also understood to be acquitted of any <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> prosecution for the same offence; but, on the contrary, if he made his peace with the king, still he might be prosecuted at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> of the party. And so, in England, if a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> be acquitted on an indictment of murder, or found guilty, and pardoned by the king, still he ought not (in strictness) to go at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, but be imprisoned or let to bail till the year and day be past, by virtue of the statute 3 Hen. VIII. c. 1, in order to be forthcoming to answer any appeal for the same felony, not having as yet been punished for it: though, if he hath been found guilty of manslaughter on an indictment, and hath had the benefit of clergy, and suffered the judgment of the law, he cannot afterwards be appealed: for it is a maxim in law, "that nemo bis punitur pro eodem delicto." Before this statute was made, it was not usual to indict a man for homicide within the time limited for appeals; which produced very <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> inconvenience. If the appellee be acquitted, the appellant (by virtue of the statute of Westm. 2. 13 Edw. I. c. 12,) shall suffer one year's imprisonment, and pay a fine to the king, besides restitution of damages to the party for the imprisonment and infamy which he has sustained: and, if the appellant be incapable to make restitution, his abettors shall do it for him, and also be liable to imprisonment. This provision, as was foreseen by the author of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLETA">Fleta</a>, proved a great discouragement to appeals; so that thenceforward they ceased to be in common <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>. If the appellee be found guilty, he shall suffer the same judgment, as if he had been convicted by indictment: but with this remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a>, that on an indictment, which is at the suit of the king, the king may <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a> and remit the execution; on an appeal which is at the suit of a private subject, to make an atonement for the private wrong, the king can no more pardon it, than he can remit the damages required on an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTERY">battery</a>. In like manner as, while the wergild continued to be paid as a fine for homicide, it could not be remitted by the king's authority. And the ancient usage was, so late as Henry IV's time, that all the relations of the slain should drag the appellee to the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of execution: a custom, founded upon that <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> spirit of family resentment which prevailed universally through <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> after the irruption of the northern nations, and is peculiarly attended to in their several codes of law; and which prevails even now among the wild and untutored inhabitants of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>: as if the finger of nature had pointed it out to mankind, in their rude and uncultivated state. However, the punishment of the offender may be remitted, and discharged by the concurrence of all parties interested; and as the king by his pardon may frustrate an indictment, so the appellant by his release may discharge an appeal: "nam quilibet potest renunciare juri pro se introducto."

APPEARANCE

Pages 525-525

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, signifies a defendant's filing a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> special bail, on any <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> issued out of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of judicature.

APPELLA

Pages 503-503

among physicians, a name given to those whose prepuce is either wanting <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> shrunk, so that it can no longer cover the glans. Many authors have supposed this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of the word Apella warranted from the passage in Horace, credat Judaeus Apella non ego. But, according to Salmasius and others, Apella is the proper name of a certain Jew, and not an adjective signifying circumcised.

APPELLANTS

Pages 525-525

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, an appellation given to such of the catholic clergy as <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a> from the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> unigenitus to a general <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>.

APPELLATION

Pages 525-526

the name by which anything is known <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> distinguished when spoken of. See NAME. Nothing can be more foreign to the original meaning of many words and proper names, than their present appellations, frequently owing to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of those things being forgotten, or an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> in which they were expressed. Who, for example, when the crier of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> bawls out, "O yes, O yes," would dream that it was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCLAMATION">proclamation</a> commanding the talkers to become hearers, being the French word Oyez, "listen," retained in our courts ever since the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> pleadings were held in French? Or would any person suppose that the headland on the French <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, near <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALAIS">Calais</a>, called by our seamen Blackness, would be so titled from its French name of Blanc Nez, or the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">White</a> Headland. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> Henry the Eighth having taken the town of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOULOGNE">Boulogne</a> in France, the gates of which he brought to Hards in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>, where they are still remaining, the flatterers of that reign highly magnified this <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, which, Porto Bello like, became a popular subject for signs; and the port or harbour of Boulogne, called Boulogne Mouth, was accordingly set up at a noted inn in Holborn. The name of the inn <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> outliving the sign and fame of the conquest, an ignorant painter, employed by a no less ignorant landlord, to paint a new one, represented it by a bull and a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> gaping <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> mouth (answering to the vulgar <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRONUNCIATION">pronunciation</a> of Bull and Mouth). The same piece of history gave being to the bull and gate, originally meant for Boulogne gate, and represented by an embattled gate or entrance into a fortified town. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BARBER">barber</a>'s pole has been the subject of many conjectures; some conceiving it to have originated from the word poll, or head, with several other conceits as far-fetched and as unmeaning: but the true intention of that party-coloured <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STAFF">staff</a> was to show that the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the shop practised <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURGERY">surgery</a>, and could breathe a vein as well as mow a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARD">beard</a>; such a staff being to this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, by every village practitioner, put into the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> of a patient undergoing the operation of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHLEBOTOMY">phlebotomy</a>. The white band which encompasses the staff, was meant to represent the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FILLET">fillet</a>, thus elegantly twined about it. Nor were the chequers, (at this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> sign of a public <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>) less expressive, being the representation of a kind of draught-board called tables, and showed that there that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAME">game</a> might be played. From their <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, which was <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>, and the similarity to a lattice, it it was corruptly called the red lettuce, which word is frequently used by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> writers to signify an alehouse. The Spectator has explained the sign of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELL">bell</a>-savagé inn plausibly enough, in supposing it to have been originally the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of a beautiful <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> found in the woods, called in French la belle sauvage. But another reason has since been assigned for that appellation, namely, that the inn was once the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of Lady Arabella <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">Savage</a>, and familiarly called Bell Savage's Inn, probably represented, as at present, by a bell and a savage or wild <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, which was a rebus for her name; rebusses being much in fashion in the 16th century; of which the bolt and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-TUN">tun</a> is an instance. The three blue balls prefixed to the doors and windows of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAWNBROKERS">pawnbrokers</a> shops, by the vulgar humorously enough said to indicate that it is two to one that the things pledged are never redeemed, was in reality the arms of a set of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> from <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LOMBARDY">Lombardy</a>, who were the first that publicly <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LENT">lent</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> on pledges. They dwelt together in a street, from them named Lombard Street, in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, and also gave their name to another at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. The appellation of Lombard was formerly all over <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> considered as <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYNONYMOUS">synonymous</a> with that of usurer. At the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> of yeomen of the guards, they used to wait at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> on all <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> solemnities, and were ranged near the buffets; this procured them the name of buffeters, not very unlike in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> to the jocular appellation of beef-eaters, now given them; though probably it was rather the voluntary <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MISNOMER">misnomer</a> of some wicked <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a>, than an accidental corruption arising from ignorance of the French language. The opprobrious <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of bum <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAILIFF">bailiff</a>, so constantly bestowed on the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a>'s officers, is, according to Judge Blackstone, only the corruption of bound bailiff, every sheriff's officer being obliged to enter into bonds and to give security for his good behaviour, previous to his appointment. A cordonnier seems to have no relation to the occupation it is meant to express, which is that of a shoemaker. But cordonnier, originally spelt cordaunier, is the French word for that trade; the best <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a> used for shoes coming originally from Cordova in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>. Spanish-leather shoes were once famous in England. APPELLATIVE names, in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>, in contradistinction to proper names, are such as stand for universal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a>, or a whole <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of beings, whether general or special. Thus, fish, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIRD">bird</a>, man, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, river, are common or appellative names; and so are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TROUT">trout</a>, eel, lobster; for they all agree to many individuals, and some to many <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>. See Name.

APPELLEE

Pages 526-526

among lawyers, the person against whom an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a> is brought. See APPEAL.

APPELLES

Pages 503-504

one of the most celebrated painters of antiquity. He was born in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Cos, and flourished in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Alexander the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>, with whom he was in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> favour. He executed a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> of this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, holding a thunderbolt in his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>; a piece, finished with so much skill and dexterity, that it used to be said there were two Alexanders; one invincible, the son of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a>; the other inimitable, the production of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APELLES">Apelles</a>. Alexander gave him a remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of his regard: for when he employed Apelles to draw Campaspe, one of his mistresses, having found that he had conceived an affection for her, he resigned her to him; and it was from her that Apelles is said to have drawn his Venus Anadyomene. One of Apelles's <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> excellencies was his making his pictures exactly resemble the persons represented; insomuch that the physiognomists are said to have been able to form a judgment of the person's <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DESTINY">destiny</a> as readily from his portraits as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they had seen the originals. But what is called <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">grace</a> was the characteristic of this <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a>. His <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a> was so famous for <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>, that Protogenes discovered by a single line that Apelles had been at his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. Protogenes lived at <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RHODES">Rhodes</a>: Apelles sailed thither, and went to his house with great eagerness to see the works of an artist who was known to him only by name. Protogenes was gone from home; but an old woman was left watching a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> piece of canvass, which was fitted in a frame for <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>. She told Apelles that Protogenes was gone out; and asked him his name, that she might inform her <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> who had inquired for him. "Tell him (says Apelles) he was inquired for by this person?"—at the same time taking up a pencil, he drew on the canvass a line of great delicacy. When Protogenes returned, the old woman acquainted him with what had happened. That artist, upon contemplating the fine stroke of the line, immediately pronounced that Apelles had been there; for so finished a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> could be produced by no other person. Protogenes, however, himself drew a finer line of another <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>; and, as he was going away, ordered the old woman to show that line to Apelles if he came again; and to say, "This is the person for whom you are inquiring." Apelles returned, and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> the line; he would not for shame be overcome; and therefore, in a colour different from either of the former, he drew some lines so exquisitely delicate, that it was utterly impossible for finer strokes to be made. Protogenes now confessed the superiority of Apelles, flew to the harbour in search of him, and resolved to leave the canvass with the lines on it for the astonishment of future artists. Apelles showed great liberality of mind towards Protogenes. With <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> enlarged by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> and literature, he was incapable of harbouring little jealousies of noble competitors; on the contrary, he was the first who made the works of Protogenes to be valued as they deserved among the Rhodians. He acknowledged that Protogenes was in some respects superior to himself; but that in one particular himself excelled, viz., in knowing when to take his hand from the picture; an art which Protogenes had not yet learned, and therefore over-worked his pieces. Apelles equally disapproved of too elaborate diligence, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> too hasty negligence in execution. A studied work of Protogenes he esteemed less on the one account; and on the other, when a silly painter once brought him a picture, and said, "This I painted in a hurry,"—he replied, "Though you had not told me so, I perceived it was painted in haste: but I wonder you could not execute more such pieces in the same time." There are two stories related of Apelles, which show him to be at once an artist of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a>, in amending even trifling improprieties, when pointed out to him by competent judges; and yet of self-confidence sufficient to make him know the perfection and value of his own paintings. It was customary with Apelles to expose to public view the works which he had finished, and to hide himself behind the picture, in order to hear the remarks passed on it by persons who chanced to view it. He once overheard himself blamed by a shoemaker for a fault in the slippers of some picture: he corrected the fault which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> had noticed; but on the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> following the shoemaker began to animadvert on the leg; upon which Apelles with some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGER">anger</a> looked out from behind the canvass, and bade him keep It is well known that Alexander forbade any one besides Apelles to paint his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTRAIT">portrait</a>. We are not, however, to conclude from this, that Alexander was a more skilful judge of painting than he was of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>. Like Augustus, he cherished the fine arts more from vanity than <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>. A remarkable proof is given of this prince's inability to discern merit, and of the painter's freedom in expressing the mortification he felt, when a work of his was not sufficiently commended. "Alexander (says Ællian, lib. ii. c. 3. Var. Hist.) having viewed the picture of himself which was at Ephesus, did not <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a> it as it deserved. But when a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> was brought in, and neighed at seeing the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of a horse in the picture, as though it had been a real horse; O <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>! (said Apelles) this horse seems to be by far a better judge of painting than you." It happened more than once that the horses drawn by him were mistaken for real ones, by living horses which saw and neighed at the pictures. In his finishing a drawing of this animal, a remarkable circumstance is related of him. He had painted a horse returning from <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, and had succeeded to his wishes in describing every other mark that could indicate a mettlesome steed, impatient of restraint; there was wanting nothing but a foam of a bloody hue issuing from the mouth. He again and again endeavoured to express this, but his attempts were unsuccessful. At last, with vexation, he threw against the reins of the horse a sponge which had in it many colours; a mixture of which coming out of the sponge, and tinging the reins, produced the very effect desired by the painter. The works of Apelles were all admired; but the most celebrated were the picture of Alexander in the temple of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIANA">Diana</a> at Ephesus, and that of Venus emerging from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. Alexander was drawn with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a> in his hand; and such relief was produced by the chiaro scuro in this piece, that the fingers seemed to shoot forward, and the thunderbolt to be out of the picture. His Venus Ἀναδυόμενη was esteemed the most exquisite figure which the pencil could create: it is therefore extolled by the Roman poets Propertius and Ovid; and the poet of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIDON">Sidon</a>, Antipater, has left us the following Greek epigram on it: Ταῖς αναδυόμεναι ἀπὸ μαλέως ἀγῇ Σαλαμίνας Κύριον Ἀπέλλει πολὺς ὁρᾷ γεράφιδες, Ως ἂν συμμετέχῃσι διασκέψασθαι καὶ τοῦ Εὐλάβειν ὑδάτι ἀφορᾶ ἀπὸ πλοκαμάτων, Αἴτια τῶν εἰσεισι Ἀθηνῶν τε καὶ Ἑρᾶ "Οὐκ ἔστι σοι μεῖζον ἢ ἐν τῇ ἐκείνητι." Anth. iv. 12. Graceful as from her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATAL">natal</a> sea she <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a>, Venus, the labour of Apelles, view: With pressing hand her humid locks she wrings, While from her tresses drips the frothy <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DEW">dew</a>: Ev'n Juno and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a> now declare, "No longer we contend whose form's most rare."

APPERCEPTION

Pages 526-526
or ADPERCEPTION, a term used by Leibnitz and his followers for consciousness.

APPETITE

Pages 526-526

in Medicine, a certain painful <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> uneasy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSATION">sensation</a>, always accompanied with a desire to eat or drink.—An excessive appetite is called by physicians bulimy or fames canina; a defect or loss of it anorexy; and that after things improper for food, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICA">pica</a>. APPIA via, a way reaching from Rome through <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPUA">Capua</a> to Brundusium, between 330 and 350 miles <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>. Appius Claudius, surnamed Cæcus, in the year of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> 441, carried it from the Porta Capena to Capua (Livy, Frontinus). It was afterwards carried on to Brundusium; but by whom, or when, is uncertain. It was laid with very hard <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, brought from a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> distance, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, and squared (Diodorus); and it was so wide, that several waggons could go abreast. Statius calls it the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a>. Its course is described by Horace, Strabo, and Antonine.

APPIAN

Pages 526-526

an eminent writer of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMAN_HISTORY">Roman <a clas</a>s="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> in Greek, under the reigns of Trajan and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HADRIAN">Hadrian</a>. He was of a good family in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>; whence he went to Rome, and there distinguished himself so well as an advocate, that he was chosen one of the procurators of the empire, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> was committed to him. He did not complete the Roman history in a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a>; but wrote distinct histories of all nations that had been conquered by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, in which he placed every thing relating to those nations in the proper order of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. His style is plain and simple; in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of Phocius, he has shown the greatest knowledge of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> affairs, and the happiest <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TALENT">talent</a> at describing them, of any of the historians; for while we read him, we in a manner see the battles which he describes. Of all this voluminous <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> there remains only what treats of the Punic, Syrian, Parthian, Mithridatic, and Spanish wars, with those against <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HANNIBAL">Hannibal</a>, the civil wars, and the wars in Illyricum, and some fragments of the Celtic <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Gallic wars.

APPIUS CLAUDIUS

Pages 526-526

a Sabine by birth, one of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> inhabitants of Regillum: His shining merit having drawn the envy of his fellow citizens upon him, he retired to Rome with all his family. Appius was admitted into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>, and was made <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a> with Publius Servilius Priscus, in 258 from the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> of Rome; but he was hated by the plebeians, being an austere opposer of their clamours and seditions. The Claudian family <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> one of the most illustrious of the patrician families in Rome; and several in succession of the name of Appius supported the same stern character that distinguished their first founder.

APPLAUSE

Pages 526-527

an approbation of something, signified by clapping the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, still practised in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-THEATRES">theatres</a>.—Applause, in antiquity, differed from <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACCLAMATION">ACCLAMATION</a>, as the latter was articulate and performed with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>, the former with the hands. Among the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, mans, applause was an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> musical kind of noise, made by the audience <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> spectators to express their satisfaction. There were three <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of applause, denominated from the different noises made in them, viz. Bombus, Imbrices, and Testae; the first a confused din, made either by the hands or the mouth; the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> and third, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEATING">beating</a> on a sort of sounding vessels placed in the theatres for this purpose. Persons were instructed to give applause with skill; and there were even masters who professed to teach the art. The proficient in this way let themselves out for hire to the vain-glorious among the poets, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTORS">actors</a>, &c. and were properly disposed to support a loud applause. These they called Laudicenni, and Σασοκερες. At the end of the play, a loud peal of applause was expected, and even asked of the audience, either by the chorus or the persons who spoke last. The formula was Spectatores plaudite, or Valete et plaudite. The plausores, or applauders, were divided into choirs, and disposed in theatres opposite to each other, like the choristers in cathedrals, so that there was a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONCERT">concert</a> of plaudences.

APPLE

Pages 527-527

the fruit of the pyrus malus. See Pyrus, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Apple of the Eye, a name not unfrequently given to the pupil. See Anatomy. Apples of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">Love</a>. See Lycofersonicon, Botany Index. Mad Apples. See Melongena, Botany Index.

APPLEBY

Pages 527-527

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> town of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WESTMORELAND">Westmoreland</a>, where the assizes are held, is seated on the banks of the river Eden, which almost surrounds it. It was formerly a very considerable town, and had <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> privileges: but it is <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> ago gone to decay, and now only consists of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> houses in one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> street, which runs with an easy ascent from <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> to south; at the head of which is the castle, almost entirely surrounded by the river. It has two churches; a town-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALL">hall</a>, in which the assizes are held; a county jail; and an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a> for a governess and twelve widows, founded in 1651 by a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Clifford. It is governed by a mayor, twelve aldermen, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, and two sergeants at mace, &c. It contained 2160 inhabitants in 1811, and sends two members to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. W. Long. 3. 52. N. Lat. 54. 3°.

APPLICATION

Pages 527-527

in a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, is the laying two things together, in order to discover their agreement <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> disagreement. Application, in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">Geometry</a>, is used either for <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a>; for applying one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> to another, whose areas, but not <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, shall be the same; or, for transferring a given line into a circle or other figure, so that its ends shall be in the perimeter of the figure. Application, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOLOGY">Theology</a>, is particularly used, by some divines, for the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> whereby our Saviour transfers, or makes over to us, what he had earned or purchased by his holy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. Accordingly it is by this application of the merits of Christ that we are to be justified and entitled to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">grace</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a>. The sacraments are the ordinary means or instruments whereby this application is effected.

APPOINTEE

Pages 527-527

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, the same as aguiseé: Thus we say, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> appointée, to signify that with two <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> at the end cut off, so as to terminate in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a>.

APPOINTMENT

Pages 527-527

in a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, the same as Assignment. Appointment, in a particular sense, denotes a pension <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> salary given by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> lords and princes to persons of worth and parts, in order to retain them in their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> is chiefly used among the French. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of France gave <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> appointments to several of the officers in his service. Appointments differ from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WAGES">wages</a>, in that the latter are fixed and ordinary, being paid by the ordinary treasurers; whereas appointments are annual gratifications granted by <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREVET">brevet</a> for a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> uncertain, and are paid out of the privy purse.

APPOSER

Pages 527-527

R signifies an examiner. In the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of exchequer there is an officer called the foreign apposer. In the office of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONFIRMATION">confirmation</a>, in the first liturgy of Edward VI. the rubric directs the bishop, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> such as he shall appoint, to appose a child; and a bishop's examining chaplain was anciently called his poser.

APPOSITION

Pages 527-527

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>, the placing two <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> more substantives together, in the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, without any copulative conjunction between them; as Ardebat Alexim, deliciæ domini. APPRaiser (from <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AD">ad</a>, "to," and pretium, "value"), one who <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RATES">rates</a> or sets a value upon goods, &c. He must be a skilful and honest person. It is not a business of itself, but is practised by brokers of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a> furniture; to which set of men the word is chiefly applied: Yet upholsterers and other brokers are employed, or even any person or persons who are supposed to be skilled in the commodities to be appraised or valued. They are employed in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, executions brought in upon goods, or of stock to be turned over from one person to another, or divided between copartners; and are called sworn appraisers, from their taking an oath to do <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> between party and party. They sometimes appraise on behalf of both sides, each party agreeing to have the same appraiser or appraisers; sometimes in opposition, each party choosing one or more of a side; and sometimes by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPUTATION">deputation</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TRUSTEES">trustees</a>, masters in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CHANCERY">chancery</a>, &c.

APPRAISING

Pages 527-527

the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of rating, valuing <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> setting a price on goods, by a person who is a competent judge, and is authorized thereto. See APPRAISER.

APPREHENSION

Pages 527-527

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, signifies the seizing a criminal, in order to bring him to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>.

APPRENTICE

Pages 527-528

APPRENTICE, (from apprendre, "to learn,") one who is bound by covenant to serve a tradesman <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> artificer a certain <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, upon condition of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>'s instructing him in his art or mystery. Apprentices may likewise be bound to husbandmen, or even to gentlemen; and they, as well as tradesmen in England, are compellable to take the children of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a>, whom the overseers, with the consent of two justices, may bind till the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 24 years. Apprentices may be discharged on reasonable cause; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> any, whose premium has been less than ten pounds, run away from their masters, they are compellable to serve out the time of absence, or give satisfaction for it, at any <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> within <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years after <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPIRATION">expiration</a> of the original <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a>. Apprentices <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> a settlement in that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> where they last served 40 days; and by the 5th of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>, c. 4, they have an exclusive <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> the trade in which they have been instructed, in any <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of England. However, the resolutions of the courts have in general rather confined than extended the restriction of this statute. See Blackstone's Com., vol. i. p. 426, &c. In France, the sons of tradesmen, living in their father's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> till seventeen years of age, are reputed to have served an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPRENTICESHIP">apprenticeship</a>. In that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, the times of serving are different in the different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROFESSIONS">professions</a>, from three years to eight. After serving out an apprenticeship, the person becomes what they call an aspirant, or candidate for mastership, and is to be examined by proper officers as to his skill and proficiency, and also to exhibit a chef d'œuvre or masterpiece in the art he has been bred to, before he be suffered to set up to practise for himself. Anciently, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BENCHERS">benchers</a> in the inns of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> were called apprentices of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>, in Latin apprentici juris nobiliores; as appears by Mr Selwyn's <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOTE">note</a> on Fortescue: and so the learned Plowden styles himself. Sir Henry Finch, in his Nomotechnia, writes himself, apprentice de ley: Sir Edward <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COKE">Coke</a> in his Inst. says Apprentici legis, in pleading, are called homines consiliarii et in lege periti: and in another <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, apprentices and other counsellors of law. Apprentices indentures and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of clerkship, pay of duty 6s. Parish indentures are excepted, and pay 6d. only, by 5 William III. c. 21. For fees given with apprentices, clerks, or servants, bound or articled by indentures, from 1l. to 50l. masters pay for every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> 6d.; and for fees above 50l. one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHILLING">shilling</a> in the pound. 8 Ann. c. 9. For an account of the more recent statutes and regulations on this subject, see APPRENTICE, SUPPLEMENT.

APPRENTICESHIP

Pages 528-529

the servitude of an apprentice, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DURATION">duration</a> of his indenture. <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">Seven</a> years seem anciently to have been, all over <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, the usual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> established for the duration of apprenticeships in the greater <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of incorporated trades. All such incorporations were anciently called <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a>, which indeed is the proper Latin name for any incorporation whatever. The university of smiths, the university of taylors, &c. are expressions which we <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> meet with in the old charters of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>. When those particular incorporations which are now peculiarly called universities were first established, the term of years which it was necessary to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a>, in order to obtain the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of arts, Apprenticeship appears evidently to have been copied from the term of apprenticeship in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> trades, of which the incorporations were much more ancient. As to have wrought seven years under a master properly qualified was necessary in order to entitle any person to become a master, and to have himself apprentices in a common trade; so to have studied seven years under a master properly qualified was necessary to entitle him to become a master, teacher or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> (words anciently <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYNONYMOUS">synonymous</a>), in the liberal arts, and to have scholars or apprentices (words likewise originally synonymous) to study under him. By the 5th of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>, commonly called the statute of apprenticeship, it was enacted, that no person should for the future <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> any trade, craft, or mystery at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> exercised in England, unless he had previously served to it an apprenticeship of seven years at least; and what before had been the bye-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> of many particular corporations, became in England the general and public law of all trades carried on in market towns. For though the words of the statute are very general, and seem plainly to include the whole <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, by interpretation its operation has been limited to market towns; it having been held, that in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> villages a person may exercise several different trades, though he has not served a seven years apprenticeship to each, they being necessary for the convenience of the inhabitants, and the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of people frequently not being sufficient to supply each with a particular set of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. By a strict interpretation of the words, too, the operation of this statute has been limited to those trades which were established in England before the 5th of Elizabeth, and has never been extended to such as have been introduced since that time. This limitation has given occasion to several distinctions which, considered as rules of <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol18.html#article-POLICE">police</a>, appear as foolish as can well be imagined. It has been adjudged, for example, that a coachmaker can neither himself make, nor employ journeymen to make his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COACH">coach</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHEELS">wheels</a>, but must buy them of a master wheelwright, this latter trade having been exercised in England before the 5th of Elizabeth. But a wheelwright, though he has never served an apprenticeship to a coachmaker, may either himself make, or employ a journeyman to make, coaches; the trade of a coachmaker not being within the statute, because not exercised in England at the time when it was made. The manufacturers of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MANCHESTER">Manchester</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIRMINGHAM">Birmingham</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WOLVERHAMPTON">Wolverhampton</a>, are many of them upon this account not within this statute; not having been exercised in England before the 5th of Elizabeth. In France the duration of apprenticeships is different in different towns and in different trades. In <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, five years is the term required in a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> number; but before any person can be qualified to exercise the trade as a master, he must, in many of them, serve five years more as a journeyman. During this latter term he is called the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a> of his master, and the term itself is called his companionship. In Scotland there is no general law which regulates universally the duration of apprenticeships. The term is different in different corporations. Where it is <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, a part of it may generally be redeemed by paying a small fine. In most towns, too, a very small fine is sufficient to purchase the freedom of any corporation. The weavers of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> and hempen cloth, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> of the country, as well as all other artificers subservient to them, wheelmakers, reedmakers, &c. may exercise their trades in any town corporate without paying any fine. In all towns corporate, all persons are free to sell <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTCHER">butcher</a>'s meat upon any lawful <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WEEK">week</a>. Three years is in Scotland a common term of apprenticeship, even in some very nice trades; and in general there is no country in Europe in which corporation laws are so little oppressive. Apprenticeships were altogether unknown to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECIPROCAL">reciprocal</a> duties of master and apprentice make a considerable article in every <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> code. The Roman law is perfectly silent with regard to them. There is no Greek or Latin word which expresses the idea we now annex to the word apprentice; a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> bound to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> at a particular trade for the benefit of a master during a term of years, upon condition that the master shall teach him that trade. Long apprenticeships Dr Smith considers as altogether unnecessary. The arts which are much superior to common trades, such as those of making clocks and watches, contain no such mystery as to require a long course of instruction. The first <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of such beautiful <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MACHINES">machines</a>, indeed, and even that of some of the instruments employed in making them, must, no doubt, have been the work of deep thought and long time, and may justly be considered as among the happiest efforts of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> ingenuity: but when both have been fairly invented and are well understood; to explain to any young <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, in the completest manner, how to apply the instruments, and how to construct the machines, cannot well require more than the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LESSONS">lessons</a> of a few weeks; perhaps those of a few days might be sufficient. In the common mechanic trades, those of a few days might certainly be sufficient. The dexterity of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, indeed, even in common trades, cannot be acquired without much practice and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>. But a young man would practise with much more diligence and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> from the beginning he wrought as a journeyman, being paid in proportion to the little work which he could execute, and paying in his turn for the materials which he might sometimes spoil through awkwardness and inexperience. His <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> in this way generally would be more effectual, and always less tedious and expensive. The master, indeed, would be a loser; he would lose all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WAGES">wages</a> of the apprentice, which he now saves, for seven years together. In the end, perhaps, the apprentice himself would be a loser. In a trade so easily learnt he would have more competitors; and his wages when he came to be a complete workman, would be much less than at present. The same increase of competition would reduce the profits of the masters as well as the wages of the workmen. The trades, the crafts, the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a>, would be all losers: but the public would be a gainer: the work of all artificers coming in this way much cheaper to market.

APPRISING

Pages 529-529

in Scots <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, the name of that <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> by which a creditor formerly carried off the estate of his debtor for payment. It is now abolished, and adjudications are appointed in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of it. Adjudications, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a>, resignation, clarè constat, cognition of heirs, heritable <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONFIRMATION">confirmation</a>, novodamus, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> and original <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> of surrender, retour, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEISIN">seisin</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> in Scotland, pay by different acts Apprising 4s. qd. duty.

APPROACH

Pages 529-529
or APPROACHING, in a general sense, the acceding or coming together of two or more things.

APPROACHES

Pages 529-529

in Fortification, the works thrown up by the besiegers, in order to get nearer a fortress, without being exposed to the enemy's cannon.

APPROACHING

Pages 529-529

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARDENING">Gardening</a>, the inoculating <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> ingrafting the sprig of one tree into another, without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> it off the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARENT">parent</a> tree.

APPROBATION

Pages 529-529

is more particularly used, in speaking of recommendations of books, given by persons qualified <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> authorized to judge of them. Those appointed to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> licenses and imprimaturs, frequently express their approbation of books. Books were formerly subjected to a licensor in England, (see 13th Car. II. c. 33.), which <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> is <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> since expired; and being incompatible with the noble principles of the Revolution, has never since been, and it is hoped never <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be, revived.

APPROPRIATION

Pages 529-530

in the canon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>, a severing of a benefice <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> to the proper and perpetual <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of some <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. See the article PARSON. The contrivance of appropriations seems to have sprung from the policy of the monastic orders, who have never been deficient in subtle inventions for the increase of their own power and emoluments. At the first establishment of parochial clergy, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITHES">tithes</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> were distributed in a fourfold <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a>; one for the use of the bishop, another for maintaining the fabric of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, a third for the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a>, and the fourth to provide for the incumbent. When the sees of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> became otherwise amply endowed, they were prohibited from demanding their usual share of these tithes, and the division was into three parts only. And hence it was inferred by the monasteries, that a small <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> was sufficient for the officiating <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>; and that the remainder might well be applied to the use of their own fraternities (the endowment of which was construed to be a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of the most exalted piety), subject to the burden of repairing the church and providing for its constant supply. And therefore they begged and bought, for masses and obits, and sometimes even for <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, all the advowsons within their reach, and then appropriated the benefices to the use of their own corporation. But, in order to complete such appropriation effectually, the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s license, and consent of the bishop, must first be obtained; because both the king and the bishop, may some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other have an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>, by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAPSE">lapse</a>, in the presentation to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENCH">bench</a>; which can never happen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it be appropriated to the use of a corporation, which never dies; and also because the law reposes a confidence in them, that they <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> not consent to anything that shall be to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a> of the church. The consent of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> also is necessarily implied, because the appropriation can be originally made to none but to such spiritual corporation as is also the patron of the church; the whole being indeed nothing else but an allowance for the patrons to retain the tithes and glebe in their own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, without presenting any clerk, they themselves undertaking to provide for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the church. When the appropriation is thus made, the appropriators and their successors are perpetual parsons of the church; and must sue and be sued, in all matters concerning the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> of the church by the name of parsons. This appropriation may be severed, and the church become disappropriate, two ways; as, first, If the patron or appropriator presents a clerk, who is instituted and inducted to the parsonage; for the incumbent so instituted and inducted is to all intents and purposes complete parson; and the appropriation being once severed, can never be reunited again, unless by a repetition of the same solemnities. And, when the clerk so presented is distinct from the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VICAR">vicar</a>, the rectory thus vested in him becomes what is called a sinecure; because he hath no cure of souls, having a vicar under him to whom that cure is committed. Also, if the corporation which has the appropriation is dissolved, the parsonage becomes disappropriate at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> law; because the perpetuity of person is gone, which is necessary to support the appropriation. In this manner, and subject to these conditions, may appropriations be made at this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>: and thus were most, if not all of the appropriations at present existing originally made; being annexed to bishoprics, prebends, religious houses, nay, even to nunneries, and certain <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> orders, all of which were spiritual corporations. At the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a> of monasteries, by statutes 27 Hen. VIII. c. 28. and 31 Hen. VIII. c. 13. the appropriation of several parsonages, which belonged to those respective religious houses (amounting to more than one third of all the parishes in England), would have been by the rules of the common law disappropriated; had not a clause in those statutes intervened, to give them to the king in as ample a manner as the abots, &c. formerly held the same at the time of their dissolution. This, though perhaps scarcely defensible, was not without example: for the same was done in former reigns, when the alien priories (that is, such as were filled by foreigners only) were dissolved and given to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>. And from these two roots have sprung all the lay appropriations or <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECULAR">secular</a> parsonages which we now see in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>; they having been afterwards granted out from time to time by the crown. See the article Parson and Vicar.

APPROVER

Pages 530-530

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, one who, professing felony in himself, appealeth <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> impeacheth another or more of his accomplices. He is so called from the French approver, comprobare, because he must prove what he hath alleged in his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> was anciently either by <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, or by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, at the choice of the appellee; and the form of this <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACCUSATION">accusation</a> may be found in Crompt. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">Just</a>. 250. APPROVERS of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>, are those who have the letting of the king's demesnes in small manors, &c. In the statute of the 1st of Ed. III. c. 8. sheriffs are called the king's approvers. It being in the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> to suffer one to be an approver, this method of late hath seldom been practised. But we have, in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BURGLARY">burglary</a> and robbery on the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> way, what seems to amount to the same by statute; it being ordained, that where persons <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with such crimes out of prison, discover two others concerned in the crime, they shall have a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a>, &c. Stat. 5th <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>, c. 31. APPROVER is particularly used, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> law writers, for a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAILIFF">bailiff</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STEWARD">steward</a>, appointed to have the care of a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANOR">manor</a>, franchise, or the like, and improve and make the most of it for the benefit of his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, the word is also written appruere.

APPROXIMATION

Pages 530-530
