in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARITHMETIC">Arithmetic</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALGEBRA">Algebra</a>, the coming nearer and nearer to a root, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> sought, without expecting to be ever able to find it exactly.

APPUI

Pages 530-530

in the manege, (q. d. rest to stay upon the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>), is the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECIPROCAL">reciprocal</a> effort between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>'s mouth and the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIDLE">bridle</a>-hand, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of the bridle on the hand of the horseman. A <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> appui of the hand, is the nice <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> up or stay of the bridle, so that the horse, being awed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSIBILITY">sensibility</a> and tenderness of his mouth, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DARES">dares</a> not rest too much upon the bitmouth, nor check or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> upon the hand to withstand it. A horse is said to have no appui, when he is too apprehensive of the hand, and cannot bear the bit. He is said to have too much appui, when he rests or throws himself too much upon the bit. Horses designed for the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> ought to have a full appui upon the hand. To give a horse a good appui, he should be galloped, and put often back.

APPULSE

Pages 530-530

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, the approach of any planet, to a conjunction with the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STAR">star</a>. It is a step towards a transit, occultation, conjunction, eclipse, &c. Mr Flamsted, M. de la Hire, and others, have given observations of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a>'s appulses to the Pleiades. Phil. Trans. No 76. p. 361. M. Acad. Science, an. 1708.

APRIES

Pages 531-531

son of Psammis, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>; the same with <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHARAOH">Pharaoh</a> Hophrah in Jeremiah and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EZEKIEL">Ezekiel</a>. He ruined <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIDON">Sidon</a>, and some say he put Jeremiah to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. He thought neither God nor <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> could dethrone him; which yet was easily done by Amasis, and he himself was strangled by the Egyptians.

APRIL

Pages 531-531

the fourth <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of the year, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> computation; but the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, according to that of the astronomers. It contains 30 days.—The word is derived from aprilis, of aperio, "I open;" because the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, in this month, begins to open her bosom for the production of vegetables. In this month the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> travels through the sign of Taurus. A PRIORI, a kind of demonstration. See Demonstration.

APRON

Pages 531-531

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUNNERY">Gunnery</a>, a piece of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> which caps <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> covers the vent or touch-hole of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUN">gun</a>.

APSIS

Pages 531-531
or Absis, signifies the bowed or arched roof of a house, room, or oven, &c. as also the ring or compass of a wheel. Apsis, in ecclesiastical writers, denotes an inner part in the ancient churches, wherein the clergy sat, and where the altar was placed. It is supposed to have been thus called, because covered with an arch or vault of its own, by the Greeks called αψίς, by the Latins absis. Apsis, in this sense, amounts to the same with what is otherwise called choir, concha, camera, and presbyterium; and stands opposed to the nave or body of the church. Apsis is more particularly used for the bishop's seat, or throne, in ancient churches. This was peculiarly called apsis gradata, because raised on steps above the ordinary stalls. It was also denominated exedra, and in latter times tribune. Apsis is also used for a reliquary, or case, wherein the relics of saints were anciently kept. It took the name apsis, from its being round or arched at the top; or perhaps from the place where it was kept. The apsis was commonly placed on the altar: it was usually of wood, sometimes also of gold and silver, with sculptures, &c. Apsis, in Astronomy, a term used indifferently for either of the two points of a planet's orbit, where it is at greatest or least distance from the sun or earth; and hence the line connecting those points is called the line of the apsides. The word is Greek, and derived from ἀπειρον, to connect. The apsis, at the greatest distance from the sun, is called the aphelion, and at the greatest distance from the earth the apogee; while that at the least distance from the sun is termed the periheilion, and at the least distance from the earth the perigee. APSIRTIDES. See Absorus.

APTERA

Pages 531-531

(Strabo, Stephanus); APTYRON, (Pliny); Afteria, (<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>): An inland town of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a>, whose port was Cisamus, on the west side of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, (Strabo); 12 miles to the south of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CYDONIA">Cydonia</a> towards the Montes Leuci, and as many from the Sinus Amphimales. So called from the Sirens, who, being there vanquished in song by the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSES">Muses</a>, stript themselves of their wings, and out of grief leaped into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, (Stephanus). There was a town of Lycia of the same name. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 25° N. Lat. 35° 50'.

APTHANE

Pages 531-531

a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> anciently given to the higher degrees of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> in Scotland. See <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THANE">Thane</a>.

APTITUDE

Pages 531-531
or Aptness, is often used, in speaking of the talents of the mind, for a promptitude, or disposition to learn things with ease and expedition: in which sense aptness amounts to the same with what the Greeks call εὐδοξία, bona índoles, and we sometimes docility. Charlton divides aptness into three parts, viz. acuteness, sagacity, and memory.

APTOTE

Pages 531-531

among grammarians, an indeclinable noun, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> one which has no <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VARIATION">variation</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>.

APULEIUS

Pages 531-532

Lucius, a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATONIC">Platonic</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, universally known by his performance of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">Golden</a> Ass. He lived in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> century, under the Antonines; and was born at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MADURA">Madura</a>, a Roman colony in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>. He studied first at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARTHAGE">Carthage</a>, then at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, and afterwards at Rome, where he learned the Latin tongue without the help of a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>. He was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of a curious and inquisitive disposition, especially in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> matters: this prompted him to take several journeys, and to enter into several <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. He spent his whole fortune almost in travelling; so that, at his return to Rome, when he was about to dedicate himself to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OSIRIS">Osiris</a>, he had not <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> enough to defray the expence attending the ceremonies of the reception, and was obliged to pawn his clothes to raise the necessary sum. He supported himself afterwards by pleading causes: and as he was a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> master of eloquence, and of a subtle genius, many considerable causes were trusted to him. But he availed himself more by a good <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> than by his pleadings; a widow, named Pudentilla, who was neither young nor handsome, but wanted a husband and was very rich, took a great fancy to him. This marriage drew upon him a troublesome <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUIT">suit</a>. The lady's relations, pretending he made <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of sorcery to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> her heart and money, accused him of being a magician before Claudius Maximus proconsul of Africa. Apuleius was under no great difficulty of making his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>. As Pudentilla was determined, from considerations of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, to enter upon a second marriage, even before she had seen this pretended magician, the youth, deportment, pleasing conversation, vivacity, and other agreeable qualities of Apuleius, were charms sufficient to engage her heart. He had the most favourable opportunities too of gaining her friendship, for he lodged some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> at her <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>: Pudentilla's eldest son having Apuleius having a great friendship for him, was likewise desirous of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MATCH">match</a>, and solicited him in favour of Pudentilla. "Do you make a wonder said Apuleius, in his defence) that a woman should marry again, after having lived a widow 13 years? It is much more wonderful that she did not marry again sooner. You think that <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGIC">magic</a> must have been employed to prevail with a widow of her <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> to marry a young man; on the contrary, this very circumstance shows how little occasion there was for magic." He offered to prove by his marriage-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a>, that he got nothing of Pudentilla but a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> of a very moderate sum, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> he survived her and had children by her. He was also obliged to make such confessions in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> as Pudentilla would gladly have excused. He said she was neither handsome nor young, nor such as could any ways tempt him to have recourse to enchantments: moreover, he added, that Pontianus her son proposed the marrying his mother to him only as a burden, and the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of a friend and philosopher. He also took notice of many inconveniences which attend the marrying of widows, and spoke highly of the advantages of a maid above a widow: "A handsome virgin (said he), let her be ever so <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a>, is abundantly portioned; she brings to her husband a heart quite new, together with the flower and first <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of her <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>. It is with great reason that all husbands set so great a value upon the flower of virginity: all the other goods which a woman brings her husband are of such a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, that he may return them again, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he has a mind to be under no obligation to her: that alone cannot be restored, it remains in the possession of the first husband. If you marry a widow, and she leaves you, she carries away all that she brought you." Upon which passage Mr Bayle makes a very coarse remark, viz. "That this good which is never taken back out of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of a husband, is very chimerical; and that there is never a baker nor a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTCHER">butcher</a>, who would lend sixpence upon this unperishable possession." The apology is still extant, and is reckoned a very fine piece. Apuleius was extremely indefatigable in his studies: and composed several books, some in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>, and others in prose; but most of them have been lost. He took great <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> in declaiming, and was heard generally with great applause: When he declaimed at Oecec, the audience cried out with one <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>, that they ought to confer upon him the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of citizen. The citizens of Carthage heard him with great satisfaction, and erected a statue to him; and several other cities did him the same honour. Several critics have published notes on Apuleius's Golden Ass, and there have been translations of it into different languages.

APULIA

Pages 532-532

now PUGLIA, a territory of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, bordering on the Adriatic, and extending from the river Frento to Tarentum in length, and from the Adriatic to the Lucani in breadth. Apuli the people (Horace); divided into the Apulia Daunia, now called Puglia Pinna <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITANATA">Capitanata</a>; and into the Apulia Peucetia, now Terra di <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARI">Bari</a>, (Pliny, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>). Apulia abounded in sheep, which yielded the finest <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a> (Martial). It is now the east side of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>.

APYCNI SUONI

Pages 532-532

in Music, sounds distant one <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> more octaves, and yet concord.

APYCNOS

Pages 532-532

in Music, is said of the diatonic genus, on account of its having spacious intervals, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHROMATIC">chromatic</a> and enharmonic.

APYROUS

Pages 532-532

a word applied to denote that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of some bodies, by which they resist the most violent fire without any sensible <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a>. Apyrous bodies ought to be distinguished from those which are refractory. Refractory substances are those which cannot by violent <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> be fused, whatever other alteration they may sustain. But a body, properly speaking, apyrous, can neither be fused by heat, nor can undergo any other change. Diamonds were <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> thought to be possessed of this property. But some late experiments have shown, that diamonds may be entirely dissipated <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> evaporated by heat, and are therefore not entitled to be ranked among apyrous substances. Perhaps there is no body in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> essentially and rigorously apyrous. But it is sufficient that there be bodies apyrous relatively to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of fire which art can produce, to entitle them to that name.

AQUA

Pages 532-535

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> frequently met with in the writings of physicians, chemists, &c. for certain medicines, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> menstruums, in a liquid form, distinguished from each other by peculiar epithets, as AQUA Alexiteria, AQUA Aluminosa, AQUA Mirabilis, &c. for which see <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHARMACY">PHARMACY</a>. AQUA Extincta, or Extinguished <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">Water</a>, is aquafortis into which some <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-RIVER_WATER">river water</a> has been poured, in order to qualify it, and render it less corrosive. Its <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> is to get the silver from the aquafortis that served to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> from it. Aqua Fortis, a name given by artists to nitric acid of a certain strength, from its dissolving power. See <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHEMISTRY">CHEMISTRY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Aqua Marina, a name by which the jewellers call the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BERYL">beryl</a>, on account of its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-green <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. See BERYL. Aqua Regia, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> of nitric and muriatic acid, in different proportions according to the purpose for which it is intended. It is usually made by dissolving in nitric acid, sal ammoniac, or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, both which are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBINATIONS">combinations</a> of muriatic acid with alkali. When made with sal ammoniac, the common proportion is one part of this salt to four parts of nitric acid; but to dissolve <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PLATINA">platina</a>, equal parts are requisite. A purer aqua regia may be made by simply mixing the two <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACIDS">acids</a>. It is particularly used as a menstruum for gold; it likewise dissolves all other <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-METALS">metals</a>, except silver. The gold dissolved in aqua regia is, in fact, dissolved in the oxygenated muriatic acid only, which gives out its <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXYGEN">oxygen</a> to the gold, and then dissolves the oxide: for metals are not soluble in acids until they are oxidated. See CHEMISTRY Index. Aqua Secunda, aquafortis diluted with much pure water. It is employed in several arts, to clear the surface of metals and certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>. Aqua Tofana, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POISON">poison</a> much used in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> in the seventeenth century. See SUPPLEMENT. Aqua Vitæ, is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> understood of what is otherwise called brandy, or spirit of wine either simple, or prepared with aromatics. Some, however, distinguish Aquae Augustae (<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>); Aquae Tarbellicae (Antonine); Aquensis Civitas, in the Notitia. Now Acqs, or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DAX">Dax</a>, a town in Gascony, on the river Adour, famous for its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1. 40. N. Lat. 43. 56. Aquae Bilbilitanæ, (Antonine): baths 24 miles to the west of Bilbilis. Now Banos de <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALHAMA">Alhama</a>, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARAGON">Aragon</a>. Aquæ Calideæ, (Ptolemy); Aquæ Solis, (Antonine); a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of the Belgæ in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, famous for its hot waters. Now Bath in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOMERSETSHIRE">Somersetshire</a>. W. Long. 1. 5. Lat. 51. 20. Aquæ Calideæ, (Ptolemy); Aquicaldensis, (Pliny); formerly in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> repute, and a public bath; whose ruins still remain, testimonies of the Roman <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a>. Now Orense, in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GALICIA">Galicia</a>, still famous for its baths; on the river Minho, 54 miles south-east of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSTELLA">Compostella</a>. W. Long. 8. 30. N. Lat. 42. 30. Also a place in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARTHAGE">Carthage</a>, (Strabo). Other Aquicaldenses, to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of Gerunda in Catalonia, (Ptolemy). Aquæ Calideæ, a colony between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Serbetes and Savus, in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MAURITANIA">Mauritania</a> Caesariensis, (Ptolemy). Aquæ Celeinae, (Ptolemy); or Cilinae, (Antonine). Now Caldas, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAMLET">hamlet</a> on the Minho, in Galicia. Aquæ Convenarum, a hamlet of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAUL">Gaul</a>, in Aquitaine, (Antonine), and on the borders of the Convenæ, or le Cominge, at the foot of the Pyrenees, near the source of the Garonne. Now Bagnères. W. Long. 3. 39. N. Lat. 42. 20. Aquæ Cutiliae, a lake of the Sabines, in the territory of Reat (Pliny); Locus Cutiliensis, (Varro); with a moveable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in it, (Seneca, Pliny); supposed to be the centre of Italy, (Varro). The waters were medicinal, and extremely <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, good for a weak stomach and in weak nerves; they seemed to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> by a kind of suction, which approached to a bite, (Pliny). Vespasian used them every <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>; and there he died, (Sueton. Xiphilin from Dio). Now Lago di Contigliano. Aquæ Flavieæ, a town on the confines of Galicia and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>, so called from Vespasian and Titus. The inhabitants are called Aquiflavienses on coins. Now called Chiaves, a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> hamlet; but the ruins of its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> testify its former grandeur. W. Long. 6. 6. N. Lat. 41. 40. Aquæ Helvetiae, described by T. Cicetus as a municipal town, and much frequented for its excellent water; and though he does not mention its name, Cluverius supposes it to be <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BADEN">Baden</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>, on the rivulet Limat, which soon after falls into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AAR">Aar</a>. It is called the Upper, to distinguish it from another called the Lower Baden, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALSACE">Alsace</a>. E. Long. 8. 49. N. Lat. 47. 55. Aquæ Merom (Joshua), famous for the defeat of Jabin: supposed to be the lake called Samachonites, or Semechonites, by Josephus; into which the river Jordan falls, before it comes to the sea of Genesereth, or Galilee. Aquæ Pannoniae, famous baths of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>, now called Baden, 28 miles to the south of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIENNA">Vienna</a>. Aquæ Patavinæ, are baths in the territory of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> near <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PADUA">Padua</a>, (Pliny); called Fontes Aponti (Livy, Martial). Now Bagni d'<a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABANO">Abano</a>. E. Long. 13. 48. N. Lat. 45. 15. Aquæ Quintianæ, put by Ptolemy in room of the Aquæ Cilince of Antonine. Now supposed to be Sarria, a town of Galicia, on a rivulet of the same name, three leagues to the south of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LUGO">Lugo</a>. Aquæ Sextiae, a colony to the north of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARSEILLES">Marseilles</a>, so called both from the founder Sextius Clavinus, and from its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of water, and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of cold and hot <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a>; built after the defeat of the Salyes, or Salvii, whose territory in the south of Provence, reached from the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RHONE">Rhone</a> on the borders of Italy, (Livy, Velæius, Strabo, Ptolemy). By an inscription the colony appears to have been either increased or renewed by Augustus. In the Notitia it is called Civitas Aquensis. Now <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIX">Aix</a>. Here the Teutones and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CIMBRI">Cimbri</a> were defeated with great slaughter by Marius. E. Long. 6. 4. N. Lat. 48. 4. Aquæ Statiellæ, or Statiellorum, (Pliny), a town in Liguria, on the river Bormia. Now <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACQUI">Acqui</a>, a town of Montferrat. E. Long. 8. 40. N. Lat. 44. 45. Aquæ Tauri, hot waters or baths in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUSCANY">Tuscany</a>, at the distance of three miles from the sea, said to be discovered by a bull, hence the appellation. There are still to be seen the ruins of these baths. Now Aquapendente, in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORVIETO">Orvieto</a>. E. Long. 12. 40. N. Lat. 42. 20. Aqueduct, in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HYDRAULICS">Hydraulics</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, a structure formed for conveying water from one place to another, over grounds that are unequal. The word is compounded of the Latin substantive aqua, water, and ductus, a channel by which that water may be conducted. Architects distinguish two kinds of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AQUEDUCTS">aqueducts</a>; the visible, and the subterraneous.—The visible are constructed in valleys or marshes, and protracted in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a> or latitude as the situation requires. They are composed of adminicula for supporting the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a> and confining the stream, and of arcades.—The subterraneous are formed, by piercing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, and conducting them below the surface of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. They are built of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> hewn or rough; and covered above with vaults, or with flat stones, which may be termed flags; these flags shelter the waters from the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>. They divide them still into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> and triple aqueducts; that is to say, such as are supported either by two or by three ranges of arcades. Such was the aqueduct which Procopius records to have been built by Cosroes <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of the Persians, for the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Petra in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINGRELIA">Mingrelia</a>: it had three conduits upon the same line, each elevated above the other. Frequently aqueducts are paved. Sometimes the waters flow through a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> channel of clay. Frequently they are conveyed by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> into reservoirs of the same metal, or into troughs of hewn stone. The channels are cut with an imperceptible <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a>, that the current may be accelerated by its own <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">Parallel</a> to its course, on each side, is cut a narrow footpath, where people may walk when necessary. By conduits, or grooves, the waters are conveyed into <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> cisterns, but not forced above their original <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a>. To make them rise and issue from their apertures. Aqueduct apertures with force, they must be confined in tubes of a small diameter, and abruptly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> from a considerable declivity. Aqueducts of every kind were long ago the wonders of Rome; the vast quantities of them which they had; the prodigious expense employed in conducting waters over arcades from one place to another, at the distance of 30, 40, 60, and even 100 miles, which were either <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> or supplied by other labours, as by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> mountains and piercing rocks; all this ought to surprise us: nothing like this is undertaken in our times: we dare not even think of purchasing public convenience at so dear a rate. Appius the censor advised and constructed the first aqueduct. His example gave the public <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a> a hint to cultivate these objects; and the force of prodigious and indefatigable labour diverted the course of rivers and floods to Rome. Agrippa, in that year when he was ædile, put the last <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> to the magnificence of these works. It is chiefly in this respect that the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> so much resembles the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> city of Rome. For this advantage, she is peculiarly indebted to Sextus V. and to Paul V., who for grandeur and magnificence emulated the masters of the universe*. There are still to be seen, in different places contiguous to Rome, striking remains of these aqueducts; arches continued through a long space, over which were extended the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a> which carried the water to the city. The arches are sometimes low, sometimes raised to a vast height, to humour the tumulities or depressions of the ground. There are some which have two arcades; one constructed above the other; and this precaution was observed, lest the height of a single arcade, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> extended as far as the situation required, might render the structure less firm and permanent. They are commonly of bricks: which by their cement cohere so strongly, that the parts are not separated without the utmost difficulty.—When the elevations of the ground were enormous, it became necessary to form subterraneous aqueducts. These carried the waters to such aqueducts as were raised above ground, in the declivity or at the foot of mountains. If the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> channel of the water was not susceptible of a downward bias but by passing through a rock, through this they cut a passage at the same height with the superior aqueduct: such a one may be seen above the city of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TIVOLI">Tivoli</a>, and at the place called Vivacaro. The canal which formed the course of the aqueduct is hewn out of the rock to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of more than a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a>, about five feet in height and four in breadth. There is one thing, however, which deserves to be remarked. It is, that these aqueducts, which might have been directed in a straight line to the city, did not arrive at it but by frequent and winding mazes. Some have said that this oblique track was pursued to avoid the expense which must attend the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> of arcades to an extraordinary height; others, that it was their intention to diminish the impetuosity of the current; which, rolling in a straight line through an immense space, must always have increased its velocity, must have worn the canals by perpetual and forcible attrition, and of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> afforded an impure and unwholesome draught to the inhabitants. But since there was so great a descent between the cascade of Tivoli and Rome, it is demanded why they should go to draw water from the same river at the distance of more than 20 miles higher; nay, of more than 30 miles, if we reckon the curvatures of its <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> through that mountainous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>? It is replied, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a> of obtaining the water more salubrious and more limpid, was sufficient to make the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> think their labour necessary, and their expense properly bestowed; and to those who reflect that the waters of this river were impregnated with mineral particles, and by no means wholesome, the answer <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> appear satisfactory. If any one will <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> his eyes upon Plate 128th of the Antiquities of Father Montfaucon, he will see with how much care these immense works were constructed. From distance to distance spiraments were left, that, if the water should happen to be stopped by any accident, it might gradually disemboque, till they could clear its ordinary passage. There were likewise, even in the very canals which conveyed the water, cavities considerably deeper than its internal surface, into which the stream was precipitated, and where it remained stagnant till it was refined from mud and feculence; and ponds, where it might expand itself till it was purified. The aqueduct of the Aqua <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MARCIA">Marcia</a> had an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> of Vol. iv. 16 feet in diameter. The whole was composed of three different kinds of stone; one of them reddish, another <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>, and a third of an earth colour. Above, there appeared two canals; of which the highest was fed by the new waters of the Tiberone, and the lower by what they called the Claudian river. The entire edifice is 70 Roman feet <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>. Near this aqueduct, we have in Father Montfaucon the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of another with three canals; the highest supplied by the water called Julia, that in the middle from Tepula, and the lowest from the Aqua Marcia. The arch of the aqueduct of the Aqua Claudia is of hewn stone, very beautiful: that of the aqueduct of the Aqua Neronia is of bricks: they are each of them 72 Roman feet in height. The canal of the aqueduct which was called the Aqua Appia, deserves to be mentioned for a singularity which is observed in it; for it is not, like the others, plain, nor gradual in its descent; but much narrower at the lower than the higher end. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a> Frontinus, who superintended the aqueducts under the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Nerva, mentions <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> of them which had each 13,594 pipes of an inch in diameter. Vigerus observes, that, in the space of 24 hours, Rome received 500,000 hogsheads of water. We might likewise have mentioned the aqueduct of Drusus, and that of Riminius: but we shall satisfy ourselves with observing here, that Augustus caused all the aqueducts to be repaired; and afterwards <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> to other monuments of the same kind, and still more important, which give the most striking <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> of Roman magnificence. One of these monuments is the aqueduct of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METZ">Metz</a>, of which a great number of arcades still remain. These arcades crossed the Moselle, a river which is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> and vast at that place. The copious sources of Gorze furnished water for the representation of a sea fight. This water was collected in a reservoir: from thence it was conducted by subterraneous canals formed of hewn stone, and so spacious that a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> could walk erect in them: it traversed the Moselle upon its superb and lofty arcades, which may still be seen at the distance of two Aqueduct two leagues from Metz; so nicely wrought and so firmly cemented, that, except those parts in the middle which have been carried away by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ICE">ice</a>, they have resisted, and will still resist, the severest shocks of the most violent seasons. From these arcades, other aqueducts conveyed the waters to the baths, and to the place where the naval engagement was mimicked. If we may trust Colmcarus, the aqueduct of Segovia may be compared with the most admired labours of antiquity. There still remain 159 arcades, wholly consisting of stones enormously large, and joined without <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MORTAR">mortar</a>. These arcades, with what remains of the edifice, are 102 feet high; there are two ranges of arcades, one above another. The aqueduct flows through the city, and runs beneath the greatest number of houses which are at the lower end. After these exorbitant structures, we may be in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> believed when we speak of the aqueduct which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIV. caused to be built near <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAINTENON">Maintenon</a>, for carrying water from the river Bucq to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSAILLES">Versailles</a>: it is perhaps the greatest aqueduct which now subsists in the world: it is 700 fathoms in length, and contains 242 arcades.

AQUAMBOE

Pages 535-535

one of the greatest monarchies on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUINEA">Guinea</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, stretching 20 miles in breadth, and ten times that space in length from east to west. According to Bosman, the coast is divided into a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of petty royalties, but all of them subject to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Aquamboe, who indiscriminately uses an unlimited authority over them and the meanest of his subjects. His despotism gave rise to a proverbial saying, that "there are only two ranks of men at Aquamboe; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> family, and slaves." The natives of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> are haughty, turbulent, and warlike; and their power is formidable to all the neighbouring nations. They grievously infest such nations as are tributaries to the king of Aquamboe, entering their territories by troops, and carrying off from the inhabitants whatever they think proper; nor do they ever meet with any opposition from the inhabitants, as they are sensible the king would not fail to resent this as an indignity offered to him. AQUAPENDENTE. See Fabricius.

AQUARIANS

Pages 535-535
Christians in the primitive church who consecrated water in the eucharist instead of wine. This they did under pretence of abstinence and temperance; or, because they thought it universally unlawful to eat flesh or drink wine. Epiphanius calls them Encratites, from their abstinence; St Austin, Aquarians, from their use of water; and Theodore, who says they sprang from Tatian, Hydroporastae, because they offered water instead of wine. Besides these, there was another sort of Aquarians, who did not reject the use of wine as unlawful; for they administered the eucharist in wine at evening service; but, in their morning assemblies, they commonly used water, for fear the smell of wine should discover them to the heathens.

AQUARIUS

Pages 535-535

the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">Water</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARRIER">carrier</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, the 11th sign of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZODIAC">zodiac</a>, reckoning from Aries; from which also the 11th <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the ecliptic takes its name.—The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> moves through Aquarius in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a>; it is marked thus, ♒. The poets feign, that Aquarius was <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GANYMEDE">Ganymede</a>, whom <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> ravished under the shape of an eagle, and carried away into heaven, to serve as a cupbearer, in the room of Hebe and Vulcan; whence the name.—Others hold, that the sign was thus called, because, when it appears in the horizon, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> usually proves rainy. The stars in the constellation Aquarius, in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>'s catalogue, are 45; in Tycho's 41; in Hevelius's 47; in Flamsted's 108. AQUARTIA. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

AQUATIC

Pages 535-535

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, an appellation given to such things as live <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> grow in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>.

AQUATINTA

Pages 535-536

a method of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ETCHING">etching</a> on <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, lately invented, by which a soft and beautiful <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> is produced, resembling a fine <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> colours <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INK">ink</a>. Previous to the operation upon the plate, the following powder must be prepared.—Take of asphaltum and fine transparent rosin, equal parts, suppose two ounces of each, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> them separately. Through a muslin sieve (which may be formed with <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of a chipbox of three or four inches diameter) sift upon a sheet of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> a thin stratum of the asphaltum, above which sift a similar layer of the rosin, and upon this another layer of asphaltum, continuing these <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALTERNATE">alternate</a> layers till both of the powders are exhausted; then <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> the mixtures through the same sieve upon the paper once or twice, or till both appear to be sufficiently incorporated; when the powder is ready for <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>. Some, instead of the above mixture, use <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUM">gum</a> sandarach pounded. The main <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> is as follows:—A copperplate being polished in the usual way, lay the etching ground upon it, and etch the outlines of your <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> in the manner directed under the article ETCHING: The ground is then to be softened with a little grease, and wiped off with a piece of rag; leaving, however, as much grease upon the plate as <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> to dim the copper. You now sift your powder upon the surface of the plate; after which, strike the other side of it pretty smartly against the edge of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, in order to discharge it of the loose powder: This done, with a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>-vice hold the back of the plate over a chafing <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DISH">dish</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARCOAL">charcoal</a> fire, till it become so hot as to give pain upon being touched with the back of the hand; and the powder which adhered to the grease <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> now be fixed to the plate. The plate being then suffered to cool, take turpentine <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VARNISH">varnish</a> mixed with <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>; and with a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a> dipt in it, cover all the lights or places where there is no <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> or shades. A rim or border of bees-wax is now to be raised under the plate: Then having reduced the aquafortis to a proper strength by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a> or water, you pour it on, and let it stand five minutes for the first or lightest <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a>: after which, pour it off; and having washed the plate with water, set it on edge to dry: Then with the varnish stop up your <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> shades: pour on the aquafortis for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> tint, and let it stand five minutes more; proceeding in the same manner for every tint till you produce the darkest shades. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> a bold open ground is wanted in any part, this requires an after operation: The ground must be laid as the other, by sifting on the powder; only this powder is much coarser, and the plate must be much more heated in order that the particles of the powder may spread, and form small circles: even good clean rosin will do by itself. In etching landscapes, the sky and distant objects are also performed by a second operation, and the powder is sifted upon the plate with a finer sieve. If the trees or any part of the fore-ground require to be higher finished, the plate must be entirely cleansed from grease with <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>, and a ground laid in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> way of etching; when you may finish as highly and neatly as you please with the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEEDLE">needle</a> or point, by stippling with dots, and biting up those parts, or by a rolling-wheel. The preceding is the method for <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINTS">prints</a> of one single tint. But if different colours are to be expressed, there will be required as many different plates, each plate having only the part etched upon it which is designed to be <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with its proper colour; unless (as may happen in particular subjects) some of the colours are so distant from each other as to allow the printer room to fill them in with his rubber without blending them; in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, two or more different colours may be printed from the same plate at once.—Where different plates are necessary, a separate one, having a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIN">pin</a> in each corner, must be provided as a sole or bottom to the aquatinta plates; and these again must be exactly fitted, having each a small hole in their corners for passing over the pins of the sole; the said pins serving the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> purpose of retaining the plates successively in their due position, and of directing the printer in placing the paper exactly on each plate so as not to shift; by which means each tint or colour will be exactly received on its proper <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>.—This is the method practised at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. A landscape or similar subject, however, may be printed off at once in the different proper colours, by <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> these upon the plate. In this case, the colours must be pretty thick in their consistence; and the plate must be carefully wiped in the usual way after the laying on of each tint, as well as receive a general wipe upon its being charged with all the tints. This art is kept as secret as possible by those who practice it; and it is believed that no particular explanation or directions, before the present, have been communicated to the public. In order to succeed, however, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> care and judgment are requisite; and much depends upon a certain nicety of management, which is only attainable by practice.

AQUAVIVA

Pages 536-536

a town of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARI">Bari</a>. AQUEDUCT. See Aqueduct.

AQUEOUS

Pages 536-536

in a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, something partaking of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> that abounds with it. Aquae Humour. See Anatomy, p. 276.

AQUILA

Pages 536-536

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a>, a synonyme of the eagle. See Falco. Aquila, the Eagle, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, a constellation of the northern hemisphere; usually joined with Antinous. The stars in the constellation <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AQUA">Aqua</a> and Antinous, in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>'s catalogue, are 15; in Tycho's 19; in Hevelius's 42; in the Britannic catalogue, 71. Aquila, a fine <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of Abruzzo, seated on a hill, on the banks of the river Pescaro, near its source. It has an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> castle, and is a bishop's see immediately under the pope. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> about it produces <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> plenty of saffron. It was very near being all destroyed by an earthquake, in February 1703. The first shock was so terrible, that the inhabitants abandoned the city; but returning to vespers, it being <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANDLEMAS">Candlemas</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, the shocks followed one another with such violence, that 24,000 people perished, and great numbers were wounded; 800 were killed in one single <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>; many other churches, monasteries, noble buildings, and the townhouse, were either swallowed up <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> overturned, together with the greater <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the city and its walls. Aquila stands 30 miles from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, and about 16 from the confines of the pope's dominions. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 14. 20. N. Lat. 42. 20.

AQUILEIA

Pages 536-536

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the Carni, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Veneti, and a noble Roman colony, which was led thither between the first and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> Macedonian wars, (Livy). It is washed by two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, the Natiso and Turrus, (Pliny). The reason of leading this colony was, in order to be a bulwark against the neighbouring barbarians. The colony was afterwards increased with 1500 families by a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DECREE">decree</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>, (Livy); from which it became a very famous port town, (Herodian). The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Julian ascribes the appellation to the augury of an eagle at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> it; but <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Vossius on Mela, to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> plenty of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the town were called Aquilegia. The harbour, at the mouth of the Natiso, is distant 60 stadia from the city; so that ships of burden are towed up the river, (Strabo). In 452 it was besieged by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATTILA">Attila</a> with an innumerable <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOST">host</a> of barbarians. The walls were assaulted by a formidable train of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTERING">battering</a> rams, moveable turrets, and engines that threw <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, darts, and fire; and the monarch of the Huns employed the forcible impulse of hope, fear, emulation, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>, to subvert the only <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARRIER">barrier</a> which delayed the conquest of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. Aquileia was at that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> one of the richest, the most populous, and the strongest of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> cities of the Hadriatic <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a>. Three months were consumed without effect in the siege; till the want of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> and the clamours of his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> compelled Attila to relinquish the enterprise, and reluctantly to issue his orders that the troops should strike their tents the next morning and begin their retreat. But as he rode round the walls, pensive, angry, and disappointed, he observed a stork preparing to leave her nest in one of the towers, and to fly with her infant family towards the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. He seized, with the ready penetration of a statesman, this trifling incident which chance had offered to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>; and exclaimed in a loud and cheerful tone, that such a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIRD">bird</a>, so constantly attached to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, would never have abandoned her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> seats, unless those towers had been devoted to impending ruin and solitude. The favourable <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OMEN">omen</a> inspired an assurance of victory; the siege was renewed and prosecuted with fresh vigour; a large <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREACH">breach</a> was made in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the wall from whence the stork had taken her flight; the Huns mounted to the assault with irresistible fury; and the succeeding <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a> could scarcely discover the ruins of Aquileia. The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, however, is still called Aquileia; and there are several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a> and antiquities to be seen in it, which are worthy of a traveller's notice; and, though dwindled into a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> village, it gives a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRIARCH">patriarch</a> of Aquileia.

AQUILICUM

Pages 536-537
or Aquilliciana, in Roman antiquity, sacrifices performed in times of excessive drought, to obtain rain of the gods.

AQUILINE

Pages 537-537

something belonging to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> resembling an eagle: Thus an aquiline nose is one bent somewhat like an eagle's beak.

AQUILO

Pages 537-537

is used by Vitruvius for the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> that which blows at 45° from the north toward the east point of the horizon.—The poets gave the name aquilo to all stormy winds dreaded by the mariner.

AQUILUS

Pages 537-537

among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, a dark <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> dusky <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> approaching to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>. Hence some of the Heathen gods were called dii aquili, q. d. nieri.

AQUIMINARIUM

Pages 537-537

in antiquity, a kind of lustral vessels, wherein the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> carried their holy <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPIATION">expiation</a> and other <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> offices.

AQUINAS

Pages 537-537

ST THOMAS, styled the Angelical <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOCTOR">Doctor</a>, was of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and noble family of the counts of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AQUINO">Aquino</a>, descended from the kings of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARAGON">Aragon</a>; and was born in the castle of Aquino, in the Terra di Lavora in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the year 1224 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 1225. He entered into the order of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMINICANS">Dominicans</a>; and, after having taught school <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> in most of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a> of Italy, at last settled at <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>; where he spent the rest of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> of lectures, and in acts of piety; and was so far from the views of ambition or profit, that he refused the archbishopric of that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, when it was offered him by Pope Clement IV. He died in 1274, leaving an amazing <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of writings, which were printed at <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> in 17 vols. folio, in the year 1490. He was canonized by Pope John XXII. in the year 1323; and Pius V. who was of the same order with him, gave him, in 1567, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of the Fifth Doctor of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, and appointed his festival to be kept with the same solemnity as those of the other four doctors. His authority has always been <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ROMAN_CATHOLICS">Roman Catholics</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Herbert, in his life of Henry VIII. tells us, that one of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> reasons which induced that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> to write against <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUTHER">Luther</a> was, that the latter had spoken contemptuously of Thomas Aquinas.

AQUINO

Pages 537-537

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, and Terra di Lavora; a bishop's see, but ruined by the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Conrade, and now consisting of about 35 houses. It was the birthplace of the poet Juvenal, and of Thomas Aquinas. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 14. 30. N. Lat. 41. 32.

AQUINUM

Pages 537-537

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> municipal town, and a Roman colony on the borders of the Sannites, washed by the river Melpha (Strabo). The inhabitants are called Aquinates. Now <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AQUINO">Aquino</a>, but almost in ruins, in the territory of Lavora. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. Aquinum 17. 11. N. Lat. 41. 35.

AQUITANIA

Pages 537-537

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, one of the three <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> divisions of Gallia Comata (Cæsar); bounded by the Garonne, the Pyrenees, and the ocean: this is the Aquitania Caesariana, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Vetus. Augustus set the different boundaries, viz. the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOIRE">Loire</a>, the Cevennes, the Pyrenees, and the ocean (Strabo). It was called Galia Aquitanica (Pliny); and in the old Notitia Provincia Aquitanica. The people are called Aquitani (Cæsar). Now comprising Guienne (which seems to be a corruption of Aquitania) and Gascony.

AR

Pages 537-537

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a> of Moab, in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a> Petraea (Moses), and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> residence, situated on the east side of the river Arnon. It was called also Rabba (Joshua); and to distinguish it from Rabba of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMMONITES">Ammonites</a>, Rabbat Moab, and on coins Rabbatha Moma (Reland). Eusebius says it was called Areopolis in his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, from Ar and Polis. The inhabitants are called Areopolitæ. St Jerome says that this <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> was entirely destroyed by an earthquake when he was a young <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>.

ARA THURIBULI

Pages 537-537

the altar of incense, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, a southern constellation, not visible in our hemisphere, consisting, according to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>, of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> stars; and according to Sharp's Catalogue, annexed to that of Mr Flamsted, of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> stars.

ARABESQUE

Pages 537-537
or Arabesk, something done after the manner of the Arabians. Arabesque, Grotesque, and Morcesque, are terms applied to such paintings, ornaments of friezes, &c. where there are no human or animal figures, but which consist wholly of imaginary foliage, plants, stalks, &c. The words take their rise from hence, that the Moors, Arabs, and other Mahometans, use these kind of ornaments; their religion forbidding them to make any images or figures of men or other animals.

ARABIA

Pages 537-568

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, famous from the remotest antiquity for the independency of its inhabitants named during the vast conquests of the Assyrians, Persians, Greeks, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>; and, in later times, for being the centre of an empire equal, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not superior, in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> to any that ever existed. This country, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> at least the greater <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of it, was in the earliest ages called Arubah. Concerning the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ETYMOLOGY">etymology</a> of this word there are various conjectures. It has most generally been derived from the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> word אָרְבַּי, signifying the west, mixture, or traffic; but, according to M. Volney, Arab, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of these countries, signifies a solitude or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DESERT">desert</a>. In its largest extent, Arabia lies between the 12th and 35th degrees of N. Lat. and the 36th and 61st of E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. Its greatest length from <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> to south is about 1430 miles, and its breadth from east to west is 1200. It is bounded on the west by <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALESTINE">Palestine</a>, part of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, the isthmus of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUEZ">Suez</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RED_SEA"><a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">Red</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>, called by the Arabs the sea Al Koloom; on the east by the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUPHRATES">Euphrates</a>, the Persian <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ORMUS">Ormus</a>; on the north, by part of Syria, Diyar Beer, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-IRAK">Irak</a>, and Khuzestan; and on the south by the straits of Babelmandel and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> ocean. It grows narrower as we approach the frontiers of Syria and Diyar Beir. Becr; and, by reason of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROXIMITY">proximity</a> of the Euphrates to the Mediterranean, may be looked upon as a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a>, and that one of the largest in the whole world. —Arabia Proper, however, is much narrower, including little more than what was comprehended by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> under the name of Arabia Felix, which we shall presently describe; and here the Arabs have been settled almost since the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a>. The first <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of the peninsula of Arabia was into Arabah and Kedem, as we learn from Scripture; the first of which implies the west, and the other the east, denoting the situation of the two countries. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a> was the first who divided the peninsula we speak of into three parts, Arabia Petraea, Arabia Deserta, and Arabia Felix, which division has generally prevailed since his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. Arabia Petraea, on the east was bounded by Syria and Arabia Deserta; on the west, by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, or rather the isthmus of Suez, which separates Asia from <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, and the Hieropolitan gulf or western arm of the Red sea; on the north, by Palestine, the lake <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASPHALTITES">Asphaltites</a>, and Cælosyria; and on the south by Arabia Felix. This tract did not admit of much cultivation, the greatest part being covered with dry sands, or rising into rocks, interspersed here and there with some fruitful spots. Its <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a> was Petra, which by the Syrians was styled Rukam, and in Scripture Joktheel. Several other cities of Arabia Petraea are mentioned by Ptolemy; but as it is very improbable such a barren country should abound with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> cities, we must look upon them as inconsiderable places. Arabia Deserta was bounded on the north by the Euphrates, which separated it from Mesopotamia; on the west, by Syria, Judæa, and Arabia Petraea; on the east, by a ridge of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> which separated it from <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BABYLONIA">Babylonia</a> and Chaldea; on the south, by Arabia Felix, from which it was likewise separated by several ridges of hills. By far the greatest part of this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, as well as the former, was a lonesome desert, diversified only with plains covered with sand, or mountains consisting of naked rocks and precipices; nor were they ever, unless sometimes at the equinoxes, refreshed with <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>. The few vegetables which they produced were stinted by a perpetual drought, and the nourishment afforded them by the nocturnal dews was greatly impaired by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> in the daytime. Throughout the deserts were found huge mountains of sand, formed by the violence of the winds that continually blew over them in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>-time, though they ceased in the night. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WELLS">Wells</a> and fountains were for the most part exceedingly rare; however, notwithstanding the sterility of these countries, the vast plains of sand <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> now mentioned were interspersed with fruitful spots, which appeared here and there like so many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> in the midst of the ocean. These being rendered extremely delightful by their verdure, and the more so by the neighbourhood of those frightful deserts, the Arabs encamped upon them; and having consumed every thing they found upon one, removed to another, as is the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of their descendants the Bedoueens at this day. These fruitful spots were likewise frequent in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBYA">Libya</a>, and by the Egyptians called auases, or abases, as we learn from Strabo. The barren part of Arabia Felix, bordering upon the Red sea, was in like manner interspersed with abases; which Arabia probably gave the name of Abaseni to a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> settled there, and in the adjacent fertile region. A body of these, it is said, crossing the straits of Babelmandel, passed into Ethiopia, which from them received the name of Abassia. From this account of Arabia Deserta, we may reasonably conclude, that the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> said by Ptolemy to have been situated in it were places of very little <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>. Arabia Felix was bounded on the north by the two kingdoms just described; on the south, by the Red sea; on the east and west, by part of that sea, together with the Arabian and Persian gulfs. In Strabo's time, it was divided into five provinces, by the oriental historians called Yaman, Hejaz, Tahamah, Najd, and Yamama. In this district stood several towns, particularly Nysa, famous for being the birthplace of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a>; and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSA">Musa</a>, or Muza, a celebrated emporium or harbour, where the Arabian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> resorted with their frankincense, spices, and perfumes. These two were situated in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Yaman. In that of Hejaz stood the still more famous cities of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECCA">Mecca</a> and Medina; also Thaisa or Taisa, Gjudda or Joddo, Yanbo or Al Yanbo, and Madian, the Modiana of Ptolemy, and the Midian or Madiam of Scripture. At what time the above-mentioned kingdoms were first peopled we have no certain accounts. The most p[...] considerable nations inhabiting Arabia Petraea, in the early ages, were the Ishmaelites, the Nabatei or Na-batheans, the Cedrei or Kedareni, and the Agareni or Hagareni; and of these the Ishmaelites were the most powerful, if they did not comprehend all the rest; and if the Hagareni were not the same people with them, they must at least have been nearly related. Kimchi, an oriental historian, insinuates, that they were originally the children of Hagar by an Arab, after she had left <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABRAHAM">Abraham</a>. In after ages, the names of all the nations situated here were absorbed in that of Saracens, by which the Ishmaelites are distinguished in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a> Targum. A nation is also mentioned by Pliny, called Arraceni, and Saraceni by Ptolemy and Dioscorides, which was probably no other than the Ishmaelites above mentioned. In Arabia Deserta several tribes resided, all of whom were very obscure, except the Aisite and Arrei. The former are supposed by Bochart to have been <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOB">Job</a>'s countrymen, and the latter to have been the same with the Hagareni, Arracei, or Saraceni, above mentioned. Arabia Felix was inhabited by many different tribes; the most remarkable of which were the Sabei, Gerrai, Minei or Minnei, Atramite, Marinata, Catabani, Ascitae, Homerite, Sapphorite, Omanite, Saraceni, Nabathei, Thamydeni, and Bnizomenæ; but neither their limits nor situation can now be determined with any manner of precision. According to the oriental historians, the Arabs are to be divided into two classes; viz. the old lost <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARA">Ara</a>-bians, and the present. The most famous tribes among the former were those of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AD">Ad</a>, Thamud, Tasm, Jades, Jorham, Amalek, Amtem, Hasbem, Abil, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">Bar</a>. Concerning these, though now entirely lost and swallowed up among other tribes, there are some remarkable traditions, of which the following may serve as a specimen. The tribe of Ad deduced their origin from Ad the son of Aws, or Uz, the son of Aram, the son of Shem, who, after the confusion of tongues, settled in Al Abkaf, or the winding sands in the province of Hadramant, on the confines of Yaman, where his posterity greatly multiplied. Their first <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> was Sheddad, the son of Ad, who built a stately <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, and made a delightful garden in the deserts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADEN">Aden</a>, which he designed as an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of the celestial paradise. This garden he called Irem: and when it was finished, he set out with a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> retinue to take a view of it; but, having some thoughts of assuming divine honours, he was destroyed by a tempest from heaven, while yet a day's journey from his paradise. The garden and palace, however, were preserved, though invisible, as a monument of divine vengeance.
