The aræometer, or waterpoise, is usually made of glass; consisting of a round hollow <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a>, which terminates in a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> slender neck hermetically sealed at top: there being first as much running <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a> put into it as <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> serve to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a> or keep it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWIMMING">swimming</a> in an erect position. The stem is divided into degrees (as represented Plate XXXVI. fig. 23.) and by the depth of its <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> into any liquor, the lightness of that liquor is concluded: for that fluid in which it sinks least must be heaviest; and that in which it sinks lowest lightest. Mr <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOMBERG">Homberg</a> has invented an aræometer, described in Phil. Transact. No 262, thus: A is a glass bottle or matrass, with so slender a neck that a drop of water takes up in it above five or six <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>, or half of an inch. Near that neck is a small <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPILLARY">capillary</a> tube D, about six inches long, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to the neck.—To fill the vessel, the liquor is poured in at the mouth B (which is widened to receive a funnel), till it run out at D, that is, till it rise in the neck to the mark C, by which means you have always the same bulk or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of liquor; and consequently, by means of the balance, can easily tell, when different liquors fill it, which weighs most, or is most intensely heavy. Some regard, however, is to be had in these trials to the season of the year, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>; because some liquors rarefy with heat and condense with cold more than others, and accordingly take up more or less room. By means of this instrument, the ingenious author has made a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> to show the different weights of the same bulk of the most considerable chemical liquors both in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> and winter as follows: | Liquor | Weighed in summer | In winter | |-----------------|-------------------|-----------| | Quicksilver | 11 oz. dr. gr. | 11 oz. dr. gr. | | <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">Oil</a> of tartar | 01 03 08 | 01 03 13 | The instrument itself weighed, when empty, one drachm twenty-eight grains. See HYDROMETER in this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, and ARÆOMETER in the Supplement. ARÆOPAGUS. See <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AREOPAGUS">AREOPAGUS</a>. ARÆOSTYLE, in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> used by Vitruvius, to signify the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> which can be made between columns. ARÆOTICS, in Medicine, remedies which rarefy the humours, and render them easy to be carried off by the pores of the skin.

ARAFAH

Pages 579-579

the ninth <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> of the last <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of the Arabic year, named Dhoulhegiat; on which the pilgrims of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECCA">Mecca</a> perform their devotions on a neighbouring mountain called Arafa. The Mahometans have a very <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> veneration for this mountain, because they believe that <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADAM">Adam</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVE">Eve</a>, after they were banished out of Paradise, having been separated from each other during 120 years, met afterwards on this mountain. *ARAFAT, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> GIBEL EL ORHAT, the mountain of knowledge, a mountain in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a> near Mecca. The Mahometans say this was the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where Adam first met with and knew his wife Eve after their expulsion from Paradise. This mountain not being <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> enough to contain all the devotees that come annually in pilgrimage to Mecca, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a> are set up all round it to show how far it reaches. The pilgrims are clad in robes of humility and mortification, with their heads uncovered. They seem to be very much affected; for the tears flow <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHEEKS">cheeks</a>, and they sob and sigh most bitterly, begging earnestly for <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REMISSION">remission</a> of sins, and promising to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> a new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. They continue here about four or five hours, and at half an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> after sunset they all decamp to perform a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> duty called Asham nomac. After this, they all receive the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of hajgees, which is conferred upon them by the imam or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>. This being pronounced, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRUMPET">trumpet</a> sounds, and they all return to Mecca. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARAGON">ARAGON</a>. See ARRAGON.

ARAHUM

Pages 580-580
or Harahum, in ancient writers, denotes a place consecrated or set apart for holy purposes. Hence the phrase in araha jurare, or conjurare, "to make oath in the church;" because, by the Ripuarian laws, all oaths were to be taken in the church on the relics of the saints.

ARAL

Pages 579-580

a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> lake in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Khowarazim, lying a little to the eastward of the Caspian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. Its length from <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> to south is said to be near 150 miles, and its breadth from east to west about 70. The shore on the west side is <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> and rocky, and destitute of good <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>: yet there are abundance of wild horses, asses, antelopes, and wolves; as also a fierce creature called a jolhart, which the Tartars say is of such a prodigious strength as to carry off a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>. It is surprising that this lake should be quite unknown to geographers till within these few years. Several great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, which were supposed to run into the Caspian sea, are now known to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> into this lake, particularly the Sihun <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Sirr, and the Ghibun or Amo, so often mentioned. mentioned by the Oriental historians. This lake, like the Caspian sea, has no visible outlet. Its water is also very <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>; and for that reason is conveyed by the neighbouring inhabitants by small narrow <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a> into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> pits, where the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, by exhaling the water, leaves them a sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of salt. The same kinds of fish are found in the Aral that are found in the Caspian sea. The former is also called the Lake of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EAGLES">Eagles</a>.

ARAM

Pages 580-580
or Aramea Regio, in Ancient Geography, the Hebrew name of Syria, so called from Aram the son of Shem, (Moses, Josephus). ARAM Beth-Rehob, in Ancient Geography, was that part of Syria lying to the north of Palestine; because Rehob was its boundary towards that quarter, (Moses); allotted to the tribe of Asher, (Judges); where it joins Sidon, (Joshua). ARAM-Dammasek, or Syria Damascena, in Ancient Geography, a principal part of Syria, and more powerful than the rest (2 Sam.), taking its name from Damascus, the principal city. ARAM-Maacha, in Ancient Geography, a district of Syria, at the foot of Mount Hermon, (2 Samuel, 1 Chronicles); on the borders of the half tribe of Manasseh, on the other side the Jordan, called the coast of Maachathii, (Moses, Joshua). ARAM-Naharaim, in Ancient Geography, i.e. Aram or Syria of the Rivers, or Mesopotamia, situated between the Euphrates and Tigris; which is the reason of the name. ARAM-Soba or Zoba, in Ancient Geography, which David conquered, was a country near the Euphrates, where afterwards Palmyra stood; the Euphrates bounded it on the east, as the land of Canaan and Syria Damascena did on the west, (2 Samuel).

ARAMONT

Pages 580-580

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUEDOC">Languedoc</a> in France, seated on the river <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RHONE">Rhone</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 4° 52'. N. Lat. 43° 54'.

ARANJUEZ

Pages 580-581

a town in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of New Castile, where the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> has a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> and gardens which are reckoned the most delightful in the world. This <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> is 20 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MADRID">Madrid</a>, by a noble <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a>, planted on each side with trees, lately made at the expense of 120,000l. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a>. It is delightfully situated at the conflux of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TAGUS">Tagus</a> and Jarama; which run through the gardens, and add new <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> to this charming spot, where art and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> seem to go <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> in hand with the most pleasing and rural simplicity. On one side fine avenues of stately oaks and lofty elms convey the truest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> of magnificence, while they afford the most reviving <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a>; on the other, the sudden transitions to lawns and wilderness, the cascades of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> breaking through the thickets, the tuneful songs of numberless birds sheltered in these cool recesses, the occasional appearance and passage of the monarch attended by the grandees of his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>; all these objects united, and concentrated in one point, fill the imagination with pleasing ideas, and impress the mind of a traveller with a thousand agreeable sensations. The general situation is in a very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> plain surrounded with large hills, of a most disagreeable aspect indeed, but seldom appearing, being well hidden by the noble rows of trees that extend across the flat in every <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>. The main body of the palace is an old <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, to which have been lately added two new wings. The first <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the building was erected by <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> II, who purchased the estate, planted many of the avenues, and, in order to extend his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHASE">chase</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> to indulge his splenetic disposition, had all the vines that grew on the hills rooted up. By that means he drove away the inhabitants, and rendered the environs of his villa a perfect <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DESERT">desert</a>.—The apartments are good; but contain nothing very particular to take off from the enjoyment of so many fine objects abroad. In one of the new wings is a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-PLAYHOUSE">playhouse</a>, and in the other a chapel. Part of the ceiling of the former was painted by Mengs, who was also sent to Rome to paint a holy family for the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> altar in the chapel. There are <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> fine pictures of Luca Jordano in the apartment called El Cabinete Antiguo, and six others in that De los Mayordomos. The portraits of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> and duchess of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUSCANY">Tuscany</a>, by Mengs, are in a new apartment, called the king's dressing-room. In the chapel, over the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> altar, there is a fine <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> of the Annunciation, by Titian, presented by him to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> V, and brought from the convent of Juste, after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORCELAIN">porcelain</a> cabinet, where there are several large pieces of the king's own manufacture, is also an object of curiosity to a traveller. As to the gardens, the whole of them may be thrown into three grand divisions, distinguished by the names of La Huerta Valenciana, Los Deleites, and El Cortijo. In the Huerta Valenciana, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARDENING">gardening</a> are carried on in the same manner as in that fruitful province, and they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLOUGH">plough</a> with horses. In the Cortijo they <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> oxen, as in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANDALUSIA">Andalusia</a>; and in other places they scratch up the ground with mules, as is still practised in some parts of Spain. Whichever way one looks round, a constant variety pleases the eye, and enraptures the mind. At one moment the sturdy buffalo moves before you, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> his heavy burden; soon after, the slow camel, with his ponderous load; while the swift zebra with his striped garment frisks over the plains. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> you approach the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARM">farm</a>, every object of convenience is consulted, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAIRY">dairy</a> every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of neatness. The Dutch cow enjoys a luxuriant pasture, the brood mares greatly enliven the landscape, and the stables are filled with the most excellent horses; and an immense nursery furnishes all manner of trees and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. The fine avenue, which serves also for a public walk, called Calle de Reyna, has nothing equal to it at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSAILLES">Versailles</a>. It is three milcs <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, quite straight from the palace gate, crossing the Tagus twice before it loses itself in the thickets, where some noble spreading elms and weeping poplars hang beautifully over the deep still pool. Near this road is a flower garden for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, laid out with great <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> by Mr Wall during his ministry. The gay variety of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARA">ARA</a> At this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of year is particularly pleasing to the eye; but its beauty soon fades on the approach of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>. As the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> grows hot, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> that choose to walk retire to a garden in an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of the Tagus, on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> side of the palace. This is a heavenly place, cut into various walks and circular lawns, which in their primitive state may have been very stiff and formal; but in the course of a century, Nature has obliterated the regular forms of art; the trees have swelled out beyond the line traced for them, and destroyed the enfilade by advancing into the walks or retiring from them. The sweet flowering <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHRUBS">shrubs</a>, instead of being clipped and kept <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, have been allowed to shoot up into trees, and hang over the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> and fountains they were originally meant to serve as humble fences to. The jets-d'eau dash up among the trees, and add fresh verdure to the leaves. The terraces and balustrades built along the river, are now overgrown with roses, and other luxuriant bushes, hanging down into the stream, which is darkened by the large trees growing on the opposite banks. Many of the statues, groups, and fountains, are handsome, some masterly; the works of Algardi: all are placed in charming <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of view, either in open circular spots, at a distance from the trees, or else in gloomy arbours, and retired <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> of the wood. The banks of this wood, called the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-ILA">Ila</a>, are also enlivened by elegant yachts for the amusement of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> family. The town or village formerly consisted of the palace, its offices, and a few miserable huts, where the ambassadors, and the attendants of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, endeavoured to lodge themselves as well as they could, but always very uncomfortably; many of the habitations were vaults half underground. What determined the king to build a new town, and to embellish the environs, was an accident that happened at the nuncio's; a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COACH">coach</a> broke through the ceiling of his dining-room, and fell in upon the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>. The court then began to apply very considerable sums to the purpose of erecting proper dwellings for the great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of persons that flock to the place where the sovereign resides; near 15,000 are supposed to live here two or three months in spring; the king keeps 115 sets of mules, which require a legion of men to take care of them. Above a million sterling has been laid out at Aranjuez since the year 1763; and it must be acknowledged, that wonders have been performed: several fine streets drawn in straight <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> pavements, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> row of trees before the houses, and a very noble road in the middle; commodious hotels for the ministers and ambassadors; great squares, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a>, churches, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>, and an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMPHITHEATRE">amphitheatre</a> for bull feasts, have been raised from the ground; besides the accession of two new wings to the palace. Neatness and convenience have been more studied and sought for than show in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, but altogether the place has something truly magnificent in the coup d'œil.

ARARAT

Pages 581-582

the name of the mountain on which <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOAH">Noah</a>'s ark rested, after the abatement of the waters of the universal deluge. Concerning this mountain there are various conjectures; though it is almost universally allowed to be in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMENIA">Armenia</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">Major</a>. Some are of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that it is one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> which divide Armenia on the south from Mesopotamia and that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASSYRIA">Assyria</a> inhabited by the Curds; from whom these mountains took the name of Cardu <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Cardu, by the Greeks turned into Gordyæi, &c. Others, that it lies towards the middle of Armenia, near the river Araxes, above 280 miles distant from the above mentioned mountains, making it belong to Mount Taurus; but the Armenians are positive that Noah's Ararat is no other than a mountain to which they now give the name of Mavis, which lies about 12 leagues to the east of Eriwan, and four leagues from the Aras. It is encompassed by several petty hills: on the tops of them are found many ruins, thought to have been the buildings of the first men, who were, for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, afraid to descend into the plains. It stands by itself, in form of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>-loaf, in the midst of a very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> plain, detached, as it were, from the other mountains of Armenia, which make a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> chain. It consists, properly speaking, of two hills; the lesser of which is the more sharp and pointed: the higher, on which it is said the ark rested, lies to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west of it, and rises far above the neighbouring mountains. It seems so <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> and big, that, when the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> is clear, it may be seen four or five days journey off; yet travellers think the height is not extraordinary. Chardin is of opinion that he passed a part of Mount <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAUCASUS">Caucasus</a> which is higher; and Pouillet thinks the height of Mount Masis, or Ararat, not above twice as <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> as that of Mount Valerian near <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. They therefore think that its being visible at such a great distance is owing to its lonely situation in a vast plain, and upon the most elevated part of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, without any mountains before it to obstruct the view. Nor is the snow with which it is always covered from the middle upwards any argument of its height; for in this country, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ICE">ice</a> hath often been observed in the mornings of the middle of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>. (See Armenia). Certain it is, however, that this mountain hath never yet been ascended; which the Armenians pretend was owing to the interposition of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGELS">angels</a>, in order to disappoint the curiosity of those who wanted to advance to such a sacred <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> as that whereon the ark rested: but the excess of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a> may very reasonably be supposed able to frustrate all such attempts, without any supernatural interposition. The most distinct account we have of this mountain is that given by M. Tournefort: which, however, being much swelled with immaterial circumstances, it is needless to trouble our readers with at length. He tells us, that this mountain is one of the most disagreeable sights upon <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, without either houses, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a>, trees, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHRUBS">shrubs</a>; and seems as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> continually wasting and mouldering away. He divides it into three regions: The lowermost, he says, is the only one which contains any <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> creatures, and is occupied by a few miserable shepherds that tend scabby flocks; and here are also found some partridges: the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> is inhabited by crows and tigers; and all. the rest is covered with snow, which half the year is involved in thick <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a>. On the side of the mountain that looks towards <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ERIVAN">Erivan</a> is a prodigious precipice, from whence rocks of an immense size are continually tumbling <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> with a hideous noise. This precipice seems quite perpendicular; and the extremities are rough and blackish, as if smutted with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> of the mountain is loose, and on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> parts it is impossible to take a firm step; so that our traveller encountered great difficulties in his ascent and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> of this mountain; being often obliged, in order to avoid the sand, to betake himself to places where great rocks were heaped on one another, under which he passed as through caverns, or to places full of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, where he was forced to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAP">leap</a> from one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> to another. If we may believe Struys, a Dutch writer, however, all these difficulties may be surmounted. He assures us, he went five days journey up Mount Ararat, to see a Romish hermit: that he passed through three regions of clouds; the first dark and thick, the next cold and full of snow, and the third colder still; that he advanced five miles every <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>; and when he came to the place where the hermit had his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CELL">cell</a>, he breathed a very serene and temperate air; that the hermit told him, that he perceived neither <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> nor <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> all the 25 years he had dwelt there; and that on the top of the mountain there reigned a still greater tranquillity, whereby the ark was preserved uncorrupted. He farther pretends, that the hermit gave him a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> made out of the wood of the ark, together with a certificate; a formal copy of which the author has given in his sham relation.

ARASSI

Pages 582-582

a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a>, populous, and trading town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the territory of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENOA">Genoa</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 7. 20. N. Lat. 44. 3.

ARATEIA

Pages 582-582

in antiquity, a yearly festival celebrated at Sicyon, on the birth <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> of Aratus, wherein <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> honours were paid by a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> consecrated to this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, who for distinction's sake wore a ribband bespangled with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> and purple spots. The Arateia were solemnized with much pomp of music, the choristers of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a> attending.

ARATUS

Pages 582-582

a Greek poet, born at Soli, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Solae, a town in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CILICIA">Cilicia</a>, which afterwards changed its name, and was called Pompictopolis, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of Pompey the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>. He flourished about the 124th, or according to some, the 126th Olympiad, in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILADELPHUS">Philadelphus</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>. He discovered in his youth a remarkable poignancy of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a>, and capacity for improvement; and having received his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> under Dionysius Heracleotes, a Stoic <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, he espoused the principles of that <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a>. Aratus was physician to Antigonus Gonatus, the son of Demetrius Poliorcetes, king of Macedon: this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> being a great encourager of learned men, sent for him to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, admitted him to his intimacy, and encouraged him in his studies. The Phenomena of Aratus, which is still extant, gives him a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> to the character of an astronomer as well as a poet; in this piece he describes the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the stars, and shows the particular influences of the heavenly bodies, with their various dispositions and relations. He wrote this poem in Greek <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>: it was translated into Latin by Cicero; who tells us, in his first book De Oratore, that the verses of Aratus are very noble. This piece was translated by others as well as Cicero; there being a translation by Germanicus Caesar, and another into elegant verse by Festus Avienus. An edition of the Phenomena was published by Grotius, at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>, in quarto, 1600, in Greek and Latin with the fragments of Cicero's version, and the translations of Germanicus and Avienus; all which the editor has illustrated with curious notes. He was certainly much esteemed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, since we find so great a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of scholiasts and commentators upon him. There are several other works also ascribed to Aratus. Suidas mentions the following: Hymns to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAN">Pan</a>; Astrology and Astrothesy; a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of Antidotes; an Encomium on Theopropus; an Epitaph on Antipater, and wife of Antigonus; an Epicedium of Cleombrotus; a Correction of the Odyssey; and some Epistles in prose. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>, in his Georgics, has imitated or translated many <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> from this author; and St Paul has quoted a passage of Aratus. It is in his speech to the Athenians (Acts xvii. 28.) wherein he tells them, that some of their own poets have said, Τοῦ γὰρ ἐκεῖ γένος ἔστιν: "For we are also his offspring." These words are the beginning of the fifth line of the Phenomena of Aratus.

ARAUCA

Pages 582-582

a fortress and town of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHILI">Chili</a>, in South <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>; situated in a fine valley, on a river of the same name. The bravery of the natives drove the Spaniards out of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> even without fire arms. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 73. 20. S. Lat. 38. 10. See Araucania, Supplement.

ARAUUSIO

Pages 582-582
or Civitas Arausiensis, or Arausiconum (Notitia); Colonia Secundanorum (Mela, Pliny, Coins); so called, because the veterans of the second legion were there settled: The capital of the Cavares, in Gallia Narbonensis. Now Orange, in the west of Provence, on an arm of the rivulet Egue, which soon after falls into the Rhone, from which it is distant a league to the east, at the foot of a mountain. Here is an ancient amphitheatre to be still seen. E. Long. 4. 46. N. Lat. 44. 10.

ARAXES

Pages 582-583

now the Aras, a river of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMENIA">Armenia</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">Major</a>, which takes its rise in a mountain called Ablos, where the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUPHRATES">Euphrates</a> also hath its origin. From this mountain it runs eastward with a serpentine course, discharging itself into the Caspian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, after a run of upwards of 500 miles, during which it receives some consider- siderable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>. Some have imagined that it hath its rise in Mount Ararat; but Tournefort assures us that it comes no nearer that mountain than 12 miles. The Araxes is a very rapid river, and is supposed to be the Gihon mentioned by Moses. Besides this <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> rapidity, it is very apt to overflow after rains; so that they have in vain endeavoured to build bridges over it; though some of them appear, from the few <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a> remaining, to have been built of the best materials, and in the strongest manner. Such is the vehemence of its current after the thawing of the adjacent snows, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> some fierce rains, that neither banks nor dikes can resist it; so that nothing can be more terrible than the noise and violence of its waves at such times: but in winter, when its waters are low, it is fordable in some places on camels.

ARBA

Pages 583-584

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Illyria, now Arbe, in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of Quarnaro. Of this island, which has been but slightly noticed by geographers, we have the following <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> by the able Fortis. In the Roman times, it is probable that there were no other cities in Arbe but that which bears the name of the island, in the neighbourhood of which ancient monuments are frequently dug up. This city of Arbe, though the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a small island, not above thirty miles round, wholly uncultivated, and uninhabitable in the highest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> that faces the channel of Morlaccia, has always maintained itself with <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECORUM">decorum</a>. That it was inhabited by civilized people in the Roman times, is evident, by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a> that have been frequently discovered there, and others still remaining at Arbe. In the lower times it suffered all the calamities to which the neighbouring countries were subjected, but it always recovered itself with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> even after <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a>. The archives of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a> of Arbe contain some ancient papers that are truly valuable, and they are kept with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> jealousy; by them it appears, that in the eleventh century, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a> were not rare among the inhabitants. Arbe was subject to the kings of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>; afterwards it became dependent on Venetian feudatories; and at last was taken under the immediate dominion of the most serene republic, by which a governor is appointed who has the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">count</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of people on the island does not much exceed three thousand souls, distributed in a few parishes, which might be officiated by a small number of priests: Yet, through a monstrous inconsistency that falls very heavy on the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> inhabitants, they have to maintain no less than three <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a> of friars, and as many of nuns, besides the considerable <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of near sixty priests, who have a very scanty provision. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> of Arbe is none of the happiest; the winter season is horrid, especially when agitated by the violent northerly winds, which sometimes transform the intermediate seasons into winter, and cause the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> itself to disappear. These furious winds do great damage to the island, particularly in the winter and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>. Two years ago, about twelve thousand sheep perished in one night, of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> pastures of the mountain; where, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> over all <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DALMATIA">Dalmatia</a>, they are left in the open <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> the whole year round. The <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> fog raised by the dread- ful commotion of the waves, which often roar between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of Arbe and the opposite <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALPS">Alps</a>, in the narrow channel of Morlaccia, consumes all the buds of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> and corn, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it happens to be driven upon the island by the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>; and it is followed by a cruel scarcity of every kind of product. This calamity communicates its baneful influence, even to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> of the animals left on the pastures, that becomes ill tasted, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of the bitterness and bad nourishment of the food. Abstracting from these irregularities, the air of Arbe is healthful; nor ought the constant summer fevers among the inhabitants to be attributed to its influence, as they are, more probably, derived from unwholesome food, and a way of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> differing little from that of the Hottentots. The appearance of the island is exceedingly pleasant. On the east it has a very <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> mountain, of the same substance as the Morlaccia, of which it was once a part. At the foot of this mountain, the rest of the island is extended to the westward, and divided into beautiful and fruitful plains interspersed with little hills fit to bear the richest products. At the extremity that looks to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, a delightful promontory, called Loparo, stretches into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>; it is crowned with little hills, which almost quite enclose a fine cultivated plain. Near this promontory are the two small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> of S. Gregorio and Goli, very useful to shepherds and fishers. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Arbe, that faces the Morlaccia mountains, is quite steep and inaccessible; and the channel between them is extremely dangerous, being exposed to furious winds, and without a single port on either side. The <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> and narrow island of Dolin, lying <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to the island of Arbe, along the coast of Barbado, forms a channel less dangerous, though by no means so secure as it is beautiful to look at. There are several harbours in the neighbourhood of the city of Arbe, by which the trade of the best part of the island is facilitated. The city stands on a rising ground between two harbours, which form a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a>; it contains about a thousand inhabitants, among whom are many noble families, but few of them are rich. Among the most remarkable curiosities of the island, the Arbegiani are proud of many egregious relics, and particularly of the head of S. Christofano their protector; but the lovers of sacred antiquity <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> find something much more singular in the three heads of Shadrach, Meshchek, and Abednego, which are venerated there with great <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>. Four of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> gentlemen are keepers of the sanctuary, and to their care the precious records of the city are also committed. Among these records there is a transaction of 1518, by which the city of Arbe promises to the doge of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, Ottone Orfeo, a tribute of some pounds de sarta serica, "of wrought silk," and in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of contravention, pounds de uzzo obrito, "of pure gold." In the last <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> there was a learned bishop of Arbe, named Ottavio Spaderi, who would not permit the relics of S. Christofano to be exposed to the public veneration, on the solemnity of the saint's <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, because he doubted of their authenticity. The mob rose, and was going to throw him <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> from the top of the hill on which the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> stands; nor did the tumult cease after the day was past. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> sent an armed vessel to deliver the prelate from the danger he was in; and the pope thought proper to give him a more tractable spouse in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> of Arbe is not the same in every situation; nay it would be difficult to find a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> where there is so great a variety in so little space. There is a very great <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between the ground of the extremity of the mountain above the channel of Barbado, and the sides of it on the one part towards the island, and on the other facing the ridge of Morlacka. Nor is the top of the mountain itself always of the same structure: for in some parts it is extended in a fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> plain, partly woody and partly cultivable; in other places it is quite rocky, and composed of bare marble. The ground at the foot of the mountain, where it stretches towards the shore, opposite to Jablanaz, is nothing but marble; and in the district of Barbado it is gravelly, and a good soil for vines. The wine of Barbado is of excellent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, and in great estimation; hardly any other product is cultivated along that coast, as the vines succeed so well, notwithstanding the negligent culture. Below the pretended ruins of Colento the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> bears vines, olives, mulberry, and other fruit trees, and also corn in the lowest parts. All the lower part of the island is composed alternately of little hills and valleys, and of a substance for the most part very different from that of the mountain and its adjacencies. As the organization of the mountain is wholly of marble, so that of the hills is generally arenaceous. The whetstone forms a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> part, and frequently contains ostracites and lenticulares; the exterior stratum is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> friable. The valleys, which according to appearances should be full of sand, are provided with an excellent soil, with such a mixture of very minute sand as is requisite to keep it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">Springs</a> of fresh <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> are by nature well distributed over the island, and maintain a proper humidity when the summer is not excessively dry; so that the dark verdure of the hills covered with wood, the luxuriance of the vines, and freshness of the corn ground, form a spectacle extremely cheerful and agreeable. The island of Arbe would have everything requisite for the subsistence of its small <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a>, if the land was cultivated by a people less stupid and lazy. It produces, however, firewood, of which many cargoes are annually sent to Venice; corn, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, excellent wine, brandy, and silk, since very ancient times; it also exports <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIDES">hides</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, sheep, hogs, and horses of a good breed. There is also abundance of good salt made on the island; and the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a> of tunny and mackerel, notwithstanding it is managed in a slovenly and awkward manner, makes no inconsiderable article of trade to the Arbegiani, who like all their neighbours, find their account in selling this commodity to strangers rather than to the Venetians. Yet, with all these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> products, the island is very far from being rich, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> even in a tolerably flourishing state; because there is much land left uncultivated, and the peasants are lazy. ARBACES governed Media under <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SARDANAPALUS">Sardanapalus</a>. Seeing him <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPINNING">spinning</a> among a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of his women, he stirred up his people to revolt, and dethroned Sardanapalus: who thereupon burnt himself in his <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>. Arbaces being crowned, began the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONARCHY">monarchy</a> of the Medes, which lasted 317 years under <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> kings, till <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTYAGES">Astyages</a> was expelled by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CYRUS">Cyrus</a>. Arbaces reigned 22 years, and died A.M. 3256. See MEDIA.

ARBBERG

Pages 585-585

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTON">canton</a> of Bern, with a handsome castle, where the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAILIFF">bailiff</a> resides. It is seated on the river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AAR">Aar</a>, in a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 7° 15' N. Lat. 47° 0'.

ARBEIA

Pages 584-585

now Irbil, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASSYRIA">Assyria</a>, lying in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 44° 5', N. Lat. 35° 15'. It is famous for the last and decisive <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> fought in its neighbourhood between Alexander the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DARIUS">Darius</a> Codomannus. This battle was fought 331 years before Christ, and the event of it determined the fate of the Persian empire. Arrian relates, that Darius's <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> consisted of a million of foot and 40,000 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>; according to Diodorus, there were 200,000 horse and 800,000 foot; Plutarch relates, that the horse and foot together made up a million: and Justin gives us exactly half Diodorus's <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>. The Macedonian army, according to Arrian consisted of 40,000 foot and 7000 horse. Upon receiving notice of the vast strength of the Gillies' enemy, Alexander expressed neither surprise nor <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPREHENSION">apprehension</a>; but having "commanded a halt, he encamped four days, to give his men rest and refreshment. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a> being fortified by a good intrenchment, he left in it the sick and infirm, together with all the baggage; and, on the evening of the fourth <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, prepared to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a> against the enemy with the effective <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of his army, which was said to consist of 40,000 infantry and 7000 horse, unencumbered with anything but their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> and armour. The march was undertaken at the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> watch of the night, that the Macedonians, by joining battle in the morning, might enjoy the important advantage of having an entire day before them, to reap the full <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of their expected victory. About half way between the hostile <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMPS">camps</a>, some eminences intercepted the view of either army. Having ascended the rising ground, Alexander first beheld the barbarians, drawn up in battle <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARRAY">array</a>, and perhaps more skillfully marshalled than he had reason to apprehend. Their appearance, at least, immediately determined him to change his first <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a>. He again commanded a halt, summoned a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>; and different <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> being proposed, acceded to the single <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of Parmenio, who advised that the foot should remain <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STATIONARY">stationary</a> until a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DETACHMENT">detachment</a> of horse had explored the field of battle and carefully examined the disposition of the enemy. Alexander, whose conduct was equalled by his courage, and both surpassed by his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a>, performed those important duties in person at the head of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> horse and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> cohort. Having returned with unexampled celerity, he again assembled his captains, and encouraged them by a short speech. Their ardour corresponded with his own; and the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>, confident of victory, were commanded to take rest and refreshment. "Meanwhile Darius, perceiving the enemy's approach, kept his men prepared for <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a>. Notwithstanding the great length of the plain, he was obliged to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> his <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a>, and form in two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>, each of which was extremely deep. According to the Persian <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> occupied the centre of the first line, surrounded by the princes of the blood and the great officers of his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>; and defended by his horse and foot guards, amounting to 15,000 chosen men. These splendid troops, who seemed fitter for parade than battle, were flanked on either side by the Greek mercenaries and other warlike battalions, carefully selected from the whole army. The <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> wing consisted of the Medes, Parthians, Hyrcanians and Sace; the left was chiefly occupied by the Bactrians, Persians, and Car- The various nations composing this immense <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOST">host</a> were differently armed, with swords, spears, clubs, and hatchets; while the horse and foot of each <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> were promiscuously blended, rather from the result of accident than by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>. The armed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARIOTS">chariots</a> fronted the first line, whose centre was farther defended by the elephants. Chosen squadrons of Scythian, Bactrian, and Cappadocian cavalry advanced before either wing, prepared to bring on the action, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> after it began to attack the enemy in flank and rear. The unexpected approach of Alexander within sight of his tents prevented Darius from fortifying the wide <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of his camp; and, as he dreaded a nocturnal assault from enemies who often veiled their designs in darkness, he commanded his men to remain all night under arms. This unusual <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, the gloomy silence, the long and anxious <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPECTATION">expectation</a>, together with the fatigue of a restless night, discouraged the whole army, but inspired <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> terror into those who had witnessed the miserable disasters on the banks of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANICUS">Granicus</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISSUS">Issus</a>. "At daybreak Alexander disposed of his troops in a manner suggested by the superior numbers and deep order of the enemy. His main body consisted of two heavy-armed phalanxes, each amounting to above 16,000 men. Of these the greater part formed into one line; behind which he placed the heavy-armed men, reinforced by his targeteers, with orders, that when the outspreading wings of the enemy prepared to attack the flanks and rear of his first line, the second should immediately wheel to receive them. The cavalry and light infantry were so disposed on the wings, that while one part resisted the shock of the Persians in front, another, by only facing to the right or left, might take them in flank. Skilful archers and darters were posted at proper intervals, as affording the best <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> against the armed chariots, which (as Alexander well knew) must immediately become useless whenever their conductors or horses were wounded. "Having thus arranged the several parts, Alexander with equal judgment led the whole in an oblique direction towards the enemy's left; a manoeuvre which enabled the Macedonians to avoid contending at once with superior numbers. When his advanced battalions, notwithstanding their nearness to the enemy, still stretched towards the right, Darius also extended his left, till, fearing that by continuing this movement, his men should be drawn gradually off the plain, he commanded the Scythian squadrons to advance, and prevent the farther <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENSION">extension</a> of the hostile line. Alexander immediately detached a body of horse to oppose them. An equestrian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a> ensued, in which both parties were reinforced, and the barbarians finally repelled. The armed chariots then issued forth with impetuous violence; but their appearance only was formidable; for the precautions taken by Alexander rendered their assault harmless. Darius next moved his main body, but with so little order, that the horse, mixed with the infantry, advanced, and left a vacancy in the line, which his generals wanted <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> or vigilance to supply. Alexander seized the decisive moment, and penetrated into the void with a wedge of squadrons. He was followed by the nearest sections of the phalanx, who rushed forward with loud shouts, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they had already pursued the enemy. In this part of the field, the victory was not long doubtful; after a feeble resistance the barbarians gave way; and the pusillanimous Darius was foremost in the flight. "The battle, however, was not yet decided. The more remote divisions of the phalanx, upon receiving intelligence that the left wing, commanded by Parmenio, was in danger, had not immediately followed Alexander. A vacant space was thus left in the Macedonian line, through which some squadrons of Persian and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> horse penetrated with celerity, and advanced to the hostile camp. It was then that Alexander derived signal and well-earned advantages from his judicious order of battle. The heavy-armed troops and targeteers, which he had skilfully posted behind the phalanx, speedily faced about, advanced with a rapid step, and attacked the barbarian cavalry, already entangled among the baggage. The enemy, thus surprised, were destroyed or put to flight. Meanwhile the danger of his left wing recalled Alexander from the pursuit of Darius. In advancing against the enemy's right, he was met by the Parthian, Indian, and Persian horse, who maintained a sharp conflict. Sixty of the Companions fell; Hephaestion, Coenus, and Menidas, were wounded. Having at length dissipated this cloud of cavalry, Alexander prepared to attack the foot in that wing. But the business was already effected, chiefly by the Thessalian horse; and nothing remained to be done, but to pursue the fugitives, and to render the victory as decisive as possible. "According to the least extravagant accounts, with the loss of 500 men, he destroyed 40,000 of the barbarians, who never thenceforth assembled in sufficient numbers to dispute his dominion in the east. The invaluable provinces of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BABYLONIA">Babylonia</a>, Susiana, and Persis, with their respective capitals of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BABYLON">Babylon</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUSA">Susa</a>, and Persepolis, formed the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a> of his skill and valour. The <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver found in those cities amounted to thirty millions <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a>; the jewels and other precious spoil, belonging to Darius, sufficed, according to Plutarch, to load 20,000 mules, and 5000 camels." The consequences of this victory the reader <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> find narrated under the article <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">PERSIA</a>.

ARBITER

Pages 585-585

in the Civil <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, implies a judge nominated by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> chosen voluntarily by the two contending parties, in order to decide their differences. The civilians make a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between arbiter and arbitrator, though both found their power on the compromise of the parties; the former being obliged to judge according to the customs of the law, whereas the latter is at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> his own <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a>, and accommodate the differences in the manner that appears to him most <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> and equitable.

ARBITRARY

Pages 585-586

that which is left to the choice <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> arbitration of men, or not fixed by any positive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INJUNCTION">injunction</a>. Arbitrary <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">Punishment</a>, in Law, denotes, such punishments as are by statute left to the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a> of the judge. It is a general rule in arbitrary punishments, that the judge cannot inflict <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. Hence all punishments that are not <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> have acquired the name of arbitrary. arbitrary punishments, even although they be expressly pointed out by statute.

ARBITRATION

Pages 586-586

is where the parties, injuring and injured, submit all matters in dispute, concerning any personal chattels <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> personal wrong, to the judgment of two or more arbiters or arbitrators; who are to decide the controversy; and, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they do not agree, it is usual to add, that another person be called in as umpire (imperator or impor), to whose sole judgment it is then referred; or frequently there is only one arbitrator originally appointed. This decision, in any of these <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, is called an award. And thereby the question is as fully determined, and the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> transferred or settled, as it would have been by the agreement of the parties or the judgment of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>.

ARBITRATOR

Pages 586-586

a private extraordinary judge, chosen by the mutual consent of parties, to determine controversies between them. See ARBITER and ARBITRATION.

ARBOIS

Pages 586-586

a small populous town of France, in the department of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JURA">Jura</a>, formerly Franche Compte, famous for its wines. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 5° 40'. N. Lat. 46° 55'.

ARBON

Pages 586-586

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> town in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>, on the south banks of the lake <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSTANCE">Constance</a>, in Thurgaw. It has a castle built by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, and is under the jurisdiction of the bishop of Constance. In the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, the Swiss have a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to put in a garrison. The Popish and Protestant religions are equally tolerated in this town. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 9° 30'. N. Lat. 4° 38'.

ARBOR

Pages 586-586

in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICS">Mechanics</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of a machine, which serves to sustain the rest; also the axis <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> spindle on which a machine turns, as the arbor of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRANE">crane</a>, windmill, &c. Arbor <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIANA">Diana</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Arbor Vite. See Thuja, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> Index.

ARBORIBONSSES

Pages 586-586

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, priests of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JAPAN">Japan</a>, who live an erratic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and subsist on alms. They dwell in caverns, and cover their heads with bonnets made of the bark of trees.

ARBORIST

Pages 586-586

a person skilled in that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a> which treats of trees. ARBORESCENT <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STAR">Star</a>-fish, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZOOLOGY">Zoology</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of asterias. See Asterias.

ARBOUR

Pages 586-586

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARDENING">Gardening</a>, a kind of shady bower, formerly in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> esteem; but of late rejected on account of its being damp and unwholesome. Arbours are generally made of lattice <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, either of wood <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>; and covered with elms, limes, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORN">horn</a>-beams; or with creepers, as honeysuckles, jasmines, or <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>; either of which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> answer the purpose very well, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> rightly managed. ARBROATH. See ABERBROTHICK.

ARBURG

Pages 586-586

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTON">canton</a> of Bern, on the river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AAR">Aar</a>. It is small, but very strong, being seated on a rock, and defended by a good fortress cut out of the rock. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 7° 55'. N. Lat. 47° 10'.

ARBUSCULA

Pages 586-586

is used by Bradley to denote a little <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DWARF">dwarf</a> tree, above the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHRUBS">shrubs</a>, but below that of trees; such, e.g. as the elder.

ARBUSTUM

Pages 586-586

implies a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> multitude of trees planted for the fruit's sake. The word was more peculiarly applied to a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> planted with trees for fastening vines to, which are hence called by Columella arbustive. ARBUSTUM is sometimes also used to denote an orchard, or field wherein trees are planted at such distance that there is room for ploughing and growing corn between.

ARBUTHNOT

Pages 586-587

John, M.D. the son of an Episcopal clergyman in Scotland, was born soon after the Restoration at Arbuthnot near <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTROSE">Montrose</a>. After acquiring a competent knowledge of the elementary parts of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, he was sent to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of Aberdeen, where the buddings of those <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> qualities and those sallies of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a>, which contributed so much to his future greatness, soon made their appearance. Having there gone through a course of academical studies, and obtained the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of physic, he went to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, in order to reap the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> both of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> and acquired abilities. He then began to display his talents, in teaching <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>, in which he was very expert. "An <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">Examination</a> of Dr Woodward's Account of the Deluge," &c. in 1607, first made him known to the learned world. This performance was received with great applause; and in 1700 a treatise "On the Usefulness of Mathematical Learning" still increased his reputation. A very interesting <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> "On the Regularity of the Births of both Sexes," demonstrating from authentic proofs the universal similarity which is observed by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> in this circumstance, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> from these several <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> and moral inferences, which he presented to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>, Meanwhile, in his own proper profession, he was acquiring considerable eminence, and was appointed, on account of his great medical knowledge, physician extraordinary to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> George of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>, and shortly afterwards one of the physicians in ordinary to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>. He was admitted in 1710 a fellow of the college. He formed about this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> a very intimate acquaintance, which lasted with unabating tenderness and affection during the rest of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, with these great literary men, Pope, Gay, and Swift. In 1714 he engaged in an extensive <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, of making a satire upon all the abuses of science in every branch in cooperation with Pope and Swift, which was to be written under the form of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of a fictitious character, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a> ironical style. The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> was never finished, but the "<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a> of Martinus Scribnerus," published in Pope's works, form a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a>; of which, much is the performance of Dr Arbuthnot. It is very probable, that the whole of the first book is of his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>, in which the great profoundness of knowledge that is discerned, and the good-natured pleasantry with which the satire is directed, has gained it the character of one of the most original, learned, and interesting pieces in the English <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. Those parts which relate to anatomy, the manners and customs of antiquity, and logic, are particularly his performance. On the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Queen Anne, he made a visit to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, in order to drive away the melancholy, which attended him on account of that circumstance, which was a severe stroke to him, and destructive not only to his personal, but also to his political views. Returning from thence, as his medical services were no longer required at St James's, he retired from it, and followed at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> the practice of his profession; yet he did not thence give up his literary pursuits, but pursued them with great ardour, although <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> intervals take <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> between the times of his publications. A <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> entitled "Tables of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> Coins, Weights, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">Measures</a>," explained and exemplified in several dissertations, in a 4to vol. appeared in 1727, which is the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of his serious performances. Although there are several inaccuracies in it, which could hardly be avoided in so intricate a subject, it is a work of great merit, and has ever since been considered as the standard authority. A treatise "On the Nature and Choice of Aliments," which was published in 1732, and another published in 1733, "On the Effects of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">Air</a> on <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">Human</a> Bodies," finish the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIST">list</a> of his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a> works. Both these were well received by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a>, and continue to be still esteemed, and are occasionally read and quoted. Respecting his humorous works, which were the productions of his leisure hours, they are so confounded with those of his contemporaries, that it is not easy to distinguish them. But a piece which, independent of any other, would raise him to the character of the first humorous writer in the English language, entitled the "History of John Bull," is confidently ascribed to him. This is conducted with great wit and humour, and all the circumstances and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> are most admirably adapted. Among his several avowed ironical pieces are "A Treatise concerning the Altercation <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Scolding of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">Ancients</a>," and the "Art of Political Lying." In the year 1751, there were published two small volumes, entitled "The Miscellaneous Works of Dr Arbuthnot," but the greatest part of what they contain is denied by his son to be of his composition. As it was customary for him, when any comical occurrence took place, which struck his fancy, to write concerning it in a large folio which lay in his parlour; it is very probable, that many slight and imperfect essays, which had gone out of his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REMEMBRANCE">remembrance</a>, might get abroad into the world. Through all his pieces of this kind there runs a vein of good-natured pleasantry; and this tends to confirm the character given of him by Swift, to a lady who desired to know his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> concerning Dr Arbuthnot, "He has more wit than we all have, and his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> is equal to his wit." Although his writings are free from that <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GALL">gall</a> and rancour, too <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> among party writers, yet they cannot be said to be altogether free from a party spirit. He, however, cannot be excused in one instance, of allowing his personal dislike to overrule his humanity, viz. in the "Memorandums of the six days preceding the death of a late <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">Right</a> Reverend" (meaning Bishop Burnet). The indignation of a virtuous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> towards an infamous character, is sufficient to justify his severity in his bitter "Epitaph on <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLONEL">Colonel</a> Chartres:" and this severity was probably aggravated by party spirit.
