Although he had no proper poetical <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TALENT">talent</a>, yet he made an effort to try his genius in that kind of composition. A piece, published in Dodsley's collection, is valuable for its philosophical sentiment, which is entitled ΓΝΩΘΙ ΣΕΑΤΤΟΝ, Know thyself. He was also skilled in music; and Sir J. Hawkins mentions an anthem and a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURLESQUE">burlesque</a> song, which are ascribed to him. In these occupations he passed his days, amid all the pleasures that can render <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> life happy, in the affection and estimation of his friends, beloved and esteemed by all his literary associates, who have each taken great pains to celebrate their mutual friendship. Swift in one of his poems sincerely laments that he is "Far from his kind Arbuthnot's aid, Who knows his art, but not his trade." Pope has dedicated to him an epistle, called a "Prologue to the Satires." He was full of humility and resignation in all the dispensations of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a>. Of his two sons, he witnessed the death of one; and the other, with some daughters, survived him. At length, from an invertebrate asthma, he fell into a dropsical disorder; and, in order to try the effect of a change of air, he repaired to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAMPSTEAD">Hampstead</a>, but without the least gleam of hope respecting a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a>, as he assured his friends Pope and Swift. Returning to his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> in London, he died February 27, 1734-5. His latest letters display a great serenity of mind, an exemplary piety, a contempt of vice, and a glowing desire of virtue. (Gen. Biog.)

ARC

Pages 587-589

JOAN OF, generally called the Maid of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORLEANS">Orleans</a>, one of the most famed heroines in the annals of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, was born about the beginning of the 15th century at Domremy, near Vaucouleurs in Lorraine, where her father, a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEASANT">peasant</a>, named James d'Arc, resided. When she was able in the least <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> to earn a sustenance for herself, her parents, who were but <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a>, put her to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> at a small inn, where she... formed several offices, more properly belonging to the other <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEX">sex</a>, such as riding the horses to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> without a saddle, and attending them in the fields, and many other similar services, which greatly displayed her masculine <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> of body. At the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> when <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> VII. was reduced to a very low condition, and the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> had been overrun by the English, Joan, probably then at the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 27 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 28, imagined that she <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> several visions, and that in one of these she was commanded by St Michael, to go immediately to the relief of Orleans, at that time closely besieged by the English <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, and then to procure the consecration of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHEIMS">Rheims</a>. In February 1429, her parents took her to the governor of Vauclercours, named Baudricourt, who at first held her pretended <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSPIRATION">inspiration</a> to be no more than an idle tale, and treated it with the contempt such a thing would have deserved; but at last induced by her entreaties, he sent her to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHINON">Chinon</a>, where the king then was, in order that she might be introduced to him. Charles, whether it proceeded from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARNEST">earnest</a> or not, in order to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> her, determined to present her to a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBLES">nobles</a>, where no mark of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> tended to distinguish him from them; and, it is asserted, that she immediately recognized him, and informed him of secrets which he had endeavoured to conceal from every person. She boldly engaged to accomplish the two objects of her mission, and required that they should arm her with a consecrated <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, which lay in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of St Catharine of Pierbois; and although she had never seen it, she accurately described every particular concerning it. The manner in which she acted inspired many with confidence; and certain doctors of the church were appointed to inspect into the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of her inspiration, and matrons to give proofs of her virginity. The report which they gave was very favourable; but being next put into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, they treated her as frantick, and demanded that she should shew them a miracle. She answered, that although she had not any at that time to present, she would soon accomplish one at Orleans. At length being fully armed and mounted, she was sent to Orleans along with the army destined for its relief. By displaying a consecrated banner, she soon cleansed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a> of intemperance; and by her whole deportment, animated the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> by her exemplary enthusiasm. Entering Orleans, she introduced a convoy, and boldly attacking the English in their forts, she routed them with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> slaughter, and struck them with such a panic that they were even obliged to raise the siege with great precipitation. The dignity of a superior mind and a brave heroism reigned through all her actions. Various other successes followed in a short time, and the dismayed English everywhere fled before the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> of a conquering enemy, whom they had but lately contemned. Joan now thinking it proper to perform her other <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> of crowning the king at Rheims, proceeded with him through the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, in order to receive submission of the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> as he marched, which he did without any opposition. Arriving at Rheims, the keys of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> were delivered to him, and, entering the town, he was anointed and crowned with the holy <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> of Clovis, Joan standing by his side in full armour, and displaying her consecrated banner. Charles filled with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a> for her important services, ennobled her family, and conferred upon it the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of the Sys, with a conforable estate in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>. The two objects of her mission being now accomplished, Joan prepared to retire into the country; but Dunois, the general, being sensible of her importance on account of her pretended inspiration, endeavoured to persuade her to remain in arms until the English should be fully driven from the country; which by his persuasions he effected. Advised by him, she <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> herself into <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-COMPEIGNE">Compeigne</a>, then closely besieged by the English and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BURGUNDY">Burgundy</a>. Having there made a sally upon the enemy, she drove them from their entrenchments; but being basely deserted by her followers, she was taken prisoner. Upon her capture, the English enjoyed a malignant gratification, and resolved to show her no mercy on account of the change she had occasioned in their affairs. The duke of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEDFORD">Bedford</a>, the regent, having ransomed her from the captors, appointed a criminal prosecution against her upon the charges of employing sorcery and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGIC">magic</a>, and of being impious. He was joined in the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACCUSATION">accusation</a> by the clergy, and by the university of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. She was carried in irons before an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROUEN">Rouen</a>, where several capricious interrogatories were put to her during a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> of about four months, to which she answered with steadiness and gravity. Among several other questions, she was interrogated why she had assisted at the coronation of Charles with her standard in her hand. She boldly replied, "Because the person who shared in the danger, had a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to share in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a>." Her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> was not so strong concerning her pretended inspiration and visions, which were the most dangerous <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of the attack. She appealed to the pope upon being accused on these grounds of impiety and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERESY">heresy</a>; but her <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a> was not allowed. At length she was condemned of being a blasphemer and sorceress, and accordingly delivered over to the power of the civil <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a>. A view of the dreadful <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> that awaited her, at last overpowered her <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a>; and she endeavoured to escape it, by making a disavowal of her pretended revelations, and a full renunciation of her errors. Her <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> was then changed into perpetual imprisonment, but this punishment did not assuage the fury of her barbarous enemies. They craftily laid a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s dress in her chamber, and she, induced by the sight of an apparel in which she had gained so much <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, put it on; and upon being discovered, her enemies condemned her to the stake, interpreting the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> into a relapse of heresy. She suffered her punishment in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1431, at the market-<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of Rouen, with great firmness; and even the English themselves beheld the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> with tears. Her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> for ever cast an indelible stigma on the character of her cruel prosecutors. Charles did nothing towards avenging her cause: but ten years afterwards, contented himself with procuring the restoration of her <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> by the pope, and a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVERSION">reversion</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a>. She was styled in that <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a>, a "<a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARTYR">martyr</a> to her <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, her country, and her king." In their enthusiastic admiration, her countrymen were not slow in honouring her memory. Many marvellous stories were related by them concerning her death. Some supposed that she was not actually dead, and continually expected, that, as formerly, she would come, and at their head <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> them on to victory. A consist- ent and uniform judgment respecting the actions and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> of this personage cannot be made by posterity. That she gave herself up to the influence of a heated fancy, and that she was confident in the idea of her divine inspiration, and that this notion was so improved by certain favourites of Charles, as to excite the emotions of the public, seems to be the most probable supposition. That the appearance of the Maid of Orleans tended to give a decisive turn to the contest between the English and the French, has never in the least been questioned. The praise and exploits of this noble heroine have formed the subject of various works both in prose and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>. In verse, that of Voltaire is very licentious and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURLESQUE">burlesque</a>, and is an injury to her memory; but it has in a great degree been repaired by that most spirited and sublime poem of Southey, in English, which represents her in the most lively and striking colours of heroism and virtue; and by that of Chapelain, although it did not meet with such success. (Gen. Biogr.)

ARCADE

Pages 589-589

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, is used to denote any opening in the wall of a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> formed by an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a>.

ARCADI

Pages 589-589
or **ARCADIANS**, the name of a learned society at Rome. See ACADEMY.

ARCADIA

Pages 589-589

an inland district in the heart of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PELOPONNESUS">Peloponnesus</a> (Strabo). It is mountainous, and fitter for pasture than corn; and therefore chiefly celebrated by bucolic <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> pastoral poets, who feign <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAN">Pan</a> the god of shepherds, to be the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUARDIAN">guardian</a> of it (<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>). It has to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> Achaia, to the east <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARGOS">Argos</a> and Locrinia, Messenia to the south, and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIS">Elis</a> to the west. According to Pliny, the wine of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> cured barrenness in women, and inspired the men with rage; and the berries of the yew gathered there were so strong a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POISON">poison</a>, that whoever slept or took refreshment under that tree was sure to die. In Strabo's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> there were few cities remaining in it, most of them being destroyed in the Grecian wars. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUSTATHIUS">Eustathius</a> says, that the country was anciently called *Pelasia*, from Pelasgos, who brought the people, from roots, herbs, and leaves of trees, to feed on acorns, especially beech mast; as Artemidorus observes, that the Arcadians usually lived on acorns. It was also called *Lycaonia*, *Gigantis* and *Parrhasia* (Stephanus). The Arcadians are greatly commended for their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of, and skill in, music, (Virgil, Polybius). To imitate the Arcadians, is to labour and toil for the benefit of others, never conquering their own, but the enemies of others (<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HESYCHIUS">Hesychius</a>). This probably took its rise from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Arcadians being accustomed to hire themselves out as mercenaries to foreign nations. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a> commends their martial prowess, their pastures, their sheep, and their country well watered. The gentilitious name is *Arcades*; who boasted of their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> antiquity, and that they were older than the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a> (Apollonius Rhodius, Nonnius, Plutarch, Ovid, Statius). They were the first who had a year of three months, and therefore called *Proceleni*, because their year was <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> to that adjusted in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a> to the course of the moon (Censorinus).

ARCANGIS

Pages 589-589

in the Turkish armies, an inferior kind of infantry, which serve as *enfans perdus*, and to harass and pillage the enemy's frontiers. The Arcangis are an order inferior to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JANIZARIES">Janizaries</a>; and when any of them distinguish themselves, are usually preferred into the Janizaries order. They have no pay, but are Arcangis to subsist on their plunder.

ARCANUM

Pages 589-589

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a villa of Q. Cicero, Tully's <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>, in Latium, (Cicero). Now Arce, in the Terra di Lavora, in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, on the borders of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAMPAGNA">Campagna</a> di Roma, on the river Melpis, between Arpinum and Aquinum.

ARCESILAUS

Pages 589-589

a celebrated Greek <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, about 300 years before the Christian era, was born at Pitane, in Eolis. He founded the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> academy, which is called the second school. He was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> erudition, and well versed in the writings of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>. He was remarkable for the severity of his criticisms; but nevertheless he knew how to accommodate himself to the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, and pursue the allurements of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>. He had a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of disciples. His doctrines were different in several respects from those of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> school: and perhaps he was led into this diversity of opinions by many <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> errors in the ancient school, such as the incredible arrogance of the dogmatists, who pretended to assign causes for all things; the mysterious <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> they had thrown upon the doctrine of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a>; the entirely discarding the testimony of the senses; the objection of the Pyrrhonists, who now began to <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROACH">broach</a> their opinions; the powerful opposition of the Stoics and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIPATETICS">Peripatetics</a>, who discovered the feeble parts of the Academic <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>. These might have given cause to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REFORM">reform</a> the ancient school, and to found a new one. The middle school, therefore, laid it <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> as a principle, that we could know nothing, nor even assure ourselves of the certainty of this position; from whence they inferred, that we should affirm nothing, but always suspend our judgment. They advanced, that a philosopher was able to dispute upon every subject, and bring conviction with him, even upon contrary sides of the same question; for there are always reasons of equal force both in the affirmative and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEGATIVE">negative</a> of every argument. According to this doctrine, neither our senses nor even our reason, are to have any <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a>: and therefore, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> affairs, we are to conform ourselves to received opinions. Arcesilaus was succeeded by his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LACYDES">Lacydes</a>.

ARCH

Pages 589-590

a concave <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> hollowed piece of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, constructed in such a manner that the several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a> of which it is composed keep one another in their places. The terms arch and vault properly differ only in this, that the arch expresses a narrower, and the vault a broader piece of the same kind. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> in the form of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a> is, that some are circular, and others elliptical; the former having a larger or smaller <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of a circle, the other of an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELLIPSIS">ellipsis</a>. What are called strait arches, are those frequently used for doors and windows, the upper and under edges of which are straight and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a>, and the ends and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a>... joints all pointing toward a centre. The space between two piers of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> is called an arch, because usually arched over. Triumphal Arches are magnificent entries into cities, erected to adorn a triumph, and perpetuate the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a>. The arches of Titus and Constantine make at this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> among the ruins of old Rome. Arch, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>, signifies <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>, or of the first class: as archangel, archbishop, &c. ARCHÆUS, or ARCHEUS. See ARCHEUS.

ARCHANGEL

Pages 590-590

an angel occupying the eighth <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> in the celestial <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HIERARCHY">hierarchy</a>. See ANGEL and HIERARCHY. Archangel, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Russia, in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Dwina, situated on the east side of the river Dwina, about six miles from the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">White</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 39° N. Lat. 64° 30'. The city extends about three miles in length and one in breadth. It is rich, populous, built in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, and is a metropolitan see. It rose from a castle built on the spot by Basilo-witz II. to protect the increasing trade brought there by the discovery of the White sea by the English, and took its name from a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> built in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the archangel Michael. Before this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> the commercial intercourse between Russia and the northern parts of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> had been long carried on by the Hanseatic <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>; which usually sailed to Revel <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NARVA">Narva</a>, and from thence passed through Dorpt or Plescof and Novogorod, where their factories were established. The accidental discovery of Archangel, in 1553, deprived the Hanseatic towns of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of this lucrative <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, and transferred it to the English. On the 11th of May, in the above-mentioned year, three ships sailed from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPTFORD">Deptford</a>, in order to explore the northern seas, under the command of Sir Hugh Willoughby. Two of these vessels penetrated as <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> as the 72d <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of latitude, to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Spitzbergen; and being afterwards forced by stress of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of the river Arzina in Russian <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAPLAND">Lapland</a>, both their crews were frozen to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. Richard <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHANCELLOR">Chancellor</a>, who commanded the other ship, called the Bonaventure, discovering the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> bordering upon the White sea, landed near the mouth of the Dwina, in a bay, which he denominated the Bay of St Nicholas, from a convent of that name near the present port of Archangel. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CZAR">czar</a> Iwan Basilowitch, being informed of his arrival, invited him to his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, where he was hospitably entertained, and the czar indulged the English with a free trade in his dominions: in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of this permission, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> was incorporated in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>; and being encouraged by particular privileges from the czar, set on foot a considerable commerce, to the mutual advantage of both nations. This traffic the English for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> enjoyed without competition. The Dutch, however, and other nations, gradually insinuated themselves into this commerce; which they carried on to a very great disadvantage, as not being favoured with those privileges which the czar had granted to the English company. These were at last suddenly annihilated by <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXIS">Alexis</a> Michaelowitch; who in 1648 banished the English merchants from all his dominions. The cause of this expulsion is generally imputed to the resentment which the czar conceived against the English for the execution of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I. with whom he was closely connected by Archangel leagues of amity and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a>: but in effect he abolished the company's privileges in the year before that event; and his indignation against the English for their rebellion, Mr Cox affirms, was only a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRETEXT">pretext</a>; the real <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a> being derived from the offers made by the Dutch to pay duties of export and import to the amount of 15 per cent. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they were indulged with the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of carrying on as free a trade as the English throughout his dominions. For not long afterwards, the czar suffered William Prideaux, Cromwell's <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGENT">agent</a>, to reside at Archangel; and permitted the English to renew their commerce in that port upon the same footing with other foreigners. And upon this footing alone our merchants ever after <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to trade. The commodities chiefly imported into Archangel, were <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver stuffs and laces, gold wire, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COCHINEAL">cochineal</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDIGO">indigo</a>, and other drugs for <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DYEING">dyeing</a>; wine, brandy, and other distilled spirits. The customs arising to the czar were computed at 200,000 rubles a-year, and the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of foreign ships at 400 annually. But upon the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> of Petersburg, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> the Great abolished the immunities of Archangel, and removed the commerce of the White sea to the havens of the Baltic. Still, however, its exports of tar were considerable; in 1730, to the amount of 40,000 lasts, of 11 barrels each. It sends, during winter, great quantities of the rawaga, a small <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of three-finned cod, to Petersburg frozen. In 1752 <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a> again restored the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> immunities of Archangel; and its present trade is not inconsiderable. It supplies the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of Archangel, part of those of Nishnei-Novgorod and Casan, with European commodities; and draws in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a> from those parts corn, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>, coarse <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, cordage, sails, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MASTS">masts</a> and tallow, which are mostly conveyed by the Dwina: it forms also a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> with the northern and western parts of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIBERIA">Siberia</a>, from whence the merchants procure furs, skins, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>. The houses of Archangel are generally of wood, but well contrived; and every chamber is provided with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STOVE">stove</a>, as a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FENCE">fence</a> against the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, which is here excessive in the winter. The streets are paved with broken pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> and rubbish, disposed so unskilfully, that one cannot walk over it without running the risk of falling, except when the streets are rendered smooth and equal by the snow that falls and freezes in the winter. Notwithstanding the severity of the cold in this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, there is always plenty of good <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>; butchers meat, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POULTRY">poultry</a>, wild fowl: and fish, in a great variety, are sold surprisingly cheap. The most remarkable edifice in Archangel is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> townhouse, built of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a> in the Italian manner, and divided into three parts. One of these consists of large commodious apartments, for the accommodation of merchants, strangers as well as natives: here they are permitted to reside with their merchandise till the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of October, when all the foreign ships set sail for their respective countries. Then, too, the native traders are obliged to remove their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> from the townhouse. In 1793 great part of this city and suburbs was destroyed by fire, but has since been elegantly rebuilt.

ARCHBISHOP

Pages 590-591

the name of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITARY">dignitary</a> of Archbishops were not known in the east till about the year 320; and though there were some soon after this who had the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a>, yet that was only a personal <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, by which the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> of considerable cities were distinguished. It was not till of late that archbishops became metropolitans, and had suffragans under them. Athanasius appears to be the first who used the title Archbishop, which he gave occasionally to his predecessor; Gregory Nazianzen, in like manner, gave it to Athanasius; not that either of them were entitled to any jurisdiction, nor even any precedence in virtue of it. Among the Latins, Isidore Hispalensis is the first that speaks of archbishops. He distinguishes four orders <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> degrees in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HIERARCHY">hierarchy</a>, viz. patriarchs, archbishops, metropolitans, and bishops. The archbishop, beside the inspection of the bishops and inferior clergy in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> over which he presides, exercises episcopal jurisdiction in his own <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a>. He is <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUARDIAN">guardian</a> of the spiritualities of any vacant see in his province, as the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> is of the temporalities; and exercises ecclesiastical jurisdiction in it. He is entitled to present by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAPSE">lapse</a> to all the ecclesiastical livings in the disposal of his diocesan bishop, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not filled within six months. He has likewise a customary <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREROGATIVE">prerogative</a>, upon consecrating a bishop, to name a clerk or chaplain to be provided for by such bishop; in lieu of which it is now usual to accept an option. He is said to be enthroned when vested in the archbishopric; whereas bishops are said to be installed. The ecclesiastical <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of England is divided into two provinces, viz. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>. Canterbury hath the following suffragan bishoprics appertaining to it, St Asaph, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANGOR">Bangor</a>, Bath and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WELLS">Wells</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRISTOL">Bristol</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHICHESTER">Chichester</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LITCHFIELD">Litchfield</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COVENTRY">Coventry</a>, St <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a>'s, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELY">Ely</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXETER">Exeter</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GLOUCESTER">Gloucester</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREFORD">Hereford</a>, Landaff, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LINCOLN">Lincoln</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWICH">Norwich</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, Peterborough, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROCHESTER">Rochester</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALISBURY">Salisbury</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINCHESTER">Winchester</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORCESTER">Worcester</a>. To York appertaineth the bishoprics of Carlisle, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHESTER">Chester</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DURHAM">Durham</a>; to which may be added the bishopric of Sodor and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">Man</a>, whose bishop is not a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. See Canterbury and York. The archbishop of Canterbury had anciently, viz. till the year 1152, jurisdiction over <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a> as well as England, and was styled a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRIARCH">patriarch</a>, and sometimes alterius orbis <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPA">papa</a>, and orbis Britannici pontifex. Matters were done and recorded in his name thus, Anno pontificatus nostrii primo, &c. The first archbishop of Canterbury was Austin, appointed by King <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ETHELBERT">Ethelbert</a>, on his conversion to Christianity, about the year 598. He was also regatus natus. He even enjoyed some special marks of royalty; as, to be <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> of a bishopric, which he was of Rochester; and to make knights, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a> moneys, &c. He is still the first peer of England, and the next to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> family; having precedence of all dukes and all <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> officers of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>. It is his privilege, by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>, to crown the kings and queens of this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. He may retain and qualify eight chaplains; whereas a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> is allowed by statute only six. He has, by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>, the power of probate of wills and testaments, and granting letters of administration. He has also a power to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> licenses and dispensations in all <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> formerly sued for in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of Rome, and not repugnant to the law of God. He accordingly issues special licenses to marry, to hold two livings, &c., and he exercises the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of conferring degrees. He also holds several courts of jurisdiction: as, court of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a>, court of audience, prerogative court, and court of peculiars. The archbishop of York has the like <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> in his province as the archbishop of Canterbury. He has precedence of all dukes not of the royal blood; and of all officers of state, except the lord <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a>. He has also the rights of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">count</a> palatine over Hexamshire. The first archbishop of York was <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PAULINUS">Paulinus</a>, appointed by Pope Gregory about the year 622. He had formerly jurisdiction over all the bishops of Scotland; but in the year 1470, Pope Sextus IV. created the bishop of St Andrew's archbishop and metropolitan of all Scotland. Scotland, whilst episcopacy prevailed in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, had two archbishops, of St Andrew's and Glasgow; of which the former was accounted the metropolitan; and, even before it arrived at the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of an archbishopric, resisted with great spirit all the attempts of the archbishops of York in England to become the metropolitans of Scotland. The sees of Argyll, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GALLOWAY">Galloway</a>, and the Isles, were suffragans to Glasgow; all the others in the kingdom to St Andrew's. Ireland has four archbishops; of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMAGH">Armagh</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>, Cashel, and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-TUAM">Tuam</a>; of which the former is <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIMATE">primate</a> of all Ireland.

ARCHBISHOPRIC

Pages 591-591

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">Ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> subject to the jurisdiction of an archbishop.

ARCHBUTLER

Pages 591-591

one of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> officers of the German empire, who presents the cup to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> on solemn occasions. This office belongs to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a>.

ARCHCHAMBERLAIN

Pages 591-591

an officer of the empire, much the same with the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> chamberlain in England. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRANDENBURG">Brandenburg</a> was appointed by the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> bull archchamberlain of the empire.

ARCHCHANCELLOR

Pages 591-591

a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> officer, who, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> times, presided over the secretaries of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>. Under the two first races of the kings of France, when their territories were divided into Germany, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARLES">Arles</a>, there were three archchancellors: and hence the three archchancellors still subsisting in Germany; the archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MENTZ">Mentz</a> being archchancellor of Germany, the archbishop of Cologn, and the archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREVES">Treves</a>.

ARCHCOUNT

Pages 591-591

a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> formerly given to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>, on account of his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> power and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RICHES">riches</a>.

ARCHDEACON

Pages 591-592

an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITARY">dignitary</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> officer next to a bishop, whose jurisdiction extends either over the whole <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> or only a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of it. He is usually appointed by the bishop himself; and hath a kind of episcopal authority, originally derived from the bishop, but now independent and distinct from his. He therefore visits the clergy; and has his separate <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> of offenders by spiritual censures, and for hearing all other causes of ecclesiastical cognizance. There are 60 archdeacons in England. Archdeacon's Court, is the most inferior court in the whole ecclesiastical polity. It is held in the archdeacon's absence, before a judge appointed by himself and called his official; and its jurisdiction is sometimes in concurrence with, sometimes in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXCLUSION">exclusion</a> of, the bishop's court of the diocese. From hence, however, by statute 24 Hen. VIII. c. 12, there lies an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a> to that of the bishop.

ARCHDRUID

Pages 592-592

the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> pontiff of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRUIDS">druids</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>. See Druid.

ARCHDUKE

Pages 592-592

a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> peculiar to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>; all the sons of which are archdukes, and the daughters archduchesses. See <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">Duke</a>.

ARCHELAUS

Pages 592-592

the son of Apollonius, one of the greatest sculptors of antiquity, was a native of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IONIA">Ionia</a>, and is thought to have lived in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Claudius. He executed, in marble, the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOTHEOSIS">apotheosis</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>. This masterpiece in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a> was found in 1568, in a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> named Fratocchia, belonging to the princes of Colonna, where, it is said, the emperor Claudius had a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. Father Kircher, Cupertino, Spanheim, and several other learned antiquaries, have given a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> and explication of this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>.

ARCHERS

Pages 592-592

a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITIA">militia</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> soldiery armed with bows and arrows. The word is formed of arcus, "a bow;" whence arcuarius, and even arquus, and arquites, as they are also denominated in the corrupt state of the Latin tongue. Archers were much employed in former times; but they are now laid aside, excepting in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> and some of the eastern countries; where there are companies of archers still subsisting in their armies, and with which they did terrible execution at the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEPANTO">Lepanto</a>.—As an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a>, the practice of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHERY">archery</a> is still kept up in many places. See the article Archery. In France, the officers who attend the lieutenants de <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol18.html#article-POLICE">police</a> and provosts, to make captures, seizures, arrests, &c., are called archers; though their arms be only halberds or carbines. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> they say, the archers of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> prevot de l'hôtel; of the prevot des marchands; the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> archers; the archers de guet, or of the watch, &c.—Small parties of archers, called also gens de maréchaussée, are continually patrolling on the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a>, to secure them against robbers.—The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRIAGES">carriages</a> of Lyons, &c., are always escorted by a party of archers. To the diligence of these archers or marshal's men, it is partly owing, that persons now travel in all parts of France in the utmost security; there being fewer robberies on the highway in that whole <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> in a year than about <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> in a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WEEK">week</a>.

ARCHERY

Pages 592-597

the art <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SHOOTING">shooting</a> with a bow and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARROW">arrow</a>. In most nations, the bow was anciently the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> implement of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>; and by the expertness of the archers alone was often decided the fate of battles and of empires.—In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> archery was greatly encouraged in former times, and many statutes were made for the regulation thereof; whence it was that the English archers in particular became the best in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, and procured them many signal victories. The <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTILLERY">Artillery</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">Company</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, though they have <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> disused the weapon, are the remains of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> fraternity of bowmen or archers. Artillery (artillerie) Archer is a French <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> signifying archery; as the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s gia, vol. bowyer is in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> styled artilleur du roy: And from that <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> the English seem to have learnt at least the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>-bow archery. We therefore find that William the Conqueror had a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of bowmen in his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> at the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HASTINGS">Hastings</a>, when no mention is made of such troops on the side of Harold: And it is supposed that these Norman archers <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> with the arbalét (or cross-bow), in which formerly the arrow was placed in a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GROOVE">groove</a>, being termed in French a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUADREL">quadrel</a>, and in English a bolt. Of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> when shooting with the long bow first began among the English, at which exercise they afterwards became so expert, there appear no certain accounts. Their chronicles do not mention the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of archery as expressly applied to the cross bow, or the long bow, till the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Richard I., who was killed by an arrow at the siege of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIMOGES">Limoges</a> in Guienne, which Hemmingford mentions to have issued from a cross bow.—After this, which happened in 1199, there appear not upon record any notices of archery for nearly 150 years, when an order was issued by Edward III., in the 15th year of his reign, to the sheriffs of most of the English counties for providing 500 <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> bows and 500 bundles of arrows, for the then intended war against France. Similar orders are repeated in the following years; with this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> only, that the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GLOUCESTERSHIRE">Gloucestershire</a> is directed to furnish 500 painted bows as well as the same number of white. The famous battle of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRESSY">Cressy</a> was fought four years afterwards, in which our chroniclers state that we had 2800 archers, who were opposed to about the same number of the French, together with a circumstance which seems to prove, that by this time we used the long bow, whilst the French archers shot with the arbalest. The circumstance alluded to is as follows: Previously to the engagement there fell a very heavy <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>, which is said to have much damaged the bows of the French, or perhaps rather the strings of them. Now the long bow (when unstrung) may be most conveniently covered, so as to prevent the rain's injuring it; nor is there scarcely any addition to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> from a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>; whereas the arbalest is of a most inconvenient form to be sheltered from the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>. As therefore, in the year 1342, orders were issued to the sheriffs of each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> county to provide 500 bows, with a proper proportion of arrows, it seems probable that these were long bows, and not the arbalet. At the above-mentioned battle, the English ascribed their victory chiefly to the archers.—The battle of Poictiers was fought A.D. 1356, and gained by the same means. Sometimes the archers gained <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> victories without even the least assistance from the men-at-arms; as particularly, the decisive victory over the Scots at Homildon, A.D. 1402. In that bloody battle, the men-at-arms did not strike a stroke, but were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> spectators of the valour and victory of the archers. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Douglas, who commanded the Scotch army in that <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, enraged to see his men falling thick around him by showers of arrows, and trusting to the goodness of his armour (which had been three years in making), accompanied by about eighty lords, knights, and gentlemen, in complete armour, rushed forward, and attacked the English archers <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>-in-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. But he soon had reason to repent his rashness. The English arrows were so sharp and strong, and discharged with so much force, that no armour could repel them. The earl of Douglas, after receiving five wounds, was made prisoner; and all his brave companions were either killed or taken. <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> de Comines acknowledges, what our own writers assert, that the English archers excelled those of every other nation; and Sir John Fortescue says again and again,—“that the might of the realme of England standyth upon archers.” The superior dexterity of their archers gave the English a great advantage over their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> enemies the French and Scots. The French depended chiefly on their men-at-arms, and the Scots on their pikemen; but the ranks of both were often thinned and thrown into disorder by flights of arrows before they could reach their enemies. James I. of Scotland, who had seen and admired the dexterity of the English archers, and who was himself an excellent archer, endeavoured to revive the exercise of archery among his own subjects, by whom it had been too much neglected. With this view, he ridiculed their awkward manner of handling their bows, in his humorous poem, of Christ’s Kirk on the Green; and procured the following <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> to be made in his first <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, A.D. 1424, immediately after his return to Scotland: “That all men might busk <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THAME">thame</a> to be archares fra the be 12 years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>; and that ilk ten pounds worth of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> thair be made bow markes, and speciallie near paroche kirks, quhairin upon halte dayis men may cum, and at the leist schute thyse about, and have usage of archarie; and whasa usis not archarie, the laird of the land sal rais of him a wedder; and gif the laird raises not the said pane, the king’s shiref, or his ministers, sal rais it to the king.” But the untimely death of that excellent <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> prevented the effectual execution of this law. There is not found any <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of parliament of Henry V. in relation to archery, and all the orders in Rymer till the battle of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGINCOURT">Agincourt</a> relate to great guns, from which he seems at first to have expected more considerable advantage than from the training of bowmen. It should seem, however, that this sort of artillery, from its unwieldiness, bad and narrow <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a>, together with other defects, was as yet but of little use in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> operations. In the year 1417 this king therefore ascribes his victory at Agincourt to the archers, and directs the sheriffs of many counties to pluck from every goose six wing-feathers for the purpose of improving arrows, which are to be paid for by the king. In 1421, though the French had been defeated both at Cressy, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POITIERS">Poitiers</a>, and Agincourt, by the English archers, yet they still <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> the use of the cross bow; for which reason, Henry V. as <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Normandy, confirms the charters and privileges of the balistarii, who had been long established as a fraternity in his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROUEN">Rouen</a>. In the fifth of Edward IV. an act passed, that every Englishman, and Irishman dwelling with Englishmen, shall have an English bow of his own height, which is directed to be made of yew, wych, hazel, ash, or awburne, or any other reasonable tree according to their power. The next <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> also directs that butts shall be made in every township, which the inhabitants are obliged to shoot up and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> every feast <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, under the penalty of a halfpenny when they shall omit this exercise. In the 14th year, however, of this same king, it appears by Rymer’s Exdera, that 1000 archers were to be sent to the duke of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BURGUNDY">Burgundy</a>, whose pay is settled at sixpence a day, which was a considerable sum in these times, when the value of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> was so much higher than it is at present. This circumstance seems to prove, very strongly, the great estimation in which archers were still held. In the same year, Edward, preparing for a war with France, directs the sheriffs to procure bows and arrows, “as most specially requisite and necessary.” On the war taking <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> with Scotland, eight years after this, Edward provides both ordnance and archers; so that though the use of artillery (as we now term it) was then gaining ground, yet that of the bow and arrow was not neglected. Richard III. by his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to archery, was able to send 1000 bowmen to the duke of Bretagne, and he availed himself of the same troops at the battle of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOSWORTH">Bosworth</a>. During the reign of Henry VII. however, there appears no order relative to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUNPOWDER">gunpowder</a> or artillery; whilst on the other hand, in 1488, he directs a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> levy of archers to be sent to Brittany, and that they shall be reviewed before they embark. In the 19th year of his reign, the same king forbids the use of the cross bow, because “the long bow had been much used in this realm, whereby <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> and victory had been gotten against outward enemies, the realm greatly defended, and much more the dread of all Christian princes by reason of the same.” During the reign of Henry VIII. several statutes were made for the promotion of archery. The 8th Eliz. c. 10. regulates the price of bows, and the 13th Eliz. c. 14. enacts, that bow staves shall be brought into the realm from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANSE">Hanse</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> and the Eastward; so that archery still continued to be an object of attention in the legislature. In Rymer’s Exdera there is neither statute or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCLAMATION">proclamation</a> of James I. on this head; but it appears by Dr Birch’s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of his son (Prince Henry), that at eight years of age, he learned to shoot both with the bow Archery, bow and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUN">gun</a>, whilst at the same time this prince had in his establishment an officer who was styled bow-bearer. The king granted a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a> to the Artillery Company, by which the powers they had received from Henry VIII. were considerably extended. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I. appears, from the dedication of a treatise entitled The Bowman's <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">Glory</a>, to have been himself an archer; and in the eighth year of his reign he issued a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> mayor, and several of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRIVY_COUNCIL">privy <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, to prevent the fields near London being so enclosed as to "interrupt the necessary and profitable exercise of shooting," as also to lower the mounds where they prevented the view from one mark to another. Catharine of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a> (<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> to Charles II.) seems to have been much pleased with the sight at least of this exercise; for in 1676, by the contribution of Sir Edward <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUNGERFORD">Hungerford</a> and others, a silver badge for the marshal of the fraternity was made, weighing 25 ounces, and representing an archer <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> the long bow (in the proper manner) to his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-EAR">ear</a>, with the following inscription: Regine Catharinae Sagittarii. The supporters are two bowmen, with the arms of England and Portugal. In 1682 there was a most magnificent cavalcade and entertainment given by the Finsbury archers, when they bestowed the titles of "duke of Shoreditch," "marquis of Islington," &c. upon the most deserving. Charles II. was present upon this occasion; but the day being rainy, he was obliged soon to leave the field. So lately as the year 1753 targets were erected in the Finsbury fields, during the Easter and Whitsun holidays; when the best shooter was styled <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> for the ensuing year, and the second <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIEUTENANT">Lieutenant</a>. Why this military weapon was so decisive in the battles of former days, the following reasons may be suggested. Before the introduction of fire arms the enemy could only be struck at a distance by slings, the how used by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, or the cross bow; to all which the English long bow was infinitely superior. As for slings, they never have been used in the more northern parts of Europe by armies in the field; nor does their use indeed seem to have been at all convenient or extensively practicable, for two principal reasons: In the first place, slingers cannot advance in a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a> body, on account of the space to be occupied by this weapon in its rotatory <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>; in the next place, the weight of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a> to be carried must necessarily impede the slingers greatly in their movements. The bow of the ancients again, as represented in all their reliefs, was a mere toy compared with that of our <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>; it was therefore chiefly used by the Parthians, whose attacks (like those of the present Arabs) were desultory. As for the cross bow, it is of a most inconvenient form for carriage, even with the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> improvements; and, in case of rain, could not easily be secured from the weather. After the first shot, moreover, it could not be recharged under a considerable time, whilst the bolts were also heavy and cumbersome. The English long bow, on the other hand, together with the quiver of arrows, was easily carried by the archer, as easily secured from the rain, and recharged almost instantaneously. It is not therefore extraordinary, that troops, who solely used this most effectual weapon, should generally obtain the victory, even when opposed to much more numerous armies. It may be urged, that these losses having been experienced by our enemies, must have induced them to practise the same <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of warfare.—But it is thought that the long bow was not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> used even in England till the time of Edward III. when the victory at Cressy sufficiently proclaimed the superiority of that weapon. It required, however, so much training before the archer could be expert, that we must not be surprised <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> soon afterwards this military exercise was much neglected, as appears by the preambles of several ancient statutes. Whilst the military tenures subsisted, the sovereign could only call upon his tenants during war, who therefore attended with the weapons they had been used to, and which required no previous practice. On the other hand, the English archers were obliged by acts of parliament, even in time of peace, to erect butts in every <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a>, and to shoot on every <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUNDAY">Sunday</a> and holiday, after repairing perhaps to these butts from a considerable distance, whilst the expense of at least a yew bow is represented as being a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> which they were scarcely equal to. The king and parliaments of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> having thus compelled the inhabitants to such training, the English armies had (it should seem) the same advantage over their enemies as the exclusive use of fire-arms would give us at present. It appears also, by what hath been already stated, that the long bow continued to be in estimation for more than two centuries after gunpowder was introduced, which probably arose from muskets being very cumbersome and unwieldy. It is well known that rapid movements are generally decisive of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMPAIGN">campaign</a>; and for such the archers were particularly adapted, because, as they could not be annoyed at the same distance by the weapons of the enemy, they had scarcely any occasion for armour. The flower of ancient armies likewise was the cavalry, against which the long bow never failed to prevail, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> were too large objects to be missed: and hence the great number of French <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> who were prisoners at Cressy, Poitiers, and Agincourt; for being dismounted (if not wounded) whilst they were also clad in heavy armour, they could not make their escape. The same reason accounts for the English obtaining these signal victories with so inferior numbers; for the nobility and gentry thus becoming prisoners, the other parts of the French army made little or no resistance. No wonder, therefore, that in England the greatest anxiety was shown to promote the exercise of this most important weapon, and that so many statutes were made for that purpose. In Scotland, also, little less attention, though apparently not with equal success, was shown to the encouragement of the art. In both kingdoms, it was provided, that the importers of merchandise should be obliged, along with their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, to import a certain proportion of bows, bow staves, and shafts for arrows. In both, every person was enjoined to hold himself provided in bows and arrows, and was prescribed the frequent use of archery. In both, a restraint was imposed upon the exercise of other games and sports, lest they should interfere with the use of the bow; for it was intended, that people should be made expert in the use of it as a military weapon, by habituating them to the familiar exercise of it as an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> of amusement. As there was no material difference between the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a> and bodily strength of the two people, it might be supposed that the English and Scots wielded the bow with no unequal vigour and dexterity: but from undoubted historical monuments it appears that the former had the superiority; of which one instance has been already narrated. By the regulations prescribed in their statute book for the practice of archery, we find that the English shot a very long bow, those who were arrived at their full growth and maturity being prohibited from shooting at any mark that was not distant upwards of 220 yards. In the use of the bow, great dexterity as well as strength seems to have been requisite. Though we hear of arrows at Cheviot <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHASE">Chase</a> which were a yard long, yet it is by no means to be supposed that the whole band made use of such, or could draw them to the head. The regulation of the Irish statute of Edward IV. viz. that the bow should not exceed the height of the man, is allowed by archers to have been well considered; and as the arrow should be half the length of the bow, this would give an arrow of a yard in length to those only who were six feet <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>. A strong man of this size in the present times cannot easily draw above 27 inches, if the bow is of a proper strength to do execution at a considerable distance. At the same time it must be admitted, that as our ancestors were obliged by some of the old statutes to begin shooting with the long bow at the age of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a>, they might have acquired a greater slight in this exercise than their descendants, though the latter should be allowed to be of equal strength. As the shooting with the long bow was first introduced in England, and practised almost exclusively for nearly two centuries, so it hath occasioned a peculiar method of drawing the arrow to the ear and not to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>. That this is contrary to the usage of the ancients is very clear from their reliefs, and from the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMAZONS">Amazons</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> off one of their paps, as it occasioned an impediment to their shooting. The Finsbury archer is therefore represented in this attitude of drawing to the ear, both in the Bowman's Glory, and in the silver badge given by Catharine to the Artillery Company. Not many years ago there was a man named Topham, who exhibited surprising feats of strength, and who happened to be at a public <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> near Islington, to which the Finsbury archers resorted after their exercise. Topham considered the long bow as a plaything, only fit for a child; upon which one of the archers laid him a bowl of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNCH">punch</a>, that he could not draw the arrow two-thirds of its length. Topham accepted this bet with the greatest confidence of winning; but bringing the arrow to his breast instead of his ear, he was greatly mortified by paying the wager, after many fruitless efforts. As to the distance to which an arrow can be shot from a long bow with the best elevation of 45 degrees, that must necessarily depend much both upon the strength and slight of the archer; but in general the distance was reckoned from eleven to twelve score yards. The butts for exercise, as above noticed, were directed to be distant upwards of 220 yards. There is indeed a tradition, that an attorney of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WIGAN">Wigan</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANCASHIRE">Lancashire</a> (named <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEIGH">Leigh</a>) shot a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a> in three flights; but the same tradition states, that he placed himself in a very particular attitude, which cannot be used commonly in this exercise. According to Neade, an archer might shoot six arrows in the time of charging and discharging one musket. The archers consider an arrow of from 20 to 24 drop weight to be the best for flight or hitting a mark at a considerable distance, and that yew is the best material of which they can be made. As to the feathers, that of a goose is preferred; it is also wished, that the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIRD">bird</a> should be two or three years old, and that the feather may drop of itself. Two out of three feathers in an arrow are commonly white, being plucked from the gander; but the third is generally <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> or gray, being taken from the goose; and, from this difference in point of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, informs the archer when the arrow is properly placed. From this most distinguished <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> therefore the whole arrow sometimes receives its name: And this, by-the-by, affords an explanation of the gray goose wing in the ballad of Cheviot Chase. Arrows were armed anciently with flint or metal heads, latterly with heads of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>; of these there were various forms and denominations. By an act of parliament made the 7th of Henry IV. it was enacted. That for the future all the heads for arrows and quarrels should be well boiled or brased, and hardened at the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> with <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STEEL">steel</a>; and that every arrow head or quarrel should have the mark of the maker; workmen disobeying this order, were to be fined and imprisoned at the king's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a>, and the arrow heads or quarrels to be forfeited to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>. Arrows were reckoned by sheaves, a sheaf consisting of 24 arrows. They were carried in a quiver, called also an arrow case, which served for the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGAZINE">magazine</a>; arrows for immediate use were worn in the girdle. In ancient times phials of quicklime, or rather combustible <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, for <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> houses or ships, were fixed on the heads of arrows, and shot from long bows. This has been also practised since the use of gunpowder.
