Neade says, he has known by <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>, that an archer may shoot an ounce of fireworks upon an arrow twelve score yards. Arrows with wildfire, and arrows for fireworks, are mentioned among the stores at Newhaven and Berwick, in the 1st of Edward VI. The force with which an arrow strikes an object at a moderate distance, may be conceived from the account given by King Edward VI. in his journal; wherein he says, that 100 archers of his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> shot before him two arrows each, and afterwards altogether; and that they shot at an inch board, which some pierced quite through and struck into the other board; <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> pierced it quite through with the heads of their arrows, the board being well-seasoned <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>; their distance from the mark is not mentioned. To protect our archers from the attacks of the enemy's horse, they carried long stakes pointed at both ends; these they planted in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, sloping before them. In the first of Edward VI. 350 of these were in the stores of the town of Berwick, under the article of archers stakes; there were also at the same time eight bundles of archers stakes in Pontefract castle. To prevent the bowstring from striking the left arm, Archery. arm, the arm is covered with a piece of smooth <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, fastened on the outside of the arm; this is called a bracer; and to guard the fingers from being cut by the bowstring, archers wore shooting gloves. Chaucer, in his prologue to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a> Tales, thus describes an archer of his day: And he was clade in cote and hode of grene, A sheaf of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PEACOCK">peacock</a> arwes bright and keen, Under his belt he bare full thriftily: Wel coude he dresse his takel yewmanly, His arwes dropned not with fetheres lowe, And in his hand he bare a mighty bowe, A not <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a> hadde he, with browne visage, Of wood craft coude he wel all the usage; Upon his arms he had a gai bracer, And by his side a swerd and a bokeler, And on the other side a gaie daggere Harneised wel, and sharpe as pointe of spere: A cristofre on his breast of silver shene, A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORN">horn</a> he bare, the baudrick was of grene, A forester was he sothely as I gesse. Though archery continued to be encouraged by the king and legislature for more than two centuries after the first knowledge of the effects of gunpowder, yet by the latter end of the reign of Henry VIII, it seems to have been partly considered as a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASTIME">pastime</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTHUR">Arthur</a>, the elder <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> of Henry, is said to have been fond of this exercise, insomuch that a good shooter was styled Prince Arthur. We are also informed that he pitched his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TENT">tent</a> at Mile End in order to be present at this recreation, and that Henry his brother also attended. When the latter afterwards became king, he gave a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINDSOR">Windsor</a> to those who should excel in this exercise; and a capital shot having been made, Henry said to Barlow (one of his guards), "If you still win, you shall be duke over all archers." Barlow therefore having succeeded, and living in Shoreditch, was created duke thereof. Upon another occasion, Henry and the queen were met by 200 archers on Shooter's hill, which probably took its name from their assembling near it to shoot at marks. This king likewise gave the first charter to the Artillery Company in the 29th year of his reign, by which they are permitted to wear dresses of any colour except purple and scarlet, to shoot not only at marks but birds, if not pheasants or herons, and within two miles of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> palaces. They are also enjoined by the same charter not to wear furs of a greater price than those of the martin. The most material privilege, however, is, that of indemnification for <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a>, if any person passing between the shooter and the mark is killed, provided the archers have first called out fast. The following <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of an archer, his bow, and accoutrements, is given in a MS. written in the time of Queen <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>. "Captains and officers should be skilful of that most noble weapon, and to see that their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> according to their draught and strength have good bowes, well nocked, well strynged, every strange whippe in their nocke, and in the myddes rubbed with wax, braser and shutting glove, some spare strynges trymed as aforesaid, every man one shefe of arrows, with a case of leather defensible against the rayne, and in the same fower and twentie arrowes, whereof eight of them should be <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> than the residue, to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GALL">gall</a> or astoyne the enemye with the hailshot of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> Archery. arrows, before they shall come within the danger of the harquebuss shot. Let every man have a brigandine, or a little cote of plate, a skull or hufkyn, a mawle of leade of five foote in lengthe, and a pike, and the same hanging by his girdle, with a hook and a dagger; being thus furnished, teach them by musters to marche, shoote, and retire, keepinge their faces up on the enemy's. Sumtyme put them into great nowmbers, as to battell apparteyneth, and thus use them often times practised, till they be perfecte; for those men in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTEL">battel</a> ne skirmish can not be spared. None other weapone maye compare with the same noble weapon." The long bow, as already observed, maintained its place in our armies long after the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of firearms. Nor have there been wanting experienced soldiers who were <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADVOCATES">advocates</a> for its continuance, and who in many <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> even preferred it to the harquebus or musket. King Charles I. twice granted special commissions under the great <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEAL">seal</a> for enforcing the use of the long bow. The first was in the 4th year of his reign: but this was revoked by proclamation four years afterwards, on account of divers extortions and abuses committed under sanction thereof. The second, anno 1633, in the ninth year of his reign, to William Neade and his son, also named William, wherein the former is styled an ancient archer, who had presented to the king a warlike invention for uniting the use of the pike and bow, seen and approved by him and his council of war; whereof his majesty had granted them a commission to teach and exercise his loving subjects in the said invention, which he particularly recommended the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> officers of his trained bands to learn and practise; and the justices and other chief magistrates throughout England, are therein enjoined to use every means in their power to assist Neade, his son, and all persons authorized by them in the furtherance, propagation, and practice of this useful invention. Both the commissions and proclamation are printed at large in Rymer. At the breaking out of the civil war, the earl of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a> issued a precept, dated in November 1643, for stirring up all well affected people by benevolence, towards raising a company of archers for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the king and parliament. Archery with the long bow continues to be used as a manly exercise by the inhabitants of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENEVA">Geneva</a>, and in many parts of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>; nor is it totally neglected in Great <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. There are several <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a> of archers in England; the chief of which are, the Woodmen of Arden, and the Toxophilite. But the most noted <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> of this kind, now existing, is The Royal Company of Archers in Scotland.—The ancient records of this Company having been destroyed by fire about the beginning of the last century, no authentic traces of their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> now remain. It is said that they owe their origin to the commissioners appointed in the reign of James I. of Scotland for enforcing and overseeing the exercise of archery in different counties. Those commissioners, who were in general men of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> and power, picking out amongst the better sort of people under their cognizance the most expert archers, formed them into a company, and upon perilous occasions made a present of their services to the king as his chief body guards; in which situa- tion they often distinguished themselves for their loyalty, their courage, and skill in archery. This rank of the king's principal body guards the Royal Company still claims, within seven miles of the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a> of Scotland. Certain it is, that by an act of the privy council of Scotland, in 1677, this company was recognized under the name and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of "His Majesty's Company of Archers;" and by the same act a piece of plate of the value of 20l. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a> was ordered to be given to be shot for by them at their annual parades, called Weapons-showings, and to be called The King's Prize. At this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> the Royal Company consisted, as it does at present, of the principal nobility and gentry of Scotland. But their unfortunate <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to anti-revolution principles, upon that event's taking place, put almost a period to their existence: Their public parades or marches were discontinued, and the royal prize was withheld. Upon the accession of Queen <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>, their former splendour was revived; and in the year 1703 they obtained a royal charter, confirming in general terms all their former <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> and privileges, and conferring others upon them. But their partiality to the family of Stuart was at various after periods the cause of a temporary prosperity and decline. These unhappy differences of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> having totally subsided, the Royal Company are now more numerous and flourishing than ever, and perhaps even more dexterous archers. His present Majesty, as a mark of his royal <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRONAGE">patronage</a> and approbation, has been pleased to revive the royal prize, which for the first time was shot for upon the 28th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1788 by a numerous and respectable meeting. The Woodmen of Arden and the Toxophilite have lately been pleased to admit the members of the Royal Company to the freedom of their societies: these grants have been followed by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECIPROCAL">reciprocal</a> diplomas from the Royal Company; so that the three chief societies of archers in Britain may be said to be now incorporated into one. The prizes belonging to this Company, and which are annually shot for, are, 1. A silver arrow, given by the town of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MUSSELBURGH">Musselburgh</a>, which appears to have been shot for as early as the year 1603. The victor in this, as in the other prizes, except the king's prize, has the custody of it for a year, then returns it with a medal appended, on which are engraved any motto and device which the gainer's fancy dictates. 2. A silver arrow given by the town of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEEBLES">Peebles</a>, A.D. 1626. 3. A silver arrow given by the city of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, A.D. 1709. 4. A silver punch bowl of about the value of 50l. made of Scottish silver at the expense of the Company, A.D. 1720. And, 5. The king's prize above mentioned, which becomes the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of the winner. All these prizes are shot for at what is termed Rovers, the marks being placed at the distance of 185 yards. Besides these, there is another prize annually contended for at butt or point-blank distance, called the Goose. The ancient manner of shooting for this prize was, a living goose was built in a turf butt, having the head only exposed to view; and the archer who first <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol11.html#article-HIT">hit</a> the goose's head was entitled to the goose as his reward. But this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>, on account of its barbarity, has been long ago laid aside; and in place of the goose head, a mark of about an inch diameter is affixed upon each butt, and the archer who first hits this mark is captain of the butt shooters for a year. The affairs of the Company are managed by a preses and six counsellors, who are chosen annually by the whole members. The council are vested with the power of receiving or rejecting the candidates for admission, and of appointing the Company's officers civil and military. The Royal Company now consists of above 1000 members, among whom are most of the Scottish nobility of the first distinction. A number of the Company meet weekly during the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> season at Edinburgh, in the Meadows, where they exercise themselves in shooting at butts or rovers: And in the adjoining ground they have a handsome <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, erected within these 12 years, with suitable offices, whither they adjourn after their exercise, and where they hold their elections and other meetings relative to the business of the society. The uniform of the Royal Company of Archers is tartan, lined with white, and trimmed with green and white fringes; a white sash with green tassels; and a blue <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BONNET">bonnet</a>, with a St Andrew's cross and feathers. The Company have two standards. The first of these bears, on one side <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARS">Mars</a> and Venus encircled in a wreath of thistles, with this motto, "In peace and war." On the other, a yew tree, with two men dressed and equipped as archers, encircled as the former; motto, Dat gloria vires. The other standard displays, on one side, a lion rampant <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULES">gules</a>, on a field or, encircled with a wreath; on the top, a thistle and crown; motto, Nemo me impune lacesset. On the other, St Andrew on the cross, on a field argent; at the top, a crown; motto, Dulce pro patria periculum. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">ARCHES</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, in English <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> polity, is a court of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a>, belonging to the archbishop of each <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>; whereof the judge is called the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAN">dean</a> of the arches, because he anciently held his court in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of St <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> le bow, (Sancta <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARIA">Maria</a> de arcibus), though all the principal spiritual courts are now holden at Doctors Commons. His proper jurisdiction is only over the 13 peculiar parishes belonging to the archbishop in London; but the office of dean of the arches having been for a long time united with that of the archbishop's principal office, he now, in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of the last-mentioned office, receives and determines appeals from the sentences of all inferior ecclesiastical courts within the province. And from him there lies an appeal to the king in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CHANCERY">chancery</a> (that is, to a court of delegates appointed under the king's great seal), by statute 25th Hen. VIII. c. 19, as supreme head of the English church, in the place of the bishop of Rome, who formerly exercised this jurisdiction; which circumstance alone will furnish the reason why the Popish clergy were so anxious to separate the spiritual court from the temporal.

ARCHETYPE

Pages 597-597

the first <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODEL">model</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>; which is copied after to make another like it. Among minters, it is used for the standard <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> by which the others are adjusted. The archetypal world, among Platonists, means the world as it existed in the idea of God before the visible <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREATION">creation</a>.

ARCHIATER

Pages 598-598

ARCHITRUS, properly denotes <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> physician of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> who retains several. The word is formed of ἀρχής, principium, "chief;" and ἰατρός, medicus, a "physician."

ARCHICOLYTHUS

Pages 597-598

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> churches: the ministers whereof were divided into four orders <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> degrees, viz. priests, deacons, subdeacons, and acolythi; each of which had their chiefs. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of the acolythi was called archiacoluthus.

ARCHIDAPIFER

Pages 598-598

(from ἀρχής, and δαπήδης, "<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEWER">sewer</a>,") <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> sewer, is a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> officer of the empire. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BAVARIA">Bavaria</a> is archidapifer. The palatine of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a> at one <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> pretended this office was annexed to his <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALATINATE">palatinate</a>; but he has since desisted.

ARCHIEROSYNES

Pages 598-598

in the Grecian antiquity, a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> vested with authority over the rest of the priests; and appointed to execute the more sacred and mysterious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>.

ARCHIGALLUS

Pages 598-598

in antiquity, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> of Cybele, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of the eunuch priests of that <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a>, called Galli.

ARCHIGERONTES

Pages 598-598

in antiquity, the chiefs <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> masters of the several companies of artificers at <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>. Some have mistaken the archigerontes for the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a>-priests appointed to take the confession of those who were condemned to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>.

ARCHIGUBERNUS

Pages 598-598

ARCHIGUBERNATA, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> ARCHIGUBERNITES, in antiquity, the commander of the imperial ship, or that which the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> was aboard of. Some have confounded the office of archigubernus with that of praefectus classis, or <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a>, but the former was under the command of the latter. Potter takes the proper office of the archiguberneta to have been, to manage the marine affairs, to provide commodious harbours, and order all things relating to the sailing of the fleet, except what related to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>.

ARCHIL

Pages 598-598

ARCHILLA, ROCHELLA, ORSIELLE, is a whitish moss which grows upon rocks, in the Canary and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> de Verd <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, and yields a rich purple tincture, fugitive, indeed, but extremely beautiful. This weed is imported to us as it is gathered. Those who prepare it for the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the dyer, grind it betwixt <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, so as to thoroughly bruise, but not to reduce it into powder; and then moisten it occasionally with a strong spirit of urine, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> urine itself mixed with quicklime; in a few days it acquires a purplish <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>, and at length a blue <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. In the first it is called Archil; in the latter, Lacmus or Litmase. The dyers rarely employ this drug by itself, on account of its dearness and the perishableness of its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> use they make of it is, for giving a bloom to other colours, as pinks, &c. This is effected by passing the dyed cloth or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a> through hot <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> lightly impregnated with the archil. The bloom thus communicated soon decays upon exposure to the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>. Mr Hellot informs us, that by the addition of a little solution of tin, the drug gives a durable dye; that its colour is at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> changed towards a scarlet; and that it is the more permanent in proportion as it recedes the more from its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> colour. Prepared archil very readily gives out its colour to water, to volatile spirits, and to spirit of wine; it is the substance principally made use of for colouring the spirits of thermometers. As exposure to the air destroys its colour upon cloth, the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXCLUSION">exclusion</a> of the air produces a like effect in these hermetically sealed tubes, the spirits of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> thermometers becoming in the compass of a few years colourless. M. l'Abbe Nollet observes (in the French <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a> for the year 1742), that the colourless spirit, upon breaking the tube, soon resumes its colour, and this for a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of times successively; that a watery tincture of archil, included in the tubes of thermometers, lost its colour in three days; and that, in an open deep vessel, it became colourless at the bottom, while the upper <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> retained its colour. See Colour-Making. A solution of archil in water, applied on <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a> marble, stains it of a beautiful violet or purplish blue colour, far more durable than the colour which it communicates to other bodies. M. du Fay says he has seen pieces of marble stained with it, which in two years had suffered no sensible change. It sinks deep into the marble, sometimes above an inch; and at the same time spreads upon the surface, unless the edges be bounded by wax or other like substances. It seems to make the marble somewhat more brittle. Linnaeus informs us, in the Swedish Transactions for the year 1742, that the true archil moss is to be found on the western coasts of England.

ARCHILOCHIAN

Pages 598-598

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, applied to a sort of verses, of which Archilocheus was the inventor, consisting of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> feet; the four first whereof are ordinarily dactyls, though sometimes spondees; the three last trochees, as in Horace, Solvitur acris hyems, grata vice veris et Favoni.

ARCHILOCHUS

Pages 598-599

a famous Greek poet and musician, was, according to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a>, cotemporary with Candaules and Gyges, kings of Lydia, who flourished about the 14th Olympiad, 724 years before Christ. But he is placed much later by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> chronologists; viz. by Blair 686, and by Priestley 660 years, before Christ. He was born at Paros, one of the Cyclades. His father Telesicles was of so <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>, that he was chosen by his countrymen to consult the oracle at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DELPHI">Delphi</a> concerning the sending a colony to Thasos: a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> that he was of one of the most distinguished families upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>. However, he is said to have sullied his birth by an ignoble <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> with a slave called Enipo, of which <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> our poet musician was the fruit. Though Archilocheus showed an early genius and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> and music, these arts did not prevent his going into the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, like other young men of his birth; but in the first engagement at which he was present, the young poet, like Horace, and like our own Suckling, lost his buckler, though he saved his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> by the help of his heels. It is much easier, said he, to get a new buckler than a new existence. This pleasantry, however, did not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> his reputation; nor could his poetry <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> prayers prevail upon Lycambes, the father of of his mistress, to let him marry his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>, though she had been <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> promised to him. After these mortifications, his life seems to have been one <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> tissue of disgrace and resentment. Archilochem proprio rabies armavit iambo. Hor. Art. Poet. 79. Archilocheus, with fierce resentment warm'd, Was with his own severe iambics arm'd. Francis. The rage of Archilocheus was proverbial in antiquity; which compared the provoking this satirist to the treading upon a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SERPENT">serpent</a>: A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> not very severe, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it be true that Lycambes, and, as some say, his three daughters, were so mortified by his satire, as to be driven to the consolation of a halter. In this piece, many adventures are mentioned, full of defamation, and out of the knowledge of the public. There were likewise many loose <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> in it; and it is said to have been on account of this satire that the Lacedæmonians laid a prohibition on his verses*. However, according to Plutarch, there is no bard of antiquity by whom the two arts of poetry and music have been so much advanced as by Archilocheus. To him is attributed particularly the sudden transition from one rhythm to another of a different kind, and the manner of accompanying those <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> upon the lyre. Heroic poetry, in hexameter <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>, seems to have been solely in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> among the more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> poets and musicians; and the transition from one rhythm to another, which lyric poetry required, was unknown to them; so that if Archilocheus was the first author of this mixture, he might with propriety be styled the Inventor of Lyric Poetry, which, after his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, became a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of versification wholly distinct from heroic.—To him is likewise ascribed the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of Epodes. See Epode. Our poet-musician is generally ranked among the first victors at the Pythic games: and we learn from <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PINDAR">Pindar</a>, that his muse was not always a termaugant; for though no mortal escaped her rage, yet she was at times sufficiently tranquil and pious to dictate hymns in praise of the gods and heroes. One in particular, written in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>, acquired him the acclamations of all <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>; for he sung it in full <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> at the Olympic games, and had the satisfaction of receiving from the judges the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of victory consecrated to real merit. This <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HYMN">hymn</a>, or ode, was afterwards sung in honour of every victor at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OLYMPIA">Olympia</a>, who had no poet to celebrate his particular exploits. Archilocheus was at last slain by one Callondax Corrax, of the island of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAXOS">Naxos</a>; who, though he did it in fight, according to the laws of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, was driven out of the temple of Delphi, by command of the oracle, for having deprived of life a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> consecrated to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSES">Muses</a>. The names of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a> and Archilocheus were equally revered and celebrated in Greece, as the two most excellent poets which the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> had ever produced. This appears from an epigram in the Anthologia; and from Cicero, who ranks him with poets of the first class, and in his Epistles tells us, that the grammarian <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOPHANES">Aristophanes</a>, the most rigid and scrupulous critic of his time, used to say, that the longest poem of Archilocheus always appeared to him the most excellent.

ARCHILUTE

Pages 682-682

Arcileuto, a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> lute, having its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASS">bass</a> strings lengthened after the manner of the theorbo, and each row doubled, either with a little <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OCTAVE">octave</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> an unison. It is used by the Italians for playing a thorough bass. ARCHYTAS of Tarentum, was a Pythagorean <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, and also well skilled in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">geography</a>. He lived in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a>, and, according to report, interposed his influence with Dionysius the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a>, in order to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of that renowned philosopher. According to this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">date</a>, it would appear that Jamblichus is mistaken when he asserts, that he was a hearer of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYTHAGORAS">Pythagoras</a>, and the testimony of a writer mentioned by Photius, would seem more worthy of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a>, that he was the eighth successive preceptor of the Pythagorean school. But his fame was not confined to the circle of literature; for so eminent were his <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> talents, that, in opposition to an express <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, that no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> should be chosen more than once the general of its armies, he was elevated to that important station no less than <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> times. He adopted the sentiments of Pythagoras; in his dissertations on <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SPECULATIVE">speculative</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>. He taught in morality, that there is nothing so destructive to man as <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>; that in every condition of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, virtue is to be pursued for its own merit, and that every <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> is incompatible with virtue. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a> was indebted to Archytas for his general heads of arrangement, entitled his "Ten Categories," and very probably for that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> idea in his Ethics, that virtue consists in avoiding excesses. By discovering the duplication of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUBE">cube</a> by means of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONIC_SECTIONS">conic sections</a>, and the method of finding two <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> proportionals between two given <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>, he displayed his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> knowledge in mathematics. He is reported to have invented several curious hydraulic <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MACHINES">machines</a>, and to have made a kind of winged automaton; and his genius is likewise honoured with the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of the screw and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRANE">crane</a>. In a beautiful ode, Horace records his sad fate, in being <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> upon the Apulian shore, an unburied corpse; and mentions him as an excellent astronomer and geographer. Te maris et terrae numeroque carentis arenae Mensorem colibit, Archytas, Pulveres evagui prope litus parva Matinum Munera: nec quidquam tibi prodest Aeria tentasse domos, animoque rotundum Percurrisse polum, miratur. Archytas, what avails thy nice survey Of ocean's countless sands, of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>? In vain thy mighty spirit once could soar To orbs celestial, and their course explore. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> here, upon the tempest-beaten strand, Yon <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> confin'd, till some more liberal <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> Shall strew the pious dust in funeral rite, And wing thee to the boundless realms of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>. Francis. A singular <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a>, and a firm command of his passions, were the leading features in his moral character. In his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGER">anger</a> he never chastised any of his servants. He said one <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> to a certain dependant who had disobliged him, "What should I have done to you if I had not been angry?" He maintained a uniform decency not often observed in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> writings. A small treatise, entitled Περὶ τῆς Παντος Φυσικῆς, "On the Universe," and some other small fragments, "On <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">Wisdom</a>," and "On the Good and Happy Man," are the only pieces ascribed to this philosopher that are still extant.

ARCHIMAGUS

Pages 599-599

the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> of the Persian <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGI">Magi</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> worshippers of fire. He resided in the highest fire temple; which was held in the same veneration with them as the temple of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECCA">Mecca</a> among the Mahometans. Zoroaster first settled it at Balch; but after the Mahometans had overrun <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a> in the 7th century, the Archimagus was forced to remove from thence into Kerman, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Persia, lying on the southern ocean, where it hath <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DARIUS">Darius</a> Hystaspes took upon himself the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of Archimagus: for Porphyry tells us, he ordered before his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, that, among the other titles, it should be engraven on his monument, that he had been <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">Master</a> of the Magi; which plainly implies that he had borne this office among them, for none but the Archimagus was master of the whole <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a>. From hence it seems to have proceeded, that the kings of Persia were ever after looked on to be of the sacerdotal tribe, and were always initiated into the sacred order of the Magi, before they took on them the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, and were inaugurated into the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>.

ARCHIMANDRITE

Pages 599-599

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, was a name given by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> to what we now call an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABBOT">abbot</a>. Father Simon observes, that the word mandrite is Syriac, and signifies a solitary monk.

ARCHIMEDES

Pages 599-600

one of the most eminent of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> mathematicians, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRACUSE">Syracuse</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, about the year 180 before the Christian era. Hiero, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Syracuse, deemed it an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to have this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> for his relative and friend. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> does not inform us, to whom he was indebted for the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of literature, but he flourished about 50 years after Euclid. It is reported, that he was indebted to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> for much of his knowledge; but other accounts indicate, that he conferred more knowledge than he received from that celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>; and, in particular, Diodorus mentions, that Egypt was indebted to him for the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of the screw-<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUMP">pump</a>, for <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> off <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. And the same author narrates, that he was the inventor of several other useful <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MACHINES">machines</a>, which conveyed his fame to every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of the globe. The following passage from Livy, proves, that he was dexterous both for the inventing warlike machines, and also for his accurate observation of the heavenly bodies: "Unicus spectator caeli siderumque, mirabilior tamen inventor ac machinator bellicorum tormentorum," &c., lib. xxiv. It appears also, that in Cicero's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, he had become proverbial for his skill in solving problems. In a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to Atticus, he informs him, that he is now freed from a difficulty, which he termed an Archimedean problem, lib. xiii. ep. 28. It may perhaps be impossible distinctly to ascertain the different inventions of this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>; but from the following passage, it appears that he formed a glass sphere, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> some kind of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANETARIUM">planetarium</a>, which, with no small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of accuracy, represented the phenomena of the heavenly bodies. Hence says Claudian <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>, in parvo cum cerneret æthera vitro, Risit, et <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AD">ad</a> superos talia dicta dedidit: Huccine Huccine mortalis progressa <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POTENTIA">potentia</a> curae? Jam meus in fragile ludet orbe labor, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JURA">Jura</a> poli, rerumque fidem, legesque deorum, Ecce Syracosius transtulit arti senex. Inclusus variis famulatur spiritus astris, Et verum certis motibus urget opus. Percurrat proprium mentitus signifer annum, Et simulata novo <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CYNTHIA">Cynthia</a> mense redit. Jamque suum volvens audax industria mundum Gaudet, et humana sidera mente regit. Quid falsa insontem tonitru Salmoenea miror? Emula naturae parva reperta manus. "When in a glass's narrow sphere confin'd, Jove <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> the fabric of th' Almighty mind; He smil'd, and said, 'Can mortals art alone Our heav'nly labours mimic with their own? The Syracusan's brittle <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> contains Th' eternal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> that through all <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> reigns, Fram'd by his art, see stars unnumber'd burn, And in their courses rolling orbs return; His <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, through various signs describe the year, And every <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> his mimic moons appear. Our rival's laws his little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a> bind, And rule their motions by a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> mind: Salmoeneus could our <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a> imitate; But Archimedes can a world create.'" In the following <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> the same machine is mentioned by Ovid. Arte Syracosia suspensus in aere clauso, Stat globus, immensi parva figura poli.

ARCHITECTURE

Pages 601-635

In the utmost latitude of the word, signifies the art of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> in general; but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> is most frequently applied only to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of such buildings as are necessary for the purposes of civil <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, such as houses, churches, halls, bridges, porticoes, &c. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of Architecture. The origin of this art, like that of most others, is totally unknown. We are assured, however, that it is as old as <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAIN">Cain</a>: for Moses tells us that he built a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>; though what were the materials, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> how the buildings were constructed, we are entirely ignorant. It is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> said, that the first materials employed in building were branches and twigs of trees, wherewith men constructed huts; such as the wigwams in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> among the American Indians at present. This, however, appears disputable. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> shelter afforded by hollows in the sides of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> or rocks, it may be supposed, would much more readily suggest the idea of using <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> as materials for building houses. Indeed, considering that tents were not invented before the days of Jabal, Tubal Cain's <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>, it is very probable that such temporary houses as the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> wigwams were not originally known; otherwise the method of covering <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a> with the skins of beasts, instead of small branches or twigs, must very soon have taken <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. These temporary houses seem to have come into use only when men began to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> an idle wandering life, like the Tartars, and could not be at the trouble of constructing durable habitations in every place where they were obliged to wander with their cattle; and Jabal perhaps from them took the hint of making portable houses or tents. Accordingly we see, that no nations, except those who are in a perpetually unsettled state, make use of such wretched materials. Even in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, where the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> has appeared in the rudest form, they were no sooner collected into <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> bodies under the emperors of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEXICO">Mexico</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERU">Peru</a>, than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> buildings began to be erected. We are not, therefore, to look for the origin of architecture in any single <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>; but in every nation, when the inhabitants began to leave off their <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> way of life, and to become civilized: and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> there is any nation to be found which hath been always in a civilized state, we may be assured that architecture hath always had an existence there. But whatever may be in this, the origin of regular buildings hath been deduced from the construction of the meanest huts in a very natural and plausible manner by several authors. "Anciently (says Vitruvius) men lived in woods, and inhabited caves; but in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, taking perhaps example from birds, who with great industry build their nests, they made themselves huts. At first they made Primitive these huts, very probably, of a conic <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>; because huts. Plate XXXVII: Fig. 1. ing them in a point at the top; covering the whole with reeds, leaves, and clay, to screen them from tempests and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>. "But finding the conic figure inconvenient on account of its inclined sides, they changed both the form and construction of their huts, giving them a cubical figure, and building them in the following manner: Having marked out the space to be occupied by the hut, they fixed in the ground several upright trunks of trees to form the sides, filling the intervals between them with branches closely interwoven and covered with clay. The sides being thus completed, four <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> beams were placed on the upright trunks; which, being well joined at the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a>, kept the sides firm, and likewise served to support the covering or <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> of the building, composed of many <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOISTS">joists</a>, on which were laid several beds of reeds, leaves, and clay. "Insensibly mankind improved in the art of building, and invented methods to make their huts lasting and handsome as well as convenient. They took off the bark, and other unevenesses, from the trunks of the trees that formed the sides; raised them, probably above the dirt and humidity, on stones; and covered each of them with a flat stone or slate, to keep off the rain. The spaces between the ends of the joists were closed with clay, wax, or some other substance; and the ends of the joists covered with thin boards cut in the manner of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIGLYPHS">triglyphs</a>. The position of the roof was likewise altered: for being, on account of its flatness, unfit to throw off the rains that fell in great abundance during the winter season, they raised it in the middle; giving it the form of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GABLE">gable</a> roof, by placing rafters on the joists, to support the earth and other materials that composed the covering. "From this simple construction the orders of architecture took their rise. For when buildings of wood were set aside, and men began to erect <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> and stately edifices of stone, they imitated the parts which <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> had introduced into the primitive huts; insomuch that the upright trees, with the stones at each end of them, were the origin of columns, bases, and capitals, and the beams, joists, rafters, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STRATA">strata</a> of materials that formed the covering, gave birth to architraves, friezes, triglyphs, and cornices, with the corona, the mutules, the modillions, and the dentils. "The first buildings were in all likelihood rough and uncouth; as the men of those times had neither <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> nor tools: but when, by <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> experience and reasoning upon it, the artists had established certain rules, had invented many instruments, and by great practice had acquired a facility in executing their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a>, they made quick advances towards perfection, and at length discovered certain manners of building, which succeeding ages have regarded with the highest veneration." Among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Egyptians, Assyrians, and Persians, this art was carried to an incredible length. The pyramids of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> are such structures as would exceed the power of the most potent monarch on earth to raise at this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>. The largest of these, according to the account of M. Coguet, is near 500 feet <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, and contains 315,590 solid fathoms. It is composed of stones enormously large; many of them being 30 feet long, four feet high, and three in breadth; and all this huge <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of building was coated over with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> flags of marble.—The structure called the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LABYRINTH">labyrinth</a>, in the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, according to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a>, who <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> it, excelled every thing which he could have conceived from the imagination either of himself or others. Within the same circuit of walls they had enclosed 3000 halls, 12 of which were of a singular form and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>; and of these, half were above, and half below ground; and the whole was terminated by a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYRAMID">pyramid</a> 40 fathoms high. All this prodigious mass of building was composed of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> marble, and the walls were adorned with engravings.—The <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-OBELISKS">obelisks</a> were not less astonishing; the largest of them being entire pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANITE">granite</a>, no less than 180 feet high.—Near Andera, in Upper Egypt, are the ruins of a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of gray granite, the ceilings of which are supported by columns of such thickness, that four men can scarcely fathom them. The ceilings themselves are composed of stones of the same kind, six or <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> feet in breadth and 18 feet in length. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALL">hall</a> is 112 feet long, 60 high, and 58 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>. The roof of the whole edifice is a terrace, on which the Arabs formerly built a very large village, the ruins of which are still visible. Among the Babylonians and Persians, too, such immense piles of building have been raised, as appear utterly inconceivable and incredible to many <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> authors, where their former <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a> is not demonstrable by ruins visible at this day. The ruins of Persepolis, the ancient <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, were so stupendous in the time of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-AVICENNA">Avicenna</a> the Arab physician, that his countrymen could not believe such structures possible to be erected but by evil spirits. Of their extraordinary magnificence, indeed, we may have some idea from the account of the staircases belonging to the palace. The remains, some time ago, consisted of 95 steps of white marble, so broad and flat, that 12 horses might conveniently go up abreast. In these vast structures, however, the nations of whom we speak seem to have regarded the greatness, rather than the elegance or usefulness of their works. In the remarkable pyramids and obelisks of Egypt this is exceedingly for great conspicuous; but whether it was so in the labyrinth or not, in the palace at Thebes above mentioned, it is impossible to determine, unless the buildings were entire, and we knew for what purpose they had been designed. If the kings who built the pyramids designed to immortalize their memories by building, they certainly could not have fallen upon any thing more proper for this purpose; though even in this they have somehow or other failed, the names of those who erected them not being certainly known even in the time of Herodotus. It is certain, however, that neither the ancient Assyrians nor Babylonians knew the method of constructing the use of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a>. The roofs of all their halls were flat, and covered with prodigiously large stones, some of them so big as to cover a whole room singly. Their manner of building was also quite destitute of what is now called <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>; the columns were ill proportioned, and their capitals executed in the poorest manner imaginable. This was observed by the Greeks, who improved upon the proportions formerly used, and were the inventors of three of the five orders of architecture, viz. the Doric, Ionic, and Corinthian. "Anciently and of (says Vitruvius) they were ignorant of the art of proportioning the various parts of a building: they used columns; but they cut them at hazard, without rules, without without principles, and without having any <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to the proportions which they ought to give them: they placed them likewise without any regard to the other parts of the edifice. Dorus, son of Helen and grandson of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEUCALION">Deucalion</a>, having caused a temple to be built at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARGOS">Argos</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of Juno, that edifice was found by chance to be constructed according to the taste and proportions of the order which afterwards they called Doric. The form of this building having appeared agreeable, they conformed to it in the construction of edifices which they afterwards had to build. "About the same time, the Athenians sent into <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> a colony under the conduct of Ion, nephew of Dorus: this undertaking had very good success. Ion seized on <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARIA">Caria</a>, and there founded many cities. These new inhabitants thought to build <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>. They proposed for a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODEL">model</a> that of Juno at Argos: but, ignorant of the proportion which they ought to give to the columns, and in general to the whole edifice, they sought for rules capable of regulating their operation. These people wanted, in making their columns sufficiently strong to support the whole edifice, to render them at the same time agreeable to the sight. For this purpose, they thought to have given it the same proportion that they found between the foot of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> and the rest of his body. According to their ideas, the foot made a sixth <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the human height: in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>, they gave at first to a Doric <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLUMN">column</a>, taking in its chapiter; six of its diameters; that is to say, they made it six times as high as it was thick: afterwards they added to it a seventh diameter. "This new order of architecture was not long in giving birth to a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a>: they would immediately go beyond the first <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a>. The Ionians tried to throw still more delicacy and elegance into their edifices. They employed the same method which they had before put in practice for the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of the Doric order: but instead of taking for a model the body of a man, the Ionians were regulated by that of a woman. With a view to make the columns of this new order more agreeable and more pleasing, they gave them eight times as much height as they had diameter. They also made channellings all along the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a>, to imitate the folds of the robes of women: the volutes of the chapiter represented that part of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> which hung in curls on each side of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a>. The Ionians added, lastly, to these columns a base, which was not in use in the Doric order." According to Vitruvius, these bases were made in the manner of twisted cords, as a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> for the columns. This order of architecture was called Ionic, from the name of the people who had invented it. Such is the account given by Vitruvius of the origin of improvements in the proportion of columns. Had these improvements, however, existed in such early times, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>, who was greatly <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POSTERIOR">posterior</a> to them, would certainly have made mention of something of that kind; but in all his writings he gives us no account of anything like a column of stone, but uses a word which would rather incline us to think that his columns were nothing more than bare posts. It is remarkable, that improvements in architecture did not take place in any nation till after, or about, the time that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a> was taken by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEBUCHADNEZZAR">Nebuchadnezzar</a>. The grandest buildings erected among the Assyrians seem to have owed their existence to this monarch; and it can scarce be imagined that he would not endeavour to imitate the architecture of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a>'s temple, to which, by his conquest of Jerusalem, he had full access. It is also remarkable, that the dimensions of the two pillars, Jachin and Boaz, set up by Solomon, very nearly correspond with those of the Doric order, first invented by the Greeks, and which originally came from their colonies settled in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASIA_MINOR">Asia <a cl</a>ass="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINOR">Minor</a>. The height of Solomon's pillars, without the chapiter, was 18 cubits; that of the chapiter itself was five cubits; the circumference was 12 cubits; from whence, according to the Scripture <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, we may reckon the diameter to have been exactly four cubits. Had they been a single <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUBIT">cubit</a> higher, they would have been precisely of the same height with columns of the original Doric order. We do not indeed <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> to assert, that this famous temple gave a model of architecture to the whole world; although it is scarcely conceivable but imitations of it, as far as it could be known, must have taken place among many nations. Notwithstanding all their defects, however, the Egyptian buildings undoubtedly had an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> of vast grandeur and magnificence, if we may <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> given of one of their banqueting rooms by Vitruvius. The usual size of one of these rooms was from 100 to 150 feet in length, and its breadth somewhat more than half its length. At the upper end, and along the two sides, they placed rows of pillars tolerably well proportioned to one another, though not of any regular order; and at the lower part they made a magnificent and spacious entrance: this, with its ornaments seems to have taken up one end of the building entire. We are not told that there were any pillars there; though perhaps they placed two or more toward the angles on each side, for uniformity, the central space being enough for an entrance in the grandest and most august manner. Those rows of columns were set at a distance from the wall, forming a noble portico along the two sides and upper end of the building. Upon the pillars was laid an architrave; and from this was carried up a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> wall with three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> columns, answering directly to those below, and in proportion one-fourth smaller in all their parts. Between these three quarter columns were placed the windows for enlightening the building. From the tops of the lower pillars to the wall was laid a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a>; this covered the portico overhead within, and made on the outside a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATFORM">platform</a>, which was surrounded by a corridor with rails and balusters. This was terraced, and served as a plain for people to walk on; and from this they could look through the windows <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> into the room. To this terrace there was no covering required, as the Egyptians were in no fear of rain. The Egyptians decorated this sort of building with <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a>; and no kind of ornament could answer it so well, as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> cannot <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> upon statues to such advantage in any <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>, as when it comes from above, in such a regular, proportioned, and uninterrupted manner. We have already taken notice, that among the ancient Egyptians, Persians, and Babylonians, the vast strength and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of their buildings seems to have been what they chiefly valued; and in this they certainly as much excelled the Greeks and modern nations, as the latter excel them in the beautiful proportion and elegance of their structures. There are not wanting, however, some modern authors, who endeavour to deprive the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> of what is justly their due, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> have every thing to be exaggerated which seems beyond the power of modern princes to accomplish. In this way M. Goguet remarkably distinguishes himself; and that without giving any reason at all, but merely that he takes it into his head. Speaking of the wonders of ancient <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BABYLON">Babylon</a>, “All these works (says he), so marvellous in the judgment of antiquity, appear to me to have been extremely exaggerated by the authors who have spoken of them. How can we conceive, in effect, that the walls of Babylon could have been 318 feet high, and 81 in thickness, in a compass of near ten leagues?” To this we may easily reply, that the pyramids of Egypt, and the immense wall which divides <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TARTARY">Tartary</a>, show us, that even such a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> as the wall of ancient Babylon is said to have been is not altogether incredible. The lowest computation of the dimensions of the Chinese wall is, that it extends in length 1200 miles, is 18 feet high at a medium and as many thick; according to which computation, it must contain 9,504,000 solid fathoms; and yet, if we may credit the Chinese historians, this immense mass of building was finished in five years. If therefore we can suppose Nebuchadnezzar, or whoever fortified the city of Babylon, to have been capable of employing as many men for ten years as were employed in raising the Chinese wall, we may suppose him able to have fortified the city of Babylon as strongly as it is said to have been; for the mass of building is not quite <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> that of the Chinese wall, though nearly so, amounting to 18,189,600 solid fathoms. When our author afterwards gasconades about the works of the French <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>, it is difficult to avoid <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAUGHTER">laughter</a> at hearing him declare, that “infinitely more <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> has been expended, and much more genius required, as well as more power, taste, and time, to finish <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSAILLES">Versailles</a>, with all its defects, than to construct a pyramid, or erect an obelisk.” The genius, taste, and time, we shall not dispute; but as the same author confesses that 100,000 men were employed for 30 years together in the construction of the largest pyramid, we think the power may justly be doubted. This doubt will appear still the more reasonable, when we consider what time the above-mentioned <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of men would have taken to accomplish some of the works of which M. Goguet boasts so much. The canal of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUEDOC">Languedoc</a>, he tells us, extends in length upwards of 70 leagues, and required the removal of two millions of cubic fathoms of earth. This was no doubt a great work; but had 100,000 men been employed upon it at once, they must have removed this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of earth in three weeks, supposing each to have removed only a single fathom a-day. Nor can we imagine, that any modern work will at all stand in competition with the works of the ancients as to greatness, whatever they may do in other respects. As to the improvements in architecture, the Greeks were undoubtedly the first European nation who began to distinguish themselves in this way. Whence they took the first hint of improvement, we have no means of knowing; though, as we have already hinted, it is scarce credible but that Solomon’s temple must have somewhat contributed thereto; especially as we learn from Scripture, that the capitals of the columns there were ornamented in the richest manner. The origin of the Doric and Ionic orders we have already given an account of from Vitruvius; to which we may add, that the volutes, which are the peculiar ornament of the Ionic capital, are by some said to represent the natural curling down of a piece of bark from the top of a beam, which is supposed to have been the first kind of column. The Corinthian order was not invented till long after the others, and is said to have taken its rise from the following accident: A <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASKET">basket</a> had been set upon the ground, and covered with a square tile; there grew near it a plant of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACANTHUS">acanthus</a> or bear’s breech; the leaves <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> up and covered the outer surface of the basket; and, as the stalks rose up among them, they soon reached the tile which overhung the edges of the basket at the top; this stopping their course upwards, they curled and twisted themselves into a kind of volutes. In this situation a sculptor, Callimachus, saw it; the twisted part of the stalk represented to him the volutes of the Ionic capital, which, as they were here smaller, and more numerous, appeared in a new form: he saw the beauty of raising them among leaves, and was struck with the representation of a noble and lofty capital; which being afterwards put into execution, has been universally admired. In their private houses the Greeks had greater conveniences, but much less magnificence, than the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, houses as the former reserved the use of their grandest architecture for their temples and public buildings. The entrance to their private houses, however large they were, was always small, narrow and plain. The whole edifice usually consisted of two courts, and several ranges of buildings. The porter’s lodge, if such a phrase may be allowed, was usually on the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> of this narrow entrance, and opposite to this were the stables. From this entrance one came into the first or smaller <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>. This had piazzas on three sides; and on the fourth, which was usually the south side, there were buttments of pilasters, which supported the more inward parts of the ceiling. A space being thus left between the one and the other, they had places for the lodgings of men and maid servants, and such as had the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> care of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. Upon the same floor with these buttments they had several regular apartments, consisting of an antechamber, a chamber, and closets; and about the piazzas, rooms for eating and other <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> purposes. Opposite to the entrance was a lobby, or vestibule, through which lay the passage into the several rooms; and through this, in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a>, one entered a large passage, which led into the larger or principal square. Round this they had four piazzas, which, in the common way of building, were all of one height; but in more magnificent houses, they made that which faced the great entrance loftier, and every way nobler, than the other three. A nobleman of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RHODES">Rhodes</a> added this to the common method of building; and it was thence called the Rhodian manner. In this more noble part of the building were the apartments of the family. These were adorned with lofty galleries, and here were the best rooms: they were called the men’s apartments; for, in rude times, the Greeks lodged their wives and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> relations in the best rooms of the first court, where they had also their separate and detached place. The two sides of this larger court were kept for the reception of visitors; and servants were appointed to wait upon them. The <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the house entertained his guests the first day in his own apartments; but after this, how long soever they staid, they lived without restraint in one of those separate piazzas, and joined the family only when they chose it. Thus was the upper end and two sides of the great court disposed of; and its lower end, being the same range of building that was the upper end of the first court, held the lady of the house and her female friends. The Romans borrowed their architecture from the Greeks, but did not imitate them in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a> of their private dwellings. They placed the principal front of their house towards the south, and on this they bestowed all the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECORATION">decoration</a> of expensive ornament. They had here lofty galleries and spacious rooms, and everything carried an air of greatness and show. In their country houses they preserved the same situation and the same front, but the inner distribution was different. At the entrance they placed the meaner and more offensive offices, after the manner of the Greeks. The first gallery, which received the stranger at his entrance, had on one side a passage to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KITCHEN">kitchen</a>, and on the other to the stalls where they kept cattle, that their noise or smell might not be offensive within, while yet they were in readiness for all services. These stalls were placed to the left, as in the Greek houses; on the right was the kitchen, which had its light from above, and its chimney in the middle. Farther within the building were placed on one side <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATHING">bathing</a> rooms, and on the other family conveniences, in the manner of our butteries and store rooms; the bathing rooms were on the left, and the others on the right. Backwards, and full to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, they placed their cellars, for fear of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, and over these were other store rooms. From this part of the structure one came into the court: for in these there generally was only one court: this was taken up by servants, and those who had the care of the cattle; and on each side there were stalls for the cattle. In front from the entrance, but very far from all these annoyances, stood the nobler apartments for the master of the family. How magnificent the Romans were in their temples and public buildings, is yet to be seen in what remains of them, and which are not only models for all modern architects, but have never been surpassed or even equalled to this day.
