In the ruined churches there are several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a> round the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOULDINGS">mouldings</a> of the tombstones; and over an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a>, behind <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Glandore's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, is an inscription in relief done in a masterly manner, but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> unknown.

ARDRAH

Pages 684-684

a small territory <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUINEA">Guinea</a> properly so called. It lies at the bottom of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of St Thomas, and has a town called Ardres, supposed to be the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>. The inhabitants are very licentious, and have neither temple nor any <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> worship. However they are very courageous; and their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> was <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a>, till lately that the king of Dahomy made <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> upon this and the neighbouring territories, brought them under subjection, and burnt the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, particularly Ardres. The <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> is very unwholesome to Europeans: yet the natives live to a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>; but the smallpox makes great destruction among them. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is fertile in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> corn, palm wine, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, which last all the year; and they make a great <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>.

ARDRES

Pages 684-684

a town of France, in Lower Picardy, now the department of the Straits of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALAIS">Calais</a>. Here was an interview between Francis I. and Henry VIII., <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of England in 1520. It is seated in the midst of a morass, eight miles south of Calais. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a> 2. 0. N. Lat. 50. 35.

ARDS

Pages 684-684
BARONY OF, in the county of Down in Ireland: it is a narrow slip of land, in some places three and in none above six miles broad; but the soil is for the most part tolerably good. It lies between the lake of Strangford and the sea, and in the south part it is opposite to Leacale. Sir Thomas Smith obtained a patent for this barony from Queen Elizabeth, and sent his natural son with a colony to possess it; but he was intercepted and slain by an Irishman. After Sir Thomas's death, Ards was granted by James I. to some of the Scots nobility.

ARDUBA

Pages 684-684

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the Pannonians. It was taken by Germanicus about the 7th year of the Christian era; but its <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REDUCTION">reduction</a> was more owing to the disagreement that reigned among the inhabitants than to the valour of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>. The greater <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the citizens were for submitting; but the women, more fond of their ancient laws and liberties than the men, joined some Roman deserters, and falling upon their husbands, killed a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of them: but being at last overcome by the men, who then submitted to the Romans, the women either threw themselves headlong from the tops of the walls, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a>, setting fire to their houses, burnt themselves and their children to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>.

AREBO

Pages 684-684
or AREBON, a town on the Slave coast of Guinea, in Africa, seated at the mouth of the river Formosa. The English had once a factory there, as the Dutch have still. It is a large oblong place, indifferently well peopled, and furnished with houses built of reeds and leaves. E. Long. 5. 5. N. Lat. 5. 0.

ARELATE

Pages 684-685
or Arelatum, is a town of Gallia Narbonensis, situated on the Rhone, denoting a town on, or beyond, a marsh, according to the particular situation. situation of the speaker; called Arelate Sextanorum (Pliny, Mela, Coin), because it had a colony of the sixth legion. Writers of the lower age call it Arelas, -atis, (Prudentius, Ausonius). There was a double Arelas, one on each side of the river, and joined by a bridge, (Ausonius); that on the left side is thought to have been built by Constantine. Tiberius's father was sent by Julius Caesar at the head of the colony, (Suetonius); and hence the appellation Julia Paterna, as appears from an inscription. It was a favourite place of the Romans, and greatly ornamented; and hence called Gallula Roma, (Ausonius). It is now called Arles. E. Long. 5. N. Lat. 43° 40'.

AREMBERG

Pages 685-685

a small town of Germany, in the circle of Westphalia, defended by a castle. It is the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of the same name, and was erected into a principality by the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Maximilian II. In favour of John de Ligne, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> of Barbazon, who took the name of Aremberg. It is seated on the river Aer. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 6. 44. N. Lat. 50° 27'.

AREMORICA

Pages 685-685
or Armorica, a part of Gaul, between the Sequana and Ligeris, (Caesar, Hirtins); denoting a country on, or beyond the sea, ar moer, or are moer, Celtic. Pliny indeed says, that Aquitania was formerly called Aremorica; but in this he stands alone. In the lower age, the term Armorica was confined to Bretagne in France.

ARENA

Pages 685-685

in Roman antiquity, a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where the gladiators fought; so called from its being always strewed with sand, to conceal from the view of the people the blood spilt in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a>. Nero is said to have strewed the arena with <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> dust.

ARENACUM

Pages 685-685
or Arenacus, one of the four towns or larger villages in the island of the Batavi, (Tacitus). Now Arnhem, in Guelderland. E. Long. 5. 20. N. Lat. 52° 2.

ARENARIUM

Pages 685-685

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> writers, denotes a cemetery <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> burying ground. The arenae were properly a kind of pits, or holes, under ground, wherein the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> not only buried their dead, but held their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> assemblies in times of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a>.

ARENARIUS

Pages 685-685

in antiquity, gladiators who combated with beasts in the arena <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMPHITHEATRE">amphitheatre</a>. The arenarii were slaves of the lowest <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>; so that, though manumitted, they were not capable of being Roman citizens. They were the same with what were otherwise called Bestiarii.

ARENSBERG

Pages 685-685

a small town of Germany, in the circle of Westphalia, upon the river Roer. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 8. 20. N. Lat. 51° 25'.

ARENSBURG

Pages 685-685

an episcopal and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> town of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIVONIA">Livonia</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, seated in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of Osel, in the Baltic <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 22. 40. N. Lat. 58° 15'.

AREOLA

Pages 685-685

among anatomiasts, the coloured circle surrounding the nipple of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>.

AREOPAGUS

Pages 687-688

sensible old men as the senators of Areopagus were should sell at so low a price the trouble of ascending so <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>. As to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of the judges which composed the Areopagus, some authors, attentive only to a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of Solon's regulations, by which he enacted, that for the future, none but the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> archons should be admitted members of the Areopagus, have imagined, that this tribunal was filled anew every year, and that it never consisted of more than nine magistrates. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, and some others, are refuted by the circumstantial account which <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIOGENES">Diogenes</a> Laertius gives us of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONDEMNATION">condemnation</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOCRATES">Socrates</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> had wished to substitute a rational <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a> for the fabulous and extravagant system of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> which prevailed in his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. His project, however laudable, appeared impious in the eye of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>. Information was laid against him before the Areopagus, and he had as many accusers as fellow-citizens. After the charges and the answers were heard, they proceeded to suffrages. The opinions were divided, but not equally, for the number of those who condemned him exceeded by 281 the number of those who declared him innocent. He made an ironical reply to this iniquitous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a>, by telling his judges, that he took it for granted they would admit him to a maintenance in the Prytaneum. On this sarcasm, 82 of those who had voted in his favour forsook him, went over to the opposite party, and condemned him to die. Here then we have 361 judges who condemn; to whom <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we add those who persist in acquitting him, the number must be very considerable. Of all the judgments of the Areopagus, the most famous one, excepting that of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARS">Mars</a>, was the sentence which they passed on Orestes. His <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a>, which happened under Demophon the 12th <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, in 375 of the Attic era, owed all its fame to a remarkable circumstance, that gave rise to a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> which was observed ever afterwards. Orestes had killed his mother. He was accused before the Areopagus, and cited to appear in that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>. He would have lost his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of the equal <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of the votes, had not <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a>, moved with his misfortunes, declared herself for those who had absolved him, and joined her suffrage to theirs. Thus Orestes was saved. In veneration to this miracle, the Areopagites, whenever the suffrages were equally divided, decided in favour of the accused, by granting him what they termed the shell of Minerva. Cephalus and Dedalus were condemned by the Areopagus <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> before the time of Orestes. We find in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> authors some decisions of this tribunal, which bear the strongest marks of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, though their objects are not interesting. We shall here quote an anecdote from Aulus Gellius, and Valerius Maximus, of a woman who was accused of having poisoned her husband and her son. She was taken and brought before Dolabella, who was then pro-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>. She was no sooner in his presence than she owned the fact: and added, that she had very good reasons for putting her husband and her son to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>.—"I had (said she) to my first husband a son whom I tenderly loved, and whose virtues rendered him worthy of my affection. My <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> husband, and the son whom I bare to him, murdered my favourite child. I thought it would have been unjust to have suffered Areopagus those two monsters of barbarity to live. If you think, Arequi Sir, that I have committed a crime, it is your <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> to punish it; I certainly never shall repent of it." This affair embarrassed Dolabella. She was afterwards sent to the Areopagus; and that court, when they had examined her a long time, ordered her and her accuser to appear before them again a hundred years after, from the first <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> of her trial. We must not, however, suppose that the Areopagus always preserved its old reputation; for such is the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> affairs, that perfection, with regard to them, is a violent, and consequently a transitory state. <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERICLES">Pericles</a>, who lived about 100 years after Solon, to flatter the people and win them to his party, used his utmost efforts to weaken the authority of the Areopagus, which was then disliked by the multitude. He took from it the cognizance of many affairs which had before come under its jurisdiction; and to forward his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of humbling it, employed the eloquence of Ephialtes, whose talents were formidable, and who was an avowed enemy to the great men of Athens. The Areopagus itself seemed to second the endeavours of a man who projected its ruin, and by its misconduct hastened its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a>. The old rules of the court, by which none were admitted its members but those whose unexceptionable conduct would support its majesty, seemed too severe. They grew less delicate in their choice; and presuming that the faults with which they dispensed, would soon be reformed in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> of so many good examples, vice imperceptibly crept among them: corruption, at first secret and timid, grew insensibly open and daring, and made such progress, that the most shameful crimes were soon exhibited on the stage; and they were not copied from the low and abandoned multitude, but from those senators, once the venerable and austere censors of idleness and of vice. Demetrius, the comic poet, wrote a piece which he entitled The Areopagites, where he strips the mask off those hypocritical legislators, who were now equally apt to be seduced by wealth and by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>. So much had the Athenian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> degenerated in the days of Isocrates, cir. 340 years before the Christian era. Before this tribunal St Paul was called to give an account of his doctrine, and converted Dionysius one of their number. The end of this court of judicature is as obscure as its origin, which was derived from very remote antiquity. It existed, with the other magistracies, in the time of Pausanias, i.e. in the 2d century. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> of its subsequent <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DURATION">duration</a> is not ascertained; but a writer, who lived under the emperors Theodosius the Elder and Younger, in the 5th century, mentions it as extinct.

AREQUIBA

Pages 688-689

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERU">Peru</a> in South <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, situated in W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 73°, S. Lat. 17°. It is one of the most beautiful cities in all Peru, being delightfully situated in the valley of Quilca, 100 leagues from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIMA">Lima</a>, and 20 from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, with which it communicates by a fine river. The entrance into the harbour is rather shallow for ships of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> burden; but when once they are entered, they may ride securely in 18 fathoms <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. This city was founded in 1539, by order of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DON">Don</a> Francisco Pizarro, in a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> known likewise by the name of Arequia; but its situation being found disadvantageous, disadvantageous, the inhabitants obtained leave to remove to the place where the city now stands. The houses are built with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, and vaulted; and, contrary to what is usual in warm countries, they are lofty, neatly furnished within, and finely decorated on the outside. The inhabitants are also exempt from many diseases <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> in other parts of Peru; which perhaps is owing to their keeping the streets clean by means of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a> which extend to the river. The temperature of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> is extremely good; and though sometimes a slight <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FROST">frost</a> is perceivable, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a> is never excessive, nor the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> troublesome, so that the surrounding fields are clothed with perpetual verdure. These <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> advantages, however, are considerably allayed by its being very subject to earthquakes, by which it has already been five times laid in ruins; notwithstanding which, it is populous, and has among its inhabitants some of the noblest families in America.

ARES

Pages 689-689

a word of Paracelsus's, by which he would express that power of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> in the whole material world, by which <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> are divided into individuals. ARETÆUS of Cappadocia, a Greek physician of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of the Pneumatists, lived in the reign of Augustus, according to some; according to others, under Trajan <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Adrian. He wrote several treatises in the Ionian dialect, on acute diseases, and other medicinal subjects; some of which are still extant. The best edition of his works is that of Boeckhaave, in Greek and Latin, with notes, printed in 1731; that of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WIGAN">Wigan</a>, printed at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a> in 1723, in folio, is also much esteemed.

ARETHUSA

Pages 689-689

a celebrated fountain near the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRACUSE">Syracuse</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, famous for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of its waters, and the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of fishes it contained. Many fables were invented by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> concerning this fountain. They had also a notion that the river ALPHEUS ran under <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> through the waters of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, without mixing with them, from <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PELOPONNESUS">Peloponnesus</a> to Sicily. Mr Brydone informs us, that it still continues to send forth an immense quantity of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, rising at once to the size of a river, but is entirely abandoned by the fishes it formerly contained in such plenty. At some distance from Arethusa is a fountain of fresh water, which boils up very strongly in the sea, insomuch that, after piercing the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> water, it may be sometimes taken up very little affected by it. This fountain Mr Brydone thinks the ancients were ignorant of, or they would not have failed to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> it as an argument for the submarine journey of the Alpheus. Mr Swinburne describes this once famous fountain as a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> pool of water near the quay, defended from the sea by a wall, and almost hidden by houses on every other side. The water is not salt, but brackish, and fit for no purpose but washing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>. "This (says he) is the celebrated fountain of Arethusa, whose soft poetical name is known to every reader. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FABLE">fable</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NYMPH">nymph</a> and her constant lover Alpheus, the excellency of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, and the charms of its situation, are themes on which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> poets have indulged their fancy, and exercised their pens. Alas, how altered! rubbish chokes up its wholesome sources; the waves have found a passage through the rocks, which repeated earthquakes have split; and not a fish is to be seen in it. Sometimes, after an earthquake, it has been left dry; and, at other times, the whole <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of its waters has been tainted by subterraneous effluvia. Its fountain head probably lies among the neighbouring hills." ARETHUSA. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. ARETIA. See Botany Index.

ARETIN

Pages 689-691

GUIDO, famous for his musical improvements, lived in the 13th century. He was a native of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AREZZO">Arezzo</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUSCANY">Tuscany</a>; and having been taught the practice of music in his youth, and probably retained as a chorister in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the Benedictine <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> founded in that city, he became a monk professed, and a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> of the order of St Benedict. In this retirement he seems to have devoted himself to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of music, particularly the system of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, and, above all, to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REFORM">reform</a> their method of notation. The difficulties that attended the instruction of youth in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> offices were so <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a>, that, as he himself says, ten years were generally consumed barely in acquiring the knowledge of the plain song; and this consideration induced him to labour after some amendment, some method that might facilitate instruction, and enable those employed in the choral office to perform the duties of it in a correct and decent manner. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> we may <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> those legendary accounts that are extant in old monkish <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a>, we should believe he was assisted in his pious intention by immediate communications from heaven: some speak of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of the syllables as the effect of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSPIRATION">inspiration</a>: and Guido himself seems to have been of the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, by his saying it was revealed to him by the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a>, as some interpret his words, in a dream: but graver historians say, that being at vespers in the chapel of his monastery, it happened that one of the offices appointed for that <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> was the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HYMN">hymn</a> * to St John. UT queant laxis R.Esonare fibris Mira gestorum F.Amuli tuorum SOLve pollutis L.Abiis reatum, Sanete Joannes. During the performance of the hymn, he remarked the iteration of the words, and the frequent returns of UT, RE, MI, FA, SOL, LA: he observed likewise a dissimilarity between the closeness of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYLLABLE">syllable</a> MI and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> open <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> of LA, which he thought could not fail to impress upon the mind a lasting idea of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONGRUITY">congruity</a>; and immediately conceived a thought of applying these six syllables to perfect an improvement either then actually made by him, or under consideration, viz. that of converting the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> tetrachords into hexachords. Struck with the discovery, he retired to his study, and having perfected his system, began to introduce it into practice; the persons to whom he communicated it were the brethren of his own monastery, from whom it met with but a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a> reception, which in the epistle to his friend, he ascribes undoubtedly to its true cause, envy: however, his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> with the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABBOT">abbot</a>, and his employment in the chapel, gave him an opportunity of trying the efficacy of his method on the boys who were training up for the choral service, and it exceeded the most sanguine <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPECTATION">expectation</a>. "To the admiration of all (says <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Baronius) a boy there- by learnt, in a few months, what no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, though of great ingenuity, could before that attain in several years." The fame of Guido's invention soon spread abroad, and his method of instruction was adopted by the clergy of other countries. We are told by Kircher, that Hermannus, bishop of Hamburgh, and Elviricus bishop of Osnaburg, made <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of it; and by the authors of the Histoire Litteraire a la France, that it was received in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and taught in all the monasteries in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. It is certain that the reputation of his great skill in music had excited in the pope a desire to see and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONVERSE">converse</a> with him; of which, and of his going to Rome for that purpose, and the reception he met with from the pontiff, he himself has given a circumstantial account in the epistle hereafter mentioned. The particulars of this relation are very curious; and as we have his own authority, there is no room to doubt the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of it. It seems that John XX. or as some writers compute, the 19th pope of that name, having heard of the fame of Guido's school, and conceiving a desire to see him, sent three messengers to invite him to Rome. Upon their arrival, it was resolved by the brethren of the monastery, that he should go thither attended by Grimaldo the abbot, and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of the canons of the church of Arezzo. Arriving at Rome, he was presented to the holy father, and by him received with great kindness. The pope had several conversations with him, in all which he interrogated him as to his knowledge in music; and upon sight of an antiphonary which Guido had brought with him, marked with the syllables agreeable to his new invention, the pope looked upon it as a kind of prodigy; and ruminating on the doctrines delivered by Guido, would not stir from his seat till he had learned perfectly to sing off a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>: upon which he declared that he could not have believed the efficacy of the method, if he had not been convinced by the experiment he had himself made of it. The pope would have detained him at Rome; but labouring under a bodily disorder, and fearing an injury to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> from the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and the heats of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, which was then approaching, Guido left that city upon a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> to revisit it, and explain to his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLINESS">holiness</a> the principles of his new system. On his return home-wards, he made a visit to the abbot of Pomposa, a town in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FERRARA">Ferrara</a>, who was very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARNEST">earnest</a> to have Guido <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> in the monastery of that place; to which invitation it seems he yielded, being, as he says, desirous of rendering so great a monastery still more famous by his studies there. Here it was that he composed a tract on music, entitled Micrologus, i.e. "a short discourse;" which he dedicated to Theobald bishop of Arezzo; and finished, as he himself at the end of it tells us, under the pontificate of John XX., and in the 34th year of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. Vossius speaks also of another musical treatise written by him, and dedicated to the same person. Most of the authors who have taken occasion to mention Guido, speak of the Micrologus as containing the sum of his doctrine; but it is in a small tract, entitled Argumentum <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOVI">novi</a> Cantus inveniendi, that his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a> of his use of the syllables, with their several mutations, and in short his whole doctrine of solmisation, is to be found. This tract makes up <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of an epistle to a very dear and intimate friend of Guido, whom he addresses thus, "Beatissimo atque dulcisissimo fratri Michaeli;" at whose request the tract itself seems to have been composed. Whether Guido was the author of any other tracts, is not easy to determine. It nowhere appears that any of his works were ever printed, except that Baronius, in his Annales Ecclesiastici, tom. xi. p. 73, has given at length the epistle from him to his friend Michael of Pomposa, and that to Theobald bishop of Arezzo, prefixed to the Micrologus: and yet the writers on music speak of the Micrologus as of a book in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of every one. Martini cites several manuscripts of Guido; namely, two in the Ambrosian library at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a>, the one written about the twelfth century, the other less ancient; another among the archives of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> of Pistoja, a city in Tuscany; and a third in the Medico-Laurenziano library at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a>, of the 15th century; these are clearly the Micrologus. Of the epistle to Michael of Pomposa, together with the Argumentum novi Cantus inveniendi, he mentions only one, which he says is somewhere at <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RATISBON">Ratisbon</a>. Of the several tracts above mentioned, the last excepted, a manuscript is extant in the library of Baliol <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>. Several fragments of the two first, in one volume, are also among the Harleian manuscripts now in the British <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSEUM">Museum</a>, No. 3199; but so very much mutilated, that they afford but small satisfaction to a curious inquirer. Aretin, Leonard, one of the most learned men of the 15th century, was secretary to the republic of Florence, and translated from the Greek into Latin some of the Lives of Plutarch, and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>'s Ethics: he also composed three books of the Punic <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, that may serve as a supplement to those wanting in Livy; the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the transactions in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> during his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; that of ancient <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>; that of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOTHS">Goths</a>; that of the republic of Florence; and many other books. He died in 1443, aged 74. Aretin, Francis, a man of great <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a>, and well acquainted with the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. He translated into Latin the Commentaries of St Chrysostom upon St John, and about 20 homilies of the same father; he also translated the Letters of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHALARIS">Phalaris</a> into Latin, and wrote a treatise De bulneis Putelarum. He studied at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIENNA">Sienna</a>, about the year 1443; and afterwards taught <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> there with such reputation, that they called him the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> of Subtleties, and his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a> became a proverb. He displayed his talents chiefly in disputes, in which nobody could withstand him. He gave his opinions in law with so much confidence, so to assure those who consulted him that they should carry their cause: nor did <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> contradict him; for it was a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> saying at the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a>, such a cause has been condemned by Aretin, it must therefore be lost. He taught also in the university of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PISA">Pisa</a>, and in that of Ferrara. He was at Rome under the pontificate of Sixtus IV. but did not stay here <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>; for he soon perceived that the great hopes which he had built upon his reputation would come to nothing. This pope, however, declared he would have given him a cardinal's hat, had he not thought he should have done a public injury by depriving the youth of such an excellent professor. When old age would not permit him to go through the duties of his office, they dispensed with his reading of of lectures, and his salary was <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a>. He continued, however, sometimes to mount the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a>; and although his lectures had now but little spirit in them, yet he had still many hearers on account of his reputation. One day when the students were gone to some public shows, there were but 40 persons in his auditory; which so mortified him, that he threw away his book: and crying out, "Aretin shall never explain law to a few persons," retired in a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>, and would teach no more. He was severe in his temper, and never kept a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> longer than a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> or two; for it was a maxim of his, "that new-hired servants always served best." He was honoured with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a>, and spent all his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> in celibacy; and his way of living was so parsimonious, that he was thereby enabled to amass a great <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of wealth. He had designed this wealth for the maintenance of a college; but he altered his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a>, and left it to his relations. Aretin, Peter, a native of Arezzo, who lived in the 16th century. He was famous for his satirical writings; and was so bold as to carry his invectives even against sovereigns, and from thence got the title of the Scourge of Princes. Francis I., the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> V., most of the princes of Italy, several cardinals, and many noblemen, courted his friendship by presents, either because they liked his compositions, or perhaps from an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPREHENSION">apprehension</a> of falling under the lash of his satire. Aretin became therupon so insolent, that he is said to have got a medal struck, on one side of which he is represented with these words, IL DIVINO ARETINO; and on the reverse, sitting upon a throne, receiving the presents of princes, with these words, I PRINCIPI TRIBUTATI DA POPOLI, TRIBUTANO IL SERVIDO LORO. Some imagine that he gave himself the title of Divine, signifying thereby that he performed the functions of a god upon <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, by the thunderbolts with which he struck the heads of the highest personages. He used to boast, that his lampoons did more service to the world than sermons; and it was said of him, that he had subjected more princes by his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEN">pen</a> than the greatest had ever done by their arms. Aretin wrote many irreligious and obscene pieces; such are his dialogues, which were called Ragionamenti. There is likewise imputed to him another very obscene performance, De omnibus Venerei schematibus. It was about the year 1525 (says Mr Chevillier*) that Julio Romano, the most famous painter of Italy, instigated by the enemy of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALVATION">salvation</a> of mankind, invented drawings to engrave 20 plates; the subjects are so immodest that I dare only name them. Peter Aretin composed sonnets for each <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>. George Vasari, who relates this in his Lives of the Painters, says, he does not know which would be the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMPURITY">impurity</a>, to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> one's eyes upon the drawings of Julio, or to dip into the verses of Aretin." Some say that Aretin changed his libertine principles; but however this may be, it is certain that he composed several pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>. He wrote a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARAPHRASE">paraphrase</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENITENTIAL">penitential</a> psalms, and another on <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GENESIS">Genesis</a>; he wrote also the Life of the Virgin <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>, and that of St Catharine of Sienna, and of St Thomas Aquinas. He was author likewise of some comedies. He died in the year 1556, at the age of 65.

ARETOLOGI

Pages 691-691

in antiquity, a sort of philosophers, chiefly of the Cynic <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Stoic tribe, who having no school or disciples of their own, haunted the tables of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> men, and entertained them in their banquets with disputations on virtue, vice, and other popular topics. These are sometimes also denominated Circulatores Philosophi. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, the word is derived from the Greek ἀγήρων, virtue, and λόγος, discourse. Some authors choose to derive the word from ἀγήρων, gratus, "agreeable;" and define Aretologi, by persons who strive to divert and entertain their audience with jokes and pleasant tales; which latter seems the more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> explication.

AREZZO

Pages 691-691

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUSCANY">Tuscany</a>, seated in the territory of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a>, on the declivity of a hill that overlooks the neighbouring plain, between the Citta di Castelli and Florence. It is an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> city and a bishop's see; and was famous for a kind of earthen <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARE">ware</a> much esteemed by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>. It was greatly fallen to decay when Cosmo de Medicis took it under his protection; since which it has been recovering gradually. It is famed for being the birthplace of Meceenas. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 12. 2. N. Lat. 43° 27'.

ARGEA

Pages 691-691
or ARGEL, in Roman antiquity, thirty human figures made of rushes, thrown annually by the priests or vestals into the Tiber, on the day of the ides of May.—Plutarch, in his Roman Questions, inquires why they are called Argae. There are two reasons assigned. The first, that the barbarous nations who first inhabited those parts cast all the Greeks they could meet with into the Tiber: for Argians was a common name for all Grecians; but that Hercules persuaded them to quit so inhuman a practice, and to purge themselves of the crime by instituting this solemnity. The second, that Evander, an Arcadian, and a sworn enemy of the Argians, to perpetuate that enmity to his posterity, ordered the figures of Argians to be thus cast into the river.

ARGEIA

Pages 691-692
or ARGOLIS, a district of Peloponnesus, situated between Arcadia to the west, the Egean sea to the east, Laconia and the Sinus Argolicus to the south, and to the north the territory of Corinth and the Sinus Saronicus (Livy, Ptolemy); so called from Argos, the capital: Now Romania di Morea. By the Greeks the people were called Argii, from Argi or Argos; by the Romans, Argivi, Argives. They were a colony who migrated, it is said, from Egypt, under the command of Inachus. Polemon and Ptolemy Mendesius, ancient Greek writers, inform us, that Inachus was contemporary with Amosis, who demolished Avaris, and expelled the shepherds out of Egypt. If, with some learned chronologers, we suppose Inachus to have begun to reform the Argives B.C. 1856, and to have died B.C. 1808, he must have been coeval with Amosis, who reigned in Upper Egypt 15 years before the expulsion of the shepherds, and 10 years after that event, which happened B.C. 1826. Inachus was styled the Son of the Ocean, because his origin was not known, or because he had come by sea into Greece. Before his arrival the inhabitants were rude and barbarous. These he united and civilized, and instructed in various arts. His son Phoroneus instituted the laws of government, and, on that account, has been called the first king in Argos, the first of men, and the father of mortals. The family of Inachus, after having kept possession of the ARGENTARIUS is frequently used in Roman writers for a money-changer or banker. The argentarii were moneyed people, who made a profit either by the changing, or lending of money at interest. These had their tabernae, or offices, in the forum Romanum, built there as early as the reign of L. Tarquinius Priscus. The argentarii and sceptratores were much hated on account of their covetousness and extortion.

ARGENTATI MILITES

Pages 692-692

in antiquity. Livy, lib. vi. speaks of argentati milites, as distinguished from aurati. Aquinas supposes these to have been similar to the argyrae and chrysaspides; but the descriptions do not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUADRATURE">quadrature</a>. Livy only represents the argentati as clothed in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> coats.

ARGENTEUIL

Pages 692-692

a town of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">Isle</a> of France, seated on the river <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEINE">Seine</a>, five miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. It is a very beautiful <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, with fine vineyards. In the environs are quarries of stucco. In the Benedictine priory they pretend to have the seamless coat of Christ. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2. 28. N. Lat. 48. 52.

ARGENTIERE

Pages 692-692

a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the Archipelago, near Milo. It is about 18 miles in compass; and is full of barren <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, producing nothing but barley, cotton, and a few <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAPES">grapes</a> fit only for eating. The barley and cotton are sown round the only village there is in the island. The ladies are handsome enough, have no other employment but making cotton stockings, and take up with the sailors, who put into the port. The men all <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, and in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> become good pilots. They have very little <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, are very ignorant, and of very bad morals. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">Justice</a> is administered by an itinerant cadi, who is sometimes the only Musulman in the whole island. The only article relating to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> is the terra cinerea so highly esteemed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>; it is a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> chalk, which is very heavy, without <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, and crumbles easily; they use it in washing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 23. 10. N. Lat. 36. 50. ARGENTINA. See <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ARGENTINUS

Pages 692-692

a deity worshipped by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, as the god of silver <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a>; as Æsculapius, whom they made his father, was the god of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, which was in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> before silver.

ARGENTON

Pages 692-692

a town and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of France, in the department of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDRE">Indre</a>, divided into two by the river <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CREUSE">Creuse</a>. Here was formerly a castle; but it was demolished by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a> XIV. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1. 38. N. Lat. 40. 30.

ARGENTORA

Pages 692-692

Argentina, (Notitiae); Argentoratum, (<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>); Argentoratus, (Amnian); a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the Tribocci; one of the fifty forts built by Drusus on the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>, (Florus): an appellation formed by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> from the German, Argen Strassen <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Straaten, "unsafe <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a> for travellers," from the marauding parties of the garrisons that infested the roads. Now <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-STRASBOURG">Strasbourg</a>, in Lower <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALSACE">Alsace</a>, on the rivulet Ill, near the Rhine. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 7. 35. N. Lat. 48. 38.

ARGENTUM ALBUM

Pages 692-693

in our old customs, silver <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BULLION">bullion</a> that anciently passed for <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>. By Doomsday <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TENURE">tenure</a>, some rents to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> were paid in argento albo, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> silver pieces of money; other rents in libris ursis et pensatis, in metal of full <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> and purity: in the next <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, that rent which was paid in money, was called blanch fearn, and and afterwards <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> rent; and what was paid in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>, was termed <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> mail.

ARGENTUM DEI

Pages 693-693

God's <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENNY">penny</a>, anciently signified <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARNEST">earnest</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> money given to bind a bargain; in some places called erles, or <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARLES">arles</a>, and by the civilians and canonists, arrha. Et capit de praedicto Henrico tres denarios de argenti Dei prae manibus. ARGENTUM MUSIVUM is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASS">mass</a> consisting of silver-like flakes, used for the colouring of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLASTER">plaster</a> figures, and for other purposes, as pigment. It consists of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMALGAM">amalgam</a> of equal parts of tin, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISMUTH">bismuth</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a>. It is to be mixed with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> of eggs, or spirit <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VARNISH">varnish</a>, and then applied to the intended <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, which is afterwards to be burnished.

ARGESTES

Pages 693-693

is used by Vitruvius for the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> which blows from that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of the horizon, which is 75° from the south and westward. Ricciolus uses the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> to denote the wind which blows at 22° 30' from the west towards the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, coinciding with that which is otherwise called west-north-west.

ARGIL

Pages 693-693

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of ardea. See ARDEA, ORNITHOLOGY <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ARGIVI

Pages 693-693
or ARGII, the people of Argeia or Argolis. See ARGEIA.

ARGO

Pages 693-693

in antiquity, a ship <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> vessel celebrated among the poets; being that wherein the Argonauts, of whom Jason was the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>, made their expedition in quest of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLEECE">fleece</a>. Jason having happily accomplished his enterprise, consecrated the ship Argo to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEPTUNE">Neptune</a>; or, as others say, to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a>, in the isthmus of Corinth; where, they add, it did not remain <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> before it was translated into heaven, and made a constellation. The generality of authors represent the ship Argo as of a long make, resembling the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> galleys; and furnished with thirty benches of rowers. It could not, however, be of any <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> bulk, since the Argonauts were able to carry it on their backs from the Danube to the Adriatic <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>.

ARGO NAVIS

Pages 693-693

the Ship Argo, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, is a constellation in the southern hemisphere, whose stars in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>'s catalogue, are 45; in Tycho's 11; in the Britannic catalogue, and Sharp's Appendix, 64.

ARGOB

Pages 693-693

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTON">canton</a> lying beyond Jordan, in the half tribe of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANASSEH">Manasseh</a>, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of Bashan, one of the most fruitful on the other side of Jordan. In the region of Argob there were sixty cities, called Bashan-havoth-jair, which had very <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> walls and strong gates, without reckoning many villages and hamlets which were not enclosed, Dent. iii. 4, 14; and 1 Kings iv. 13. But Argob was more particularly the name of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the region of Argob, which Eusebius says was 15 miles west from Gerasa. ARGONAUTA. See <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONCHOLOGY">CONCHOLOGY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ARGONAUTIC

Pages 693-693

something belonging to the Argonauts. The Argonautic expedition is one of the greatest epochs <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> periods of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> which Sir <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Newton endeavours to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a>, and from thence to rectify the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">chronology</a>. This he shows, by several authorities, to have been one <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a> or about 30 years earlier than the taking of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">Troy</a>, and 43 years later than the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a>. See CHRONOLOGY. Dr Bryant, however, rejects the history of the Argonautic expedition as a Grecian <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FABLE">fable</a>, founded indeed on a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a> derived from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, and ultimately referring to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOAH">Noah</a>'s preservation, &c., in the ark. But although we are not to believe all the romantic stories which poets, and even some <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a> historians, have told us of these famous adventurers, yet it seems unreasonable to discredit entirely the Argonautic expedition. See ARGONAUTS.

ARGONAUTICA

Pages 693-693

in literary <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, denotes poems on the subject and expeditions of the Argonauts. We have the Argonautics of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORPHEUS">Orpheus</a> in epic <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>, published by H. Stephens; the Argonauticon of Valerius Flaccus, in eight books of Latin heroics, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of Apollonius, with respect to which Burman observes that the imitator has often surpassed the original; the Argonautics of Apollonius Rhodius, an heroic poem, consisting of four books, opus, as Quintilian calls it, non contentendum.

ARGONAUTS

Pages 693-694

in antiquity, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of illustrious Greeks, who embarked along with Jason, in the ship Argo, from <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLCHIS">Colchis</a>, with a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> to obtain the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLEECE">fleece</a>. The occasion of this expedition is thus represented by Greek writers. Phryxus, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">flying</a> with his sister Helle from the rage of their stepmother Ino, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CADMUS">Cadmus</a>, went on board a ship, whose ensign was a golden ram, and sailed to Colchis (now <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINGRELIA">Mingrelia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEORGIA">Georgia</a>). Helle was drowned by the way, in that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> which from her was called the Hellespont, now the Dardanelles. This, according to some, was the ground of the poetical <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FABLE">fable</a>, that a ram with a golden fleece swam away with them to Colchis; and that the Argonauts undertook their famed expedition, in order to find that fleece. But Strabo and Arrian inform us, that it was a practice of the Colchians to collect <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> on Mount <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAUCASUS">Caucasus</a> by extending fleeces across the beds of the torrents; and as the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> passed, the metallic particles remained entangled in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>; hence, according to those historians, the adventure was named the expedition of the golden fleece. Sir <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Newton thinks that this expedition was really an embassy sent by the Greeks, during the intestine divisions of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> in the reign of Amenophis, to persuade the nations upon the coasts of the Euxine and the Mediterranean seas, to take that opportunity of shaking off the yoke of Egypt, which Sesostris had laid upon them; and that fetching the golden fleece, was only a pretence to cover their true design. But the most judicious and satisfactory account of the Argonautic expedition seems to be that given by Dr Gillies in his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>. "The northern districts of Thessaly being peculiarly exposed to the dangerous fury of invaders, the petty princes of that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> entered into a confederacy for their mutual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>. They assembled in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> and autumn at Thermopylae, a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> afterwards so illustrious, and then governed by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMPHICTYON">Amphictyon</a>, a descendant of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEUCALION">Deucalion</a>, whose name is immortalized in the Amphictyonic <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>. The advantages which the confederates derived from this <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, were soon perceived by their neighbours. The central states gradually acceded..." Argonauts, ed to their <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a>; and about the middle of the 14th century before Christ, Acrisius <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARGOS">Argos</a>, and other princes of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PELOPONNESUS">Peloponnesus</a>, were allowed to share the benefits and security of this useful <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASSOCIATION">association</a>. See Amphictyons. "After this event, the Amphictyons appear to have <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> confined themselves to the original purpose of their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a>. The states, whose <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> were directed by this <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a>, found sufficient occupation in defending their own territories; and near a century elapsed, before they undertook, by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> consent, any distant expedition. But it was not to be expected that their restless <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a> could always be exhausted in defensive <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. The establishment of the Amphictyons brought together the chiefs most distinguished by birth and bravery. <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">Glory</a> and emulation prompted them to arms, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> directed those arms against the barbarians. Jason, Admetus, and other chieftains of Thessaly, having equipped a small fleet in the neighbouring harbour of Iolcos, and particularly the ship Argo of superior size and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> to any before known, were animated with a desire to visit foreign lands, to plant colonies in those parts of them that appeared most delightful, and to retort on their inhabitants the injuries which Greece had suffered from strangers. The princes of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> having proclaimed this spirited design over the central and southern provinces, the standard of enterprise and glory was speedily surrounded by the flower of the Grecian youth, who eagerly embraced this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> opportunity to signalize their manly valour. <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PELEUS">Peleus</a>, Tydeus, Telamon, and in general the fathers of those heroic chiefs who in the succeeding <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> shone with distinguished lustre in the plains of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">Troy</a>, are numbered among the leaders of the Argonauts. They were accompanied by the chosen warriors, and by the venerable prophets, of their respective tribes; by an Esculapius, the admired father of the healing art; and by the divine <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORPHEUS">Orpheus</a>, whose sublime genius was worthy to celebrate the amazing <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of their adventures. "These adventures, however, have been too much adorned by the graces of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, to be the proper subject of historical <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>. The designs of the Argonauts are veiled under the allegorical, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> at least doubtful, phrase, of carrying off the golden fleece; which, though easily explained, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we admit the report that the inhabitants of the eastern banks of the Euxine extended fleeces of wool, in order to collect the golden particles which were carried <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> by the torrents from Mount Caucasus, is yet described in such various <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> writers, that almost every <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> who examines the subject, thinks himself entitled to offer, by way of explanation, some new conjecture of his own. But in opposition to the most approved of these conjectures, we may venture to affirm, that the voyage to Colchis was not undertaken with a view to establish extensive plans of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, or to search for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of gold, far less to learn the imaginary art of converting other substances into that precious metal; all such motives expressing a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of speculation and refinement unknown in that age to the gallant but uninstructed youth of Thessaly. The real object of the expedition may be discovered by its consequences. The Argonauts fought, conquered, and plundered; they settled a colony on the shores of the Euxine; and carried into Greece a daughter of the king of Colchis, the celebrated Medea, a princess of Egyptian <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTRACTION">extraction</a>, whose crimes and enchantments are condemned to eternal infamy in the immortal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EURIPIDES">Euripides</a>." Argonauts of St Nicholas, was the name of a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> order instituted by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> III, king of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, in the year 1382, for the advancement of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>, or, as some say, merely for preserving amity among the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBLES">nobles</a>. They wore a collar of shells, enclosed in a silver <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRESCENT">crescent</a>, whence hung a ship, with this device, Non credo temporis, "I do not trust <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>." Hence these Argonaut knights came to be called knights of the shell. They received the order of St <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASIL">Basil</a>, archbishop of Naples; and held their assemblies in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of St Nicholas, their <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRON">patron</a>.

ARGOPHYLLUM

Pages 694-694
White-leaf (Forst. Nov. Gen.) a genus of the monogynia order, belonging to the pentandria class of plants. The capsule is trilocular; the nectarium is pyramidal, pentagonal, and the length of the corolla. There is but one species, the nitidum or glossy, a native of New Caledonia. This genus has great affinity with the ivy; but differs in the nectarium, and perhaps in the fruit.

ARGOS

Pages 694-696

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> name of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PELOPONNESUS">Peloponnesus</a>; from Argos, one of the kings, (<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>, Strabo). Argos, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, and an inland town, of Argolis <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Argelia. It had different surnames; as Achaeum, from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, or an ancient people, (Homer); Hippium, from its breed of horses; and Inachium, from the river Inachus, which runs by, or from Inachus the founder of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, whose name was also given to the river. The Argives related, that this was one of the river gods who adjudged the country to Juno, when she contended for it with <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEPTUNE">Neptune</a>, which deity in return made their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> to vanish; the reason why the Inachus flowed only after <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>, and was dry in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>. The source was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, not copious, on a mountain in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCADIA">Arcadia</a>, and the river served there as a boundary between the Argives and Mantineans. Ancient Argos stood chiefly on a flat. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> were near the surface; and it abounded in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WELLS">wells</a>, which were said to have been invented by the daughters of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DANAUS">Danaus</a>. This early peopleage lived in the acropolis or citadel, which was named <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LARISSA">Larissa</a>, and accounted moderately strong. On the ascent was a temple of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a> on the ridge, which in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> century <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> the seat of an oracle. The woman who prophesied was debarred from <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> with the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MALE">male</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEX">sex</a>. A lamb was sacrificed in the night monthly; when, on tasting of the blood, she became possessed with the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>. Farther on was a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STADIUM">stadium</a>, where the Argives celebrated games in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of Nemean <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>, and Juno. On the top was a temple of Jupiter, without a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROOF">roof</a>, the statue off the pedestal. In the temple of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a> there, among other curious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>, was a wooden Jupiter, with an eye more than <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a>, having one in the forehead. This statue, it was said, was once placed in a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of Priam, who fled as a suppliant to the altar before it, when <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">Troy</a> was sacked. In this <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> was also the brazen tower in which Danaë, being confined there by her father, was deflowered by Jupiter. Argos retains its original name and situation, stand- ing near the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> which are the boundary of the plain, with Napoli and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> in view before it. The shining houses are whitened with lime or <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLASTER">plaster</a>. Churches, mud-built cottages and walls, with gardens and open areas, are interspersed, and the town is of considerable <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>. Above the other buildings towers a very handsome mosque shaded with solemn cypresses; and behind is a lofty hill, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> and naked, of a conical form, the summit crowned with a neglected castle. The devastations of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> have effaced the old city. We look in vain (says Mr Chandler) for vestiges of its numerous edifices, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>, the gymnasium, the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>, and monuments, which it once boasted, contending even with <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a> in antiquity and in favours conferred by the gods. **Argos Amphilocheum**, (<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUCYDIDES">Thucydides</a>), a city of Arcarnania, (<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SCYLAX">Scylax</a>, Pliny); its territory Amphilochia: situated on the east side of the Sinus Ambracius, (Thucydides); distant an hundred and eighty stadia to the south-east of Ambracia, (Polybius). Also called Argia Amphilocheis, (Mela); Amphiloci and Amphilocheici the people. (Stephanus). The name is from Amphilocheus, son of Amphiaraus; and from Argos, the name of his country, in Peloponnesus, (Thucydides). **Argos Hippium.** See Argos in Peloponnesus, supra. **Argos Hippium,** the ancient name of Arpi; but Lampe is a still more ancient; afterwards called Argyrippa, and Argippa; built by, and the residence of, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIOMEDES">Diomedes</a>, on the Cerbalus, (<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>); afterwards a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and populous city, (Livy): A town of Apulia; now in ruins, and the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> called Arpi. **Argos Pelasgicum,** (Homer); an appellation denoting Thessaly; so called from the Pelasgi. **Argos Portus,** a port of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUSCANY">Tuscany</a>, (Strabo): now Porto Ferrajo, in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-ELBA">Elba</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 11. 30. N. Lat. 42. 35. **Arguim,** an island on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, about sixteen miles distant from <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLANCO">Blanco</a>, situated in W. Long. 16. 30. N. Lat. 20. 20. It is scarce two miles in length; notwithstanding which, it was a bone of contention for 87 years between the Portuguese, Dutch, English, and French; and, after a variety of fortune, has at last been totally abandoned. This island was first discovered by the Portuguese in 1444, when a fleet bound to the east touched at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARGUIN">Arguin</a>, and from some little trade carried on with the natives, it was imagined that a settlement there might be of some advantage to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>. In <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, a fort was erected on the island, and the Portuguese enjoyed the peaceable possession of it till 1638. At this time, the Dutch having received a minute account of the condition of the island, resolved to attack it: and accordingly landed without molestation from the garrison, which was too weak to oppose them. The Portuguese, however, defended themselves with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> intrepidity, and at last surrendered upon <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> terms.
