The Dutch immediately set about repairing the fortifications, and securing it in the best manner they could: however, in 1665, the fort was reduced almost to a heap of rubbish by an English squadron; but as the fortifications were totally destroyed, and only a small garrison left there, it was easily retaken by the Dutch the next year. They now redoubled their diligence in strengthening the island, entering into <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> with Moorish chiefs, procuring a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of families to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> under protection of the fort, and giving extravagant prices for <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUMS">gums</a>, in order to monopolize the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUM">gum</a> trade. By this means the gum trade of the French <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENEGAL">Senegal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">Company</a> was almost entirely destroyed; upon which they fitted out a squadron, dispossessed the Dutch, and had the island finally ceded to them by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of Nimeguen. Though the Dutch now seemed to be finally expelled, they resolved not to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> so easily with such a valuable settlement. Under pretence of being subjects of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRANDENBURG">Brandenburg</a>, therefore, they erected one of the forts which had been demolished, and there maintained themselves in spite of the utmost endeavours of the French Company to dispossess them. Numberless were the memorials, protests, rescripts, &c. which were published on this occasion, till a new war in 1701 put an end to them. In 1717, however, the French Company having found all their remonstrances ineffectual, fitted out a new squadron; but this armament did not arrive at Arguin before Feb. 26. 1721. The Dutch defended themselves with such intrepidity and conduct as had almost baffled the utmost efforts of the French; but the latter having found means to draw off a Moorish <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> from his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLEGIANCE">allegiance</a>, the Dutch were obliged to evacuate Arguin, and retire to Portendic, where they fortified themselves, determining to watch a favourable opportunity for recovering their settlement at Arguin. This was not long wanting, by means of the weakness of the garrison and the imprudence of Duval the French <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTOR">director</a>, who having quarrelled with the Moors, was surprised, defeated, and killed by them; in consequence of which, the settlement fell again into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the Dutch on the 11th of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1722. In 1723, the Dutch were attacked by another French squadron under the command of the Sieur Rigadiere. This <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> boasted that the fort could not hold out one <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>; but though he prevailed so far as to get possession of the cisterns which contained the water of the besieged, he was at last shamefully repulsed, and forced to raise the siege with precipitation. The Dutch, however, did not long enjoy the possession which they had so bravely defended; for, in 1725, their fort was entirely demolished by the French under Du Casse, and has never since been rebuilt by any European <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>. **Argument,** in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">Rhetoric</a> and Logic, an inference drawn from premises, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of which is indisputable, or at least highly probable. See Logic. **Argument,** in matters of literature, denotes also the abridgement or heads of a book, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMEDY">comedy</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a>, &c. See Syllabus. **Argumentation,** the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of inventing, or framing arguments, of making inductions, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> conclusions. See Induction, &c. Argumentation, according to Cicero, is the delivering or unfolding of an argument.—The <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of argumentations is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPOSITIONS">propositions</a>; the form, their due disposition, with regard to one another, so as a conclusion may be drawn from them. See Enthymeme, Proposition, Ratiocination, Sorites, Syllogism, &c. **Argus,** in fabulous history, was the son of Aristor, and had 100 eyes, 50 of which were always open. Juno made choice of him to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> Io, whom Jupiter had. ARGUS had transformed into a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> heifer; but Jupiter, pitying Io for being so closely confined, sent <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a>, who, with his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLUTE">flute</a>, charmed Argus to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a>, sealed up his eyes with his caduceus, and then cut off his head; when Juno, to reward his fidelity, turned him into a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PEACOCK">peacock</a>, and placed his eyes in his tail. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARGUS_SHELL">ARGUS-shell</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORCELAIN">porcelain</a> shell, beautifully variegated with spots, resembling in some <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> those in a peacock's tail.

ARGUTIAE

Pages 696-696

witty and acute sayings, which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> signify something further than what their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> words at first sight seem to import. Writers on <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a> speak of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of argutiae, viz. ARGUTIAE <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AB">ab</a> alieno, when something is said, which seems repugnant either to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of a thing, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>, the laws, &c. which yet in reality is consistent therewith; or when something is given as a reason of another, which yet is not the reason of it. For instance, Si <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAIUS">Caius</a> nihil didicisset, errasset minus; again, Aurum hoc seculum est, quia pluriinus jam curo honos venit. Argutiae ab allusione, those wherein allusion is made to some <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FABLE">fable</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a>, proverb or the like; e.g. Multi umbrae captant et carmen amittunt. Argutiae à comparatis, when two things are compared together, which yet at first sight appear very different from each other, but so as to make a pretty kind of simile or dissimile; e.g. Par est pauper nil cupiens principi omnia habenti. Argutiae à repugnantibus, when two things meet in a subject, which yet regularly cannot be therein; or when two things are opposed to each other, yet the epithet of the one is attributed to the other, e.g. Dum tacent clamant.

ARGYLLSHIRE

Pages 696-698

one of the counties of Scotland, supposed to have formed the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the Caledonian <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, when the eastern provinces of Scotland submitted to the irresistible power of the Roman empire. It is bounded on the east by the shires of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERTH">Perth</a> and Dunbarton; on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVERNESS">Inverness</a>; on the west and south by the Irish <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> and the frith of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLYDE">Clyde</a>, which enter into various bays, sounds, and inlets, round the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, and form both in the main <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, many spacious and commodious harbours. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> is subdivided into the districts of Kintyre, Knapdale, Argyll Proper, Cowal, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LORN">Lorn</a>. Within the same <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> are also comprehended several Hebridian islands, of which two <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> three are of considerable <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>. Its length from south to north, between the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MULL">mull</a> of Kintyre and the point of Ardnamurchan, where it joins the shire of Inverness, is about 114 miles, and its breadth, in several places, including the isles, is 70. The total superficies is calculated at 3800 <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles, of which 1063 are insular, and 2735 on the main land. Similar to the other parts of the Highlands of Scotland, this county presents a very wild and horrid prospect of hills, rocks, and huge <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, piled upon each other in a stupendous and dreadful disorder, bare, bleak, and barren to the view; or, at best covered with shaggy heath, which appears <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> and dismal to the eye, except in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, when it is variegated with an agreeable bloom of a purple <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. Hence lofty mountains, deep glens, inlets of the sea entering far into the land, form the most striking features in the general aspect of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. Cruacha-Ben in this county is one of the loftiest mountains in Scotland; and where this county meets the confines of Perth and Dunbarton, the mountains contiguous to Ben-Lomond are but little inferior in height to that mountain. The Loch Fine, Loch Etive, Linnhe Loch, are inlets of the sea. The district of Kintyre enters into the north channel, and is almost divided from the main land at the narrow isthmus of Tarbat. The district of Cowal is also nearly peninsulated by Loch <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a> on one side and Loch Fine on the other. The interior parts of the county are interspersed with a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of small fresh-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>. A barrenness of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> and scanty vegetation prevail chiefly on the summits of the great mountains, which exhibit great masses of stratified rocks or groups in a columnar form. Even a number of the glens are barren, and afford little pastureage, and are covered in several places with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> fragments, which have been separated and precipitated from the impending rocks. On the declivities of the hills and the banks of the lakes there are, however, numerous woods interspersed, which unite with the lofty mountains to form a most romantic <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a>. In a run of several miles, fertility, verdure, and cultivation, reign through the valley of Glenorchay. Remains of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> forests are still very extensive in various places; and these consist chiefly of oakes, ashes, pines, and birches. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> of the country, towards the southern parts, descends the nearest to an equality with that of the sea. The elevation of the country is highest towards the interior parts of the counties of Perth and Inverness. The mountains and forests abound with fallow-deer, roes, stags, and all kinds of wild <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAME">game</a>; and all over the sea coast, the moors, the heaths, and on the lakes, the wild fowl are numerous. The mountains feed an innumerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of black cattle, which run wild among the hills in winter as well as summer. The circumambient sea, with its lochs, bays, and harbours, pours forth myriads of fish; and in several places of the county <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, and other <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-METALS">metals</a> and minerals, have been dug out. Yet, notwithstanding these numerous local advantages, Argyllshire, as well as many other parts of the Highlands, struggles with many great obstacles in the way of improvement. The want of long <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEASES">leases</a> is one of the most material. What inducement can a person have to manure or cultivate a piece of land which he may have taken, when his first <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> is to erect a hut for himself; and after all the disagreeable inconveniences attending it, he holds his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARM">farm</a> year by year, dependant on the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> of his landlord? When he also reflects, that by cultivating his ground in such a manner, the rent which he was this year scarcely able to pay, may be nearly doubled the next year, how can he be able to defray the expense necessarily attending such an improvement, when he is uncertain of a competent return for his labour? It is hoped that proprietors will at length see the manifest advantage that will arise from granting long leases, both to themselves and their tenants; and, by so doing, either to encourage the tenants to build houses, by paying any expense that may remain unpaid at the end of the lease, or build houses for the tenants themselves; and, by these means, they would have surer payment of their rents, which would be augmented; their grounds would be greatly improved, and their vassals would enjoy comfort and ease. Another great obstacle to the general improvement is the rugged <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> of this county, which renders the great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a> few in number, and the intersected roads for the purpose of conveying manure to the grounds being still in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> rudeness. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> branch of husbandry followed over the greatest part of this county is the management of sheep, black cattle, and goats. In former times, the ordinary animal stock consisted mostly of black cattle: but within these last 20 years a more skilful method of managing flocks of sheep than was formerly practised, having been introduced by the farmers of the low country; these have been multiplied with great <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> and assiduity. Cows and oxen now form only the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> considerable branch of the animal stock. Barley, oats, and potatoes, are the principal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of crop; and, in some places, the proper manner of tillage has been made <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of, excellent manures have been laid upon the ground, and the most suitable <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROTATION">rotation</a> of crops has been adopted. In years of ordinary plenty it would appear, that besides affording a considerable surplus to the breweries and distilleries, the grain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> produced in this county is a sufficient sustenance for its inhabitants. Besides the great profits arising from the iron works and the salmon <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FISHERIES">fisheries</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> of woods has brought much <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> into Argyll, and still continues to be equally beneficial to the labourer and the landlord. When the projected canal shall be completed, and some villages and harbours erected, the populous county of Argyll (Mr Knox affirms) will become one of the most valuable provinces of the British empire. Washed on both sides by the sea; deeply indented by navigable lakes and bays; having an easy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> with the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a> grounds on the north Highlands, with Glasgow and the trading <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> on the Clyde, with <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITEHAVEN">Whitehaven</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-LIVERPOOL">Liverpool</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRISTOL">Bristol</a>, and other marts on the west coast of England; we may easily conceive, that the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> is at no great distance when Argyllshire will become a great commercial county. To corroborate this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, he observes, that after a vessel gets under sail from this coast, she enters at once into the Atlantic, where she meets with no interruption till she makes the coast of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a> or the West Indies. The line, therefore, which <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> out for the inhabitants is that of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>-making, fishing, ship-<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, freight or the carrying trade, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOAP">soap</a> and glass-making, by means of the kelp upon their shores, and sand found upon the islands of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JURA">Jura</a> and Gigha, which is adapted for the latter. In this district the deeds of the celebrated Fingal, whose invincible arm gave a check to the progress of the conquerors of the world, were mostly achieved. Many of the scenes of the battles of that illustrious <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a> and his gallant followers, which are so beautifully described by <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OSSIAN">Ossian</a>, are still pointed out, and many very ancient monuments still display the warlike spirit of its former inhabitants. In the course of the eighth and ninth centuries, Argyll, along with the neighbouring isles, was conquered by the Danes and Norwegians. For five or six centuries it <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> under the dominion of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWAY">Norway</a>, and during that period, was under the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> administration of feudal chieftains, generally of Norwegian <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTRACTION">extraction</a>, who each maintained an almost independent <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. Along with the Hebridean isles, all the western parts of Argyll became the conquest of the Scottish monarchs in the 14th century. Some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> after, Macdonald, the representative of this region, obtained leave from the Scottish <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> to hold his possessions as a feudatory to that kingdom; but the turbulent spirit of him and his family could not remain in quietude, and therefore their rebellions were punished with forfeiture. Their estates and titles were bestowed on the Campbells; and these have ever since retained them in peace and loyalty, beloved and honoured by their country. The county of Argyll gives the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> to the chief of this family. He likewise enjoys several other important posts under the crown, and is the chief of the Scottish <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>. His vassals are so numerous, that in former times he could on occasion bring 3000 or 4000 fighting men into the field. Argyllshire is generally peopled by this clan, and affords a great number of castles and seats belonging to gentlemen who hold of the duke, and boast themselves descended from his family. Argyllshire sends one member to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>; it is also the seat of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCIAL">provincial</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYNOD">synod</a>. It contains two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> boroughs and 49 parishes; the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of which is as follows: | Parishes | Population in 1755 | Population in 1790-1798 | |----------------|-------------------|------------------------| | Ardchattan | 2195 | 2400 | | Ardnamurchan | 5000 | 4542 | | Campbelltown | 4597 | 8700 | | Craignish | 769 | 770 | | Dunoon | 1757 | 1683 | | Glassary | 2757 | 2568 | | Glenorchy | 1634 | 1869 | | <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVERARY">Inverary</a> | 2757 | 1832 | | Invercaolin | 944 | 504 | | Kilbrandon | 1492 | 2060 | | Kilcalmonell | 1925 | 2448 | | Kilchrenan | 1030 | 1124 | | Killinian | 1793 | 1417 | | Killean | 2391 | 1911 | | Kilmadan | 806 | 351 | | Kilmartin | 1150 | 1337 | | Kilmore | 1200 | 1886 | | Kilninver | 1045 | 1178 | | Knapdale, North| 1369 | 1009 | | Knapdale, South| 1202 | 1524 | | <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LISMORE">Lismore</a> | 2812 | 3326 | | Lochgoylehead | 1505 | 1012 | | Morven | 1223 | 1764 | | Saddel | 1369 | 1341 | | Southend | 1391 | 1300 | | Strachur | 1193 | 1061 | **ISLANDS** | Mull | Torosay | Kilninian | |----------------|------------------|-----------| | | 1012 | 1685 | | | 1733 | 3002 | | | | 3281 | | | | Islay | ARI Parishes. Population in 1790—93. 30 Islay { Kilarow Kilchoman } 5344 9500 Jura and Colonsay, &c. 1097 1838 Coll and Tirry 2702 3457 35 Gigha and Cara 514 614 Small isles 943 1339 Total, 63,291 76,101 Population in 1811 85,585 See ARGYLESHERE, SUPPLEMENT.

ARGYRASPIDES

Pages 698-698
or ARGYROASPIDES, in antiquity, persons armed with silver bucklers, or bucklers silvered. The argyraspides, according to Quintus Curtius, made the second corps of Alexander's army; the first was the phalanx.—According to Justin's account, lib. xii. cap. 7. Alexander having penetrated into India, and extended his empire as far as the ocean; for a monument of his glory, ordered the armour of his soldiers, and the housings of his horses, to be adorned with silver. And hence commanded them to be called argyraspides, from the Greek ἀγγύς, silver, and μορις, buckler. By this author it should seem, that Alexander's whole army were called argyraspides.—After that prince's death, the argyraspides despised all other chiefs of the army, disdaining to obey any other, having borne arms under Alexander. ARGYRIPÆ, See Argos Hippium.

ARGYRUNTUM

Pages 698-698

a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> town of Illyria (<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>, Pliny). Now Novigrad, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DALMATIA">Dalmatia</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 17° 30'. N. Lat. 44° 30'.

ARHUSEN

Pages 698-698

a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUTLAND">Jutland</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>, to the south of Wilburg, about 60 miles in length and 30 in breadth. It contains two <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> cities, called Arhusen and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RANDERS">Randers</a>; besides several market <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> of less <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOTE">note</a>, and upwards of 300 villages. Arhusen, one of the capitals, is advantageously situated on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of the Baltic <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, at the mouth of the river Guda, which runs through it; and it is surrounded with forests full of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAME">game</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 10° 0'. N. Lat. 56° 12'.

ARIADNE

Pages 698-698
daughter of Minos king of Crete. Theseus being sent to destroy the Minotaur, Ariadne was so taken with him, that, as a testimony of her love, she gave Theseus a clue of thread to guide him out of the labyrinth. Theseus, having killed the Minotaur, carried off the Athenians he had relieved, together with Ariadne: whom, however, he afterwards forsook.

ARIAN

Pages 698-698

and Ariana, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, whether the same <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> distinct countries authors are not agreed. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a> has only Aria, and knows nothing about Ariana. Pliny mentions only Ariana, and says nothing about Aria; but distinguishes between the Arii and Ariani: <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARTHIA">Parthia</a>, he says, has the Arii to the east, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARAMANIA">Caramania</a> and the Ariani to the south; from which it is conjectured, the Ariani extended farther than the Arii, and comprised the Gedrosii and the Drange. Arrian has only Aria and Arii, and is silent about Ariana. But Strabo gives more extensive bounds to Ariana than to Aria, without particularly defining them; only in general he says, that Ariana begins from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, and quotes Eratosthenes; according to whom, Ariana is bounded by the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDUS">Indus</a> on the east; on the south by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>; by Paropamisus on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, and by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, quite to the Porte Caspiae; on the west by the same boundaries by which Parthia is separated from Media, Caramania from Paratacene and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>: and thus Ariana is extremely extensive.—Aria has its limits thus described by Ptolemy: On the north, some parts of Margiana and Bactriana; on the east, the Paropamiside; on the south the Drangianæ: and Strabo says, the Arii adjoin to the Paropamiside on the east.

ARIANA

Pages 698-698

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, an extensive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, comprising Paropamisus, Arachosia, Drangiana, and Gedrosia, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we suppose it to reach to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. See ARIA.

ARIANNA

Pages 698-698

a small village six miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east from the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUNIS">Tunis</a>. Here is a beautiful range of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Carthaginian aqueduct, 74 feet <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, supported by columns 16 feet <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, and which still increased in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a> the nearer it approached <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARTHAGE">Carthage</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a> are all <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIAMOND">diamond</a> cut. Near this spot several ancient mattamones, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> subterraneous magazines for corn, have been discovered within these few years, capable of containing 100 bushels, strongly arched with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> square stones. The Moors have already begun to demolish them, it being their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> to do so with everything beautiful as soon as it comes to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>.

ARIANO

Pages 698-699

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a> in the Ulterior Principality, with a bishop's see. Mr Swinburne describes it as an ugly <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, built upon the uneven summit of a mountain, with an extensive look-out on all sides, but exposed to every blast that blows. It does not appear to be so old as the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>; therefore may be supposed to owe its rise to the demolition of some neighbouring town, and to the advantages its situation afforded for discovery and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>. It is but a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, without out trade <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>; having declined ever since the desolation caused by an earthquake in 1456. It reckons about 14,000 inhabitants, and no less than 20 parishes and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a>, besides an ill-endowed <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>. The wine made here is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a>, like <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> Champagne, which it also resembles in a certain tartness, exceedingly refreshing in hot <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> lies upon a soft argillaceous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>. At a small distance to the east is a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> consisting of layers of volcanic earths, interspersed with thick <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STRATA">strata</a> of oyster shells. Below the town is a convent of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMINICANS">Dominicans</a>, whose <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, within these last hundred years, has been thrice rebuilt, having been as often thrown to the ground by earthquakes. The last and most destructive happened in 1732, fatal to all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> that lies along the eastern verge of the Apennines. In order to secure a retreat in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of future accidents, which from their situation they have every reason to expect, these fathers have constructed a small <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> of wood, the parts of which being joined together with strong <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> chains, are contrived so as to have a proper play, and by yielding to the oscillatory <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, return easily to their equilibrium. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 15° 19'. N. Lat. 41° 8'.

ARIANS

Pages 699-699

followers of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARIUS">Arius</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRESBYTER">presbyter</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a> about the year 315; who maintained that the Son of God was totally and essentially distinct from the Father; that he was the first and noblest of those beings whom God had created, the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> by whose subordinate operation he formed the universe; and therefore inferior to the Father both in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>: also, that the Holy Ghost was not God, but created by the power of the Son. The Arians owned that the Son was the Word, but denied that Word to have been eternal. They held, that Christ had nothing of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> in him but the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>, to which the Λόγος <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Word was joined, which was the same as the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> in us. See Lardner's Credibility, &c., vol. ix. book i. c. 69. The Arians were first condemned and anathematized by a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> at Alexandria in 320, under Alexander, bishop of that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>; who accused Arius of impiety, and caused him to be expelled from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a> of the church; and afterwards by 380 fathers in the general council of Nice, assembled by Constantine in the year 325. But, notwithstanding that, it was not extinguished; on the contrary, it became the reigning <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, especially in the east, where it obtained much more than in the west. Arius was recalled from banishment by the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Constantine in two or three years after the council of Nice, and the laws that had been enacted against him were repealed. In the year 335, Athanasius, his zealous opponent, was deposed and banished into <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAUL">Gaul</a>, and Arius and his followers were reinstated in their privileges, and received into the communion of the church. In little more than a year after this, he fell a victim to the resentment of his enemies, and died a tragic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, occasioned probably by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POISON">poison</a>, or some other violence. The Arian party found a protector in Constantius, who succeeded his father in the empire of the east; and the zeal with which he abetted them produced many animosities and tumults to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of his death in the year 362. They underwent various revolutions, persecuting and oppressed, under succeeding emperors, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> they had in the civil power, till at length Theodosius the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> exerted every possible effort to suppress and disperse them. The Arians were divided into various sects, of which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> writers give an account under the names of Semi-Arians, Eusebians, Aetians, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EUNOMIANS">Eunomians</a>, Acacians, Psathyrians, and others. But they have been <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> distributed into three classes, viz. the Genuine Arians, Semi-Arians, and Eunomians. Arianism was carried in the fifth century into <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a> under the Vandals; and into <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> under the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOTHS">Goths</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, the Gauls, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, were also deeply infected with it; and towards the commencement of the sixth century, it was triumphant in many parts of Asia, Africa, and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. But it sunk almost all at once, when the Vandals were driven out of Africa, and the Goths out of Italy, by the arms of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTINIAN">Justinian</a>. However, it revived again in Italy under the protection of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOMBARDS">Lombards</a> in the seventh century. Erasmus seems to have aimed in some <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> to restore Arianism at the beginning of the sixteenth century, in his Commentaries on the New <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>. Accordingly, he was reproached by his adversaries with Arian interpretations and glosses, Arian tenets, &c. To which he made little answer, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> that there was no <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERESY">heresy</a> more thoroughly extinct than that of the Arians: Nulla heresis magis extincta quam Arianorum. But the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> of things was soon changed. Servetus, a Spaniard by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, published in 1531 a little treatise against the Trinity, which once more revived the opinions of the Arians in the west. Indeed he rather showed himself a Photinian than an Arian; only that he made <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the same <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> of Scripture, and the same arguments against the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> of our Saviour, with the proper Arians. It is true, Servetus had not, properly speaking, any disciples; but he gave occasion after his death to the forming of a new system of Arianism in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENEVA">Geneva</a>, much more subtle and artful than his own, and which did not a little perplex Calvin. From Geneva the new Arians removed to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>, where they gained considerable ground; but at length became Socinians. The appellation Arian has been indiscriminately applied, in more <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> times, to all those who consider <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ as inferior and subordinate to the Father; and whose sentiments cannot be supposed to coincide exactly with those of the ancient Arians. Mr Whiston was one of the first divines who revived this controversy, in the beginning of the 18th century. He was followed by Dr Clarke, who published his famous book, entitled, "The Scripture Doctrine of the Trinity, &c. In <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of which he was reproached with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Semi-Arian. He was also threatened by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONVOCATION">convocation</a>, and combated by argument. Dr <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATERLAND">Waterland</a>, who has been <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with verging towards Tritheism, was one of his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> adversaries. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of this controversy during the present century may be found in a pamphlet entitled, "An Account of all the considerable Books and Pamphlets that have been wrote on either side, in the Controversy concerning the Trinity, from the Year 1712; in which also is contained an Account of the Pamphlets written this last Year, on each side, by the Dissenters, to the End of the Year 1719." Published in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> 1720.

ARICA

Pages 700-700

a port town of South <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Los Charcas, in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERU">Peru</a>. It was formerly a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, but the earthquakes, which are frequent here, have almost entirely ruined it; for there are no more than 150 families, which are most of them blacks, mulattoes, and Indians. Most of the houses are made with canes <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> reeds, set upright and bound together with cords or thongs; and as it never rains here, they are covered only with mats, which makes the place look at a distance like a heap of ruins. The vale of Arica is about a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> wide, and six leagues <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, next the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, and is all a barren <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, except the spot where the old town stood, which is divided into little meadows of clover grass, and plots for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a> canes, with a few olive and cotton trees intermixed. This vale grows narrower as it runs eastward; and a league up there is a village, where they begin to cultivate pimento or Jamaica <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEPPER">pepper</a>, which is planted throughout all the rest of the vale; and there are several farms, which produce nothing else, that bring in the value of 80,000 crowns yearly. The Spaniards of Peru are so used to this pepper, that they dress no <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> without it. W. Long. 70. 15. S. Lat. 18. 26.

ARICINA

Pages 699-700

in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">Mythology</a>, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SURNAME">surname</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIANA">Diana</a>; under which appellation she was honoured in the forest Aricino, so called from Aricia a princess of the blood <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>. Hippolytus, to whom this princess was married, is said to have erected a temple to Diana in this forest, where he was concealed after his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESURRECTION">resurrection</a> by Esculapius, and to have established a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> and festivals.

ARICONIUM

Pages 700-700

a town of the Silures, (Antonine); now <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREFORD">Hereford</a>, (Camden). W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2. 42. Lat. 52. 6.

ARIDAS

Pages 700-700

a kind of taffety, manufactured in the East Indies from a shining thread which is got from certain herbs, whence they are styled aridas of herbs.

ARIDULLAM

Pages 700-700

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, a kind of zarich found in the East Indies. See ZARNICH.

ARIES

Pages 700-700

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, a constellation of fixed stars, drawn on the globe, in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of a ram. It is the first of the twelve signs of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZODIAC">zodiac</a>, from which a twelfth <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the ecliptic takes its denomination.

ARILLUS

Pages 700-700

an improper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> invented by Linnaeus, and defined to be the proper exterior coat <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> covering of the seed which falls off spontaneously. All seeds are not furnished with an arillus; in many, a dry covering, or scarf skin, supplies its <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. In jasmine; <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol11.html#article-HOUND">hound</a>'s tongue, cynoglossum; cucumber; fraxinella; dictamnus; <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STAFF">staff</a>-tree, celastrus; spindle-tree, euonymus; African spirea, diosma; and the coffee-tree, coffee; it is very conspicuous. In the genus hound's tongue, four of these arilli or proper coats, each enfolding a single reed, are affixed to the stylus; and in this circumstance, says Linnaeus, does the essence of the genus consist. In fraxinella, the arillus is <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> to two seeds. The staff tree has its seeds only half involved with this cover. The arillus is either baccatus, succulent, and of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of a berry; as in the spindle tree, euonymus—Cartilagineus, cartilaginous, or gristly; as in the African spirea, diosma—Coloratus, coloured; as in the staff-tree—Elasticus, endued with elasticity, for dispersing the seeds; as is remarkable in the African spirea, diosma, and fraxinella—Scaber, rough and knotty; as in hound's tongue. Although covered with an arillus or other dry coat, seeds are said to be naked (semina nuda) when they are not enclosed in any <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of pericarpium or fruit vessel; as in the grasses, and the labiati or lipped <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> of Tournefort, which correspond to the didynamia gymnosperrmia of Linnæus. Seeds are said to be covered (semina tecta) when they are contained in a fruit vessel, whether <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPSULE">capsule</a>, pod, or pulpy pericarpium, of the apple, berry, or cherry kind: (See SEMEN). This exterior coat of the seed is, by some former writers, styled calyptra. See CALYPTRA. The different skins or coverings of the seeds are adapted, say naturalists, for receiving the nutritive juices, and transmitting them within.

ARIMANUS

Pages 700-701

the evil god of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Persians. The Persian <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGI">Magi</a> held two principles; a good demon <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> god, and an evil one: the first the author of all good, and the other of all evil: the former they supposed to be represented by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, and the latter by darkness, as their truest symbols. The good principle they named Yezad or Yesdan, and Ormazd or Hormizda, which the Greeks wrote Oromazes; and the evil demon they called Ahriaman, and the Greeks Arimanus. Some of the Magians held both these principles to have been from all eternity; but this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a> was reputed <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HETERODOX">heterodox</a>: the original doctrine being, that the good principle only was eternal, and the other created.—Plutarch (De Æside et Osiride, p. 369.) gives the following account of the Magian traditions in relation to these gods, and the introduction of evil into the world, viz. That Oromazes consisted of the most pure light, and Arimanus of darkness; and that they were at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> with each other: That Oromazes created the gods; the first, the author of benevolence; the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>; the third, of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RICHES">riches</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> which attends good actions; and that Arimanus made as many, who were the authors of the opposite evils or vices: that then Oromazes, triplicating himself, removed as far from the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> as the sun is from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and adorned the heaven with stars, appointing the dog <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STAR">star</a> for their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUARDIAN">guardian</a> and leader: that he also created 24 other gods, and enclosed them in an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGG">egg</a>; but Arimanus having also made an equal <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, these last perforated the egg, by which means evil and good became mixed together. However, the fatal <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> come, when Arimanus, the introducer of plagues and famine, must be of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> utterly destroyed by the former, and annihilated; then the earth being made plain and even, mankind shall live in a happy state, in the same manner, in the same <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, and using one and the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. Theopompus writes, that, according to the Magians, the said two gods, during the space of 3000 years, alternately conquer, and are conquered; that for other 3000 years, they will will wage perpetual war, fight and destroy the works of each other; till at last <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HADES">Hades</a> (or the evil spirit) shall perish, and men become perfectly happy, their bodies needing no food, nor casting any shadow, i.e. being perfectly transparent.

ARIMASPI

Pages 701-701

(Pliny), a people of Sarmatia Europea, to the south of the Montes Ripheci, said by Mela to have but one eye; a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FABLE">fable</a> broached by Aristeas Proconnesius, according to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a>.

ARIMATHEA

Pages 701-701

a town of Judea, (Evangelists); thought to be the same with Ramatha, 1 Sam. i. and thus in the tribe of Ephraim (<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WELLS">Wells</a>).—This <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> is now called Ramla; and is in a very ruinous state, containing nothing but rubbish within its boundaries. The aga of Gaza resides here in a serai, the floors and walls of which are tumbling <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>. He maintains about one hundred horsemen, and as many Barbary <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>, who (says Mr Volney) are lodged in an old Christian <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, the nave of which is used as a stable, and in an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> khan, which is disputed with them by the scorpions. The adjacent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is planted with lofty olive trees, disposed in quincunces. The greatest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of them are as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> as the walnut trees of France; but they are daily perishing through <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, the ravages of contending factions, and even from secret mischief: for, in these countries, when a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEASANT">peasant</a> would <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> himself of his enemy, he comes by night, and saws <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> cuts his trees <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to the ground, and the wound, which he takes care to cover, draining off the sap like an issue, the olive tree languishes and dies.—Amid the plantations, we meet, at every step, with dry wells, cisterns fallen in, and vast vaulted reservoirs, which prove that, in ancient times, this town must have been upwards of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> and a half in circumference. At present it scarcely contains two hundred families. The little <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> which is cultivated by a few of them, belongs to the mufti, and two or three persons related to him. The rest content themselves with <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPINNING">spinning</a> cotton, which is chiefly purchased by two French houses established there. The only remarkable antiquity at Ramla, is the minaret of a ruined mosque on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> to Yafa, which is very lofty; and by an Arabic inscription appears to have been built by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SULTAN">sultan</a> Saladin.

ARIMINUM

Pages 701-701

a town of Umbria, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Romagna, at the mouth of the Ariminus, on the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>. The seizing on it by Caesar gave rise to the civil <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. Now called <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIMINI">Rimini</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 13° 30'. Lat 44° 8'.

ARIOLI

Pages 701-701

in antiquity, a kind of prophets, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> conjurers, who by abominable prayers, and horrible sacrifices at the altars of idols, procured answers to their questions concerning future events. *Isid. Orig.* lib. viii. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 9. These are also called *hatrioli*, and the operation *hatriolation*. Sometimes they were denominated *aruspices* or *haruspices*. The *arioli* were distinguished by a slovenly dress, disorderly and matted beards, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, &c.

ARION

Pages 701-701

an admirable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, much more famous in poetic <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> than Bucephalus in that of Alexander. Authors speak variously of his origin, though they agree in giving him a divine one. His production is most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> ascribed to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEPTUNE">Neptune</a>. This god, according to some, raised him out of the ground by a stroke of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIDENT">trident</a>; according to others, he begat him upon the body of the fury Erinnyes; according to others, upon that of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CERES">Ceres</a>, whom he ravished in the form of a horse, she having previously assumed the form of a mare to elude his pursuit. This horse was nursed by the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEREIDS">Nereids</a>; and being sometimes yoked with the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> horses of Neptune to the chariot of this god, he drew him with incredible swiftness threw the sea. He had this singularity in him, that his <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> feet resembled those of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>. Neptune gave him to Capreus <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALICARNASSUS">Halicarnassus</a>. Capreus made a present of him to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>; who mounted him when he took the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIS">Elis</a>, gained the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a> with him in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> against Cygnus the son of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARS">Mars</a> near Troezena, and at last made a present of him to Adrastus. It is under this last <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> that Arion has signalized himself the most: he won the prize for <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACING">racing</a> at the Nemean games, which the princes who went to besiege Thebes instituted in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of Archemorus; and was the cause that Adrastus did not perish in this famous expedition as all the other chiefs did.

ARIOSTO

Pages 701-702

Lodovico, the famous Italian poet, and author of Orlando Furioso, was born at the castle of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REGGIO">Reggio</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LOMBARDY">Lombardy</a> in 1474. His father, who was <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">major</a> domo to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">Duke</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>, lived to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of his fortune, so left but little at his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. Ariosto, from his childhood, showed <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> marks of genius, especially in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>; and wrote a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMEDY">comedy</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> on the story of Pyramus and Thisbe, which his brothers and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SISTERS">sisters</a> played. His father being utterly unlearned, and rather regarding profit than his son's inclination, compelled him to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> the civil <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>, in which having plodded some years to no purpose, he quitted it for more pleasing studies; yet often lamented, as Ovid and Petrarch did before him, and our own <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILTON">Milton</a> since*, that his father banished him from the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSES">Muses</a>. At the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 24, Ariosto lost his father, and found himself perplexed with family affairs. However, in poem, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AD">Ad</a> about six years he was, for his good parts, taken into Patrem. the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DON">Don</a> Hippolito, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol9.html#article-ESTE">Este</a>. At this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> he had written nothing but a few sonnets; but now he resolved to make a poem, and chose Bayardo's Orlando Inamorato for a groundwork. However, he was prevented <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> for a great many years, and was chosen as a fit person to go on an embassy to Pope Julius II. where he gave such satisfaction, that he was sent again, underwent many dangers and difficulties, and at his return was highly favoured. Then, at his leisure, he again applied himself to his poem; but soon after he incurred the cardinal's displeasure for refusing to accompany him into <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>; by which he was so discouraged, that he deferred writing for 14 years, even till the cardinal's death. After that, he finished by degrees, in great perfection, that which he began with great <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPECTATION">expectation</a>. Duke Astolfo offered him great promotions <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he would serve him; but preferring <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a>, he refused this and other great offers from princes and cardinals, particularly from Leo X. from all whom he received notwithstanding great presents. The duke of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FERRARA">Ferrara</a> delighted Ariosto delighted so much in his comedies, of which he wrote five, that he built a stage on purpose to have them played in his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, and enabled our poet to build himself a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> in Ferrara, with a pleasant garden, where he used to compose his poems, which were highly esteemed by all the princes in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, who sent him many presents; but he said, "he would not sell his liberty for the best cardinal's hat in Rome." It was but a small, though convenient house: being asked, why he had not built it in a more magnificent manner, since he had given such noble descriptions of sumptuous palaces, beautiful porticoes, and pleasant fountains, in his Orlando Furioso? he replied, That words were cheaper laid together than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>. Upon the door was the following inscription: Parva, sed apta mihi, sed nulli obnoxia, sed non Sordida, parta meo sed tamen ære, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOMUS">domus</a>. Which Mr <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HARRINGTON">Harrington</a> thus translates: This house is small, but fit for me, but hurtful unto none; But yet not sluttish, as you see, yet paid for with mine own. In his diet he was temperate, and so careless of dainties, that he was fit to have lived in the world when they fed upon acorns. Whether he was ever married, is uncertain. He kept <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> with one <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>, to whom, it was reported, he was married privately, and a lady Genevera, whom he silly mentions in the 24th book of his Orlando, as poets are apt to intermix with their fictions some real amours of their own. He was urged to go <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a> to Pope Clement, but would by no means accept this embassy. He translated the Menecmi of Plautus: and all his own comedies were so esteemed, that they were frequently acted by persons of the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>; and when his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LENA">Lena</a> was first represented, Ferdinand of Este, afterwards marquis of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASSA">Massa</a>, so far honoured the piece as to speak the prologue. He began one of his comedies in his father's lifetime, when the following incident shows the remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TALENT">talent</a> he had for poetry. His father one <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> rebuked him sharply, charging him with some great fault; but all the while he returned him no answer. Soon after, his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> began on the same subject: but he easily refuted him, and with strong arguments justified his own behaviour. "Why then (said his brother) did you not satisfy my father?" "In <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> (said Lodovico) I was thinking of a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> in my comedy; and methought my father's speech to me was so suited to the part of an old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s chiding his son, that I forgot I was concerned in it myself, and considered it only to make it a part of my play." It is also reported of Ariosto, that coming by a potter's shop, he heard him singing a stave out of his Orlando, with so bad a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">grace</a>, that, out of all <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATIENCE">patience</a>, he broke with his stick several of his pots. The potter, in a pitiful tone, asking what he meant by wronging a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> man that had never injured him? "You rascal (he replied), I have not done thee half the wrong thou hast done me: for I have broken but two <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> three pots of thine, not worth so many halpence; whereas thou has broken and mangled a stanza of mine worth a mark of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>." Ariosto was tall, of a melancholy <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPLEXION">complexion</a>, and so absorbed in study and meditation, that he often forgot himself. His <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> was drawn by Titian in a masterly manner. He was honoured with the laurel by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> V. He was naturally affable, always assuming less than was his due, yet never putting up a known injury, even from his superiors. He was so fearful on the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, that, whenever he went out of a ship, he would see others go before him; and, on <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>, he would alight from his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> on the least <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPREHENSION">apprehension</a> of danger. He was of an amorous disposition, and left two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> sons. He enjoyed the friendship of the most eminent men of learning of his time, most of whom he mentions with great respect in the last <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTO">canto</a> of his Orlando Furioso. His <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> was but weakly, so that he was obliged to have recourse to physicians the greatest part of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. He bore his last sickness with great <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> and serenity; and died at Ferrara the 8th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1533, according to Sir John Harrington, being then 59 years of age. He was interred in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of the Benedictine monks, who, contrary to their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>, attended his funeral. He had a bust erected to him, and the following epitaph, written by himself, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSCRIBED">inscribed</a> upon his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a>: Ludovicici Ariostii humantur ossa Sub hoc marmore, seu sub hac humo, seu Sub quidquid voluit benignus haeres, Sive haerede benignior comes, seu Opportunitas incidens viator; Nam scire haud potuit futura: sed nec Tanti erat, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VACUUM">vacuum</a> sibi cadaver Ut urnam cuperet parare, Vivens ista tamen sibi paravit, Quæ scribi voluit suo sepulchro, Olim si quod haberet id sepulchrum: Ne cum spiritus hoc brevi peracto Prescripto spatio misellos artus, Quos ægre ante reliquerat, poscet, Hac et hac cinerem huc et huc revellum Dum noscat proprium, diu vagetur.

ARIPO

Pages 702-702

a town on the western <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Ceylon, at the mouth of the river Sarunda. To the east of this town, is a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a>, where they fish for pearls. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 8°. 25'. N. Lat. 8°. 42'.

ARISBA

Pages 702-702

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LESBOS">Lesbos</a> (Herodot.).—Another of Troas on the continent, and to the south-east of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABYDOS">Abydos</a> (Polyb.): the rendezvous of Alexander's <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> after the passage of the Hellespont (Arrian); a colony of the Mitylenians (Stephanus); taken and plundered by <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACHILLES">Achilles</a> (<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>.) The residence of Axylus, celebrated by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a> for his hospitality, which gained him the character of Friend of mankind.

ARISI

Pages 702-702

the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> name for the plant which produces the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>. See ORYZA, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ARISTA

Pages 702-702
or AWN, among botanists, a long needle-like beard, which stands out from the husk of a grain of corn, grain, &c. ARISTÆUS, son of Apollo and Cyrene, whom, for the many services he had rendered to mankind by his knowledge of all profitable arts, the gods placed among the stars; so that he is the Aquarius in the zodiac. The resemblance of his history to that of Moses has been curiously discussed by Huetius.

ARISTANDER

Pages 702-703

a famous soothsayer under Alexander the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>, over whom he gained a wonderful Aristarchus, a Grecian <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAMOS">Samos</a>, one of the first that maintained that the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> turns upon its own centre. We are not sure of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> in which he lived; and have none of his works but a Treatise of the greatness and distance of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">Sun</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">Moon</a>, translated into Latin by Frederic Commandine, and published with Pappus's explanation in 1572. Aristarchus, a celebrated grammarian, much esteemed by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a> Philometor, who committed to him the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> of his son. He applied himself chiefly to criticism, and made a revisal of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>'s poems, but in too magisterial a way; for such verses as he did not like he treated as spurious. He commented on other poets. Cicero and Horace made <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of his name to express a very rigid critic. ARISTIDA. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ARISTIDES

Pages 704-704

a painter <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APELLES">Apelles</a>, flourished at Thebes about the 122d Olympiad. He was the first, according to Pliny, who expressed character and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> mind, and its several emotions; but he was not remarkable for softness of colouring. "His most celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> was of an infant (on the taking of a town) at the mother's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>, who is wounded and expiring. The sensations of the mother were clearly marked, and her fear lest the child, upon failure of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILK">milk</a>, should suck her blood." "Alexander the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> (continues the same author) took this picture with him to Pella." Junius (in his Treatise de Pictura Veterum) conjectures that the following beautiful epigram of Æmilianus was written on this exquisite picture: Ἐλκει, φάλαγξ, πυρὰ μήτηρ: οὐ μὴ τῇ μαζῇ αἰμαλίζῃς Εἰκόνων ὑποτασσεῖς καὶ πᾶσα Φράμης. Ἡ δὲ γυνὴ ξύφεσθαι λιποτὸν ἀλλὰ τα μῆτρας Φιλέτη καὶ μὴ αἰδὼν παίδωναμιν εἰμιν. Elegantly translated thus: Suck, little wretch, while yet thy mother lives, Suck the last drop her fainting bosom gives! She dies! her tenderness survives her breath, And her fond <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> is provident in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. Webb's Inquiries, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIAL">Dial</a>. vii. p. 161.

ARISTIPPUS

Pages 704-706

the founder of the Cyrenaic <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, was the son of Aretades, and born at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CYRENE">Cyrene</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBYA">Libya</a>. He flourished about the 96th Olympiad. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> reputation of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOCRATES">Socrates</a> induced him to leave his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and remove to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, that he might have the satisfaction of hearing his discourses. He was chiefly delighted with those discourses of Socrates that related the most to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>: which he asserted to be the ultimate end in which all <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> consists. His manner of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> was agreeable to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>: for he indulged himself extremely in all the luxuries of dress, wine, and women. Though he had a good estate, and three country seats, yet he was the only one of the disciples of Socrates who took <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> for teaching; which being discovered by the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, he asked Aristippus, How he came to have so much? Who in reply asked him, How he came to have so little? Upon his leaving Socrates, he went to Ægina, as Athenæus informs us, where he lived with more freedom and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a> than before. Socrates sent frequent exhortations to him, in order to reclaim him; but all in vain; and with the same view he published that discourse which we find in Xenophon. Here Aristippus became acquainted with Laïs, the famous courtezan of Corinth; for whose sake he took a voyage to that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>. He <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> at Ægina till the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Socrates, as appears from <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a>'s Phædo, and the epistle which he wrote upon that occasion. He returned at last into his own country Cyrene, where he professed philosophy, and instituted a sect which, as we observed above, was called the Cyrenaic, from the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and by some writers the Hedonic <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> voluptuous, from its doctrines. During the height of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a> of Dionysius the Sicilian <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a>, a great many philosophers resorted to him; and among the rest Aristippus, who was tempted thither by the magnificence of that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>. Dionysius asking him the reason of his coming, he replied, "That it was in order to give what he had, and to receive what he had not:" or, as others represent it, "That when he wanted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>, he went to Socrates; but now as he wanted money, he was come to him." He very soon insinuated himself into the favour of Dionysius; for being a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of a soft easy temper, he conformed himself exactly to every place, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, and person, and was a complete <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the most refined complaisance. We have several remarkable <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> concerning him during his residence at that court, mentioned by <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIOGENES">Diogenes</a> Laertius. Dionysius, at a feast, commanded that all should put on women's purple habits, and dance in them.
