But Plato refused, repeating these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>: I cannot in this gay effeminate dress Disgrace my manhood or my <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEX">sex</a> betray. But Aristippus readily submitted to the command, and made this reply immediately: — At feasts, where nirth is free, A sober mind can never be corrupted. At another time, interceding with Dionysius in behalf of a friend, but not prevailing, he <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> himself at his feet: being reproved by one for that excess of humility, he replied, "That it was not he who was the cause of that submission; but Dionysius, whose ears were in his feet." Dionysius showed him three beautiful courtezans, and ordered him to take his choice. Upon which he took them all three away with him, alleging that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> was punished for preferring one to the other two: but when he had brought them to his door, he dismissed then, in order to show that he could either enjoy Aristippus, or reject with the same indifference. Having desired money of Dionysius, the latter observed to him, that he had assured him a wise man wanted nothing. "Give me (says he) what I ask, and we <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> talk of that afterwards." When Dionysius had given it him, "Now (says he), you see I do not want." By his complaisance he gained so much upon Dionysius, that he had a greater regard for him than for all the rest of the philosophers, though he sometimes spoke with such freedom to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>, that he incurred his displeasure. When Dionysius asked, Why philosophers haunted the gates of rich men, but not rich men those of philosophers: he replied, "Because the latter know what they want, and the others not." Another time, Dionysius repeating (out of Sophocles, as Plutarch affirms, who ascribes this to Zeno) these verses, He that with tyrants seeks for bare support, Enslaves himself, though free he came to court: he immediately answered, He is no slave, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he be free to come. Diogenes, as Laertius informs us, related this in his Lives of the Philosophers; though others ascribe this saying to Plato. Aristippus had a contest with Antisthenes the Cynic philosopher; notwithstanding which, he was very ready to employ his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> at court for some friends of Antisthenes, to preserve them from death, as we find by a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> of his to that philosopher. Diogenes followed the example of his master Antisthenes in ridiculing Aristippus, and called him the court spaniel. We have many apophthegms of his preserved.—To one who asked him what his son would be the better for being a scholar? "If for nothing else (said he), yet for this alone, that when he comes into the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>, one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> will not sit upon another." When a certain person recommended his son to him, he demanded 500 drachmas; and upon the father's replying, that he could buy a slave for that sum, "Do so (said he), and then you will be master of a couple." Being reproached, because, having a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> depending, he see'd a lawyer to plead for him, "<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">Just</a> so (said he), when I have a great <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPPER">supper</a> to make, I always hire a cook." Being asked what was the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between a wise man and a fool, he replied, "Send both of them together naked to those who are acquainted with neither of them, and then you will know." Being reproved by a certain person (who, according to Mr Stanley, was Plato) for his costly and voluptuous feasts, "I warrant you (said he), that you would not have bestowed three farthings upon such a dinner;" which the other confessing, "Why, then (said he), I find myself less indulgent to my palate than you are to your covetous humour?" or, as it is otherwise represented, "I find, that I <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> my belly and you love your money." When Simus, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a> to Dionysius, showed him his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> magnificently furnished, and paved with costly marble, (for he was a Phrygian, and consequently profuse;) Aristippus spit in his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a>: upon which the other growing angry, "Why, truly (said he), I could not find a fitter place." His <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> carrying after him a great <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of money, and being ready to sink upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> under his burden, Aristippus, burden, he bid him throw away all that was too much for him to carry. Horace mentions this fact in his third satire of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> book: Quid simile isti Græcus Aristippus qui servos projicere aurum In media jussit Libya, quia tardius irent Propter onus segnes. Being asked, what things were most proper for children to be instructed in? he answered, "Those which might prove of the greatest advantage to them when they came to be men." Being reproached for going from Socrates to Dionysius, he replied, "That he went to Socrates when he wanted serious instruction, and to Dionysius for diversion." Having received money of Dionysius at the same time that Plato accepted a book only, and being reproached for it, "The reason is plain (says he), I want money, and Plato wants books." Having lost a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARM">farm</a>, he said to one who seemed excessively to compassionate his loss, "You have but one field; I have three left: why should not I rather grieve for you?" Plutarch, who relates this, in his book De Tranquillitate Animi, observes upon it, that it is very absurd to lament for what is lost, and not to rejoice for what is left. When a person told him, "That the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> for his sake was lost," he replied, "That it was better so, than that he should be lost for the land." Being cast by shipwreck ashore on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RHODES">Rhodes</a>, and perceiving mathematical schemes and diagrams drawn upon the ground, he said, "Courage, friends; for I see the footsteps of men." After he had lived a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> time with Dionysius, his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> Arete sent to him, to desire his presence at Cyrene, in order to take care of her affairs, since she was in danger of being oppressed by the magistrates. But he fell sick in his return home, and died at Lipara, an Eolian island. With regard to his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> opinions, like Socrates, he rejected the sciences as they were then taught, and pretended that logic alone was sufficient to teach <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> and fix its bounds. He asserted, that pleasure and pain were the criterions by which we were to be determined; that these alone made up all our passions; that the first produced all the soft emotions, and the latter all the violent ones. The assemblage of all pleasure, he asserted, made true happiness, and that the best way to attain this was to enjoy the present moments. He wrote a great many books: particularly the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of Libya, dedicated to Dionysius; several Dialogues; and four books of the Luxury of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>. There are four epistles of his extant in the Socratic collection published by Leo Allatius. Besides Arete his daughter, whom he educated in philosophy, Aristippus had also a son, whom he disdained for his stupidity. Arete had a son who was named Aristippus from his grandfather, and had the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SURNAME">surname</a> of Mητροδιάκονος, from his mother's instructing him in philosophy. Among his auditors, besides his daughter Arete, we have an account of Ἀθηνίας of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMAIS">Ptolemais</a>, and Antipater of Cyrene. Arete communicated the philosophy which she received from her father to her son Aristippus, who transmitted it to Theodorus the Atheist, who instituted the sect called Theodorean. Antipater communicated the philosophy of Aristippus to Epitimeses his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a>; Epitimeses to Parabates; Parabates to Hegesias and Anniceris: and Aristiphus these two last improving it by some additions of their own, obtained the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> each of them of giving a name to the Hegesian and Annicerian sect.

ARISTO

Pages 706-706

a Stoic <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of Zeno the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of the Stoics, flourished about 290 years before the Christian era. He differed but little from his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> Zeno. He rejected logic as of no <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY"><a class="xref" hr</a>ef="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> as being above the reach of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> understanding. It is said, that being bald, the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> burnt his head; and that this caused his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>.—There is a saying of his recorded, which might render the doctrine of Aristippus less odious than it ordinarily is; (see Aristippus). He used to say, "That a philosopher might do those of his hearers a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a> who put a wrong interpretation upon good meanings; as for example that the school of Aristippus might send out debanchees, and that of Zeno cynics:" which seems to imply, that the doctrine of this philosopher never produced this effect but when it was misunderstood. He should also have added, that every teacher is therefore obliged to forbear laying <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> ambiguous maxims, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> to prevent false glosses being put upon them.

ARISTOCRACY

Pages 706-706

a form of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> where the supreme power is vested in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> persons of the state. The word is derived from αὐτος, optimus, and ἐπιμερος, "I govern." The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> writers of politics prefer the aristocratical form of government to all others. The republic of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> is an aristocracy. Aristocracy seems to coincide with oligarchy; which, however, is more ordinarily used to signify a corruption of an aristocratical state, where the administration is in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of too few, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> where some one or two usurp the whole power.

ARISTOGITON

Pages 706-706

a famous Athenian, who, with Harmodius, killed <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HIPPARCHUS">Hipparchus</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, about 513 years before the Christian era. The Athenians erected a statue to him.

ARISTOMENES

Pages 706-706

a general of the Messenians, renowned for his valour and virtue. See Messenia.

ARISTOPHANES

Pages 706-707

a celebrated comic poet of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>. He was <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOCRATES">Socrates</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EURIPIDES">Euripides</a>; and most of his plays were written during the Peloponnesian <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. His imagination was warm and lively, and his genius particularly turned to raillery. He had also <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> spirit and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a>; and was a declared enemy to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a>, and to all those who wanted to oppress their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. The Athenians suffered themselves in his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to be governed by men who had no other views than to make themselves masters of the commonwealth. Aristophanes exposed the designs of these men, with great <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a> and severity, upon the stage. <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLEON">Cleon</a> was the first whom he attacked, in his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMEDY">comedy</a> of the Equites; and as there was not one of the comedians who would venture to personate a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of his great authority, Aristophanes played the character himself, and with so much success, that the Athenians obliged Cleon to pay a fine of five talents, which were given to the poet. He described the affairs of the Athenians in so exact a manner, that his comedies are a faithful <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of that people. For this reason, when Dionysius <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRACUSE">Syracuse</a> desired to learn the state and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of Athens, Plato sent him the comedies of Aristophanes, telling him, these were the best representations thereof. He wrote above 50 comedies; but there are only 11 extant which are perfect: these are Plutus, the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">Clouds</a>, the Frogs, Equites, the Acharnenses, the Wasps, Peace, the Birds, the Ecclesiazusa <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">Female</a> Orators, the Thesmophoriazusa or Priestesses of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CERES">Ceres</a>, and Lysistrata. The Clouds, which he wrote in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIDICULE">ridicule</a> of Socrates*, is the most celebrated of all his comedies. Madam Dacier tells us, she was so much charmed with this performance, that after she had translated it, and read it over 200 times, it did not become the least tedious to her, which she could not say of any other piece; and that the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> which she received from it was so exquisite, that she forgot all the contempt and indignation which Aristophanes deserved for employing his wit to ruin a man who was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> itself, and the greatest ornament of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Athens. Aristophanes having conceived some aversion to the poet Euripides, satirizes him in several of his plays, particularly in his Frogs and his Thesmophoriazusa. He wrote his Peace in the 10th year of the Peloponnesian war, when a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of 50 years was concluded between the Athenians and the Lacedemonians, though it <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> but <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years. The Acharnenses was written after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERICLES">Pericles</a> and the loss of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, in order to dissuade the people from intrusting the safety of the commonwealth to such imprudent generals as Lamachus. Soon after, he represented his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-AVES">Aves</a> or Birds; by which he admonished the Athenians to fortify Decelea, which he calls by a fictitious name Nephelococcygia. The Vespa, or Wasps, was written after another loss in Sicily, which the Athenians suffered from the misconduct of Chares. He wrote the Lysistrata when all <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a> was involved in war; in which comedy the women are introduced debating upon the affairs of the commonwealth; when they come to a resolution, not to go to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a> with their husbands till a peace should be concluded. His Plutus, and other comedies of that kind, were written after the magistrates had given orders that no person should be exposed by name upon the stage. He invented a peculiar kind of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>, which was called by his name, and is mentioned by Cicero in his Brutus; and Suidas says, that he also was the inventor of the tetrameter and octameter verse. Aristophanes was greatly admired among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, especially for the true Attic elegance of his style. The time of his death was unknown; but it is certain he was living after the expulsion of the tyrants by Thrasybulus, whom he mentions in his Plutus and other comedies. There have been several editions and translations of this poet. Nicodemus Frischin, a German, famous for his classical knowledge, in the 16th century, translated Plutus, the Clouds, the Frogs, the Equites, and the Acharnenses, into Latin verse. Quintus Septimus Florens rendered into Latin verse the Wasps, the Peace, and Lysistrata; but his translation is full of obsolete words and phrases. Madam Dacier published at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1692, a French version of Plutus and the Clouds, with critical notes, and an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> of them according to the rules of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>. Mr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a> Theobald likewise translated these two comedies into the English, and published them with remarks. The most noble edition of this author is that published by Ludolphus Kuster, at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a>, in folio, in 1710, and dedicated to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> Montague <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALIFAX">Halifax</a>.

ARISTOTELIA

Pages 707-707

in antiquity, annual feasts celebrated by the citizens of Stagyra, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>, who was born there; and in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a> for his having procured from Alexander the rebuilding and repeopling of that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, which had been demolished by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a>.

ARISTOTELIAN

Pages 707-707

something that relates to the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>. ARISTOTELIAN <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">Philosophy</a>, the philosophy taught by Aristotle, and maintained by his followers. The Aristotelian is otherwise called the Peripatetic Philosophy. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIPATETICS">Peripatetics</a>.

ARISTOTELIANS

Pages 707-707

a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of philosophers, otherwise called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIPATETICS">Peripatetics</a>. The Aristotelians and their dogmata prevailed for a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> while in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a>; even in spite of all the efforts of the Cartesians, Newtonians, and other corpuscularians. But the systems of the latter have at length gained the pre-eminence; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEWTONIAN_PHILOSOPHY">Newtonian <a class="</a>xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> in particular is now very generally received. The principles of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARISTOTLE_S_PHILOSOPHY"><a class="xref" href="</a>vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>'s philosophy, the learned agree, are chiefly laid <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> in the four books de Caelo; the eight books of Physical Auscultation, Φυσική αναγνώσις, belonging rather to logic, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METAPHYSICS">metaphysics</a>, than to physics. Instead of the more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> systems, he introduced <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, form, and privation, as the principles of all things; but he does not seem to have derived much benefit from them in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY"><a class="xref" hr</a>ef="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> philosophy. His doctrines are, for the most <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a>, so obscurely expressed, that it has not yet been satisfactorily ascertained what were his sentiments on some of the most important subjects. He attempted to refute the Pythagorean doctrine concerning the twofold <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>; and pretended to demonstrate, that the matter of the heavens is ungenerated, incorruptible, and subject to no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a>; and he supposed that the stars were carried round the earth in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> orbs. The reader <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> find a distinct account of the logical part of his philosophy, by Dr Reid professor of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MORAL_PHILOSOPHY">moral philosophy</a> in the university of Glasgow, and in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> volume of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Kames's Sketches of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">Man</a>. Mr Harris has published a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMENTARY">commentary</a> on his Categories, under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Philosophical Arrangements.

ARISTOTLE

Pages 707-708

the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of the Peripatetic philosophers, born at Stagyra, a small <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> in Macedon, in the 99th Olympiad, about 384 years before the birth of Christ. He was the son of Nicomachus, physician to Amyntas the grandfather of Alexander the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>. He lost his parents in his infancy; and Proxenes, a friend of his father, who had the care of his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, taking but little notice of him, he quitted his studies, and gave himself up to the follies of youth. After he had spent most of his patrimony, he entered into the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>; but not succeeding in this profession, he went to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DELPHOS">Delphos</a> to consult the oracle what course of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> he should follow; when he was advised to go to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>. He accordingly went thither about 18 years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, and studied under <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a> till he was 37. By this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> he had spent his whole fortune; and we are told that he got his living by selling powders, and some receipts in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHARMACY">pharmacy</a>. He Aristotle followed his studies with most extraordinary diligence, so that he soon surpassed all in Plato's school. He ate little, and slept less; and that he might not oversleep himself, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIOGENES">Diogenes</a> Laertius tells us, that he lay always with one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> out of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a>, having a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> in it, which, by its falling into a basin of the same metal, awakened him. We are told that Aristotle had several conferences with a learned Jew at Athens, and that by this means he instructed himself in the sciences and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> of the Egyptians, and thereby saved himself the trouble of travelling into <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>. When he had studied about 15 years under Plato, he began to form different tenets from those of his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, who became highly piqued at his behaviour. Upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Plato, he quitted Athens; and retired to Atarneus, a little city of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSIA">Mysia</a>, where his old friend Hermias reigned. Here he married Pythias, the sister of this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, whom he is said to have loved so passionately, that he offered sacrifice to her. Some time after, Hermias having been taken prisoner by Meranion, the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>'s general, Aristotle went to Mitylene the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LESBOS">Lesbos</a>, where he remained till <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> king of Macedon having heard of his great reputation, sent for him to be <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a> to his son Alexander, then about 14 years of age: Aristotle accepted the offer; and in eight years taught him <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY"><a class="xref" hr</a>ef="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> philosophy, ethics, politics, with a certain sort of philosophy, according to Plutarch, which he taught nobody else. Philip erected <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of Aristotle; and for his sake rebuilt Stagyra, which had been almost ruined by the wars. The last fourteen years of his life he spent mostly at Athens, surrounded with every assistance which men and books could afford him for prosecuting his philosophical inquiries. The <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> of Alexander's name, which then filled the world, ensured tranquillity and respect to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> whom he distinguished as his friend: but after the premature death of that illustrious protector, the invidious jealousy of priests and sophists inflamed the malignant and superstitious fury of the Athenian populace; and the same odious passions which proved fatal to the offensive virtue of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOCRATES">Socrates</a>, fiercely assailed the fame and merit of Aristotle. To avoid the cruelty of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a>, he secretly withdrew himself to Chalcis in Euboea. This <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> was sufficiently justified by a prudent regard to his personal safety; but lest his conduct should appear unmanly, when contrasted with the firmness of Socrates in a similar situation, he condescended to apologise for his flight, by saying, that he was unwilling to afford the Athenians a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> opportunity "to sin against philosophy." He seems to have survived his retreat from Athens only a few months; vexation and regret probably ended his days. Besides his treatises on philosophy, he wrote also on <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, rhetoric, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>, &c. to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of 400 treatises, according to Diogenes Laertius; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> more, according to Francis Patricius of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>. An account of such as are extant, and of those said to be lost, may be seen in Fabricius's Bibliotheca Graeca. He left his writings with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOPHRASTUS">Theophrastus</a>, his beloved <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> and successor in the Lyceum; and forbade that they should ever be published. Theophrastus, at his death, trusted them to Neleus, his good friend and disciple: whose heirs buried them in the ground at Scopis, a town of Troas, to secure them from the king of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERGAMUS">Pergamus</a>, who made great search everywhere for books to adorn Aristotle's library. Here they lay concealed 160 years, until, being almost spoiled, they were sold to one Apellicon, a rich citizen of Athens. Sylla found them at this man's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, and ordered them to be carried to Rome. They were some time after purchased by Tyrannion a grammarian: and Andronicus of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RHODES">Rhodes</a> having bought them of his heirs, was in a manner the first restorer of the works of this great <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>; for he not only repaired what had been decayed by time and ill keeping, but also put them in a better order, and got them copied. There were many who followed the doctrine of Aristotle in the reigns of the 12 Caesars, and their numbers increased much under Adrian and Antoninus: Alexander Aphrodisius was the first professor of the Peripatetic philosophy at Rome, being appointed by the emperors Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus; and in succeeding ages the doctrine of Aristotle prevailed among almost all men of letters, and many commentaries were written upon his works. The first doctors of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> disapproved of the doctrine of Aristotle, as allowing too much to reason and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>; but Antoninus bishop of Laodicea, Didymus of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>, St Jerome, St Augustin, and several others, at length wrote and spoke in favour of it. In the sixth age <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOETHIUS">Boethius</a> made him known in the west, and translated some of his pieces into Latin. But from the time of Boethius to the eighth age, Joannes Damascenus was the only man who made an abridgement of his philosophy, or wrote any thing concerning him. The Grecians, who took great pains to restore learning in the 11th and following ages, applied much to the works of this philosopher, and many learned men wrote commentaries on his writings: amongst these were Alfarabins, Algazel, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-AVICENNA">Avicenna</a>, and Averroes. They taught his doctrine in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, and afterwards at Cordova in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>. The Spaniards introduced his doctrine into France, with the commentaries of Averroes and Avicenna; and it was taught in the university of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, until Amauri having supported some particular tenets on the principles of this philosopher, was condemned for <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERESY">heresy</a>, in a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> held there in 1210, when all the works of Aristotle that could be found were burnt, and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> of them forbidden under pain of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXCOMMUNICATION">excommunication</a>. This prohibition was confirmed, as to the physics and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METAPHYSICS">metaphysics</a>, in 1215, by the pope's legate; though at the same time he gave leave for his logic to be read, instead of St Augustin's, used at that time in the university. In the year 1265, Simon, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a> of St Cecil, and legate from the holy see, prohibited the reading of the physics and metaphysics of Aristotle. All these prohibitions, however, were taken off in 1366; for the cardinals of St Mark and St Martin, who were deputed by Pope Urban V. to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REFORM">reform</a> the university of Paris, permitted the reading of these books which had been prohibited; and in the year 1448, Pope Stephen approved of all his works, and took care to have a new translation of them into Latin.

ARISTOXENUS

Pages 708-710

one of the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> musical writers, was born at Tarentum, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> in Magna Graecia, now <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALABRIA">Calabria</a>. He was the son of a musician, and it appears that he lived about the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Alexander the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> and his successors. His Harmonics ARI <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARITHMETIC">ARITHMETIC</a> Is a science which explains the properties of numbers, and shows the method <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> art of computing by them. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of Arithmetic. At what time this science was first introduced into the world, we can by no means determine. That some <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of it, however, was coeval with the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> is absolutely certain. We cannot conceive how any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> endowed with reason can be without some knowledge of numbers. We are indeed told of nations in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a> who have no word in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> to express a greater <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> than three; and this they call pectarraroincoroae: but that such nations should have no idea of a greater number than this, is absolutely incredible. Perhaps they may compute by threes, as we compute by tens; and this may have occasioned the notion that they have no greater number than three. But though we cannot suppose any <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, or indeed any single person, ever to have been without some knowledge of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between greater and smaller numbers, it is possible that mankind may have subsisted for a considerable time without bringing this science to any perfection, or computing by any regular <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a>, as 10, 60, &c. That this, however, was very early introduced into the world, even before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a>, we may gather from the following <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> in Enoch's prophecy, as mentioned by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APOSTLE">apostle</a> Jude: "Behold, the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> cometh with ten thousands of his saints." This shows, that even at that time men had <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> of numbers as <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> as we have at this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, and computed them also in the same manner, namely, by tens. The directions also given to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOAH">Noah</a> concerning the dimensions of the ark, leave us no room to doubt that he had a knowledge of numbers, and of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> likewise. When Rebekah was sent away to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABRAHAM">Abraham</a>'s son, her relations wished she might be the mother of thousands of millions; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they were totally unacquainted with the rule of multiplication, it is difficult to see how such a wish could have been formed. It is probable, therefore, that the four <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FUNDAMENTAL">fundamental</a> rules of Arithmetic have always been known to some nation or other. No doubt, as some nations, like the Europeans formerly, and the Africans and Americans now, have been immersed in the most abject and deplorable state of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a>, they might remain for some time unacquainted with numbers, except such as they had immediate occasion for; and, when they came afterwards to improve, either from their own industry, or hints given by others, might fancy that they themselves, or those from whom they got the hints, had invented what was known <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> before. The Greeks were the first European nation among whom arithmetic arrived at any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of perfection. M. Goguet is of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that they first used pebbles in their calculations: a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of which he imagines is, that the word ἀριθμός, which comes from ἀρίθμειν, a little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, or flint, among other things, signifies to calculate. The same, he thinks, is probable of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>; and derives the word calculation from the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a> (calculi) in their first arithmetical operations. If this method, however, was at all made use of, it must have been but for a short time, since we find the Greeks very early made use of the letters of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPHABET">alphabet</a> to represent their numbers. The 23 letters of their alphabet taken according to their order, at first denoted the numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9, 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80, 100, 200, 300, 400, 500, 600, 700, and 800; to which they added the three following, Θ, Ψ, Δ, to represent 6, 92, and 900. The difficulty of performing arithmetical operations by such marks as these may easily be imagined, and is very conspicuous from <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHIMEDES">Archimedes</a>'s treatise concerning the dimensions of a circle. The Romans followed a like method; and besides <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> for each <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of classes, they introduced others for five, fifty, and five hundred. Their method is still used for distinguishing the chapters of books, and some other purposes. Their numeral letters and values are the following: I V X L C D M One, five, ten, fifty, one hundred, five hundred, one thousand. Any number, however great, may be represented by repeating and combining these according to the following rules: 1st, When the same <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> is repeated twice, or oftener, its value is represented as often. Thus II signifies two; XXX thirty; CC two hundred. 2d, When a numeral letter of lesser value is placed after one of greater, their values are added: thus XI signifies signifies eleven, LXV sixty-five, MDCXXVIII one thousand six hundred and twenty-eight. 3d, When a numeral letter of lesser value is placed before one of greater, the value of the lesser is taken from that of the greater: thus IV signifies four, XL forty, XC ninety, CD four hundred. Sometimes IC is used instead of D for 500, and the value is increased ten times by annexing O to the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>.

ARITHMETIC

Intermediate Decimals. late, is equal to one whose numerator is the circulating figures, and its denominator a like <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of 9's. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the numerator be 1, the vulgar fraction is reduced to that form by multiplying both terms into the circle of the decimal; and if the numerator be more than 1, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> decimal is found by multiplying that which corresponds to the numerator 1 into any other numerator. Thus \( \frac{7}{9} = .142857_1 = \frac{142857}{999999} \) and \( \frac{7}{9} = .027_1 = \frac{27}{999} \). Hence we may infer, that pure circulates are equal in value to vulgar fractions whose numerators consist of the circulating figures, and denominators of as many 9's as there are places in the circle. To <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> this in another point of view, we shall reduce a vulgar fraction, whose numerator consists entirely of 9's, to a decimal. \[ \begin{<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARRAY">array</a>}{c} \frac{7}{9} = .142857_1 = \frac{142857}{999999} \\ \frac{9}{9} = .375000_1 = \frac{375000}{999999} \\ \end{array} \] The remainder is now the same as the dividend, and therefore the quotient must circulate; and, in general, since any number with 3 cyphers annexed, may be divided by 1000, without a remainder, and quotes the significant figures; therefore, when divided by 999, it must quote the same figures, and leave an equal remainder. This also applies to every divisor which consists entirely of 9's. Circles of two places, therefore, signify ninety-ninth parts; circles of 3 places, signify <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> hundred and ninety-ninth parts; and so on. The value of circulating decimals may also be illustrated by adding the values of the places. Thus, if two figures circulate, the first circle signifieth hundredth parts, and every following circle signifies one hundred times less than the preceding; and their values added, as in p. 649. col. 2. par. 3. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> approach nearer to ninety-ninth parts than any assigned <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a>, but will never exactly complete it. All denominators which are powers of 3, except 9, produce pure circulates; and the number of places in the circle is equal to the quotient of the denominator divided by 9. Thus, \( \frac{7}{9} = .037_1 \), a circle of 3 places, and 27 divided by 9 = 3. \( \frac{1}{9} = .012345679_1 \), a circle of 9 places, and 81 divided by 9 = 9. These decimals may be formed, by dividing the numerator by the component parts of the denominator. In the first example, the component parts of the numerator are 9 and 3. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> by 9 quotes a pure circulate, and the circulating <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> is not 3, 6, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 9, if the vulgar fraction be in its lowest terms. And any other repeating figure divided by 3 quotes a pure circulate of 3 places; for the first individual must leave a remainder of 1 or 2. If the first remainder be 1, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> remainder is 2, (because, if 1 be prefixed to the repeating figure, and the 3's be <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> out, the result is 2), and, for a like reason, the third individual clears off without a remainder. If the first remainder be 2, the second is (twice 2 or 4, with the 3's cast out, or) 1, and the third 0; so the circle is always complete at 3 places, and the division begins anew. The sum of such a circle cannot be a multiple of 3; for since the repeating figure is not 3, nor any of its multiples, the sum of 3 places is not a multiple of 9, and therefore cannot be divided by 9, nor twice by 3, without a remainder. Again, If the decimal equal to \( \frac{7}{9} \) be divided by 3, we shall obtain the decimal equal to \( \frac{1}{3} \). The dividend, as we have shown already, is a pure circulate of 3 places, whose sum is not a multiple of 3. Therefore, when divided by 3, the first circle leaves a remainder of 1 or 2, which being prefixed to the second, and the division <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a>, the remainder at the end of the second circle, is 2 or 1, and at the end of the third circle, there is no remainder; all which may be illustrated by casting out the 3's. The division being completed at 9 places, finishes the circle; and it may be shown, as before, that the sum of these places is not a multiple of 3. The learner will apprehend all this if he reduce these, or the like vulgar fractions, to decimals, by successive divisions. \[ \begin{array}{c} 27 = 9 \times 3, \text{and } 9(1.000.1111_1, \text{and } 3) \times 1111_1(0.037_1, \\ 81 = 27 \times 3, \text{and } 3) \times 37.037_1(0.012345679_1. \end{array} \] For the same reason, if any circulating decimal, not a multiple of 3, be divided by 3, the quotient will circulate thrice as many places as the dividend; and if any circulate obtained by such division be multiplied by 3, the circle of the product will be restricted to one-third of the places in the multiplicand. All vulgar fractions, whose denominators are multiples of 2, 5, or their powers, except those already considered, produce mixed circulates; for they may be reduced by dividing by the component parts of the denominator. The first divisor is 2, 5, or some of their powers, and therefore gives a fine quotient. The second divisor is none of the numbers enumerated p. 650. col. 2. par. 2. and therefore gives a circulating quotient when the significant figures of the dividend are exhausted, and cyphers annexed to the remainder. \[ \begin{array}{c} Ex. \frac{7}{9} = \frac{216}{27} = \frac{27 \times 8}{27}, \\ 216 \times 1.000(0.004629_1, \text{or } 8) \times 1.000_1, \\ 864 \times 27 = 125(0.004629_1, \\ 108_1. \end{array} \] All mixed circulates are derived from vulgar fractions. The reader will easily perceive, that when a decimal is formed from a vulgar fraction, whose numerator is 1, when the remainder 1 occurs in the division the decimal is a pure circulate; but if any other remainder occurs twice, the decimal is a mixed circulate. We are to show that this last will never happen, unless the divisor be a multiple of 2, 5, or their powers. If two numbers be prime to each other, their product will be prime to both; and if two numbers be proposed, whereof the first does not <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> the second, it will not measure any product of the second, if the multiplier be prime to the first. Thus, because 7 does not measure 12, it will not measure any product of 12 by a multiplier prime to 7. For instance, it will not measure $12 \times 3$, or 36. Otherwise, the quotient of 12 divided by 7, or $\frac{12}{7}$ multiplied by 3, would be a whole number, and $5 \times 3$ would be measured by 7, which it cannot be, since 5 and 3 are both prime to 7. Now, if we inspect the foregoing operation, we shall perceive that the product of 136, the remainder where the decimal begins to circulate, multiplied by 999, is measured by the denominator 216. But 999 is not measured by the denominator, otherwise the decimal would have been a pure circulate; therefore 126 and 136 are not prime to each other, but have a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> measure, and that measure must apply to 864, a multiple of 126, and to 1000, the sum of 136 and 864; see p. 642, col. 2, par. ult. &c. But it was proven, p. 649, col. 1, par. 1. that no numbers, except the powers of 5 and 2, measure a number consisting of 1 with cyphers annexed; consequently the denominator must be measured by a power of 2 or 5. The reader will perceive, that the exponent of the power must be the same as the number of cyphers annexed to 1, or as the number of figures in the finite <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the decimal. We shall now recapitulate the substance of what has been said with respect to the formation of decimals: 2, 5, and their powers, produce finite decimals, by p. 649, col. 1, par. 3, &c. and the number of places is measured by the exponent of the power; 3 and 9 produce pure repeaters (p. 649, col. 2, par. 2.) The products of 2, 5, and their powers, by 3 or 9, produce mixed repeaters by p. 649, col. 2, par. ult.; their products by other multipliers, produce mixed circulates by p. 649, col. 2, par. ult.; and all numbers of which 2 and 5 are not aliquot parts, except 3 and 9, produce pure circulates. To find the form of a decimal corresponding to any denominator, divide by 2, 5, and 10, as often as can be done without a remainder; the number of divisions shows how many finite places there are in the decimal, by p. 651, col. 2, par. 3. If the dividend be not exhausted by these divisions, divide a competent number of 9's by the last quotient, till the division be completed without a remainder: the number of 9's required show how many places there are in the circle; and the reason may be inferred from p. 650, col. 2, par. 5. We shall conclude this subject by marking <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the decimal produced by vulgar fractions, whose numerator is 1, and denominator 30; and under that the reader may observe their connexion with the denominators. Rules for reducing intermediate decimals to vulgar fractions. I. "If the decimal be a pure repeater, place the repeating figure for the numerator, and 9 for the denominator." II. "If the decimal be a pure circulate, place the circulating figures for the numerator, and as many 9's as there are places in the circle for the denominator." III. "If there be cyphers prefixed to the repeating or circulating figures, annex a like number to the 9's in the denominator." IV. "If the decimal be mixed, subtract the finite part from the whole decimal. The remainder is the numerator; and the denominator consists of as many 9's as there are places in the circle, together with as many cyphers as there are finite places before the circle." Thus, $235.62 = \frac{23562}{99999}$ From the whole decimal $23562$ We subtract the finite part $235$ and the remainder $23327$ is the numerator. The reason may be illustrated by dividing the decimal into two parts, whereof one is finite, and the other a pure repeater or circulate, with cyphers prefixed. The sum of the vulgar fractions corresponding to these will be the value of the decimal sought. $235.62$, may be divided into $235\overline{62}$ by Rule I. and $.000\overline{62} = \frac{62}{99999}$ by Rules II. III. In order to add these vulgar fractions, we reduce them to a common denominator; and, for that purpose, we multiply both terms of the former by 99, which gives $\frac{23327}{99999}$; then we add the numerators. $235$ or by method explained p. 628, col. 1, par. 3. $\begin{array}{c} 99 \\ 2115 \\ 2115 \\ \end{array}$ Sum of numerators. $23500$ $23265$ or $23562$ $62$ $235$ $23265$ $23265$ $23327 - 23327$ The value of circulating decimals is not altered, though one or more places be separated from the circle, and considered as a finite part, providing the circle be completed. For example, .27 may be written $2\overline{72}$, $\frac{27}{99}$, or $\frac{27}{99}$, which is also the value of .27. And if two or more circles be joined, the value of the decimal is still the same. Thus, $27\overline{72} = \frac{2772}{9999}$, which is reduced by dividing the terms by 101 to $\frac{27}{99}$. All circulating decimals may be reduced to a similar form, having a like number both of finite and circulating places. For this purpose, we extend the finite part of each as far as the longest, and then extend all the circles to so many places as may be a multiple of the number of places in each. Ex.: .34725; extended, .34725725725725, 14562, 14562456245624, Here the finite part of both is extended to two places, and the circle to 12 places, which is the least multiple for circles of 3 and 4 places. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">Sect</a>. II. Addition and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SUBTRACTION">Subtraction</a> of Intermediate Decimals. To add repeating Decimals. "Extend the repeating figures one place beyond the longest finite ones, and when you add the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLUMN">column</a>, carry to the next by 9." Ex.: .37524 or .37524 .23 .296 .8 88888 .328 .42 .643 643 .469 .7548 .73 73333 .30 .31 To subtract repeating Decimals. "Extend them till they become similar (p. 652, col. 1, par. ult. &c.) and when you add the right-hand column, include the figure which would have been carried if the circle had been extended further." This occurs in Ex. 2. Note 3. The sum of the circles must be considered as a similar circle. If it consist entirely of cyphers, the amount is terminate. If all the figures be the same, the amount is a repeater. If they can be divided into parts exactly alike, the amount is a circle of fewer places; but, for the most part, the circle of the sum is similar to the extended circles. III. Multiplication of Intermediate Decimals. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">Case</a> I. "When the multiplier is finite and the multiplicand repeats, carry by 9 when you multiply the repeating figure: The right-hand figure of each line of the product is a repeater; and they must be extended and added accordingly." Ex. .13494 .376 9446x 800668 4048333 .0495246x If the sum of the right-hand column be an even number of 9's, the product is finite; otherwise, it is a repeater. Case II. "When the multiplier is finite, and the multiplicand circulates, add to each product of the right-hand figure the carriage which would have been brought to it if the circle had been extended. Each line of the product is a circle similar to the multiplicand, and therefore they must be extended and added accordingly." The product is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> a circulate similar to the multiplicand; sometimes it circulates fewer places, repeats, or becomes finite; it never circulates more places. Ex. .3746x X .235 1. .674, X .78 235, 2. .37, X .86 3. .625, X .42 187,32, 4. .4793, X .48 1123,93, 5. .375, X .124 7492,92, 6. .2963, X .36 .08804,19, Case III. "When the multiplier repeats or circulates, find the product as in infinite multipliers, and place under it the products which would have arisen from the repeating or circulating figures, if extended." Ex. 1st.] .958+.8 2d.] .784+.36 8 7664 4704 7664 2352 7664 7664 28224 7664 28224 .8513 .284,09, It is evident, that if a repeating multiplier be extended to any length, the product arising from each figure will be the same as the first, and each will stand one place to the right hand of the former. In like manner, if a circulating multiplier be extended, the product arising from each circle will be alike, and will stand as many places to the right hand of the former as there are figures in the circle. In the foregoing examples, there are as many of these products repeated as is necessary for finding the total product. If we place down more, or extend them further, it will only give a continuation of the repeaters or circulates. This is obvious in Ex. 1st and 2d. As the learner may not comprehend it so readily in Ex. 3d. when the multiplicand is a circulate, and consequently each line of the product is also a circulate, we have divided it into columns, whose sums exhibit the successive circles. The sum of the first column is $38,961037$, and there is a carriage of 1 from the right-hand column, which completes $38,961038$. This one is supplied from the three first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> of the second column, the sum of which is $999999$, and being increased by 1 in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of the carriage from the third column, amounts to $1,000000$, and therefore carries 1 to the first column, and does not affect the sum of the remaining lines, which are the same as those of the first column. The third column contains two sets of these lines, which amount to $999999$, beside the lines which compose the circle. Each of these sets would be completed into $1,000000$ by the carriage from the 4th column, if extended, and each would carry 1 to the second column. One of these would complete the sum of the three first lines, and the other would complete the sum of the circle. In like manner, if the circles be extended ever so far, the increasing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRIAGES">carriages</a> will exactly answer for the increasing deficiencies, and the sum will be always a continuation of the circle; but the product could not circulate, unless the sum of the lines marked off in the second column had consisted entirely of 9's; or had been some multiple of a number of 9's; and the circles must be extended till this take place, in order to find the complete product. The multiplication of interminate decimals may be often facilitated, by reducing the multiplier to a vulgar fraction, and proceeding as directed p. 643. col. 1. Thus, \[ \begin{align*} 4th.] & \quad .3824 \times \frac{7}{5} = \frac{2}{5} \\ & \quad 7 \\ & \quad 26768 \\ & \quad 9)2.6768 \\ & \quad 9742 \\ & \quad 68 \\ & \quad 90)8.832 \\ & \quad 9813. \end{align*} \] Therefore, in order to multiply by 3, we take one-third part of the multiplier; and, to multiply by 6, we take two-thirds of the same. Thus, \[ \begin{align*} 6th.] & \quad .784 \times \frac{3}{7} = \frac{2}{7} \\ & \quad 3)1.7522 \\ & \quad 2613 \\ & \quad 58408 \end{align*} \] As the denominator of the vulgar fractions always consists of 8's, or of 9's with cyphers annexed, we may <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRACTION">contraction</a> explained p. 631. col. 1. par. ult. &c.; and this will <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> us exactly to the same operation which was explained p. 653. col. 2. par. ult. &c. on the principles of decimal arithmetic. \[ \begin{align*} 8th.] & \quad .735 \times 3.26 = \frac{855}{365} \\ & \quad 323 \\ & \quad 323 \\ & \quad 1390 \\ & \quad 1470 \\ & \quad 1668 \\ & \quad 2205 \\ & \quad 834 \\ & \quad 99)2(37405 \\ & \quad 237405 \\ & \quad 2374 \\ & \quad 23 \\ & \quad 239803, \end{align*} \] When the multiplier is a mixed repeater or circulate, we may proceed as in Ex. 5th and 8th; or we may divide the multiplier into two parts, of which the first is finite, and the second a pure repeater or circulate, with cyphers prefixed, and multiply separately by these, and add the products. Thus, \(.384 \times .23\) or by \(.2 = .0768\) or thus, \(.384\) and by \(.05 = .02138\) \(.23\) \(.09813\) \(9)1920\) \(2132\) \(768\) \(09813\) In the following examples, the multiplicand is a repeater; and therefore the multiplication by the numerator of the vulgar fraction is performed as directed p. 653. col. 2. par. 2. In Ex. 13th, we have omitted the products of the divisor, and only marked down the remainders. These are found, by adding the left-hand figure of the dividual to the remaining figures of the same. Thus, 363 is the first dividual; and 3, the left-hand figure, added to 63, the remaining figures, gives 66 for the first remainder; and the second dividual, 666, is completed by annexing the circulating figure 6. The reason of which may be explained as follows. The highest place of each dividual shows, in this example, how many <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HUNDREDS">hundreds</a> it contains; and as it must contain an equal number of ninety-nines, and also an equal number of units, it follows, that these units, added to the lower places, must show how far the dividual exceeds that number of ninety-nines. The figure of the quotient is generally the same as the first place of the dividual, sometimes one more. This happens in the last step of the foregoing example, and is discovered when the remainder found, as here directed, would amount to 99, or upwards; and the excess above 99 only, must in that case take to complete the next dividual. The number of places in the circle of the product is sometimes very <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a>, though there be few places in the factors: but it never exceeds the product of the denominator of the multiplier, multiplied by the number of places in the circle of the multiplicand. Therefore, if the multiplier be 3 or 6, the product may circulate three times as many places as the multiplicand; if the multiplier be any other repeater, nine times as many; if the multiplier be a circulate of two places, ninety-nine times as many; thus, in the last example, .01, a circulate of two places, multiplied by .102, a circulate of two places, produces a circulate of twice 99, or 198 places. And the reason of this limit may be inferred from the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the operation; for the greatest possible number of remainders, including 0, is equal to the divisor 99; and each remainder may afford two dividuals, if both the circulating figures, 3 and 6, occur to be annexed to it. If the multiplier circulate three places, the circle of the product, for a like reason, may extend nine hundred and ninety-nine times as far as that of the multiplicand. But the number of places is often much less. The multiplication of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDETERMINATE">indeterminate</a> decimals may be proven, by altering the order of the factors, (p. 628, col. 2, par. 2,) or by reducing them both to vulgar fractions in their lowest terms, multiplying these as directed p. 643, col. 2, par. 3, and reducing the product to a decimal. Sect. IV. Division of Indeterminate Decimals. Case I. "When the dividend only is indeterminate, proceed as in common arithmetic; but, when the figures of the dividend are exhausted, annex the repeating figure, or the circulating figures in their order, instead of cyphers, to the remainder." Ex. The foregoing method is the only one which properly depends on the principles of decimal arithmetic; but it is generally shorter to proceed by the following rule. "Reduce the divisor to a vulgar fraction, multiply the dividend by the denominator, and divide the product by the numerator." Ex. 1st.] Divide .37845 by $8 = \frac{3}{8}$. 2d.] Divide .65328 by $8 = \frac{3}{8}$. Note 1. Division by 3 triples the dividend, and division by 9 increases the dividend one half. Note 2. When the divisor circulates, the denominator of the vulgar fraction consists of 9's, and the multiplication is sooner performed by the contraction explained p. 628. col. 1. par. 1. It may be wrought in the same way, when the divisor repeats, and the denominator, of consequence, is 9. Note 3. If a repeating dividend be divided by a repeating or circulating divisor; or, if a circulating dividend be divided by a similar circulating dividend; or, if the number of places in the circle of the divisor be a multiple of the number in the dividend; then the product of the dividend multiplied by the denominator of the divisor will be terminate, since like figures are subtracted from like in the contracted multiplication, and consequently no remainder left. The form of the quotient depends on the divisors as explained at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, p. 649. col. 1. par. 1.—p. 651. col. 2. par. 3. Note 4. In other <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, the original and multiplied dividend are similar, and the form of the quotient is the same as in the case of a finite divisor. See p. 655. col. 2. par. ult. &c. Note 5. If the terms be similar, or extended till they become so, the quotient is the same as if they were finite, and the operation may be conducted accordingly; for the quotient of vulgar fractions that have the same denominator is equal to the quotient of their numerators. Chap. XI. OF THE <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTRACTION">EXTRACTION</a> OF ROOTS. The origin of powers by involution has already been explained under the article <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALGEBRA">Algebra</a>, No 66. There now remains therefore only to give the most expeditious methods of extracting the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUBE">cube</a> roots; the reasons of which will readily appear from what is said under that article. As for all powers above the cube, unless such as are multiples of either the square and cube, the extraction of their roots admits of no deviation from the algebraic canon which must be always constructed on purpose for them. If the root of any power not exceeding the seventh power be a single <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGIT">digit</a>, it may be obtained by inspection, from the following <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> of powers. Sect. I. Extraction of the Square Root. Rule I. "Divide the given number into periods of two figures, beginning at the right hand in integers, and pointing toward the left. But in decimals, begin at the place of hundreds, and point toward the right. Every <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> will give one figure in the root." II. "Find by the table of powers, or by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a>, the nearest lesser root of the left-hand period; place the figure so found in the quot; subtract its square from the said period, and to the remainder bring down the next period for a dividual or resolvend." III. "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">Double</a> the quot for the first part of the divisor; inquire how often this first part is contained in the whole resolvend, excluding the units place; and place the figure denoting the answer both in the quot and on the right of the first part; and you have the divisor complete." IV. "Multiply the divisor thus completed by the figure put in the quot; subtract the product from the resolvend, and to the remainder bring down the following period for a new resolvend, and then proceed as before." Note 1st. If the first part of the divisor, with unity supposed to be annexed to it, happen to be greater than the resolvend, in this case place o in the quot, and also on the right of the partial divisor; to the resolvend bring down another period; and proceed to divide as before. Note 2. If the product of the quotient figure into the divisor happen to be greater than the resolvend, you must go back and give a lesser figure to the quot. Note 3. If, after every period of the given number is brought down, there happen at last to be a remainder, you may continue the operation, by annexing periods or pairs of cyphers, till there be no remainder, or till the decimal part of the quot repeat or circulate, or till you think proper to limit it. Ex. 1st. Required the square root of 133225. Square number 133225(365 root 9 1 div. 66)432 resolvend. 396 product. Vol. II. Part II. 2 div. 725)3625 resolvend. 3625 product. 2d.] Required the square root of 72, to eight decimal places. After getting half of the decimal places, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> by contracted division for the other half; and obtain them with the same accuracy as if the work had been at large. 3d.] Required the square root of .2916. If the square root of a vulgar fraction be required, find the root of the given numerator for a new numerator, and find the root of the given denominator for a new denominator. Thus the square root of $\frac{3}{4}$ is $\frac{3}{2}$, and the root of $\frac{3}{5}$ is $\frac{3}{5}$; and thus the root of $\frac{3}{5} = \frac{3}{5}$. But if the root of either the numerator or denominator cannot be extracted without a remainder, reduce the vulgar fraction to a decimal, and then extract the root, as in Ex. 3d. above. Sect. II. Extraction of the Cube Root. Rule I. "Divide the given number into periods of three figures, beginning at the right hand in integers, and pointing toward the left. But in decimals, begin at the place of thousands, and point toward the right. The number of periods shows the number of figures in the root." II. "Find by the table of powers, or by trial, the nearest lesser root of the left-hand period; place the figure so found in the quot; subtract its cube from the said period; and to the remainder bring down the next period for a dividual or resolvend." The divisor consists of three parts, which may be found as follows: 40 III. "The first part of the divisor is found thus: "Multiply the square of the quot by 3, and to the pro- duct annex two cyphers; then inquire how often this first part of the divisor is contained in the resolvend, and place the figure denoting the answer in the quot." IV. "Multiply the former quot by 3, and the pro- duct by the figure now put in the quot; to this last product annex a cypher; and you have the second part of the divisor. Again, Square the figure now put in the quot for the third part of the divisor; place these three parts under one another, as in addi- tion; and their sum will be the divisor complete." V. "Multiply the divisor, thus completed, by the figure last put in the quot, subtract the product from the resolvend, and to the remainder bring down the following period for a new resolvend, and then pro- ceed as before." Note 1. If the first part of the divisor happen to be equal to or greater than the resolvend; in this case, place o in the quot, annex two cyphers to the said first part of the divisor, to the resolvend bring down another period, and proceed to divide as before. Note 2. If the product of the quotient figure into the divisor happen to be greater than the resolvend, you must go back, and give a lesser figure to the quot. Note 3. If, after every period of the given number is brought down, there happen at last to be a remainder, you may continue the operation by annexing periods of three cyphers till there be no remainder, or till you have as many decimal places in the root as you judge necessary. Ex. 1st. Required the cube root of 12812904.
