ARIUS

Pages 746-747

a divine of the fourth century, the head and founder of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARIANS">Arians</a>, a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a> which denied the eternal <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> and substantiality of the Word. He was born in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBYA">Libya</a>, near <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>. Eusebius, bishop of Nicomedea, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> favourite of Constantia, sister of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Constantine, and wife of Licinius, became a zealous promoter of Arianism. He took Arius under his protection, and introduced him to Constantia; so that the sect increased, and several <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> embraced it openly. There arose, however, such disputes in the cities, that the emperor, in order to remedy these <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIS">dis</a>- orders, was obliged to assemble the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of Nice, where, in the year 325, the doctrine of Arius was condemned. Arius was banished by the emperor, all his books were ordered to be burnt, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> pu- nishment was denounced against whoever dared to keep them. After five years' banishment, he was recalled to Constantinople, where he presented the emperor with a confession of his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, drawn up so artfully, that it fully satisfied him. Notwithstanding which, Athana- sius, now advanced to the see of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>, refused to admit him and his followers to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a>. This so enraged them, that by their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, they procured that prelate to be deposed and banished. But the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Alexandria still refusing to admit Arius into their communion, the emperor sent for him to Constantinople; where, upon delivering in a fresh con- fession of his faith in terms less offensive, the emperor commanded Alexander, the bishop of that church, to receive him the next <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> into his communion: but that very evening Arius died. The manner of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> was very extraordinary: as his friends were conducting him in triumph to the great church of Constantinople, Arius, pressed by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a>, stepped aside to ease himself; himself; but expired on the spot, his bowels gushing out. But the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERESY">heresy</a> did not die with the heresiarch: his party <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> still in great <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> at court. Athanasius, indeed, was soon recalled from banishment, and as soon removed again; the Arians being countenanced by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, and making and deposing bishops as it best served their purposes. In short, this sect continued with great lustre above 300 years: it was the reigning <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> for above two centuries: it was on the throne both in the east and west; it prevailed in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, France, Pannonia, and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>; and was not extirpated till about the end of the 8th century. This heresy was again set on foot in the west by Servetus, who, in 1551, wrote a little treatise against the mystery of the Trinity. After his death Arianism got footing in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENEVA">Geneva</a>; from whence it removed into <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>; but at length degenerated, in a great <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, into Socinianism. Erasmus seems to have aimed at reviving Arianism, in his Commentaries on the New <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>; and the learned Grotius seems to lean a little that way. With regard to the state of Arianism in England, it may be sufficient to observe, that from the numerous publications of that <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> which are daily making their appearance, it seems to be rather a growing, than exploded, doctrine there.

ARIUS MONTANUS

Pages 700-700

a learned Spanish divine, employed by <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> II. of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> to publish another edition of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a>, after that of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Ximenes; which he finished with applause, and died at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEVILLE">Seville</a> in 1589.

ARK

Pages 747-748
or Noah's Ark, a floating vessel built by Noah, for the preservation of his family, and the several species of animals, during the deluge. The ark has afforded several points of curious inquiry among the critics and naturalists, relating to its form, capacity, materials, &c. The wood whereof the ark was built is called in the Hebrew Gopher wood, and in the Septuagint square timbers. Some translate the original cedar, others pine, others box, &c. Pelletier prefers cedar on account of its incorruptibility, and the great plenty of it in Asia; whence Herodotus and Theophrastus relate, that the kings of Egypt and Syria built whole fleets thereof, instead of deal. The learned Mr Fuller, in his Miscellanies, has observed, that the wood whereof the ark was built was nothing but that which the Greeks call κυπαρισσος, or the cypress tree; for, taking away the termination, ku-par and gopher differ very little in sound. This observation the great Bochart has confirmed, and shown very plainly that no country abounds so much with this wood as that part of Assyria which lies about Babylon. In what place Noah built and finished his ark is no less made a matter of disputation. But the most probable opinion is, that it was built in Chaldea, in the territories of Babylon, where there was so great a quantity of cypress in the groves and gardens in Alexander's time, that that prince built a whole fleet out of it for want of timber. And this conjecture is confirmed by the Chaldean tradition, which makes Xisuthrus (another name for Noah) set sail from that country. The dimensions of the ark, as given by Moses, are 300 cubits in length, 50 in breadth, and 30 in height; which some have thought too scanty, considering the number of things it was to contain; and hence an argument has been drawn against the authority of the relation. To solve this difficulty, many of the ancient fathers and the modern critics have been put to very miserable shifts: But Buteo and Kircher have proved geometrically, that taking the common cubit of a foot and a half, the ark was abundantly sufficient for all the animals supposed to be lodged in it. Snellius computes the ark to have been above half an acre in area. Father Lamy shows, that it was 110 feet longer than the church of St Mary at Paris, and 64 feet narrower; and if so, it must have been longer than St Paul's church in London, from west to east, and broader than that church is high in the inside, and 54 feet of our measure in height; and Dr Arbuthnot computes it to have been 81,062 tons. The things contained in it were, besides eight persons of Noah's family, one pair of every species of unclean animals, and seven pair of every species of clean animals, with provisions for them all during the whole year. The former appears, at first view, almost infinite; but if we come to a calculation, the number of species of animals will be found much less than is generally imagined; out of which, in this case, are excepted such animals as can live in the water; and Bishop Wilkins shows that only 72 of the quadruped kind needed a place in the ark. By the description Moses gives of the ark, it appears to have been divided into three stories, each ten cubits or 15 feet high; and it is agreed on, as most probable, that the lowest story was for the beasts, the middle for the food, and the upper for the birds, with Noah and his family; each story being subdivided into different apartments, stalls, &c. though Josephus, Philo, and other commentators, add a kind of fourth story under all the rest; being, as it were, the hold of the vessel, to contain the ballast and receive the filth and faeces of so many animals: but F. Calmet thinks, that what is here reckoned a story, was no more than what is called the keel of ships, and served only for a conservatory of fresh water. Drexelius makes 300 apartments; F. Fournier, 333; the anonymous author of the questions on Genesis, 400; Buteo, Temporarius, Arias Montanus, Hostus, Wilkins, Lamy, and others, suppose as many partitions as there were different sorts of animals. Pelletier makes only 72, viz. 36 for the birds, and as many for the beasts. His reason is, that if we suppose a greater number, as 333 or 400, each of the eight persons in the ark must have had 37, 41, or 60 stalls to attend and cleanse daily, which he thinks impossible to have been done. But it is observed, that there is not much in this: to diminish the number of stalls without the diminution of animals is in vain; it perhaps being more difficult to take care of 300 animals in 72 stalls than in 300. As to the number of animals contained in the ark, Buteo computes that it could not be equal to 500 horses; he even reduces the whole to the dimensions of 56 pair of oxen. F. Lamy enlarges it to 64 pair of oxen, or 128 oxen; so that, supposing one ox equal to two horses, if the ark had room for 256 horses, there must have been room for all the animals. But the same author demonstrates, that one floor of it would suffice for 500 horses, allowing nine feet square to a horse. As to the food in the second story, it is observed by Buteo from Columella, that 30 or 40 pounds of hay ordinarily suffices for an ox a day; and that a solid cubit of hay, as usually pressed down in our hay ricks, Ark weighs about 40 pounds; so that a square cubit of hay is more than enough for one ox in one day. Now it appears, that the second story contained 150,000 solid cubits; which divided between 266 oxen, will afford each more hay, by two-thirds, than he can eat in a year. Bishop Wilkins computes all the carnivorous animals equivalent, as to the bulk of their bodies, and their foods, to 17 wolves, and all the rest to 280 beves. For the former he allows 1825 sheep; and for the latter, 109,500 cubits of hay: all which will be easily contained in the two first stories, and a deal of room to spare. As to the third story, nobody doubts of its being sufficient for the fowls, with Noah, his sons, and daughters. Upon the whole, the learned bishop remarks, that of the two, it appears much more difficult to assign a number and bulk of necessary things to answer the capacity of the ark, than to find sufficient room for the several species of animals already known to have been there. This he attributes to the imperfection of our list of animals, especially those of the unknown parts of the earth; adding, that the most expert mathematician at this day could not assign the proportion of a vessel better accommodated to the purpose than is here done: and hence he finally concludes, that the capacity of the ark, which had been made an objection against Scripture, ought to be esteemed a confirmation of its divine authority; since, in those ruder ages, men, being less versed in arts and philosophy, were more obnoxious to vulgar prejudices than now; so that, had it been a human invention, it would have been contrived, according to those wild apprehensions, which arise from a confused and general view of things, as much too big as it had been represented too little. But it must be observed, that, besides the places requisite for the beasts and birds, and their provisions, there was room required for Noah to lock up household utensils, the instruments of husbandry, grains, and seeds to sow the earth with after the deluge; for which purpose it is thought that he might spare room in the third story for 36 cabins, besides a kitchen, a hall, four chambers, and a space about 48 cubits in length to walk in. Ark of the Covenant, a small chest or coffer, three feet nine inches in length, two feet three inches in breadth, and two feet three inches in height, in which were contained the golden pot that held manna, and Aaron's rod, and the tables of the covenant. This coffer was made of shittim wood, and covered with a lid, which was made of solid gold. The ark was reposed in the holiest place of the tabernacle. It was taken by the Philistines, and detained 20, some say 40 years, at Kirjath-jearim; but the people being afflicted with emerods on account of it, returned it with divers presents. It was afterwards placed in the temple. The lid or covering of the ark was called the propitiatory or mercy-seat; over which were two figures placed called Cherubims, with expanded wings of a peculiar form. Here the Schechinah rested both in the tabernacle and temple in a visible cloud: hence were issued the Divine oracles by an audible voice; and the high-priest appeared before this mercy-seat once every year on the great day of expiation; and the Jews, wherever they worshipped, turned their faces towards the place where the ark stood. In the second-temple there was also an ark, made of the same shape and dimensions with the first, and put in the same place, but without any of its contents and peculiar honours. It was used as a representative of the former on the day of expiation, and a repository of the original copy of the holy Scriptures, collected by Ezra and the men of the great synagogue, after the captivity. And in imitation of this, the Jews to this day have a kind of ark in their synagogues, wherein their sacred books are reposed. This they call aron. Leo of Modena gives a description thereof in his Account of the Customs and Ceremonies of those of his Nation. "The Jews (says he), in the eastern side of their synagogues, have an ark, or armory, called aron, in memory of the ark of the covenant. In this are preserved the five books of Moses, written on vellum, with ink made on purpose," &c. Some have supposed that the figure of this ark is still remaining on the triumphal arch of Titus at Rome; though Villalpandus and others, with greater reason, are of opinion, that it is the table of shew bread. Prideaux's Con. vol. i. p. 209. Tertullian calls this ark Armarium Judai- cum; whence the phrase, to be in the armory of the synagogue, q. d. in the number of canonical writings. A chest or coffer, very nearly resembling the Jewish ark, and called the house of the God, was found in Huacheine, one of the islands in the southern sea. Mr Banks could obtain no other information concerning it than what the name imports. Hawkesworth's Account, &c. vol. ii. p. 252.

ARKLOW

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-port town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WICKLOW">Wicklow</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEINSTER">Leinster</a>. ARKWRIGHT

Pages 748-748

Sir Richard, celebrated for his <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of machinery in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPINNING">spinning</a> and carding cotton, was originally a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BARBER">barber</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> circumstances, but acquired by his inventions a very <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> fortune. About the year 1767, when he had quitted the profession of a barber, and went up and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the country buying <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, he came to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WARRINGTON">Warrington</a>. At that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, it is said, he had some <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> project in view, of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of a perpetual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>. One John Kay, a clockmaker of that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, becoming acquainted with him, endeavoured to dissuade him from this scheme, but said that much <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> might be made by spinning cotton, which he promised to describe to him. Arkwright urged as an objection, that that scheme had been the ruin of many; but he came to Kay's bedside next morning, and asked him <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he could make a small engine at a moderate expense, as this Kay had been employed to make a cotton-spinning engine for a Mr Hayes, who likewise employed himself in making cylindrical carding engines, and who was brought as a witness on the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> in which Arkwright's patent was set aside in 1795. Mr Hayes proved, that he had invented an engine of a similar <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> to Arkwright's, but had not brought it to perfection. Arkwright and Kay made application to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHERTON">Atherton</a>, Esq. now of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-LIVERPOOL">Liverpool</a>, to make such an engine; but he refused to undertake it, from the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> poverty of the former, although on the evening of the same <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> he undertook to give Kay the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of a smith, and watch-tool maker, to make the heavier parts of the engine; and Kay agreed to instruct the workmen, and to make the clockmakers share of it. In this manner Arkwright's

ARLES

Pages 751-751

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of France, in the department of the Mouths of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RHONE">Rhone</a>, formerly Provence, seated on the east side of the Rhone, on a hill, whose declivity is towards the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>. It is an archbishop's see; and is celebrated for its antiquities both within and without the city. Those of which any remains are now to be seen are the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMPHITHEATRE">amphitheatre</a>, the obelisk, the elysian fields, the sepulchres, columns with their capitals, busts, pedestals, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AQUEDUCTS">aqueducts</a>, with some remains of the capitol, and the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a> of their gods. The other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> monuments are entirely destroyed. Under the amphitheatre, in 1675, they found the statue of Venus, which was worshipped by this city; and has been since carried to the castle of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSAILLES">Versailles</a>. It is a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>-piece which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> always be admired by connoisseurs. The amphitheatre is one of the most remarkable pieces of antiquity. It was built by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, but the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> is unknown, though some say by Julius Caesar. It is of an oval form, and about 400 yards in circumference, and the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a> is 34 yards in height. The middle, called the arena, is 142 yards wide and 104 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>. The porticoes <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> piazzas are three stories, built with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a> of a prodigious size. Each of them consists of 60 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a>, which still remain; and the walls are of surprising thickness, but gone to decay. The obelisk is the only one of this kind to be seen in France. It seems to be one of the forty brought from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> to Rome, because it is of the same oriental <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANITE">granite</a> with them. They are generally full of hieroglyphic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>; but this is quite smooth. In 1675, it was found in a private garden near the walls of the city, not far from the Rhone. It consists of one piece; and is 52 feet <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, and 7 in diameter at the base. It is now supported with four lions made of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRONZE">bronze</a>; and on the top a blue <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a> is placed, with the arms of France, and over that a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>. The Pagans burying <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> called the Elysian Fields, is without the city, upon an agreeable hill, divided into two parts. The first, called Montaure, has very few tombs, they having been broken to build the walls of gardens, which are made in that place. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, called Eliscomps, contains a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>. Those of the Pagans have the letters D. M. which signify Dit's Manibus. Those of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> have a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>. Pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, silver, and bronze, are found here; as also urns, lamps, and cups, without number. Here is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> academy of sciences, consisting of thirty members, who must be natives, gentlemen, and inhabitants of the city. It enjoys the same privileges as that at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. Arles is surrounded with marshy <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>, which renders the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> full of vapours, and makes it not very wholesome. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 4° 48'. N. Lat. 43° 0'.

ARLEUX

Pages 751-751

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> town in France, in the department of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a>, with a castle. It was taken by the French in 1645, and retaken by the allies in 1711; but the French got possession again the same <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3° 6'. N. Lat. 50° 20'.

ARLON

Pages 751-751

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> town of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, formerly a strong <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, but now dismantled. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 5° 28'. N. Lat. 49° 4'.

ARM

Pages 752-752

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, is used for the branch of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> river. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a> are only parted by an arm of the sea. St George's arm in the Mediterranean is the Thracian Bosphorus. ARM is also used figuratively for power. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECULAR">secular</a> arm is the lay or temporal authority of a secular judge; to which recourse is had for the execution of the sentences passed by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> judges. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> sheds no blood: even the judges of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INQUISITION">inquisition</a>, after they have found the person guilty, surrender him to the secular arm. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of Antioch, held in 341, decrees, that recourse be had to the secular arm to repress those who refuse obedience to the church: for secular arm, they here <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> exterior power.

ARMACALES

Pages 752-752

a river of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BABYLON">Babylon</a> (Abydenus); called Posca Regia, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> Trench <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Cut (Polybius); the Royal River (<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>); Almarchur (Pliny); Naarmalcha, (Ammian); a factitious channel or cut, made by Nabuchodonosor, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORN">horn</a> or branch of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUPHRATES">Euphrates</a>, (Abydenus). The Euphrates naturally divides into two channels, one passing through Babylon, the other through <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SELEUCIA">Seleucia</a>, and then falls into the Tigris; the factitious channel between these two is the Royal River; which mixes with the Tigris, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> lower <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> than Seleucia, at Apamea, (Ptolemy).

ARMADA

Pages 752-754

a Spanish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a>, signifying a fleet of men of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. The armada which attempted to invade England in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>, is famous in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>. This armada, to which the Spaniards, in confidence of success, gave the name of Invincible, consisted of 150 ships, most of which were greatly superior in strength and size to any that had been seen before. It had on board near 20,000 <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>, and 8000 sailors, besides 2000 volunteers of the most distinguished families in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>. It carried 2650 <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> guns, was victualled for half a year, and contained such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> stores, as only the Spanish monarch, enriched by the treasures of the Indies and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, could supply. The troops on board were to be joined by 34,000 more which the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Parma had assembled in the neighbourhood of Nieuport and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUNKIRK">Dunkirk</a>. For transporting these, he had, with incredible labour, provided a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of flat-bottomed vessels, and had brought sailors to navigate them from the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> in the Baltic. Most of these vessels had been built at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTWERP">Antwerp</a>; and as he durst not venture to bring them from thence by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> to Nieuport, lest they should have been intercepted by the Dutch, he was obliged to send them along the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHELDT">Scheldt</a> to Ghent, from Ghent to <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRUGES">Bruges</a> by the canal which joins these towns, and from Bruges to Nieuport by a new canal which he dug on the present occasion. This laborious undertaking, in which several thousand workmen had been employed, was already finished, and the duke now waited for the arrival of the Spanish fleet; hoping, that as soon as it should approach, the Dutch and English ships which cruised upon the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> would retire into their harbours. When the news reached England that this mighty fleet was preparing to sail, terror and consternation universally seized the inhabitants. A fleet of not above 30 ships of war, and those very small in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a>, was all that was to oppose it by sea. All the commercial towns of England, however, were required to furnish ships for reinforcing this small <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a>. The citizens of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, instead of fifteen vessels, which they were commanded to equip, voluntarily fitted out <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> the number; and the gentry and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> equipped 43 ships at their own <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Howard of Effingham was <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a>: and under him served Drake, Hawkins, and Forbisher, all of them renowned as seamen of courage and capacity. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> fleet was stationed at <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLYMOUTH">Plymouth</a>. A smaller squadron, consisting of 40 vessels, English and Flemish, was commanded by Lord Scymour, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> son of Protector Somerset, and lay off Dunkirk in order to intercept the duke of Parma. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> forces of England were more numerous than those of the enemy, but inferior in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>. An <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of 20,000 men was disposed in different bodies along the south coast, with orders to retire backwards and waste the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they could not prevent the Spaniards from landing; 22,000 foot and 1000 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, under the command of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEICESTER">Leicester</a>, were stationed at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TILBURY">Tilbury</a>, in order to defend the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>; and the principal army, consisting of 34,000 foot and 2000 horse, commanded by Lord Hunsdon, was reserved for guarding the queen's person, and appointed to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a> whithersoever the enemy should appear. These armies, though all the Spanish forces had been able to land, would possibly have been sufficient to protect the liberties of their country. But as the fate of England, in that event, must depend on the issue of a single <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, all men of serious reflection entertained the most awful apprehensions of the shock of at least 50,000 veterans, commanded by experienced officers, under so consummate a general as the duke of Parma. The queen alone was undaunted. She issued all her orders with tranquillity, animated her people to a steady resistance, and employed every resource which either her <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> situation <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> her foreign alliances could afford her. She even appeared on horseback in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a> at Tilbury; and riding through the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>, discovered a cheerful and animated countenance, exhorted the soldiers to remember their duty to their country and their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, and professed her intention, though a woman, to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> them herself into the field against the enemy, and rather perish in battle than survive the ruin and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a> of her people. "I know (said she, intrepidly) I have but the weak and feeble arm of a woman; but I have the heart of a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>, and of a king of England too!" The heroic spirit of Elizabeth communicated itself to the army, and every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> resolved to die rather than <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DESERT">desert</a> his station. The Spanish armada was ready in the beginning of May; but its sailing was retarded by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of the marquis marquis of Santa Croce the admiral, and that also of the vice-admiral the duke of Paliano. The command of the expedition was therefore given to the duke of <a class="xref" href="../1823/vol0.html#article-MEDINA_SIDONIA">Medina Sidonia</a>, a man entirely unexperienced in sea affairs. This promotion, in some <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, served to frustrate the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, which was also rendered less suc- cessful by some other accidents. Upon leaving the port of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LISBON">Lisbon</a>, the armada next <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> met with a vio- <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LENT">lent</a> tempest, which sunk some of the smallest of their shipping, and obliged the fleet to put back into the harbour. After some time spent in refitting, they put again to sea. Being descried by Fleming, a Scotch <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIRATE">pirate</a>, who was roving in those seas, he immediately sailed towards the English fleet, and informed the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AD">ad</a>- miral of their approach. Effingham had <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> time to get out of port when he <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> the Spanish armada com- ing full sail towards him, disposed in the form of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRESCENT">crescent</a>, and stretching the distance of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> miles from the extremity of one <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> to that of the other. The English admiral considering that the Spaniards would probably be much superior to him in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> fight, by reason of the size of their ships and the number of their troops, wisely resolved to content himself with harassing them in their voyage, and with watching at- tentively all the advantages which might be derived from storms, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> winds, and such like fortuitous ac- cidents. It was not <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> before he discerned a favour- able opportunity of attacking the vice-admiral Recal- do. This he did in person; and on that occasion <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIS">dis</a>- played so much dexterity in working his ship, and in loading and firing his guns, as greatly alarmed the Spaniards for the fate of the vice-admiral. From that time they kept much closer to one another; notwith- standing which, the English on the same day attacked one of the largest galleasses. Other Spanish ships came up in time to her relief; but in their hurry one of the principal galleons, which had a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the trea- sure on board, ran foul of another ship, and had one of her <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MASTS">masts</a> broken. In <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of this misfortune she fell behind, and was taken by Sir Francis Drake; who on the same day took another capital ship, which had been accidentally set on fire. Several other encounters happened, and in all of them the English proved victorious, through the great advantage which they derived from the lightness of their ships, and the dexterity of the sailors. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SPA">Spa</a>- niards in that <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> did not sufficiently understand nau- tical <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICS">mechanics</a>, to be able to avail themselves of the unusual magnitude of their ships. The English sail- ed round them, approached or retired, with a ve- locity that filled them with amazement, and did in- finitely greater execution with their cannon; for while every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> of theirs proved effectual, their ships suf- fered very little damage from the enemy, whose guns were planted too <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, and generally spent their force in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>. The Spaniards, however, still <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to advance till they came opposite to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALAIS">Calais</a>; there the duke de Medina having ordered them to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCHOR">anchor</a>, he sent information to the duke of Parma of his arrival, and entreated him to hasten the embarkation of his forces. Farnese accordingly began to put his troops on board. But at the same time he informed Medina, that, agree- ably to the king's instructions, the vessels which he had prepared were proper only for transporting the troops, but were utterly unfit for fighting; and for this reason, till the armada were brought still nearer, and the coast cleared of the Dutch ships which had blocked up the harbours of Nieuport and Dunkirk, he could not stir from his present station, without expos- ing his army to certain ruin, the consequence of which would probably be the entire loss of the Nether- lands. In compliance with this request, the armada was ordered to advance; and it had arrived within sight of Dunkirk, between the English fleet on the one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and the Dutch on the other, when a sudden calm put a stop to all its motions. In this situation the three fleets remained for one whole day. About the mid- dle of the night a breeze sprung up; and Lord Howard had recourse to an expedient which had been happily devised on the day before. Having filled eight ships with pitch, sulphur, and other combusti- ble materials, he set fire to them, and sent them be- fore the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> against the different divisions of the Spa- nish fleet. When the Spaniards beheld these ships in flames ap- proaching towards them, it brought to their remem- brance the havoc which had been made by the fire ships employed against the duke of Parma's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> at the siege of Antwerp. The darkness of the night in- creased the terror with which their imaginations were overwhelmed, and the panic flew from one end of the fleet to the other. Each crew, anxious only for their own preservation, thought of nothing but how to escape from the present danger. Some of them took time to weigh their anchors, but others cut their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CABLES">cables</a>, and suffered their ships to drive with <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLIND">blind</a> precipitation, without considering whether they did not thereby ex- pose themselves to a greater danger than that which they were so solicitous to avoid. In this confusion the ships ran foul of one another: the shock was dreadful, and several of them received so much damage as to be rendered unfit for future <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>. When daylight returned, Lord Howard had the satisfaction to perceive that his stratagem had fully produced the desired effect. The enemy were still in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> disorder, and their ships widely separated and dispersed. His fleet had lately received a great aug- mentation by the ships fitted out by the nobility and gentry, and by those under Lord Seymour, who had left Justin de <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NASSAU">Nassau</a> as alone sufficient to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> the coast of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>. Being bravely seconded by Sir Francis Drake and all the other officers, he made haste to improve the advantage which was now presented to him, and attacked the enemy in different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> at the same time with the utmost impetuosity and ardour. The engagement began at four in the morning and lasted till six at night. The Spaniards displayed in every encounter the most intrepid bravery; but, from the causes already mentioned, they did very little exe- cution against the English; while many of their own ships were greatly damaged, and twelve of the largest were either run <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGROUND">aground</a>, or sunk, or compelled to sur- render. It was now evident that the purpose of the armada was utterly frustrated. The Spanish admiral, after many unsuccessful encounters, prepared therefore to make his way home; but as the winds were contrary to his return through the Channel, he resolved to take the the circuit of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>. The English fleet followed him for some time; and had not their ammunition fallen short, through the negligence of the public offices in supplying them, they had obliged the armada to surrender at <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a>. Such a conclusion of that vain-glorious enterprise would have been truly illustrious to the English, but the event was scarcely less fatal to the Spaniards. The armada was attacked by a violent storm in passing the Orkneys; and the ships, having already lost their anchors, were obliged to keep at sea, while the mariners, unaccustomed to hardships, and unable to manage such unwieldy vessels, allowed them to drive on the Western isles of Scotland, or on the coast of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, where they were miserably wrecked. Not one half of the fleet returned to Spain, and a still smaller proportion of the soldiers and seamen; yet <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a>, whose command of temper was equal to his ambition, received with an air of tranquillity the news of so humbling a disaster. "I sent my fleet (said he) to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a> the English, not the elements. God be praised that the calamity is not greater!" This calamity, however, was sensibly felt all over Spain, and there was scarcely a single family of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> that did not go into <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOURNING">mourning</a> for the death of some near relation; insomuch that Philip, dreading the effect which this universal <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> of sorrow might produce upon the minds of the people, imitated the conduct of the Roman <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> after the battle of Cannae, and published an edict to abridge the time of public mourning.

ARMADILLA

Pages 754-754

in Spanish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, denotes a squadron of men of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of six <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> eight, from twenty-four to fifty pieces of cannon, which the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> maintains, to prevent foreigners from trading with the Spaniards and the Indians, both in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of war and peace. The vessels of this armadilla are those that have been so much talked of, under the name of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUARDA">guarda</a> costas. They have even power to take all Spanish merchant ships they meet with on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> that have not licenses from the king. The South <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> has its armadilla as well as the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> sea. The ordinary abode of the former is at Calao, the port of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIMA">Lima</a>; that of the latter at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARTHAGENA">Carthagena</a>.

ARMADILLO

Pages 754-754

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZOOLOGY">Zoology</a>, a synonyme of the dasypus. See DASYPUS, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAMMALIA">MAMMALIA</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ARMAGEDDON

Pages 754-754

a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> spoken of in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVELATION">Revelation</a> (xvi. 16.), which literally signifies the mountain of Maggeddon <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEGIDDO">Megiddo</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> situated in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> plain at the foot of Mount Carmel, where <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> Josiah received his mortal wound in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> against <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECHO">Necho</a> king of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>. At Armageddon, the three unclean spirits, coming out of the dragon's mouth, shall gather together the kings of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> to the battle of the great <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> of God Almighty (Rev. xvi. 13. 14.). The word armageddon, according to Mr Poole, does not signify any particular place, but is here an allusion, as some think, to that of Megiddo, mentioned Judges v. 19, where Barak overcame Sisera with his great <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, and where Josiah was slain (2 Kings xxiii. 30.). Others translate this word, the mountain of the gospel, and others, the mountain of apples or <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>.

ARMAGH

Pages 754-754

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, bounded by <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOUTH">Louth</a> on the south; Lough-Neagh, on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRONE">Tyrone</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONAGHAN">Monaghan</a>, on the west; and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">Down</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> on the east, from which it is separated by the river Newry. It is in length 32 miles, in breadth 20; and is divided into five baronies, containing about 290,786 acres, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 454 English <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles. Both the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> are good, especially the latter, which is said to be the richest in Ireland; only there is a certain tract in it called the Feves, that is, hilly and barren. The county of Armagh sends two members, and the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> one, to the imperial <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. Armagh, standing near the river Kalin, gives name to the county, and is the see of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIMATE">primate</a> of all Ireland. It is said to have been founded by St Patrick in the fifth century: and in 1142, it was constituted an archbishopric, together with <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>, Cashel, and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-TUAM">Tuam</a>, by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Papyreo, with the consent of the kings, dukes, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>, abbots, and states of Ireland. This Papyreo was sent into Ireland by Pope Eugenius, to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REFORM">reform</a> the abuses that had crept into the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. Here was anciently a famous <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> built by St Columbo, or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLUMBANUS">Columbanus</a>, about the year 610. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> was often burnt, but as often rebuilt and enlarged, and particularly by Patrick Scanlain, about 1262. His successor Nicholas, son of Molissa, besides books, rich <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> vestments, and other things, bestowed on it an annual pension of twenty marks. He appropriated also to his see the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANOR">manor</a> of Dromyskin. He died the 10th of May, 1303. This town was first subjected to the English by John de Courcy; but afterwards entirely destroyed by Tir Oen, or O'Neal, in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. However, it was afterwards recovered, rebuilt, and garrisoned by the English. The see of Armagh is valued in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s books, by an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> taken anno 30th Henry VIII. at 182l. 17s. 5½d. Irish <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> per annum, which amounts to 187l. 18s. c½d. the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between Irish and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STERLING">Sterling</a> money being at that time one-fourth. But by an extent returned in the 15th of James I. it is valued at 400l. sterling per annum, and pays so much first <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> to this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>. It is reputed to be worth annually 8000l. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> of Armagh is composed of five dignitaries and four prebendaries, who have voices in every capitular <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a>. The dignitaries are thus ranked, viz. a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAN">dean</a>, chanter, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a>, and archdeacon. There are also eight vicars choral, and an organist, attendant on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the cathedral. The vicars choral were anciently fewer; and of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> only one <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>. Primate Marsh added another priest, but without increasing the number of vicars. In the year 1720, Primate Lindsay obtained a new <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a> for enlarging the number of the said vicars to eight, and laid out upwards of 4000l. on a purchase, in augmentation of the estate of the choir. See ARMAGH, Supplement.

ARMAGNAC

Pages 754-754

formerly a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Guienne in France, which with Gascony now forms the department of Gers, is 55 miles in length, and 40 in breadth; bounded on the west by the river Garonne, on the south by Bigorre and Bearn, on the west by Gascony, and on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by Condomois and Agenois: Auch is the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> town. It is fertile in corn and wine, and carries on a considerable trade in brandy, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, and bonchretin pears, which are excellent.

ARMAMAXI

Pages 754-755

in antiquity, a kind of Scythian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARIOTS">chariots</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRIAGES">carriages</a>, composed of two <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHEELS">wheels</a>, variouly ously adorned with crowns, shields, breastplates, and other spoils, carried in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESSION">procession</a> after the images of the gods and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> men.

ARMAMENT

Pages 755-755

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> body of forces, raised and provided with the furniture of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, either for <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>.

ARMATURA

Pages 755-755

in a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, is the same with what we otherwise call armour. ARMATURA is more particularly used in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> art, for a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a>, performed with missive weapons, as darts, spears, arrows, and the like. In this sense, armatura stands contradistinguished from palaria; the latter being the exercise of the heavy-armed, the former of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>-armed. The armatura was practised with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> diligence among the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>; they had their campiductores, on purpose to instruct the tyrones <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> young <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> in it. Under it were included the throwing of the spear or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JAVELIN">javelin</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SHOOTING">shooting</a> with bows and arrows, &c. ARMATURA is also an appellation given to the soldiers who were light-armed. ARMATURA is also a denomination given to the soldiers in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>'s retinue. Of these we find two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, mentioned in the Notitia Imperii, called the armaturae seniores and armaturae juniores. Their commander was entitled tribunus armaturarum.

ARMED

Pages 755-755

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, is used when the horns, feet, beak, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> talons, of any beast or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIRD">bird</a> of prey, are of a different <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> from the rest of their body. ARMED Ship, a vessel occasionally taken into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, and employed to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> some particular <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, or attend on a fleet. She is therefore armed and equipped in all respects like a ship of war, and commanded by an officer of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a>, who has the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> and commander. All ships of this sort are upon the establishment of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s sloops, having a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a>, master, purser, surgeon, &c.

ARMENIA

Pages 755-760

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, anciently divided into Armenia <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">Major</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINOR">Minor</a>. Armenia Major, according to Strabo, was bounded on the south by Mount Taurus, which separated it from Mesopotamia; on the east, by the two Medias; on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IBERIA">Iberia</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBANIA">Albania</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rather that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of Mount <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAUCASUS">Caucasus</a> which surrounds them both; and on the west, by Armenia Minor, or the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> Paryadres, some Pontic nations, and the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUPHRATES">Euphrates</a>. The most considerable cities were Artaxata, Tigranocerta, and Theodosiopolis.—Armenia Minor was bounded on the east by the Euphrates; on the south by Mount Taurus, which separated it from <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CILICIA">Cilicia</a>; on the west and north by a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> chain of mountains, called in different places Mons Scordiscus, Amanus, and Antitaurus, by which it was separated from Cappadocia. Whence this tract received the name of Armenia is not determined. The Greeks suppose it to be so called from one Armenus who attended Jason in the Argonautic expedition, and afterwards settled in this country. Others, transforming Armenia into Aramia, derive its name from Aram the son of Shem, or from one of the kings of Armenia <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> that name. Bochart imagines it to be a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRACTION">contraction</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AAR">Aar</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> word signifying a "mountain," and Mini signifying "metal," and which was the name of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Armenia mentioned by the prophet Jeremiah. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a> derives the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Armenians from the Phrygians, by reason that several Phrygian words were crept into the ancient Armenian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. But Strabo reckons them to have been originally Syrians, which Bochart looks upon to be the most probable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>. Armenia is said to have been very early advanced to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. Berosus makes one Sytha the first founder of this <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONARCHY">monarchy</a>, whose successor Bardanes, he says, was driven out by Nimus <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASSYRIA">Assyria</a>. Plutarch mentions one Araxes king of Armenia, who in a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> with the Persians, being assured of success by an oracle, provided he sacrificed his two daughters, caused the two daughters of one Miesalcus, a nobleman of his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, to be sacrificed in their stead, flattering himself that he thereby complied with the oracle. But Miesalcus did not fail to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of his own daughters by putting the king's two daughters to death, and pursued himself so closely, that he was drowned in attempting to swim across the Araxes, which was then called Helmus. The Armenians were in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> subdued by the Medes, to whom <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTYAGES">Astyages</a> made them tributaries, but allowed them to be governed by their own kings; but on the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a> of the Median empire by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CYRUS">Cyrus</a>, the kingdom was reduced to the form of a province, and they were governed by Persian prefects or lieutenants. On the destruction of the Persian empire by Alexander the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>, Armenia fell into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the Macedonians; to whom it <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> subject till the beginning of the reign of Antiochus the Great: This <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> having appointed two prefects, called Zadriades and Artaxias, to govern Armenia, they excited the people to a revolt, and caused themselves to be proclaimed kings of the provinces over which they presided. Antiochus being then very young, they were attended with success beyond their <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPECTATION">expectation</a>; which encouraged them to attempt the enlargement of their territories. Accordingly, invading the neighbouring countries, they took from the Medes the provinces of Caspiana, Phaunitis, and Basoropida; from the Iberians Chorzena and Gogorena on the other side of the Cyrus; from the Chalybes and Mossynæci, the provinces of Pareneta and Herexena, which bordered on Armenia Minor. On this occasion, the above-mentioned <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of the kingdom into Armenia Major and Minor first took <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. Artaxias became king of Armenia Major and Zadriades of Armenia Minor; and this distinction subsists even at this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>. By whom Artaxias was succeeded is not known; neither have we any account of the transactions of his reign, farther than that Antiochus led a powerful <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> against him and Zadriades, but without being able to recover a single province. Upon this he concluded a peace, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGNING">designing</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> upon them at a proper opportunity; portunity; but they having entered into <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> with the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, by that means secured themselves in the possession of their kingdom. After this, Artaxias was defeated and taken prisoner by Antiochus Epiphanes; but, somehow or other, seems to have been restored to his kingdom. From this time we meet with a chasm in the Armenian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> for 70 years; during which all we know is, that Tigranes, the king's son, was delivered up as an hostage to the Parthians; from whence it is plain, that the Armenians had been carrying on an unsuccessful war with that <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>. On the news of his father's death, however, the Parthians set the young king at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, having first obliged him to give up a considerable part of his kingdom by way of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RANSOM">ransom</a>. Tigranes being thus restored to his father's kingdom, was prevailed upon in the beginning of his reign to enter into an alliance with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MITHRIDATES">Mithridates</a> Eupator against the Romans, whose power began to give jealousy to all the princes of Asia. One of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> was, that Mithridates should have the cities and conquered countries, and Tigranes the captives and plunder. In <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of this, Tigranes was to invade Cappadocia, which he had lately been obliged, by a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DECREE">decree</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> of Rome, to give up to Ariobarzanes. But before either of the princes took the field, a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> was solemnized with all possible magnificence between Tigranes and Cleopatra the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Mithridates. Immediately after the nuptials, Tigranes set out on his intended expedition; and Ariobarzanes, on the first news of his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a>, abandoned his kingdom and fled to Rome. Thus Tigranes, without fighting a stroke, enriched himself with the booty, and then proclaimed Ariarathes, Mithridates's son, king of Cappadocia, to the universal satisfaction of the people. In the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time, the Syrians being harassed with a long and intestine war of the Seleucidse, invited Tigranes to come and take possession of their country; which he accordingly did, and kept it for 18 years, till he was driven out by Pompey, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a> reduced to the form of a Roman province. Encouraged by this success, he next invaded Armenia Minor; defeated and killed King Artanes, who opposed him with a considerable army; and in one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMPAIGN">campaign</a> made himself <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the whole kingdom. From Armenia Minor he marched against the Asiatic Greeks, the Adiabennians, the Assyrians, and the Gordians; carrying all before him, and obliging the people wherever he came to acknowledge him sovereign. From this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> expedition he returned home loaded with booty, which he soon after increased by the spoils of Cappadocia, invading that kingdom a second time at the instance of Mithridates, who had been obliged by the Romans to withdraw his forces from thence. From Cappadocia Tigranes, besides other booty, brought back into Armenia no fewer than 300,000 captives, having surrounded the country with his numerous forces in such a manner that none could escape. These, together with the prisoners he had taken in his two first expeditions, he employed in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Tigranocerta, which they afterwards peopled. In the mean time Mithridates, who had concluded a peace with the Romans for no other end than to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> time, sent a solemn embassy to Tigranes, inviting him to enter into a second alliance against the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> enemy. This he at first declined; but in the end was prevailed upon by his wife Cleopatra to send him considerable supplies, though he never came heartily into the war, not caring to provoke the Romans, who on their part kept fair with him, taking no notice for the present of the supplies he had sent Mithridates. That unfortunate prince being soon after defeated by Lucullus, was forced to fly for shelter into Armenia, where he met with a very <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a> reception from his son-in-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>, who would neither see him, treat with him, nor own him as his relation; however, he promised to protect his person, and allowed him in one of his castles a princely retinue, and a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> suitable to his former condition. Though this total overthrow of Mithridates might have opened the eyes of Tigranes, and made him oppose with all his might the growing power of the Romans, he foolishly left them to finish their conquest of Pontus, while he marched at the head of a very numerous army against the Parthians, with a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> to recover from them the dominions they had formerly extorted from him before they set him at liberty. These he easily retook; and not satisfied with what formerly belonged to him, he added to them all Mesopotamia, the countries that lay about <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINUS">Ninus</a> and Arbela, and the fruitful province of Mygdonia; the Parthians, though at that time a mighty people, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">flying</a> everywhere before him. From Mesopotamia Tigranes marched into Syria to quell a rebellion which had been raised by Cleopatra, surnamed Selene; who after the death of her husband Antiochus Pius, reigned jointly with her sons in that part of Syria which Tigranes had not seized on. The malcontents were quickly reduced; and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> herself was taken prisoner, and confined to the castle of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SELEUCIA">Seleucia</a>, where she was soon after put to death by the king's orders. From Syria Tigranes passed into Phoenicia, which he subdued either entirely or in great part, spreading far and wide the terror of his arms, insomuch that all the princes of Asia except those who were in alliance with the Romans, either in person or by their deputies, submitted and paid homage to the conqueror. The king, having now subdued all Syria to the borders of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, and being elated with a long course of victories and prosperous events, began to look upon himself as far above the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> of other crowned heads. He assumed the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of King of kings, and had many kings waiting upon him as menial servants. He never appeared on horseback without the attendance of four kings dressed in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIVERY">livery</a>, who ran by his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>; and when he gave answers to the nations that applied to him, the ambassadors stood on either side the throne with their hands clasped together, that attitude being of all others then accounted among the orientals the greatest acknowledgment of vassalage and servitude. In the midst of all this haughtiness, however, he was unexpectedly visited by an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a> from Lucullus the Roman general, who, without any <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a>, told him, that he came to demand Mithridates king of Pontus, who had taken refuge in his dominions, and, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of his refusal, to declare war against him. Notwithstanding his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> opinion of himself, Tigranes returned a mild answer to this message: in which, however, he refused to deliver up his father-in-law; and being Armenia, being highly provoked at Lucullus for not giving him the title of King of kings in his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a>, he did not so much as bestow upon him the title of general in his answer. In the mean time, being informed that Zarbiens king of the Gordians had entered into a private alliance with the Romans, he put him, his wife, and children to death; and then, returning into Armenia, received with the greatest pomp imaginable his father-in-law Mithridates, whom till that time he had not admitted into his presence, though he had resided a year and eight months in his dominions. They had several private conferences; and at last Mithridates was sent back to Pontus with 10,000 horse, to raise there what disturbances he could. Lucullus, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, hearing the king's <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> to protect Mithridates, immediately began his march for Armenia, at the head of only two legions of foot and 3000 horse, having left 6000 men in Pontus to keep that country quiet. Having passed the Euphrates without opposition, he detached two parties; one to besiege a city where he heard that Tigranes's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a> and concubines were kept; and the other, under Sextilius, to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLOCK">block</a> up Tigranocerta, in order to draw the king to a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>. But Tigranes, after having put to death the scout that brought him the first intelligence of the approach of the Romans, made towards Mount Taurus, which he had appointed for the place of the general rendezvous. The Roman general then despatched Muræna in pursuit of the king; who, having overtaken him in a narrow <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a>, defeated him, and, besides all the baggage, carried off a great many prisoners, the king himself have fled in the beginning of the skirmish. After this, he sent out several parties to scour the country, in order to prevent the innumerable forces of Tigranes from joining into one body. This, however, he was not able to effect; Tigranes was joined by such numbers of Gordians, Medes, Adiabenians, Albanians, Iberians, &c. that before he left Mount Taurus, his army consisted, according to Plutarch, of 150,000 foot armed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>-a-pee, 35,000 <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIONEERS">pioneers</a>, 20,000 archers and slingers, and 55,000 horse. Lucullus was so far from being dismayed at this formidable army, that the only fear he had was lest the king should follow the advice of Mithridates, which was, not to engage the Romans, but, by ravaging the country, distress them for want of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>. In order to draw him to a battle, therefore, he formed the siege of Tigranocerta, imagining that Tigranes would never suffer that fine city to be taken without making an attempt to relieve it. The event fully answered his expectations: Tigranes having called a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of war, it was unanimously resolved to attack the Romans; and Taxilis, whom Mithridates sent to dissuade the king from venturing a battle, was in danger of losing his head on account of the advice he gave. The Roman general finding Tigranes disposed to come to an engagement, left Muræna with 6000 men to carry on the siege, while he himself marched against the king's vast army with only 10,000 men according to some, and the highest computations make them no more than 18,000. The Romans were at first greatly disheartened; but being encouraged by Lucullus, they immediately broke the Armenian army, who betook themselves to flight almost at the first onset. The Romans pursued them till night, making a most terrible slaughter. Plutarch informs us, that of the Armenians, 100,000 foot were killed, and that very few of the cavalry escaped; whereas of the Romans only five men were killed and 100 wounded. Antiochus the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> mentioning this battle, says that the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> never beheld the like: and Livy, that the Romans never fought to such a disadvantage; the conquerors not amounting to a twentieth part of the conquered. Tigranes in his flight having met with his son in as forlorn a condition as himself, resigned to him his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> robes and diadem, desiring him to shift for himself and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> those royal ensigns. The young prince delivered them to a trusty friend, who, being taken by the Romans, consigned them to Lucullus. While the king was making his escape after this terrible overthrow, he was met by Mithridates, who was marching to his assistance at the head of a considerable army.
