Arras, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Araxes, is also the name of a river of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEORGIA">Georgia</a>, which discharges itself into the Caspian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARRAY">Array</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, the ranking or setting forth of a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JURY">jury</a>, or inquest of men impannelled on a cause. <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">Battle</a>-Array, the order or disposition of an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, drawn up with a view to engage the enemy. See Army. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARRAYERS">Arrayers</a>, or Arragers, Arraitores, is used in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> statutes, for such officers as had care of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> armour, and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> them duly accoutred in their kinds. In some reigns, commissioners have been appointed for this purpose. Such were the commissioners of array appointed by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I. in the year 1642. Arrefars, the remainder of a sum due, or <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> remaining in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of an accountant. It likewise signifies the money due for rent, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WAGES">wages</a>, &c. or what remains unpaid of pensions, taxes, &c. Arrentation, in the forest laws, implies the licensing the owner of lands in a forest to enclose them with a low hedge and a small ditch, in consideration of a yearly rent. Arreoyes, a secret <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> of a very singular kind, in Otaheite. See Supplement. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARREST">Arrest</a>, in English Law, (from the French word arrestor, to stop or stay), is the restraint of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s person, obliging him to be obedient to the law; and is defined to be the execution of the command of some <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of record or office of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>. An arrest is the beginning of imprisonment; where a man is first taken, and restrained of his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, by power or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of a lawful warrant. Arrests are either in civil or criminal <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>. 1. An arrest in a civil cause is defined to be the apprehending or restraining one's person by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> in execution of the command of some court. An arrest must be by corporal seizing or touching the defender's body; after which the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAILIFF">bailiff</a> may justify breaking open the house in which he is, to take him: otherwise he has no such power; but must watch his opportunity to arrest him. For every man's house is looked upon by the law to be his castle of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASYLUM">asylum</a>, wherein he should suffer no violence. Which principle is carried so far in the civil law, that, for the most part, not so much as a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> citation or summons, much less an arrest, can be executed upon a man within his own walls. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEERS">Peers</a> of the realm, members of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, and corporations, are privileged from arrests; and of course from outlawries. And against them the process to enforce an appearance must be by summons and distress infinite, instead of a captus. Also clerks, attorneys, and all other persons attending the courts of justice (for attorneys being officers of the court, are always supposed to be there attending) are not liable to be arrested by the ordinary process of the court, but must be sued by <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BILL">bill</a> (called usually a bill of privilege), as being personally present in court. Clergymen performing divine <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, and not merely staying in the church with a fraudulent <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, are for the time privileged from arrests, by statute 50 Edw. III. c. 5, and 1 Rich. II. c. 16.; as likewise members of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONVOCATION">convocation</a> actually attending thereon, by statute 8 Hen. VI. c. 1. Suitors, witnesses, and other persons, necessarily attending any courts of record upon business, are not to be arrested during their actual attendance, which includes the necessary coming and returning. Seamen in the king's service are privileged from arrests for debts under 20l. (1 Geo. II. c. 14. and 14 Geo. II. c. 38.) and soldiers or <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARINES">marines</a> are not liable to arrests for a debt of less than 10l. (30 Geo. II. c. 6. 11.). And no arrest can be made in the king's presence, nor within the verge of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, nor in any <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where the king's justices are actually sitting. The king hath moreover a special <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREROGATIVE">prerogative</a> (which indeed is very seldom exerted), that he may by his writ of protection privilege a defendant from all personal and many real suits, for one year at a time, and no longer; in respect of his being engaged in his service out of the realm. And the king also by the common law might take his creditor into his protection, so that no one might sue or arrest him till the king's debt was paid: but by the statute 25 Edw. III. c. 19. notwithstanding such protection, another creditor may proceed to judgment against him, with a stay of execution, till the king's debt be paid; unless such creditor <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> undertake for the king's debt, and then he shall have execution for both. And, lastly, By statute 29 Car. II. c. 7. no arrest can be made, nor process served, upon a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUNDAY">Sunday</a>, except for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREASON">treason</a>, felony, or <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREACH">breach</a> of the peace. 2. An arrest in a criminal cause is the apprehending or restraining one's person, in order to be forthcoming to answer an alleged crime. To this arrest all persons whatsoever are, without distinction, equally liable; and doors may be broken open to arrest the offender: but no man is to be arrested, unless <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with such a crime as will at least justify holding him to bail when taken. There is this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> also between arrests in civil and criminal cases, that none shall be arrested for debt, trespass, or other cause of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, but by virtue of a precept or commandment out of some court; but for treason, felony, or breach of the peace, any man may arrest with or without warrant or precept. But the king cannot command any one by word of mouth to be arrested; for he must do it by writ, or order of his courts, according to law: nor may the king arrest any man for suspicion of treason, or felony, as his subjects may; because <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he doth wrong, the party cannot have an action against him. Arrests by private persons are in some cases commanded. Persons present at the committing of a felony lony must <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> their endeavours to apprehend the offender, under penalty of fine and imprisonment; and they are also, with the utmost diligence to pursue and endeavour to take all those who shall be guilty thereof out of their view, upon a hue and cry levied against them. By the vagrant <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a>, 17 Geo. II. c. 5., every person may apprehend beggars and vagrants; and every private person is bound to assist an officer requiring him to apprehend a felon. In some cases likewise arrests by private persons are rewarded by law. By the 4 and 5 William and Mary, c. 8., persons apprehending highwaymen, and prosecuting them to a conviction, are entitled to a reward of 40l.; and if they are killed in the attempt, their executors, &c. are entitled to the like reward. By the 6 and 7 William III. c. 17., persons apprehending counterfeiters and clippers of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a>, and prosecuting them to conviction, are entitled to 40l. By 5 Ann. c. 31., persons who shall take any one guilty of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BURGLARY">burglary</a>, or the felonious breaking and entering any house in the daytime, and prosecute them to conviction, shall receive the sum of 40l. within one <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> after such conviction. With regard to arrests by public officers, as watchmen, constables, &c. they are either made by their own authority, which differs but very little from the power of a private person; or they are made by a warrant from a justice of peace. See WARRANT. ARREST of Judgment, in Law, the assigning <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> reason why judgment should not pass: as, Want of notice of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a>; a material defect in the pleading; when the record differs from the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEED">deed</a> impleaded; when persons are misnamed; where more is given by the verdict than is laid in the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a>, &c. This may be done either in criminal or civil cases.

ARRESTMENT

Pages 776-776

in Scots <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, signifies the securing of a criminal till <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> till he find caution to stand trial, in what are called bailable crimes. In civil <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, it signifies either the detaining of strangers, or natives in meditatio fugae, till they find caution judicio sisti, or the attaching the effects of a stranger in order to found jurisdiction. But, in the most general acceptation of the word, it denotes that diligence by which a creditor detains the goods or effects of his debtor in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of third parties till the debt due to him be either paid or secured. See LAW.

ARRESTO FACTO SUPER BONIS

Pages 776-776

&c. a writ brought by a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DENIZEN">denizen</a> against the goods of aliens found within this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, as a recompense for goods taken from him in a foreign <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>.

ARRESTS

Pages 776-776

in Farriery, mangy tumours upon a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>'s hinder legs, between the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAM">ham</a> and the patern.

ARRETIUM

Pages 776-776

(Cicero, Caesar); Arrhetium, (<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>); Urbs Arrhetinorum, (Polybius); one of the twelve <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUSCANY">Tuscany</a>, near the Arnis and Clanis, situated in a pleasant valley. Now <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AREZZO">Arezzo</a>, 42 miles east of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 13. 18. N. Lat. 43. 15.

ARRHABONARI

Pages 776-776

a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, who held that the eucharist is neither the real <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> blood of Christ, nor yet the sign of them; but only the pledge or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARNEST">earnest</a> thereof.

ARRHEPHORIA

Pages 776-776

a feast among the Athenians, instituted in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HERSE">Herse</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Cecrops. The word is composed of ἀγέλλειν, mystery, Arrhephoria, and φέρω, I carry; on account of certain mysterious things which were carried in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESSION">procession</a> at this solemnity.—Boys, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a>, as some say, girls, between <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> and twelve years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, were the ministers that assisted at this feast, and were denominated ἀγέλλεις. This feast was also called Hersiphoria, from the daughter of Cecrops, already mentioned.

ARRIAN

Pages 776-776

a famous <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> and historian under the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HADRIAN">Hadrian</a> and the two Antonines, was born at Niconedia in Bithynia. His <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> learning and eloquence procured him the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> Xenophon, and raised him to the most considerable dignities at Rome, even the consulship itself. We have four books of his Dissertations upon Epictetus, whose scholar he had been; and his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of Alexander the Great, in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> books, is greatly admired by the best judges.

ARRIEGE

Pages 776-776

a department in the south of France, at the foot of the Pyrenees, and named from a river which flows through it. The southern <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> is covered with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, which afford pasture to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> quantities of cattle; in the northern parts corn of all kinds, and vines, are cultivated. There are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, silver, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, and coal. There are a few <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> of cottons and woollens. The superficial <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of the department is 529,540 hectares, and its <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> in 1815 was 222,936. Foix is the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> town.

ARRIERE

Pages 776-776

the hinder <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POSTERIOR">posterior</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of any thing. ARRIERE Ban, in the French customs, was a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCLAMATION">proclamation</a>, whereby the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> summoned to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> all that held of him, both his vassals, i.e. the noblesse, and the vassals'of his vassals. ARRIERE Fec, or Fief, is a fee dependent on a superior one. These fees commenced, when the dukes and counts, rendering their governments <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> in their families, distributed to their officers parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> domains which they found in their respective provinces, and even permitted those officers to gratify the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> under them in the same manner.

ARROBAS

Pages 776-776
or AROBA, a weight used in Spain, Portugal, and the foreign dominions of both. The arrobas of Portugal, is also called arata, and contains thirty-two Lisbon pounds; that of Spain contains twenty-five Spanish pounds. In Peru it is called arruse.

ARROE

Pages 776-776

a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>, in the Baltic <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, a little south of the island of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FUNEN">Funen</a>. It is eight miles in length, and about two in breadth; and produces corn, aniseed, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> cattle, and horses. It has three parishes, the most considerable of which is Kopin. It stands at the south side of the island, in the bottom of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>, and has a port with some trade. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 9. 40. N. Lat. 55. 20.

ARROJO DE ST SERVAN

Pages 776-776

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, in Extremadura. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 5. 20. N. Lat. 38. 40.

ARRONDEE

Pages 776-776

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>, the arms of which are composed of sections of a circle, not opposite to each other so as to make the arms bulge out thicker in one <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> than another; but the sections of each arm lying the same way, so that the arm is everywhere of an equal thickness, and all of them terminating at the edge of the escutcheon like the plain cross.

ARROW

Pages 776-787

a missive weapon of offence, slender, pointed, pointed, and barbed, to be <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> with a bow. See <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHERY">Archery</a>. Arrow-Makers, are called fletchers; and were formerly, as well as <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOWYERS">bowyers</a>, persons of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> in the commonwealth. Arrow-heads and quarrels were to be well boched or brased, and hardened at the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> with <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STEEL">steel</a>; the doing of which seems to have been the business of the arrow-smith. Arrow-Head. See Sagittaria, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Arrow-Root. See Maranta, Botany Index. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARSACES">Arsaces</a>, otherwise <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MITHRIDATES">Mithridates</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of the Parthians, spoken of in the first book of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MACCABEES">Maccabees</a>, xiv. 2. He considerably enlarged the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARTHIA">Parthia</a> by his good conduct and valour. See Parthia. Arschin, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> used in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a> to measure stuffs. Four arsins make three yards of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. Arsenal, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> or public <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGAZINE">magazine</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> appointed for the making and keeping of arms, necessary either for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> or assault. Some derive this word from arx, a fortress; others from ars, denoting a machine; others again from arx and senatus, because this was the defence of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>: but the more probable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> derives it from the Arabic darsena, which signifies arsenal. The arsenal of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> is the place where the galleys are built and laid up. The arsenal of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> is that where the cannon or great guns are cast. Arsenic. See <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINERALOGY">Mineralogy</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a> Index. Arsenius, a deacon of the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, of great learning and piety. He was pitched upon by the pope to go to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Theodosius, as <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a> to his son Arcadius. Arsenius arrived at Constantinople in the year 383. The emperor happening one <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> to go into the room where Arsenius was instructing Arcadius, his son was seated, and the preceptor standing; at this he was exceedingly displeased, took from his son the imperial ornaments, made Arsenius sit in his place, and ordered Arcadius for the future to receive his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LESSONS">lessons</a> standing uncovered. Arcadius, however, profited but little by his tutor's instructions, for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> after he formed a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of despatching him. The officer to whom Arcadius had applied for this purpose, divulged the affair to Arsenius, who retired to the deserts of Scete, where he passed many years in the exercises of the most strict and fervent <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>. He died there, at 95 years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARSHOT">Arshot</a>, a town of the Austrian <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, situated about 14 miles east of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MECHLIN">Mechlin</a>, in E. Long. 4. 45. N. Lat. 51. 5. Arsinoe, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, on the west side of the Arabian <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a>, near its extremity, to the south of Hieropolis, (Strabo, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>); called Cleopatris by some. Another Arsinoe, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CILICIA">Cilicia</a>, (Ptolemy); and the fifth of that name in Cilicia, (Stephanus); with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> or station for ships, (Strabo). A third Arsinoe, in the south of Cyprus, with a port between Citium and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALAMIS">Salamis</a>, (Strabo). A fourth, an inland town of Cyprus, called Marium formerly, (Stephanus). A fifth in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of Cyprus, between Acamas and Soli, (Strabo); so called from Arsinoe, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> of Egypt, Cyprus being in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the Ptolemies. A sixth Arsinoe, a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> town of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CYRENE">Cyrene</a>, formerly called Teuchira. A seventh Arsinoe, in the Nomos Arsinoites, to the west of the Heracloteos, on the western <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NILE">Nile</a>, formerly called Crocodilorum Urbs, (Strabo); the name Arsinoe <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> under Adrian, (<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">Coin</a>). Ptolemy calls this Arsinoe an inland <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a>, and therefore at some distance from the Nile, with a port called <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMAIS">Ptolemais</a>. An eighth Arsinoe, a maritime town of Lycia; so called by Ptolemy <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILADELPHUS">Philadelphus</a>, after the name of his consort, which did not hold long, it afterwards recovering its ancient name Patara, (Strabo). A ninth, a town of the Troglodyte, near the mouth of the Arabian gulf, which towards Ethiopia is terminated by a promontory called Diré, (Ptolemy). This Arsinoe is called <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BERENICE">Berenice</a>, and the third of that name in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>, with the distinction Epideres; because situated on a neck of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> running out a great way into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. Arsis and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THESIS">Thesis</a>, in Music, is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> applied to compositions in which one <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> rises and the other falls. Arsmart. See Persicaria, Botany Index. Arson, in English <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, is the malicious and wilful <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> or outhouse of another <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>; which is felony at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> law. This is an offence of very great malignity, and much more pernicious to the public than simple theft: because, first, it is an offence against that <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of habitation which is acquired by the law of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> as well as by the laws of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>; next, because of the terror and confusion that necessarily attends it; and, lastly, because in simple theft the thing stolen only changes its <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, but still remains in esse for the benefit of the public; whereas, by burning, the very substance is absolutely destroyed. It is also frequently more destructive than <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> itself, of which too it is often the cause: since murder, atrocious as it is, seldom extends beyond the felonious <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> designed, whereas fire too frequently involves in the common calamity persons unknown to the incendiary, and not intended to be hurt by him, and friends as well as enemies. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARSURA">Arsura</a>, in ancient customs, a term used for the melting of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> or silver, either to refine them, or to examine their value.—The method of doing this is explained at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> Book of the Exchequer, ascribed to Gervaise, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> De officio Militis Argentariorii, being in those days of great <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, on account of the various places and different manners in which the king's <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> was paid. Arsura is also used for the loss or diminution of the metal in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a>. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> was said tot ardere denarios, to lose so many pennyweights. Arsura is also used for the dust and sweepings of silversmiths, and others, who <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> in silver, melted <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>. Art is defined by <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACON">Bacon</a>, a proper disposal of the things of nature by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> thought and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>, so as to answer the several purposes of mankind; in which sense art stands opposed to nature. Art is principally used for a system of rules serving to facilitate the performance of certain actions; in which sense it stands opposed to science, or a system of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SPECULATIVE">speculative</a> principles. Arts are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> divided into useful or mechanic, liberal or polite. The former are those wherein the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> hand and body are more concerned than the mind; of which kind are most of those which furnish us with the necessaries of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and are popularly known by the name of trades; as <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAKING">baking</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREWING">brewing</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARPENTRY">carpentry</a>, smithery, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEAVING">weaving</a>, &c.—The latter are such as depend more on the labour of the mind than that of the hand; they are the produce of the imagination, their essence consists in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>, and their end is <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>. Of this kind are <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, music, &c. Progress of the Arts. Some useful arts must be nearly coeval with the human <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a>; for food, clothing, and habitation, even in their original simplicity, require some art. Many other arts are of such antiquity as to place the inventors beyond the reach of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a>. Several have gradually crept into the world without an inventor. The busy mind, however, accustomed to a beginning in things, cannot rest till it finds or imagines a beginning to every art. The most probable conjectures of this nature the reader may see in the historical introductions to the different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>. In all countries where the people are barbarous and illiterate, the progress of arts is extremely slow. It is vouched by an old French poem, that the virtues of the loadstone were known in France before the year 1180. The mariner's compass was exhibited at Venice anno 1262, by Paulus Venetus, as his own <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a>. John Goya of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMALFI">Amalfi</a> was the first who, many years afterward, used it in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>; and also passed for being the inventor. Though it was used in China for navigation long before it was known in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, yet to this day it is not so perfect as in Europe. Instead of suspending it in order to make it act freely, it is placed upon a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a> of sand, by which every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the ship disturbs its operation. Hand-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MILLS">mills</a>, termed querns, were early used for <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRINDING">grinding</a> corn; and when corn came to be raised in greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>-mills succeeded. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">Water</a>-mills for grinding corn are described by Vitruvius. <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">Wind</a>-mills were known in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, and in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a> as early as the seventh century; and yet no mention is made of them in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> till the fourteenth. That they were not known in England till the reign of Henry VIII. appears from a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a> book of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTHUMBERLAND">Northumberland</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> with that king, stating an allowance for three mill-horses, "two to draw in the mill, and one to carry stuff to and from the mill." Water-mills for corn must in England have been of a later <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">date</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> had mirror-glasses, and employed glass to imitate crystal vases and goblets; yet they never thought of using it in windows. In the 13th century, the Venetians were the only people who had the art of making crystal glass for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRRORS">mirrors</a>. A clock that strikes the hours was unknown in Europe till the end of the 12th century. And hence the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of employing men to proclaim the hours during night; which to this day continues in Germany, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>, and England. Galileo was the first who conceived an idea that a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENDULUM">pendulum</a> might be used for measuring time; and Huygens was the first who put the idea in execution, by making a pendulum clock. Hook, in the year 1660, invented a spiral <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> for a watch, though a watch was far from being a new invention. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">Paper</a> was made no earlier than the 14th century; and the invention of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a> was a century later. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">Silk</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> were long established in Greece before silk-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORMS">worms</a> were introduced there. The manufacturers were provided with raw silk from <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>; but that commerce being frequently interrupted by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, two monks, in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTINIAN">Justinian</a>, brought eggs of the silk-worm from Hindostan, and taught their countrymen the method of managing them.—The art of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> made a very slow progress. To encourage that art in England, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> for murder was remitted, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the criminal could but read, which in law <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> is termed benefit of clergy. One would imagine that the arts must have made a very rapid progress when so greatly favoured; but there is a signal <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of the contrary: for so small an edition of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a> as 600 copies, translated into English in the reign of Henry VIII. was not wholly sold off in three years. The people of England must have been profoundly ignorant in Queen <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>'s time, when a forged clause added to the 20th article of the English creed passed unnoticed till about 50 years ago. The discoveries of the Portuguese on the west <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, is a remarkable instance of the slow progress of arts. In the beginning of the 15th century, they were totally ignorant of that coast beyond <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> Non, 28 degrees north latitude. In 1410, the celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> Henry of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a> fitted out a fleet for discoveries, which proceeded along the coast to Cape Bajadore in 28 deg., but had not courage to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> it. In 1418, Tristan Vaz discovered the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> Porto Santo; and the year after, the island <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MADEIRA">Madeira</a> was discovered. In 1439, a Portuguese <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> doubled Cape Bajadore; and the next year the Portuguese reached Cape <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLANCO">Blanco</a>, lat. 20 degrees. In 1446, Nuna Tristan doubled Cape de Verd, lat. 14.40. In 1448, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DON">Don</a> Gonzallo Vallo took possession of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AZORES">Azores</a>. In 1449, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> of Cape de Verd were discovered for Don Henry. In 1471, Pedro d'Escovar discovered the island St Thomas and Prince's island. In 1484, Diego Cam discovered the kingdom of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGO">Congo</a>. In 1486, Bartholomew Diaz, employed by John II. of Portugal, doubled the Cape of Good Hope, which he called Cabo Tormentoso, from the tempestuous <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> he found in the passage. The exertion of national spirit upon any particular cause art, promotes <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a> to prosecute other arts. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, by constant <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a>, came to excel in the art of war, which led them naturally to improve upon other arts. Having, in the progress of society, acquired some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> and polish, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TALENT">talent</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> broke forth. Nevius composed in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> books of the Punic war; besides comedies, replete with bitter raillery against the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>. Ennius wrote annals, and an epic poem. Lucius Andronicus was the father of dramatic poetry in Rome. Pacuvius wrote tragedies. Plautus and Terence wrote comedies. Lucilius composed satires, which Cicero esteems to be slight and void of erudition. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FABIUS_PICTOR">Fabius Pictor</a>, Cincius Alimentus, Piso Frugi, Valerius Antias, and Catto, were rather annalists than historians, confining themselves to naked facts, ranged in order of time. The genius of the Romans for the fine arts was much inflamed by Greek learning, when free intercourse between the two nations was opened. Many of those who made the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> in the Roman state commenced menced authors; Cæsar, Cicero, &c. Sylla composed <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMOIRS">memoirs</a> of his own transactions, a work much esteemed even in the days of Plutarch. The progress of art seldom fails to be rapid, when a people happen to be roused out of a torpid state by some fortunate change of circumstances. Prosperity, contrasted with former abasement, gives to the mind a spring, which is vigorously exerted in every new pursuit. The Athenians made but a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> figure under the tyranny of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PISISTRATUS">Pisistratus</a>; but upon regaining freedom and independence, they were converted into heroes. <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILETUS">Miletus</a>, a Greek city of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IONIA">Ionia</a>, being destroyed by the king of Persia, and the inhabitants made slaves, the Athenians, deeply affected with the misery of their brethren, boldly attacked the king in his own dominions, and burnt the city of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SARDIS">Sardis</a>. In less than ten years after, they gained a signal victory at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARATHON">Marathon</a>; and, under Themistocles, made head against that prodigious <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> with which <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-XERXES">Xerxes</a> threatened utter ruin to Greece. Such prosperity produced its usual effects: arts flourished with arms, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a> became the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a> for sciences, as well as for fine arts. The reign of Augustus Caesar, which put an end to the rancour of civil war, and restored peace to Rome, with the comforts of society, proved an auspicious era for literature; and produced a cloud of Latin historians, poets, and philosophers, to whom the moderns are indebted for their taste and talents. One who makes a figure rouses emulation in all: one catches fire from another, and the national spirit is everywhere triumphant: classical works are composed, and useful discoveries made in every art and science. With regard to Rome, it is true, that the Roman <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> under Augustus was in effect despotic: but despotism, in that single instance, made no obstruction to literature, it having been the policy of that reign to hide power as much as possible. A similar revolution happened in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUSCANY">Tuscany</a> about three centuries ago. That <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> having been divided into a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of small republics, the people, excited by mutual hatred between small nations in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> neighbourhood, became ferocious and bloody, flaring with <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> for the slightest offence. These republics being united under the great <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Tuscany, enjoyed the sweets of peace in a mild government. That comfortable revolution which made the deeper <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> by a retrospect to recent calamities, roused the national spirit, and produced ardent application to arts and literature. The restoration of the royal family in England, which put an end to a cruel and envenomed civil war, promoted improvements of every kind; arts and industry made a rapid progress among the people, though left to themselves by a weak and fluctuating administration. Had the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, upon that favourable turn of fortune, been blessed with a succession of able and virtuous princes, to what a height might not arts and sciences have been carried! In Scotland, a favourable <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> for improvement was the reign of the first Robert, after shaking off the English yoke; but the domineering spirit of the feudal system rendered every attempt abortive. The restoration of the royal family mentioned above, animated the legislature of Scotland to promote manufactures of various kinds: but in vain; for the union of the two crowns had introduced despotism into Scotland, which sunk the genius of the people, and rendered them heartless and indolent. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">Liberty</a>, indeed, and many other advantages, were procured to them by the union of the two kingdoms; but the salutary effects were long suspended by mutual enmity, such as commonly subsists between neighbouring nations. Enmity gradually wore out, and the eyes of the Scots were opened to the advantages of their present condition; the national spirit was roused to emulate and to excel; talents were exerted, hitherto latent; and Scotland at present makes a figure in arts and sciences above what it ever made while an independent kingdom. Another cause of activity and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANIMATION">animation</a>, is the being engaged in some important <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of doubtful event; a struggle for liberty, the resisting a potent invader, or the like. Greece, divided into small states frequently at war with each other, advanced literature and the fine arts to unrivalled perfection. The Corsicans, while engaged in a perilous war for defence of their liberties, exerted a vigorous national spirit; they founded a university for arts and sciences, a public library, and a public bank. After a long stupor during the dark ages of Christianity, arts and literature revived among the turbulent states of Italy. The Royal Society in London, and the Academy of Sciences in Paris, were both of them instituted after civil wars that had animated the people and roused their activity. As the progress of arts and sciences toward perfection is greatly promoted by emulation, nothing is more fatal to an art or science than to remove that spur, as where some extraordinary genius appears who soars above rivalry. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">Mathematics</a> seem to be declining in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>; the great Newton, having surpassed all the ancients, has not left to the moderns even the faintest hope of equalling him; and what man <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> enter the lists who despairs of victory! In a country thinly peopled, where even necessary arts want hands, it is common to see one person exercising more arts than one: in several parts of Scotland, one man serves as a physician, surgeon, and apothecary. In every populous country, even simple arts are split into parts, and each part has an <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a> appropriated to it. In the large <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> of ancient Egypt, a physician was confined to a single <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>. In mechanic arts that method is excellent. As a hand confined to a single operation becomes both expert and expedient, a mechanic art is perfected by having its different operations distributed among the greatest number of hands: many hands are employed in making a watch, and a still greater number in manufacturing a web of woollen cloth. Various arts or operations carried on by the same man, invigorate his mind; because they <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> different faculties; and as he cannot be equally expert in every art or operation, he is frequently reduced to supply want of skill by thought and invention. Constant application, on the contrary, to a single operation, confines the mind to a single object, and excludes all thought and invention: in such a train of life, the operator becomes dull and stupid, like a beast of burden. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> is visible in the manners of the people: in a country where, from want of hands, several occupations must be carried on by the same person, the people are knowing and conversable: in a populous country, where manufactures flourish, they are ignorant and unsociable. The same effect is equally visible in countries where an art or manufacture is confined to a certain class of men. It is visible in Indostan, where the people are divided into casts, which never mix even by <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>, and where every man follows his father's trade. The Dutch lint-boors are a similar instance: the same family carries on the trade from <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a> to generation; and are accordingly ignorant and brutish even beyond other Dutch peasants. The inhabitants of Buckhaven, a sea-port in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Fife, were originally a colony of foreigners, invited hither to teach our people the art of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a>. They continue fishers to this day, marry among themselves, have little intercourse with their neighbours, and are dull and stupid to a proverb. Useful arts pave the way to fine arts. Men upon whom the former had bestowed every convenience, turned their thoughts to the latter. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">Beauty</a> was studied in objects of sight; and men of taste attached themselves to the fine arts, which multiplied their enjoyments, and improved their benevolence. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SCULPTURE">Sculpture</a> and painting made an early figure in Greece; which afforded plenty of beautiful originals to be copied in these imitative arts. Statuary, a more simple <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> than painting, was sooner brought to perfection: the statue of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> by Phidias, and of Juno by Polycletes, though the admiration of all the world, were executed long before the art of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a> was known. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLODORUS">Apollodorus</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZEUXIS">Zeuxis</a> his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a>, who flourished in the 9th Olympiad, were the first who figured in that art. Another cause concurred to advance statuary before painting in Greece, viz. a great demand for <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> of their gods. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, as a fine art, made a slower progress. Proportions, upon which its elegance chiefly depends, cannot be accurately ascertained, but by an infinity of trials in great buildings: a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODEL">model</a> cannot be relied on; for a large and a small <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, even of the same form, require different proportions. From the fine arts mentioned, we proceed to literature. It is agreed, among all antiquaries, that the first writings were in verse, and that writing in prose was of a much later date. The first Greek who wrote in prose was Pherecides Syrus: the first Roman was Appius Caecus, who composed a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECLAMATION">declamation</a> against Pyrrhus. The four books of the Chatah Bhade, which is the sacred book of Hindostan, are composed in verse stanzas; and the Arabian compositions in prose followed long after those in verse. To account for that singular fact, many learned pens have been employed; but without success. By some it has been urged, that as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> is the only record of events where writing is unknown, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> originally was composed in verse for the sake of memory. This is not satisfactory. To undertake the painful task of composing in verse, merely for the sake of memory, would require more foresight than ever was exerted by a barbarian: not to mention that other means were used for preserving the memory of remarkable events; a heap of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, a pillar, or other object that catches the eye. The account given by Longinus is more ingenious. In a fragment of his treatise on verse, the only part that remains, he observes, "that measure or verse belongs to poetry, because poetry represents the various passions with their language; for which reason the ancients, in their ordinary discourse, delivered their thoughts in verse rather than in prose." Longinus thought, that anciently men were more exposed to accidents and dangers, than when they were protected by good government and by fortified cities. But he seems not to have adverted, that fear and grief inspired by dangers and misfortunes, are better suited to humble prose than to elevated verse. It may be added, that however <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> poetical diction may be when one is animated with any vivid <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>, it is not supposable that the ancients never wrote nor spoke but when excited by passion. Their history, their laws, their covenants, were certainly not composed in that tone of mind. An important article in the progress of the fine arts, which writers have not sufficiently attended to, will perhaps explain this mystery. The article is the profession of a bard, which sprung up in early times before writing was known*, and died away gradually as writing became more and more common†. The songs of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BARDS">bards</a>, being universal favourites‡, were certainly the first compositions that writing was employed upon: they would be carefully collected by the most skilful writers, in order to preserve them in perpetual <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REMEMBRANCE">remembrance</a>. The following part of the progress is obvious. People acquainted with no written compositions, but what were in verse, composed in verse their laws, their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> ceremonies, and every memorable transaction that was intended to be preserved in memory by writing. But when subjects of writing multiplied, and became more and more involved; when people began to reason, to teach, and to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARANGUE">harangue</a>; they were obliged to descend to humble prose: for to confine a writer or speaker to verse in handling subjects of that nature would be a burden unsupportable. The prose compositions of early historians are all of History. A writer destitute of art is naturally prompted to relate facts as he <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> them performed: he introduces his personages as speaking and confering; and he himself relates what was acted, and not spoke. The historical books of the Old <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a> are composed in that <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a>; and so addicted to the dramatic are the authors of those books, that they frequently introduce God himself into the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIALOGUE">dialogue</a>. At the same time, the simplicity of that mode is happily suited to the poverty of every language in its early periods. The dramatic mode has a delicious effect in expressing sentiment, and every thing that is simple and tender. Read, as an instance of a low incident becoming, by that means, not a little interesting, Ruth i. 8. to iv. 16. The dramatic mode is far from pleasing so much in relating bare historical facts. Read, as an example, the story of Adonijah in I Kings i. 11—49. In that passage there are frequent repetitions; not however by the same person, but by different persons, who have occasion in the course of the story to say the same things; which is natural in the dramatic mode, where things are represented precisely as they were transacted. In that view, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>'s repetitions are a beauty, not a blemish; for they are confined to the dramatic part, and never occur in the narrative. But the dramatic mode of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>, however pleasing, is tedious and intolerable in a long history. In the progress of society new appetites and new passions arise; men come to be involved with each other in in various connexions; incidents and events multiply, and history becomes intricate by an endless variety of circumstances. Dialogue accordingly is more sparingly used, and in history plain <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NARRATION">narration</a> is mixed with it. Narration is as it were the ground work; and dialogue is raised upon it, like <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMBROIDERY">embroidery</a>. Homer is admitted by all to be the great master in that mode of composition. The narrative mode came in time so to prevail, that in a long chain of history, the writer commonly leaves off dialogue altogether. Early writers of that kind appear to have very little judgment in distinguishing capital facts from minute circumstances, such as can be supplied by the reader without being mentioned. The history of the Trojan war by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DARES">Dares</a> Phrygius is a curious instance of that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a> and creeping manner of composition. The Roman histories before the time of Cicero are chronicles merely. Cato, Fabius Pictor, and Piso, confined themselves to naked facts. In the Augustae Historiae Scriptores we find nothing but a jejune narrative of facts, commonly of very little moment, concerning a degenerate people, without a single incident that can rouse the imagination or exercise the judgment. The monkish histories are all of them composed in the same manner. The dry narrative manner being very little interesting or agreeable, a taste for embellishment prompted some writers to be copious and verbose. <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAXO_GRAMMATICUS">Saxo-Grammaticus</a>, who in the 12th century composed in Latin a history of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a> surprisingly pure at that early period, is extremely verbose and full of tautologies. Such a style, at any rate unpleasant, is intolerable in a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> tongue, before it is enriched with a stock of phrases for expressing aptly the great variety of incidents that enter into history. The perfection of historical composition which writers at last attain to after wandering through various imperfect modes, is a relation of interesting facts, connected with their motives and consequences. A history of that kind is truly a chain of causes and effects. The history of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUCYDIDES">Thucydides</a>, and still more that of Tacitus, are shining instances of that mode. Eloquence was of a later date than the art of literary composition; for till the latter was improved there were no models for studying the former. Cicero's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORATION">oration</a> for Roscius is composed in a style diffuse and highly ornamented; which, says Plutarch, was universally approved, because at that time the style of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, introduced into Rome with its <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a>, was in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> vogue. But Cicero, in a journey to Greece, where he leisurely studied Greek authors, was taught to prune off superfluities, and to purify his style, which he did to a high degree of refinement. He introduced into his native tongue a sweetness, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">grace</a>, a majesty, that surprised the world, and even the Romans themselves. Cicero observes with great regret, that if ambition for power had not drawn Julius Caesar from the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a> to command legions, he would have become the most complete orator in the world. So partial are men to the profession in which they excel. Eloquence triumphs in a popular <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a>; makes some figure in a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of law composed of many judges, very little where there is but a single judge, and none at all in a despotic government. Eloquence flourished in the republics of Athens and of Rome; and makes some figure at present in a British house of commons. The Greek stage has been justly admired among all polite nations. The tragedies of Sophocles and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EURIPIDES">Euripides</a>, in particular, are by all critics held to be perfect in their kind, excellent models for imitation, but far above rivalry. If the Greek stage was so early brought to maturity, it is a phenomenon not a little singular in the progress of arts. The Greek tragedy made a rapid progress from Thespis to Sophocles and Euripides, whose compositions are wonderful productions of genius, considering that the Greeks at that period were but beginning to emerge from roughness and barbarity into a taste for literature. The compositions of Eschylus, Sophocles, and Euripides, must have been highly relished among a people who had no idea of anything more perfect. We judge by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a>, and every work is held to be perfect that has no rival. It ought at the same time to be kept in view, that it was not the dialogue which chiefly enchanted the Athenians, nor variety in the passions represented, nor perfection in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTORS">actors</a>; but machinery and pompous <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECORATION">decoration</a>, joined with exquisite music. That these particulars were carried to the greatest height, we may with certainty conclude from the extravagant sums bestowed on them: the exhibiting a single tragedy was more expensive to the Athenians than their fleet or their armies in any single <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMPAIGN">campaign</a>. One would imagine, however, that these compositions were too simple to enchant for ever: as variety in action, sentiment, and passion, is requisite, without which the stage will not continue long a favourite entertainment: and yet we find not a single improvement attempted after the days of Sophocles and Euripides. The manner of performance, indeed, prevented absolutely any improvement. A fluctuation of passion and refined sentiments would have made no figure on the Grecian stage. Imagine the discording <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> between Brutus and Cassius in Julius Caesar to be there exhibited, or the handkerchief in the Moor of Venice: how slight would be their effect, when pronounced in a mask, and through a pipe? The workings of nature upon the countenance, and the flexions of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> expressive of various feelings, so deeply affecting in modern representation, would have been entirely lost. If a great genius had arisen with talents for composing a pathetic tragedy in perfection, he would have made no figure in Greece. An edifice must have been erected of a moderate size: new actors must have been trained to act with a bare <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a>, and to pronounce in their own voice. And after all, there remained a greater miracle still to be performed, viz. a total reformation of taste in the people of Athens. In one word, the simplicity of the Greek tragedy was suited to the manner of acting; and that manner excluded all improvements. With respect to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMEDY">comedy</a>, it does not appear that the Comedy Greek comedy surpassed the tragedy in its progress toward perfection. Horace mentions three stages of Greek comedy. The first well suited to the rough and coarse manners of the Greeks, when <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUPOLIS">Eupolis</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRATINUS">Cratinus</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOPHANES">Aristophanes</a> wrote. These authors were not ashamed to represent on the stage real persons, not even disguising their names; of which we have a striking instance in a comedy of Aristophanes, called The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">Clouds</a>, where <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOCRATES">Socrates</a> is introduced, and most contemptuously, temptuously treated. This sort of comedy, sparing neither gods nor men, was restrained by the magistrates of Athens, so far as to prohibit persons to be named on the stage. This led writers to do what is done at present; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> and manners of known persons were painted so much to the life, that there could be no mistake; and the satire was indeed heightened by this regulation, as it was an additional pleasure to find out the names that were meant in the representation. This was termed the middle comedy. But as there still remained too great scope for obloquy and licentiousness, a law was made, prohibiting real events or incidents to be introduced upon the stage. This law happily banished satire against individuals, and confined it to manners and customs in general. Obedient to this law are the comedies of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MENANDER">Menander</a>, Philemon, and Diphilus, who flourished about 300 years before the Christian era. And this is termed the third stage of Greek comedy. The comedies of Aristophanes which still remain, err not less against taste than against decency. But the Greek comedy is supposed to have been considerably refined by Menander and his contemporaries. Their works, however, were far from perfection, if we can draw any conjecture from their imitator Plautus, who wrote about a century later. Plautus was a writer of genius; and it may be reasonably supposed that his copies did not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> much short of the originals, at least in matters that can be faithfully copied; and he shows very little art, either in his compositions or in the conduct of his pieces. With respect to the former, his plots are wondrous simple, very little varied, and very little interesting. The subject of almost every piece is a young man in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> with a music girl, desiring to purchase her from the procurer, and employing a favourite slave to cheat his father out of the price; and the different ways of accomplishing the cheat is all the variety we find. In some few of his comedies the story rises to a higher tone, the music girl being discovered to be the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of a freeman, which removes every obstruction of a marriage between her and her lover. In the conduct of his pieces there is a miserable defect of art. Instead of unfolding the subject in the progress of the action, as is done by Terence, and by every modern writer, Plautus introduces a person for no other end but to explain the story to the audience. In one of his comedies, a household god is so obliging as not only to unfold the subject, but to relate before-hand every particular that is to be represented, not excepting the catastrophe. The Roman theatre, from the time of Plautus to that of Terence, made a rapid progress. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a> defines comedy to be "an imitation of light and trivial subjects, provoking <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAUGHTER">laughter</a>." The comedies of Plautus correspond accurately to that <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-DEFINITION">definition</a>: those of Terence rise to a higher tone. Nothing is more evident than the superiority of Terence above Plautus in the art of writing; and, considering that Terence is a later writer, nothing would appear more natural, if they did not copy the same originals. It may be owing to genius that Terence excelled in purity of language and propriety of dialogue; but how account for his superiority over Plautus in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> and conduct of a play? It will not certainly be thought, that Plautus would imitate the worst constructed plays, leaving the best to those who should come after him. This difficulty does not seem to have occurred to any of the commentators. Had the works of Menander and of his contemporaries been preserved, they probably would have explained the mystery; which for want of that light will probably remain a mystery for ever. Homer has for more than 2000 years been held the Epopée prince of poets. Such perfection in an author who flourished when arts were far short of maturity, is truly wonderful. The nations engaged in the Trojan war are described by him as in a progress from the shepherd state to that of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a>. Frequent mention is made in the Iliad of the most eminent men being shepherds. Andromache, in particular, mentions seven of her brethren who were slain by <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACHILLES">Achilles</a> as they tended their father's flocks and herds. In that state, garments of woollen cloth were used; but the skins of beasts, the original clothing, were still worn as an upper garment; every chief in the Iliad appeared in that dress. Such indeed was the simplicity of this early period, that a black ewe was promised by each chief to the man who would undertake to be a spy. In times of such simplicity, literature could not be far advanced; and it is a great doubt, whether there was at that time a single poem of the epic kind for Homer to imitate or improve upon. Homer is undoubtedly a wonderful genius, perhaps the greatest that ever existed: his fire, and the boldness of his conceptions, are inimitable. But in that early age, it would fall little short of a real miracle, to find such ripeness of judgment, and correctness of execution, as in modern writers are the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of long experience and progressive improvements during the course of many centuries. Accordingly, that Homer is far from being so ripe, or so correct, cannot escape the observation of any reader of taste and discernment. One striking particular is, his digressions without end, which draw our <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> from the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> subject. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIOMEDES">Diomedes</a>, for instance, meeting with Glaucus in the field of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, and doubting from his majestic <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>, whether he might not be an immortal, inquires who he was, declaring that he would not fight with a god. Glaucus lays hold of this very slight opportunity, in the very <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of action, to give a long history of his family. In the mean time the reader's <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATIENCE">patience</a> is put to a trial, and his ardour cools. Again, Agamemnon desiring advice how to resist the Trojans, Diomedes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> forward; but before he offers advice, gives the history of all his progenitors, and of their characters, in a long train. And, after all, what was the sage advice that required such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREFACE">preface</a>? It was, that Agamemnon should exhort the Greeks to fight bravely. At any rate, was Diomedes so little known, as to make it proper to suspend the action at so critical a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNCTURE">juncture</a>, for a genealogical history? There is a third particular which justly merits censure; and that is, an endless number of minute circumstances, especially in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of battles, where they are most improper. The capital beauty of an epic poem is, the selection of such incidents and circumstances as make a deep impression, keeping out of view every thing low or familiar. An account of a single battle employs the whole fifth book of the Iliad and a great part of the sixth: yet in the whole there is no general action; but unknown warriors, whom we never heard of before, killed at a distance with an arrow or a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JAVELIN">javelin</a>; lin; and every wound described with anatomical accuracy. The whole seventeenth book is employed in the contest about the dead body of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATROCLUS">Patroclus</a>, stuffed with minute circumstances, below the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of an epic poem. In such scenes the reader is fatigued with endless particulars; and has nothing to support him but the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MELODY">melody</a> of Homer's versification. Having traced the progress of the fine arts toward maturity, in a summary way, the decline of these arts comes next in order. An art, in its progress toward maturity, is greatly promoted by emulation; and, after arriving at maturity, its downfall is not less promoted by it. It is difficult to judge of perfection but by comparison; and an artist, ambitious to outstrip his predecessors, cannot submit to be an imitator, but must strike out something new, which, in an art advanced to ripeness, seldom fails to be a degeneracy. This cause of the decline of the fine arts may be illustrated by various instances. The perfection of vocal music is to accompany passion, and to enforce sentiment. In ancient Greece, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of music was well understood; which being confined within its proper sphere, had an enchanting influence. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARMONY">Harmony</a> at that time was very little cultivated, because it was of very little use: melody reaches the heart, and it is by it chiefly that a sentiment is enforced, or a passion soothed; harmony, on the contrary, reaches the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-EAR">ear</a> only; and it is a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of undoubted experience, that the most melodious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIRS">airs</a> admit but of very simple harmony. Artists, in later times, ignorant why harmony was so little regarded by the ancients, applied themselves seriously to its cultivation; and they have been wonderfully successful. But they have been successful at the expense of melody; which in modern compositions, generally speaking, is lost amid the blaze of harmony. These compositions tickle the ear by the luxury of complicated sounds, but seldom make any impression on the heart. The Italian <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPERA">opera</a>, in its form, resembles the Greek tragedy, from which it is evidently copied; but very little in substance. In the latter, music being made subservient to sentiment, the dialogue is nervous and sublime; in the former, the whole <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> is laid on music; and the dialogue, devoid of sentiment, is weak and spiritless. Restless man knows no <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> mean, but will be attempting innovations without end. By the same ambition, architecture has visibly declined from its perfection. The Ionic was the favourite order when architecture was in its height of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a>. The Corinthian order came next; which, in attempting greater perfection, has deviated from the true simplicity of nature; and the deviation is still greater in the Composite order. With respect to literary productions, the first essays of the Romans were very imperfect. We may judge of this from Plautus, whose compositions are abundantly rude, though much admired by his contemporaries, being the best that existed at that time. The exalted spirit of the Romans hurried them on to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> and beautiful; and literary productions of all kinds were in perfection when Augustus reigned. In attempting still greater perfection, the Roman compositions became a strange jumble of inconsistent parts: they were tumid and pompous; and, at the same time, full of antitheses, conceit, and tinsel <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a>. Every thing new in the fine arts pleases, though less perfect than what we are accustomed to; and, for that reason, such compositions were generally relished. We see not by what gradual steps writers, after the time of Augustus, deviated from the patterns that were before them; for no book of any moment after that time is preserved till we come down to Seneca, in whose works nature and simplicity give place to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> thought and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASTARD">bastard</a> wit.
