He was a great corrupter of the Roman taste; and after him nothing was relished but brilliant strokes of fancy, with very little regard to sentiment: even <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a> and Cicero made no figure in comparison. Lucan has a forced elevation of thought and style very difficult to be supported; and, accordingly, he sinks often into puerile reflections; witness his encomium on the river Po; which, says he, would equal the Danube, had it the same number of tributary streams. Quintilian, a writer of true and classical taste, who was protected and encouraged by Vespasian, attempted to stem the tide of false writing. His <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a> is composed in an elegant style; and his observations contain every delicacy of the critical art. At the same time flourished Tacitus, possessing a more extensive knowledge of the nature of man than any other author, ancient or modern, if Shakespeare be not excepted. His style is original, concise, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a>, and comprehensive; and, in what is properly called his history, perfectly correct and beautiful. He has been imitated by several, but never equalled by any. Brutus is said to be the last of the Romans for love of liberty: Quintilian and Tacitus may be said to be the last of the Romans for literary genius. Pliny the younger is no exception; his style is affected, turgid, and full of childish brilliancy. Seneca and Pliny are proper examples of writers who study show more than substance, and who make sense yield to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOUND">sound</a>. The difference between these authors and those of the Augustan age, resembles the difference between Greek and Italian music. Music, among the Greeks, limited itself to the employment to which it is destined by nature, viz. to be the handmaid of sense, to enforce, enliven, or sweeten a sentiment. In the Italian opera, the mistress is degraded to be handmaid; and harmony triumphs with very little regard to sentiment. Another great cause that precipitates the downfall of every fine art is despotism. The reason is obvious; and there is a dismal example of it in Rome, particularly with regard to eloquence. We learn from a dialogue accounting for the corruption of the Roman eloquence, that in the decline of the art it became fashionable to stuff harangues with impertinent poetical quotations, without any view but ornament merely; and this also was long fashionable in France. It happened unluckily for the Romans, and for the world, that the fine arts were at their height in Rome, and not much upon the decline in Greece, when despotism put an end to the republic. Augustus, it is true, retarded their fall, particularly that of literature; it being the policy of his reign to hide despotism, and to give his government an air of freedom. His court was a school of urbanity, where people of genius acquired that delicacy of taste, that elevation of sentiment, and that purity of expression, which characterise the writers of his time. He honoured men of learning, admitted them to his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, and was bountiful to them. It would be painful to follow the decline of the fine arts in Rome to their their total extirpation. The tyranny of Tiberius, and of subsequent emperors, broke at last the elevated and independent spirit of the brave Romans, reduced them to abject <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a>, and left not a spark of genius. The science of law is the only exception, as it flourished even in the worst of times: the Roman lawyers were a respectable body, and less the object of jealousy than men of power and extensive landed <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>. Among the Greeks also, a conquered people, the fine arts decayed; but not so rapidly as at Rome: the Greeks, farther removed from the seat of government, being less within the reach of a Roman <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a>. During their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEPRESSION">depression</a>, they were guilty of the most perilous conceits: witness verses composed in the form of an axe, an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGG">egg</a>, wings, and such like. The style of Greek authors, in the reign of the emperor Adrian, is unequal, obscure, stiff, and affected. Lucian is the only exception that may be made. We scarcely need any other cause but despotism, to account for the decline of statuary and painting in Greece. These arts had arrived at their utmost perfection about the time of Alexander the Great; and from that time they declined gradually with the vigour of a free people; for Greece was now enslaved by the Macedonian power. It may in general be observed, that when a nation becomes <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STATIONARY">stationary</a> in that degree of power which it acquires from its <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> and situation, the national spirit subsides, and men of talents become rare. It is still worse with a nation that is sunk below its former power and pre-eminence; and worst of all when it is reduced to slavery. Other causes concurred to accelerate the downfall of the arts mentioned. Greece, in the days of Alexander, was filled with statues of excellent workmanship; and there being little demand for more, the later statuaries were reduced to heads and busts. At last the Romans put a total end both to statuary and painting in Greece, by plundering it of its finest pieces; and the Greeks, exposed to the avarice of the conquerors, bestowed no longer any money on the fine arts. The decline of the fine arts in Rome is by a writer of taste and elegance ascribed to a cause different from any above mentioned, a cause that overwhelms manhood as well as the fine arts wherever it prevails; and that is opulence, joined with its faithful attendants avarice and luxury. "In ancient times (says he), when naked virtue had her admirers, the liberal arts were in their highest vigour; and there was a generous contest among men, that nothing of real and permanent advantage should long remain undiscovered. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEMOCRITUS">Democritus</a> extracted the juice of every <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERB">herb</a> and plant; and, lest the virtue of a single <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> or twig should escape him, he consumed a lifetime in experiments. Eudoxus, immersed in the study of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>, spent his age upon the top of a mountain. Chrysippus, to stimulate his inventive <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a>, thrice purified his genius with heliobore. To turn to the imitative arts; <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LYSIPPUS">Lysippus</a>, while labouring on the form of a single statue, perished from want. <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYRON">Myron</a>, whose powerful hand gave to the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> almost the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> of man and animals,—at his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> found not an heir! Of us of modern times what shall we say? Immersed in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRUNKENNESS">drunkenness</a> and debauchery, we want the spirit to cultivate those arts which we possess. We inveigh against the manners of antiquity; we study vice alone; and vice is all we teach. Where now is the art of reasoning? Where astronomy? Where is the right path of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>? What man now-a-days is heard in our <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a> to make a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOW">vow</a> for the attainment of eloquence, or for the discovery of the fountain of true <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>? Nor do we even pray for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> of body, or a sound understanding. One, while he has scarce entered the porch of the temple, devotes a gift in the event of the death of a rich relation; another prays for the discovery of a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a>; a third for a ministerial fortune. The senate itself, the exemplary preceptor of what is good and laudable, has promised a thousand pounds of gold to the capitol; and, to remove all reproach from the crime of avarice, has offered a bribe to Jupiter himself. How should we wonder that the art of painting has declined, when, in the eyes both of the gods and men, there is more beauty in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of gold than in all the works of Phidias and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APELLES">Apelles</a>."—In England, the fine arts are far from such perfection as to suffer by opulence. They are in a progress, it is true, toward maturity; but they proceed in a very slow pace. There is still another cause that never fails to undermine a fine art in a country where it is brought to perfection, abstracting from every one of the causes above mentioned. It is remarked a little above, that nothing is more fatal to an art or to a science than a performance so much superior to all of the kind as to extinguish emulation. This remark is exemplified in the great Newton, who having surpassed all the ancients, has not left to his countrymen even the faintest hope of rivalling him; and to that cause is attributed the visible decline of mathematics in Great Britain. The same cause would have been fatal to the arts of statuary and painting among the Greeks, even though they had continued a free people. The decay of painting in modern Italy is, probably, owing to the same cause: Michael Angelo, Raphael, Titian, &c., are lofty oaks that bear down young <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> in their neighbourhood, and intercept from them the sunshine of emulation. Had the art of painting made a slower progress in Italy, it might have there continued in vigour to this day. Velleius Paterculus says judiciously, "Ut primo <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AD">ad</a> consequendos quos priores ducimus accendiur; ita, ubi aut praeteriri aut equire eos posse desperavimus, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STADIUM">stadium</a> cum spe senescit; et quod adequi non potest, sequi desinit: praeteritoque eo in quo eminere non possimus, aliquid in quo nitamur conquirimus." The decline of an art or science proceeding from the foregoing cause, is the most rapid where a strict comparison can be instituted between the works of different masters. The superiority of Newton above every other mathematician can be ascertained with precision; and hence the sudden decline of that science in Great Britain. In Italy a talent for painting continued many years in vigour, because no painter appeared with such superiority of genius as to carry perfection in every branch of the art. As one surpassed in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGNING">designing</a>, one in colouring, one in graceful attitudes, there was still scope for emulation. But when at last there was not a single perfection but what one or other master had excelled in, from that period the art began to languish. Architecture continued longer in vigour than painting, because the principles of comparison in the former are less precise than in the latter. The artist who who could not rival his predecessors in an established mode, sought out a new mode for himself, which, though perhaps less elegant or perfect, was for a time supported by <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOVELTY">novelty</a>. Useful arts will never be neglected in a country where there is any <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol18.html#article-POLICE">police</a>; for every man finds his account in them. Fine arts are more precarious. They are not relished but by persons of taste, who are rare; and such as can spare great sums for supporting them are still more rare. For that reason, they will never flourish in any country, unless patronized by the sovereign, or by men of power and opulence. They merit such <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRONAGE">patronage</a>, as one of the springs of government; and a capital spring they make, by multiplying amusements, and humanizing manners; upon which account they have always been encouraged by good princes. General <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEORY">Theory</a> of the Polite Arts. The essence of the polite arts, as before observed, consists in expression. The end of these arts is pleasure; whereas the end of the sciences is instruction and utility. Some of the polite arts, indeed, as eloquence, poetry, and architecture, are frequently applied to objects that are useful, or exercised in matters that are instructive, as we shall show more particularly in their proper place; but in these <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, though the ground-work belongs to those sciences which employ the understanding, yet the expression arises from the inventive faculty. It is a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> that is designed by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a>, to which the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSES">Muses</a> add the colouring, and the Graces the frame. This union forms therefore the perfection of the art, according to that sententious and well known precept of Horace: Omne tulit punctum, qui miscuit utile dulci. Under the denomination therefore, of Polite Arts, we comprehend, 1. Eloquence; 2. Poetry; 3. Music; 4. Painting; 5. Sculpture; 6. Graving; 7. Architecture; 8. Declamation; 9. <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DANCING">Dancing</a>. Particular descriptions of these arts are given under their respective names. This branch of the present article is intended as a general introduction to them; and, as such, will be occasionally referred to. There is one very essential reflection, which it appears to us proper to make in the first place, on the polite arts in general. All the rules in the world are not sufficient to make a great poet, an able orator, or an excellent artist; because the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> necessary to form these, depends on the natural disposition, the fire of genius, which no human art can confer, but which is the pure gift of heaven. The rules, however, will prevent a man from being a bad artist, a dull orator, or a wretched poet; seeing they are the reflections of the greatest masters in those arts, and that they point out the rocks which the artist should shun in the exercise of his talents. They are of use, moreover, in facilitating his labours, and in directing him to arrive by the shortest and surest road at perfection. They refine, strengthen, and confirm his taste. Nature, abandoned to herself, has something constantly wild and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a>. Art, founded on <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> and sagacious rules, gives her elegance, dignity, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITENESS">politeness</a>; and it is impossible to sacrifice properly to the Graces, without knowing the incense that is pleasing to them. Beauty is the object of all the polite arts. It is not, however, so easy, as it may seem, to give a clear and determinate idea of what we precisely mean by that term*. Many able writers, who have treated expressly on the subject, have shown that they were totally ignorant of what it was. It is one of these expressions that we comprehend immediately, that present* See the us with a clear and precise idea, that leave a distinct article impression on our minds, when it is simply written or Beauty- pronounced; but which philosophers envelope in darkness, when they attempt to elucidate it by definitions and descriptions; and the more, as mankind have different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> of beauty, their opinions and tastes being as various as their understandings and physiognomies. We may say, however, in general, that beauty results from the various perfections of which any object is susceptible, and which it actually possesses; and that the perfections which produce beauty consist principally in the agreeable and delightful proportions which are found, 1. Between the several parts of the same object; 2. Between each part and the whole together; 3. Between the parts and the end or design of the object to which they belong. Genius, or invention, is that faculty of the mind by which beauty is produced. Taste†, disposition, or rather the natural <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSATION">sensation</a> of† See Taste. the mind refined by art, serves to guide the genius in discerning, embracing, and producing, that which is beautiful of every kind. From whence it follows, that the general theory of the polite arts is nothing more than the knowledge of what they contain that is truly beautiful and agreeable; and it is this knowledge, this theory, which modern philosophers call by the Latin name of aesthetica. It should be constantly remembered, that the essence of the polite arts consists in expression. This expression lies sometimes in the words, and sometimes in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEN">pen</a>; sometimes in sounds and their harmony, and at others in corporeal attitudes; sometimes in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a> or in the chisel, and at others in the graver; sometimes in a proper disposition or judicious employment of the mechanic arts, and at others merely in their manner of acting. From whence arise those arts that we have mentioned, and which are described in their order. The general theory of the polite arts, or esthetics, First gene-necessarily supposes, therefore, certain rules; but these general rules are of no great number. The first is, That whoever would devote himself to the polite arts, should above all things consult his genius; divest himself of self-love; and examine if he be a true son of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a>, and cherished by the Muses: for In vain, rash author, dost thou strive to climb, By lofty verse, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARNASSUS">Parnassus</a>' height sublime, If heaven does not by secret powers inspire, Or if thy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATAL">natal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STAR">star</a> darts not poetic fire. This precept with regard to poetry in particular, is applicable to all the polite arts in general: for their most happy success is founded on imagination. By Imagina-this term, we understand, in general, a faculty of the tion what. mind, a particular genius, a lively invention, a certain subtle spirit, which gives a facility in discovering something new. But it is necessary also to describe just bounds to this term new, which must not be here taken in an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> sense. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a> wisely remarks, and Inven-that, even in his time, there was nothing new under the the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>. In fact, all that exists, and all that is capable of being discovered in the known world, has already been discovered. The fine arts in their imitations of nature, in their expressions, can borrow images, figures, comparisons, from those things only that exist and are known. As there have been from the beginning of the world to our days, millions of authors in each of the polite arts, almost all the possible <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBINATIONS">combinations</a> of the various subjects have been produced by their lively imaginations; and when we hear the ignorant part of mankind talk of a work of wit or of art that is entirely new, that offers ideas which were before utterly unknown, that had never entered into the brain of any other man, we should refer such assertions to the class of popular errors: and reflect on those stories we every day hear of certain empirics, who pretend to be alone possessed of marvellous methods of cure by means of simples; as if there were any plant, any stalk of grass that grows in our world, that can have escaped the researches of botanists. But the novelty, of which we here speak, consists in the ingenious use of combinations of all the various objects of nature, that are new, happy, and agreeable, that have not yet been exhausted, and which appear even to be inexhaustible; and of the use which the artist makes of all new discoveries, which he turns to his advantage by a judicious application. Invention therefore supposes a considerable <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FUND">fund</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRELIMINARY">preliminary</a> knowledge, such as is capable of furnishing ideas and images, to form new combinations. But there is no art by which invention itself can be produced; for that, as we have already said, is the gift of heaven; and it is an endowment which we cannot even make use of whenever we please. We would rather say, therefore, that invention consists in producing, in works of genius, that which is unexpected; an object, a harmony, a perfection, a thought, an expression of which we had no idea, that we could not foresee, nor hope to find, where the artist has so happily placed it, and where we perceive it with delight. This idea appears applicable to such of the polite arts as affect the mind by the hearing as well as by the sight; and it is a matter that is highly essential. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> rule is, That every artist ought incessantly to labour in the improvement of his taste; in acquiring that sensible, refined, and clear discernment, by which he will be enabled to distinguish the real beauties in each object, the ornaments that are agreeable to it, and the proportions and relations that subsist among the several parts: and by this faculty, he will be regulated in the employment of his natural talents. This labour consists not only in the profound reflections he will make on the properties of objects, as they relate to the fine arts, but also in a constant, assiduous study of the grand models of beauty. The third rule to be observed in the practice of the polite arts, is the imitation of nature. Every object in the universe has its peculiar nature, of which the artist should never lose sight in his manner of treating it. In vain will he otherwise ornament his work with the most refined and most brilliant strokes; for, if nature be not justly imitated, it will for ever remain imperfect. The sublime Homer has sometimes sinned against this rule: for, as the gods have a nature peculiar to themselves; it cannot be a just imitation when we <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> to them passions that are scarcely pardonable in mortals, and make them frequently <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONVERSE">converse</a> in a language that is at once vulgar and ridiculous. It was not to imitate nature, to put in the mouth of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a>, at the moment of a decisive battle, a harangue that must become tedious by its excessive length, and which certainly could not have been heard by the thousandth part of a numerous army: but we have already touched upon some of the faults that are strewed over the poems of that great man; to multiply or dwell upon them would be ungrateful. We must, however, observe that this imitation of nature, which appears at first view so simple and so easy, is of all things the most difficult in practice; and that it requires a discernment so sagacious, and an expression so happy, as is rarely bestowed by heaven on mortal man. Perspicuity forms the fourth rule of expression. In all the fine arts, in general, an obscure, perplexing, ed, ambiguous, and elaborate expression, is always bad. The true striking beauty must be manifest and perceptible to the most ignorant of mankind as well as the most learned. Those are even false or inferior beauties that have occasion for a covering, a kind of veil that may make them appear greater than they really are: true beauty wants no veil, but shines by its native lustre. From the union of the true imitation of nature with perspicuity of expression arises that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> which is so essential in the productions of the fine arts. In all the polite arts, and in all the subjects they embrace, there must necessarily reign an elevation of sentiment, that expresses each object in the greatest perfection of which it is susceptible; that imitates nature in her most exalted beauty. This makes the fifth general rule. The design of the fine arts being to excite pleasure by the expression of that which is beautiful, every artist should raise himself above his subject; and, choosing the most favourable light wherein to place it, should there embellish it with the greatest, most noble, and beautiful ornaments, that his own genius can suggest; still, however, observing a strict imitation of nature. From the observation of these two last rules results the sublime, which is the union of the greatest perspicuity with the strictest truth and most exalted elevation possible. It is necessary to remark here, that the most simple and common subjects are susceptible of a sublime that is agreeable to their nature. An idyl or landscape may be as sublime in their kinds as an epic poem or a history piece. When Moses begins the book of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GENESIS">Genesis</a>, with these words, In the beginning God created the heaven and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>; or when he tells us, that God said, Let there be light, and there was light; these expressions are sublime in the highest degree, because they are perfectly clear, true, and elevated. Every author should therefore endeavour after the sublime in every subject that he undertakes; and this makes the sixth and last general rule in the practice of the polite arts. But if he cannot attain to this, it is, however, indispensably necessary that he constantly make use of expressions that are noble and refined. Every thing that is low, indecent, or disagreeable, is naturally repugnant to the sublime. See the articles ARTS, Fine, and DRAMA, in the SUPPLEMENT. ART is also an appellation given to several superstitious practices, as, St <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANSELM">Anselm</a>'s art, St Paul's art, &c. ART and Part, in Scots Law. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCESSORY">Accessory</a>.

ARTA

Pages 787-787

by some called Larta, a town of Lower <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBANIA">Albania</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, with a Greek archbishop's see. It is a pretty <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> town, and contains, according to Mr Hobbhouse, about 5000 inhabitants, of which less than a fourth are Mahometans. It had formerly a castle, but this has been suffered to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> to decay. Arta is situated at the distance of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> eight miles from the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> to which it gives name. The neighbouring grounds produce <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAPES">grapes</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>, oats, and maize; and there is some little trade in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, cotton, cloths, &c. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 21. 15. N. Lat. 39. 20.

ARTABA

Pages 787-787

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> of capacity used by the Persians, Medes, and Egyptians. The Persian artaba is represented by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a> as bigger than the Attic medimnus by three Attic choenixes: from which it appears that it was equal to 6½ Roman modii; consequently that it contained 166½ pounds of wine <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, or 126½ pounds of wheat. The Egyptian artaba contained five Roman modii, and fell short of the Attic medimnus by one modius; consequently held 133½ pounds of water or wine, 100 pounds of wheat, or 62 of flour.

ARTABAZUS

Pages 787-787

the son of Pharnaces, commanded the Parthians and Chorasmians in the famous expedition of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-XERXES">Xerxes</a>. After the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALAMIS">Salamis</a>, he escorted the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> to the Hellespont with 60,000 chosen men; and after the battle of Platæa, in which Mardonius engaged contrary to his advice, he made a noble retreat, and returned to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> with 40,000 men under his command.

ARTAXATA

Pages 787-787

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> residence and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMENIA">Armenia</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">Major</a> (Strabo, Pliny, Juvenal), and built according to a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HANNIBAL">Hannibal</a>, for <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> Artaxias, after whom it was called. It was situated on an elbow of the river Araxes, which formed a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a>, and surrounded the town like a wall, except on the side of the isthmus, but this side was secured by a rampart and ditch. This town was deemed so strong, that Lucullus, after having defeated Tigranes, durst not lay siege to it; but Pompey compelled him to deliver it up without striking a blow. It was then levelled with the ground; but the Armenians have a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a>, that the ruins of it are still to be seen at a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> called Ardachat. Sir John Chardin says, that it has the name of Ardachat from Artaxias, whom in the East they call Ardechier. Here are the remains of a stately <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> which the Armenians take to be that of Tiridates who reigned in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Constantine the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>. One <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a> of this <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> is but half ruined, and there are many other fine antiquities which the inhabitants call Taet Trudat, that is, the throne of Tiridates. Tavernier also mentions the ruins of Artaxata between <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ERIVAN">Erivan</a> and Mount Ararat, but does not specify them. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> geographers mention another <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the same name, likewise situated on the Araxes, but in the northern <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of Media, known among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> by the name of Acropatia.

ARTAXERXES

Pages 787-787

the name of several kings of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>. See PERSIA. Vol. II. <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">Part</a> II.

ARTEDI

Pages 787-787
Peter, an eminent naturalist, was born in Sweden in the year 1705, in the province of Angermania. Although his parents were poor, yet it appears they found means to give him a liberal education, and with this view they sent him to the college of Hornsland. Intending to embrace the ecclesiastical profession, he went in 1724 to Upsal; but being fond of the study of href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural history, he yielded to the bent of inclination, and directed his attention towards medicine. In natural history he made rapid progress, and soon arose to considerable eminence, particularly in the knowledge of Ichthyology. His reputation for natural knowledge was high when Linnaeus arrived at Upsal in the year 1728. A lasting friendship was formed between these two great men. Confining his botanical studies to the umbelliferous plants, he suggested a new mode of classification; but Arvedi was much better acquainted with chemistry than botany. His attention was chiefly directed to ichthyology, the classification of which he greatly reformed, and new-modelled upon philosophical principles. This arrangement added greatly to his reputation as a naturalist. When the two friends were about to leave Upsal, Linnaeus to go to Lapland, and Arvedi to England, they reciprocally bequeathed to each other their manuscripts and books upon the event of death. In the year 1735, they, however, met again at Leyden, where Arvedi was introduced to Seba, and employed in preparing for the press the third volume of that eminent naturalist's Theaurus, which chiefly related to fishes. Arvedi formed the resolution, as soon as that work was finished, to return to his native country, to publish the fruits of his own labours; but unfortunately as he was returning home from Seba's house on the evening of September 27, 1735, the night being dark, he fell into the canal and was drowned. According to agreement, his manuscripts came into the hands of Linnaeus, and he published his Bibliotheca Ichthyologica, and Philosophia Ichthyologica, together with a life of the author, at Leyden in the year 1738. (Gen. Biog.) ARTEDIA. See BOTANY Index.

ARTEMIDORUS

Pages 787-788

famous for his Treatise on <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DREAMS">Dreams</a>. He was born at Ephesus, but took upon him the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SURNAME">surname</a> of Daldianus in his book, by way of respect to his mother <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> Daltis. He styled himself the Ephesian in his other performances. He not only bought up all that had been written concerning the explication of dreams, which amounted to many volumes; but he likewise spent many years in traveling, in order to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> an acquaintance with fortune-tellers; he also carried on an extensive correspondence with all the people of this sort in the cities and assemblies of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and the most populous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>; collecting at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> all the old dreams, and the events which are said to have followed them. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> which he wrote on dreams consisted of five books: the first three were dedicated to one Cassius Maximus; and the last two to his son, whom he took a good <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of pains to instruct in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and interpretation of dreams. This work, though filled with frivolous observations, contains some things that are interesting. It was first printed in Greek at <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> in 1518; and Rigaltius published an edition at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, in Greek and Latin, in 1603, and added some notes. Artemidorus wrote also a treatise upon Auguries, and another... other upon Chiromancy; but they are not extant. He lived under the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANTONINUS_PIUS">Antoninus Pius</a>.

ARTEMISIA

Pages 788-788
queen of Caria, and the daughter of Ligdamis, marched in person in the expedition of Xerxes against the Greeks, and performed wonders in the sea-fight near Salamis, 480 years before the Christian era. Being pursued by an Athenian vessel, she attacked one of the Persian ships, commanded by Demasithynus, king of Calyndus, her enemy, and sunk it; on which the Athenians, thinking that her ship was on the side of the Greeks, ceased their pursuit; but Xerxes was the principal person imposed upon in this affair; for believing she had sunk an Athenian vessel, he declared, that "the men had behaved like women, and the women like men." Xerxes intrusted her with the care of the young princes of Persia, his sons, when, agreeably to her advice, he abandoned Greece, in order to return to Asia. These great qualities did not secure her from the weakness of love: she was passionately fond of a man of Abydos, whose name was Dardanus, and was so enraged at his neglect of her, that she put out his eyes while he was asleep. The gods in order to punish her for this, inspired her with a still stronger passion for him; so that the oracle having advised her to go to Leucas, which was the usage of desperate lovers, she took the leap from thence, and was interred at that place.—Many writers confound this Artemisia with the former, the wife of Mausolus.

ARTEMISIUM

Pages 789-789

a town of Oenotria, (Stephanus): now S. Agatha, in the Hither <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALABRIA">Calabria</a>, on the river Pisaurs, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> la Foglia, distant eight miles from the Tuscan <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>.—Another of the Contestani, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, (Strabo); otherwise called Dianium: now <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DENIA">Denia</a>, on the sea <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VALENCIA">Valencia</a>.

ARTERIOTOMY

Pages 789-789

the opening an artery, with <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> to procure an evacuation of blood. See <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>.

ARTERY

Pages 789-789

in Anatomy, a conical tube <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> canal which conveys the blood from the heart to all parts of the body. See Anatomy.

ARTHITIS

Pages 789-789

in Medicine, the Gout. See the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a> subjoined to Medicine.

ARTHRODIA

Pages 789-789

in Anatomy, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of articulation, wherein the flat head of one bone is received into a shallow socket in the other. The humerus and scapula are joined by this species of articulation.

ARTHUR

Pages 789-791

the celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a> of the Britons, is said to have been the son of Uther Pendragon <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, and to have been born in 521. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> is a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of wonders. It is said that he killed four hundred and seventy Saxons with his own <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> in one <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>; and, after having subdued many mighty nations, and instituted the order of the Knights of the Round <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">Table</a>, died A.D. 542, of wounds which he received in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>. The most particular detail of his story and his exploits is that given by <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GEOFFROY_OF_MONMOUTH">Geoffroy of Monmouth</a>: but the probable there is so blended with the marvellous and the extravagant, that not only the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of the whole, but even the reality of Arthur's existence, has been called in question. In this controversy, Mr Whittaker has taken much pains to vindicate the existence, and discriminate between the real and the fabulous transactions, of the British worthy. "Many of the actions (he observes) attributed to Arthur by the Welsh chronicles of Britain, are as absurd in themselves as they are spurious in their authority. Written, as those narratives were, many centuries after the facts, and being merely the authentic accounts of Arthur, embellished with the fictions and distorted by the perversions of folly; they are inconsistent equally with the state of the times, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the continent and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>. And the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> of the forgers, and the credulity of their abettors, can be equalled only by the injudiciousness and incredulity of the opponents to both. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> some accounts of Arthur and Cunobeline in these histories be certainly spurious, others are as certainly genuine. And the relations of Suetonius, Dio, and Nennius, are not to be rejected, because of the falsehoods which imposture has grafted upon them, and absurdity admitted with them. "The existence of Arthur is evinced by that of the fables, which have at once annihilated his actions and his name with the misjudging critic. And the reasoner's own arguments really turn against himself, and demonstrate the point which they were intended to disprove. The annals of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WALES">Wales</a> have <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> laboured in Arthur's commendation. The Highlanders have long had a poetical history of his exploits in their own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. The whole island is in traditionary possession of his character; and 600 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 700 places within it are still distinguished by his name. "The genuine actions of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> are mentioned by his own historians, with a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a> and conciseness that is no bad argument of the truth, and with a particularity of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> that is a good <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> of the facts. They are noticed by men, whom the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of the hero had exempted from all temptation to flattery: they are recited by persons, whom a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROXIMITY">proximity</a> to the time had precluded from all possibility of mistake: and they are attested by the best historical authority, writers who lived cotemporary with him, authors who conversed with his warriors, and historians that wrote within a few years after him. He is spoken of as the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> father of the British heroes by the aged Llomarch, a writer actually cotemporary with him, and some time resident at his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>. One of his greater actions is incidentally recorded by Taliesin, an historical bard living under Maelwn Gwined, who was a sovereign among the Britons in the days of Arthur, Gildas, and Llomarch. Another of his considerable exploits is casually intimated by Myrddin Wyllt or Merlinus Caledonius, who complains of the severe treatment which he himself received from Rydderch Hael, a king cotemporary with Urien Reged, and engaged with him in a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> against the Saxons on the death of Ida in 509. And all his actions are particularly recited by Nennius. "In the Historia Britonum of this last author, Arthur's victories over the Saxons are thus recorded. The first battle was fought at the mouth of the river which is denominated Glam. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, third, fourth, and fifth, were upon another river, that is called Douglas, and lies in the region Linuis. The sixth was on a stream, which bears the appellation of Bassas. The seventh was in the wood of Celidon, that is, in Cat Coit Celidon. The eighth was at Castle Gannon; and the ninth was at the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the Legion. The tenth was on the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the river Ribroit; the eleventh at the hill Aged Cathregonion; and the twelfth at Mount Badon. These twelve battles of Arthur are described to us in the same manner as Vortimer's three. Only the general facts are mentioned, and only the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> names of places are recited, in both." Arthur, from the whole <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> and aspect of the history, the remarkable conciseness with which the notices are given, and the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> ease with which the places are pointed out, the detail appears to have been drawn up at the distance only of a few years from the transactions, and when these little references were sufficiently understood." Mr Whittaker proceeds to ascertain the scenes of Arthur's battles; after which he gives a relation of them with a surprising particularity. A severe critic might be apt to say, as Dr Kippis observes, that it requires all our <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> in the author's judgment, as well as in his ingenuity and learning, not to suspect that he sometimes allows too much scope to fancy and conjecture. However, the whole of what he hath advanced is singularly curious, and deserves peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> and consideration. And no one can help admiring the penetration with which he hath formed such a regular detail of facts, from the combined aid of history, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROMANCE">romance</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a>. According to Mr Whittaker, Arthur's <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> exploits were against the northern Saxons, whilst he was only <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of the Silures, and Ambrosius was the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DICTATOR">dictator</a> or pendragon of the Britons. "In a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> probably of five campaigns, and in a succession certainly of eleven victories, this great commander had repelled the Saxons from the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of Flavia, dislodged them from all Maxima, and possessed them of all Valenta. And these were successes so unchequered with misfortunes, so great in themselves, and so beneficial to the public, that the name of Arthur claims the first <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIST">list</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a>, and the better one of patriot, heroes." The twelfth battle of Arthur was fought in the south of England, after he was elected to the pendragonship, against Cedric the Saxon. "This (says Mr Whittaker) was a most extraordinary victory, and completes the circle of Arthur's military glories." In the author's account of this prince's conduct in peace, he asserts, that "Arthur <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> that an appointment was wanted, which should at once be a more regular and more honourable <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIGNATURE">signature</a> of merit; by the certainty of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> and the greatness of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, call out all the worth of all the worthy in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, and collect it round the throne of the pendragon. Accordingly he established a military order. It was the first that had ever been instituted in the island; and it has since been imitated by all the nations on the continent. By means of this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASSOCIATION">association</a>, Arthur raised among the provincials a general glow of ingenuous heroism, the first spirit of chivalry that ever appeared in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>; that manly and honourable gallantry of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>, which has made him and his worthies the subject of romantic histories over all the west of it. By this, and this alone, could he have been what history represents him, the Revered Father of the British Heroes in general, even to the conclusion of the sixth century, and nearly the middle of the seventh. The order naturally survived its founder. And the members of it were denominated the Warriors of Arthur, though the persons were born half a century after his death." Mr Whittaker goes on to inform us, that under the prudent management of Arthur for 20 years together, a fair prospect dawned upon the Britons, and long scenes of future glories opened to their imaginations. "But the gay vision was destroyed at once by the commencement of a civil war. Many <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> still remained in ruins, the memorial of the former wars, and the disgrace of the present. The diffused spirit of chivalry was turned upon the nation, and heroism became the tool of dissension. And the dreadful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a> of civil evils was begun and consummated, at once, by the death of the renowned Arthur in battle. Thus died the incomparable hero in 542." To these observations it may not be improper to add the following account of the discovery of Arthur's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a>, which appears to be tolerably well authenticated. Henry II. who was the first of the Plantagenet line, being, in the last year of his reign, at <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEMBROKE">Pembroke</a>, and hearing there a Welsh bard singing to his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HARP">harp</a> the story of Arthur, concluding with an account of his death, and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BURIAL">burial</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCHYARD">churchyard</a> of Glastonbury between two pyramids; the king instantly gave orders that the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> should be inquired into, and the body dug up. This was done as the king directed; and at the depth of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> feet was found a vast <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, whereon was fastened a leaden <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>, with this inscription on the inside: Hic Jacet Sepultus Inclytus Rex Arturius in Insula Avalonia; i.e., "Here lies the famous King Arthur, buried in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of Avalon." <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGGING">Digging</a> still lower, they found the king's body in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a> of a tree, his beautiful <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> lying by him, with long flowing <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> bright as <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, which, however, sunk into dust when touched. The king's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> were very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> sized; and in his skull there were ten wounds or more, all cicatrizated, except that of which he died. This discovery was made in the year 1189, as Giraldus Cambrensis tells us, who saw these bones, and examined the whole matter carefully. There was also a table containing this story, set up in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> of Glastonbury, and the leaden cross with the inscription remained there till the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a> of the monastery, where it was seen by the great antiquary Leland; but what is become of it since does not appear. Of the different places above alluded to as being distinguished by our hero's name, and serving to evince his existence, the following may be mentioned as one of the principal. **Arthur's Seat**, a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> hill in the neighbourhood of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, said to have been so denominated from a tradition that King Arthur surveyed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> from its summit, and had also defeated the Saxons in its neighbourhood. This hill rises by a steep and rugged ascent, till it terminates in a rocky point near 700 feet high from the base, being more than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> the height of the cross on the top of St Paul's, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, which is 340 feet. On the south it is in many parts a perpendicular rock, composed of basaltic pillars regularly pentagonal or hexagonal, about three feet in diameter, and from 40 to 50 feet in height. Contiguous upon the west, and partly connected with it at the base, are <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALISBURY">Salisbury</a> Crags, of inferior height, but exhibiting an appearance equally singular and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a>. They present to the city an awful <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a> of broken rocks and precipices, forming a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMPHITHEATRE">amphitheatre</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> rock; and backward from the craggy verge above, the hill forms an extensive <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> slope, the surface affording pasture to numerous flocks of sheep. The crags, besides ores, spars, rock <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, and here and there, it is said, some precious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, afford an inexhaustible supply of stone for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAVING">paving</a> the streets. streets and other purposes. In quarrying, a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the crags has been worn <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> into a spacious shelf, having the appearance of a lofty terrace, and stretching a considerable length. From hence is a near and distinct prospect of the city, with its environs and the adjacent country. But from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PINNACLE">pinnacle</a> called Arthur's Seat the view is more noble and extensive. The traveller may here sit and survey at his ease the centre of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, besides having a complete view of Edinburgh and its castle, on which he looks down as if seated among the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a>. In a word, the German ocean, the whole course of the Forth, the distant Grampians, and a large portion of the most populous and best cultivated part of Scotland, form a landscape sublime, various, and beautiful. The denomination of this hill, derived as above, has been adduced as an argument against those who dispute the existence of the British Arthur. That derivation, however, though probable, is not without uncertainty. For Arthur's Seat is said to be derived, or rather corrupted, from A'rd Sech, a "place or field of arrows," where people <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> at a mark: And this not improperly; for among these cliffs is a dell or recluse valley, where the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> can scarcely reach, now called the Hunter's Bog, the bottom of it being a morass. The adjacent crags are supposed to have taken their name from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Salisbury, who in the reign of Edward III. accompanied that prince in an expedition against the Scots. ARTICHOKE. See Cinara, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ARTICLE

Pages 791-791

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>, denotes a particle used in most languages for the declining of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-NOUNS">nouns</a>, and denoting the several <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> and genders thereof. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> arises chiefly hence, that in languages which have no different terminations, to express the different states and circumstances of nouns, there is something required to supply that office. The Latins have no articles; but the Greeks, and most of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> languages, have had recourse to them, for fixing and ascertaining the vague signification of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> and appellative names. The Greeks have their ἐν, the eastern tongues their ἐν emphaticum; the Italians their il, lo, and la; the French their le, la, and les; the Germans their der, das, dat. The English also have two articles, a and the; which being prefixed to substantives, apply their general signification to some particular things. Some grammarians make the article a distinct <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of speech; others <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> have it a pronoun, and others a noun adjective. See Grammar. Articles are of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, as they contribute to the more neat and precise expressing of several properties and relations, which must otherwise be lost. And hence one great advantage of such languages over the Latin, in that the article being either expressed <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> left out, makes an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, which the Latins cannot distinguish. Thus when the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVIL">devil</a> said to our Saviour, Si tu es Filius dei, it may either be understood, "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> thou art a son of God," or, "if thou art the son of God?" The Italians even prefix articles to proper names, which do not naturally need any, because they themselves signify things individually. Thus, they say, il Ariosto, il Tasso, il Petrarca. Even the French join the article to the proper names of kingdoms, provinces, &c. as la Suede, la Normandie. And we likewise annex it to the names of certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>; as, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>, the Danube, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALPS">Alps</a>, &c. ARTICULATE sounds, are such sounds as express the letters, syllables, or words of any <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPHABET">alphabet</a> or language; such are formed by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>, and by some few birds, as parrots, &c.

ARTICULATION

Pages 791-791

in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, is the connexion of parts that consist of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNEES">knees</a>, such as the pods of French honeysuckles, which when ripe divide into so many parts as there are knees or joints; also those parts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> which swell into nodes or joints, and which usually send forth branches.

ARTIFICER

Pages 791-792

a person whose employment it is to manufacture any kind of commodity, as in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, &c. such are smiths, brasiers, carpenters, &c. The Roman artificers had their peculiar <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>, where they assembled and chose their own <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRON">patron</a>, to defend their causes; they were exempted from all personal services. Taruntenus Paternus reckons 32 <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of artificers, and Constantine 35, who enjoyed this privilege. The artificers were incorporated into <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> colleges <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> companies, each of which had their tutelar gods, to whom they offered their worship. Several of these, when they quitted their profession, hung up their tools, a votive offering to their gods. Artificers were held a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> below <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>, and argentarii or <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>-changers, and their employment more sordid. Some deny, that in the earliest ages of the Roman state artificers were ranked in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of citizens: others, who assert their citizenship, allow that they were held in contempt, as being unfit for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, and so <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> that they could scarcely pay any taxes. For which reason they were not entered among the citizens in the censor's books; the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of the census being only to see what number of persons were yearly fit to bear arms, and to pay taxes towards the support of the state. It may be added, that much of the artificers business was done by slaves and foreigners, who left little for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> to mind but their husbandry and war. By means of the arts, the minds of men are engaged in inventions beneficial to the whole <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a>; and thus prove the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> preservative against the barbarism and brutality, which ever attend on an indolent and inactive stupidity. By the English laws, artificers in wool, iron, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STEEL">steel</a>, brass, or other metal, going out of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> into any foreign <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> without license, are to be imprisoned three months, and fined in a sum not exceeding one hundred pounds. And such as going abroad, and not returning on warning given by our ambassadors, &c. shall be disabled from holding lands by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVISE">devise</a>, from receiving any legacy, &c. and be deemed aliens. Stat. 5 Geo. I. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 27. By 23 Geo. II. cap. 13. § 1. penalty is also inflicted on seducing artificers to go abroad. Ramazini has a treatise on the diseases of artificers.

ARTIFICIAL

Pages 792-792

in a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, denotes something made, fashioned, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> produced by art, in contradistinction from the production of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. ARTIFICIAL is also frequently used for factitious. Thus we have artificial sal ammoniac, artificial <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BORAX">borax</a>, &c. ARTIFICIAL Fire-works are compositions of inflammable materials, chiefly used on solemn occasions, by way of rejoicing. See <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYROTECHNY">PYROTECHNY</a>. ARTIFICIAL <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTNING">Lightning</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTRICITY">ELECTRICITY</a> and LIGHTNING. ARTIFICIAL <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">Lines</a>, on a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECTOR">sector</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a>, are certain lines so contrived, as to represent the logarithmic sines and tangents; which, by the help of the line of numbers, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> solve all questions in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIGONOMETRY">trigonometry</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>, &c. pretty exactly. ARTIFICIAL Magnets. See MAGNETS.

ARTIGI

Pages 792-792

indeclinable, (Pliny); Artigis, (<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>); a town of the Turduii, in Bætica. Now <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALHAMA">Alhama</a>.

ARTILLERY

Pages 792-795

in its general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, denotes the offensive <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPARATUS">apparatus</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, particularly of the missile kind. Among the French the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> was anciently appropriated to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHERY">ARCHERY</a>. In its <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> acceptation it signifies fire-arms, mounted on their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRIAGES">carriages</a> and ready for <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, with their balls, their bombs, their grenades, &c. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> we take the term in a more extensive meaning, it includes the powder, the matches, instruments for fire-works, the utensils of ordnance, the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MACHINES">machines</a> which facilitate their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> and transport them, the vehicles over which they <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRAVERSE">traverse</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, every thing necessary to them, and all that enters into the form of a train of artillery. The same word, still farther extended in its meaning, likewise comprehends the men destined for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the artillery; the people who provide the artillery with materials and implements when engaged, the cannoniers, the bombardiers, the officers of every <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>, and engineers of every kind. By artillery is likewise understood the science which the officers of artillery ought to possess. This science teaches to know the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of all the materials and ingredients which enter into the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> and the structure of every thing relative to the artillery, such as nitre, sulphur, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARCOAL">charcoal</a>; the properties of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> and fire; the composition and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUNPOWDER">gunpowder</a>; the materials for fire-works; the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a>, proportions, &c. of the different warlike machines; the arrangement, movement, and whole management, of cannon, &c. in the field <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> in sieges, in such manner, that each of them, according to the length of its tube and the diameter of its bore, may be situated in the best <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> and at the properest distance for execution, and that the whole train taken together may reciprocally assist and support each other with the greatest advantage. Artillery has undergone many changes from its origin to the present <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. The artillery of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> were the catapulta, the balista, the different kinds of slings, &c. In latter ages, the Franks used the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HATCHET">hatchet</a> as a missile weapon, throwing it in the same manner as the Americans do theirs called the tomahawk. The Gascon and Genoese were excellent <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>-bow men. The Swiss owed their victories to their strength and skill in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the pike, halberd, and espadon or two-handed <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>; and the victories of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRESSY">Cressy</a>, Poictiers, and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGINCOURT">Agincourt</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> occasion the valour and skill of the English archers to be transmitted <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to latest posterity. See ARCHERY. The chevalier Folard was extremely attached to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> machines first mentioned, and seemed even to prefer them to our fire-arms; an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> which must appear not a little extraordinary from such a person. Father Daniel might well be mistaken in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> which he made between the effects of ancient and modern artillery, and in his conclusion that the latter was of little use; the situation of this good father removed him from the scenes of war and the opportunities of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>. But it is astonishing, that one so learned in the military art as the commentator of Polybius, who had ocular demonstration of the success of modern artillery, should have declared so violently against it. Whatever be the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> with these authors and their maxims, it may be asserted that cannon is one of the most singular discoveries which have been made amongst men; and by little and little it has changed the whole art of war, and of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> influenced the whole system of policy in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. The era of artillery is dated from the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of Cressy in 1346, because it is only from that <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> that cannon were mentioned in battle. Edward III. of England successfully employed some pieces of artillery placed in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of artillery was then known in France as well as in England; but probably <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> VI. marched with so much hurry and precipitation to attack his enemy, that he left his cannon as useless encumbrances behind him. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> arts considerably retarded the progress of artillery; and that of which they were then possessed was so unwieldy and imperfect, that they could not possibly discern its importance and efficacy in practice. After the invention of gunpowder, the Spaniards were the first who armed <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of their foot with muskets and harquebusses, and mixed them with the pikes. In this they were soon imitated by most other nations; though the English had not entirely laid aside their favourite weapon the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> bow, and generally taken to The use of fire-arms, during the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>. The first muskets were very heavy, and could not be fired without a rest; they had matchlocks, and barrels of a wide bore, that carried a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of powder, and did execution at a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> distance. The musketeers on a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a> carried only their rests and ammunition; and had boys to bear their muskets after them, for which they were allowed great additional pay. They were very slow in loading, not only by reason of the unwieldiness of the pieces, and because they carried the powder and balls separate, but from the time it took to prepare and adjust the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MATCH">match</a>; so that their fire was not near so brisk as ours is now. Afterwards a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> kind of matchlock musket came into use; and they carried their ammunition in bandoliers, which were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> belts that came over the shoulder, to which were hung several little <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> of wood covered with <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, each containing a charge of powder: the balls they carried loose in a pouch, and they had also a priming <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORN">horn</a> hanging by their side. Matchlocks were, about the beginning of this century, universally disused in Europe, and the troops were armed with firelocks; to which, much about the same time, the bayonet being added, pikes also were laid aside; which latter change, whether it was for the better or not, is a point that still admits of dispute among the best military writers, who are divided in their opinions about it, though most of them disapprove of it. The old English writers call those large muskets calivers; the harquebus was a lighter piece that could be fired without a rest. The matchlock was fired by a match, fixed by a kind of tongs in the serpentine or cock, which by pulling the trigger was brought down with great quickness upon the priming in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAN">pan</a>, over which there was a sliding cover, which was drawn back by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> at the time of firing. There was a great <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of nicety and care required to fit the match properly to the cock, so as to come down exactly true on the priming, to blow the ashes from the coal, and to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> the pan from the sparks that fell from it: a great deal of time was also lost in taking it out of the cock, and returning it between the fingers of the left hand, every time that the piece was fired; and wet <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> often rendered the matches useless. However, most writers allow that they were very sure, and less apt to miss fire than the firelock. The firelock is so called, from producing fire of itself, by the action of the flint and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STEEL">steel</a>. The most ancient invention of this sort is the wheel lock, which we find mentioned in Luigi Collado's Treatise of Artillery, printed at <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, 1586, as then lately invented in Germany. This sort of lock was used till within these hundred years, especially for pistols and carbines. It was composed of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> steel wheel, with an axis, to which was fastened a chain, which, by being wound round it, drew up a very strong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>: on pulling the trigger, the spring acting, whirled the wheel about with great velocity, and the friction of the edge of it (which was a little notched) against the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> produced the fire; the cock was made so as to bring the stone upon the edge of the wheel, part of which was in the pan, and touched the priming; they used any <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> hard pebble for that purpose, which served as well as flint. These locks were inconvenient, took time to <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> up (or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAN">span</a>, as they termed it), and sometimes would not go off; an instance of which may be seen in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUDLOW">Ludlow</a>'s <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a>.
