The Indian historians speak of it with raptures. Cabul is the residence of the kings of Candahar. It has at all times been of much importance, as the frontier of India towards the river Oxus, which flows into the Caspian sea, and towards Tartary. In ancient times, it always was a great commercial magazine, as well as an important fortress. To this day, it is on the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> road by which the commerce of the southern parts of the Russian empire is carried on with India. It is at present noted for its vast <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a> of horses and cattle, the first of which are brought hither by the Usbee Tartars; and merchants resort to these markets from Persia, China, and Tartary. Near the mouth of the river Kameh, the city of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATTOCK">Attock</a> stands upon the Indus. Attock signifies forbidden; this being the original boundary of Hindoostan, towards the north-west, which the Hindoos were prohibited to pass. Here the river is three quarters of a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a> broad, and the water is cold, and the stream rapid and turbulent, having much black sand suspended in it. To this place the Indus descends from the lofty mountains of Imaus, and the high region of Tartary. The remainder of its course, therefore, lies through a country little known, and so rude in its soil and climate, as scarcely to admit even of the most slender population. Returning to the ocean, it is to be observed, that the most eastern of the branches into which the Indus is divided towards its mouth, flows into the bay or gulf of Cutch, which advances far into the country, receiving the river Puddar. This river, and the bay into which it flows, form one side of the fertile peninsula of Guzerat, the other side of the same peninsula being contiguous to the gulf of Cambay. The western parts of the peninsula of Guzerat are mountainous and woody. The rest is extremely rich, and once famed for a very considerable commerce of its productions. Here stood, in former times, on the promontory of Guzerat in the neighbourhood of Diu, one of the last remaining possessions of the Portuguese in India, the great temple or <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PAGODA">pagoda</a> of Sumnat. It was destroyed in the eleventh century by Mahmud, the greatest of the princes of that race of Tartars called Turks. He was the sovereign of Ghizni, which we have already noticed as a town in the kingdom of Candahar, upon one of the streams that fall into the Indus from the north-west. Being a most fanatical Mahometan, he undertook 12 holy wars, as they were called, against the unbelieving nations of India. Lahore, Moultan, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DELHI">Delhi</a>, were compelled to open their gates to him, and he at last reached and conquered the rich peninsula or kingdom of Guzerat. On the payment of a tribute, the rajahs preserved their dominions, and the people their lives and fortunes; but to the religion of the country Mahmud was inexorable. Many hundred <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a> or pagodas were levelled with the ground. Many thousand idols were demolished; and the servants of the Arabian prophet were stimulated, and rewarded, by the precious materials of which they were composed. The pagoda of Sumnat was at this time conspicuous beyond all the retreats of Indian <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>. Its magnificence and its destruction deserve well to be noticed, as indicating the character of two Asiatic nations: the riches and devout superstition of the one, and the furious fanaticism which the other had been able to diffuse over a great part of the world. This pagoda, or temple, was endowed with the revenue of 2000 villages; 2000 Brahmans were consecrated to the service of the deity, whom they washed each morning and evening with water from the distant Ganges. The subordinate ministers consisted of 300 musicians, 300 barbers, and 500 <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DANCING">dancing</a> girls, conspicuous for their birth or beauty. Three sides of the temple were protected by the ocean: the narrow isthmus was fortified by a natural or <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> precipice, and the city and adjacent country were peopled by a nation of fanatics. They confessed the sins and the punishment of Kinnoge and Delhi; but they boasted, that if the impious stranger should presume to approach their holy precincts, he would surely be overwhelmed by a blast of the divine vengeance. By this challenge the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> of Mahmud was animated to a personal <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> of the strength of this Indian deity. Fifty thousand of his worshippers were pierced by the spears of the Moslems; the walls were scaled; the sanctuary was profaned; and the conqueror aimed a blow of his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> mace at the head of the idol. The trembling Brahmans are said to have offered ten millions <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a> for his ransom; and it was urged by the wisest counsellors, that the destruction of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> image would not change the hearts of the Gentoes, and that such a sun might be dedicated to the relief of the true <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELIEVERS">believers</a>: "Your reasons," replied the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SULTAN">sultan</a>, "are specious and strong; but never in the eyes of posterity shall Mahmud appear as a merchant of idols." He repeated his blows, and a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a> of pearls and rubies, concealed in the belly of the statue, explained in some degree the devout prodigality of the Brahmans. The fragments of the idol were distributed to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAZNA">Gazna</a>, Mecca, and Medina. <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAGDAD">Bagdad</a> listened, says the historian, Gibbon, to the edifying tale; and Mahmud was saluted by the vol. v. caliph, with the title of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUARDIAN">Guardian</a> of the fortune and faith of Mahomet. Adjoining to the peninsula of Guzerat, and at the city of bottom of the gulf of Cambay, stands the city of that Cambay name, which once was the capital of a considerable kingdom. It is situated in a great manufacturing country, which furnishes large quantities of coarse unbleached cotton cloth, for Persia, Arabia, Egypt, and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABYSSINIA">Abyssinia</a>; also blue cloths for the same countries, and for the English and Dutch trade on the western coast of Africa; likewise blue and white checks to be used as mantles in Arabia and Turkey, some coarse, and others enriched with gold; muslins for turbans, gauzes, mixed stuffs of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a> and cotton, and shawls made of the Cashmerian wool. This country also sends annually to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURAT">Surat</a>, Bengal, China, Persia, and Arabia, immense quantities of raw cotton, as well as rich embroideries of various kinds. From the bottom of the gulf of Cambay, the peninsula of western India may be said to begin in the strictest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>. est sense; as a line of coast here commences, which proceeds without interruption, or any considerable <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENDING">bending</a>, to Cape Comorin, the southern part of the peninsula, after which the coast suddenly turns to the north-east; and the bay of Bengal bounds the peninsula on the east. From Cambay to Cape Comorin, the western coast of the peninsula may be divided into three unequal parts. The first extends from the most advanced part of the gulf southward, a little beyond the city of Surat. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> tract of coast, which is more extensive than this, in a fourfold proportion, is called the coast of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONCAN">Concan</a>, or the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIRATE">pirate</a> coast. To the southward of this, the coast of the peninsula, all the way to Cape Comorin, receives the appellation of the Malabar coast. The first of these divisions, lying upon the eastern shore of the gulf of Cambay, consists of a low country, into which the rivers descend from the upper part of the peninsula of Hindostan. After passing Surat, however, the physical structure of the peninsula assumes a peculiar character well worthy of attention. The Concan and Malabar coasts which form almost the whole of the western shores of the peninsula are extremely low, and a narrow stripe of level land, of from 40 to 50 miles in breadth, runs along the coast of Surat to Cape Comorin. At the back of this stripe of low land, a chain of mountains runs parallel to the sea shore. They are called the Ghauts, and rise to a surprising height, opposing to the west a lofty wall of rugged and precipitous rocks. The whole chain seems one continued crest or wall, inaccessible to the summit, unless by paths which have been worked by the hand of man, and which cannot be ascended, even by a single traveller, without the fatiguing labour of many hours. From the root of these rocks, the plain towards the sea is variegated with small hills, which gradually descend into a level and fertile country, blest with a cool and healthy air. The small hills near the foot of the Ghauts are clothed with forests of the most valuable <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>; and from the sides of the mountains magnificent cataracts descend, forming torrents which facilitate the conveyance of the timber to the sea coast.

ASIDE

Pages 881-881

in the drama, something said by an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTOR">actor</a>, which some, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> even all the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTORS">actors</a> present are supposed not to hear; a circumstance justly condemned as being unnatural and improbable.

ASIITO

Pages 881-881

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERUGIA">Perugia</a>, and in the pope's territories. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 23. 40. N. Lat. 43. 0.

ASINARA

Pages 881-881

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, on the western <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SARDINIA">Sardinia</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 8. 30. N. Lat. 41. 0.

ASINIUS POLLIO

Pages 881-881

a Roman <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a> and orator, distinguished himself under Augustus by his exploits and his literary works. He is frequently mentioned with praises by Horace and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>, and is said to have collected the first library at Rome. He died at Frescati, at 80 years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>.

ASIONGABER

Pages 881-881

ESIONGEBER, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> EZIONGEBER, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a> Petraæ, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of Elath, a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the Arabian <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a>: the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOCK">dock</a> or station for the ships of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a> and Jehoshaphat; an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> town, mentioned also by Moses. It was afterwards called <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BERENICE">Berenice</a> (Josephus).

ASISIA

Pages 881-882
or ASSISTA, a town of Liburnia (Ptolemy, Antonine), now in ruins, but exhibiting many monuments of antiquity. It is the Assesia or Asseria of Pliny. This author, after having specified the Liburnian cities that were obliged to attend the congress or diet of Scardona, adds to the catalogue the free Asserians, immunesque Asseriates; and this people, who created their own magistrates, and were governed by their own municipal laws, were no doubt more rich and powerful than their neighbours. The vestiges of the walls of Asseria that still remain, are a sufficient proof of this; for their circumference is clearly distinguishable above ground, and measures 3600 Roman feet. The space enclosed by them forms an oblong polygon, and they are built with common Dalmatian marble; but not taken from the hill on which they stand, for that furnishes only soft stone. The walls are invested, both inside and out, with this marble: some of the stones are ten feet long, and they are all of considerable dimensions. The thickness of these fortifications is commonly about eight feet: but at the narrowest extremity, which falls towards the foot of the hill, they are eleven feet thick; and, in some parts, their height still above ground reaches to near 30 feet. An antiquary, or even a simple lover of the fine arts, or of erudition, the abbé Fortis observes, cannot help wishing at Podgraje (the modern name of Asseria). Asseria), that some powerful hand quicquid sub terra est in apertum profert: and such a wish becomes stronger when he reflects, that since the destruction of that city no search has ever been made under ground, with a view to discover any thing curious; and yet these walls without doubt enclose a valuable deposite of antiquities, thrown down in heaps, who knows by what cause; perhaps naturally, by an earthquake, or perhaps by a sudden inundation of barbarians, which is still worse. The gate now demolished, the considerable height of the walls to be seen in several places from without, some pieces of thick walls that still appear levelled to the ground among the bushes, are circumstances which give ground to hope that many costly monuments might be recovered out of these ruins. The magnificence of the remaining wall, and the many pieces of well-cut stone and fine marbles scattered over the contiguous fields, afford sufficient proof that both good taste and grandeur once flourished in that country. In the midst of the rubbish which covers the remains of Asseria, the parish church of the little village stands insulated; it is built of broken pieces of ancient ruins, taken as they happened to be nearest, mixed with mutilated inscriptions and fragments of noble cornices.

ASISIO

Pages 882-882
or ASITO, a city of the pope's territories in Italy, situated about 16 miles east of Perugia. E. Long. 13. 35. N. Lat. 43. ASKELON. See ASCALON.

ASKERON

Pages 882-882

a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> five miles from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DONCASTER">Doncaster</a>, noted for a medicinal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>. It is a strong sulphurous <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and is slightly impregnated with a purging <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>. It is recommended internally and externally in strumous and other ulcers, scabs, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEPROSY">leprosy</a>, and similar complaints. It is good in chronic obstructions, and in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORMS">worms</a> and foulness of the bowels.

ASKRIG

Pages 882-882

a town in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> riding of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 0. 5. N. Lat. 53. 50.

ASLANI

Pages 882-882

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">Commerce</a>, a silver <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a>, worth from 115 to 120 aspers. See <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASPER">ASPER</a>.

ASMONEUS

Pages 882-882
or ASSAMONEUS, the father of Simon, and chief of the Asmoneans, a family that reigned over the Jews 126 years.

ASNA

Pages 882-882
or ESNA, a town in Upper Egypt, seated upon the Nile, and occupying the site of the ancient Latopolis. It is near the cataracts of the Nile, and is the last place of any magnitude on the side of Nubia. It contains several monuments of antiquity; and among the rest an ancient Egyptian temple, pretty entire, all painted throughout, except in some places that are effaced by time. The columns are full of hieroglyphic figures. This structure is considered by Denon as one of the most perfect monuments of ancient architecture he had seen. A little way from thence are the ruins of an ancient nunnery, said to be built by St Helena, surrounded with tombs.—Asna is the principal town in these parts, and the inhabitants are rich in corn and cattle. They drive a considerable trade into Lower Egypt and Nubia, by means of the Nile, and also by the caravans that pass over the desert. The inhabitants are all Arabs, except about 200 Copts, the ancient inhabitants, and a sort of Christians. They are under the government of the Turks, who have a cadi, and the Arabs have two sheriffs of their own nation. E. Long. 32. 35. N. Lat. 23. 15.

ASOLA

Pages 882-882

a town of the Bressan in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, belonging to the republic of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 14. 18. N. Lat. 45. 15.

ASOPH

Pages 882-882

a town of Cuban <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TARTARY">Tartary</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, seated on the river <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DON">Don</a>, near its mouth, a little to the east of the Palus Maeotis, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> of Asoph. It has been several times taken and retaken of late years; but in 1739, the contending powers agreed that the fortifications should be demolished; and the town remains under the dominion of Russia. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 39. 5. N. Lat. 47. 18.

ASOPUS

Pages 882-882

a river of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHRYGIA">Phrygia</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">Major</a>, which, together with the Lycons, washes Laodicea (Pliny).—Another of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOEOTIA">Boeotia</a>, which running from Mount Citheron, and watering the territory of Thebes, separates it from the territory of Plateae, and falls with an east course into the Euripus, at Tanagra. On this river Adrastus <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Sicyon built a temple to Nemesis, thence called Adrasteia. From this river Thebes came to be surnamed Asopides, (Strabo). It is now called Asopo. A third Asopus, a river of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PELOPONNESUS">Peloponnesus</a>, which runs by Sicyon, (Strabo); and with a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west course falls into the Sinus Corinthiacus, to the west of Corinth.—A fourth, a small river of the Locri Epinomidi, on the borders of Thessaly, (Pliny); rising in Mount Oeta, and falling into the Sinus Maliacus. Asopus, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LACONIA">Laconia</a>, (Pausanias); on the Sinus Laonicus, with a port in a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a>, between Boe to the east, and the mouth of the Eurotas to the west. The citadel only remains standing, now called by the sailors Castel Rompano.

ASOR

Pages 882-882
or HASOR, in Ancient Geography, a town of the tribe of Judah, to the south-west, on the borders of Ascalon, (Joshua); as also Hasor-Hadata, translated by the Seventy Arwen Kain (id).—Another Asor, Asorus, or Hazor, a town of Galilee; called the capital of all the kingdoms to the north of Palestine. It was taken by Joshua; the inhabitants were put to the sword, and their houses burnt. It was afterwards rebuilt (Judges, i Sam.); but remained still in the hands of the Canaanites, though in the lot of the tribe of Naphtali, (Joshua). It lay to the north of the Lachus Samachonites, called in Scripture the Waters of Merom (Josephus).

ASOW

Pages 882-883

a celebrated and important fortress of Russia, once a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of considerable trade, but now demolished. It was situated in the district of Bachmut, near the place where the Greeks many centuries ago built the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Tanaïs, which was very famous for its trade, and underwent many vicissitudes. The Genoese, who settled a trade with Russia soon after the discovery of Archangel by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHANCELLOR">Chancellor</a>, became masters of this place, and gave it the name of Tana <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Catana: but the Tartars, who were very powerful in these parts, seem to have been in possession of it <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> before: for, as Busching informs us, there are Asow coins yet extant, on which is the name of Tacktamysz Kan. From the Geneese it fell into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the Turks, lost its trade, and became an inconsiderable town. In 1637, it was taken by the Cossacks, who defended it against the Turks in 1641, and next year set fire to it, and blew it up. The Turks rebuilt it with strong fortifications. The Russians laid claim to it in 1672, and took it in 1696; but, by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of Pruth in 1711, it was restored to the Turks. In 1736, the Russians became masters of Asow; but by the treaty of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELGRADE">Belgrade</a> they were obliged to relinquish it, and entirely destroy the place.

ASP

Pages 883-883

in *<a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>*, a small poisonous kind of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SERPENT">serpent</a>, whose bite gives a speedy but easy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. It is said to be thus denominated from the Greek *άσπις*, shield, in regard to the manner of its lying convolved in a circle, in the centre of which is the head, which it exerts, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> raises, like the umbo or umbilicus of a buckler. This <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of serpent is very frequently mentioned by authors; but so carelessly described, that it is not easy to determine which, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> any of the species known at present, may properly be called by this name. It is said to be <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, and about the banks of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NILE">Nile</a>; and Bellonius mentions a small species of serpent which he had met with in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and which had a sort of callous excrescence on the forehead, which he takes to have been the aspis of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>. It was with the asp that Cleopatra is said to have despatched herself, and prevented the designs of Augustus, who intended to have carried her captive to adorn his triumphal entry into Rome. But the fact is contested: <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">Brown</a> places it among his vulgar errors. The indications of that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>'s having used the ministry of the asp, were only two almost insensible pricks found in her arm; and Plutarch says it is unknown what she died of. At the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, it must be observed, that the slightness of the pricks found in her arm furnishes no presumption against the fact; for no more than the prick of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEEDLE">needle</a> point dipt in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POISON">poison</a> was necessary for the purpose. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACON">Bacon</a> makes the asp the least painful of all the instruments of death. He supposes it to have an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFFINITY">affinity</a> to opium, but to be less disagreeable in its operation; and his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> seems to correspond with the accounts of most writers, as well as with the effects described to have been produced upon Cleopatra. The ancients had a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLASTER">plaster</a> called *διαστίχωμα*, made of this terrible animal, of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> efficacy as a discutent of strumae and other indurations, and used likewise against pains of the gout. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>, and skin or exuviae, of the creature, had also their share in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">materia medica</a>.

ASPASTICUM

Pages 883-883

(from *ἀσπασμός*, "I salute.") in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> writers, a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> apartment, adjoining to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> churches, wherein the bishop and presbyters sat, to receive the salutations of the persons who came to visit them, desire their blessing, or consult them on business.—This is also called *aspasticum diaconicum*, *receptorium*, *metatorium*, or *mesatorium*, and *salutorium*: in English, "greeting-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>."

ASPECT

Pages 883-883

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, denotes the situation of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a> and stars with respect to each other. There are five different aspects. 1. Sextile aspect is when the planets <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> stars are 60° distant, and marked thus *. 2. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-QUARTILE">quartile</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUADRATURE">quadrature</a>, when they are 90° distant, marked □. 3. Trine, when 120° distant, marked Δ. 4. Opposition, when 180° distant, marked Ω. And, 5. Conjunction, when both in the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, marked &. Kepler, who added eight new ones, defines aspect to be the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> formed by the rays of two stars meeting on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, whereby their good or bad influence is measured: for it is to be observed, that these aspects being first introduced by astrologers, were distinguished into benign, malignant, and indifferent; the quartile and opposition being accounted malign; the trine and sextile, benign or friendly; and the conjunction, indifferent. **ASPEN TREE**. See Populus, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ASPER

Pages 883-883
or Aspre, in Commerce, a Turkish coin, three of which make a Medine.

ASPERIA ARTERIA

Pages 883-883

in Anatomy, the same with the windpipe <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> trachea. See Anatomy <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ASPERIFOLIATE

Pages 883-884
or Asperifolious, among botanists, such plants as are rough-leaved, having their leaves... Asperifoliæ leaves placed alternately on their stalks, and a monopetalous flower divided into five parts.—They constitute an order of plants in the *Fragmenta methodi naturalis* of Linnæus, in which are these genera, viz. tournefortia, cerinthe, symphytum, pulmonaria, anthusa, lithospermum, myosotis, heliotropium, cynoglossum, asperugo, lycopsis, echium, borrago: *magis minusve oleaceae, mucilaginosae, et glutinosae sunt.* Lin. In the present system, these are among the pentandra monogynia. **ASPERIFOLIÆ PLANTÆ**, rough-leaved plants; the name of a class in Hermannus, Boerhaave, and Ray's methods, consisting of plants which have four naked seeds, and whose leaves are rough to the touch. In Tournefort's System, these plants constitute the third section or order of the second class; and in Linnæus's Sexual Method, they make part of the pentandra monogynia.

ASPERITY

Pages 884-884

the inequality of the surface of any body, which hinders the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> from passing over it freely.—From the testimony of some <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLIND">blind</a> persons, it has been supposed that every <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> hath its particular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of asperity: though this has been denied by others. See the article **BLIND**.

ASPEROSA

Pages 884-884

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>; it is a bishop's see, situated on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of the Archipelago. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 25° 20' N. Lat. 40° 38'.

ASPHALTITES

Pages 884-885

so called from the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of bitumen it produces; called also the Dead <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>; and from its situation, the East sea, the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">Salt</a> sea, the sea of Sodom, the sea of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DESERT">Desert</a>, and the sea of the Plain, in the sacred writings: A lake of Judea. Many things have been said and written of this famed, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they were indeed true, rather infamous lake: such as that it arose from the submersion of the vale of Siddim, where once stood, as is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> reported, the three cities which perished in the miraculous conflagration, with those of Sodom and Gomorrah, for their unnatural and detestable wickedness: on which account this lake has been looked upon as a lasting monument of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> judgment of God, to deter mankind from such abominations. Hence it is added, that the waters of the lake are so impregnated with salt, sulphur, and other bituminous stuff, that nothing <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> sink or live in it; and that it casts such stench and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a>, that the very birds die in attempting to fly over it. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> likewise of the apples that grew about it, fair without, and only ashes and bitterness within, were looked upon as a farther monument of God's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGER">anger</a>. So likewise the description which many travellers give not only of the lake, but of all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> round about, of the whole appearing dreadful to behold, all sulphurous, bituminous, stinking, and suffocating: and lastly, what hath been farther affirmed of the ruins of the five cities being still to be seen in clear <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, and having been actually seen in these latter times; all these surprising things, and ill-grounded notions, though commonly, and so <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, received among <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, have been of late so much exploded, not only by the testimony of very credible witnesses, but even by arguments drawn from Scripture, that we must give them up as inventions, unless we will suppose the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of all these things to have been entirely changed. Those, in particular, of bodies not sinking in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and of birds being stifled by the exhalations of it, appear now false in fact, though it is true, that the quantity of saline matters, with which it is impregnated, renders it so much specifically heavier than fresh water, that bodies will not so easily sink. Its waters were found, by Dr Marcei in 1807, to have a specific gravity of 1,211; but Klapproth, a German chemist, found it to be 1,245, which is much higher than that of sea water. But objects of all kinds above this specific gravity are found to sink in it; birds fly over it without injury, and according to Chateaubriand fishes live in it. The substances it holds in solution are nearly the same as are found in sea water; nitrates of lime, of soda, and of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGNESIA">magnesia</a>. To reconcile these things with the experiments which Pliny* tells us had been made by Vespasian, is impossible, without supposing lib. v. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. that those ingredients have been since much exhausted, §5, which is not very probable. With respect to its salt, we are told, the Arabs make quantities of it from that lake, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> pits about the shore, which they fill with that water, and leave to be crystallized by the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>. This salt is in some <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> much commended by Galen, as very wholesome, and a strengthener of the stomach, &c. on account of its unpleasant bitterness. What likewise relates to the constant smoke ascending from the lake, its changing the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of its water three times a-<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, so confidently affirmed by Josephus †, ‡ <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELL">Bell</a>. Jud. and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, and confirmed by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> Radziwill lib. v. cap. and other moderns, who pretend to have been eyewitnesses of it, is all now in the same manner exploded by authors of more <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">date</a>, and of at least equal candour. The unhealthiness of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> about the lake was affirmed by Josephus and Pliny, especially on the west; the monks that live in the neighbourhood confirm the same, and would have dissuaded Dr Pococke from going to it on that account; and, as he ventured to go and bathe in it, and was two days after seized with a dizziness, and violent pain in the stomach, which lasted near three weeks, they made no doubt but it was occasioned by it; and he doth not seem to contradict them. As to the water, it is, though clear, so impregnated with salt, that those who dive into it come out covered with a kind of saline <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>. There is one remarkable thing relating to this lake, generally agreed on by all travellers and geographers, viz. that it receives the waters of Jordan, a considerable river, the brooks of Jabbok, Kishon, Arnon, and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a>, which flow into it from the adjacent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, and yet never overflows, though there is no visible way to be found by which it discharges that great influx. Some naturalists have been greatly embarrassed to find a discharge for these waters; and have therefore been inclined to suspect the lake had a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> with the Mediterranean. But, besides that we know of no <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> to corroborate this supposition, it has been demonstrated, by accurate calculation, that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVAPORATION">evaporation</a> is more than sufficient to carry off the waters brought by the river. It is, in fact, very considerable; and frequently becomes sensible to the eye, by the fogs with which the lake is covered at the rising of the sun, and which are afterwards dispersed by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>. It is enclosed on the east and west with exceeding <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> mountains, many of them craggy and dreadful to behold. On the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> it has the plain of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERICHO">Jericho</a>; or, if we take in both sides of the Jordan, it has the Great Plain, properly so called, on the south; which is open, and extends beyond the reach of the eye. Josephus gives this lake 580 furlongs in length, from the mouth of the Jordan to the town of Segor, on the opposite end, that is about 22 leagues; and about 150 furlongs or 5 leagues, in its greatest breadth; but our modern accounts commonly give it 24 leagues in length, and 6 or 7 in breadth. On the west side of it is a kind of promontory, where they pretend to show the remains of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">Lot</a>'s metamorphosed wife. Josephus says, it was still standing in his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; but when Prince Radziville inquired after it, they told him there was no such salt pillar or statue to be found in all that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a>. However, they have found means, about a century after him, to recover, as they pretended to assure Mr Maundrell, a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLOCK">block</a> or stump of it, which may in time grow up, with a little art, into its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> bulk. It is to be observed here, that the name of Dead sea is not to be found in the sacred writings; but hath been given to this lake because no creature will live in it, on account of its excessive saltness, or rather bituminous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>; for the Hebrews <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> sulphur, nitre, and bitumen, under the general name of salt. However, some late travellers have found cause to suspect the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> report of its breeding no living creature; one of them having observed, on the shore, two or three shells of fish like those of an oyster, and which he supposes to have been thrown up by the waves, at two miles distance from the mouth of the Jordan, which he there takes notice of, lest they should be suspected to have been brought into the lake by that way. And Dr Pococke, though he neither <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> fish nor shells, tells us, on the authority of a monk, that some sort of fish had been caught in it; and this is confirmed by Chateaubriand, who visited the shores of the lake in 1807. Mr Volney, however, affirms that it contains neither animal nor vegetable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. We see no verdure on its banks, nor are fish to be found within its waters. But he adds, that it is not true that its exhalations are pestiferous, so as to destroy birds <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">flying</a> over it. "It is very common (says he) to see swallows skimming its surface, and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIPPING">dipping</a> for the water necessary to build their nests. The real cause which deprives it of vegetables and animals is the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> saltness of the water, which is infinitely stronger than that of the sea. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> around it, equally impregnated with this salt, produces no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>; and the air itself, which becomes loaded with it from evaporation, and which receives also the sulphureous and bituminous vapours, cannot be favourable to vegetation: hence the deadly aspect which reigns around this lake. In other respects, the ground about it, however, is not marshy; and its waters are limpid and incorruptible, as must be the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> with a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a> of salt. The origin of this mineral is easy to be discovered; for on the south-west shore are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of fossil salt, of which I have brought away several specimens. They are situated in the side of the mountains which extend along that border; and, from time immemorial, have supplied the neighbouring Arabs, and even the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>. We find also on this shore fragments of sulphur and bitumen, which the Arabs convert into a trifling article of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>; as also hot fountains, and deep crevices, which are discovered at a distance by little pyramids built on the brink of them. We likewise find a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, which, on rubbing, emits a noxious smell, burns like bitumen, receives a polish like <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> alabaster, and is used for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAVING">paving</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>-yards. At intervals, we also meet with unshapen blocks, which prejudiced eyes mistake for mutilated <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a>, and which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> with ignorant and superstitious pilgrims for monuments of the adventure of Lot's wife; though it is nowhere said she was metamorphosed into stone like Niobe, but into salt, which must have melted the ensuing winter." It is on account of this bitumen that it hath had the name of Asphaltite lake, it being reported to have thrown up great quantities of that drug, which was much in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> among the Egyptians, and other nations, for <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMBALMING">embalming</a> of dead bodies. Josephus assures us, that in his days it rose in lumps as big as an ox without its head, and some even larger. But whatever it may have formerly done, we are assured by Mr Maundrell and others, that it is now to be found but in small quantities along the shore, though in much greater near the mountains on both sides the lake. But the contrary is since affirmed by two or more late* travellers; one *Pococke's of whom tells us, that it is observed to float on the sur-Travels, face of the water, and to come on the shore after windy P 56° weather, where the Arabians gather it, and put it to all the uses that common pitch is used for; even in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of some medicines; and another † tells Shaw's us, he was there informed, that it was raised at certain Travels, times from the bottom, in large hemispheres, which, P 374° as soon as they touch the surface, and are acted upon by the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> air, burst at once, with great noise and smoke like the pulvis fulminans of the chemists, dispersing themselves about in a thousand pieces. From both these judicious authors we may conclude the reason of Mr Maundrell's mistake, both as to the lake's throwing it up only on certain seasons (that reverend <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> might chance to be there at the wrong time); and likewise as to his not observing it about the shores, seeing the Arabs are there ready to gather it as soon as thrown up: all of them describe it as resembling our <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> pitch, so as not to be distinguished from it but by its sulphureous smoke and stench when set on fire; and it has been thought to be the same with that which our druggists sell under the name of bitumen Judaicum, or Jewish pitch, though we have reason to think that this last is factitious, and that there is now none of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> asphaltum brought from Judea. It hath, moreover, been confounded with a sort of blackish combustible stone thrown on the shore, and called by some Moses's stone, which being held in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANDLE">candle</a>, will soon burn, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> a smoke and intolerable stench; but with this extraordinary <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, that though it loses much of its <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> and colour, it becoming in a manner white, yet it diminishes nothing in its bulk. But these, Dr Pococke tells us, are found about two or three leagues from the shore. He concludes, however, from it, that a stratum of that stone under the lake is probably one part of the matter that feeds the subterraneous fire, and causes the bitumen to boil up out of it. See ASPHALTITES, Supplement.

ASPHALTUM

Pages 885-886

Bitumen Judaicum, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Jews Pitch, is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> bitumen, of a dusky <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> on the outside, and a deep shining <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> within; of very little... Asphaltum little <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>; and having scarcely any smell, unless heated, when it emits a strong pitchy one. It is found in a soft or liquid state on the surface of the Dead <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>, and by <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> grows dry and hard. The same kind of bitumen is met with likewise in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, in other places of the world, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, and in some places of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, as the Carpathian hills, France, Neufchatel, &c. There are several kinds of Jews pitch in the shops: but none of them are the genuine sort, and have little other <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> to their name than their being artificially compounded by Jews; and as they are a medley of we know not what ingredients, their medicinal <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> begins to be deservedly laid aside, notwithstanding the discutient, resolvent, pectoral, and other virtues attributed to this bitumen by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>. The true asphaltum was formerly used in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMBALMING">embalming</a> the bodies of the dead. The thick and solid asphalts are at present employed in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, as pitch for ships; as the fluid ones, for <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> in lamps, and for varnishes. Some writers relate, that the wall of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BABYLON">Babylon</a>, and the temple of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>, were cemented with bitumen instead of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MORTAR">mortar</a>. This much is certain, that a true <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> bitumen, that for instance which is found in the district of Neufchatel, proves an excellent cement for walls, pavements, and other purposes, uncommonly firm, very durable in the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>, and not penetrable by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. The watch and clock makers use a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of asphaltum, fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAMP">lamp</a> black, and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> of spike or turpentine, for <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> the black figures on <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIAL">dial</a> plates: this composition is prepared chiefly by certain persons at Augsburg and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUREMBERG">Nuremberg</a>. See the preceding article.

ASPHURELATA

Pages 886-886

in **<a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>**, are semi-metallic fossils, fusible by fire, and not malleable in their purest state, being in their native state intimately mixed with sulphur and other adventitious <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, and reduced to what are called ores. Of this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of fossils there are only five bodies, each of which makes a distinct genus; viz. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTIMONY">antimony</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISMUTH">bismuth</a>, cobalt, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZINC">zinc</a>, and quicksilver.

ASPICUETA

Pages 886-886

MARTIN DE**, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOCTOR">Doctor</a> of Navarre, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> **Doctor Navarrus**, was descended of a noble family, and born the 13th of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1491, at Varasayn, a small <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Navarre, not far from Pampeluna. He entered very young into the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> of regular canons at Roncevaux, where he took the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>, which he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to wear after he left the convent. He studied classical learning, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MORAL_PHILOSOPHY">moral <a class="</a>xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>, at Alcala, in New Castile, adopting chiefly the system of Petrus Lombardus, commonly called the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">Master</a> of the Sentences. He applied to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FERRARA">Ferrara</a>, and taught it with applause at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOULOUSE">Toulouse</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAHORS">Cahors</a>. After being first professor of canon law at <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALAMANCA">Salamanca</a> for 14 years, he quitted that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> to be professor of law at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COIMBRA">Coimbra</a>, with a larger salary. The duties of this office he discharged for the space of 20 years, and then resigned it to retire into his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, where he took care of his nieces, the daughters of his deceased brothers. Having made a journey to Rome to plead the cause of Bartholomeo de Caranza archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOLEDO">Toledo</a>, who had been accused of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERESY">heresy</a> before the tribunal of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INQUISITION">inquisition</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, and whose cause was, by the Pope's order, to be tried in that city, Aspicueta's writings, which were well known, procured him a most <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> reception. Pope Pius V. made him assistant to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Francis Aciat, his vice <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENITENTIARY">penitentiary</a>; and Gregory XIII. never passed by his door without calling for him, and stopped sometimes a whole <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> to talk with him in the street. His name became so famous, that even in his lifetime the highest encomium on a learned <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> was to call him a Navarrus. He was consulted as an oracle. By <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEMPERANCE">temperance</a> he prolonged his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> to a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> length. His economy enabled him to give substantial proofs of his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a>. Being very old, he used to ride on a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MULE">mule</a> through the city, and relieved all the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> he met; to which his mule was so well accustomed, that it stopped of its own <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACCORD">accord</a> at the sight of every poor man, till his master had relieved him. He refused several honourable posts in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> and state, that he might have leisure to correct and improve the works he had already written, and compose others. He died at the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 94, on the 21st of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1586. He wrote a vast <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of treatises, all which are either on morality or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> law.

ASPIRATE

in **<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>**, denotes words marked with the spiritus <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASPER">asper</a>. See **ASPER**.

ASPIRATION

among grammarians, is used to denote the pronouncing a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYLLABLE">syllable</a> with some vehemence.

ASSANCALA

a strong town in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMENIA">Armenia</a>, near the river <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARRAS">Arras</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> between <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ERZERUM">Erzerum</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ERIVAN">Erivan</a>, and noted for its hot <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a>. It stands on a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> hill, and has walls round it, strengthened with towers. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 41. 30. N.
